Founded in 1948, the event aims to present the latest innovations from around the world to companies and the public, helping inventors explore business opportunities and gain feedback from potential users. ■

Mongolia on track to meet tourist arrival target this year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:51:13 CST
22:51:13 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Mongolia is on track to meet its target of receiving 1 million foreign tourist arrivals this year, local media reported on Saturday, citing the Mongolian Tourism Organization.
The Asian country has received 919,104 foreign tourist arrivals since the beginning of the year, reaching 91.9 percent of its annual target, according to the tourism organization.
Mongolia recorded more than 847,000 foreign tourist arrivals in 2025, marking a 5-percent increase from the previous year.
The Mongolian government views tourism as a key sector in diversifying the country's economy, which has traditionally relied heavily on mining exports.
However, the country's tourism industry has long faced seasonal challenges due to its harsh continental climate, characterized by long, severe winters and relatively short summers.
To address these challenges, the government has been promoting the development of year-round tourism. As part of these efforts, it has extended its "Years to Visit Mongolia" campaign through 2028, aiming to attract at least 1 million foreign visitors annually. ■

Over 1,400 displaced after Mayon Volcano eruption in N. Philippines
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:51:10 CST
22:51:10 KST

MANILA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Over 1,400 people in Albay province in the northern Philippines have been evacuated since Friday after the Mayon Volcano erupted, according to local officials.
The evacuees, who lived within the volcano's 6-km permanent danger zone (PDZ), were moved to safer areas. The Philippine National Police has strictly prohibited entry to the PDZ due to potential hazards.
The Mayon Volcano experienced a "moderately explosive eruption" at around 11:53 a.m. local time Friday, generating a plume that rose 3,000 meters above the crater. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology on the same day raised the volcano's alert level from 2 to 3, with Level 5 being the highest.
Mayon, famed for its near-perfect conical shape, is one of the Philippines' most active volcanoes and has a long history of explosive eruptions that have triggered mass evacuations. ■

China's "porcelain capital" wins Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:51:04 CST
22:51:04 KST

FUZHOU, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The global observance of 2026 World Cities Day was held on Saturday in east China's Fuzhou, with five cities, including China's "porcelain capital" Jingdezhen, honored with the fourth-cycle Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities, also known as the Shanghai Award.
The event runs from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2. Apart from Jingdezhen, the other four recipients of the Shanghai Award, which recognizes cities for achievements in sustainable urban development, are Addis Ababa in Ethiopia, Santiago de Cali in Colombia, Istanbul in Türkiye, and Katowice in Poland.
The event brings together senior United Nations officials alongside representatives from national governments, local authorities, international organizations, academic institutions, the private sector, and community networks to share best practices and advance practical solutions to common urban challenges.
In December 2013, the 68th United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution designating Oct. 31 as World Cities Day starting in 2014. It was the first international day proposed by the Chinese government at the United Nations.
Ceramic culture has long been an ideal medium for cross-civilization dialogue. As a cornerstone commodity of the ancient Silk Road, Jingdezhen porcelain was a defining cultural symbol, through which the world came to know China and China reached out to the world.
Building on this legacy, Jingdezhen has embraced a model of development that combines cultural preservation with creative renewal. Former porcelain factories have been reimagined as cultural and creative districts, old streets are lined with ceramic-themed installations, and historic neighborhoods have been carefully preserved and revitalized.
The city is home to more than 3,200 inheritors of intangible cultural heritage in ceramic craftsmanship. It has also been named in the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Crafts and Folk Art.
Jingdezhen's recognition is just one example of China's broader urban renewal efforts.
Urban renewal also holds huge potential for investment and consumption. China has set a target of renovating 1,500 old streets and factory compounds from 2026 to 2030, bringing in new industries and business models to inject fresh momentum into urban development.
"Converting old streets and factory sites into cultural and creative districts drives growth in dining, retail and entertainment," said Yan Yuejin, deputy director of the E-house China R&D Institute. ■

China Focus: Xinjiang's past and present: weighty monographs present authentic regional history
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:50:55 CST
22:50:55 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- A set of books covering the general and religious histories of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region has been praised as a landmark cultural achievement and an academic bulwark against hostile propaganda and misconceptions about the region.
Since a September launch in Beijing, libraries across Xinjiang have listed the two books as authoritative sources, while the works also drew significant attention at a major book fair in the region's Hotan Prefecture.
Compiled over more than two years by the Xinjiang Academy of Social Sciences, the books present an authentic history of Xinjiang, spanning from the Paleolithic Age to the present. Experts and scholars have praised the set of books as a comprehensive work of historical research on Xinjiang and a significant cultural project.
Wu Yiqun, dean of the School of History at Xinjiang University, said the monographs draw on solid historical materials to correct misconceptions, presenting robust academic theories based on rigorous research to build academic agreement on the subject.
The books, as primary source material, will play a key role in clarifying matters and building consensus in college and university teaching and research, Wu added.
To guarantee the books' authoritativeness, the compilation group convened more than 100 seminars, gathering experts from across the country in disciplines such as history, ethnic studies, religion, archaeology and border governance.
The books have emerged at an appropriate time as hostile forces at home and abroad constantly concoct false narratives about Xinjiang, said Li Tao, Party chief and vice president of the academy.
One of the books, focusing on the history of Xinjiang, is considered the country's first general history work on the region, covering a wide range of fields within a complete and standardized academic format.
With support from a wealth of historical records, archaeological artifacts and statistical data, the book traces central governments' administration of Xinjiang throughout history, affirming that Xinjiang has been an inseparable part of China since ancient times.
The book also vividly outlines the tremendous changes Xinjiang has undergone over more than 70 years, as it has developed from poverty into a moderately prosperous society in all respects.
The second book deals with the history of religions in Xinjiang, delineating the region's religious landscape and how it took shape.
The book presents core themes of how multiple religions, including Shamanism and other primitive religions, Buddhism, Taoism, and Islam, have developed and coexisted, as well as their adaptation to the Chinese context, said Yu Shangping, the chief editor of the book and vice president of the academy.
According to the book, the coexistence of multiple religions, with one or two predominating, has been a basic feature of Xinjiang's religious landscape. It concludes that, in the region's history, no single religion has ever existed alone.
The set of works is underpinned by abundant archaeological artifacts, historical documents and academic achievements, all aimed at presenting history as it truly happened, said Ren Hong, director of the academy's institute of religious studies.
Tian Kang, Party chief of the Xinjiang Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, said the books' solid historical conclusions should be woven into exhibition hall interpretations to tell the true stories about Xinjiang. ■

Australia's diesel stocks rise to 34 days amid global supply disruptions

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

22:50:53 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Australia's diesel stocks have risen to the equivalent of 34 days of consumption amid continued uncertainty and disruptions in international fuel supply chains, Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said on Saturday.
The level was three days higher than a week earlier, while stocks of aviation fuel stood at 29 days, up one day, Bowen told a press conference.
He said 43 ships carrying fuel were currently on their way to Australia, while 3.1 billion liters of fuel had been secured for delivery over the next four weeks, 100 million liters more than in the previous week's update.
Bowen said Australia's fuel supply remained "solid and secure" despite continued uncertainty in global supply chains, including disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz over the past 24 hours.
The government was working with domestic refineries to maintain production and with trading partners in Southeast Asia, the Middle East and elsewhere to secure supplies, he said.
Bowen said he had seen the reports that four oil tankers had caught fire and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz, adding that Australia highlights continued uncertainty in the region and difficulties in moving fuel through the strategic waterway. ■

Across China: Roses honoring two late women who served rural China go on sale
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:50:45 CST
22:50:45 KST

KUNMING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Two Chinese roses named after the women who died while helping rural communities went on sale in China earlier this week, following public calls to honor them with the flowers.
One is a gosling-yellow rose called "Wenxiu." The other, "Jiaolong," has soft-pink petals and a faint fragrance. Both were bred by the Flower Research Institute of the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences and have independently developed Chinese intellectual property rights.
"Wenxiu" honors Huang Wenxiu, who returned to her hometown in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region after earning a master's degree in Beijing. She volunteered to work in Baini village of Leye County, helping residents improve their livelihoods.
In June 2019, Huang was caught in a flash flood while returning to the village. She died at 30.
The pink rose bears the name of He Jiaolong, who once served as deputy head of Zhaosu County in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. She became widely known in 2020 after a video of her riding a horse across snowy grasslands to promote local tourism went viral.
She later worked to help Xinjiang farmers sell their produce online. In January this year, she fell from a horse while filming promotional material for an agricultural sales campaign. She died three days later, aged 47.
Both roses were named at the suggestion of internet users. During separate online campaigns to select names in late 2025 and early 2026, "Wenxiu" and "Jiaolong" drew widespread support and were adopted by the breeders.
The institute later donated rose plants to Guangxi and Xinjiang, where the women had worked.
The flowers were developed in Yunnan, China's largest fresh-cut flower producer. The southwestern province produced 22.15 billion stems in 2025, while roughly seven in 10 fresh-cut flowers sold across China come from Yunnan.
Yunnan's flower industry also has an international reach. Its fresh-cut flower exports reached 1.22 billion yuan (about 181.7 million U.S. dollars) in 2025, with shipments reaching 64 countries and regions.
Despite the industry's scale, Chinese growers have long relied on rose varieties developed overseas.
Cai Yanfei, a researcher at the institute, said that producing a new variety takes years of crossbreeding, screening and field observation to ensure its desirable characteristics remain stable.
The two varieties went on sale through e-commerce platforms on Thursday. Initial supplies were limited, but more flowers are expected to become available in December, Cai said.
For Huang's family, the rose is more than a new commercial variety.
In March, her elder sister, Huang Aijuan, traveled to Yunnan to receive the first plants. Wearing a pale-yellow blouse, she held a blooming "Wenxiu" rose in her hands, her eyes filling with tears.
"A flower so full of life, bearing Wenxiu's name, is the best tribute to her," she said. ■

Personal data of cumulative 260 mln people compromised in Japan since April amid cyberattack surge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:50:40 CST
22:50:40 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Personal information on a cumulative total of about 260 million people was compromised in Japan from the start of the current fiscal year in April to mid-October, according to data recently released by the Personal Information Protection Commission.
The total, roughly twice Japan's population, includes many people who were counted more than once because they were affected by multiple incidents.
The figures are based on data leak cases reported to the commission between April 1 and Oct. 16 by businesses handling personal information, excluding financial and telecommunications firms, suggesting the actual scale could be even larger.
According to the data, a total of 2,094 incidents of unauthorized access to personal information were reported during the period. Of these, six incidents each resulted in the leak of personal information on more than 10 million people.
The number of breach incidents has been on the rise, surging in October in particular. A total of 830 incidents were reported in the first half of October alone, compared with 303 in the whole of September. In fiscal 2025, a total of 1,256 incidents were reported for the entire year, according to Kyodo News.
The trend is borne out by a string of recent reports in Japanese media.
On Wednesday alone, several companies and institutions, including Sony Life Insurance Co., discount retailer Don Quijote, video game publisher Bandai Namco Entertainment Inc., and Kyushu University and its affiliated hospital, said personal data may have been compromised following unauthorized access to their websites or other systems.
On Friday, more Japanese companies reported possible leaks, including Muji brand operator Ryohin Keikaku Co., restaurant chain operator Matsuya Foods Holdings Co., and All Nippon Airways Co.
"The number of large-scale leaks is increasing rapidly, and the government is taking the situation very seriously," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said at a press conference Friday, adding that the government will compile a package of emergency countermeasures quickly. ■

22:48:43 KST

On the night of October 31, the Ukrainian Armed Forces struck the Russian solid-fuel rocket propellant plant Kamensky Combine in the Rostov region with Neptune missiles and drones.
This was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the Ukrainian Navy.
According to military command, the strike damaged at least four production facilities and caused a fire in the finished goods warehouse.
The Federal State Unitary Enterprise Kamensky Combine is located in the city of Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, the Rostov region, at coordinates 48.322833, 40.243132.
According to OSINT-Varta, this is one of the largest chemical plants in southern Russia, which fulfills state defense contracts and specializes in the production of gunpowder, explosives, and ammunition components.
The plant’s products are used in cartridges ranging from 5.45 to 14.5 mm in caliber, as well as in artillery and mortar ammunition, grenades, and rounds for 23–30 mm cannons.
The company also collaborates with the Russian JSC Scientific-Research Institute of Polymer Materials on the development of new high-energy compositions for propellants and artillery gunpowder.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the plant also produces solid rocket fuel for the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple launch rocket systems.
The governor of the Rostov region confirmed a nighttime airstrike on Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and four districts in the region.
This is not the first strike on the facility. As previously reported by Militarnyi, on the night of August 24, 2026, Ukrainian drones had already struck its production facilities.
Footage released by the military captured the drones hitting their targets, after which a fire broke out on the premises.

Pope Leo tries to stay neutral as basketball rivals descend on Vatican
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:47:19 CET
22:47:19 KST

VATICAN CITY, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Popes have received heads of state, royalty and pilgrims by the busload in the Vatican’s Paul VI Audience Hall. On Saturday, Pope Leo received his old college basketball team and, in a show of sportsmanship that went only so far, their opponents.
Leo, the first American pope, greeted the men’s and women’s teams from his alma mater Villanova, where he graduated in 1977, and from their rival Notre Dame, before roughly 7,000 players, guests and supporters.
Villanova, home of the Wildcats, is in Pennsylvania, while Notre Dame, whose teams are known as the Fighting Irish, is in Indiana but has strong support in the part of Chicago where the pope, born Robert Prevost, was raised.
“Growing up on the south side of Chicago, we oftentimes heard, ‘Go Irish.’ But as you all know, Prevost graduated from Villanova,” Leo said.
“So the Pope doesn’t take sides. Prevost has another opinion, but we won’t do that now,” he added, to cheers and laughter from the audience.
The two Catholic universities will settle matters on the court on Sunday, when their men’s and women’s teams face off at Rome’s Palazzo dello Sport in the Eternal City Tip-Off, opening the US college basketball season.
Turning more serious, Leo acknowledged the natural urge to cheer, often passionately, for one’s own side but reminded the crowd that rival teams “are certainly not enemies”.
For Notre Dame, the challenge on Sunday is obvious: beating a team whose most famous alumnus has a direct line to heaven. Villanova, meanwhile, may have found the ultimate sixth man.
(Reporting by Gavin Jones and Yesim Dikmen; Editing by Alex Richardson)

Mideast leaders call for calm as fears mount of renewed war in the region
Regional leaders called for calm Saturday as fears of a new escalation between the US, Israel and Iran grow.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs said the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace.
Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Waleed ElKhereiji told the audience that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the crisis with Iran.
“If you look at … the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region," he said. But he said no one can predict the outcome of the efforts.
Concerns are rising about a return to an all-out Iran war.
Speaking at the same event, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
“We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere,” he said.
Syria's Foreign Minister said Saturday that border security is a shared responsibility between his country and Jordan and that a high-level meeting is expected next month to discuss arrangements.
Speaking Saturday at the security forum in Bahrain, Assad al-Shibani said there are no “skirmishes” between the countries.
The announcement came after Jordanian strikes in Syria raised tensions between the neighbors.
Jordan said the strikes over Syria last week killed 20 militants from the extremist Islamic State group, but acknowledged that civilians had also been killed in the attacks.
Syrian authorities reported seven people killed in the strikes, most of them women and children.
Separately, al-Shibani said Syria is in discussions to evaluate joining the Mecca Pact, the Saudi-led defense alliance that includes Turkey and Pakistan.
“Whether Syria joins or not, Syria thinks the region is in dire need of a structure that protects its security,” he said.

Humanitarian mission from Oleshky arrives in Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in a post on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
Representatives of the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, medical workers, psychological support services, and volunteer organizations are working at the reception site. Mobile heating points have been set up and hot meals are being provided.
Wheelchairs have been provided for people with limited mobility. A designated area for animals has also been set up, with water and food available. A separate vehicle has been allocated to transport animals as part of the humanitarian mission.
As reported, on October 23, 2026, an agreement to conduct a humanitarian mission in Oleshky was officially confirmed. International humanitarian mediation was provided by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump and her team. Ukraine's Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed the agreement on the Ukrainian side, while Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova confirmed it on the Russian side. Lubinets headed the Ukrainian negotiating team tasked with implementing the mission, while Lantratova led the Russian side.
As part of the mission, the ombudsmen of Ukraine and Russia, acting as heads of the negotiating teams, agreed to establish a ceasefire; clear transport routes to Oleshky of mines; deliver humanitarian aid; and allow anyone who wished to leave to do so, either for Ukrainian government-controlled territory or for the Russian Federation.
To facilitate the humanitarian mission, Ukraine and Russia agreed to observe a ceasefire in the area of temporarily occupied Oleshky from October 27 until 22:59 on November 1.

Four days before his stunning electoral comeback, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, got his first smartphone.
Lula, who turned 81 last Tuesday, had long said he wanted to avoid an endless stream of calls during his rare moments off, and he began his presidential campaign by sticking to an old habit: using aides’ phones – only when necessary.
Then he suffered an unexpected first-round defeat to the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who had neither his father Jair Bolsonaro’s charisma nor much of a record as a two–decade legislator – and Lula realised he had lost both in the ballot box and in the digital arena.
The veteran leftist, who contested his first election more than 40 years ago, overhauled his digital strategy, began recording selfie-style videos – and went on to beat Bolsonaro by more than 4.4m votes.
There are many explanations for how he managed to boost turnout and win over other candidates’ voters. Some analysts point to an organic student mobilisation that held mass protests across Brazil, others to a package of government benefits Lula approved at the last minute in a transparent attempt to use government spending to curry favour with the electorate.
But many analysts, and the president himself, point to the incumbent’s reinvention of his social media use as a key reason for his victory.
Interestingly, neither Lula’s campaign created nor ran what was ultimately the driving force behind the shift: a WhatsApp group called “Lula’s Army”.
In the days leading up to the vote, its nearly 11 million followers – up from just 60,000 after the first round – received daily “missions” to try to win over voters and make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.
Leading the “army” was the man Lula praised in his victory speech as “our general”, whose role was “raising the morale of our troops every day”: 42-year-old congressman André Janones.
“I have no doubt that Lula’s army determined the outcome of the election,” Janones said, saying that he is not modest “because modesty sometimes comes very close to hypocrisy. I know how much bigger I came out of this election.”
In his view, the contest had three main fronts. The first was candidate versus candidate, “and on that Lula was winning by a mile because he had much more experience”. The second was mobilisation on the streets, “and we were bringing many more people out to the protests”.
But the third: “You don’t have to be very clever to realise that we were losing on social media.”
Although Lula had more followers, Bolsonaro’s content generated up to five times more engagement.
The incumbent’s campaign also complained to the electoral court of alleged interference by Meta in the senator’s favour, including a 24-hour period in which Lula was unable to boost ads on Instagram, which the company later acknowledged but blamed on a technical error.
Janones said he realised the solution was to boost organic engagement among Lula’s voters.
One of his most successful strategies came a week before the election, when “soldiers” were told to post a photo making an “L” sign for Lula with their thumb and index finger while wearing the yellow Brazil football shirt, a national symbol that had been appropriated by Bolsonaro supporters over the past decade.
Domestic worker Sidneia dos Santos Araujo, 63, took part “because the shirt of Lula supporters is the Brazilian one. Bolsonaro supporters should be wearing the United States shirt,” she said this week, citing the Bolsonaro clan’s “subservience” to US president Donald Trump and noting how the senator fled to Miami.
A day after Lula’s victory, Araujo created a template on Google Drive that allowed followers of the “army” to create their own “certificate”, which would declare that during their “military service” they “maintained excellent performance and exemplary conduct … and are therefore deserving of this distinction as a ‘soldier’”. The certificates, which went viral, came complete with copies of the signatures of “marshal” Lula and “commander” Janones.
Janones said that, above all, he wanted to create a “sense of community: the feeling that we are not alone”.
According to Raquel Recuero, a researcher at the Federal University of Pelotas, this was one of the channel’s biggest achievements: it gave voters “a sense of purpose and the chance to channel their energy into doing something to help Lula”.
Other young, digitally native politicians have also been credited with reshaping Lula’s social media strategy, including 21-year-old Ana Elisa Santos, known as Ana Elisa, who became the youngest congresswoman elected from Minas Gerais in this election.
The night after Lula’s first-round defeat, Elisa recorded a hugely popular video saying the left needed to be more “humble” and to “learn” how to use social media because “there is no longer any separation between social media and the streets … The grassroots are also on Instagram and TikTok.”
She was called to a meeting with Lula and is said to have persuaded the president to record the selfie-style videos he had previously refused to make.
Meanwhile, Janones urged each WhatsApp group member to bring in one more person. One day, while recording a video alongside the president, the congressman said that if they reached 5 million followers, Lula would buy a mobile phone and join the “army” himself.
“People think we only say that for the cameras, but it’s real: Lula really didn’t have a mobile phone,” said Janones.
The group hit its target, and when an allied politician gave the president a phone as a gift, Lula finally joined it. “I’m not going to say he’s an expert now, but he’s there, following it, and has been sending some content,” said Janones.
Recuero believes it will be difficult to keep “Lula’s army” engaged now because there is a “social cost” to being so digitally committed – Janones himself suffered a cardiac arrhythmia after the first presidential debate and had to spend 24 hours in hospital. It was the only day the group went silent.
But Janones believes there is a path forward for the group, perhaps not engaged 24/7 as it had been, but focused on special moments, such as trying to secure passage of legislation important to Lula.
“We can’t leave the campaign trail any more,” he said, noting that despite Lula’s election, Bolsonaro’s party secured an unprecedented number of seats in congress. The “army”, he said, is what will “guarantee Lula’s ability to govern”.

Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:35:51 UTC
22:35:51 KST

Israel voted for Israel: Why Gaza wasn’t on the ballot
Despite genocide, regional war and isolation, Israel’s election revealed little appetite for political alternatives.
Israel’s parliament remains in deadlock.
After one of the highest voter turnouts in decades, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority in the October 27 polls.
Netanyahu’s camp came first, with 53 seats, five more than the main opposition bloc. The Arab parties surged to a record 19 seats but have been relegated to merely observing coalition negotiations.
Viewed from a distance, the results could appear startling.
The judicial reforms ushered in at the start of Netanyahu’s government term in 2022 provoked the largest street protests in Israel’s history, while the prime minister himself is still embroiled in a corruption trial dating back to 2019. Alleged failures ahead of the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, that triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip have still to be reckoned with, despite overwhelming public pressure to do so. Moreover, the genocide has led to growing international isolation, while also providing the pretext for multiple attacks on countries across the region – the latest of which, undertaken with the United States on Iran in February, continues to roil energy markets around the world.
Nevertheless, roughly 2.38 million Israelis on Tuesday made the journey to the polls to back Netanyahu’s coalition, led by his Likud party, while some 2.21 million cast their ballots for the opposition alliance.
Between the two, little space was given to examine the multiple war crimes Israel stands accused of having carried out in Gaza, where Israeli attacks have killed more than 74,500 people and left much of it in ruins, or government complicity in the surging violence and pogroms in the occupied West Bank, where a United Nations commission of inquiry said on Monday that Israel had been committing crimes against humanity, including extermination, torture and rape.
Gaza did not make the ballot
Analysts said the fact that neither Gaza nor the West Bank were a deciding factor in how Israelis voted on Tuesday was largely because they already represented an area of broad agreement across both alliances.
Instead, the election was fought on largely internal issues: the power of Israel’s courts, whether members of the ultra-Orthodox minority should be exempted from military service, and whether the government’s alleged culpability in missing the warnings of the October 2023 attack should be examined.
Leading Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani said the issues were pitched to the Israeli public along broadly similar lines to those used by the politicians enacting the policies.
“I don’t think the problem is simply that people are uninformed or disengaged,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Many Israelis know that Gaza has been devastated, even though they are exposed to a very selective representation of that devastation. But knowing something and recognising its moral and political implications are different things,” Shenhav-Shahrabani added, providing one explanation for the absence of empathy displayed by many Israelis in the face of the widely reported suffering of Palestinians in Gaza.
“Ordinary people, who love their families, care for their friends, and consider themselves decent human beings, can participate in or acquiesce to a political order that produces immense suffering for others,” he said.
For Shenhav-Shahrabani, there has been “a powerful mechanism of denial” at work. “Not necessarily denial of the facts, but denial of their meaning,” he said.
Security on the agenda
For Netanyahu’s supporters, however, this denial could be traced to something more personal.
“The Likud is a tribe, or perhaps a cult and, as far as they are concerned, Dear Leader is always right,” Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman said of the prime minister’s base, which has sustained his rule for a cumulative 19 years – roughly a quarter of Israel’s entire existence.
“For them, the enemy, straight after the Arabs, is the left, and they would vote for Netanyahu regardless of his faults,” added Bregman, a senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.
For much of this electorate, the vote was less a judgement on the government’s conduct than a choice between competing claims to political legitimacy – or as Israeli academic Roi Zur put it, a contest over “the heart and soul of democracy” and the future of Jewish and Israeli identity.
“The most important thing, I think, for turnout among Netanyahu’s supporters is the understanding, or the belief, that the alternative coalition would be weaker on security,” said Zur, an expert on voter behaviour who teaches at Essex University.
What Netanyahu had been particularly successful in doing, he continued, was creating “this campaign of fear and the belief that he is the only one who can deal with this situation, that he is the only strong enough prime minister”.
“The idea that Netanyahu is the only and the strongest leader that can lead Israel through these recent times and the post-October 7 war.”
War and occupation, according to Shenhav-Shahrabani, were not choices to be made on the ballot paper.
Instead, they had become the prism through which, over decades, Israelis had come to view “security, citizenship, and the very meaning of democracy”.
“That is why replacing Netanyahu, important as it may be, would not by itself resolve the deeper problem.”

UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:30:43 UTC
22:30:43 KST

Ministry of Defence officials have privately accused a UK police force of wrongly handing over the investigation of an American fighter pilot who strangled a British woman to the US military, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.
Cambridgeshire police allowed the US military police to quickly take control of the investigation into Capt Jacob Wulfson after he had been accused of sexually assaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat.
The decision meant Wulfson was not tried in an English criminal court. Instead he was prosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbase in neighbouring Suffolk.
Ministry of Defence officials said the Cambridgeshire force should “absolutely” not have let the US military police take over the investigation in a clear breach of a long-established agreement with the US.
The disclosure of the case by the Guardian in June provoked immediate criticism from Downing Street, which said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.
The government to set up a high-level inquiry to examine how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to the US military police.
The Ministry of Defence, which is responsible for handling the military relationship with the US, is one of the key departments taking part in the inquiry.
A batch of documents, disclosed via the Freedom of Information Act, revealed the private views of MoD officials about the Steele case, which centres on an obscure agreement signed by the US and the UK decades ago.
Under the terms of the agreement, police in the UK have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes by Americans stationed in the country.
The MoD officials made it clear the agreement was “pretty unambiguous” and only permitted the US military to acquire jurisdiction over investigations in a “narrow set of circumstances”. These circumstances are: if the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or if they were committed against another member of their armed forces or property.
In a memo written on 8 July, MoD officials based in Washington wrote: “The Steele case does not, on the surface, appear to meet the bar for a visiting force to be awarded jurisdiction.” In the agreement, the US military is formally known as a visiting force.
Four days earlier, the MoD officials had referred to the Steele case in an email to colleagues, saying: “The decision-making on this specific case seemed at odds with what is very clear” in the agreement.
Another MoD official agreed that “as best as we understand the facts, this should absolutely have been for the UK courts”.
An unidentified Greater Manchester police officer wrote in an email to MoD officials on 6 July that Cambridgeshire police had “wrongly, in my view” handed over the Wulfson investigation to the US military.
Cambridgeshire police said they were conducting a review of the case with what they called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers. The force said it “remained engaged with the victim”.
“We are working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making,” they added.
The US military aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK.
The Americans often ask police in the UK if they can take over the prosecution of their military personnel – requests the police agree to, even when they have primary responsibility for investigating them.
A series of cases uncovered this year by the Guardian have highlighted concerns that British victims are required to give evidence in US courts martial, an unfamiliar legal system that often does not afford the same protections as that of a court in the UK.
Wulfson was off-duty when he assaulted Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair talked on the Tinder dating app.
Steele testified at Wulfson’s court martial, which was held on his airbase at Lakenheath, Suffolk in April, that her experience was “degrading and distressing”.
The verdict and sentence were decided by an all-male jury of Wulfson’s fellow air force officers. All the lawyers were American. Steele was subjected to invasive and aggressive questioning by Wulfson’s lawyer.
Wulfson was convicted of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted of sexual assault. He was dismissed from the US Air Force and confined to a military jail on Lakenheath for six months.
The cross-government inquiry, which includes officials from the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is looking at how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.
The inquiry, which also involves police chiefs, is scrutinising a series of cases uncovered by the Guardian this year.
In each case, police handed over the investigations to US military police even though the American perpetrators were off-duty and the British victims had no connection to the armed forces.
They were tried in US courts martial on American bases. Tyrion Davis allegedly raped two women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault, but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.
Hannes Marschalek allegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girl and four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He negotiated a plea bargain at a court martial and admitted a charge of indecent conduct. He won an appeal in a US military court that quashed his conviction on technical grounds. This ruling is now being challenged.
The US has more than 12,000 US military personnel in the UK, stationed in at least 15 bases and facilities. The two biggest bases are at Lakenheath and Mildenhall, in Suffolk. Significant numbers of American military personnel live in East Anglia.

'Indira Gandhi's assassination cannot justify 1984 anti-Sikh riots': Hardeep Puri ahead of 42nd anniversary

Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri spoke out about the lasting impact of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, firmly stating that no justification exists for the violence inflicted upon the Sikh community
NEW DELHI: Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri on Saturday said the assassination of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was a profound tragedy but stressed that it could not justify the violence subsequently inflicted on the Sikh community during the 1984 anti-Sikh riots.Ahead of the 42nd anniversary of the riots on November 1, Puri said, "The assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, regardless of one’s perspective, was a profound tragedy. The collective punishment subsequently inflicted upon the Sikh community cannot be justified under any circumstances."Speaking about the scale of the violence, Puri said an official death toll of 3,325 was recorded across the country, with Delhi alone accounting for 2,733 deaths. He also described November 1 as a painful reminder for Sikh families who lost relatives and saw their homes reduced to ashes.Puri also credited senior advocate HS Phoolka for his decades-long efforts to secure justice for the victims of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, saying he had remained committed to the legal battle despite threats and repeated delays."One individual who has dedicated over four decades to helping the victims secure justice, remaining steadfast in his resolve and, alongside their legal counsel, keeping these cases alive despite threats and persistent delays, is HS Phoolka," Puri said.
1984 anti-Sikh riotsThe anti-Sikh violence broke out across several parts of India following the assassination of then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by two of her Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984.The assassination came months after Operation Blue Star, a military operation ordered by Indira Gandhi's government to remove armed militants from the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar.
The violence intensified in Delhi over the following days, with Sikh men, women and children targeted in attacks. Homes, shops and businesses belonging to members of the community were looted and set on fire. Several neighbourhoods in the national capital witnessed widespread killings and destruction.The violence also triggered allegations of organised attacks and political complicity, leading to several investigations, commissions and prolonged court battles.The demand for accountability and justice has continued for decades, with survivors and families of victims pursuing legal action against those accused of involvement in the violence.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Russian outlet ASTRA on October 31, an analysis of eyewitness photographs indicated that the fire broke out at the Bashneft-Novoil facility. Initial reports suggest that the refinery’s L-35 catalytic reforming unit may have been affected.

Bashneft-Novoil is part of Bashneft, a subsidiary of Russia’s state-controlled oil company Rosneft. The facility processes approximately 7.3 million metric tons of crude oil annually and produces gasoline, diesel, aviation kerosene, and industrial lubricants.
Local authorities declared a drone threat at approximately 5:40 a.m. local time, while Russia’s aviation regulator temporarily suspended operations at Ufa airport.
Footage circulating online showed thick smoke rising from the industrial zone, with residents reporting explosions and air defense activity.
Initial reports differed on the exact location of the strike. Eyewitness accounts also raised the possibility that two facilities were affected, although this has not been verified.
The northern industrial zone of Ufa contains three major refineries—Bashneft-Novoil, Bashneft-UNPZ, and Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim—with a combined annual processing capacity of approximately 23.5 million metric tons.

Burnham opens door to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:19:23 UTC
22:19:23 KST

Burnham opens door to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
The prime minister has ruled out financial reparations despite longstanding Caribbean demands ahead of Commonwealth leaders’ summit.
Britain’s prime minister has opened the door to a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, while ruling out financial reparations.
Andy Burnham set out his position in a Guardian article on Friday, ahead of a Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Sunday.
The Commonwealth comprises 56 countries, mostly former British colonies, whose Caribbean members have long pressed Britain to acknowledge slavery’s legacy and offer redress.
Burnham offered structured talks with countries and campaign groups affected by slavery, including discussions on whether Britain should issue an official state apology.
“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them,” Burnham wrote.
He expressed “sorrow and regret” for the suffering of millions of enslaved people, but rejected calls for financial compensation.
“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” he said.
The stance maintains the position of previous British governments, despite his willingness to discuss an apology.
Instead, he proposed an international effort to ease the debt burden on poorer nations by extending repayment periods and cutting interest rates.
Burnham also said that former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown will assist with the initiative, adding that more than 40 percent of the world’s poorest and most vulnerable countries spend more on debt interest than on healthcare.
Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley welcomed the opening for talks but reiterated her government’s position on reparations.
In a statement reported by the Guardian on Saturday, she said cooperation could also cover healthcare, education, development and fairer borrowing terms.
Antigua’s Prime Minister Gaston Browne, who is hosting the summit, welcomed the debt initiative and promises of cooperation on renewable energy.
CARICOM, the regional bloc of Caribbean countries, has drawn up a 10-point plan for reparations.
Its demands go beyond payments to include an apology, support for health and education, as well as measures to address the economic and social damage left by slavery.
The dispute surfaced at the last Commonwealth summit in Samoa in 2024, when leaders called for discussions about reparations, despite opposition from then Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
King Charles III will also attend the summit. However, Buckingham Palace has said he will not issue a formal apology for slavery during his trip, despite calls from countries in the region.

At least 12 civilians were killed and several others injured in a drone strike in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region Friday while collecting grain spilled from a truck damaged in an earlier attack, local authorities and hospital sources confirmed Saturday.
The attack took place in the town of Rama, where residents had gathered to collect sorghum scattered across the road after a privately owned truck transporting grain for local traders was struck Thursday night.
Local sources told Ethiopian news outlet Addis Standard that 12 people died at the scene, while several others sustained injuries, some of them serious.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), which monitors violence worldwide, also documented the Friday attack, recording 12 deaths plus injuries and property damage.
The latest incident comes amid renewed fighting in Tigray, where drone operations have raised concerns over civilian safety.
Earlier in October, separate drone strikes in Medebay Terer killed seven civilians, including an 8-year-old girl, and injured six others. Other attacks in the Hintalo district also caused civilian deaths, including a 2-year-old child.
The escalation extends beyond Tigray, with drone strikes causing casualties in the neighboring Amhara region and western Oromia.
On Thursday, a strike at the Hayiq Jari 2 Turk displacement camp in Amhara killed at least 16 civilians and injured 22 others.
Ethiopia’s northern conflict has also heightened tensions with neighboring Eritrea, which Addis Ababa has accused of supporting armed groups and sending troops into Tigray.
Eritrea has rejected the accusations, as concerns grow over the risk of another regional confrontation.

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Dutch professor Jan Rotmans, who has terminal cancer, is developing an artificial intelligence version of himself to preserve his knowledge and deliver lectures after his death, local media reported Saturday.
The 65-year-old professor of transition studies said his digital twin would be developed using his books, scientific publications and recorded lectures, Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported.
The first online version is expected to become available by the end of 2026, with plans to eventually develop a hologram capable of appearing on stage.
Rotmans said recordings of his voice, image and facial expressions had already been made to help create the digital version.
The project is being developed by studio The Synths, which previously created a digital likeness of former Dutch footballer Ruud Gullit.
Rotmans, who has had metastatic prostate cancer for nearly two years, said his condition remained stable and that recent medical results had been encouraging.
He also expressed hope that he would be able to interact with his AI counterpart and learn from its responses.
However, the professor acknowledged the technology's limitations, including the possibility that it could generate inaccurate information or statements he would not endorse.
He said the system would undergo extensive testing before being made available.
AI expert warns of risks
Iris van Rooij, an artificial intelligence professor at Radboud University, criticized the project, describing it as an undesirable development.
She warned that people interacting with such digital models could mistakenly attribute human qualities, including emotions and intelligence, to artificial intelligence systems.
Rotmans, however, stressed that the digital twin was not intended to replace him personally but to ensure that his knowledge remained accessible to future generations.
He said he accepted the potential risks associated with the project and expected other researchers to pursue similar initiatives.

'Northern women and esotericism': Life after death explored at Finnish National Gallery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:10:35 UTC
22:10:35 KST

The relationship between spirit and matter, questions related to life after death and the existence of the spirit world are the key themes of the exhibition "Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" at Ateneum Art Museum, Finnish National Gallery.
The Latin words arcana and borealis mean "hidden knowledge" and "the north", two elements at the heart of the Finnish National Gallery's latest exhibition.
"Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" is the first large-scale museum show to examine how female artists from across the Nordic region and Sápmi have engaged with esotericism, spirituality and alternative systems of knowledge from the 19th century to the present day.
The exhibition brings together more than 200 works by 50 artists and features both well-known and overlooked artists, including Hilma af Klint, Tyra Kleen and Tove Jansson.
Previously the connection between modern art and esotericism, occultism and magic has been explored mainly through famous male artists, according to Dr Marja Lahelma, Chief Curator at Ateneum Art Museum and co-curator of the exhibition.
"For quite a long time art history has been dominated by narratives focusing on male artists and on this notion of the individual genius. Our focus is on women and we also draw attention to this idea of communality and working together," Dr Lahelma explained to Euronews Culture.
Art, spirituality and handicraft
"Arcana Borealis shows how the boundaries between art and spirituality, fine art and craft, object and process, individual authorship and collective making begin to blur when viewed through the lens of artist women and esotericism" added Dr Nina Kokkinen from University of Turku, co-curator of "Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" .
The range of materials featured in the exhibition is exceptionally wide, including textiles, ceramics, metal engravings, and traditional media from sacral art, such as stained glass and mosaics.
Handicraft involves matrilineal transmission of tradition, that is, passing down knowledge and skills from one woman to the next. Sámi duodji, the traditional Sámi craft tradition, brings together spirituality, the tacit knowledge passed on from one generation to another, and values related to nature.
Some of the artists gathered on the exhibition were saying that they were guided by some kind of non human agency whether it was angels or guiding spirits, or in some cases a source of nature.
Halloween or Kekri
"This is a perfect exhibition to visit for Halloween, or Kekri as we say in Finnish. Esotericism is about light and darkness. We can explore themes such as death in art through this esoteric theme and sometimes the hidden knowledge, the secret knowledge that esotericism is all about, can be found through exploring darkness rather than light," explained Dr Marja Lahelm.
Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism at Ateneum Art Museum, Finnish National Gallery is on open until 28 February 2027.

A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:09:49 UTC
22:09:49 KST

A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
- Date:
- October 31, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.
- Share:
In the hills of north-west Morocco, overlooking the river that gives the site its name, research at Oued Beht is bringing to light a previously unknown chapter of the region’s past. The discovery of a substantial built structure suggests that, during the second millennium BC, communities in north-west Africa were actively shaping their environment. They were also engaging in broader networks of interaction across the Mediterranean world.
Previous research by the Oued Beht Archaeological Project had already brought to light what is likely the earliest and largest agricultural complex ever discovered in Africa outside the Nile Valley. It dates to around 5,400 to 4,900 years ago. New excavations carried out in 2023 – in which we took part – have now deepened our understanding of the site.
Our new study shows how we uncovered the earliest known large-scale construction of a probably defensive nature in north Africa beyond the Nile Valley. It’s about 4,000 to 3,500 years old.
It’s not known exactly what threats these wall-like structures were designed to counter. They likely relate to increasing competition over land, resources, and possibly control of movement through the landscape, rather than to “invaders”. Constructions like these suggest communities felt the need to protect themselves or assert power over strategic locations.
This discovery pushes back the evidence for organized defensive architecture in the Maghreb and suggests that societies in this region at this time were more complex and structured than previously believed.
Our study also reveals how the ridge of Oued Beht would become a focal point again in the medieval period, during the 11th to 13th centuries AD. The same defensive structure was rebuilt, a hamlet or farm was established on a nearby hilltop, and people were buried in a cemetery between the two areas.
Together these findings provide rare archaeological insights into rural communities during both prehistoric and medieval times. They help us understand how societies developed and maintained themselves in a region too often left out of the history books.
A prehistoric hub in the Maghreb
For a long time, the later prehistory of north Africa’s Maghreb region (the Mediterranean countries of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia) has been poorly understood. Compared with neighboring areas such as Iberia in south-western Europe or Athens in the eastern Mediterranean, archaeological evidence was often fragmentary. In the last few years this has changed completely.
Excavations at Oued Beht have revealed a large concentration of human activity spread across at least ten hectares. The earliest major phase dates to the mid-fourth and early third millennia BC, or the Final Neolithic period.
Environmental evidence from plant and animal remains in the prehistoric era indicates a farming community cultivating crops such as barley and wheat. They also exploited wild plants and kept livestock.
The site was also an important center of craft production. Thousands of polished stone axes and other tools have been discovered, along with finely made pottery, sometimes decorated with painted patterns.
It’s still uncertain whether prehistoric Oued Beht functioned as a permanent village, a seasonal center, or something less familiar. But it was clearly a major focus in the landscape of north-west Morocco.
The defensive wall
The presence of potentially ancient earthworks and walls had been noted since the 1930s. The French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann first documented a configuration of three walls, with the fourth side protected by the natural scarp of the ridge, describing a defensive éperon barré (barred spur). Their precise nature and date remained uncertain until now.
New excavations have clarified the existence of a multi-phase ditch, rampart and wall built across a narrow section of the Oued Beht ridge between the river and a ravine. This cut off and protected the ridge’s southern tip.
Radiocarbon dating of deposits associated with these structures gave us the timelines in our study.
They place its original construction at a time equivalent to the Bronze Age of the remaining western Mediterranean. This makes it the earliest confirmed defensive construction in north Africa outside Egypt.
What was this construction for?
This structure raises important questions about the society that built it. Building an embankment and ditch system required planning, coordination and the mobilization of labor. This suggests a community capable of organizing complex construction initiatives.
During the earlier Neolithic phase, activity at Oued Beht focused on the larger and more open northern area of the site. By the period of our new study, focus had shifted to the narrower, more defensible southern ridge. This may reflect a shift in settlement strategies.
Mediterranean connections
The second millennium BC was a dynamic period across the Mediterranean. In southern Iberia, Argaric societies (about 2200-1550 BC) in today’s Europe were developing complex, often hilltop settlements. They were characterized by planned architecture, advanced metallurgy (especially bronze production), and marked social hierarchies visible in burial practices. These communities often constructed fortified sites, and strategically located settlements controlling surrounding territories.
Increasing evidence suggests that communities in north-west Africa were connected to wider Mediterranean networks. This includes today’s Spain and Portugal. The discoveries at Oued Beht indicate that the Maghreb was not isolated. It participated in broader processes shaping the western Mediterranean.
The defensive system at the site may reflect wider transformations in social organization and regional interaction. There may have been growing competition over resources, control of movement, and more formalized leadership structures.
Rewriting history
The discoveries at Oued Beht highlight how much remains to be learned about the deep history of north Africa. The defensive wall shows that communities here were able to coordinate large construction projects and points to social transformations that are only very tentatively beginning to be recognized.
The medieval remains demonstrate that the ridge was used again many centuries after the prehistoric settlement had been abandoned. Oued Beht was not simply a single-period settlement but a landscape repeatedly selected by different communities across millennia.
As research continues, this location may become key to understanding how societies in the Maghreb evolved from early farming communities to the medieval rural world.

Oleshky residents reach Ukrainian-controlled territory after escaping Russian occupation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:04:04 UTC
22:04:04 KST

Oleshky residents reach Ukrainian-controlled territory after escaping Russian occupation
CHERNIHIV OBLAST — Evacuees from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory on Oct. 31 after an arduous 19-hour journey.
The city's residents, who had been trapped in a worsening humanitarian crisis for months on end, arrived to an emotional reception at the border crossing with Belarus by relatives, health workers with ambulances, aid organizations, police, and media.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the mission was successful, thanking all parties involved, including U.S. First Lady Melania Trump.
"When there is the attention of the world, there is the salvation of people," Zelensky wrote.
"Further de-escalation steps and a real approach to peace are also needed."
Disembarking the buses to step on Ukrainian-controlled soil for the first time in years, many residents broke out in tears.
Liudmyla Burychenko, 39, said she always had faith that residents would eventually be evacuated, and decided to leave Oleshky as soon as the opportunity presented itself. She arrived with her husband, Valentyn. Their son had left the occupied town earlier.
“There were drones there flying around (in recent months). We took shelter in the basement,” Burychenko told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, and Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova, had coordinated the operation.
"This is an extraordinarily important moment," Lubinets wrote upon arrival in Ukraine.
"Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who have waited so long to be rescued are finally safe."
According to the Ombudsman, the oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest had only recently turned one.
Officials have not yet disclosed the exact number of those evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled territory, citing security reasons amid the highly sensitive operation.
The evacuation followed a temporary ceasefire agreement reached between Ukraine and Russia, with mediation by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump. The arrangement was intended to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the departure of civilians wishing to leave Oleshky.
According to Lubinets, the ceasefire will last until 11 p.m., making it the longest halt to the fighting in any area since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.
This is the largest publicly-known humanitarian operation involving civilians from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
Ukraine has regularly facilitated the return of its citizens, including children, from occupied areas, but the Oleshky mission was unprecedented, both in its scale and in the role played by a U.S.-mediated ceasefire in Kherson Oblast to allow civilians to leave safely.
Some relatives who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said their loved ones had stayed in Russian-occupied Oleshky out of fear of Russian filtration checks.
Holding her young daughter in her arms, Iryna Mohylna waited for her godfather to return. She last spoke to him on Oct. 27 and later saw a video of him boarding an evacuation plane.
"It's the pain of what has happened and of what is still to come… I understand his age and why he chose not to leave. He spent his whole life working, building something for himself, and now he has to leave it all behind. It's impossible to put into words."
The first leg of the day-long journey was to Armiansk in occupied Crimea, where residents could choose whether to go to Russia or Ukraine.
According to Newsmax journalist Alex Salvi, who was one of the only non-Russian journalists granted access to the mission inside Oleshky itself, the approximately 750 people who registered for evacuation were split between 11 buses going to Ukraine, and only four taking those who chose Russia.
From Armiansk, the buses took residents to Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, where they boarded four planes to Belarus, according to David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary faction.
The planes carrying the evacuees landed in Gomel in Belarus, from where they were brought to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
For years, Oleshky residents were trapped in the embattled town with the Russian soldiers stationed among civilian houses. The town, located on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River across from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Moscow's full-scale invasion.
In recent months, residents faced severe shortages of food, drinking water, electricity, and medical supplies. Russian forces had effectively blockaded the town, preventing humanitarian organizations from delivering aid.
Andrii Zhydenko, director of Chernihiv Regional Hospital, said that more than 30 employees from the hospital were waiting to assist the evacuees, with transfers to Kyiv hospitals available if needed.
"It's a celebration because we're bringing our Ukrainians home," Zhydenko told reporters. "You know how much they suffered there. It is simply genocide in the 21st century."
For many of those leaving Oleshky, the evacuation offered a way out of a worsening humanitarian crisis that had made survival increasingly difficult.
According to Mohylna, the blockade of Oleshky began in earnest in October last year, and by December, supplies and groceries were no longer being brought into the city.
"It was survival. Traveling around the city was very dangerous because of the mines," she said.
"I was talking on the phone with my godfather and I heard an explosion from the sound. Then I read in a telegram that a person had been blown up by a mine."
Mined roads, constant drone attacks, and Russian interrogations at checkpoints made independent evacuation extremely dangerous. In September, one person was killed and four others were injured by landmines while attempting to flee the area, according to the head of the exiled Oleshky City Military Administration, Tetiana Hasanenko.
Before the war, Oleshky had a population of around 24,000. By October, only around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, were believed to remain there, according to Ukrainian officials.
read also
How did Russia act on the ground?
The evacuation was accompanied by a significant Russian media presence, with numerous Russian journalists attending the operation, compared with only two Ukrainian and two American journalists.
Russia also appeared to be seeking to present a carefully staged picture of the humanitarian mission. According to Oleshky residents interviewed by the Media Initiative for Human Rights (MIHR), Russian forces selected an evacuation route that avoided the town's most heavily destroyed areas, while clearing the road of debris, damaged military equipment, and rubble ahead of the operation.
One resident told MIHR that Russian forces were effectively creating an image for American television that "it's not that terrible in Oleshky," despite entire neighborhoods having been reduced to ruin.
Kseniia Arkhipova, an evacuation volunteer from Oleshky who is now based in Ukrainian-controlled territory, said that Russia had violated the terms of the agreement by starting the evacuation early.
Footage broadcast by TASS also appears to show civilians being moved with only Russian forces present and before the agreed-upon date of departure, Oct. 30. TASS also showed interviews with people it claimed were evacuated from Oleshky on Oct. 29.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that residents would have a choice — either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there."
A source familiar with the events unfolding on the ground, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said on Oct. 29 that Russia was already taking steps to ensure as few people as possible left for Ukraine.
They said that patients at the city's only functioning hospital were being registered and told they faced filtration if they left, Russian forces had refused to go house-to-house to inform sick and immobile people that the evacuation was happening, and those living in outlying villages had been told they could be shot if they approached the assembly point.
Some residents expressed fears in local Telegram chats that they could be taken to "concentration camps."

'Only we will decide when it ends': Khamenei threatens US and Israel as Iran talks advance

Arab media outlets continued reporting Saturday on alleged progress in negotiations between Iran and the United States aimed at preventing a resumption of hostilities, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday. The Qatari newspaper "Al-Araby Al-Jadeed," which earlier reported a breakthrough in the talks, said around midday that an Iranian deputy foreign minister had arrived in Doha, Qatar's capital. The newspaper did not identify which deputy minister had made the trip.
Reuters also reported that Iranian representatives arrived in Doha on Saturday following more than 12 hours of talks in Tehran on Friday. A source familiar with the negotiations told the news agency that Qatari officials were in continuous contact with the Americans but did not confirm reports earlier in the day that a U.S. delegation was also on its way to Qatar.
The reported arrival came as Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, issued a defiant statement following what was described as a meeting with senior military commanders. Once again, Iranian authorities released a written statement attributed to Khamenei without an accompanying photograph. Iran's supreme leader has not been seen publicly since his appointment to the position, or since he was wounded in Israel's opening strike against Iran on Feb. 28, which targeted the residential compound of his father, Ali Khamenei.
According to the Iranian statement, Khamenei warned that if Israel and the United States launched another attack, Iran would determine the timing and conditions for ending the fighting. He added that he had ordered an update to the military's target list to "ensure that all tangible and intangible assets of the American-Zionist enemy" (as stated in the original) would be within the reach of Iranian forces.
Khamenei instructed the senior commanders he reportedly met to maintain combat readiness for a major confrontation and respond to any attack without geographical limitations. He also praised Iran's proxy organizations. According to the report, those who met with Khamenei included Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps; Ali Abdollahi, Iran's military chief of staff; and Amir Hatami, commander of the Iranian army.
The Qatari report published Saturday morning, citing unidentified sources, claimed that "an American delegation will join the talks in Doha to conduct direct negotiations with the Iranian delegation." It did not specify when that would happen, and, as noted, Reuters quoted a source who cast doubt on that claim. Nevertheless, the report said the move could pave the way for an announcement that negotiations were resuming following an agreement on preliminary measures concerning Iran's nuclear program, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and economic incentives for Iran, with China and Russia serving as guarantors of the agreement.
Saudi television channels Al Arabiya and Al Hadath reported overnight that they had obtained a draft proposal being discussed by mediators. The draft has not been confirmed by either party or by the Qataris. According to the reports, it includes an initial Iranian commitment concerning the future of its nuclear stockpile, discussions on arrangements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, daily talks on confidence-building measures between Iran and the United States, an agreed timetable for implementing commitments by both countries and a possible role for China as a guarantor of any agreement.
"Every Iranian action concerning its nuclear program will be met with a corresponding U.S. action concerning sanctions. Clear procedures will be established to address any delay or noncompliance by Iran," the Saudi channels reported. "Neither Iran nor the United States will be required to make concessions without receiving a corresponding commitment." The reports also referred to "a clear definition of Iran's and the United States' commitments at every stage of the agreement."
The Lebanese newspaper "Al-Akhbar," which is affiliated with Hezbollah, reported Saturday, citing "knowledgeable sources," that Iran does not oppose reciprocal commitments concerning the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the lifting of the naval blockade. According to the report, Iran's reservations concern the provision dealing with nuclear concessions, under which Tehran would allow inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency to access its nuclear facilities. In return, Washington would reportedly lift some sanctions and release a portion of Iran's frozen assets. Tehran has repeatedly insisted that any negotiations on the nuclear issue would take place only after an official declaration ending the war and the implementation of concrete measures.
