Affordability, AI and Iran: Americans on the key issues guiding their midterm votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:00:45 UTC
22:00:45 KST

Millions of Americans will head to the polls on 3 November in elections that will determine control of the Republican-held House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships of 36 states.
The midterms come amid mounting public frustration over issues ranging from the rising cost of living and immigration to the climate crisis, artificial intelligence, big tech and the US’s overseas wars. Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 36%, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted this month.
Voters across the US described to the Guardian their concerns and disillusionment with the current political climate, with one characterizing the country under the Trump administration as a “rogue nation, ungoverned by the rule of law”. (Some respondents only shared their first name or declined to share their name for privacy reasons.)
For many, the cost of living is a central concern ahead of the midterms, particularly as inflation reaches 3.7%.
Kathryn Warren, a retired staff member from Dare county schools who lives on Hatteras Island, North Carolina, said she and her husband had already voted early.
“We are dying on the vine in this economy. We live in a remote area and the cost of gas is taking a big chunk of our social security. Groceries and medicine are outrageous. The medicine that keeps me alive costs $7,000 a month before insurance. In what world is that reasonable?” Warren said.
A 36-year-old counsellor in Tennessee described financial pressures compounded by health issues and expressed concern about the US “sliding into an authoritarian state”.
“I have a migraine medication that costs nearly $2,000 out-of-pocket for a month’s supply. My health insurance has agreed to pay for five months. That’s it. After 24 years of chronic migraines, I have tried everything under the sun and this is the first medication that has ever reduced the pain levels, so it isn’t like I can try some cheaper, knock-off brand. But I find it absurd and financially prohibitive to spend that much on medication every month,” she said.
Vicki Stein, a 66-year-old retired marketing communications professional from Alpine Township, Michigan, said she had already voted for Democrats across the ticket.
“Working Americans can’t afford healthcare, let alone gas nor groceries due to tariffs, and children are losing Snap benefits while we blow our gold on [Israeli prime minister Benjamin] Netanyahu’s war. We can’t even trust our lettuce under this administration’s [Department of Health and Human Services],” she said, referring to a cyclospora outbreak across 27 states this summer that was traced to contaminated lettuce.
George, a 23-year-old business school graduate in Houston, Texas, also linked the affordability crisis to the administration’s policies, criticizing “Trump’s idiotic tariff scheme”.
“The priorities of both parties are clearly more in line with billionaires than regular people … It has been heartening to see politicians like [James] Talarico abandon that side of politics to focus on affordability and quality of life for average Americans. Who cares about 1% of the population when everyone is struggling?”
George also criticized the US’s war in Iran and called for the US to divest from Israel, saying: “Billions upon billions of American taxpayer dollars spent on killing children. No matter how you cut it, all we get from our investment in Israel is a mountain of dead bodies. Any politician who refuses Aipac money or promises to stop funding Israel’s perma-war has my vote and many other Americans’ as well.”
Opposition to the US war in Iran and military aid to Israel remains a driving concern among voters.
Joel Young, a 66-year-old retired civil litigator in Albuquerque, New Mexico, said: “The single most important issue in any election for federal office is whether the candidate or incumbent will approve another dollar, weapon, or material to support Israel, or support the US’s historical pattern of cover for Israel’s apartheid regime and program of ethnic cleansing in place since 1948, which has now clearly become genocidal.”
A 30-year-old machine operator and father in Bogalusa, Louisiana, who voted for Trump in 2024, also criticized the “evil war against Iran which must end”.
“Every day it continues is another day that the president scandalizes our service members, taxpayers and nation. It’s also another day of stealing present day purchasing power from embattled American workers, stealing future prosperity from our children through a climbing national debt and stealing tranquility from people in the Middle East,” he added.
Beyond economic pressures and foreign policy, voters also raised concerns about the growing influence of AI and big tech.
Dave Neps, a 74-year-old retired teacher in Georgia, said: “I’m … concerned about the AI financial bubble. This market reminds me of the dotcom crash in the late 90s and the financial crash in 2008. My wife and I lost money both times in those markets. Now I’m looking at a pension and a country that’s heavily invested in AI that so many of us don’t want. Give these guys time and they’ll just turn it into another commodity that we’ll have to pay for like cable TV.”
Joy, a 47-year-old insurance executive in north Georgia, similarly raised concerns about the expansion of datacenters and the influence of technology companies on local government.
“I live in rural Georgia where they are buying off local officials to build datacenters and the county and city reps are ignoring their constituents and offering massive tax incentives,” she said, calling for datacenter moratoriums.
The climate crisis and environmental protection were also prominent concerns, particularly among older voters who described witnessing the degradation of natural spaces over their lifetimes.
David Tucker, a 57-year-old registered nurse in Washington, said: “The climate crisis and public lands protection are my main concerns, along with protecting democracy and healthcare funding cuts. I grew up in Utah and spent a lot of time camping and fishing with my parents and siblings on public forests and deserts. Natural spaces and our ecosystem are essential for our survival.”
Similarly, Kaye, a 71-year-old resident of Bothell, Washington, said: “While Donald Trump is evil and incompetent in so many ways, the degradation of the planet is my greatest concern as it is larger than all of us and we’re so close to a tipping point that will be catastrophic. I’m old enough to have known a world with more birds and animal species; where the forests, coasts and plains were so much more alive. Our vile destruction of the land that feeds us is tragic.”
Another 78-year-old Washington resident similarly described the climate crisis as the “biggest threat to the planet and causes suffering, disease, fear, inequality”.
“A candidate with a clear track record of ethical standards, who is direct about the threat, and who can muster a coalition to face it will have my vote. This issue is bigger than political affiliation,” she added.
Immigration enforcement and fears of voter intimidation were other major concerns, with some readers expressing alarm about potential federal interference in the midterm elections.
Katie, a 34-year-old arts professional in Denver, Colorado, pointed to the killings of two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, by federal immigration agents in Minnesota earlier this year.
“Maga lost America when they murdered Renee Good and Alex Pretti. First and foremost I’m concerned about Trump’s immigration secret police, and I am voting for candidates who will defund and prosecute ICE,” Katie said.
Julie Stielstra, a retired librarian living in rural Kansas, said she was worried about the potential presence of immigration agents and armed individuals at polling stations. Stielstra said she would be working as a poll worker the following week.
“I am apprehensive about the possible presence of ICE, which has been active in my state recently … [and] armed government agents or self-appointed ‘poll watchers’ who may be intimidating at best. I trust my county clerk’s vigilance and honor, but worry about federal minions and officials who could disrupt or try to negate or overturn our ballots,” she said.
Those concerns extended beyond intimidation at polling stations to the possibility that the Trump administration could challenge the election results.
Richard Corcoran, a 63-year-old licensed clinical social worker in Lumberton, North Carolina, said: “I do not have faith that the federal government under Trump and Republican control of Congress and the supreme court will respect the outcome of this election. I expect problems in the aftermath,” he said.
Michael Pitts-Campbell, a 78-year-old law enforcement retiree living in Brookings, Oregon, similarly worried that Trump would reject a Democratic victory.
“My biggest concern is that if the results of the election are overwhelmingly Democratic, Trump will claim that the election results are false. Whether the appropriate member of the government attempts to not certify the vote or not seat the new representatives and senators, the proclamation from Trump will only widen the current political chasm,” he said.
But even among voters hoping for a Democratic victory, there was little consensus that the party would be prepared to deliver the changes they want.
Several readers expressed concern that Democrats could fail to use a potential congressional majority to enact effective change.
For a 52-year-old insurance professional in New Lenox, Illinois, their “biggest fear is that despite a likely massive Democrat wins, they will not have the guts to do what is necessary to prosecute this administration and pass laws that are sorely needed limiting the powers of the president, abolishing [the Department of Homeland Security] and establishing Medicare for all”.
D Turner, a California resident, similarly said: “I’m concerned that the reflexive centrist impulses of current Democratic leadership and advisers will assume that if they just get a majority, everything will be back to normal. There is so much hard work that needs to be done to preserve the rights of all.”
Brad Southard, a 54-year-old teacher in Irvine, California, criticized Democratic leaders for focusing “too much on courting the illusive ‘undecided middle’ to the detriment of the needs of working-class people”.
“I worry that the party will again choose to seize defeat from the jaws of victory by supporting pro-corporate neoliberal candidates and policies and refuse to pay attention to the real material pain felt by so many Americans,” Southard added.
For other voters, disillusionment extended beyond either party’s leadership, reflecting a broader lack of faith in the US political system.
Mark, a 68-year-old retiree in Parma, Ohio, said both parties had become too beholden to wealthy interests to represent ordinary Americans.
“Both political parties share the blame. The GOP has morphed into something even worse than the [Democrats]. Neither party offers policies that meet the needs of the people. Rather, both parties are captured by moneyed interests. It just turns out the GOP has openly embraced the dark side while the [Democrats] are more coy about their corruption.”

Single dose of psychedelic nasal spray reduced treatment-resistant depression symptoms for eight weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:00:43 UTC
22:00:43 KST

A single dose of a fast-acting psychedelic nasal spray appears to ease symptoms of hard-to-treat depression within a day, with benefits lasting up to eight weeks, according to a clinical trial published in JAMA. The medication, a synthetic formulation of the psychedelic compound mebufotenin, produced a brief psychoactive experience that allowed most patients to be assessed as ready to leave the clinic within two hours. These findings suggest that short-acting psychedelics may offer a practical way to deliver rapid antidepressant relief without the four- to twelve-hour clinic stays required for compounds like psilocybin.
Major depressive disorder is a mood condition marked by persistent sadness, loss of interest in daily activities, and trouble sleeping or concentrating, affecting about 290 million people worldwide. Roughly one-third of patients have treatment-resistant depression, meaning their symptoms do not adequately respond to at least two antidepressant trials. People with treatment-resistant depression tend to experience greater emotional distress, a lower quality of life, and a higher risk of suicide than those who respond to standard medications.
Existing options for treatment-resistant depression, such as esketamine nasal spray or magnetic brain stimulation, require frequent clinic visits. Psychedelic drugs, which alter perception and mood by activating docking sites for the chemical messenger serotonin in the brain, offer a potential alternative because a single dose can produce lasting relief. For instance, a clinical trial of patients with treatment-resistant depression found that one 25-milligram dose of psilocybin with psychological support reduced depression scores at three weeks compared to a 1-milligram control dose, though it carried side effects including suicidal thoughts.
Because classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD require four to twelve hours of in-clinic supervision, scientists have turned to mebufotenin, a psychedelic compound chemically known as 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine that is naturally found in toad venom and certain plants. Mebufotenin activates both serotonin 1A and 2A receptors in the brain and is rapidly absorbed and eliminated by the body, producing a brief psychedelic experience.
Earlier clinical trials tested mebufotenin by inhalation. In a 2026 randomized controlled trial of 81 patients with treatment-resistant depression, an inhaled formulation of mebufotenin produced a 58 percent remission rate at day 8 compared to 0 percent for placebo, and in an open-label follow-up phase allowing up to four retreatments, 87 percent of those who reached remission were still in remission at six months. Researchers have also developed a dry-powder nasal spray for intranasal absorption, and an earlier study of psychedelic-naive healthy adults showed that intranasal mebufotenin elicited emotional, bodily, and cognitive effects peaking within 8 to 15 minutes and resolving within 45 to 60 minutes.
Joint first authors David Feifel of the Kadima Neuropsychiatry Institute in La Jolla, California, and Mathieu Seynaeve of King’s College London, along with their colleagues, tested the nasal spray in patients with treatment-resistant depression.
The researchers conducted a Phase 2b, double-blind, randomized clinical trial, a mid-stage study designed to test doses and gauge effectiveness, between September 2023 and April 2025 at 38 sites in Australia, Germany, Poland, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Of 443 adults screened, 193 received treatment. Between 5 and 14 percent of each group did not complete the eight-week core study, with the highest rate in the control group and no withdrawals due to side effects. Participants were aged 18 to 75 (average age 41 years, 59.1 percent female) with moderate to severe major depressive disorder that had not responded to two to five antidepressant trials in their current episode, which had lasted an average of 2.6 years.
To test the spray as a standalone therapy, the two-thirds of participants taking antidepressants at screening tapered off their medications at least two weeks before dosing. Participants were randomly assigned to receive a single spray into one nostril of 8 milligrams of mebufotenin benzoate (46 participants), 12 milligrams (73 participants), or a 0.3-milligram comparator dose low enough that most participants would not feel its effects (74 participants), alongside structured psychological support before, during, and after dosing. Midway through recruitment, the randomization ratio was adjusted from an equal split to prioritize the 12-milligram and 0.3-milligram groups for the primary analysis.
The primary outcome was the change in depression severity from baseline to day 29 between the 12-milligram and 0.3-milligram groups on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale, which scores symptoms from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating worse depression. Independent, blinded raters conducted these interviews by video call at baseline and every two weeks after dosing, including days 2, 8, 29, and 57. Staff assessed discharge readiness every 30 minutes starting 90 minutes after dosing, though participants had to stay at least four hours. Statistical models controlled for baseline depression scores, geographic region, and randomization schedule.
Baseline depression scores averaged about 32 across the three groups. The trial was designed with enough participants to detect a 6-point difference; the primary comparison at day 29 found an adjusted mean difference of 5.3 points (confidence interval 1.8 to 8.9), as scores dropped by 11.1 points in the 12-milligram group versus 5.5 points in the control group. The 8-milligram group improved by 12.5 points, an adjusted difference of 6.2 points (confidence interval 2.1 to 10.2). Whether a participant had tapered off antidepressants before the trial was not associated with the primary outcome.
Improvements appeared by day 2, when both active groups had dropped about 9 points versus 3.8 in the control group, and persisted to day 57, where active-group reductions averaged about 11 points versus 5.2. At day 29, response rates (at least a 50 percent score reduction) were about one-third in both active groups versus 12 percent in the control group; remission rates (a score of 10 or less) were 26 and 18 percent for the 8-milligram and 12-milligram groups versus 8 percent for the control group. Response and remission rates were reported descriptively, without confidence intervals or statistical tests.
Both active doses outperformed the control dose across all time points on clinician-rated illness severity and self-reported quality of life. On a self-reported depression scale, the 12-milligram group improved more than the control group at all visits, while the 8-milligram group improved more at days 2 and 8, though differences at days 29 and 57 were not statistically significant.
On day 1, the 8-milligram and 12-milligram doses produced higher scores on a 0-to-5 questionnaire measuring mystical-type experiences such as a sense of unity, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability (averaging 2.4 and 2.6, versus 0.4 in the control group). Those scores did not correlate with day 29 symptom reductions, a finding that runs against evidence from other psychedelics, which the authors note has suggested that the intensity of the subjective experience predicts therapeutic outcomes.
Most participants in the active groups (85 percent for 8 milligrams and 78 percent for 12 milligrams) met discharge readiness criteria within two hours of dosing, with two-thirds ready at 90 minutes. Those criteria required that the acute psychedelic effects had fully subsided and that vital signs, orientation, and coordination had returned to normal. This rapid turnaround is the feature the researchers argue sets the spray apart from psilocybin and LSD.
Side effects were common in all three groups, reported by roughly 73 to 85 percent of participants, and 99.7 percent of events were mild or moderate. The most frequent were headache, nausea, and pain at the spray site. Headache was about as common in the control group as in the active groups (29.5 percent overall), while nausea was far more common with the active doses (33 and 40 percent) than with the control dose (3 percent). Because the 8-milligram dose had comparable efficacy to the 12-milligram dose with fewer side effects like nausea and anxiety, the researchers selected the 8-milligram dose for Phase 3 trials, which will follow patients for longer to test how long the benefits last.
Most side effects in the active groups appeared on the day of dosing and resolved within 24 hours, though one participant in the 12-milligram group had two severe panic attacks related to the drug. Temporary increases in heart rate and blood pressure resolved within an hour. No suicidal behavior occurred during the trial. Eight drug-related reports of suicidal thoughts without intent were recorded: one in the 8-milligram group, four in the 12-milligram group, and three in the control group, all mild or moderate, and those in the active groups all occurred in participants with a history of such thoughts.
These results align with an uncontrolled, open-label study of 10 women with postpartum depression, which tested an inhaled formulation rather than a nasal spray in a different patient group, and similarly found rapid relief of depressive symptoms. The findings also parallel a 2019 observational study in which 42 people who inhaled vapor from dried toad secretion containing mebufotenin reported reduced depression and anxiety four weeks later, though that study had no control group and relied on self-reported symptoms.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The trial was funded by Beckley Psytech, an AtaiBeckley company that is developing the nasal spray, and several authors are company employees or hold stock or patents related to the compound. Employees of the sponsor were involved in the trial’s design, data analysis, and the decision to publish.
Statistical adjustments for multiple comparisons were applied to the primary outcome and three key secondary outcomes; the remaining comparisons were not adjusted. The smaller size of the 8-milligram group after the randomization change may also have limited statistical power to detect differences on the self-reported depression scale at later visits.
Difficulty maintaining blinding is a recognized problem across psychedelic trials, and the authors cite it as an inherent limitation, noting that most participants and on-site clinicians guessed their treatment assignment. Blinding was better preserved among the centralized remote raters who scored the primary measure; that measure is scored through an interview in which participants describe their own symptoms. Pre-treatment expectations did not correlate with day 29 outcomes, though those expectations were measured before the first preparation visit, prior to dosing and to any knowledge of group assignment; post-dose expectancy was not measured.
In addition, the two-hour discharge figure describes an assessment rather than an actual discharge. No one was discharged at two hours because the protocol required a minimum four-hour stay. Average times to readiness were just under two hours in the active groups, with the longest cases running past four.
In an editorial published alongside the trial in JAMA, Chittaranjan Andrade of the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences in Bangalore, India, called two findings striking: that a single dose given on its own kept depression scores roughly a third lower for eight weeks, and that most patients were ready to leave within two hours rather than the four to twelve hours that psilocybin and LSD require.
At the same time, Andrade noted that the average patient improved only about 30 percent, and that the response and remission rates fall below those typically seen with ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy. In his reading, either the 8- to 12-milligram dose or the single-dose approach is insufficient, and he suggests testing higher or escalating doses, or a course of treatments as is standard with ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy.
Both the study authors and Andrade note that the trial population may underrepresent more severely treatment-resistant patients. Participants had failed a median of two antidepressants, which Andrade describes as not markedly refractory depression. The protocol also excluded people with PTSD, bipolar or psychotic disorders, any personality disorder, a first-degree family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, suicidal ideation with intent in the prior year, or prior nonresponse to ketamine or electroconvulsive therapy. Because active suicidal intent was an exclusion, Andrade notes that the trial could not examine whether the drug reduces suicidal thinking, as ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy have been shown to do.
Other constraints affect how the findings might translate to clinical care. Participants had to discontinue antidepressants so the spray could be tested on its own, which the authors note can cause withdrawal symptoms or a return of depression and may not reflect how the drug would be used in practice. Andrade adds that the trial offers no guidance on when or how patients would transition to a conventional antidepressant afterward. In addition, the study did not evaluate how much the structured psychological support contributed to the improvements, and the trial population lacked racial and ethnic diversity, as nearly 90 percent of participants were white.
Andrade argues that psychedelic research points toward a broader rethinking of how depression is treated, not just treatment-resistant depression. He questions whether it is justifiable to put patients in severe distress through antidepressants that take four to eight weeks to work when faster-acting options exist, and notes that current Canadian guidelines do not list ketamine and esketamine as third-line treatments for depression, naming them only as second-line add-ons for difficult-to-treat depression.
He also raises a point about access: in low- and middle-income countries, where newly approved psychedelics are likely to be unavailable or unaffordable, generic ketamine can be given orally at negligible cost, though he notes the evidence base for that approach needs strengthening. Andrade has published several studies on oral ketamine and cites his own work in making this argument.
He adds that psychedelics have not yet been approved by regulators and will need to be evaluated for long-term safety, including the risk of hallucinogen persisting perception disorder, a condition in which visual disturbances continue after the drug has worn off. He also calls for more detail on what the mebufotenin experience is actually like, including difficult experiences, whether patients found it unpleasant or frightening, and whether they would undergo it again.
The study, “Single Intranasal Administration of the Psychedelic Mebufotenin for Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” was authored by David Feifel, Mathieu Seynaeve, Wiesław Jerzy Cubała, Fiona Dunbar, Gerhard Gründer, Rosa María Dueñas Herrero, Chandni Hindocha, Paul Liknaitzky, Sean M. McGuigan, Sejal Mehta, Mimi Pierce, Dimitris Repantis, Claire Roberts, Frank Wiegand, and Robert Conley.
The accompanying editorial, “Treatment Approach to Major Depressive Disorder: It’s Time for a Paradigm Shift,” was authored by Chittaranjan Andrade.

Gulf states scramble to avert another U.S.-Israeli war on Iran they cannot stop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The first of two elections that many believe are the final bell before all out war is resumed against Iran is now complete. Although it seems likely that the efforts to cobble together a governing coalition in Israel, if that is even possible, will take weeks, the American midterms are expected to be the last milestone before the United States and Israel launch a massive attack on Iran.
There is no doubt that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is almost bursting with anticipation of the bloodshed to come. Donald Trump, as always, seems unsure of how to proceed, but seems very uncomfortable with the situation as it stands, while also being unwilling to make the concessions necessary to end this futile, destructive war he started for no good reason.
Iran can do little to deter an American attack, if that is what Trump decides to do. But it can retaliate with devastating consequences, which will be felt by its Gulf Arab neighbors, Israel, and the global economy.
That is why the countries of the newly created Mecca Pact—Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye—took the dramatic step of meeting Iranian officials in Tehran.
Iran trumpeted the meeting as demonstrating the seriousness with which the Sunni Muslim states take the Islamic Republic, meeting in the Iranian capital rather than in a third country.
Saudi Arabia said the meeting was aimed at mediating between the United States and Iran, but there is no evidence the United States had any part in the planning of this meeting. Indeed, the indications are the opposite; one purpose of the confab was to establish regional dialogue specifically on security matters.
Participants included Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff Field Marshall Asim Munir, Saudi Minister of Defense Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Turkish Director of National Intelligence Ibrahim Kalin. They met with Iran’s Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
The fact that the meeting included leaders of the countries’ respective militaries indicates that the description of the meeting—that it was to deal with regional security—is likely accurate.
And, while little has been made public about the substance of the meeting, it also seems fair to say that there was little progress that could have been made on the major issues—the war with U.S. and the ongoing battles between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Ansar Allah.
Little room for negotiations
Regarding Ansar Allah, Saudi Arabia was feeling Iran out to see if they would intervene with the Yemeni fighters whom the Saudis have been unable to defeat.
But Iran doesn’t have much reason to do so. While they could benefit from pulling the Saudis away from the American war effort, the compromises Tehran would have to make are far too great.
Reports out of Israel state that the Saudis offered Ansar Allah $1 billion for a ceasefire. But the Yemeni group will not budge on its understandable demand that Saudi Arabia drop its air blockade of Yemen.
This is not an issue Iran can try to mediate. If they try to get Ansar Allah to compromise on the air blockade, it undermines their argument that the United States must end its sea blockade of Iran.
Iran supports Ansar Allah’s cause, but if they thought they could get concessions from the Saudis on the kingdom’s support for American military efforts, Ansar Allah might find it reasonable to agree to a temporary ceasefire to help their ally.
But they cannot compromise on the air blockade, nor would Iran want them to. As long as Saudi Arabia maintains its efforts to block air traffic in Yemen, they can’t buy their way out of Ansar Allah attacks.
On the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the Saudis are very worried, as are all the countries of the Gulf and their neighbors. They should be, given that Trump has warned the Gulf states to get ready for a “short, intense military campaign.” Considering that the war started on February 27 was supposed to end in just a few days, or weeks at most, no one is counting on the “short” part. But it is likely to be intense, and that intensity will be felt in Iran and the Gulf Arab states.
The problem for Iran is that its interlocutors can do little to turn Trump’s mind. Even Saudi Arabia, which is in a terrible position right now if the war restarts, has few options outside of registering its reservations with Trump, which it surely has already done.
Türkiye and Pakistan have even less leverage over Trump’s decisions. If he is reckless enough to risk the consequences of restarting the war with Iran, what can they do to stop him?
And those consequences are potentially very dire.
The costs of war
Iran has made it clear that it intends to target data centers, AI hubs, and underwater fiber networks that are the backbone of the internet in addition to oil infrastructure. No one doubts they have the capability of doing so.
The amount of damage that can be inflicted on the world dwarfs anything we’ve seen until now.
That has produced fear among the Gulf states, but it has also produced tension between them and Iran. Gulf states are angry at Iran for targeting them in response to American attacks, but Iran is aggravated because the Gulf states have cooperated with Washington.
This double-edged sword was visible this week when Qatar submitted a proposal for a ceasefire and a path back to negotiations, including reciprocal but revocable steps each side could take, presumably offering each side the assurances they needed to proceed.
But at the same time, Qatar publicly supported the call for Iran to allow international traffic through the Strait of Hormuz unconditionally. That did nothing to help the case for Qatar’s proposal, which Iran eventually dismissed as a collection of random ideas rather than a serious proposal and which Trump ignored.
Vice President JD Vance, who has quietly been opposing the resumption of large-scale fighting, tried reaching out via a letter to Rezaei, but the letter reportedly offered no immediate relief from any of the pressures the U.S. is putting on Iran while demanding that any talks include the nuclear issue, which Iran insists be left to be discussed after its minimal terms are met. In other words, it was just Vance delivering Trump’s unacceptable terms in nicer language.
If that wasn’t enough to make the Vance letter a non-starter, the fact that Vance’s earlier efforts were routinely contradicted by Trump soon after empties the vice president of any credibility, even if Tehran believes he is personally sincere in his desire to avoid another round of full-scale fighting.
This leaves only one hope: that Trump, in his eternally mercurial and indecisive way, will back away from what will be a devastating conflict.
One unknown is how much Trump understands about the danger that an Iranian response presents and how certain it is that a devastating response will be coming.
Trump’s threat of a “short intense” attack would seem to imply that he is being led to believe that the United States can overwhelm Iran with devastating force. Of course, that is exactly what he tried in February, and it failed dismally. Outside of insanity, does he have any reason to think that the same action would produce a different result this time?
It could be that what the U.S. and Israel are planning is a multi-phase attack.
American planners may think the weakness of their initial strike was that they targeted Iranian leadership while devastating large areas of civilian and military infrastructure, believing that this would lead to the collapse of the Iranian government. When that failed, there was no plan B.
It may be that the idea this time is to simply start with doing as much damage to Iranian infrastructure as they can, then pinpoint where the response is coming from and take out those missile and drone launchers.
That is consistent with what Senator Chris Murphy is warning about when he says that what the Trump administration is planning is “insane.”
“It will lead to devastating escalation, and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law. There’s been open reporting as to what we may be planning and the civilian infrastructure that we may be targeting,” Murphy said. “They’ve been asked by the president to develop a plan. Whether they believe it will work or not, I do not know. But the plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests.”
The result, then, would be one of two things. If the U.S.-Israeli attack is successful, the Gulf states will suffer significant damage, but they can recover and, theoretically, come out with a weakened Iran. But that would mean that what failed in February magically works in November, and there is no evidence to support that expectation.
The other, far more likely scenario is that Iran continues to weather American and Israeli attacks and responds by devastating the Gulf states, further demolishing American positions, and inflicting a far greater degree of damage on Israel than they have in the past.
In that scenario, Gulf oil and civilian infrastructure could be damaged beyond repair. Moreover, given the region’s inherent instability—governed as it is mostly by iron-fisted dictators ruling over states of mixed and often clashing ethnicities drawn up by colonial map-makers—such a scenario could well mean the end of one or more of the Gulf states.
It is that scenario that the Mecca Pact countries are trying to avert.
They are not fools; they knew there was little that Iran could do to change the strategic playing field. Instead, they hoped that sending their top security leaders to Tehran would signal to Washington how concerned they were. They understood that the meeting, by its very existence, would give Iran a diplomatic win and, more importantly, would show that the Mecca Pact is intended to forge a new regional security system that will want to work with Iran, potentially even including it in the group someday.
The Mecca Pact countries, as well as Iran, hope that this message of the region’s strong desire to avert the oncoming catastrophe will convince Trump to back off.
Meanwhile, in Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu is even more incentivized to see the war roar back to life. With the election process in deadlock, he needs to move swiftly, before the opposition can make the case to the public that they are better suited to defeat Iran than Netanyahu.
He needs the war to make it more difficult to replace him, and he will push hard for it. He has already tried to provoke Iran into an act that would have restarted the major fighting before Trump was ready. He will surely try again before too long.

On the Norway-Russia border, the Sámi people face a growing divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:58:28 UTC
21:58:28 KST

Along the shores of the Neiden Fjord, in Norway’s northernmost county Finnmark, Nils Boine* gazes out across the water. On the horizon, the Neiden River splits around the craggy island of Skogerøya, but lurking beneath its surface is a fisherman’s bounty: hundreds of king crabs.
His grandmother was Sea Sámi, from an Indigenous coastal people whose homeland, Sápmi, stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s heavily militarised Kola Peninsula. In Finnmark’s fjords, Sea Sámi families have fished for generations. But these waters are dissected by more than currents and shoals. Since Norway and Russia fixed their border in 1826, Sámi communities in the region have been divided by a national boundary.
Two hundred years later, this Arctic community is a combination of Sámi, Norwegians, Finns, Ukrainians, Russians, and international seasonal workers. Most of the Sámi population lives in Norway, with roughly 2 percent residing in Russia.
The Sámi have established a cross-border lifestyle, supported by flexible policies, including a Norwegian-Russian agreement allowing visa-free travel for those living within 30km (18.5 miles) of the border.
Security, however, has begun to tighten since the onset of Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine. The West sees Finnmark as part of NATO’s exposed northern flank, as it is directly opposite Russia’s heavily armed Kola Peninsula. The Norwegian border town of Kirkenes has been caught in a spy war with Russia, with multiple Russian operatives having been caught posing as tourists and fishermen while trying to engage in espionage.
Now, border bureaucracy is a daily reality, and reindeer herding, language revitalisation and hunting traditions are increasingly being navigated through permits and regulations, making the wider Arctic infrastructure feel fractured.
“I have friends in Russia,” Boine says. “We used to go shopping in Russia, and go there for weekends.”
Since Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, those crossings have stopped — partly as a display of solidarity with Ukraine, and partly due to safety concerns.
“A local person was just arrested in Russia, so people are afraid to cross the border,” Boine explains. “The rumours say that he had some illegal things in his car, but he was arrested, and the [Ministry of] Foreign Affairs in Norway tried to do something, but it’s very difficult, of course, because we don’t have any diplomats in Russia.”
He is referring to the reported June arrest of a Kirkenes businessman. Lawyer John Christian Elden told the daily newspaper Verdens Gang (VG) that the man was in custody for two months under alleged “possession of weapons or ammunition". Some Kirkenes residents were left shaken by the news, as recreational hunting is common in the region. They fear accidentally crossing the Russian border with forgotten hunting ammunition that might be left in their cars.
The number of Russian tourists visiting Norway has also declined, from 250,000 in 2019 to 52,000 last year.
“Before, we had Russian guests, but not now,” Boine says. Fortunately for his family, who run a tourism company, 80 percent of customers come from Asia or Finland. Their business has emerged relatively unscathed, but other companies have not been as lucky.
“Shops in the area have lost a lot of income without Russian [tourists],” says Boine. “Several shops have had to close.”
In a landscape traditionally connected for centuries, the fragmentation of communities is deeply concerning for both the regional economy and Sámi culture. Cross-border connections are deeply rooted in the regional psyche.
For Boine, the war in Ukraine has put his friendships with people in Russia on hold.
“They are afraid to do something wrong or write something wrong,” he says quietly. “You never know what might happen if they have too close contact,” he says.
“I want to be careful.”
New technological barriers
German Henrik Hoffmann visited Kirkenes in 2021 and fell in love with its landscape and tight-knit community. Deciding to relocate permanently, the expat co-founded a tourism company, Kirkenes Tours, and began working with Sámi herders and on hiking trails along the Norwegian-Russian border.
“I was nervous the first time,” Hoffmann admits. “I kept checking my maps to make sure I hadn’t accidentally crossed [the border].”
Distracted hikers can easily step over the border by mistake, as the frontier is only marked by posts and forest clearings.
Hoffmann takes tourists along these trails, teaching them about the border’s history and its strict rules, including heavy fines for touching a Russian marker. In June 2026, three Swedish tourists were reportedly each fined 8,000 Norwegian kroner ($830) for throwing stones across the border.
The terrain looks desolate, peppered with granite rocks and scattered birch trees, but it is well-surveilled. Watchtowers dot the horizon, and security cameras are tucked among branches overhead.
Hoffmann rarely sees other civilians on this route, but he has seen increasing numbers of Norwegian military patrols. When his walks are interrupted, it is mostly by Sámi-owned reindeer.
He points towards a small herd grazing in a sheltered valley beneath a rocky crag. The reindeer – which are marked with traditional branding and earmarks – are at least a kilometre (0.6 miles) away.
Sámi families use distinctive marks, including pre-approved patterns cut into reindeer ears, to instantly identify which animal belongs to which herder. In May and June, there is a calf marking round-up, where the local siida – an organisation of Sámi herders who manage reindeer – use huskies, snowmobiles and drones to track and herd reindeer into pens. This process ensures that every calf is correctly identified. The jagged earmarking is an ancient Indigenous practice.
Alongside traditional earmarking, Sámi herders have simplified these roundups with 21st-century technology. For years, they have attached GPS tracking devices to reindeer, enabling herders to locate livestock with ease. But this is no longer a reliable method, because the area along the Russian-Norwegian border is often affected by GPS jamming and spoofing.
Aeroplanes landing in Kirkenes have even been affected by the interference, with navigation symbols blocked or replaced with false location data. The same disruption can render reindeer trackers inaccurate and useless.
Recently, Russian interference has reportedly been targeting lower elevations, too, leaving those in the hills surrounding Kirkenes – typically hikers and reindeer herders – at higher risk of having a GPS device jammed or spoofed.
“I have experienced it saying I am in Tromsø,” says Hoffmann, referring to the northern Norwegian city, about an 800km (500 miles) drive from Kirkenes.
To avoid mishaps, he always hikes with a satellite phone, and many local reindeer herders now avoid using GPS trackers because they have become unreliable.
“Now, they’re mostly using GSM trackers, which rely on the phone network,” Hoffmann explains.
Animals don’t understand borders
Walking through Finnmark's exposed borderlands means crossing paths with many types of wildlife, including the Arctic grouse, a bright-white bird that buries itself in the snow. But not all animal encounters are pleasant.
For Sámi herders, predators are an increasing concern. Finnmark’s brown bear population is steadily increasing, with bears freely crossing between Russian and Norwegian territory. Some residents believe the rise could be connected to a decline in Russian hunting activity, but since cross-border conservation has declined, it is difficult to say.
“Last year, a man was bitten,” says Hoffmann. He also reveals that at a local stable where his girlfriend goes horseback riding, a bear attacked a horse in its paddock.
Bear and wolf attacks are dangerous for reindeer, who spend much of the year wandering unattended in the remote Arctic terrain. Large animals, like bears, are also notorious for damaging reindeer fences, barriers key to preventing livestock from wandering into Russia.
For herders, these potential animal breaches illustrate how difficult it can be to control a border shaped as much by wilderness and animal wandering as by geopolitics. Norwegian authorities are now investing heavily in doing just that.
Following a report by the Norwegian National Police Directorate in 2024, the European Union awarded Norway 16.4 million euros ($18.5m) to strengthen its border surveillance. By 2033, Norway will have a fully operational Finnmark Brigade, forming a defensive presence throughout its Arctic region.
Roaming wildlife is not following the same script. Along the Pasvik River, the boundary is visible, but it rarely feels fixed.
From the birch-covered slopes of the Norwegian side, the river forms a natural border, and coloured markers are dotted evenly along the water to help boaters navigate safely.
But by early November, the river is frozen, forming an icy bridge for the wandering wildlife – and a seasonal concern for Sámi herders who fear their reindeer will run off into Russia.
Across Sápmi, the terrain is already intersected by sections of reindeer fencing. Traditionally crafted from wood, these barricades discourage livestock from venturing into forbidden grazing lands, but these man-made structures have one weakness: On snowy winter days, large snowdrifts are enough to allow opportunistic reindeer to scramble across.
Along the border, efforts have intensified to try to prevent livestock from wandering into Russia, with increased patrols and repairs by herders.
In 2023, after 42 reindeer crossed into Russia in eight months, Norway moved to replace a dilapidated 7km (4.3-miles) of the 150km (93-mile) reindeer fence along the border. Still, some Sámi herders remain sceptical.
Egil Kalliainen, a local herder, told The Barents Observer that “reindeer will keep crossing the border with or without any war".
The trouble, many say, is that cross-border cooperation is needed. “Reindeer don’t understand borders,” Hoffmann says with a wry smile.
The power of craft
On the shelves of the Ä´vv Skolt Sámi Museum sit reindeer antlers that have been polished into pocketknife handles. Nearby, there are kuska cups carved from birch burl. These are examples of duodji, traditional Sámi handicraft created through techniques with cultural meanings that have been handed down for generations.
But duodji is more than an exhibit or souvenir; it is part of a broader economy rooted in reindeer herding, local materials and border exchange. Before the geopolitical tensions of recent years, Sámi artisans and institutions could easily move goods and sell jewellery made in Russia while maintaining connections across the region.
Barriers that hinder cultural exchange and trade directly impact the material foundation of Sámi culture.
“Historically, national borders have divided Sámi and settlement areas,” said Håkon Mudenia, political adviser to the Sámi Parliamentary Council.
But now, border restrictions have made those exchanges more difficult, affecting the movement, sale and display of Sámi-made goods and limiting broader cultural cooperation. Mudenia says the council is calling for simplified customs and VAT rules for traditional Sámi handicrafts. “Barriers that hinder cultural exchange and trade directly impact the material foundation of Sámi culture,” he says.
Norwegian officials acknowledge the wider constraint. As a generational use of natural resources, duodji relies on raw materials, such as reindeer antlers or birch trees. These crafts play an important role in Sámi heritage preservation.
“Sanctions imposed on Russia have created constraints that affect the ability of Indigenous peoples to sustain cross‑border cooperation,” Marius Meisfjord Jøsevold, Norway’s state secretary at the Ministry of Local Government and Regional Development, tells Al Jazeera.
Duodji objects make Sámi culture visible, whether it is antler handles or leader pouches marked with a herder’s reindeer sign. But one part of the culture most threatened by a divided Sápmi boundary cannot be displayed on a museum shelf. It is spoken.
Language across borders
Centuries of colonisation have affected Indigenous languages in the region. Sápmi encompasses numerous Sámi communities and linguistic traditions, including Inari, Skolt and Sea Sámi communities. Each has distinct cultural differences, and there are nine surviving languages in total. Originally, the number was higher, but a handful of languages, including Akkala Sámi, are already extinct.
The 1826 delimitation of the Norwegian-Russian border was particularly damaging for Skolt Sámi lands. Separated across countries, the Skolt community faced an abrupt split.
From 1850 to 1959, the situation worsened, with Norwegianisation policies forcing Sámi children to be taught in Norwegian at state schools. As of 2026, local reports suggest there are fewer than 1,000 Skolt Sámi speakers across Norway, Finland and Russia.
With numbers so low, every speaker counts.
“Border closures and restrictions render cross-border, all-Sámi cooperation more vulnerable,” explains Mudenia, noting that opportunities for speakers to gather are of utmost importance.
In 2026, the Sámi Parliament Council supported a Skolt Sámi Year of Culture, celebrating its distinct culture within the wider Indigenous community. But Mudenia says more must be done to protect and revitalise the community.
“The Sámi Parliament has already recognised Skolt Sámi as an official language in Norway and demands that the Norwegian Parliament do the same,” he says.
For the people living along this frontier, survival has long depended on forms of mutual care ...
The battle to protect the language is part of the ongoing demand for change. The Sámi Parliament Council wants a situation where Sámi economic, social and cultural conditions are safeguarded within national contingency plans, Mudenia explains.
“The overarching goal of the Sámi Parliament Council is to continuously dismantle border obstacles across Sápmi,” he says. “State security measures and geopolitical barriers must not be designed or implemented in a way that violates Indigenous rights, international law, or the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP).”
The council, he says, “thinks that Sámi communities should be included as an integral part of the total defence framework”, while Sámi expertise and representation should be “secured in national security and emergency preparedness forums to address such hybrid threats".
Jøsevold, from the Ministry of Local Government and Regional Development, says the Sámi Parliament is an important dialogue partner for the central government.
Asked about the council’s concerns, Jøsevold emphasised the government’s commitment to consultation as defence activity expands in the North. But he did not address Mudenia’s call for national recognition of the Skolt Sámi, or for Sámi representation in national-security forums.
“In Northern Norway, increased defence activity as a result of increased tensions caused by Russia’s illegal war against Ukraine will be coordinated with Sámi representatives to ensure due consideration to Sámi culture and traditional Sámi industries,” he says.
But for the people living along this frontier, survival has long depended on forms of mutual care that are not included in defence planning or government consultations.
Community against the odds
“People think there is nothing here,” Hoffmann laughs as he scrambles up a steep embankment. The Pasvik River disappears behind the tree line, and an undulating expanse of smooth rock unfolds. A dark wooden cube appears on the horizon.
Set against a backdrop of the granite-speckled hillside, this building is a recreational shelter, one of the small public spaces designed to make the remote border landscape accessible year-round. It offers walkers, hikers, families, and herders alike a place to warm up and take shelter from the weather.
Inside, a fire sits ready to be lit; in winter, locals add an extra log before leaving, preheating the shelter for the next visitor. In another corner, a stack of children’s books forms the start of a community library.
Within these walls, it is easy to forget that NATO’s northernmost land border is a short walk away. One side of the shelter is a floor-to-ceiling window. The views are beautiful: rock-peppered hills and crevices, dipping and diving towards a hazy horizon. From this warm bench, nature is the star attraction, and the painted border markers stand forgotten.
Throughout the Varanger Peninsula, there is a determination to preserve everyday life. With the border just a few kilometres away, its largest city, Kirkenes, has become a multicultural Arctic outpost.
Along the harbour, tourists continue to disembark from Hurtigruten cruises, promising local business with their clockwork itineraries of border hikes and boat tours.
Reindeer roundups follow a seasonal calendar, not political agendas. Ocean vessels continue to collect nets of Arctic cod and baskets of king crabs, while along the Neiden River, Sámi fishermen return for the salmon season. In Kirkenes, a simple walk to the Joker supermarket could be interrupted by drifting conversations in Sámi, Norwegian, Finnish, Swedish, German, English or Russian.
“We were very surprised that we have people from Ukraine living in Kirkenes alongside Russian people in Kirkenes,” Boine admits. “I thought maybe there would be more conflict between these people, but not here.”
While many residents might have been surprised by Ukrainian refugees deciding to settle so close to the Russian border, Boine says it makes sense. “Because they speak Russian, it is easier for them to find work here,” he adds.
In February 2026, Barents Spektakel, an annual arts festival, marked the 200th anniversary of the Russian-Norwegian border. Kirkenes erupted in creative artwork and cultural displays, but the theme, “The border crossed us”, spoke volumes.
For Sámi communities, connection to these landscapes predates both the ongoing war and the 200-year-old border. There was an Arctic community before both, and across Sápmi, there is a growing determination that tightening borders will not erase it.
*Nils Boine is a pseudonym to protect the identity of a man with Sea Sámi heritage who lives near Neiden and crosses the border regularly.

He noted that nearly 80% of court cases involved ordinary people, whose stories were often hidden behind the “antiseptic language” of case files.
“Every single day we read real stories,” he said, highlighting the emotional toll of handling criminal cases and reading accounts of victims' experiences.Justice Dayal described a judge's role as applying “cold, objective reasoning and fairness” while navigating allegations, facts and the law.He also shared amusing examples of mistranslations in court documents. Poland’s president accuses Tusk of forced takeover of country’s top court
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:56:49 CET
21:56:49 KST

WARSAW, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Polish President Karol Nawrocki on Saturday accused Prime Minister Donald Tusk of staging a forced takeover of the country’s top court after the head of the court, an ally of the previous far right government, was suspended.
Late on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal’s president and an appointee of Tusk’s hard-right predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.
The move escalated a battle between Nawrocki, an ally of the previous nationalist government, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s pro-European government over control of the judiciary.
“Tonight, there was a breach of public order in the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional body,” Nawrocki said in a statement read by an aide outside the court early on Saturday, after the president had turned back mid-flight from a trip to Africa to address the situation.
He headed straight to the court where riot police were out in force as several hundred protesters demanded Swieczkowski’s reinstatement.
Nawrocki called for urgent political consultations.
Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors — the Law and Justice Party — of subverting.
“This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he said.
LONG-RUNNING POLITICAL DISPUTE
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognise appointees put forward by the other side.
The dispute dates back to 2015, when the Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.
Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.
After Tusk’s coalition took office in 2023 it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
Last month, parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government’s stated goal of restoring checks and balances.
(Reporting by Justyna Pawlak; Editing by Susan Fenton)

Feature: From hardship to mentorship, Kenya rugby veteran inspires next generation at Dakar 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:56:24 CST
21:56:24 KST

by sportswriters Wang Qi and You Huiyuan
DAKAR, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- As a teenager, Sheila Chajira could hardly have imagined that a small break in her routine would set her on a new path.
Now a two-time Olympian and veteran of Kenya's women's rugby team, Chajira remains committed to sport's transformative power, embracing a new mission at Africa's first-ever Olympic event.
"I am not just the Sheila that I know: I am a better Sheila," she said of being named an Athlete Role Model for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games (YOG).
"It's a path of helping athletes stay on the right path and attain their goals through your example and mentorship."
Orphaned at the age of nine, Chajira and her sisters moved between makeshift homes, often finding themselves back in the slums. Through it all, sport provided an anchor.
"I played football. I ran. Sports kept me going," she said. "It was just uphill. But sports took over."
In high school, Chajira never skipped her mandatory morning run before evening football training. "A friend used to tell me, 'You have a body that can play rugby. You can see what happens.' I was hesitant at first," she said.
One morning, however, she was running late. "That day I was free, I decided to go and see what rugby was all about. Since then, I never went back to football."
Rugby offered a culture that "streamlined" her life. "Coming from the slums in Kenya, you see people get married early, get pregnant, or do drugs," Chajira said. "The moment I joined rugby, I wasn't able to focus on those things. I looked forward to getting out of this place for training."
The sport taught her respect, teamwork and self-reliance while opening doors to new opportunities and connections.
Turning professional after high school seemed a natural next step, even as rugby was still in its infancy locally and making a full-time living from it remained, as Chajira put it, "a maybe thing" for women.
"We used to have two or three tournaments a year," Chajira recalled. At times, the team could not afford to travel, and matches were missed.
Her turning point came at the 2016 Rio Olympics, where rugby sevens made its Games debut and Kenya became the first African women's side to compete. "I had no idea what to expect," Chajira said, recalling a mix of excitement and uncertainty.
Drawn into a tough Pool B, the Kenyans battled through the group stage but scored just 17 points, while a dominant New Zealand topped the group with 109. Even after a 24-0 defeat to Japan, Kenya refused to fold, closing its campaign with a landmark 22-10 win over Colombia.
Although an 11th-place finish was modest on paper, the experience of "playing against the world's best of the best" filled Chajira with immense pride and showed how far the team had come.
During the group stage, Chajira found herself on the same pitch as New Zealand star Portia Woodman, an idol she had long admired.
"She gave us some advice and told us that even they didn't start up there. It was slow for them. Because they trained consistently, they were able to perform the way they did," she said.
The Rio Olympics fueled her confidence in what the Kenyan team could achieve. "If we get more support or better facilities, we can be at the top of the world," she believed.
"We knew the intensity, the consistency, and what we needed to compete at a higher level. To the younger girls, we were able to tell them how incredible it is to play in the Olympics."
Driven by greater ambition, a clearer vision and a transformed mindset, the Kenya Lionesses stepped onto the Tokyo stage, with Chajira wearing the captain's armband. Pandemic disruptions fractured their training schedule, but they climbed one place to a historic 10th-place finish.
For Chajira, being an Olympian is every athlete's dream, regardless of age. "I'm able to get opportunities that I've never expected, to get the drive of being that athlete who's able to train and play among the world's best."
Maintaining peak physical condition in a demanding, high-impact sport has been a relentless challenge.
"When you get injured and get out of this rugby space, it's always hard," she admitted. "I always tell myself: 'It is not going to happen forever; It is a phase.' Hold on to it, learn from the experience, and definitely it will end. Here I am."
Since Tokyo, the road has been marked by near-misses. A 24-7 loss to China in the Paris 2024 Olympic repechage final dashed Kenya's hopes of making a third consecutive Olympic appearance, while a 22-0 defeat to South Africa at the 2025 Africa Women's Sevens in Nairobi marked the team's fourth runner-up finish since winning the title in 2018.
Nevertheless, rugby continues to expand its footprint in Kenya. The national team secured a place on the new HSBC SVNS 2 circuit in February, with Nairobi hosting the inaugural leg. At club level, Mwamba RFC Women claimed a historic fifth consecutive Kenya Cup title in May, beating Kenya Harlequin 30-20.
"We're able to play friendlies, compete in more tournaments, and play a home game, like the HSBC SVNS 2," she noted. "We couldn't have said that rugby was a career; then we were just doing it for fun or just getting out of a dark space. But right now, it's something I'm happy to say that rugby pays."
As the game expanded, so did Chajira's influence.
Off the field, she embraced motherhood, earned her World Rugby strength and conditioning credential, mentored young talent in slum academies and took charge as head coach of the Kenya Harlequin women's side.
"There are some girls from Kibera who I coached nine years ago. They play for the senior teams right now in Harlequins, and also some of them have been called up for the training school of the national team," she said. "Seeing such things happen, I'm so proud of the journey. I'll try my best to keep on doing it."
In April, the 32-year-old veteran was selected as an Athlete Role Model for Dakar 2026. Continuing a tradition established at the inaugural YOG in Singapore in 2010, she will help guide the next generation of athletes as they emerge onto the world stage.
"Most Olympics were held outside Africa. It was a dream far away. But right now, being brought here in Africa, it's reachable," she said. "For the girls and boys who are playing local tournaments, they have something to look forward to."
Following Saturday's opening ceremony, the rugby tournament begins the next day at Complexe Iba Mar Diop. Kenya's women's squad joins Pool A alongside Australia, China, Tunisia and host Senegal.
As the only African rugby personality among the Athlete Role Models for Dakar 2026, Chajira was thrilled by the prospect of welcoming the world's finest young talents to her home continent.
"Put yourself out there. Every opportunity you get, just go with it. Just work hard, focus on what you want and you will achieve," she added. ■

Iran's supreme leader orders "immediate, effective" response to any "enemy" threat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:55:56 CST
21:55:56 KST

TEHRAN, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has ordered that any level and kind of threat from the "enemies" must be met with an "immediate and effective" response without geographical limitations, according to a statement published on the leader's website on Saturday.
He made the remarks at a meeting with the Iranian armed forces' senior commanders, including Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces Ali Abdollahi, Army's Chief Commander Amir Hatami, Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Ahmad Vahidi, the statement said.
He stressed that if the "enemies" resume military or terrorist attacks against Iran, the Iranian armed forces and people will determine the time and conditions for the war's end.
Khamenei also highlighted the necessity to "strengthen the country's military intelligence architecture, deepen home-grown defense in terms of doctrine and tactics, and advance modern defense and security capabilities using cutting-edge technologies."
The supreme leader emphasized that the country's bank of targets must be updated in such a way that "various tangible and intangible assets of the U.S.-Israeli enemy are brought within the Iranian armed forces' reach."
At the meeting, the senior military commanders presented reports on the armed forces' state of readiness, and briefed the supreme leader on the manifold rise in the country's production of various types of ammunition, as well as reconnaissance, support and combat weaponry.
The Iranian supreme leader's remarks came amid heightened U.S. threats of military action against Iran.
The United States has told several Gulf countries to prepare for a brief but intense military campaign against Iran after the U.S. midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people briefed on the conversations.
According to the report, the United States and Israel are preparing for another round of intense military operations against Iran.

Pope meets Villanova and Notre Dame basketball teams at the Vatican

Pope Leo meets with Villanova and Notre Dame basketball teams at the Vatican
Pope Leo XIV met on Saturday with the basketball teams from Villanova and Notre Dame, along with thousands of U.S. fans in Italy, ahead of the two Catholic universities' season opener later this weekend.
About 7,000 people entered the Paul VI audience hall inside the Vatican on Saturday after a special private Mass in St. Peter's Basilica.
Leo, who is an avid tennis player and sports fan, said sports bring people together and can promote values such as fraternity, solidarity and peace.
"By acting as a concrete means of bringing people together, athletics can teach the values of cooperation and mutual sharing. This is increasingly necessary in an age marked by the distance that can be created by technology," he said, according to Vatican News.
The teams are in Rome for the U.S. college basketball season opener on Sunday — an event dubbed the Eternal City Tip-Off and created to honor the U.S.-born pope. The universities' men's and women's teams will play a doubleheader at the Palazzo Dello Sport, an 11,000-seat arena about a half-hour drive from the Vatican.
Leo, who is currently recovering from lung cancer surgery, graduated from Villanova in 1977 with a Bachelor of Science in mathematics.
"Growing up on the south side of Chicago, we oftentimes heard, 'Go Irish.' But as you all know, Prevost graduated from Villanova! So, the Pope doesn't take sides. Prevost has another opinion, but we won't do that now," Leo joked during the audience, according to Vatican News.
Leo urged the teams and their families to embrace sports as a way to grow in saintliness.
"No one is born a champion, just as no one is born a saint," he said.
He warned against letting sporting rivalries get out of hand and he said he hoped the fans in Rome this weekend would actually get to know one another as they cheer, "even passionately."
"In any competition, the members of two teams, even when they have a competitive rivalry, are certainly not enemies," he said. "I hope, therefore, that despite the competitive nature of college basketball, there will be opportunities for the players and the fans of both teams to get to know each other in your days here in Rome."
Before the audience, the Rev. Robert Dowd, president of Notre Dame, acknowledged Villanova had something of an edge considering it counts the pope as an alumnus. But in an interview Saturday, he said the occasion to bring both teams together with all their fans in Rome for a papal audience and season opener was "amazing."
"That could be a little challenging, but I know that the pope is a pope for all of us, and so I'm grateful," he said. "I know in a particular way the pope talks about the importance of bridge building, and I'm sure he'll be a bridge builder when we play each other."
Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson Perez celebrated a private Mass for traveling fans in St. Peter's Basilica on Saturday morning, and asked the thousands of people in the pews to give a round of applause to the players. The English-language liturgy was unusual in that it had all the trappings of a papal Mass celebrated at the main altar and televised live by Vatican Media.
Asked about the upcoming games on the papal plane during a recent trip to France, Leo said, "They tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side."
Leo is an avid Chicago White Sox fan and has been known to follow basketball, too.
"He will know who they (the players) are. He's a true, blue Villanovan," said the Rev. Rob Hagan, Villanova's longtime team chaplain. He said Leo used to attend Villanova games at the Palestra, the Philadelphia arena known as "The Cathedral of College Basketball."
Sunday's games coincide with All Saints' Day, a major Catholic holiday.
"Our true goal, beyond emerging victorious in any one event, is to win the prize of everlasting life," Leo said.

Studios destroyed, traditions saved: Artists fight to save Sudan’s culture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:49:04 UTC
21:49:04 KST

Studios destroyed, traditions saved: Artists fight to save Sudan’s culture
Artists in Sudan are working to save culture and traditions amid the country’s war.
Port Sudan, Sudan – Awad Haroun, 45, a visual artist and theatre director, fled his home in Al-Halfaya, Khartoum North, after war destroyed a life he had worked hard to build in the capital.
He moved to Port Sudan with his wife and son, leaving behind his home, artistic workspace and the tools he needed to work, shortly after fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in April 2023.
When he fled, he carried little: Two shirts, two pairs of trousers, two books and a few torn drawing papers, expecting to return soon. Instead, he has been forced to rebuild his life far from home.
He lost not only his home but also the tools and materials he relied on to work and make a living.
In Port Sudan, he looked to use his skills in sculpture, design and decoration for some money. He has since participated in theatrical performances at Wasel Festival, organised by Ahalina Cultural Group in partnership with UNESCO, and led traditional arts workshops with cultural groups.
Awad founded Ahalina cultural group in 2013 with a group of young people, using theatre, visual arts, music and puppetry to engage with young people and promote peace and social cohesion.
Drawing, storytelling, music and play have also given children opportunities to express themselves and connect with others.
“Losing my tools does not mean I have lost my skills, and losing my workspace does not mean I have lost my ability to create,” Awad told Al Jazeera.
Awad and other displaced artists found shelter at an old school in Port Sudan, where they helped clean and prepare the building for families forced from their homes.
“Now, concerns about the possibility of eviction have left us uncertain about where we will go next,” he said.
While art cannot replace a lost home or end the war, Awad believes it can preserve memories, bring communities together and offer children space to play and express themselves.
“From the ashes, we will rise” is the motto of Ahalina cultural group. This is more than a slogan for Awad; it is a reminder to keep creating, despite everything the war has taken from him.
The war has taken a heavy toll on Sudan’s cultural life, damaging heritage sites and disrupting the livelihoods of artists across the country.
In June 2026, UNESCO estimated that Sudan’s cultural sector faced a $30m funding gap. But behind this figure are deeply personal losses: Artists killed by the war or forced to leave behind studios, galleries, artworks and the tools they need to create.
In April 2024, UNESCO reported that the Artists and Writers Union in Port Sudan had provided shelter to more than 112 displaced artists and other cultural professionals.
The challenges remain significant, but cultural initiatives have continued. In April 2026, UNESCO said its initiatives in Port Sudan had benefitted more than 350 artists, women, girls and internally displaced cultural professionals, supporting efforts to sustain Sudan’s cultural life amid the conflict.
Asim Abdelaziz, 31, a musician and filmmaker, left El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, amid escalating fighting and repeated drone attacks. He arrived in Port Sudan in November 2023, hoping to find safety and work.
Separated from his family, who are scattered between Omdurman and El Obeid, Asim lives alone in a shelter for displaced artists. The war has uprooted his life and disrupted his career, but he continues to use music to preserve Sudan’s cultural heritage and bring communities together.
In Port Sudan, he has worked with the local Artists and Writers Union, UNESCO and community organisations. He has also collaborated with the Ministry of Culture and Information and other artists on music programmes to address social issues, including hate speech and racism.
Asim said the war has spurred hate speech and deepened divisions between Sudan’s different communities. He believes art can counter these differences by promoting diversity, mutual acceptance and peaceful coexistence.
“I have seen firsthand how hate speech affects people’s lives,” Asim told Al Jazeera. “Through music, I try to remind Sudanese people that we are all brothers and sisters, and that war does not represent who we are.”
Mokhalaya, a project he founded to document and archive traditional music and rhythms from across the country a year ago, is one avenue for this.
“I hope to take the project to international festivals, introducing audiences abroad to [showcase] Sudan’s rich musical traditions and cultural diversity,” he said.
Preserving heritage is not just about safeguarding the past, but also about keeping Sudan’s cultural identity alive during a war that has displaced communities and disrupted lives, he said.
Abdelqader Hashem, secretary of the Red Sea State Writers and Artists Union, told Al Jazeera the union has supported artists and their families who fled fighting in other parts of Sudan since the war began on April 15, 2023.
“We worked to establish a shelter for displaced artists in a school in Port Sudan and sought support from local and international organisations to provide for their basic needs,” he said.
Beyond providing shelter, the union has helped displaced artists take part in the city’s cultural activities, contributing to community awareness programmes that address important societal issues such as the dangers of drug use, a growing concern in Sudan.
“We have also implemented projects in partnership with UNESCO to train children in displacement camps in handicrafts, including concrete crafts,” Hashem said.
“Most of the displaced artists have since returned to their homes in Khartoum following the Sudanese army’s recapture of the capital.”
