====================================================================================================

‘This is a robust recipe’: the experimental farm bucking the decline in UK birds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:43 UTC
21:00:43 KST

Farmer Alastair Leake is standing in a field of sprouting winter wheat, pointing at his experiment. One side was ploughed before planting, with green shoots breaking through neat rows of upturned soil. On the other, the crop was drilled directly into the earth, emerging through a messy carpet of “trash” – stems, stubble and crop residue from previous harvests.
“When we’re watching to see where the birds are landing to feed, none of them are going on to the ploughed side,” says Leake, the director of the Allerton Project farm, standing on the trashy side. “They’re all coming and feeding down here.
“That’s because that’s where the seeds, the earthworms and the insects are. On the ploughed side, they’re all buried.”
It is experiments such as these that have enabled the Allerton Project to buck the decline in farm bird populations across the UK. Farm bird abundance at Allerton has risen 145% since 1992 when monitoring began, compared with a 23% decline nationally over the same period.
“This is not some study that’s been done overnight,” Leake says. “We can be fairly confident that this is a robust recipe that we’ve got here.”
The Allerton Project is a working farm and research centre on the Leicestershire-Rutland border, where farmers and scientists have spent more than three decades testing how farming can produce food while supporting wildlife.
Frequently hosting farmers, policymakers and businesses, the 320-hectare “demonstration farm” uses a range of sustainable agriculture, habitat creation and landscape management methods to show how agriculture can be a part of environmental action.
“I don’t want people to come here and say: ‘Oh, that’s a nice nature reserve they’ve got going there’,” Leake says of his guests. “I want them to go back on to their farms and say: ‘Do you know what, I can do that.’”
Changes in farming practices across the UK have devastated farmland bird populations. An increase in pesticide use and a loss of suitable habitats have driven some species to extinction, according to the RSPB. But at Allerton, farm bird numbers are at their highest level since records began, with song thrush, blackbirds and linnets in particular on the rise.
Leake points to a “bird table”, a channel of dedicated wildlife seed mix that splits the field. In these unkempt strips found all over the farm, kale, teasel, sorghum and millet are grown to supply seeds to birds through winter.
“That is probably the most important thing we’ve done, [making] sure that there is food in the landscape for those birds to go and feed on,” he says. “If they manage to survive what we call the ‘hungry gap’, which is January, February, March, that means they’re ready to breed again.” Goldfinches love the teasel, he adds.
Adjoining the bird table is the “beetle bank”, a strip of uncultivated land planted with long, tussock-forming perennial grasses. As the grass dies down year after year, it falls over and builds a thick, fibrous blanket of dead plant material, where beetles move to hibernate.
“When it warms up in the spring, they go out into the crops and they eat the pests that attack the crops,” says Leake, adding that the beetles mean the crops do not need to be sprayed with pesticides. “But also they provide insect food for birds.”
In a nearby field, Leake showcases an innovation found in gardens all over the country: bird feeders. “We fill the barrel up with wheat and the birds come and feed off it in the wintertime,” says Leake. “It’s just what people do in the gardens, feeding birds and things, but we’re doing it for farmland birds instead.”
The less-discussed aspect of wild bird protection is predator control. Foxes and crows, for example, can prey on eggs and chicks, sometimes holding back the recovery of vulnerable ground-nesting birds. Killing predators can be contentious.
Leake says Allerton’s approach is as humane as possible, targeting predators only during nesting season, the most vulnerable time for birds. “Our approach is a much more managed one,” he says. “So we are just reducing the pressure at the critical point.”
He says these measures prove it is possible to reverse the decline in wild bird populations. “We have reached the highest number [of birds] against the backdrop of the national figure continuing to go down,” he says. “This is because we’re learning how to manage the whole estate better for nature as time moves on. We come up with new ideas, we put them in place, and that is bringing nature recovery.
“There’s no reason why this couldn’t be done across the whole country. No reason at all, given the right incentives for people to do it.”

====================================================================================================

Analysis of FDA reports finds Prozac’s sexual side effects vary widely, with some emerging years into treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:39 UTC
21:00:39 KST

A recent study published in Progress in Neuropsychopharmacology & Biological Psychiatry suggests that sexual side effects associated with the antidepressant fluoxetine are highly varied, involving severe sensory disruptions alongside changes in libido. Using computer modeling, the researchers found that the drug may interfere with immune and cellular stress proteins, offering clues about the biological mechanisms behind these symptoms.
Fluoxetine is a widely prescribed medication used to treat depression and anxiety. It belongs to a class of drugs called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications work by increasing the availability of serotonin, a chemical messenger in the brain that helps regulate mood. While effective for mental health conditions, these drugs frequently produce unwanted sexual side effects.
Lead authors Jun Li and Xing Wang, along with corresponding author Honglin Hu from Nanchang University in China, initiated the investigation to better understand these adverse reactions. Previous research pointed to serotonin as the primary culprit, as heightened serotonin activity can suppress other brain chemicals like dopamine, which drives sexual arousal. The research team suspected that other biological networks, such as inflammation and cell survival pathways, might also be involved in these side effects. They combined real-world patient reports with advanced computer simulations to explore this hypothesis.
The scientists began by extracting data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System. This public database collects voluntary reports of adverse drug reactions from patients and healthcare professionals. The team filtered the records from 2004 to 2025 to isolate cases where fluoxetine was listed as the primary suspected drug. They analyzed 997 reports related to sexual dysfunction to see if certain side effects were disproportionately associated with the medication.
The analysis revealed strong statistical signals for a wide range of sexual problems. Common issues like erectile dysfunction and decreased libido appeared frequently in the patient reports. However, the researchers observed the strongest reporting intensities for highly specific conditions. Symptoms such as a total inability to climax, decreased orgasmic sensation, and genital numbness showed unusually high reporting rates compared to traditional measures of sexual dysfunction.
Following the database analysis, the team calculated the time it took for these symptoms to appear after a patient started taking the medication. They only included reports that contained complete date information for both the start of treatment and the onset of the side effect. They used statistical distribution models to map out the timing patterns for different symptoms across the patient population.
The timing of the side effects varied greatly depending on the specific symptom. Some conditions, such as prolonged and painful erections or persistent genital arousal, emerged within the first few days of treatment. Issues related to sexual desire, such as a loss of libido, tended to surface after about four to five months. The most delayed side effects involved sensory and orgasmic disruptions, with reports of genital numbness and an inability to climax often appearing after more than two years of continuous medication use.
To understand the biological roots of these symptoms, the researchers turned to network toxicology. This computational approach maps out how drugs interact with the body by cross-referencing vast genetic and protein databases. The team first compiled a list of human proteins known to interact with fluoxetine. They then created a separate list of proteins and genes associated with human sexual dysfunction.
By comparing the two lists, the scientists identified 56 overlapping genetic targets. These shared targets operate within networks that control brain chemistry, including both serotonin and dopamine pathways. The overlapping targets were also heavily concentrated in biological pathways that regulate inflammation, immune responses, and cellular death.
The researchers built a digital map to visualize how these 56 targets interact with one another inside the body. This mapping process identified two core hub proteins that act like major intersections in a city traffic grid, handling a high volume of biological signals. The first is IL10, a protein that helps regulate the body’s inflammatory and immune responses. The second is TP53, a protein that responds to cellular stress and helps control when a damaged cell undergoes programmed death.
To see if the drug could physically influence these proteins, the team used a technique called molecular docking. This computer simulation predicts how a small drug molecule might fit into the three-dimensional structure of a larger protein. It operates much like a simulation of a key entering a lock.
The simulations showed that the fluoxetine molecule fits neatly into the structural pockets of both the TP53 and IL10 proteins. The binding affinity was notably strong for the IL10 protein. This physical compatibility suggests that the drug might directly attach to and alter the function of these proteins in the human body. The researchers suspect that fluoxetine might contribute to sexual side effects by triggering low-level inflammation or cellular stress in nerve and reproductive tissues.
Because the FDA database relies on voluntary submissions, it cannot capture the true frequency of these side effects in the general population. The reporting system also lacks complete information on drug dosages, the duration of treatment, and the patients’ other medications. These missing details prevent researchers from determining exactly how much of the drug is required to trigger a specific symptom.
The database does not track the severity of a patient’s underlying depression. Since depression itself is associated with bodily inflammation, it is difficult to isolate the medication as the sole driver of the immune system changes observed in the data. The underlying mental health condition may be contributing to the same biological pathways highlighted in the computer models.
The computer models used to predict protein interactions are entirely theoretical. While molecular docking shows that a physical bond is possible, it does not confirm how the drug behaves inside a living human body. Physical laboratory experiments and clinical trials are necessary to verify these biological mechanisms.
The study, “Deciphering the molecular mechanisms of fluoxetine-induced sexual dysfunction: Evidence from pharmacovigilance, network toxicology, and molecular docking,” was authored by Jun Li, Xing Wang, Yunfeng Zhang, Penglin Zhang, Zhenfa Tan, Ruizhen Huang, Zuhuan Xu, Zhiyu Zhou, and Honglin Hu.

Why You Shouldn't Toss Your Old Halloween Pumpkins In The Trash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The only thing scarier than Halloween? Getting rid of a sad looking jack-o’-lantern when it's over.
When confronted with a rotting, deflating carved pumpkin, your first instinct might be to beeline to the trash as quickly as possible. But experts caution against doing so—warning that trashing pumpkins, and thus sending them to landfill, can release harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
“Everybody throws them out from Halloween to right after Thanksgiving,” says Kay McKeen, executive director at Scarce, an environmental education non-profit. “It's a huge burst of methane gas that's going into the landfill all at one time.”
Why shouldn’t you trash your pumpkin?
When pumpkins are sent to landfill, they release methane, a potent greenhouse gas that, over a 20 year period, is around 80 times more powerful at trapping heat in the atmosphere when compared to carbon dioxide.
The lack of oxygen in landfills causes pumpkins to rot “anaerobically,” which releases methane. They are also full of water, and when they mix with waste and moisture it creates leachate, a toxic sludge that can pollute the environment.
Though a single pumpkin might not do much damage, if you consider how many pumpkins are trashed each autumn, it adds up.
“Maybe if we had a handful of pumpkins going into that waste stream, that might be one thing,” says Chris Enroth, horticulture educator with the University of of Illinois Extension, which organizes annual “Pumpkin Smash” events to help people recycle and compost old jack-o'-lanterns and pumpkins. “But we have millions of people who buy multiple pumpkins. We're talking about hundreds of millions of pumpkins that need to be disposed of post Halloween, and it's just a massive amount of organic material that goes into the landfill system.”
How do I get rid of my pumpkin?
Composting sidesteps many of the harms that come with sending food waste, like pumpkins, to landfill.
“When we compost something, it's really a whole system that we're creating that introduces both water and oxygen, [and uses] microbes, bacteria, fungi, all the little decomposers,” says Enroth. “When we introduce those things, we get that aerobic composting process, so we don't produce methane, and we're able to turn those pumpkins back into organic matter that has nutrients and can be put back out into the garden.”
What’s the best way to compost? If you have a curbside compost bin or designated compost for your apartment building, you can throw it there. If not, see if there are any drop-off composting sites near you. Some areas even organize dedicated events for residents to drop off old pumpkins. Since starting “pumpkin smashes” in 2014, Scarce and Illinois Extension have saved over 1,600 tons of pumpkins from landfill.
Don’t leave your pumpkin out for animals to eat or dump it in a park—they can be harmful to wildlife. While pumpkins are generally safe for most wildlife to eat, some small animals, like hedgehogs, can become sick, different animal species congregating together could increase the risk of disease, and it can attract predators to residential areas.
As you’re thinking about composting, keep in mind that it’s not just pumpkins that are compostable. Food is the single most common material sent to landfills in the U.S.—and wasted food is responsible for 58% of landfill methane emissions. If you’ve been thinking about starting your own home compost, now is the best time to do it, says Enroth. “We often recommend to folks thinking about starting a compost pile, to try it in the fall because we usually have leaves, grass clippings, things to get that pile started. And you could incorporate that pumpkin into that compost pile,” he says. “It's a really good combination of materials for you to get compost out of it next year.”

Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.
Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.
“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”
Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.
Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.
Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.
Volta’s creators included a 240-word prompt, including bullet points and a numbered list, as part of their instructions to any LLM analyzing the collected data. “You are a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment from a structured evidence bundle,” the Volta prompt says. It instructs the chatbot to produce an “executive summary” about the person, details of what they do, “what they’re worth,” and a summary of “their opsec.” It adds that the chatbot should “connect dots across fields,” for example, checking whether someone’s Wi-Fi password matches their last name. “Go deep, not wide,” the prompt says.
“The prompt is pretty carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious,” Fetterman says. “But they’re building in the expectation to potentially hit model refusals at first request. And so they plan for failover kind of cascading to more permissible models as they go down the chain. And there’s also the capability to still use the implant without the AI. The AI calls are kind of above and beyond, but the malware will still work without it.”
Some low-level cybercriminals and scammers have complained about AI slop filling up cybercrime forums, but security researchers are increasingly discovering other hackers using LLMs for coding tasks or analyzing troves of stolen information. Researchers at threat intelligence firm Crowdstrike, for example, recently told WIRED they had seen four distinct hacking groups with varying sophistication—operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian, and Russian—using AI tools to compromise dozens of targets around the world, including government entities and businesses in health care, retail, and travel.
Cisco’s Fetterman says Volta contains some clues that it may have been built to sell to a range of attackers rather than being developed for one specific actor’s campaigns. And while the malware at its core is still a traditional infostealer, the AI expansion foreshadows even more invasive and sinister activity in the future.
“If you’re able to identify your high-value targets faster, you probably have a better chance of using their credentials or authenticating using stolen tokens more often than maybe you would have if you had to do that triage yourself,” Fetterman says, referencing the fact that authentication tokens expire and passwords can be changed. “We’re seeing more advanced capabilities accessible to lower-level sophistication attackers. It’s really interesting and disturbing.”

Lopez: No undecideds here: Why Bass backers are on board, and Raman fans are fired up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- At one point it looked as though Raman had a comfortable lead over Bass.
- The latest polling shows the race is close.
Late one afternoon, at the intersection of South La Brea Avenue and Obama Boulevard, Shirley Dace cold-called fellow Angelenos and encouraged them to give L.A. Mayor Karen Bass a second term.
“I love Karen Bass because of all the experience she has,” Dace, a retired flight attendant, told me between phone calls. “Karen Bass was raised here. She knows the city. ... I’ve seen her around at different events.”
Meanwhile, roughly 10 miles to the northeast, Christian Perez and Marium Mohiuddin organized a night of door-knocking for Bass challenger Nithya Raman in Boyle Heights.
“I think she’s incredibly intelligent and I want to give her an opportunity,” said Perez.
Given the ICE raids and general denunciations of immigrants, Mohiuddin, a Muslim and Canadian immigrant, said he’s been impressed by Raman’s outreach to minority communities. And Raman is an immigrant, too.
“I want a mayor that’s going to protect me,” said Mohiuddin, who speaks out against Islamophobia and antisemitism, “and I really feel like Nithya would go to bat for us.”
You may have noticed a pattern here. Lots of positivity.
Lopez: Disney built the monorail in a year. LAX’s people mover, almost 8, hasn’t left the station
Years of delays for the SkyLink people mover at LAX have led to finger-pointing, litigation and a grand jury probe into how a $1.9-billion project has become a $3.3-billion boondoggle.
I figured that with just hours to go before election day, you’ve heard plenty from me and others about City Hall dysfunction, about each mayoral candidate’s flaws, and about undecided and uninspired voters here in the land of budget-busting rent, broken sidewalks and blue tarps.
It appeared for a while as if Raman wouldn’t even make it out of the primary, and then it looked as though she had a comfortable lead over Bass in the runoff. But if the latest poll can be trusted, it’s hard to pick a winner. So today I’m going to shed every cynical bone in my body — only temporarily, I promise — and hand the megaphone over to people who unabashedly like either Bass or Raman.
And to be honest, in connecting with these folks on the phone, by text and in person, I was inspired by their interest in civic affairs (if only there were more like them), and their belief that their vote matters.
So here goes, and I’ll start with the incumbent.
::
Shirley Dace, as she worked the phones at Bass headquarters, referred to a five-page list of personal achievements and positive developments during the mayor’s first term. Violent crime is down, solar street lights have been installed by the thousands, Metro rides are free for students, thousands of affordable housing units are on the way and thousands of homeless people have been brought indoors.
“We have a homeless problem, and I realize that,” Dace said, but she believes there’s been progress. “It takes a while to solve these problems.”
One day I happened upon a social media post by Christian Green, who said he was driving by Bass headquarters and popped in to volunteer. I reached him by phone, and the West L.A. College professor told me he volunteered for Bass four years ago, too. Green said he was once in the foster care system, and said Bass has supported foster youth initiatives dating back to her time in Congress.
Bass is the first Black woman, and first female, to be elected mayor of Los Angeles. Given the history of the city’s power structure, economy and racial makeup, Green said, “that is not something we should take lightly.”
One of Green’s students in African American studies, 23-year-old Kioi Shropshire-Maina, also works as a Bass volunteer.
“I’ve heard about her since I was a kid,” said Shropshire-Maina, a communications major.
One of the things he likes about Bass is that her career has followed a long and varied public service trajectory. She first worked in healthcare as a physician assistant at County-USC, then became a social justice activist and co-founder of the Community Coalition, followed by a leadership role in the California Assembly and 12 years in Congress.
“She’s always been kind of like the standard of public service,” said Shropshire-Maina.
He pushed back when I mentioned that Raman seems to be the candidate with more backing among younger and more progressive voters.
“I definitely think Miss Bass has a lot of youth support. I’ve seen it myself. We organize events all the time, and people turn out,” said Shropshire-Maina.
“She’s the most progressive mayor Los Angeles has ever had,” he added, saying he thinks that has played out in her approach to homelessness. She inherited a huge challenge, Shropshire-Maina said, but moved away from policies that criminalized homelessness. “It started with her executive directive ... which made government be more proactive and work across departments, and not just rely on police.”
At Bass headquarters, Shropshire-Maina worked at one phone bank table while Philip Rosen of Hollywood and Christina Schiepe of Westchester worked another table. Rosen said Bass is a pragmatic Democrat who has been dealt a lot, with homelessness and the Palisades fire, “but she’s taken accountability,” and he believes Raman will be accountable primarily to the Democratic Socialists of America.
Schiepe, who had been to Bass headquarters twice previously, is 16.
“I can’t vote, but you know, at least I can do something that could help the cause,” Schiepe said, telling me her parents also support Bass, and one issue in particular stands out for her.
“We really are not happy with the ICE raids going on at the moment,” she said, and Bass “has done a lot to kind of combat that ... and try to get them out of Los Angeles.”
Schiepe said she wants to study political science in college, so who knows. Maybe she and Shropshire-Maina will run for office one day, and I can volunteer for them.
Now on to Raman.
Jane Demian, an Eagle Rock retiree and longtime activist and volunteer, said she would have voted for Bass if the opponent were Pratt, but Raman will get her vote.
Demian thought there were some bumps in the rollout of the mayor’s homelessness plan, but she thinks Raman did a good job as head of the council’s homelessness committee. She noted that Raman was one of the founders of the SELAH neighborhood homeless coalition, which steers people in the direction of housing and case management.
“I’m not put off as others are by her DSA connection. DSA is made up of people who want to provide economic support to working people,” Damian said. The “main focus is affordable housing, healthcare, and good wages for working people.”
Just as the Bass volunteers had their scripts to work with, Raman supporters touted the candidate’s work on renter protections, cleared encampments and a reduction in homelessness in her council district. I met with Mid-City residents Perez and Mohiuddin at La Monarca in Boyle Heights, where they were distributing literature to volunteer door-knockers.
As mayoral election day nears, four people talk about how they escaped homelessness.
Perez, who works in post-production, and Mohiuddin, who works in communications, both like the specificity they hear in Raman’s comments about homelessness, City Hall accountability and greater urgency in problem-solving.
“When I see Nithya Raman speak, I see someone who’s sincere, who’s kind of a wonk,” and isn’t afraid to dive into policy minutiae, said Perez, or to forge a path independent of the political establishment or dependent on endorsements from fellow council members.
Perez and Mohiuddin voted for Bass four years ago, but don’t think she’s earned a second term.
“It’s very hard to find an Angeleno who’s happy with government,” Perez said.
The change Mohiuddin wants to see, she told me, is simple. She wants for a candidate “to say something’s going to happen, and then stick to it.”
As Perez sees it, Bass has attempted to position herself as the candidate of the people.
“But in canvassing and speaking to people throughout the city ... there’s a lot of people who are disappointed with the status quo and perhaps not enough has happened in the last four years to justify them giving [her] another shot,” he said. “So I do think there is an aspect of [voters being hungry for] fresh blood and energy in order to confront the emergencies the city is facing.”
Whatever the outcome on election day, Mohiuddin said, there will be a victory of sorts.
“We’re still going to have a woman leading the city.”

Bangladesh records deadliest dengue month as deaths reach 418
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:57:00 UTC
20:57:00 KST

Bangladesh recorded its deadliest month of the year for dengue in October, with 173 deaths as health experts warned that the outbreak is likely to persist through November and may not ease significantly until December.
The country reported 418 dengue deaths and more than 133,000 hospital admissions between Jan. 1 and Oct. 30, according to Health Ministry data. October's toll surpassed September's 148 deaths, making it the deadliest month of 2026 so far.
The surge comes as Bangladesh is also struggling with the world's worst measles outbreak, which has killed more than 1,200 people, placing additional pressure on an already overstretched health care system.
Doctors said many dengue patients were arriving at hospitals only after developing serious complications, making treatment more difficult.
At the state-run Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Dhaka, 279 dengue patients were receiving treatment after 67 new admissions in a single day, hospital director Mirza Golam Sarwar said.
"We are getting many patients in shock. Their blood pressure sometimes is too low to measure, and their oxygen levels are dropping," he said.
Medicine specialist ABM Abdullah said repeat infections, coupled with delays in diagnosis and treatment, were contributing to the rise in severe cases and deaths.
People who have previously contracted dengue face a greater risk of serious illness if infected again, he said, urging residents to eliminate mosquito breeding sites and seek medical attention as soon as symptoms appear.
The danger of repeated infections is a growing concern for residents such as Dhaka's Faisal Ferdous, who has contracted dengue three times, in 2017, 2024 and again earlier this month.
"This time, both my wife and I needed hospital treatment," said Ferdous, who is now recovering at home.
He said the couple fell ill shortly after spending several days at a hospital where their 5-year-old son was receiving treatment for an unrelated illness.
"Every bout has been difficult. After getting it repeatedly, you become increasingly concerned about the risk of severe illness," he said.
Health experts have also warned that the circulation of all four dengue virus serotypes is contributing to more severe infections. People previously infected with one serotype can develop more serious complications when subsequently infected with another.
Bangladesh has yet to introduce a dengue vaccine, although authorities are considering vaccination as a longer-term measure to tackle the disease.
Despite the October surge, entomologist Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University said the monthly death toll was unlikely to continue rising at the same pace. However, he warned that dengue transmission would probably remain high through November.
"We may see some relief, but dengue is unlikely to disappear in November. Any decline is likely to be modest, with significant improvement unlikely before December," he said.
Bashar said mosquitoes would continue emerging from breeding sites created by earlier rainfall, allowing transmission to persist even as weather conditions become drier.
He also pointed to changing rainfall and humidity patterns, partly linked to climate change, which are extending mosquito breeding seasons and allowing Aedes mosquitoes, the primary carriers of dengue, to remain active for longer.
The prolonged transmission season, combined with repeat infections and mounting pressure on hospitals, means Bangladesh is unlikely to see a substantial improvement in its dengue situation before the end of the year.

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal crisis explained: a decade-long dispute over legitimacy of the justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:52:31 UTC
20:52:31 KST

The dispute over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal began in 2015, when the two main political camps, PO and PiS, clashed over the appointment of five judges. It later escalated into a wider conflict over judicial independence, the Tribunal’s composition and the authority of its rulings.
After taking office in 2023, Donald Tusk’s coalition moved to reverse judicial reforms introduced by PiS.
The dispute entered a new phase in 2026, when President Karol Nawrocki refused to accept the oaths of several judges elected by parliament.
The standoff reached boiling point on Friday outside of the Constitutional Tribunal’s headquarters, with both sides disputing the other’s legitimacy.
Euronews explains the conflict in five key stages.
1. 2015: Five judges, two rival appointments
The crisis began in June 2015, when the outgoing PO-PSL coalition changed the law to allow parliament to elect five Constitutional Tribunal judges before the October elections.
On 8 October, the outgoing Sejm elected Roman Hauser, Andrzej Jakubecki, Krzysztof Ślebzak, Bronisław Sitek and Andrzej Sokala. President Andrzej Duda refused to accept their oaths.
After PiS won the election, the new Sejm declared the previous appointments invalid and elected five alternative candidates on 2 December. Duda accepted their oaths.
A day later, however, the Tribunal ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were constitutional, while two were not. It also said the president must accept the oaths of properly elected judges without delay.
This meant three seats had already been lawfully filled. PiS’s subsequent appointments to those seats were therefore challenged. The three disputed appointees — Mariusz Muszyński, Henryk Cioch and Lech Morawski — became known as the Tribunal’s 'stand-in judges'.
While PO-PSL had overstepped its powers by filling two seats prematurely, PiS also challenged three appointments that the Tribunal had deemed valid.
2. 2016–2023: Changes to the Tribunal and questions over independence
After taking power, PiS changed the rules governing the Tribunal, including how cases were heard, the number of judges required and voting thresholds.
In March 2016, the Tribunal ruled that the first set of changes was unconstitutional. Prime Minister Beata Szydło’s government refused to publish the judgment, arguing that it had been issued under the wrong procedures.
The dispute deepened after Julia Przyłębska became Tribunal president in December 2016. The three disputed PiS appointees were also allowed to take part in its work.
Critics said the changes undermined judicial independence and brought the Tribunal under political control. PiS argued that it was restoring the institution and reforming the justice system.
The conflict also reached European courts. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the Tribunal's composition, including Mariusz Muszyński, did not meet the requirement of a tribunal established by law.
That year, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal also issued rulings challenging the primacy of certain EU law provisions concerning the judiciary.
By 2022–2023, divisions had emerged within the Tribunal itself. Several judges questioned Przyłębska’s continued leadership, arguing that her six-year term as president had expired. She maintained that she could remain in office until the end of her nine-year judicial term.
3. 2024–2025: Tusk’s coalition attempts to reverse the reforms
After the October 2023 election, Donald Tusk’s coalition made restoring the rule of law a central priority.
In March 2024, the Sejm adopted a resolution questioning the status of the three disputed PiS appointees and Przyłębska’s authority to lead the Tribunal.
Two reform bills followed in September. They proposed changes to the appointment of judges and the institution’s functioning. President Andrzej Duda referred both to the Constitutional Tribunal for review, preventing them from taking effect.
In December 2024, Duda appointed Bogdan Święczkowski, a former national prosecutor and close associate of Zbigniew Ziobro, as Tribunal president.
Meanwhile, the government restricted the publication of Tribunal rulings in the Journal of Laws, citing concerns over the institution’s composition. Its leadership said the move was unlawful and that its judgments remained binding.
The result was a deepening institutional standoff: the government questioned the Tribunal’s legitimacy, while the Tribunal challenged the legality of the government’s actions.
4. 2026: Nawrocki refuses to accept four judges’ oaths
The crisis escalated in March 2026, when the Sejm elected six new judges to replace those whose terms were ending: Krystian Markiewicz, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, Maciej Taborowski, Magdalena Bentkowska, Marcin Dziurda and Dariusz Szostek.
President Karol Nawrocki accepted the oaths of Bentkowska and Szostek but refused the remaining four.
His office cited concerns over the appointment procedure, including deadlines and the requirement for individual votes. It also argued that the president was not obliged to accept appointments automatically.
The government maintained that the Sejm had the constitutional authority to elect judges and that the president could not block their appointments.
On 9 April, the four judges took their oaths before a notary in parliament and sent the documents to the presidential office. Nawrocki’s office and Tribunal president Święczkowski rejected the move, arguing that the oath had to be taken in the president’s presence.
The Tribunal added to the dispute on 12 May, ruling in case K 3/26 that the president was not obliged to accept every appointment and had to be physically present for the oath.
The government challenged the ruling, pointing to the disputed status of judges sitting on the panel.
In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure requiring Polish authorities not to obstruct the four judges from taking up their duties. The Venice Commission also said the president’s role in the oath should be ceremonial and that a refusal or delay should not prevent a judge from taking office.
5. October 2026: The dispute reaches the Tribunal’s headquarters
The conflict escalated again in October, when Maciej Berek also took his oath in parliament after receiving no invitation from the president.
Święczkowski refused to recognise oaths taken without the president’s presence and prevented some newly elected judges from sitting on cases.
On 30 October, judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska ordered a one-month suspension of duties for Tribunal president Święczkowski and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański, citing provisions on the temporary suspension of judges. She then took over the management of the institution.
She said the move was necessary to restore the Tribunal’s functioning and allow all judges elected by the Sejm to perform their duties.
The existing leadership rejected the decision as unlawful, arguing that there was no legal basis for suspending the president and that judges sworn in outside the presidential procedure were not full members of the Tribunal.
The confrontation then moved inside the building. After seven judges entered the headquarters accompanied by State Protection Service officers, scuffles broke out. President Nawrocki arrived during the night and described the events as an attempted takeover of a constitutional institution. He called for urgent consultations with political leaders.
On Saturday, Święczkowski said he and the remaining judges would seek to regain control of the Tribunal. Korwin-Piotrowska, meanwhile, announced that she would convene a General Assembly of judges on 3 November.
What is at stake?
Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal crisis is no longer simply about appointments or who runs the institution. It raises fundamental questions about the separation of powers, judicial independence and the authority of constitutional rulings.
The consequences extend beyond the political institutions. When judgments are not published and state bodies disagree over their legal force, uncertainty spreads to laws affecting citizens, businesses, taxation and public services.
More than a decade after the crisis began, successive governments and presidents have failed to agree on a common solution. Instead, each change of power has brought new legal interpretations and further disputes over who has the authority to decide.

Protesters begin marching in French cities
Protesters in Paris have begun marching from Porte de Bagnolet, with demonstrations also taking place in Lille and Lyon.
Demonstrations have also begun across Germany, with marches taking place in Berlin, Hamburg, Frankfurt and Dresden, among other cities:
Crowds of people have gathered in Paris for the protests, where two French student unions have called for a blockade of schools and universities on Tuesday and Thursday.
“We will block access… and then take part in the demonstration this 5 November, in response to the call from workers who are calling for a strike,” Sabrine Kharbach, the spokesperson for the Union Etudiante (Student Union), told protesters, according to Le Monde.
“If they want to ban demonstrations every week, if they want to ban the marches that have always taken place peacefully, we will show them that they are wrong.”
Manon Moret, general secretary of the National Union of Students of France (UNEF), added: “So far, the government has still not provided a concrete response to the demands of young people.”
Protesters have gathered in front of the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin. German police said an additional 1,500 officers will be deployed throughout the city.
The demonstrations coincide with Halloween, but France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has warned protesters that covering their faces with costumes for malicious intent could result in a fine of €150.
“Using Halloween as an excuse will not be a legitimate reason to cover one’s face in public spaces,” he said.
The route for the demonstration in Paris is restricted to the eastern outskirts of the capital, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton. Police have refused a request from organisers for the march to start at the Bastille and head towards Place de la Nation in the heart of Paris.
According to local media reports, a Paris court lifted the ban on the Bastille-Nation route yesterday, but the Paris police prefecture immediately appealed against the ruling to the country’s highest court, which overturned the lower court’s decision this morning.
Organisers of the protests in Germany have rejected warnings from authorities that violent groups could seek to infiltrate the demonstrations.
Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it), the group behind the protests, has urged supporters to demonstrate peacefully. It is anticipating more than 160,000 people to turn out today to demand increased funding for schools, measures to tackle the rising cost of living and stronger climate action.
“The media’s rhetoric against the protests has been stirred up, so to speak, and is actually intended to distract from our core demands with a narrative of violence,” Veronika Dinter, a spokesperson for the movement, told the German Deutschlandfunk radio.
Alexander Throm, a member of the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU), has urged that a repeat of the unrest in France “must be prevented at all costs”.
Berlin police chief Barbara Slowik Meisel said an extra 1,500 officers would be deployed in the capital, but stressed there was little evidence of any planned attacks on people or property.
Here are some of the latest images from around France:
In Paris, two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. An appeal by organisers against the decision to exclude them from the centre was rejected late on Friday night.
The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October.
Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide strike called for 5 November.
Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.
In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service.
Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”
But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.
“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.
“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.
France is bracing for a third weekend of protests, with police deploying 70,000 officers in an effort to prevent a repeat of the riots and looting that have swept the country in recent weeks.
Nationwide protests over the rising cost of living and the deteriorating education system have drawn hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets. Some demonstrations have descended into violence, with widespread looting and vandalism reported on 17 October.
Ahead of this weekend’s planned demonstrations, shops and businesses across France have boarded up their storefronts. Police have restricted access to Place de la République and Les Halles between 11pm and 6am on Saturday and Sunday and unaccompanied minors face a separate 9pm curfew around the Champs-Elysees.
The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, warned earlier this week of a “very high risk of public disorder”, saying demonstrations would be permitted but not in city centres, where authorities are concerned about the potential for violence and damage to property. The interior ministry said around 150 demonstrations were scheduled to take place nationwide.
Nuñez said authorities had identified social media posts for Halloween gatherings urging protesters to spark a “revolution”.
“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” he added.
The largely peaceful protests, which began in late September by students angry over the state of school facilities, overcrowded classrooms and what they regard as an unfair university admissions process, have since been joined by the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) activists and and trade unionists. Government pledges to overhaul the education system and reduce fuel costs have done little to quell public anger.
The protests have sparked a wave of youth-led demonstrations across Europe, with protests scheduled in more than 30 German cities today. An alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has urged supporters in cities including Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich and Cologne to take to the streets to demand greater investment in education, climate action and housing, as well as opposition to proposals to reintroduce compulsory military service. Organisers said they are expecting more than 160,000 people to take part in the demonstrations.

Healey to veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:48:14 UTC
20:48:14 KST

John Healey has said he will veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills, adding to concerns that the government is moving away from the pro-renewables agenda.
Announcing his plans, the chancellor said clean power is “how we break the grip of international gas prices on our bills”, but added the shift towards it “has to come at the right pace, in the right places, with the grid to carry it”.
New offshore wind projects lodging bids for subsidy contracts will only get signed off by ministers if they believe that all the power generated could be accommodated by Britain’s electricity grid without pushing up costs for consumers.
Writing in the Times, he said: “There’s no sense building power that can’t connect and then paying to switch it off. We will take that approach into our next renewables auction, only buying projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security.”
The move appears to be a further shift away from Labour’s target of having clean power by 2030, after Healey revealed more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget in the budget, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.
The cuts caused alarm among renewables experts, who warned they meant that Britain was unlikely to hit its targets on green heating, and were seen as a dismantling of former energy secretary Ed Miliband’s green agenda.
There is concern in government that wasted wind charges could add to energy bills, with the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which is funded through energy bills, being forced to pay wind turbines to switch off when there is not sufficient cabling capacity to transmit their power to consumers.
A National Audit Office report in September warned that homes and businesses could be faced with a potential annual bill of £7.8bn by 2030 to deal with the issue.
Healey appeared to preemptively address criticism of the plans. He said: “This is not a retreat from clean power. It is the credible route to it. Cheaper electricity will make it easier for businesses and households to electrify, strengthening our energy security and helping us decarbonise the wider economy.”
He added that “without the renewable generation added in recent years”, this year’s gas price shock “would have hit families and firms even harder.
“Those who want to rip up renewables would leave Britain more exposed to volatile markets and the dictators who exploit them.”
One casualty of the cuts announced in the budget was a reduction in the amount of money available for the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions were being undermined.
Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.
Some believe the cuts, much of which will pay for higher defence spending, are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. Allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever, pointing out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.
Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.
Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.

Below the threshold: Elkin, Sukkot, Radman among those left out of 26th Knesset after election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:45:15 UTC
20:45:15 KST

Several prominent political figures, including incumbent lawmakers and high-profile candidates, failed to secure seats in the 26th Knesset following Tuesday's elections, as their parties fell short of expectations and left familiar faces outside Israel's parliament.
Some were serving MKs, while others were candidates who had come close to securing positions considered likely to win seats. However, the final election results upended their political plans.
Yesh Atid lawmakers lose their Knesset seats
Yesh Atid ran a targeted campaign aimed at securing seats for candidates in the second group of 10 on its electoral list, particularly MKs Vladimir Beliak and Naor Shiri. The two, ranked 16th and 14th, respectively, stood out during the previous Knesset term for their work on the Finance Committee, where they led challenges against the government.
The effort, however, proved insufficient. Yesh Atid, led by Yair Lapid, secured just five seats, its share of the partnership with Bennett, leaving both lawmakers well outside the next Knesset.
The Religious Zionist Party also suffered a setback that cost MK Zvi Sukkot his seat. Sukkot, ranked seventh on the party's list, was involved in several prominent controversies during the previous Knesset term. The party won six seats in Wednesday's reported election results.
In July 2024, he was among the lawmakers who arrived at the Sde Teiman military base following the arrest of reserve soldiers suspected of abusing a Palestinian detainee. Sukkot entered the base through a breach in the fence as part of a protest against the soldiers' arrests.
He later sparked another controversy after being filmed smashing a monument with a hammer in the Palestinian village of Madama. Sukkot claimed that the monument had been erected to commemorate terrorists.
The incidents made him one of the political figures most closely associated with confrontations surrounding IDF activities and the settlement movement in the West Bank. This time, however, the Religious Zionist Party failed to win enough seats to bring him into the Knesset.
Protest leader Moshe Radman falls short
The Democrats also left a prominent figure outside parliament: protest activist Moshe Radman, who was placed ninth on the party's electoral list.
Radman, a high-tech entrepreneur and one of the leaders of the protest movement against the government's judicial reform legislation, had been among the movement's most prominent figures since it began.
He founded the high-tech protest movement, organized and led demonstrations, marches, and rallies, addressed protesters, and became one of the leading voices calling for the judicial legislation to be halted.
He later expanded his activities to include protests against the government and demands for early elections.
After joining the Democrats and securing ninth place on the party's list, Radman sought to translate his public activism into a seat in the Knesset. However, the Democrats won only eight seats, leaving him outside parliament.
Ze'ev Elkin and other prominent Likud figures left out
Several prominent figures in Likud also failed to secure Knesset seats.
Among the most notable was Minister Ze'ev Elkin, who left Likud in December 2020 to join Gideon Sa'ar's New Hope party and subsequently served as part of the National Unity Party.
Ahead of the elections, Elkin returned to Likud and competed in the party primaries, facing a difficult internal campaign.
Although he finished 17th in the nationwide primary results, the party's system of allocating positions and reserving places for designated candidates pushed him down to 32nd place on the final electoral list, too low to secure a Knesset seat. Election night results had already highlighted the uncertainty surrounding the makeup of the next Knesset.
Also left outside parliament were bereaved father Itzik Bontzel, who was assigned the 29th position on the list, MK Amit Halevi, and MK Avihai Boaron, who headed Likud's grassroots election campaign.

With the vote count complete, the makeup of the next Knesset is becoming clear. Alongside veteran politicians, several figures with high public profiles and notable personal and political stories will enter parliament.
Their election reflects a shift from the media, senior public service positions, the security establishment, and protest movements into politics. For some, it is a direct continuation of years of public activity. For others, it will be their first opportunity to try to shape policy from inside the Knesset. These are the names to know.
Yaakov Bardugo, Likud
A Channel 14 commentator and associate of Benjamin Netanyahu, Bardugo has become one of the most prominent voices aligned with the prime minister in recent years. He has a long career in public life, including serving as director-general of the Federation of Local Authorities and of Mifal Hapayis, Israel’s national lottery. He now moves from television studios to the Knesset after being given a reserved spot on Likud’s candidate list.
David Peter, Likud
A lawyer, legal commentator and former researcher at the Kohelet Policy Forum, Peter has been closely involved in the government’s legal battles in recent years. He has represented Netanyahu, Yariv Levin and Itamar Ben-Gvir in various proceedings. He enters the Knesset with extensive knowledge of the battle over the judiciary and conservative positions on constitutional law.
Shaul Meridor, Yashar

Keren Terner, B’Yachad
A former director-general of both the Transportation and Finance ministries, Terner was one of the most senior women in Israel’s public service. She and Meridor worked together in the Finance Ministry’s senior ranks during a battle over the independence of its professional staff. She publicly supported Meridor after Netanyahu attacked him, drawing criticism from Katz. The two now return to public life in different parties, Meridor with Yashar and Terner with B’Yachad.
Yoram Cohen, Yashar
Cohen headed the Shin Bet from 2011 to 2016. A member of the religious Zionist community with a long security career, he entered politics through Gadi Eisenkot’s party. In recent years, he has criticized the government’s conduct and Netanyahu’s policies, drawing on his extensive knowledge of the security
Noam Tibon, B’Yachad
A retired major-general, Tibon previously commanded the Northern Corps, the Judea and Samaria Division and the Nahal Brigade. He became particularly well known on the morning of October 7, when he and his wife set out to rescue their son and his family from Kibbutz Nahal Oz, helping rescue other residents along the way. Since then, he has been involved in the public campaign demanding accountability for the failures surrounding the war.
Moshe Feiglin, Religious Zionist Party, joint Religious Zionist Party and Zehut list
The leader of Zehut and a former Likud MK, Feiglin returns to the Knesset after years outside parliamentary politics. In the 1990s, he led opposition to the Oslo Accords. He later challenged Netanyahu for the Likud leadership and founded his own party. He is associated with support for Greater Israel, changes to the status quo on the Temple Mount and libertarian economic policies.
Rafi Ben Shitrit, Yisrael Beytenu
A former mayor of Beit She’an and longtime Likud member, Ben Shitrit left the party in which he built his political career to join Avigdor Liberman. His son, Elroi Ben Shitrit, was killed defending the Nahal Oz military outpost on October 7. Since then, he has become a leading figure in the campaign for a state commission of inquiry through the October Council.
Hanamel Dorfman, Otzma Yehudit
Ben-Gvir’s former chief of staff at the National Security Ministry, Dorfman is one of the minister’s closest associates. He was involved in the ministry’s work and its relations with the police and other law enforcement agencies. His name also surfaced in investigations by the Justice Ministry’s Police Investigation Department, in which he was questioned as a suspect. He now moves from a central role behind the scenes at the ministry to the Knesset.
Yair “Yaya” Fink, The Democrats
A social and political activist, Fink is a co-founder of Lobby 99 and a former CEO of the Darkenu movement. He was a leader of the protests against the judicial overhaul and established a reservists’ campaign for equal military service. Omri Ronen, The Democrats
A lawyer, reserve officer in the Maglan commando unit, and co-founder of Brothers in Arms, Ronen was born in Kfar Aza. He lost his grandmother in the October 7 attack and took part in the fighting in communities near the Gaza border. He was a leader of the protests against the judicial overhaul and now moves from public activism to the Knesset.

WHO Director-General commends Tokayev's contribution to advancing ‘Health for All’ concept
World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has praised Kazakhstan’s efforts in improving public health and well-being. He shared his remarks in a post on his Facebook account, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus commended President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s commitment to increasing the salaries of 77,000 healthcare workers.
“By investing in primary health care, empowering general practitioners and supporting health workers, Kazakhstan is demonstrating how political leadership can translate into better, more accessible health services for all,” he said.
The WHO Director-General also recalled Kazakhstan’s role in shaping the global “Health for All” concept, which was reflected in the Alma-Ata Declaration nearly 50 years ago.
He stressed that as the 50th anniversary of the declaration approaches in 2028, Kazakhstan continues “to set an example of turning that vision into action.’
“Political commitment to health makes a difference. Thank you, Kazakhstan, for showing the way!” he wrote.
As it was reported, in his annual address to the nation, “Kazakhstan’s Current Priorities in a New Historical Cycle,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized the need to modernize the primary healthcare system by expanding the responsibilities of general practitioners and gradually increasing funding. He instructed the Government to raise salaries for primary healthcare workers by up to 40% starting January 1, 2027.

Germany and Netherlands receive first Caracal air assault vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:42:36 UTC
20:42:36 KST

- Germany and the Netherlands received their first Caracal air assault vehicles at Rheinmetall’s Ede plant on Oct. 29, under a joint buy of more than 1,500.
- The G-Class-based Caracal will equip the Dutch 11th Air Assault Brigade and Germany’s Rapid Forces Division, which have operated together since 2014.
Germany and the Netherlands have taken delivery of their first Caracal air assault vehicles, light 4x4s built on the Mercedes-Benz G-Class for paratroopers and helicopter-borne infantry, under a joint program covering more than 1,500 vehicles, the Dutch Defense Ministry said on Oct. 30.
The vehicles were handed over on Oct. 29 at Rheinmetall Defence Nederland’s plant in Ede, in the central Netherlands. The ministry did not say how many were delivered in the first batch or when the remaining vehicles will reach units.
The Caracal is built for the Dutch 11th Air Assault Brigade and Germany’s Rapid Forces Division, known as the Division Schnelle Kräfte, which have fought as one formation since the Dutch brigade came under the German division’s command in 2014. Both armies are buying technically identical vehicles, so troops from either country can drive, repair and resupply each other’s fleets. The ministry said that would make the two forces work together even more closely.
Rheinmetall developed the Caracal with Mercedes-Benz and Armoured Car Systems. The vehicle uses the military 464 series of the G-Class chassis, ACS supplies the body, and Rheinmetall’s Ede plant installs the systems before the vehicles go to units. When Rheinmetall first showed the Caracal in 2022, it said the roughly 4.9-ton vehicle has a 249-horsepower six-cylinder diesel, a top speed of 140 km/h (87 mph), and is small enough for two to fit inside a CH-47F Chinook or CH-53K King Stallion helicopter, or to be carried slung underneath one. It can also be flown in C-130, A400M and C-17 transport aircraft.
The Dutch ministry calls the vehicle the Airborne Vehicle Air Assault Caracal and noted it should not be confused with the Airbus H225M Caracal helicopter, which the Netherlands is buying to replace its Cougar helicopters from 2030.
Germany and the Netherlands signed a framework contract with Rheinmetall in July 2023 for up to 3,058 Caracals, worth up to €1.9 billion (about $2.12 billion) including value-added tax. It covers up to 2,054 vehicles for Germany and 1,004 for the Netherlands. The two countries placed a firm order for 1,508 vehicles worth about €870 million (about $970 million) at the same time, and Germany is paying for its share from the special fund it set up in 2022 to re-equip the Bundeswehr.
The Caracal family is designed to carry different equipment on one platform, including troop transport, ambulance and supply versions. Rheinmetall unveiled a larger 6×6 version at the Eurosatory exhibition in Paris in June, with an extra payload of up to 3.3 tons compared with 1.2 tons for the 4×4, and said it hopes Germany and the Netherlands will order it through the same framework contract.

COP17: nations agree to combat biodiversity loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:41:39 KST

COP17: nations agree to combat biodiversity loss
At the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, dubbed COP17, states have agreed on measures designed to speed up the implementation of decisions taken in 2022.
These include setting aside at least 30% of the world’s land and marine areas for biodiversity.
“The agreement represents a positive outcome that demonstrates the willingness of countries to work together to achieve the objectives of the (so-called) Global Biodiversity Framework and to accelerate its implementation”, said Katrin Schneeberger, director of the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), who represented Switzerland during the final phase of the summit. The conference took place in Yerevan, Armenia, between October 19 and 30.
The parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity had adopted the Global Framework in December 2022 at the United Nations Biodiversity Conference held in Montréal, Canada. It includes 23 targets to be achieved by 2030 and long-term goals extending to 2050, addressing the main causes of biodiversity loss. As stated, one of the main targets is to set aside at least 30% of land and marine areas for biodiversity by 2030 (“30 by 30”), by establishing protected areas or implementing other effective land-based measures.
More
Biodiversity loss in Switzerland in six graphs
“Switzerland is committed to ensuring that the targets are implemented through concrete measures and that biodiversity is effectively protected in the long term,” said Schneeberger in a press release.
In Yerevan, the parties carried out an initial mid-term review of progress made towards achieving the targets set in Montreal in 2022. According to the FOEN, businesses and financial institutions play a key role in their implementation. Through innovation, investment in nature and sustainable models of production and consumption, they can make an “essential” contribution.
More
One third of Switzerland’s animal and plant species under threat
In future, it will be necessary to raise awareness of the value of nature and, for example, the importance of insect diversity for agriculture. The countries intend to collaborate more effectively and, amongst other things, to learn from the experiences gained through greater regional exchange, with a view to improving their policies.
The parties also agreed on several other technical decisions. These include a commitment to examine the issue of aquatic and mountain habitats in greater depth over the next two years.

Police catch teenagers who deliberately left scooters on 70 km/h road
Police have identified several young men who deliberately left electric scooters on a 70 km/h stretch of road near Keila, endangering people's lives. The company that owns the vehicles has temporarily suspended operations in the area.
Officers received a report in late September that an electric scooter was lying on the road near the Mudaaugu bus stop on Paldiski Highway, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) said on Saturday.
According to Hisko Vares, head of the investigation unit at Lääne-Harju Police Station, several reports of similar incidents were received over the course of the month. "Police have been informed on 10 occasions that an electric scooter had been left on the road. In one case, a car hit a scooter, but fortunately no one was injured," he said.
The head of the investigation unit said police officers gathered additional information from residents, but the investigation was complicated by the lack of surveillance cameras in the area. There were also no eyewitnesses, as far as police are aware.
"After extensive work, the perpetrators were identified as three young men aged 17, 18 and 24," Vares said.
He stress that deliberately leaving objects on the road is extremely dangerous. "The speed limit on this stretch of road is 70 km/h, and hitting an electric scooter in the dark at that speed could end extremely badly. The young men endangered other people through their actions, and it is only fortunate that no one was injured," Vares said.
The PPA has launched misdemeanor proceedings, during which all the precise circumstances will be established.
Company suspends scooter parking in the area
Hoog Mobility, the company that owns the electric scooters, told ERR it is aware of the incidents, is cooperating with police and has temporarily removed its electric scooters from the area.
"Yes, we are aware of these incidents and take them very seriously. These are not incorrectly parked scooters. The scooters were in a parking area and locked, but someone deliberately carried them from there onto the highway. This is vandalism that endangers the lives and health of drivers. Nothing like this has happened to us before, and the incidents have been confined to one area," said Drevor Rudnevs, Hoog Mobility management board member.
Several of the company's scooters have been damaged as a result of the incidents, but he did not say how extensive the damage was. "Scooters can be repaired or replaced, but a person's health cannot," Rudnevs added.
The board member said police are aware of the incidents and proceedings are ongoing: "As a precautionary measure, we have temporarily removed the parking areas in this region. We are grateful to local residents who have informed us of their observations"

The removal of the CEC

Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court

President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis.
However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters.
— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 31, 2026
On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw.
At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors.
The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her.
— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 30, 2026
Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”.
Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”.
Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”.
⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94

The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.
That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate.
As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.
That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.
However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek.
Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026
On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal.
Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence.
At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker.
The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon.

Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners.
Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki.
Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”.
On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki.

On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska.
