UN closes Somalia mission, ending three decades of political engagement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:37:21 UTC
20:37:21 KST

UN closes Somalia mission, ending three decades of political engagement
The United Nations has closed its political mission in Somalia, ending more than three decades of efforts to help the country rebuild after civil war.
The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) ceased operations on Saturday after completing a two-year transition requested by the Somali government, the mission said in a statement on X.
Its responsibilities have been gradually transferred to Somali institutions, UN agencies and the UN office supporting African Union (AU) troops under a roadmap agreed between Somalia and the UN.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Somalia’s progress but called for continued international backing amid political, security and humanitarian challenges.
Strained relations
The closure follows years of sometimes strained relations between Somali governments and the UN mission, whose involvement in domestic politics has repeatedly prompted accusations of interference.
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s government formally requested its withdrawal in 2024.
At a farewell ceremony in Mogadishu on Monday, Deputy Prime Minister Saleh Ahmed Jama hailed the closure as a “day of victory”, saying Somalia was now leaving behind the “era of transition”.
The departure comes as international support for Somalia is shrinking, even as the country faces deep political divisions and continuing violence.
Opposition leaders reject the government’s position that constitutional changes allow President Mohamud and parliament to remain in office until 2027.
Relations with some regional leaders are also strained, while al-Shabab, an armed group linked to al-Qaeda, continues to fight government forces.
The UN mission previously helped rival leaders reach election agreements, but no replacement for its mediation role has been agreed.
Mohamud has invited political opponents to talks, although major opposition groups have yet to confirm their attendance.
UN humanitarian and development agencies remain in Somalia, but their funding has been hard-hit by cuts to international aid.
In August, the UN children’s agency said 205 health and nutrition facilities had closed because of aid cuts.
AU troops also remain to support Somali forces against al-Shabab, but their operations depend heavily on a separate UN office, UNSOS, providing food, fuel, medical care and transport.
However, that vital support could end by December 2027 under a US-backed plan to close the UN office providing it, the Reuters news agency reported in September.

Russia loses about 13 warplanes in a month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:37:18 UTC
20:37:18 KST

- Russia lost about 13 military aircraft from late September through October, including seven Su-34s destroyed by Ukrainian strikes and a Tu-95MS bomber in a crash.
- Two Su-30SMs crashed on Oct. 21, and a Su-57 reportedly burned at Akhtubinsk on Oct. 29, though Russia has not confirmed the Su-57 loss.
Russia’s military aviation has lost about a dozen aircraft in roughly five weeks, including at least seven Su-34 fighter-bombers destroyed on the ground by Ukrainian missiles and drones, a Tu-95MS strategic bomber and two Su-30SM fighters in crashes, and a Su-57 stealth fighter that reportedly burned out during an engine start.
The Ukrainian open-source project Oko Gora counted 11 Russian fighter aircraft and one helicopter lost in October alone, with two more Su-34s partially damaged. Adding the Tu-95MS that crashed on Sept. 29 brings the tally to about 13 airframes since late September. Russia has confirmed only the two crashes during training flights and has not acknowledged losses from Ukrainian strikes.
The heaviest losses fell on the Su-34, the jet Russia uses most to drop glide bombs on Ukrainian cities and front-line positions. On Oct. 4, drones from Ukraine’s SBU security service hit a Su-34 and a Su-35 fighter at Khanskaya air base in Russia’s Republic of Adygea, about 500 km (310 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory, along with an ammunition depot. On the night of Oct. 14-15, Ukrainian Navy Neptune missiles struck Borisoglebsk air base in the Voronezh region, and satellite imagery showed four Su-34s destroyed and two more badly damaged. On Oct. 29, another Neptune strike destroyed two more Su-34s at Marinovka air base in the Volgograd region, with satellite images showing the wreckage at their parking spots.
That puts confirmed Su-34 losses for the month at seven destroyed, or nine counting the two damaged at Borisoglebsk. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR said Russia had about 140 Su-34s of all versions in service as of Oct. 22, and that Russian industry delivered 22 new ones between October 2025 and October 2026, Ukrinform reported. October’s losses alone equal about a third of that annual output.
On Sept. 29, a Tu-95MS bomber crashed on takeoff near Ukrainka air base in the Amur region of Russia’s Far East, killing six of the seven crew members. The Russian Defense Ministry said the aircraft was on a training flight without weapons. Russia no longer builds the Tu-95, which it uses to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles at Ukraine, and it was the first Tu-95MS lost in a crash since 2015.
On Oct. 21, a Su-30SM crashed during a training flight in the Kaliningrad region, and the Defense Ministry said both crew ejected. Russian and Ukrainian outlets reported that a second Su-30SM was lost the same day. Days later, the Russian Knights, the Russian Air Force’s aerobatic display team, announced the deaths of two of its pilots, Col. Oleg Yerofeyev and Lt. Col. Vladimir Kochetov, without saying how they died, and Ukrainian analysts have linked their deaths to the second crash. Russian authorities have not confirmed the connection.
The most unusual loss came on Oct. 29 at Akhtubinsk, the Russian Air Force’s main flight-test center in the Astrakhan region. A Su-57 fifth-generation fighter caught fire during an engine start and burned completely, the Ukrainian open-source channel Absolutely Reliable Source said, publishing satellite images of a burn scar on the airfield. Russia has not confirmed the loss. If verified, it would be the fourth Su-57 lost or damaged this year, after a Ukrainian drone strike in April and a crash near Moscow in July that Russia blamed on a technical malfunction.
The tallies also include helicopters. On Oct. 30, Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade said it destroyed a Mi-8 transport helicopter in the Luhansk region with two Hornet attack drones after the helicopter landed.
The losses span thousands of kilometers, from Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea to the Far East. The open-source project Oryx had visually confirmed 205 Russian aircraft destroyed or damaged since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, with the Su-34 the most-lost type at 48.

US Clears 500 Patriot PAC-3 Missiles for Ukraine in $2.1 Billion Sale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:36:25 UTC
20:36:25 KST

- Category
- World
US Clears 500 Patriot PAC-3 Missiles for Ukraine in $2.1 Billion Sale
The US State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) interceptors to Ukraine on October 30, but the decision does not constitute a signed contract or guarantee immediate deliveries.
The State Department announced the decision as part of the formal congressional notification process for potential foreign military sales.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under US arms export procedures, Congress generally has 30 calendar days to review the proposed transaction. A final Letter of Offer and Acceptance cannot be issued until that period expires, meaning the actual agreement and subsequent procurement arrangements remain pending.
Ukraine requested 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors, classified and unclassified spare parts, and associated logistics and program support. The State Department did not announce a contract signing date, production schedule, or expected delivery timeline.
The $2.1 billion purchase would be financed through contributions from Canada, Germany, and Norway under the JUMPSTART program, as well as Ukrainian funds backed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan. The State Department confirmed that no US funding would be involved.
Even after a contract is concluded, deliveries could take several years because of manufacturing timelines and strong global demand for Patriot interceptors.
An April 2026 analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated an average of 29 months between procurement and initial PAC-3 MSE deliveries, with additional time required to complete an order. Initial shipments in 2027 or 2028 would therefore depend on production availability and contractual arrangements, and remain unconfirmed.
The PAC-3 MSE is an advanced hit-to-kill interceptor designed to destroy ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft through direct impact. Its dual-pulse rocket motor and enhanced maneuverability extend its engagement capabilities, making it particularly important for Ukraine's defenses against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Lockheed Martin, headquartered in Bethesda, Maryland, is designated as the principal contractor. The proposed transaction would not require additional US government or contractor personnel in Ukraine, and Washington assessed that it would not adversely affect US defense readiness.
The deal comes amid an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors in Ukraine.
In mid-October, Ukraine's supplies of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles were severely depleted, with most available stocks directed to the Middle East for an extended period.
Some interceptors have continued to arrive through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which lets European partners finance US-made weapons, supplemented by small batches from other countries. By October 15, Ukraine had reportedly exhausted its available interceptors entirely, leaving almost all ballistic missiles in a recent Russian strike unintercepted.

US Cancels Traditional G20 Group Photo After European Diplomats Refuse to Stand With Lavrov
The US canceled the traditional G20 foreign ministers' group photo ahead of their October 30 meeting in Atlanta after European diplomats refused to be photographed alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
The Daily Mail reported on October 30, citing two US officials who confirmed that Secretary of State Marco Rubio canceled the photograph to prevent the controversy from disrupting the summit. Several European representatives had threatened to walk out if the photo session proceeded.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband had already announced plans to boycott any photograph involving Lavrov and requested a separate picture with close allies.
"We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years," Miliband told British lawmakers earlier in the week, citing Russia's war against Ukraine.
The two-day gathering, chaired by Rubio, brings together senior diplomats to discuss international security, trade, and economic challenges. Russia's war against Ukraine, conflicts in the Middle East, and maritime security are among the main issues.
Several G20 members also expressed concern over Washington's decision to invite Lavrov amid intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine. Ukraine, which had previously participated in G20 meetings despite not being a member, received no invitation this year. US officials explained that attendance was restricted to formal members.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas announced plans to press international partners for stronger support for Ukraine and greater accountability for Russian actions, including through the Special Tribunal and Claims Commission.
Washington's willingness to engage Moscow at the G20 extends beyond the foreign ministers' meeting. In September, the US formally invited the Russian leader Vladimir Putin to the G20 leaders' summit scheduled for December 20 in Miami, Florida.
Rubio announced the decision after meeting Lavrov and noted that the event would give Putin a chance to speak with US President Donald Trump and other world leaders. He also indicated that Washington was open to helping secure a limited ceasefire, adding that both sides had expressed interest in a truce covering grain and energy.

Ukraine's Fire Point Builds Starlink-Free Strike Technology to Reduce Foreign Dependence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:36:09 UTC
20:36:09 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine's Fire Point Builds Starlink-Free Strike Technology to Reduce Foreign Dependence
Ukrainian weapons manufacturer Fire Point has developed technology allowing its long-range strike systems to complete missions against targets in Russia and Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory without relying on SpaceX satellite connectivity.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh told Reuters in an interview published on October 30 that the company had developed technological workarounds to maintain strike capabilities despite restrictions on satellite communications.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Fire Point systems are designed to finish a mission without a satellite link," Terekh stated, emphasizing that navigation independent of external signals remains a development priority.
Terekh acknowledged that the alternative technology provides only 15% to 20% of the operational capabilities Ukraine could achieve with full Starlink coverage over Russia. She described unrestricted access as a potential game changer for strikes against high-value targets, including Russian ballistic missile launchers.
The developments follow a 10-day period in October when SpaceX restricted satellite connectivity for Ukrainian drones traveling faster than 160 kilometers per hour. The limitations disrupted drone operations and communications during ongoing strike missions. Higher-speed connectivity was subsequently restored.
Terekh also called for a predictable agreement between Ukraine and the US governing satellite communications, arguing that Ukraine's ability to defend itself should not depend on frequently changing restrictions.
Beyond satellite-independent navigation, Fire Point is expanding Ukraine's domestically developed ballistic missile capabilities. Its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, which has a range of approximately 300 kilometers, recently made its combat debut against a target in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.
Terekh explained that the FP-7 could target Russian Iskander ballistic missile launchers, which can relocate before slower Ukrainian strike drones reach them. Destroying such launchers could prevent attacks on Ukrainian cities and provide a more cost-effective defensive option than intercepting incoming missiles with US-made Patriot systems.
She also emphasized that domestic ballistic missile production eliminates the risk of foreign governments remotely disabling the weapons through a technological "kill switch."
The company is also coordinating Freyja, a pan-European project to develop an anti-ballistic missile interceptor. Terekh reported that testing against a simulated target is expected before the end of 2026, followed by an interception of a physical target by mid-2027. The project aims to expand Europe's ability to counter ballistic missile threats.
Fire Point's missile program has moved quickly from the drawing board to the battlefield. The FP-7 entered codification after roughly two years of development, with research and initial production setup costing approximately $200 million, before its first combat use was confirmed on October 1.
To overcome tight international export controls, the company has engineered critical components internally. It has also upgraded the FP-7.x Freyja interceptor, developed with nine other European nations, with a combined infrared and radar seeker designed to hold a lock through bad weather or decoys.

Ukraine’s SABER Adds Remote Fire Support to Germany’s GEREON Unmanned Ground Vehicle

Ukraine’s SABER Adds Remote Fire Support to Germany’s GEREON Unmanned Ground Vehicle
German defense technology company ARX Robotics and Ukrainian manufacturer ROBONEERS have successfully completed initial integration tests of the Ukrainian SABER combat module with the German GEREON unmanned ground vehicle, the companies announced on October 29.
The companies plan to integrate SABER weapon stations in M2 and MK 19 (M) configurations with GEREON platforms by the end of 2026. Initial deliveries will be carried out in accordance with the operational needs and requirements of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The SABER combat module is designed to adapt to the operational needs of military units, not the other way around," ROBONEERS CEO Anton Skrypnyk stated. He emphasized that integration with GEREON demonstrates the systems' interoperability and could accelerate the deployment of urgently needed capabilities to the front lines.
GEREON is a medium-sized modular unmanned ground vehicle developed by ARX Robotics. It provides mobility, power, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities, while the Ukrainian SABER remotely operated weapon station supplies fire support.
The platform can be adapted for logistics, casualty evacuation, electronic warfare, reconnaissance, combat, and counter-drone missions. SABER supports various weapon systems, ranging from assault rifles to grenade launchers, allowing military units to configure the vehicle to meet specific battlefield requirements.
According to ARX Robotics, GEREON represents the largest Western-built unmanned ground vehicle fleet currently deployed in Ukraine. Its modular architecture allows the company to adapt existing platforms to changing operational requirements.
"Modern armed forces require platforms that can adapt quickly to different missions, integrate new technologies and work seamlessly with existing systems," Maximilian Wied, CFO and co-founder of ARX Robotics, stated.
The integration marks the next phase of a strategic technical partnership signed in Kyiv on October 4, 2026, during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's visit to Ukraine. The agreement was signed in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The cooperation also builds on an earlier agreement between the two manufacturers to establish ARX Industries, a joint venture to expand production of the Ukrainian Rys Pro unmanned ground vehicle in Germany and Ukraine. The companies set an initial target of producing a four-digit number of vehicles during the venture's first year.
The partnership was signed amid a broader expansion of Ukrainian-German defense cooperation, with the two countries concluding 15 agreements during the same visit covering unmanned ground systems, drone interceptors, small missiles, radars, artillery, and air defense.
The deals also included increased production of Patriot missiles in Germany, Ukrainian orders for IRIS-T systems from Diehl Defence, and radar procurement from Hensoldt. Berlin separately announced a support package that includes funding for new interceptors designed to counter Russia's jet-powered Shahed-type drones.

Four planes carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky landed in Belarus on Saturday, the Belarusian state news agency Belta and a senior Ukrainian official said.
Hundreds of starving and exhausted residents left the town of Oleshky on Friday during a U.S.-backed local ceasefire, the first of its kind and the longest humanitarian pause in the war, which is nearing its fifth year.
"The last, fourth plane landed in Gomel," said David Arakhamia, a top Ukrainian peace negotiator and close ally of President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“In a few hours, all Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky together with a Ukrainian delegation will be on Ukrainian territory.”
Belta later reported that a convoy of buses carrying the residents had departed from the airport in Gomel, in southeastern Belarus near the border with Ukraine.
The evacuees heading for Ukraine had to take a complicated route to leave Oleshky as the frontline runs just a few kilometres away.
They traveled first by bus via Crimea to the Russian town of Anapa, before flying to Belarus, from where they will continue to Ukraine via a border crossing, Belta said.
The ceasefire was reached thanks to mediation efforts by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of the Pope. The ceasefire has been holding since Tuesday without violations, according to both Ukrainian and Russian officials. It has allowed them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town.
Supply routes to Oleshky were disrupted by fighting and drones. According to some residents, food deliveries were stopped in May, pushing hundreds of people into starvation.
It was not immediately clear how many people decided to leave Oleshky and how many opted to stay in the town. Oleshky residents had the option to travel to Russia or to return to Ukraine.
Ukrainian officials have said around 1,700 people remained in Oleshky from a pre-war population of about 24,000. According to several residents interviewed by Reuters, many of those were elderly or ill.

Oman rescues 25 from burning ship, Iran halts tankers
Oman said Friday it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack, as Iran reported three oil tankers were halted while crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has restricted maritime traffic through the strait since the Middle East war erupted on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic.
The narrow waterway, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil, has become a focal point of the conflict, with ships regularly coming under Iranian fire.
Muscat's navy "carried out an evacuation operation for 25 crew members of the merchant ship RITI, flying the Panamanian flag, after it was targeted, which led to a fire breaking out on board," Oman's Maritime Security Centre said in a statement.
The crew members were provided with medical care, the Omani statement said, without giving details.
The Marine Traffic ship-tracking website described the RITI as a crude oil tanker.
US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a video released on Friday that US forces had "successfully cleared the strait's internationally recognised primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines".
US forces remain "present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear," he added.
Cooper said he visited some of the more than 50,000 US service members in the region, repeating earlier statements that Washington has helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude via the strait since summer.
British maritime security agency UKMTO said that a ship 40 nautical miles (74 kilometres) south of Lavan island in Iran was struck on Friday by an unknown projectile, which caused a fire onboard.
"The crew of the vessel have been reported as safe and there is no reported environmental impact at this time," the UKMTO said on X.
Blockade
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said earlier that three oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified "incidents" or hitting mines.
"Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has demanded that vessels use a designated route through the strait and coordinate their passage with the country's armed forces, labelling a southern corridor closer to Oman's shores as unauthorised.
The tankers had "switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist US military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorised route", the Guards' statement said.
The Guards did not specify the nature of the "incidents" the tankers encountered, which came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had stopped in the area after hitting mines.
They said Friday's incidents occurred after the vessels received several radio warnings but disregarded them.
The IRGC said in a later statement that a supertanker carrying two million barrels of oil had stopped following an explosion "after striking a naval mine while navigating an unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz".
"This is the third oil tanker to have exploded and caught fire today as a result of attempting to pass through an unauthorised route," it added.
The United States has responded to Iran's blockade of the strait with a counterblockade of Iranian ports, further restricting Tehran's ability to export oil and conduct trade.

France braces for renewed nationwide protests as Macron's government vows tough response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:27:26 UTC
20:27:26 KST

France deployed a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Saturday in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron's government.
The demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.
"Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble," Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying "a very high risk" of unrest.
France's top administrative court confirmed on Saturday a march between the emblematic Paris squares of Republique and Bastille will be banned, rejecting a challenge by unions. Demonstrations will instead have to be held on boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, away from the main shopping areas in central Paris.
Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
Some 150 gatherings were planned across France, the interior ministry said.
The US Embassy advised travelers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.
The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron's minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for maneuver.
Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair, have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent "Yellow Vest" movement demanding action on the cost of living.
Protests spread across Europe
The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
The French government's promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.
"When I was little, I was told young people were the future," said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
"Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing."
The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April's presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
Protests are damaging the economy, costing retailers billions
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Friday showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double that when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.
Along Paris' main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry.
The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest.

Protests outside Poland’s constitutional court: What’s the crisis about?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:27:07 UTC
20:27:07 KST

Protests outside Poland’s constitutional court: What’s the crisis about?
Poland’s centrist government says it is restoring judicial independence after years of far-right political interference.
Riot police have been deployed outside Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal as a dispute over who should serve on the court escalates into a confrontation between Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government and the nationalist opposition.
Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the Warsaw building on Friday night after judges elected by the current parliamentary majority announced the suspension of the tribunal’s president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski.
The move drew condemnation from the far-right opposition Law and Justice party, known as PiS, and prompted President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally, to abandon a trip to Senegal, turning his plane around to return to Poland on Friday. Police said three people were arrested after trying to enter the court complex.
Tusk says decisive action is necessary to restore the rule of law after years of political interference in the Constitutional Tribunal under PiS. Here is what we know.
Why are Poland’s leaders fighting over the Constitutional Tribunal?
The Constitutional Tribunal decides whether laws comply with Poland’s constitution. Its rulings can prevent legislation from taking effect, making its independence and who sits on its bench politically significant.
This latest dispute can be traced back to 2015, during the transfer of power from a centrist government led by Tusk’s Civic Platform party to the far-right PiS.
The outgoing parliament elected five judges, although Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal subsequently found that only three of those appointments had a valid legal basis. The incoming PiS majority then elected replacements, including for the three seats already lawfully filled. Then-President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in the three validly elected judges.
During its eight years in government, PiS introduced broader judicial changes that critics said brought the courts under greater political influence. PiS is currently the main opposition in Poland.
“It was a power play to control who serves as a justice, in what positions, and how the court system operates in Poland,” Wojciech Przybylski, editor-in-chief of Visegrad Insight, told Al Jazeera.
“The former PiS government wanted a court system and tribunal that would allow it to pass laws that supported their ideological perspective. It also wanted control of a Constitutional Tribunal that would support its claim of sovereignty over the EU.”
Aleksandra Kustra-Rogatka, an associate professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Torun, told Al Jazeera that “after Przylebska became president of the CC, the rule of law crisis worsened. Controversial laws reformed the judicial system, and the court became seen as a rubber-stamp body and an active political player supporting illiberal policies.”
The European Court of Human Rights, which is separate from the EU, had already ruled in 2021 that an improperly appointed judge’s participation deprived a company of its right to a tribunal established by law. Then, in December 2025, the EU’s highest court ruled that the tribunal had not met the requirements of an independent court. It also found that tribunal judgements challenging the authority of EU law breached Poland’s obligations as a member state.
Tusk returned to office as prime minister in December 2023 promising to restore judicial independence, and his government has refused to recognise the tribunal’s legitimacy in its existing form and has been attempting to disregard its rulings.
Kustra-Rogatka added that “many supporters of the centrist governing camp have grown disappointed by the lack of progress in restoring the rule of law since 2023, partly constrained by the prospect of losing the 2025 presidential election”.
This year, the parliament elected eight judges to the 15-member tribunal. President Nawrocki, a supporter of Donald Trump, was elected last year and with the power to veto legislation, administered the oath to three judges but withheld it from five, who instead took their oaths without his presence. The tribunal’s president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, refused to allow those five to begin adjudicating.
What triggered the latest confrontation?
On Friday, Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced one-month suspensions of court president Swieczkowski and his deputy, Sochanski, and said she was assuming responsibility for running the tribunal.
But questions have arisen over whether Korwin-Piotrowska, who is one of the court’s 15 justices alongside Swieczkowski and Sochanski, has the authority to do this. Her claim rests on her length of judicial service overall, rather than having served longest on the tribunal.
In separate measures, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, took steps that could lead to criminal proceedings against the suspended president, Swieczkowski, and his deputy, Sochanski. Far-right critics say these measures are politically motivated and intended to apply pressure on the already suspended justices.
PiS supporters, including senior party figures, gathered outside to oppose the suspensions on Friday. Police said their deployment followed information from Korwin-Piotrowska about possible threats to judges and staff and risks to public order. They said officers were securing the grounds and had not entered the tribunal building.
Nawrocki turned back to Poland midair while flying to Senegal and arrived at the tribunal during the night. By Saturday morning, he had called urgent consultations with parliamentary representatives, describing events as a forcible takeover of a constitutional institution.
Tusk defended the effort to restore the rule of law, saying that reversing the legacy of PiS required difficult action.
What could happen next?
The confrontation raises two overlapping questions: who is entitled to sit on the tribunal, and whether the measures used to change its leadership are lawful.
Marcin Matczak, a prominent Polish lawyer, told Al Jazeera that the far-right opposition was defending its “remaining institutional stronghold”, while the centrist government wants to “restore balance to the Constitutional Tribunal”.
But restoring independence also requires scrutiny of the current government’s choices. In September, its parliamentary majority elected Maciej Berek, previously a minister in Tusk’s cabinet, to the tribunal. Some coalition members opposed the appointment, saying it contradicted promises to depoliticise the judiciary.
With parliamentary elections due next year, Matczak said Tusk might be taking a harder line to mobilise supporters frustrated by the slow pace of reform. “But that is a risky strategy: it may energise his political base while alienating more moderate voters,” he said.
A more immediate flashpoint could be a tribunal judges’ meeting that Matczak said had been called for November 3. Attempts to lift immunity could deepen the confrontation if the assembly’s composition or ability to reach the required quorum is challenged.
Matczak also warned that the scenes could establish a precedent for future governments. “A future government could invoke these events to argue that sending the police into the Constitutional Tribunal is an acceptable way to resolve a legal dispute,” he said.
“Whatever the immediate political gains, the long-term institutional consequences could be deeply damaging.”

Fire Point will not produce new cruise missiles because the “Flamingo” is sufficient: Stielerman explained Terekh’s statement on the marathon broadcast
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point has focused on producing the FP-5 “Flamingo” and developing the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles. Production of the “Flamingo” is not being discontinued.
Fire Point does not plan to create new cruise missile models, as the FP-5 "Flamingo" is sufficient for the company. Its production is being ramped up, while the developers’ main efforts are focused on ballistic missiles. Details

Iryna said that there would be no new cruise missiles and no new models. We are currently focused on producing ballistic missiles and developing ballistic missiles. And we are continuing to ramp up production of the FP-5, that is, Flamingo
He stressed that there was no talk of discontinuing production of the "Flamingo." The company simply does not intend to expand its lineup of cruise missiles.
We do not plan to make new cruise missile models because we believe that Flamingo is sufficient for our company
The company’s main focus for its developers now is ballistic technology. Fire Point is working on the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles, and on October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the first combat use of the FP-7.
Context
Several days ago, an edited fragment of an interview with Iryna Terekh circulated on social media, presented as if Fire Point had discontinued production of the FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missile. We do not plan to develop additional cruise missile models; instead, we are focusing on developing the existing model, while also directing our greatest efforts toward two ballistic models

New Saudi luxury airline forced to cancel, redivert flights under Houthi attacks - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:27:05 UTC
20:27:05 KST

Saudi Arabia's new airline, Riyadh Air, was forced to divert and cancel flights just months after it started commercial flights this summer, with Houthi attacks forcing the airline to evacuate all aircraft from its home base and halt almost all flying for two weeks, the Wall Street Journal reported last week.
Riyadh Air was intended to be part of Saudi Arabia's larger long-term economic ambitions, a high-end airline designed for wealthy tourists in the style of similar airlines from the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, according to the WSJ.
Houthi targeting of the airport in Riyadh has forced Riyadh Air to reduce its number of flights, with those remaining landing either in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, or at a small airport 200 miles from Riyadh, with passengers ferried on an hour-long ground journey to the capital.
Riyadh Air's sister carrier Saudia, an airline focused on the demand from Saudi Arabia's oil workers and pilgrimage travelers, has also been forced into disruptions by Houthi attacks, one of which killed one of its pilots and destroyed an aircraft on October 8.
Riyadh Air staff have started volunteering at hospitals where victims of the airport strikes were treated as flights are canceled and redirected and the airline moves its expensive assets from Riyadh.
Airports on Iran's target list
In addition to the Houthi threat, Iranian officials have told mediators that Tehran will be looking towards civilian targets, including airports, to retaliate against any renewed US or Israeli strikes, the WSJ wrote.
Riyadh Air also faces a renewal of its war-risk insurance policy in November, according to the report.
The airline plans to boost its number of flights, returning to semiregular scheduling using an airport in Al Qassim province, a free 4.5-hour bus ride to Riyadh, to service flights from places including London, Islamabad, and Cairo, according to Riyadh Air's website.

Gadi Eisenkot must beat Benjamin Netanyahu at his own game. He must do to Bibi what Bibi would have done to him if the roles were reversed. He must not become Benny. He did not win. In the kitchen with Henny: Short Friday shortcuts for Shabbat preparation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:26:44 UTC
20:26:44 KST

A few weeks ago, our family had the pleasure of spending Shabbat with dear friends in Ramat Beit Shemesh. Over the years, it has become a tradition to spend Parshat Noah with them. The week leading up to that Shabbat is always particularly hectic for me, as I’m busy preparing and selling my rainbow challah dough. My dear friend Gila knows just how busy I am and generously invites us to spend Shabbat with her family.
What makes these visits so special is that our families are all friends. Our husbands enjoy spending time together, our daughters are the same age, and I treasure the opportunity to catch up with Gila, whom I don’t get to see nearly often enough. It’s always a Shabbat filled with good company, wonderful conversations, and delicious food.
This year, I was especially impressed by how Gila pulled everything together. She works full-time, is a very hands-on mother, and still manages to serve an incredible variety of delicious dishes, all with a smile. What impressed me most was how simple many of the recipes were to prepare, yet how flavorful the results were.
With shorter Fridays upon us, I thought this was the perfect time to share some of the inspiration I brought home from Gila’s kitchen. These recipes are simple, require minimal hands-on preparation, and prove that a delicious Shabbat meal doesn’t have to mean spending the entire Friday cooking.
All-purpose spice mix
One of my favorite kitchen shortcuts is keeping a homemade spice mix ready to use. When you’re preparing several dishes for Shabbat, the last thing you want is to keep pulling out five or six different spices for every recipe. Having one jar of your favorite seasoning blend makes cooking quicker, easier, and creates less cleanup.
I use my spice mix on just about everything, from roasted vegetables and potatoes to chicken, fish, soups, and meat dishes. The best part is that you can make it your own. Use the spices your family enjoys, adjust the seasonings to your taste, and create a blend that works with your everyday cooking. It takes just a few minutes to prepare but saves time throughout the week.
Prep time: 5 minutes
Yield: Approximately ½ cup
1 clean, dry, empty spice jar, approximately 150-200 ml. in capacity, with a tight-fitting lid
3 Tbsp garlic powder
2 Tbsp dried onion flakes or onion powder
1 Tbsp sweet paprika
1 Tbsp dried parsley flakes
1½ tsp kosher salt
1 tsp ground black pepper
½ tsp turmeric
½ tsp ground ginger
¼ tsp hot red pepper flakes, optional
Add all the spices directly into the empty spice jar. Close the lid tightly and shake well until all the spices are evenly combined.
Store in a cool, dry place away from heat and moisture. Use to season roasted vegetables, potatoes, chicken, fish, soups, and meat dishes.
For a larger batch, double the recipe and use a larger spice container, approximately 330 g. in size.
Kitchen Tip: Keep your spice mix within easy reach when cooking. Whether you’re preparing a full Shabbat menu or a quick weekday dinner, having your favorite seasonings combined in one jar means fewer containers to open, fewer things to put away, and a little less time spent in the kitchen.
Golden roasted vegetables
I always thought I didn’t like fennel because of its licorice-like flavor. But on Friday night, when Gila served roasted fennel alongside red onions, she encouraged me to give it a try. I told her I wasn’t a fan of the licorice taste, but she explained that roasting it with a little olive oil and salt changes the flavor completely.
I decided to put some on my plate and was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed it! The roasted onions were just as delicious, and the two went beautifully together.
Inspired by Gila’s dish, I decided to add kohlrabi, which often sits right next to the fennel in the supermarket. I sliced all three vegetables, roasted them together, and ended up with a simple dish bursting with flavor. It’s a wonderful addition to a main course, alongside other side dishes, or even served with fresh bread and dips.
Yield: 4-6 servings
2 red onions, sliced into half-moons
1 fennel bulb, thinly sliced
1 kohlrabi, peeled and sliced into thin strips
3 Tbsp olive oil
1 tsp kosher salt
½ tsp ground black pepper
1 tsp balsamic vinegar, optional
Preheat the oven to 200° Celsius. Line a large baking sheet with baking paper.
Cut off the green stalks and fronds of the fennel, using only the white bulb. Trim the base, remove any tough outer layer, and slice the bulb thinly. Peel the kohlrabi and cut it into thin strips. Peel the red onions, cut them in half, and slice into half-moons.
Spread all three vegetables on the prepared baking sheet. Drizzle with olive oil, add the salt, pepper, and a small splash of balsamic vinegar, if using, and toss until evenly coated.
Roast for 30-40 minutes, gently mixing once halfway through, until the vegetables are tender and lightly caramelized around the edges.
Serve warm or at room temperature.
Pot roast with za’atar
When Gila was planning our Shabbat meals, she mentioned to her coworker Barbara that she was looking for a new meat recipe for her Friday night guests. Barbara was happy to share one of her favorites, and Gila decided to give it a try.
Before preparing the roast, Gila checked with me to make sure we didn’t have any allergies to za’atar. I assured her that za’atar was fine, but I remember wondering why anyone would put za’atar on a pot roast. Well, one bite was all it took to understand! The meat was incredibly tender and flavorful, and the za’atar added a subtle richness without overpowering the natural flavor of the beef.
What makes this recipe even better is how simple it is to prepare. Everything cooks in one large pot on the stovetop, with very little attention needed once it’s simmering. I think you could even add some small potatoes to the pot and have an entire Friday night dinner ready with hardly any extra effort.
Yields 8-10 servings
1 beef shoulder roast (Israeli cut No. 5), approximately 2-2.5 kg.
2-3 large onions, sliced
2 Tbsp olive oil
6 cloves garlic
4 Carrots, cut into strips
1 Tbsp za’atar seasoning
1-2 Tbsp All-Purpose Spice Mix (recipe above)
1 tsp kosher salt
½ tsp ground black pepper
1 cup red wine
1 cup water
Drizzle a little olive oil into a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Add the shoulder roast and sear on all sides until nicely browned, approximately 5 minutes per side. Remove the meat from the pot and set aside.
Add a little more olive oil to the same pot, followed by the sliced onions. Sauté for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add the carrot strips and garlic, and continue sautéing for another 5 minutes, until the vegetables begin to soften.
Return the roast to the pot, placing it on top of the vegetables. Sprinkle the za’atar and 1-2 Tbsp of the Everyday All-Purpose Spice Mix (recipe included in this article) over the meat.
Pour in the red wine and water, bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low and cover the pot. Cook for approximately 3½-4 hours until fork-tender. Check occasionally to make sure there is enough liquid in the pot, adding a little water if needed.
Allow the roast to cool slightly before slicing. Serve with the softened vegetables and cooking juices spooned over the meat.
Optional: Add small potatoes to the pot during the last 60-90 minutes of cooking for an easy, complete Friday night dinner.
Orange coconut cake
After Friday night dinner, Gila and her husband opened their home to the neighborhood for a gathering filled with inspiring words from my wonderful rabbi husband, as well as singing and refreshments. We all pitched in to help set up, and my daughter happily volunteered to cut one of the cakes into squares and arrange them in cupcake holders on a dessert platter.
Of course, there’s an unwritten rule that you can’t cut a cake without tasting it! My daughter, who loves baking, took her role as taste tester very seriously and was immediately impressed. She asked Gila for the recipe, which had been shared with her by her neighbor Idit, who happened to be at the gathering that evening. The original recipe came from Osem’s website, and I’ve made a few adjustments to simplify the preparation and make it my own.
My daughter noticed a flavor that was different from an ordinary vanilla cake and was surprised to discover that the secret ingredient was shredded coconut. It added a wonderful richness without making the cake grainy. The cake was incredibly light, fluffy, and moist, needing nothing more than a simple dusting of powdered sugar before serving.
Yields one 9 × 13” pan or one 24 cm. round pan
3 eggs
¾ cup sugar
1½ cups flour
2 tsp baking powder
1 package (80 g.) instant vanilla pudding mix
¾ cup oil
¼ cup shredded coconut
1 cup orange juice
Preheat the oven to 170°. Grease your cake pan.
Using an electric mixer, beat the eggs and sugar for 3-4 minutes, until light and fluffy.
Add the oil, instant vanilla pudding mix, and orange juice. Mix gently, then add the flour, baking powder, and shredded coconut. Mix on low speed just until incorporated, being careful not to overmix.
Pour the batter into the prepared pan and bake for approximately 40 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean.
Allow the cake to cool before dusting with powdered sugar, if desired.
I KNOW these shorter Fridays are going to take some getting used to, but the good news is that by the time we adjust, the days will already be getting longer again!
In the meantime, I’m looking forward to those long, cozy Friday nights filled with games, good conversation, and maybe even a chance to catch up on some reading.
Most importantly, I’ll be making sure I have a plan to keep Fridays simple. By preparing what I can throughout the week and leaving less cooking for Friday, I can spend more time enjoying Shabbat and less time rushing to get everything done.
Wishing you all a cozy Shabbat, filled with delicious food and surrounded by the people you love.■

Turkish delight: A top-notch Israeli meal at Tel Aviv's Turkish Grill - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:26:36 UTC
20:26:36 KST

Growing up in England, where a salad meant lettuce, a few tomato and cucumber slices, and bottled dressing, the Israeli custom of starting a meal with several small dishes of different salads is a welcome change.
While not unique to Israel, the custom is popular across the Middle East. I, for one, think it an excellent start to a meal with healthy vegetables served in a distinctive variety of flavors.
A remarkable variety of vegetables and spices
At Turkish Grill, a meat restaurant on the outskirts of Tel Aviv that we visited recently, there are 12 such salads served with soft, fluffy laffas (Iraqi pitas) as a first course (NIS 30 per diner).
The variety was remarkable. Think of a vegetable and there it was, transformed into a salad: corn, avocado, eggplant, tomatoes, cucumbers, sweet potatoes, beets, cabbage, and one non-vegetable, eggs, had all been turned into tasty starters.
Without describing each one, I can say that none were overly oily or spicy, except for one: the Turkish salad, which was peppery by any standards.
My favorite was the sweet potato. It was cut into small pieces, possibly fried, and then dipped in silan (date syrup). It was sweet and positively addictive.
I also liked the eggplant very much, which was roasted, and the inside turned into a spread with the familiar burnt flavor of what some call “aubergine caviar.” The corn salad had mushrooms and red pepper garnish, the avocado was very green and not too lemony, and the beetroot salad was sweet and acidic.
While enjoying the starters, a large salad arrived alongside a plate of hummus and tahini to share. Everything was very fresh and appealing.
For a main course, we received three massive skewers. One was pieces of entrecote steak, which were crisp on the outside and tender within, and tasted great. The second skewer had chunks of pargit (spring chicken), and the third held pieces of meat meant to simulate lamb, since they were dipped in lamb fat before cooking. Although not quite like the real thing, they were an acceptable substitute (skewers, NIS 42 and 63).
Good service, excellent food, and a friendly ambiance
The restaurant, which was crowded with families having an early supper, is situated in a largely Sephardi area. It was pleasant to see so many people enjoying the food and the surroundings.
They had several dessert options on the menu, but we declined and had a sweet green tea to round off the meal.
Though they didn’t have Turkish Delight, the dessert options they had were rotondo (decadent, multi-layered Italian pastry), creme brulee, chocolate soufflé, hot chocolate cake, creamino (inspired by cremino, a tri-layered chocolate confection from Italy’s Piedmont region), and handmade baklava (NIS 20-28).
It was a very enjoyable meal with good service, excellent food, and a friendly ambiance – everything a good meal out should be.
Turkish Grill
2 Ha’Avoda St., Or Yehuda
Call: 053 623 8221
Open: Sun.-Thurs. 11 a.m.-midnight; Fri. closed; Sat. after Shabbat-midnight.
Kashrut: Badatz Beit Yosef
The writer was a guest of the restaurant.

Roshel has sent nearly 3,000 Senator vehicles to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:22:17 UTC
20:22:17 KST

- Canadian manufacturer Roshel says nearly 3,000 Senator armored vehicles have gone to Ukraine, as one of its Senator MRAPs went on display at the Canadian War Museum.
- Canada committed 383 more Senators in February 2026, and Mexico, Moldova and a U.S. federal agency are also buying the vehicle.
Nearly 3,000 Senator armored vehicles built by Canadian manufacturer Roshel have now gone to Ukraine, the company said on social media as it placed one of its first-generation Senator MRAPs on permanent display at the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa.
The figure makes the Senator one of the most numerous Western-supplied armored vehicles in Ukrainian service. Roshel did not give an exact count or say how many of the vehicles were paid for by Canada, by Ukraine itself or by other donor countries.
“Nearly 3,000 Senators have gone to Ukraine, a symbol of Canadian support for those defending their country,” Roshel said.
The company’s tally has climbed steadily since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Roshel said it had delivered 1,400 Senators by the fall of 2024 and more than 2,000 by December 2025, and the Canadian Defence Review put the number at more than 2,700 this week. The Senator is used by Ukraine’s armed forces and its Border Guard Service to carry troops, evacuate wounded and run patrols and reconnaissance.
Canada’s own donations make up only part of the total. Ottawa announced its first package of 200 Senators in January 2023, worth CAD 90 million, and in February 2026 it committed another 383 Senators along with 66 LAV 6 armored vehicles from General Dynamics Land Systems Canada. Other countries have bought Senators for Ukraine through aid packages, and Ukraine has purchased some directly.
The Senator is built on a Ford F-550 heavy commercial truck chassis, a choice that lets Roshel produce it faster and more cheaply than purpose-built armored vehicles. The MRAP version, short for mine-resistant ambush-protected, meets NATO STANAG 4569 protection Levels 2 and 3 and is designed to survive the detonation of up to 8 kg (17.6 pounds) of explosives. Founded in 2016 in Brampton, Ontario, Roshel began building the Senator in 2018, mainly for police and security agencies in North America, before wartime orders from Ukraine expanded its production. Canada’s defense minister said in March that the program supports close to 500 jobs in Brampton and nearby Mississauga.
Roshel also sells the Senator well beyond Ukraine, including to U.S. federal agencies. NASA used a Senator to escort astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley to the launch pad at Kennedy Space Center for SpaceX’s Crew Dragon Demo-2 mission in May 2020, the first crewed launch from U.S. soil in nearly a decade. In November 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement awarded Roshel a sole-source contract worth about $7.3 million for 20 Senator emergency response vehicles, CBC News reported, citing procurement records that said only Roshel could deliver within 30 days. ICE said the vehicles qualify under Buy American rules because they are produced in the United States; Roshel opened a plant in Michigan in 2024. The deal drew criticism from some Canadian politicians and advocacy groups over ICE’s immigration enforcement. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is also buying a Senator for its special response team.
Elsewhere, Mexico selected the Senator MRAP earlier this year after trials with its armed forces and national guard, and Moldova’s military is due to receive more than 100 Senators funded by the European Union by May 2027. The company has also supplied vehicles to Haiti, Brazil, South Korea, Costa Rica and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

How to ‘fall back’ this weekend without losing your mind

11:19:23 UTC
20:19:23 KST

At 2 A.M. on Sunday, most of the U.S. will set the clocks back by an hour. With the switch to standard time, we’ll get earlier sunshine and darker evenings—and an extra hour of sleep.
Research suggests standard time better aligns with our circadian rhythm, or internal clock, and reduces the risk of health complications. But changing to standard time comes with some risks, too, experts say.
Between “falling back” to standard time in November and “springing forward” to daylight saving time (DST) in March, experts say the switch to DST is the bigger disruption. In the days after the March time change, scientists have measured higher rates of lost sleep and an uptick in heart attacks. After the time change in November, however, those risks are lower.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Some research suggests rates of stroke go up around both spring and fall clock changes, although the risk of death is higher in the spring, says Beth Malow, a professor of neurology and pediatrics at Vanderbilt University.
On standard time, early risers get the benefit of a little more morning sunlight. Morning light is “one of the strongest forces” that aligns our bodies’ circadian rhythm with the outside world, Malow says. That alignment helps us wake up in the morning and drift off at night more easily.
After the fall time change, you might wake up well after the sun comes up—but that poses less of a risk than cutting off your body’s internal clock early, says Jamie Zeitzer, a professor and a sleep scientist at Stanford University. “You’re basically sleeping in,” he adds.
In fact, given the overall benefits of standard time, top medical organizations, including the American Medical Association, Sleep Research Society and American Academy of Sleep Medicine have fought efforts to make DST permanent—a frequent hobbyhorse in Congress.
A major downside to standard time, however, is less time spent outdoors. Some studies also suggest moving commuting times nearer to dusk in the fall increases the risk of vehicle collisions with deer and other wildlife, which are more active around sunset.
There are certain steps you can take to ensure a more smooth transition, experts say.
Number one, don’t go into a clock change while sleep-deprived, Malow says. And try to get as much exposure to morning light as possible throughout the season. (If you’re able to access one, a light box can be helpful for this on dark mornings in the spring.) Stay alert during dark commutes, when visibility may be limited, whether they’re on a spring morning or a fall evening, Malow adds. And if you’re consistently struggling with sleep, consider seeing a doctor.
In the fall, you may need to take extra care to get regular evening exercise in. And if you, like many Americans, aren’t getting enough shut-eye on most nights, consider using the clock change to set a new sleep habit, Malow says.
If your usual bedtime is 11 P.M., for instance, try going to bed when you’re tired instead—after the time change, that will be when the clocks read about 10 P.M.—and try to stick to the new schedule. “Take advantage of the fact that your body’s now going to be ready to go to bed earlier,” she says.
If nothing else, relish “sleeping in,” Zeitzer says. “Enjoy the extra hour of sleep.”

How your brain can turn your own reflection into something unrecognizable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:19:02 UTC
20:19:02 KST

It’s Halloween night. Someone has dared you to turn off the lights and stand in front of the mirror. The rules are simple, stare into your reflection and say her name three times.
Bloody Mary. Bloody Mary. Bloody Mary.
According to the creepy urban legend, a terrifying figure will appear in the glass. Depending on which version of the story you follow, she might be a bloodied woman, a witch or a ghost seeking revenge. Sometimes, she simply appears behind you. In more sinister versions, she reaches out of the mirror.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Most of us encountered some variation of this story as children. Those brave enough to have tried it may even swear they saw a monstrous face appear in the mirror before them.
As tempting as it might be to believe that the monster you saw in mirror was something supernatural, the real explanation is perhaps even stranger. Your brain is perfectly capable of turning your own reflection into something you barely recognize.
The monster in the mirror
In 2010, Italian psychologist Giovanni Caputo published a study with the intriguing title Strange-face-in-the-mirror illusion. He asked 66 volunteers to sit approximately 40 centimeters from a mirror in a dimly lit room and look at their own faces for one minute.
Around two-thirds reported significant distortions of their faces. More than a quarter described seeing an unfamiliar person, while others reported fantastical beings, animals or the faces of relatives – sometimes deceased. Some changes began after less than a minute.
The participants weren’t being asked to summon ghosts. They were simply looking at themselves. So why would something as familiar as our own face suddenly become strange?
The explanation partly lies in the 1804 work done by Swiss physician Ignaz Paul Vital Troxler who described a curious phenomenon. When we fix our gaze on one point, objects elsewhere in our visual field can gradually fade from awareness. This is now known as the Troxler effect, or Troxler fading.
This effect happens partly because sensory neurons, which detect and transmit information about what we see, adapt to relatively constant stimulation. Our visual system is particularly interested in change: movement, shifting contrast and anything that might require our attention.
Normally, we hardly notice this process. Even when we believe we’re staring steadily, our eyes make tiny movements that continually refresh visual information. But prolonged fixation can allow relatively stable features, particularly those away from the centre of our gaze, to become less distinct.
Now imagine applying this to your face. When you stare at your own eyes in a mirror, the surrounding features remain relatively stationary. The contours of your cheeks, the edges of your nose and the outline of your mouth provide a fairly constant pattern of information.
But in dim light, those features are already harder to distinguish—so the Troxler effect alone cannot explain why someone might see an entirely different face. For that, we need to consider how the brain recognizes faces.
Human beings are extraordinarily sensitive to faces. We can recognize familiar people from surprisingly little visual information and detect subtle changes in expression.
This ability involves a network of brain regions, including the fusiform face area, which responds particularly strongly to faces. Rather than analyzing every feature independently, our visual system processes the relationships between them—including the distance between the eyes, the position of the nose and the arrangement of facial features.
When you look into a mirror, your brain isn’t simply recording what is in front of you. It interprets visual information using previous experience and expectations—and there’s perhaps no face you know better than your own. But under dim lighting, the information arriving from your eyes becomes less reliable. Shadows obscure features, contrast diminishes and the relationships between parts of the face become harder to resolve.
The brain must continue interpreting this increasingly ambiguous information. Sometimes the result is a distorted version of your own face. Sometimes it resembles another person altogether.
The mechanisms behind these illusions are still under investigation. But what makes the experience disturbing is that the reflection remains recognizably human while no longer appearing to belong to you.
Haunted mirrors
Long before children began summoning Bloody Mary, reflective surfaces were associated with spirits, prophecy and the dead.
The ancient practice of catoptromancy involved divination using mirrors. Related traditions of scrying involved gazing into reflective surfaces in the hope of seeing visions or messages hidden from ordinary sight.
Mirrors also acquired significance in mourning traditions. In some communities, they were covered following a death because of the belief they could trap the soul or reveal the dead. Other traditions have different explanations for covering mirrors – including setting aside concerns about personal appearance during mourning.
We cannot conclude that visual illusions gave rise to these customs. But it’s intriguing that prolonged staring, low illumination and the expectation of seeing something unusual feature in both supernatural mirror rituals and experiments producing perceptual distortions.
The Bloody Mary ritual adds another ingredient: anticipation. You expect something frightening, and that expectation may influence how you interpret ambiguous shadows and unfamiliar features.
In this way, the ritual creates the very conditions in which something unsettling might appear. The legend tells you what to expect, and your visual system may provide something that seems to confirm it. So, this Halloween, remember that you don’t need to believe in ghosts for something strange to happen.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Evacuated Ukrainians from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Belarus
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:18:14 GMT
20:18:14 KST

Evacuees from Russia-occupied city where residents ate weeds arrive in Ukraine
- Published
People evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have crossed into the Ukrainian controlled region of Chernihiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky has confirmed.
Residents of the frontline city had been trapped without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
The Ukrainian president thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts in brokering a local ceasefire that paved the way for their evacuation on Friday.
The evacuees were taken via Russia and Belarus before being driven across Ukraine's northern border on Saturday.
"As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region," Zelensky said in a post on X.
"All of them will receive the assistance they need. It is important that government agencies and all the regional and local authorities involved work effectively and help our people adapt."
A humanitarian ceasefire took effect across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday, providing the first few days of peace in the area in four years, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Conditions had become so desperate in Oleshky that not only was getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escape was highly dangerous because the routes out had been mined and subject to drone attack.
Bridges across the nearby River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank has been mined and is dangerous.
One resident who fled the city three weeks earlier told the BBC he had walked through 24km (15 miles) of minefields to get to safety.
The ceasefire allowed the road out of the city to be cleared of mines and humanitarian aid to be delivered.
Ceasefire measures will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.
Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Ukrainian military positions lie just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky but evacuees first had to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa, where they flew to Gomel in Belarus, before finally travelling on to Ukraine.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
Before the war, Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".
Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
Zelensky praised Lubinets and his team for helping the evacuees be moved to safety.
The Ukrainian president also thanked those who had helped bring attention to the "true humanitarian catastrophe in Ukrainian territory temporarily occupied by Russia".
The ceasefire has required close cooperation between Lubinets and Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.
But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.

Germany news: Merkel calls for first female president

- Several women are being discussed as possible successors to Frank-Walter Steinmeier, but no candidate has yet been agreed upon
- Berlin's Left Party is expected to approve coalition talks with the Social Democrats and Greens, potentially paving the way for its first mayor
- Delegates are meeting under tight security amid threats and planned protests
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, August 10, 2026:
Merkel calls for Germany's first female president
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called for a woman to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, pointing out that no woman has held the office in the country's 77-year history.
Everyone should ask "whether it might finally be time," Merkel told MagentaTV.
She said she knew women capable of doing the job but declined to name anyone.
The Federal Convention elects Germany's next head of state on January 30. Steinmeier cannot seek a third consecutive term. The presidency is mostly a ceremonial role.
Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner has the backing of Markus Soder, leader of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).
Other names being discussed include Bundestag president Julia Klockner, Education Minister Karin Prien and former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, all from Merkel's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Merkel described the debate as "strange" and criticized its "unpleasant undertone."
She also challenged her party's direction, saying the CDU's identity went beyond economic policy. "The CDU was always about building bridges to all parts of society — and that must be brought back to the forefront."
Berlin's Left Party weighs coalition talks under tight security
Berlin's socialist Left Party is expected to approve coalition negotiations with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and environmentalist Greens, potentially paving the way for the city's first Left Party mayor.
The SPD and Greens have already backed talks, which could begin on Monday. But the Left Party's youth wing opposes the alliance, calling instead for a "strong socialist opposition."
Delegates gathered under tight security in Berlin's Lichtenberg district following calls for protests accusing the party of betraying voters. Its candidate for mayor, Elif Eralp, has been given personal protection.
The Left Party won September's election with 25.7% of the vote. The governing coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and SPD lost its majority.
If the three parties reach a deal, Eralp, currently the Left Party's parliamentary leader in Berlin, could become the city's next governing mayor.

Bangladesh death toll from dengue rises, unlikely to ease before December
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:15:06 CET
20:15:06 KST

DHAKA, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Bangladesh recorded its highest monthly dengue death toll of the year in October, with experts warning the outbreak is unlikely to ease significantly before December.
The outbreak has killed 418 people and led to more than 133,000 hospital admissions this year as of October 30, according to health ministry data. October alone accounted for 173 deaths, surpassing September’s 148 and making it the deadliest month of 2026 so far.
The surge comes as Bangladesh is also battling the world’s worst measles outbreak, which has killed more than 1,200 people, placing additional strain on an already stretched healthcare system.
HOSPITALS UNDER PRESSURE
Doctors said many dengue patients were only seeking hospital admission after developing severe complications. At the state-run Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Dhaka, 279 dengue patients were being treated after 67 new admissions in a single day, hospital director Mirza Golam Sarwar said.
“We are getting many patients in shock. Their blood pressure is sometimes too low to measure, and their oxygen levels are dropping,” he said.
Medicine specialist ABM Abdullah said repeat infections and delays in diagnosis and treatment were driving severe cases and deaths.
“People who have had dengue before may face a greater risk of severe illness if they become infected again,” he said, urging people to eliminate mosquito breeding sites and seek care as soon as symptoms appear.
Dhaka resident Faisal Ferdous, 33, was diagnosed with dengue in 2017, 2024 and again earlier this month. “This time, both my wife and I needed hospital treatment,” said Ferdous, who is now at home recovering.
Ferdous said the couple fell ill shortly after spending several days at a hospital where their five-year-old son was being treated for an unrelated illness.
“Every bout has been difficult, and after getting it repeatedly, you become increasingly concerned about the risk of severe illness,” he said.
Health experts warn that the circulation of all four dengue virus serotypes is increasing the risk of severe disease. People infected with one strain can later contract another, raising the likelihood of complications. Bangladesh has yet to introduce a dengue vaccine, although authorities are considering one as a longer-term measure.
CLIMATE CHANGE EXTENDS DENGUE SEASON
Entomologist Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University said deaths were unlikely to continue rising at October’s pace, but transmission would probably persist through November.
“We may see some relief, but dengue is unlikely to disappear in November. Any decline is likely to be modest, with significant improvement unlikely before December,” he said.
Bashar said mosquitoes would continue emerging from breeding sites created by earlier rainfall, sustaining transmission even as conditions become drier. Changing rainfall and humidity patterns, partly linked to climate change, were extending mosquito breeding seasons and keeping Aedes mosquitoes active for longer, he said.
(Reporting by Ruma Paul; Editing by Susan Fenton)

TAIPEI, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an, in a close race for re-election, got an angry reception on Saturday when be briefly showed up for Taiwan’s packed annual Pride parade, following a police raid on a city gay bar earlier this month.
The raid struck a nerve in Taiwan, which legalised same-sex marriage in 2019 in a first for Asia and is proud of its reputation as a bastion of LGBTQ+ rights in a region where they are often repressed.
More than 170,000 people joined Saturday’s parade, which is east Asia’s largest Pride event.
Chiang, from the opposition Kuomintang party and who has previously expressed his support for the LGBTQ+ community, arrived at the end of the parade and stayed for only around 15 minutes.

“I already said this earlier: I apologise for the impact on those affected,” Chiang told reporters. “So on this matter, we will conduct a rigorous investigation and impose immediate discipline.”
He then posed for pictures with a few supporters as he left, surrounded by reporters and security with protesters continuing to shout.
THIS YEAR’S THEME REVISED AFTER RAID
Alan Chang, 30, said it was “ridiculous and unbelievable” that such a raid could have even happened.
“This is a country and a city that emphasises gender equality and our mayor would condone this?” he added.
Shen, who some opinion polls have put ahead of Chiang, appeared at a different part of the rally where he was warmly greeted by the crowd.

Taipei police raided the Commander D bar in the city’s main gay neighbourhood of Ximen this month and took 51 people in for questioning and arrested the owner.
Some were detained for more than six hours after police accused them of violating a law that prohibits “wantonly exposing one’s naked body or presenting a lascivious posture in a public place.”
