Loading
US voters will soon deliver a national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states and state legislatures across the country. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.
Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about extremism in US politics, their confidence in the US voting system, what they hope Congress will tackle first and their views of the president’s secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.
The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood days before voters head to the polls. The Guardian will return to its voter panel after final votes are cast.
Do you think this election cycle has seen more extreme candidates? If so, who?
Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive
 The times that we’re living through has created a certain extremism. My bias is that I see the extremism on the right. I see the extremism of Trump’s influence on the candidates, on the electorate and the people that I live with every day here in Taylor county. I’ve not been a fan of Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin. He showed his extremism from the very start, seeking to undermine the 2020 election, voting for war, supporting tariffs, never swerving from the lockstep Maga extremist playbook, essentially.
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive
 It depends on what you mean by extreme. We have certainly seen way more candidates than usual making it out of the Democratic primaries who do not take billionaire or foreign lobby money, like Angie Nixon [in Florida] or Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan]. While this shift is seen as electorally threatening to some, most of these candidates who are typically the ones labeled as “extreme” have policy prescriptions that are very close to the average American’s views, especially when it comes to topics like healthcare reform or participation in forever wars. Looking at the other side of the aisle, I do think there has been an emergence of candidates who display an “extreme” level of corruption and bigotry typically only seen coming from the White House these days. Mike Rogers [Republican Senate candidate for Michigan] comes to mind, with his main campaign strategy seemingly being a desperate bid to tie El-Sayed to anything radical or Islamist, and so does Vivek Ramaswamy’s notable doubling-down on a campaign ad implying his gubernatorial opponent [in Ohio] lied about her childhood sexual abuse.
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican
 Most of the Democratic candidates are extreme. This political cycle has produced more extreme candidates than ever before. I’m 70 years old and I’ve never been involved in active politics. I’ve always voted since I was 18 and I’ve always voted conservative Republican but I’ve never seen anything that’s so extreme. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan is one that stands out and some have already been elected like the mayor of New York [Zohran Mamdani]. I never thought I would see someone that far left voted in.
Do you think this election will be free and fair?
Sally Rasmussen 62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressive
 I believe that at the most local level, it will overwhelmingly be free and fair. And by that I mean that I have a great deal of faith in the town clerks and the county clerks, the people who, at the ground level, oversee elections and whose livelihoods, whose reputations are on the line. On the national level, I have every expectation that the extremists that are currently in power will do whatever they can to, well, to cheat, to break the law, to violate constitutional rights of the people, and to try to deny election results, as happened after the 2020 election.
Patti Fucci 46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderate
 The election itself will be free and fair as it’s conducted. However, we’re already seeing all the multiple attempts in the past two weeks of different types of intimidation from the justice department trying to interfere with elections. And we’ve seen that in California, we’ve seen it right now in Alaska, we’ve seen it here. So, they’re using the many tactics of intimidation and meddling and propaganda to interfere in the elections. But when I look at the amount of people that have already voted early, I think that’s the biggest guardrail that this election has.
Sharon Anderson 70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republican
 I can only hope. I’m thankful for the steps that the Republican party has followed with monitors and people watching the polls because, if an election is won fair and square, I am thrilled. That is the way of the people but, if there’s any cheating going on or one vote that is fraudulent, that vote should be thrown out because that’s not what this nation is based on. In some countries, people have died for fair elections and, unless we have fair elections, it’s to the good of no one.
Morgan Akin 85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderate
 Being a poll worker and observing what goes on, I think [elections] go on pretty well anywhere in the country. I think you will see a fair election. Unfortunately, maybe, delayed or not approved by the Trump administration. He’s saying if the GOP loses in Alaska, he’s not going to recognize it. [But] I think the Democrats have been anticipating this all along and have been putting together different ways of challenging him in the courts.
If your party wins next week, what are you hoping they will do first?
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive
 I am hoping Democrats immediately reinstate and expand the ACA, [the Affordable Care Act], pass a war powers resolution to end engagement with Iran, pass an AI datacenter moratorium, end all military aid to Israel, reverse the White House’s cancellation of federally approved funding, undo the blanket tariffs, release the Epstein files, and scrutinize and impeach the cabinet and president. I also hope they fight to advance Medicare for All, a substantial increase in the federal minimum wage, and robust federal job and housing programs.
Yajaira Martinez 43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voter
 Whichever party wins, I really hope they focus on doing the right thing and bring ICE under control. Right now, here in the Rio Grande valley, ICE is profiling individuals of a certain color, Hispanic people, and they are chasing them down, arresting and assaulting them. I’m not saying that they shouldn’t deport people, but it’s got to be done the right way, the legal way.
Morgan Akin 85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderate
 I hope they will first [address] gas prices, food prices, medical costs and interest rates, and all of the things that are hurting the economy right now. I don’t think it’s time to talk about impeachment or anything like that. It would just cause more problems than necessary.
Justin Daniels 45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressive
 Bring civility back to society. It seems as though there’s something going on in society, and there’s a race to the bottom. Democrats had power before, and they spend so much time arguing amongst themselves. I think that when Democrats win, the speed of which society is collapsing will slow down, but it will not stop.
Caleb Davis 22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservative

Scott Akridge 60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberal
 Stop ICE by any means necessary. Their harmful impact is threatening the lives of innocent people daily, and it makes us look like we’re run by a third world cartel. Obama deported just as many illegal immigrants, focusing on actual criminals and not using unchecked violence against families. No civilians were casually murdered on his watch.
Next, start impeachment proceedings and investigations into all the blatant and rampant corruption that the GOP has repeatedly ignored. What do you think of Pete Hegseth? What was your reaction to the idea of livestreaming an execution?
David Ferrari 19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressive

 We need a strong leader in any position that we have in the country. I think it would just be another black mark on his ability to carry out his job.

Top Democrats are fighting a billionaire tax in California. Their voters are on the other side |
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:41 UTC
20:00:41 KST

Midway through this summer, a high-quality poll found that Democrats in California were overwhelmingly in favor of the upcoming ballot measure for a one-time 5% tax on billionaire wealth.
The ratio was more than 4 to 1. But the state’s most powerful Democrats – including the governor Gavin Newsom, his near-certain successor Xavier Becerra and the Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass – have lined up with Silicon Valley billionaires who’ve raised upward of $340m to defeat the initiative.
While Newsom has led the charge against the measure, most Democratic leaders in the deep-blue state have opted to duck. California’s senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff have stayed mum on Proposition 40. The same is true of the former vice-president Kamala Harris and the former House speaker Nancy Pelosi.
“Neither wants to alienate wealthy donors or their allies in labor by publicly opposing it,” the San Francisco Chronicle noted in mid-October. “But their silence on such a high-profile measure is giving cover to the billionaires” fighting the measure.
Nine-tenths of the billionaire tax revenue from Proposition 40 would go to healthcare for Californians in need. As the New York Times reported this month, “California stands to lose around $100 billion in federal Medicaid funding over the next five years, threatening healthcare coverage for millions of low-income residents, as well as the potential closure of hospitals and other facilities.”
With so much at stake in human terms, refusal to back Proposition 40 runs directly counter to standard rhetoric from Democratic politicians about standing up to the ultra-wealthy on behalf of the disadvantaged.
The stance of Newsom and other Democratic heavyweights in the state puts them on the side of billionaires in ongoing class war. The effect is that party leaders are offering a kinder, gentler oligarchy as an alternative to the far more corrupt Trumpist version.
Overall, a semblance of party unity has taken hold with the midterm elections looming. But clashes between corporate Democrats and progressives will soon begin to escalate.
The fact that the most prominent Democrats in the country’s most populous state are at loggerheads with the party’s grassroots on Prop 40 is a bad sign, but it’s hardly an anomaly.
Every time a general election nears, party leaders fervently call for a huge turnout – but their disconnect from the party’s base discourages turnout. California’s billionaire tax proposal is unprecedented, but the response to it from Democratic party elites is part of a pattern that has undermined capacities to build populist momentum against Republicans, let alone advance progressive agendas favored by voters.
Now being vilified by an onslaught of attack ads, Proposition 40 might get buried under the avalanche of billionaire cash (with nearly half coming from the Google co-founder Sergey Brin). The proposal’s foes have out-fundraised supporters by nearly 10-1.
But whatever the election’s outcome is on 3 November, campaigning to tax the wealth of the country’s nearly 1,000 billionaires has enormous potential nationwide.
In early August, the California Democratic Party executive board, hardly a bastion of class struggle, voted to give the party’s endorsement to Prop 40. But, undeterred, Newsom has gone all-out to fight the billionaire tax proposal as well as to boost another ballot measure that would nullify any such tax.
When I contacted a former chair of the state party’s Progressive Caucus, he was matter-of-fact about the alliance of big tech moguls with the current and next governor. “When it comes to Newsom and Becerra opposing the billionaire tax,” said Amar Shergill, a Sacramento-based attorney, “you need know only two things. First, Newsom needs billionaire money for his presidential campaign. Second, Becerra needs to pay back the billionaires that made him governor. The rest of the corporate Democrats in office are some version of these stories.”
Newsom became governor in 2019, following Jerry Brown’s second eight-year stretch in the job. His unique style aside, Brown has long been a kind of prototype for the state’s Democratic leadership now typified by Newsom.
“The way you have to approach the political process is something like piloting a canoe,” Brown said in 1979 during his first stint as governor. He explained: “If you paddle a little bit on the left side, then you paddle a little bit on the right side, you keep going right down the middle.”
This year, Brown has stayed out of the battle over Proposition 40. In late October, when I emailed the former governor to ask whether he supports it, he replied: “I have not discussed the proposition. There is already a plethora of opinions on the measure.”
Weeks ago, during a BBC interview, Brown lamented: “The gains for those who succeed at the top are getting bigger and richer, and the sustenance at the bottom and the middle is getting less and less.” He added: “We obviously need a wealth tax. If Tesla wants to give Elon Musk a trillion dollars over 10 years, then the people have to take back 99% of it. Now, can you get that? No, not at this point. Can you get it in one state? No, that would not work. Can you get it in one country? Probably not. So it would take an international agreement to tax the very wealthy, so that you can’t accumulate at the level that they are today.”
Brown and Newsom share a fondness for voicing lofty principles while kicking them very far down the road, tacitly equating deference to corporate power with realism. Newsom says – with scant details – that he would support a federal tax on billionaires. Meanwhile, he claims that approval of Proposition 40 would cause many of California’s more than 200 billionaires to move out of the state, with disastrous results.
“Proposed tax hikes on the rich invariably produce grim warnings of millionaire flight which then don’t eventuate,” the journalist Harold Meyerson recently pointed out. “Even if they did in this case, as a paper for the National Bureau of Economic Research has documented, the revenue gain of roughly $100 billion that the [billionaire] wealth tax would yield wouldn’t be offset by reductions in the income tax revenue produced by the flight of every one of those 200 billionaires until 25 years had passed. If just 50 of those 200 billionaires fled, it would take a full century.”
A large majority of the 45 Democrats in the California delegation to Congress richly deserve the “corporate” label. The official website of the Proposition 40 campaign lists only two congressional endorsers in the state. One of them, Representative Ro Khanna, has emerged as California’s most visible and vocal politician advocating for Prop 40.
“It’s the most important ballot initiative in America and in the world,” Khanna declared during a recent interview on MS Now. Looking ahead, he asked: “Are we going to continue to cater to a donor class that has hollowed out jobs, hollowed out the working class, and lost us two elections to Donald Trump?”
That kind of rhetorical question could progressively reframe the race for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.
“This is a fight for the soul of the Democratic party,” Khanna told me last weekend. “Will we be beholden to billionaire donors and offer platitudes without policy like Gavin Newsom, or will we reclaim our FDR courage and offer a bold vision for our nation’s future?”
Exactly 90 years ago, speaking at Madison Square Garden on the last day of October 1936, the then president Franklin Delano Roosevelt scorned the rightwing plutocrats of the day: “They are unanimous in their hate for me – and I welcome their hatred.” Leaders of today’s Democratic party have failed to earn such hatred.
- Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book is The Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for Autocracy

Christopher Capron obituary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:41 UTC
20:00:41 KST

Christopher Capron, who has died aged 90, was a well-regarded editor of the BBC’s flagship current affairs programme Panorama, and then the corporation’s head of current affairs, during which time he was a key player in the BBC’s battle for independence in the Thatcher era. He went on to form his own production company, and in 1994 became the first independent to be awarded the contract for the BBC’s Question Time.
As editor of Panorama from 1977 until 1979, he put the emphasis on original, often investigative 50-minute stories from around the world, during a time when money never seemed to be a problem. He ran a team that included the reporters Tom Mangold and Richard Lindley, and his award-winning programmes included a 1978 investigation by Philip Tibenham and Christopher Olgiati into the German rocket company Otrag testing space technology in central Africa, which won the Golden Nymph award at the Monte Carlo television festival, and Who Killed Georgi Markov?, Michael Cockerell and Philip Harding’s 1979 report on the murder of the Bulgarian dissident on British soil that pointed to the Bulgarian secret police and the KGB, which won an Emmy.
Capron never interfered during filming unless asked, and always backed his staff, as I found in 1977 when working as a producer with Lindley on an investigation into the tactics being used by the prime minister Ian Smith’s forces in what was then Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe). We were banned from returning to the country when it was broadcast.
For Mangold, Capron was “sharp and fast in the cutting rooms, he was happy mediating endless rows between reporters and producers, he fathered some great editions”. But in 1979 it came to an end, due to the then BBC rule of each Panorama editor only having two years at the helm.
He moved on to become deputy head and then head of BBC current affairs – and yet more battles, just as Margaret Thatcher had become prime minister. While deputy, he played a key role in defending Roger Bolton, the new Panorama editor, who had been dismissed after his team had contacts with the IRA. Capron was concerned it would be seen as giving in to government pressure. Bolton said: “He was rock solid in defending me and reinstating me as editor.”
In May 1982, just as the British fleet was sailing towards the Falklands, the next editor of Panorama, George Carey, broadcast a programme that included the views of those opposed to the war, alongside the government position presented by the Conservative party chair Cecil Parkinson. “A well-balanced programme, I thought,” said Carey.
Thatcher disagreed, and so did the Panorama presenter Robert Kee, who wrote to the Times disowning his own programme. Carey went to see Capron, now head of current affairs, who quietly moved Kee off to make documentaries, and Carey kept his job. “He was very good at protecting me from the politics of the BBC,” said Carey, “which obviously included governors getting agitated about politicians – notably Thatcher”.
After becoming head of parliamentary broadcasting – something of a disappointment because the Commons was not yet keen on being broadcast – in 1987 he started Capron Productions, run from an office near his London home in Wandsworth.
One of his first commissions was a follow-up for Thames Television to the controversial report Death on the Rock, which had examined the killing of IRA men in Gibraltar by the SAS. The programme had been edited by Bolton, who had left the BBC for the Thames programme This Week, and after Thames had commissioned an independent inquiry into the programme, Capron was asked to analyse their findings. “He was ruthlessly impartial,” said Bolton. “I would have expected nothing else.”
After producing Question Time for five years, Capron closed his company in 1999 and moved to Northamptonshire, where he owned the stately home Southwick Hall. His mother had lived there until her death in 1989, but Capron chose instead to stay at the Old Rectory in Stoke Doyle, another part of the estate. But he was determined to look after the 14th-century hall that his family had owned since 1841. When there were open days, Capron would be “out front manning the car parking,” said his daughter, Naomi. “No one had a clue he owned the place.”
Born in Rochester, Kent, he was the son of Christian (nee Hepburne-Scott) and Lt Col George Capron. He attended Scaitcliffe prep school in Surrey and then Wellington college, Berkshire, where he wrote in the school magazine that he “learned very little”. He did national service in Germany, then studied French and German at Trinity Hall, Cambridge.
In 1958, while still a student, he married Edna Goldrei, “a quiet Jewish girl from a Cricklewood semi,” according to Naomi. A gifted pianist, she had won a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Music, and after their marriage, she moved to Cambridge to teach piano.
Following his graduation in 1959, Capron became a studio manager in BBC Radio, and rapidly moved up through the ranks. He got an attachment to Lime Grove Studios, and worked on several programmes including 24 Hours and Midweek, before editing Tonight and Panorama and becoming a major player in British television.
One rare occasion when his two worlds came together was in 1976, when Panorama had secured an interview with the great exiled Russian writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn. It needed to be kept very secret, and Capron, then editor of Tonight, suggested Southwick Hall as a “safe house” where Solzhenitsyn could talk.
Capron loved sport – especially cricket. He played for the BBC’s Bushmen team where he was famous for his increasingly slow bowling. Cockerell, who played with him, said his proudest moment was when he took a hat-trick in 1996 “and it was unkindly suggested that the ball was taking so long to come down that the three batsmen had dozed off”.
He is survived by Edna, and his children, Naomi and David.

Railway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruption

Passengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines at Christmas have been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works.
Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well as Birmingham New Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period.
Passengers travelling between London, north-east England and Scotland will have to negotiate the part closure of the east coast mainline on Christmas Eve. Direct trains from the capital to parts of Essex and Norfolk will also be cut for much of the festive period.
Network Rail said most routes would still stay open and that the Christmas period, when train services generally stop for 25 and 26 December, remained the best time to conduct essential works.
Engineers hope to use the quieter festive days to carry out about £152m of works to improve reliability and capacity.
The biggest engineering work is expected on the lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough. Most Great Western services to Wales and the west of England will start and finish at Reading, with some services diverting around Oxford to London Euston, from 27 December until 4 January.
The work also means Elizabeth line services west of Paddington and Heathrow Express services will not resume after Christmas until 31 January.
Birmingham’s main station, New Street, will be closed from the start of Christmas Eve until 29 December to replace overhead power supplies. No trains will stop or pass through, with rail replacement buses serving the city centre.
Passengers using east coast mainline services run by LNER and other operators may wish to avoid travel on Christmas Eve. Work at Doncaster means trains between London, north-east England and Scotland will be partly replaced by rail replacement buses from Newark to York, adding two hours to journeys.
The Great Eastern mainline out of London Liverpool Street will be closed for 10 days from Christmas Day for track replacement in east London, meaning no Greater Anglia or Elizabeth line rains will run through the area, with no direct trains from Norwich to London.
TransPennine services between Leeds and Manchester will be slowed for six weeks from Christmas Day with the closure of Huddersfield station.
Network Rail’s group director, system operator, Anit Chandarana, said: “Christmas is a time when many people want to be with family and friends, and most of the railway will be open to help them get there. We have worked with train operators to keep services running wherever we can on the busiest travel days and to provide alternative journey options where work affects the usual route.
“We are sorry that some passengers will face disruption. The days between Christmas and new year are by far the quietest of the year and give us the best opportunity to complete major projects such as the power supply upgrades at Birmingham and Paddington. Our teams will do everything they can to keep people moving, and we urge passengers to check their journeys before setting off.”

From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

For more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe.
Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground.
Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois.
Observing the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes. Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all.
“It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.”
Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators.
Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses. Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.”
Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon.
The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported the first potential detection of dark matter.
“We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations. “We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.”
Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year.
“This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson. “It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois.
Once operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles.
One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos.
Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes.
Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who used a cubic kilometre of Antarctica to detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”

====================================================================================================

‘We were mortgage-free at 45, here’s how you can do it too’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

When Adrian Massey was made redundant from his job as a food developer in 2010, the bill that worried him the most was the mortgage. Just over a decade later he and his wife, Tulay, had cleared their debt early, saving themselves £30,000 and freeing up some money to start their own business.
The couple had bought their six-bedroom home in Banbury, Oxfordshire, for £280,000 two years before he lost his job.
With an interest rate on their mortgage of 6.1%, the couple’s monthly payment was about £1,400. “It felt like a burden; a chain around my neck,” says Adrian, 50. “I started thinking about the best way to pay it down.
“It dawned on me what could happen if you overpay even a relatively modest amount. You can really start to make a difference.”
When he started his next job he set up a standing order to overpay the mortgage. “We looked at our current income and outgoings, and then, based on our spare cash, we decided how much did we want to put into clearing the mortgage without overstretching ourselves,” he says.
They decided they could afford £500 a month. After that, any pay rises they received were funnelled into the mortgage, and the couple would sometimes add a lump sum of up to £2,000 from savings.
When their five-year, fixed rate deal ended in 2013, they remortgaged to a rate of 2.5%, choosing a tracker deal that had no limits on overpayments.
The extra they paid each month started to make an even bigger difference. By 2021, Adrian and Tulay were mortgage-free – seven years ahead of schedule.
“I know that, purely from a financial point of view, there are advantages to investing more in the stock market because of the returns you get, but the freedom was more important to me,” he says. “It has meant I have been able to invest in myself and the life I want to lead, rather than being shackled to this payment.”
The money that used to go into repayments has been used to set up a business, ATM Food Innovations, and Adrian has also upped his pension contributions.
“Making the final payment felt really good; it’s a real sense of relief and liberation,” he says. “You know that whatever happens, no one can take your house away.”
Every bit helps
With interest rates rising, it is no wonder that achieving mortgage-free status is a goal for so many.
Andrew Hagger, finance expert at Moneycomms, says: “For most people, repaying the mortgage means getting rid of the biggest financial commitment hanging around your neck.
“They dream of what they could do with all the extra disposable income: holidays, update the car, home improvements, or retire early. The list is endless.”
Clearing your mortgage not only means removing what is likely to be your largest monthly expense, it can also save you thousands of pounds in interest that would have been paid over the full term.
And even small overpayments can make a big difference. On a 25-year mortgage of £200,000, with an interest rate of 5%, overpaying by just £20 a month could save you £5,700 in interest and clear your debt nine months early, according to Moneycomms.
Overpaying by £50 a month on the same loan would save you £13,400 in interest, and clear the mortgage almost two years early. A £100-a-month overpayment would save £24,530 and clear the debt three years and six months ahead of schedule.
Overpayments don’t have to be on a regular basis. You could pay off a lump sums when you come to the end of your deal, or switch to a new lender, or part-way through if the terms of your loan allow it.
In the above example, a one-off overpayment of £10,000 could save £11,870 in interest and pay off the mortgage one year and two months early.
To make an overpayment, contact your lender. Often it is as simple as making a transfer to the account.
As your overpayments start to make an impact, you will typically be offered the option to reduce either your monthly payments, or the mortgage term. If repayments are comfortable, choose the latter. This means that more of your money goes towards paying off the debt and you’ll clear the balance sooner.
One downside to overpaying is that you can’t easily get the money back if you need it, so ensure you have a savings buffer in case of an emergency; typically three to six months’ of essential outgoings is recommended.
“It’s tempting to try to throw every spare penny at the mortgage, but find a balance between making progress towards being mortgage-free and retaining enough flexibility to deal with life’s unexpected costs,” says David Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C.
Understand the terms of your mortgage: most let you overpay up to 10% of the outstanding balance each year without charges. Hollingworth says: “It’s worth checking as early repayment charges can be substantial, often 3-5% of your overpayment, which can erode, or remove, the benefit of the overpayment.”
Offset mortgages: the best of both worlds?
If you want to overpay without locking away your money, an offset mortgage can be a good alternative to a standard deal. These let you link a savings account to your mortgage. The savings balance is deducted from the amount you owe, reducing the amount of interest you are charged. For example, on a £200,000 mortgage with a savings balance of £10,000, you would be charged interest on £190,000 of the loan.
The trade-off is that you don’t earn interest on your savings, but they are accessible if you need them; any money withdrawn from the account is simply no longer offset from the mortgage balance. So, in the above example, if you withdrew £2,000 from the savings account, you would then be charged interest on £192,000 of the mortgage loan.
David Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C, says: “An offset can suit those with substantial cash savings or who receive lump sum bonuses. It allows your cash to work harder without limiting your ability to draw on it when required.”
A 25-year, £200,000 offset mortgage at a rate of 5.46%, with a £10,000 savings balance, could save £28,550 in interest costs and clear the debt one year and nine months early, Moneycomms says.
It’s worth noting that the choice of offset deals is more limited than for standard mortgages, and typically they have a higher interest rate. L&C currently lists more than 7,500 mortgage products but just 150 of them are offset deals. They are typically about 0.4-0.5 percentage points more expensive than a standard mortgage, says Hollingworth.

====================================================================================================

Does a forest matter more than a foreigner? That’s where cultures disagree most.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:36 UTC
20:00:36 KST

People around the world tend to rank their moral obligations toward others in a remarkably similar order, placing family and friends at the top and violent criminals at the bottom, according to a new study published in European Journal of Social Psychology. An analysis of university students across 41 cultural groups indicates that this general moral pecking order holds up across a wide range of societies, especially in nations culturally similar to the United States. At the same time, cultures and individuals frequently diverge when deciding whether distant humans deserve more moral consideration than animals and the natural environment.
Moral concern refers to the personal obligation people feel to care for the welfare and interests of another being or object. Psychologists and philosophers often picture this concept as a “moral circle” made up of concentric rings, where entities placed in the innermost ring receive the highest level of protection and personal responsibility, while those left outside the boundary receive none at all. Where those entities sit inside a person’s moral circle shapes everyday choices, from donating to an animal sanctuary to supporting aid for foreign refugees or favoring laws that protect old-growth forests.
To map these priorities systematically, psychologists created the Moral Expansiveness Scale, which asks people to sort 30 human and non-human entities into four rings of moral standing. When several of the same researchers first tested this tool in a 2016 study of American adults, they observed a consistent hierarchy: family and friends came first, followed by community members, then revered figures like charity workers and marginalized people at nearly identical levels, then foreign citizens and political opponents, animals and ecosystems, plants, and finally violent criminals.
Later research linked the overall size of a person’s moral circle to real-world generosity, with a 2024 global study of charitable donors showing that people who pledged at least 10 percent of their income to charity had wider moral circles and greater open-mindedness than typical citizens.
Even within Western societies, however, not everyone follows the exact same ordering when weighing human needs against the natural world. For example, a 2021 study of American adults indicated that although most participants prioritized distant or marginalized humans over animals and ecosystems, roughly one-third reversed that pattern and valued nature above people outside their own social groups. Broader social environments also shape moral boundaries, as a 2022 study across 36 countries, drawn from the same dataset by several of the same researchers, found that high perceived economic inequality and low social trust were associated with smaller moral circles overall.
What remained uncertain was whether the specific hierarchy of who matters most was a widespread feature of human psychology or largely a byproduct of Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies, since earlier tests of the ranking itself relied almost exclusively on participants from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.
To examine whether this moral ordering holds up across diverse societies and individuals, study co-lead authors Işıl Ayça Akkuş and Bastian Jaeger of the Department of Social Psychology at Tilburg University in the Netherlands, along with their colleagues, analyzed moral rankings across 41 cultural groups.
“There have been quite a lot of studies recently on mapping people’s moral hierarchy, that is, how much concern people show for the welfare and interests of different humans, non-human animals, ecosystems, AI systems, and other entities,” Jaeger told PsyPost. “Most people showed a very similar ranking, and I had the feeling that researchers were starting to treat this pattern as an established fact of how people think about the moral standing of others. But almost all research on this topic was conducted in the US or other Western countries. We wanted to test how often the same, or at least a very similar pattern actually shows up in countries across the world.”
The researchers examined survey responses from 6,561 university students across 41 cultural groups, originally collected in 2018 and 2019, with all but four groups reaching the target of at least 100 students. These groups spanned countries across Asia, Africa, Europe, North and South America, and Oceania, and separated culturally distinct regions within the same nation, such as English-speaking and French-speaking Canada as well as the Northern and Southern United States. The participants had an average age of 21.6 years, and roughly 63 percent were women, 30 percent were men, and less than 1 percent identified as another gender. On average, the student participants leaned slightly toward the political left and rated religion as slightly below moderate importance in their daily lives.
All participants completed the Moral Expansiveness Scale by assigning 30 specific entities into four concentric rings scored from 0 to 3. Placing an entity in the inner circle (3) meant the participant felt a strong moral obligation and personal responsibility to ensure its welfare, whereas the outer circle (2) reflected moderate concern with reduced personal obligation, the fringes (1) indicated minimal moral standing, and the area outside the boundary (0) meant the entity deserved no moral concern at all. The 30 entities were grouped into 10 broader categories of three items each.
Six categories covered humans: family and friends (family member, close friend, partner or spouse); ingroup members from one’s own community (fellow citizen, neighbor, co-worker); revered figures (elected leader, soldier, charity worker); stigmatized individuals (refugee, lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender person, mentally challenged person); outgroup members outside one’s national, political, or religious group (foreign citizen, political opponent, person with different religious beliefs); and villains (murderer, terrorist, child molester).
The other four covered non-human nature: high-sentience animals widely seen as having complex minds and feelings (chimpanzee, dolphin, cow); the environment (national park, old-growth forest, coral reef); low-sentience animals viewed as having simpler mental capacities (chicken, bee, fish); and plants (redwood tree, apple tree, rose bush).
To evaluate how closely each cultural group and each individual matched the typical Western hierarchy, the authors focused on 13 pairwise comparisons between categories that had consistently differed in prior Western studies, such as prioritizing family and friends over ingroup members or plants over villains. Category pairs that had historically received nearly identical scores in Western samples, such as revered versus stigmatized humans or high-sentience animals versus the environment, were left out of the 13 core comparisons.
For 26 of the cultural groups with available data, the authors also compared the group rankings against a cultural distance index, which combines nearly 200 survey and institutional indicators to measure how much a society’s broader values, beliefs, and norms differ from those of the United States. The study was not preregistered, and the authors describe their approach as primarily descriptive, intended to map patterns that future work can test directly rather than to confirm specific predictions.
At the cultural group level, the results pointed to substantial cross-cultural similarity in how people organize their moral circles. Across the 41 cultural groups, a median of 11 out of the 13 expected rankings replicated, with an average of 11.32 rankings matching the typical pattern. Twelve cultural groups matched all 13 rankings: the Northern United States, Australia, English-speaking Canada, Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Belgium, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, and Ukraine. Most of the remaining groups fell close behind, and even the most divergent kept the majority of the hierarchy intact, with Malaysia matching 8 of 13 and French-speaking Canada, Chile, Germany, and Poland each matching 9.
Family and friends occupied the highest position in every single cultural group, receiving an average rating of 2.89 out of 3.00 across all samples. At the bottom of the hierarchy, villains received the lowest moral concern in 38 of the 41 cultural groups, with an overall average score of 0.58 out of 3.00; the only exceptions were Hong Kong, Thailand, and Uganda, where criminals received scores similar to or slightly higher than plants and low-sentience animals. Three specific rankings held true in all 41 cultural groups without exception: family and friends were always ranked above ingroup members, and the natural environment was always ranked above both low-sentience animals and plants.
“Although we found some evidence for cultural differences, what really stood out to me was how similar the results were, even across countries that differ a lot from each other,” Jaeger said. “Participants from Australia, New Zealand, and the Netherlands showed a hierarchy that was very similar to the US hierarchy. These countries are all relatively similar to the US, but we also found similar patterns in Japan, Ukraine, South Africa, and Türkiye.”
Where cultures differed most was in how they weighed distant humans against non-human nature. Prioritizing human outgroup members over the natural environment was the least consistent pattern globally, appearing in only 21 of the 41 cultural groups, while prioritizing human outgroup members over high-sentience animals occurred in 26 of the 41 groups. A multilevel statistical model estimating the sources of variation at the group level indicated that 40.73 percent of the variation in whether a typical ranking held up was explained by which two categories were being compared, whereas only 13.36 percent was explained by which cultural group was being examined.
Comparing the 26 cultural groups with available cultural distance scores showed a moderate negative correlation (-0.46) between a society’s cultural distance from the United States and the number of moral rankings that matched the standard hierarchy. In other words, societies whose general values, beliefs, and social norms were closer to those of the United States tended to display a moral hierarchy more closely aligned with the pattern originally observed in American studies.
Examining individual participants rather than group averages uncovered far greater variation from person to person. Across all 6,561 students, the median individual matched 7 out of the 13 typical rankings, with an average of 6.85 rankings (or 52.75 percent across all comparisons). Only 38.25 percent of individuals placed human outgroup members above the environment, 44.72 percent placed human outgroup members above high-sentience animals, and 31.81 percent rated high-sentience animals higher than low-sentience animals. By contrast, 91.38 percent of individual participants placed family and friends above ingroup members, the most consistent ranking in the entire dataset.
“Researchers usually focus on finding differences, but I think it is also important to recognize that for some issues, people’s views are actually very similar,” Jaeger explained. “This can be an important thing to highlight in very polarized societies like the US, where many people (often mistakenly) think that others’ beliefs and values are completely different from their own. For example, privileging family above all else is usually framed as a conservative value. Our results show that, even though political differences exist, this is a view that is held by a wide majority of people in general no matter their political orientation.”
Identical group-level rankings can also hide disagreement among people within the same country. Both the Netherlands and Ukraine matched all 13 rankings at the group average level, yet 84.25 percent of Dutch students prioritized ingroup members over stigmatized individuals compared to 55.66 percent of Ukrainian students, whereas 44.34 percent of Ukrainian students prioritized high-sentience over low-sentience animals compared to 26.03 percent of Dutch students. In a statistical model analyzing all 85,293 individual comparisons, the pair of categories being compared accounted for 13.82 percent of the variation, differences between individual participants accounted for 1.30 percent, and the participant’s home country accounted for just 0.2 percent.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Although the dataset spanned 41 cultural groups, all of the participants were university students, who tend to be younger, more educated, from higher socioeconomic backgrounds, and more politically liberal than the general public in their home countries. Relying on student samples may have made the cultural groups appear more alike than they actually are, and future studies using nationally representative samples could uncover wider cultural differences.
“It is possible that nationally representative samples would lead to more cultural differences, but based on our results, we concluded that there are only modest cultural differences in people’s moral hierarchy,” Jaeger noted.
The high degree of variability among individual participants may also stem in part from how the categories were measured, as each of the 10 groups was represented by just three specific examples: chimpanzees, dolphins, and cows for high-sentience animals, and chickens, bees, and fish for low-sentience animals. The authors suggest that people may downplay the moral standing of cows to justify meat consumption and grant higher moral concern to bees because of their perceived usefulness, which could explain why fewer than a third of individuals rated the high-sentience group above the low-sentience group. Future research using a larger assortment of entities within each category could help separate genuine personal philosophies from measurement noise.
Finally, some of the specific groups on the questionnaire, such as refugees, sexual and gender minorities, and people with intellectual disabilities, were originally selected because they represent stigmatized populations in Western societies, and those social labels may not translate identically across every culture. Statistical checks of measurement invariance, which test whether people in different cultures interpret and use a survey scale in the exact same way, indicated that comparing raw average scores between nations remains challenging, though the researchers avoided this pitfall by comparing relative rankings within each culture rather than raw totals across borders.
Looking ahead, the researchers plan to examine why individuals differ so sharply when weighing human strangers against the natural world. “Although most people show maximum concern for family members, and very little concern for murderers and other deviants, concern for some other entities was more variable,” Jaeger added. “Many people were more concerned about human strangers than the rainforest and other ecosystems, but many also showed the opposite pattern. I’m curious which traits and beliefs can explain these differences in who people prioritize in their moral hierarchy.”
The study, “Exploring Cultural and Individual Differences in the Hierarchy of Moral Concern: Evidence From Student Samples Across 41 Cultural Groups,” was authored by Işıl Ayça Akkuş, Charlie R. Crimston, Kelly Kirkland, Brock Bastian, and Bastian Jaeger.

Why We Like to Be Scared
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

In a moment marked by economic anxiety, concerns over artificial intelligence, and geopolitical instability, frightening fiction is thriving. From the page to the big screen, horror has had a massive year.
In publishing, the horror sub-genre is set to break new sales records. Readers aren’t the only ones seeking a good scare. Horror films dominated the silver screen this summer, with Backrooms and Obsession grossing more than $460 million domestically and roughly $900 million globally. Both films came from young directors who cut their teeth on YouTube, with their fingers on the pulse of this generation’s anxieties and fears. Even as major franchises like Spider-Man broke box office records, audiences turned two original horror stories into blockbuster hits.
What is it about a horror story that allows it to latch its claws into our minds and pull us in? Why would we seek out an experience that produces in us a feeling of fear and anxiety? After all, we spend most of our lives trying to avoid these emotions.
The truth is that humans love to be scared. We spend our time sharing and consuming scary stories; we take our kids to haunted houses; we dedicate an entire season to all things spooky.
Understanding why we crave fear helps explain more than horror’s hold on Hollywood: It reveals how we confront uncertainty, test our limits, and find a sense of control when the world feels frightening enough already.
Who loves horror
The prevailing wisdom has long suggested that our desire for a good scare comes from the adrenaline kick we get while watching a scary movie. While this does explain some of the appeal, especially among younger consumers, research shows that many people who like horror movies aren’t necessarily looking for the rush it provides.
Curiosity, specifically about situations that can cause injury or death, is perfectly normal and common. Morbid curiosity motivates us to learn about dangers, something that all animals can benefit from.
Horror also offers a laboratory for self-learning. In my own work, I’ve found that a large portion of horror fans are “white knucklers”—people who don’t necessarily enjoy fear, but rather the opportunity to practice overcoming it. Many white knucklers report that they have learned something about themselves after a scary-play experience—for example, how they react in stressful situations, or that they should trust their instincts.
Another group of horror fans seems to enjoy scary stories because they offer a safe opportunity to work through feelings of dread, anxiety, and other difficult thoughts. We called this group the “dark copers.” While this may sound odd at first, horror fans and morbidly curious individuals reported higher levels of psychological resilience during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, even when controlling for other personality traits and demographic factors.
The logic begins to make sense once we work through what a horror story really is: a sandbox for a potentially dangerous situation.
The collective imagination of horror
Many animals show some curiosity for things that might be dangerous. Zebras will cautiously observe lions as they lounge, and minnows will swim up to a pike to keep an eye on it. However, humans are the most morbidly curious creatures of all because of our ability to ask “What if?”
In horror, the human capacity for imagination really shines.
We concoct detailed stories of possible encounters with all sorts of beings, some of which we know well, and others that live only in the darkest recesses of our minds. We play out scenarios imagining what might happen if we, or someone like us, encountered a terrible situation.
In real life, an encounter with danger is a costly way to learn. Our minds long for safe ways to learn about dangerous situations.
Because of horror’s position as a sandbox for misfortune, consumers tend to reward horror films that reflect their generation’s anxieties. For instance, the unbelievably destructive ability of atomic bombs captured the imagination of those living in the late 1940s and 1950s. Anxiety about the future of this new atomic age spawned several radiation-borne monsters, the most famous of which was the Japanese film Godzilla (1954).
Around the same time, paranoia was bubbling in the U.S. about surreptitious invaders, both alien and communist. Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956) beautifully captured these anxieties in a story about your friends and loved ones being secretly replaced by a foreign, hostile entity.
In the 21st century, “elevated horror” has taken hold, with films like The Babadook (2014) and Hereditary (2018) portraying anxieties about trauma and mental health. And then there are films like Get Out (2017) and Parasite (2019), which took on the tense social issues of race and class. While the 2026 hits Backrooms and Obsession may seem to touch on fairly unrelated topics, each has a foothold in the minds of modern consumers.
Horror in an anxious era
I would argue that the rise in interest in horror as a genre can be partly attributed to rising social anxieties. Backrooms is a masterclass in how terrifying meaninglessness can be. The endless hallways and rooms in the film are reminiscent of social media, which offers an endless tunnel of content, with mental health concerns lurking under the surface. Each room contains some variation of objects that aren’t quite right, like an AI rendering of an image. The haphazard placement gives the entire space a creepy, purposeless feel.
Meaninglessness is on the minds of this generation, too. A 2025 Gallup poll reports that 39% of Gen-Z adults feel like their life mostly lacks meaning, with slightly more saying they lack a sense of purpose. Mental health outlooks are similar, with a 2024 McKinsey survey reporting that nearly 1 in 3 Gen-Z respondents in the U.S. report poor mental health.
Over 20% of Gen-Z and Millennials in that same survey report poor or very poor social health, a topic that is explored into absurdity in Obsession. The basic plot is an old monkey’s paw-style tale: a story about a magical item granting a wish with unintended consequences. Director Curry Barker infused his story with modern anxieties about dating and social life. The main character, Bear, is a socially awkward twentysomething who can’t bring himself to tell his crush how he really feels.
In many ways, Bear’s situation resembles men of this generation more than previous generations. One survey found that 44% of Gen-Z men did not date at all as teens, compared to 32% of Millennials and 23% of Gen-X. This may be due to a lack of confidence. A 2026 study by the Wheatley Institute and the Institute for Family Studies found that only about 1 in 3 young men express confidence in their ability to approach a potential romantic partner.
In my view, this resonance is why horror has had such a good run over the past two decades. According to film producer and data maven Stephen Follows, the horror genre has grown faster in the past few decades than any other genre. While the infamous slasher era of the 1980s saw around 150 horror films per year, the 2020s have surpassed 1,500 horror films per year. Even when the film genre was suffering in 2020, horror was having a moment. As COVID-19 emptied theaters, horror held on, pushing its share of the Box Office to the highest it had ever been. Horror beat its own record for Box Office share again in 2025.
To be sure, scary stories have been with us as long as any other type of story, but we seem to be in a golden age of horror, and cultural institutions are taking note. From The Substance (2024) and Sinners (2025) to Bugonia (2025) and Frankenstein (2025), dark films with horror themes are now consistently receiving critical acclaim from the Academy.
The world has always been full of things that frighten us. One way we work through these fears is by simulating scenarios. We tell stories of the things we fear and indulge in the bad outcomes that the protagonists face from the safety of our seats.
Humans learn quite well from the mistakes of others, and horror stories trade in poor choices. In this way, horror offers us a uniquely powerful tool to process social concerns.
As our technological world enters a new area of artificial intelligence, we will unlock a whole new world of possible dangers and things to fear, and films like M3GAN (2022) will be there to help us process worries.
As we enter the unknown, we will try to prepare and cope with what comes our way in the same fashion as those before us: by diving into a good horror story.

There’s a Completely New Type of Whisky. It’s French and Made in Concrete Eggs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The vines on Bordeaux’s Right Bank next to the Dordogne were first planted by Roman troops and settlers in the first century CE. Known for Merlot-dominant blends, with its clay and limestone soils, this region of France delivers softer, fruitier wines. If you're a fan of Pomerol or St-Émilion, this is your nirvana.
It is here you will find Maison Lineti, happily shunning 2,000 years of tradition by making not wine, but whisky. French whisky. A thousand miles or so from the distilleries of Scotland and Ireland, this small company is making the spirit in a way whisky has never been made before.
Even though Maison Lineti is not making wine, it is, in what is apparently a world first, applying wine-science methods to fermentation, distillation, and maturation for its whisky. The result is a floral, fresh, mineral, and textured spirit.
After the producer hosted the prestigious World Whisky Forum in June 2025, its methods have set the industry all aflutter. Why? Not only does the product taste exceptional, Lineti's groundbreaking techniques are bringing its spirit to the bottle years faster than traditional players using traditional processes.
The masterminds behind Maison Lineti's wine-made whisky are Magali Picard, a chemical engineer who holds a doctorate in oenology from the University of Bordeaux, and her partner and cofounder, Alex Cosculluela. The company launched in 2018 with their friend Xavier Payan, who studied wine and spirits management alongside Cosculluela.
During pandemic lockdowns, while the rest of us dusted off gaming consoles or mined the more questionable parts of Netflix’s catalog, Picard sharpened her skills gained as a spirits development project manager at barrel-maker Demptos to research a more scientific approach to whisky-making—one that leaned far less heavily on barrel aging for flavor and instead looked to molecular science, sensory analysis, and copious amounts of data. At the time, Picard even posted her progress online as an open logbook of her experiments.
The conclusion Picard and Cosculluela came to after these experiments was this: a great spirit is decided at fermentation, not by age. “Whisky makers are very focused on the style of cask. It's not our vision,” says Picard.
“What we try to do is not increase the production but focus on the quality of the whisky, and more precisely on the steps before the maturation,” Picard says. “We worked on the quality of the wash—the liquid issued from the fermentation, just like in the wine industry. We worked a lot on techniques used in the wine industry. For example, the use of lactic bacteria during the fermentation, and the use of lees aging—which is a process used for champagne or Chardonnay wines to increase the rawness.”
Before fermentation, organic French barley is cold-soaked to bring out its brighter notes. Then there’s a long, seven-day fermentation that builds flavor (compared with a typical two or three days for scotch). The addition of lees aging keeps the Lineti wash in contact with the fermentation process's dead yeast cells for a full two weeks to develop more floral and fruity aromas.
Picard also employs malolactic fermentation, a secondary winemaking process where lactic acid bacteria convert sharp, tart malic acids into softer, creamier lactic acids. Such a process wouldn't be allowed in scotch production, which is strictly regulated, but EU law permits such manipulation. In wine, the process would result in a softer texture, but in Lineti's whisky, along with that creamier mouthfeel, it adds length and even more floral notes.
Maison Lineti’s wine-based, science-laden fermentation process happens in the “egg box”—a remarkable space housing seven giant concrete, egg-shaped fermenters that reach to the ceiling. Cosculluela says the concrete allows for precise temperature control, as the material much thicker than the stainless steel that’s typically used. Additionally, the lack of internal ridges in the eggs supposedly make for better movement and churn of the liquid when the yeasts are fermenting.
The tangible gains from all this work before the fruits of their labor go into barrels are not merely limited to improved and distinctive flavor profiles. Cosculluela claims that Maison Lineti’s pre-maturation may well take weeks longer than other makers, but, crucially, it saves two to four years of barrel aging. This is how Maison Lineti’s relatively young whisky somewhat magically goes toe-to-toe with single malt scotch that is many years older. (Which it does. Take our word for it.)
It also means Cosculluela and Picard end up with more booze for their buck. A faster maturation to a minimum viable product, if you will, means the angels get to steal less of Maison Lineti’s produce. The “angel’s share” is the portion of whisky that naturally evaporates through the porous wood of the casks into the atmosphere during the spirit’s aging process. Simply put, less time in Lineti’s barrels means less whisky disappears.
“Every year you lose 2 percent of your whisky, so you need to produce approximately 20 percent more than the final volume you will need at 10 years,” Cosculluela says. “So if you work on the drinkability to get something really tasty and balanced in three years, you save a lot of raw material, a lot of space in your warehouse, and a lot of energy.”
However, for Picard, this use of these winemaking skills and methods is not enough to ensure success for Maison Linetti—comprehensive data analysis is also key. Excel files document some 10,000 lines of data per batch produced.
“On the brewing part, we collect temperature, the time, the transfer yield of the pump, the water added, everything,” Cosculluela says. “For the fermentation, we collect the time and temperature every 20 minutes. For the stills, we have the ABV, the temperature, and the speed.” As a result, Cosculluela and Picard can see the direct impacts of any changes they make. “We try to change only one parameter at a time,” Cosculluela says, so that any improvements can be tracked back to exactly what was altered.
“If we develop a project on the fermentation parts, we just need a different samples from the batch, and you can collect the data in two weeks,” says Picard. “But do a study on the maturation? That needs time. We conducted one three years ago, and we've only just begun to have the final results.”
The data science isn't the only thing that's been an arduous process for Maison Lineti. Cosculluela and Picard have been tested financially, too. In July last year, after all their hard work, experiments, and graft, the company was forced into liquidation when its main wine-producing backer withdrew from the business. However, before the worst could happen, Maison Lineti secured a new unnamed investor, a French entrepreneur who, fittingly, apparently made their fortune in the luxury industry.
This new injection of cash has resulted in, just this week, Maison Lineti's whisky going on sale to the public in the UK for the first time. The intention, Cosculluela says, is to bring the spirit to the US in 2028. The launch range consists of a core expression, called Calibre No1, sitting alongside two limited editions, named “Complications,” all three clearly referencing the luxury watchmaking world in their nomenclature.
At 47.7 percent ABV, Calibre No1 single malt is WIRED's clear favorite, and the most accessible at £50 (about $67) for 70 cl (about 23.7 fluid ounces). It’s described as the DNA of the brand—sophisticated, complex, and elegant. Complication No1 is matured in ex-bourbon casks and is limited to 850 bottles. It is more focused on the malolactic fermentation, and it proposes something different altogether, in no way trying to compete with the distilleries of Scotland or elsewhere. Complication No2 is limited to 750 bottles and is all about offering a profile defined by Oloroso sherry casks. All of these whiskies are just three and a half years old, but, quite remarkably, taste much more mature.
Drinks writer and presenter Becky Paskin, who is also the former editor of The Spirits Business and Scotchwhisky.com, is unequivocal in her praise of what Maison Lineti has managed to achieve. “What they're doing is probably the most innovative thing to happen to whisky in decades,” Paskin says. “By leaning on their own background and oenology, they've created whisky that is completely unique … for now. Other producers around the world will look to what they're doing and potentially start to use some of these techniques.”
As for the undeniably subtle and interesting flavors Cosculluela and Picard are managing to conjure, Paskin thinks the whiskey world is only beginning to see the distillery's potential. "You're only just starting to see the tip of what Maison Lineti is capable of. They've got all these levers they can pull. So, ultimately, we could see very creamy, very fruity whiskies. We could see whiskies that are more malty in character, but they always have this signature floral undertone. Every distillery needs a DNA, and that's what's unique to Maison Lineti.”
The World Whisky Forum's Dave Broom, who has also written 14 books on the spirit, agrees. “I am very excited by what what has come out, but more excited by what is going to come out,” he says. “In terms of flavor production, interaction between between wood and air and spirit, down to a molecular level—that is innovation, and genuinely groundbreaking. I think [Maison Lineti] is one of the most important distilleries in the world at the moment.”

O'Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects creates "quiet yet present" garden studio in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

O’Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects creates “quiet yet present” garden studio in London
A low brick base anchors the timber structure of this pared-back garden studio, which London studio O’Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects created as a workspace for a creative couple in Highbury.
Nestled in a leafy garden of a Victorian home, the studio provides the filmmaker and artist with a calming, well-lit space with a strong visual connection to the outdoors.
O’Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects slotted it at the end of the garden to preserve views from the house over the mature garden, avoiding “compromising the sense of depth and continuity of the landscape”, the studio said.
“It was important that the building felt distinct from the house while sitting comfortably within its setting, a short walk from the rear garden door,” studio co-founder Amalia Skoufoglou told Dezeen.
“The intention was to create a building that felt quiet yet present in the garden, rather than competing with it or the Victorian house,” she added.
“The form allows the quality of the space to emerge through its proportions, construction and relationship with daylight,” Skoufoglou continued. “Its modest scale and subservient position give the studio the character of a garden building.”
O’Sullivan Skoufoglou Architects designed the material palette and low profile of the studio to complement the character of the existing house and garden, ensuring minimal visual impact.
Its low brick plinth nods to the brick boundary walls of the Victorian home and also pays homage to Victorian glasshouses, traditionally supported on low brick walls.
Above the brick plinth is a lightweight timber structure, chosen to “allow the upper part of the building to remain visually light”, Skoufoglou said.
Inside, the garden studio comprises a main open workspace and an adjoining bathroom. The focal point is its built-in desk that extends along the main east-facing window wall.
“The main window wall and the built-in desk form the focus of the interior. The desk runs alongside the generous east-facing windows, making daylight and the changing garden views an integral part of the working environment,” said Skoufoglou.
“This arrangement brings the working surface into direct relationship with natural light and views of the garden.”
Inside, the timber structure is left exposed at roof level, while the brick plinth is also left visible. Between, the walls are lined with painted pine.
Smaller windows are positioned strategically around the studio, framing views of trees while maintaining privacy from neighbouring homes.
According to the studio, the “grain of the timber, the texture of the brick and the changing daylight combine to give the space its character”.
Other London garden studios featured on Dezeen include Shou Sugi Bangers, a timber music studio by Unknown Works, and Gardenhide Studio, a hempcrete workspace by Commonbond Architects.

Trump’s ICE Crackdown Broke Miami. Will It Tank This Cuban Republican’s Campaign?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, says he started stockpiling food and water weeks ago in case of a national emergency, as he talked up the threats to the UK and said his department had already begun ramping up its spending in response.
Streeting spoke after the chancellor, John Healey, said he wanted defence spending to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 and 3.5% by 2035; having already asked Whitehall departments to find 1% cuts in their budgets for long-term investment to fund defence spending.
“I’m glad the message is getting through because my mum got in touch and said ‘payday is coming up, how much do you think I need to buy because I’m just budgeting to the end of the month?’ I’m glad that people are beginning to think about their own household resilience, making sure we’ve got sufficient supplies of bottled water, canned goods, battery-powered torches. These are all just commonsense things for the everyday challenges,” Streeting told the Times.
The defence secretary says he has bottled water, a first aid kit and a battery-powered torch on standby. He added that he was stockpiling baked beans, sweetcorn, red kidney beans, tuna, protein bars and nuts. Streeting, who recently urged all Britons to follow suit, said he had started setting aside the supplies because he wanted to “lead by example”.
He told the Times he was determined the UK should be able to deter its adversaries and “should deterrence fail, to be ready to defeat them”. Streeting said: “That is the core job. We should never lose sight of that,” adding that any additional spending must be done carefully. “Spending more money badly is not virtuous,” he said. He also told the newspaper that value for money and modernisation needed to be balanced in order to ready the UK to “fight the wars ahead”.
In June, Healey’s resignation as defence secretary was one of the final nails in the coffin of Keir Starmer’s premiership. The man who now serves as chancellor in Andy Burnham’s government accused Burnham’s predecessor, as well as the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk with inadequate funding for the defence investment plan (Dip).
“You have been unable and the Treasury has been unwilling to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats. I would not be able to accept a Dip settlement that does not give our forces the resources they need. I am now left with no other option than to submit my resignation as your defence secretary,” he wrote.
Announcing his first budget on Wednesday, Healey said he was now fully funding the defence investment plan. He reiterated the target of defence spending reaching 3% of GDP; prompting the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, to say the UK was on “a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato allies in The Hague”. But Healey was criticised for leaving details of his plan to reach that target until next year’s spending review.
Besides spending, Streeting also discussed oversight of service personnel, telling the Times the courts were in the middle of an “active campaign” to “smear the reputation and integrity of our special forces”. He also left the door open to scrutiny of special forces and the UK’s nuclear weapons by MPs and peers on the intelligence and security committee, saying they could be trusted.
