Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.
Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.
Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”
While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”
The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.
Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.
Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.
Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.
Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents.
Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said.
Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email.
There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement.
Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent. But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.

====================================================================================================

Abuse survivors to press Church on accountability during pope’s trip to South America
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:29:06 CET
19:29:06 KST

MEXICO CITY/LIMA, Oct 31 (Reuters) - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America, Peruvian abuse survivor Pedro Salinas sees reason for both hope and unease in the pope’s record confronting clerical abuse.
For a decade, Salinas watched as the Catholic Church investigated Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, the Peru-founded Catholic community he helped expose. Then, in the final days of Pope Francis’ papacy last year, the Vatican dissolved the group and its branches.
“What was achieved, nobody, absolutely nobody, could even have imagined. It was inconceivable. But it happened,” said Salinas, 63, a journalist and former member whose reporting helped expose allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse inside the group.
Robert Prevost, as Leo was known when he was a bishop in Peru and later a Vatican cardinal, quietly worked with survivors and advocates, Salinas said, attending meetings, gathering information and communicating by WhatsApp and email.
“Without him, the needle didn’t move,” Salinas said.
The first US-born pope will travel through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru November 6 to 17, ending with six days in Peru, where he arrived as a missionary in the 1980s and later became a citizen and served as bishop of Chiclayo. The Vatican said he will meet clergy abuse survivors there, as he has done on other recent trips.
Survivors say they wonder whether Leo’s approach in Peru, which they credit with helping bring about the rare step of dissolving a Catholic community, can translate into broader change across a Church where they say accountability is uneven.
“What is lacking are bishops everywhere in the world committed to this issue,” Salinas said.
Peru is preparing for a tourism bonanza during Leo’s visit. José Enrique Escardó, 56, president of a Peruvian survivors network, views the excitement from a different perspective.
While Escardó acknowledged that some survivors credit Leo with helping dissolve Sodalitium, he said the Church’s actions have not delivered sufficient justice, accountability or reparations.
“Survivors have grown tired of being told things, of being promised things, but nothing being done,” Escardó said. “We feel more abandoned. We feel deceived.”
He wants survivors to become involved in shaping Church policy and wants reparations to include psychological care and education.
The Vatican did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
‘TIP OF THE ICEBERG’
Francis, the first Latin American pope, left a complicated legacy, survivors say. Juan Carlos Cruz, the survivor whose case became central to Francis’ 2018 reckoning with abuse in Chile, credits Francis with changes including revisions to canon law, removal of the pontifical secret — the Church’s highest level of confidentiality — surrounding abuse cases and Vos Estis Lux Mundi, a Vatican framework for bishops accused of abuse or cover-up.
“We’re still at the tip of the iceberg,” said Cruz, whom Francis appointed in 2021 to the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors. “The commission has been working for years on universal safeguarding guidelines and those standards need to be applied around the world.”
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the watchdog group BishopAccountability.org, which tracks Catholic Church abuse allegations worldwide, called Vos Estis the most significant action Francis took on abuse. But she said the Vatican rarely makes clear whether an accused bishop’s resignation represents punishment.
“The public is left in the dark,” she said.
Barrett Doyle said the Vatican has not released global disciplinary data comparable with figures it provided to a United Nations committee in 2014. Her group relies on public records, media reports and investigations by prosecutors, governments and commissions to track cases.
She wants Leo to make permanent removal from ministry the universal rule for priests found under canon law to have sexually abused children, extending worldwide a policy adopted by US bishops in 2002.
“To say that no child molesters should be out to practice as priests is just such a no-brainer,” she said. “It’s a step that Leo could take now.”
Vatican officials have previously cited the difficulty of creating a single abuse reporting law across all countries and argued that removing priests can put them beyond Church supervision.
Angela Walker, executive director of the US-based Survivors Network of those Abused by Priests, said survivors increasingly turn to civil authorities because of the Church’s “incredible failure” to police itself.
“There needs to be more transparency, more openness, and more accountability,” she said. “I will believe it when I see it.”
SURVIVORS’ LONG WAIT
In Mexico, survivors pressed the Vatican on clerical abuse decades before it became a defining crisis across Latin America. Among the most notorious cases was that of Marcial Maciel, the Mexican priest who founded the Legion of Christ order and whose accusers took allegations to the Vatican in the 1990s. The Vatican ordered Maciel in 2006 to withdraw from public ministry. He died in 2008, without ever facing his accusers.
The scale of his abuse became clearer after his death. In 2019, the Legion reported that Maciel had abused at least 60 minors, among 175 instances of child abuse the order documented involving 33 priests over eight decades.
José de Jesús Barba Martin, 87, alleged Maciel abused him when he was studying for the priesthood in the 1950s. He recalled survivors struggling to be heard by Church and state authorities in the late 1990s and said an appeal he sent Pope John Paul II went unanswered.
Decades later, that experience has left him with little expectation that another appeal to Rome would bring change.
“The Church is made up of two types of men: good and bad, courageous and cowardly,” he said. “It will take a long time, and the issue will not be addressed under this pope nor the next.”
Alberto Athié, 72, a former Mexican priest who pursued clerical abuse cases from inside the Church before leaving the priesthood in 2003, sees Leo’s visit as another opportunity to push for transparency.
“I do have hope,” he said. “But my hope fades just the same … Things have to be fixed within the Church.”
Abuse survivor Sebastian Cuattromo said the Argentine Church should have been “at the international forefront” of confronting abuse under Argentine Pope Francis, but fell short of what he had hoped to see.
“There is a major outstanding debt,” Cuattromo said.
Argentina’s Episcopal Conference declined to comment.
(Reporting by Cassandra Garrison in Mexico City and Marco Aquino in Lima; additional reporting by Lucila Sigal in Buenos Aires and Joshua McElwee in Vatican City; editing by Rod Nickel)

US campaign for control of Congress enters final weekend
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:28:57 CET
19:28:57 KST

WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 31 (Reuters) - As the campaign for control of the US Congress reached its final weekend, the Trump administration stepped up its legal intervention in the Alaska Senate race while the number of Americans casting early ballots neared 50 million, a record for a midterm election.
The Department of Justice accelerated its criminal investigation in Alaska on Friday, following reports that aides to a Democratic Senate candidate recruited a retired schoolteacher from a remote fishing village to get on the ballot because he has the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The DOJ, acting on a civil lawsuit that President Donald Trump said he instigated, also filed further motions in an attempt to block the state of Alaska from certifying the Senate results if the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, loses a close race on a ballot that includes the nonpartisan candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
The closely contested race in Alaska is seen as crucial for the Democrats if they hope to take control of the Senate from Trump’s Republicans in Tuesday’s vote.
PROSECUTOR ALLEGES ‘SHAM CANDIDATE’ IN KEY ALASKA RACE
It is one of 35 races in the 100-member Senate that will set the tone for Trump’s final two years in office. Also up for grabs are all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives.
Early voter participation this cycle has set a record. More than 49 million Americans have already cast ballots, either in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day in the last midterms, in 2022.
A Democratic victory in one or both chambers could result in congressional investigations of the Trump administration, which for two years has enjoyed largely compliant Republican majorities.
Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is not scheduled to travel on Saturday, when there will be a mash-up of American traditions: politics, Halloween and college football across the country. Trump returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
The DOJ’s top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article about the supposed recruitment effort had driven a “surge” of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place “intensely and swiftly.”
The Times reported on Wednesday that aides to Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola recruited Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to run. Heyman labeled him a “sham candidate” but declined to say what crime may have been committed.
The department had already filed its civil action but, Heyman said, “when the New York Times article hit, that’s additional information that accelerated what we’ve been doing.”
Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
ADMINISTRATION GETS INVOLVED IN RACES NATIONWIDE
The Trump administration has also sued California to try to prevent the counting of ballots cast by more than 20,000 registered voters who the administration alleged could be noncitizens. It has also sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia, seeking unredacted voter rolls, part of a pattern that has alarmed election officials.
A federal judge on Friday ordered the DOJ to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration’s directives regarding alleged voting by noncitizens.
Sean Morales-Doyle, director of the voting rights and elections program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the administration’s actions parallel the tactics undertaken by election deniers in the 2020 presidential election. While the administration is unlikely to win in court, he said, the efforts could create a political atmosphere that leads to official misconduct.
“It’s about creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos, hoping that you create the political circumstances in which maybe the lieutenant governor of Alaska does feel pressure to do something that they’re not supposed to do. Maybe the governor does start to question things, too,” Morales-Doyle said.
Even so, a bipartisan majority of US voters trust the overall electoral process, with 76% saying they are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a September 30 to October 5 Reuters/Ipsos poll. Some 15% were not confident and the rest were not sure or did not answer the question. Confidence was about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.
(Reporting by Andrew Goudsward and David Morgan in Washington and Nathan Frandino in Anchorage; Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Sergio Non and William Mallard)

Scenes of the tragedy in Seoul will be cut from the new Call of Duty following criticism
Kyiv • UNN
Activision apologized and will remove 10 seconds of footage of the Itaewon crowd crush from the game after outrage from the victims’ families. The update will be released on November 12.
The American computer game publisher announced that it would remove footage of the Seoul tragedy from the shooter "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4." NBC News writes about this, reports UNN.
Details
"American video game publisher Activision announced on Friday (October 30) that it was removing controversial footage from its recently released game "Call of Duty" following a wave of outrage in South Korea sparked by the inclusion of real footage from the tragic crush during the 2022 Halloween celebrations in Seoul," the publication writes.
The world premiere of "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4," which took place last week, came just days before the anniversary of the tragedy that occurred on October 29 in Itaewon, a nightlife district of the South Korean capital, where a crowd of tens of thousands of partygoers surged uncontrollably into a narrow alley, resulting in the deaths of nearly 160 people.
The game, set against the backdrop of a fictional North Korean invasion of South Korean territory, contains approximately 10 seconds of heavily edited footage of the tragedy to illustrate what the aftermath of a Pyongyang attack might look like, although it makes no direct reference to the Itaewon crush.
Groups representing the families of the crush victims demanded that the footage be removed, saying it was horrific that the game directly recreated real scenes of people performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation "while victims lie on the cold streets amid chaos and despair."
"If the game developer has even the slightest sense of respect and compassion for the victims of the Itaewon disaster, it must take immediate action to rectify the situation," the Association of the Families of the Deceased said in a statement.
Activision apologized in its statement and said that the footage would be completely removed as part of a game update scheduled for release on November 12.
"This game is a work of fiction created to provide a realistic and immersive gaming experience," the studio said in a statement sent to South Korean state broadcaster MBC.
The scandal erupted as the families of the deceased are still awaiting answers as to why the authorities were unable to prevent the disaster four years ago. As part of the investigation, which is still ongoing, nearly two dozen officials have been charged, while three former police officers have been imprisoned.
Additional information
On Friday, October 23, the long-awaited release of the shooter "Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4" took place on PC and consoles. It was developed by the American company Infinity Ward and published by Activision.
The Modern Warfare 4 campaign focuses on a war between North and South Korea. Following the events of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III (2023), an invasion of the Korean Peninsula by the Korean People's Army threatens to destabilize the peace.
The plot centers on two main characters: Private Park (Yang Mazino), a South Korean recruit who fights side by side with his unit to defend his homeland, and Captain John Price (Barry Sloane), a former commander of Task Force 141 who is on the run after killing U.S. General Hershel Shepard.

UK PM Burnham says he is ‘open’ to formal apology for slavery, but rules out reparations
Italy
Unknown Publisher

LONDON, Oct 31 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is open to calls for a formal apology for Britain’s historical role in slavery, before attending next week’s Commonwealth summit at which he is likely to face demands for financial reparations.
Writing in the Guardian newspaper, Burnham said Britain was “offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade”, in which at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery.
“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them,” he added.
But Burnham rejected calls for financial reparations, writing: “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”
From the 15th to the 19th century, millions of Africans were sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, according to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database.
Ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week, King Charles, who is touring the Caribbean, said it was “only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past”.
Caribbean leaders are expected to press demands for reparations, which they have often framed in terms of debt relief, development finance, education, healthcare and climate resilience.
Burnham also wrote in the Guardian that he wanted to “launch a new drive on debt”, including by helping more vulnerable countries “repay over a longer time period and with better rates”.
Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne welcomed Burnham’s comments and proposals for practical assistance, though he added in a Facebook post: “The Caribbean’s longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged.”
(Reporting by Sam Tobin; Editing by Alex Richardson)

In Germany, the movement Gen Z regelt, meaning "Gen Z takes charge", has organised demonstrations in 34 cities, including Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich, Cologne and Hamburg.
Organisers are demanding greater investment in schools, housing and climate protection, alongside measures to reduce living costs. They also oppose proposals to restore compulsory military service.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder and announced the deployment of 70,000 police officers and gendarmes.
The authorities have restricted demonstrations in central Paris, with France's highest administrative court upholding a ban on a march between Place de la République and Place de la Bastille.
More than 40 Paris metro stations face closure, while police have announced restrictions on face coverings during demonstrations.
The security measures follow unrest on 17 October, when protests across France resulted in damage to shops, public buildings and businesses.
According to Reuters, France's Chamber of Commerce estimates that retailers have suffered losses exceeding €1 billion from the disruption.
The French government faces pressure over its proposed 2027 budget as public debt approaches 120 per cent of gross domestic product. Students have criticised deteriorating school buildings, overcrowded classrooms and university admissions procedures.
French authorities reported that 410,000 people participated in demonstrations last Saturday.
The protests follow demonstrations in Italy, Spain, Portugal and other European countries, where young people have raised similar concerns about education, housing and employment prospects.

Boo! See the universe’s spookiest sights in time for Halloween
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:26:35 UTC
19:26:35 KST

As ghosts, skeletons and spiders roam the streets trick-or-treating on Halloween night, they’ll have cosmic company. Throughout outer space lie stars and galaxies that resemble creepy creatures, spooky skulls and galactic ghouls. And while there’s no candy in outer space (though there is sugar), these colorful images are a treat in and of themselves.
Skeletons and disembodied heads are a hallmark of Halloween, but this phantasmic apparition, called the exposed cranium nebula, lurks above us all year long. Its brainlike appearance stems from the different phases of star death. First, the dying star ejects a bunch of hydrogen, which forms the white outer bubble, then heavier material, which creates the orange “brain” within.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The name of this nebula sounds like the title of a scary story. Called “the Ghost of Cassiopea,” its gas and dust glows like a haunted spirit because of hydrogen interacting with ultraviolet radiation from a star in the constellation Cassiopeia the Queen. When the two mix, the gas glows red, and the blue haze comes from light reflecting off space dust.
This nebula, called the Red Spider Nebula, is scuttling around space while its central star, glowing bright red in the middle, ejects bursts of gas and dust. These filaments, made up mostly of hydrogen, form the spider’s “legs.”
We all know the stories about black cats on Halloween, but what about space cats? The Cat’s Head Nebula is a collection of gas and young stars sitting within the Carina Nebula. Although the shape will someday dissipate, for now it resembles a cat turned to the right, with a glowing red eye that’s likely a young star.
The aptly named Phantom galaxy lies 32 million light-years away in the Pisces constellation. It’s called that because it has low surface brightness and is difficult to spot—but with a head-on spiral view that resembles a portal to another dimension, it certainly lives up to its haunted name.

Separately, five Palestinians were injured on Friday when illegal Israeli occupiers attacked a family harvesting olives in the Tel Rumeida neighborhood of central Hebron, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
The commission said the occupiers beat the Palestinians, used pepper spray and threw stones before stealing their olive harvest.
It also reported that occupiers completely burned an agricultural room and equipment in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron.
Palestinian farmers were prevented from working in the towns of Dura and al-Shuyukh, the commission added.
Since the beginning of the offensive, Israeli forces have imposed closures on Hebron and surrounding villages. They also seized homes in the Jilada and Ain Deir Baha neighborhoods and converted them into military barracks.
The offensive has involved forced displacement, demolition of homes and commercial properties, and destruction of infrastructure. Israeli flags were also raised over houses converted into military positions.
Nearly 5,000 Palestinians displaced
The Hebron Municipality said Tuesday that the Israeli offensive has displaced 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families.
The Palestinian Prisoners’ Society said Israeli forces arrested 110 Palestinians across the governorate between Friday and Wednesday. Military closures and the ongoing siege have also disrupted education at 66 schools, affecting 2,872 students.
Of those students, 2,198 remain under direct siege, while another 674 have been forcibly displaced and cannot reach their schools.
Displaced Palestinians have called for an end to the military closures and the lifting of the siege on their neighborhoods so they can return home and resume daily life.

‘Paycheck to paycheck’: Texas border voters shed parties amid economic woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:24:21 UTC
19:24:21 KST

‘Paycheck to paycheck’: Texas border voters shed parties amid economic woes
Voters reassess 2024 swing towards Trump as Republicans and Democrats grapple for Rio Grande Valley votes.
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Jesus Robles sells mechanical bulls.
Mainstays of bars and dance halls, once used to train rodeo riders, the bucking behemoths point to the Rio Grande Valley’s history, where Mexican and Texan Ranchero culture have long intertwined.
But the business has also been a nagging reminder of Robles’s 2024 vote, when he cast his ballot for US President Donald Trump, expecting an economic boost that would allow the company to flourish.
“I have lost tonnes of business due to our president right now,” he said, blaming Trump’s tariffs and rising fuel prices. “I ship a lot. The price of freight has doubled…. Some of my clients have been affected by immigration raids.”
Voters like Robles in 2024 helped reinforce the notion that the Rio Grande Valley, a Latino-dominated area long seen as reliably Democratic, was shifting Republican, bucking liberal hopes the ever-growing demographic would finally turn Texas blue.
His about-face in 2026, he said, underscored that no party should take voters in the region for granted.
“We focus on other countries. We focus on taxes,” said Robles, who cast his ballot on the final day of early voting in Alamo, Texas, about 50km (30 miles) from the US-Mexico border.
“But at the end of the day, I don’t feel none of these governments really help us, the people,” he added. “Because trust me, we work hard, the middle-class people work hard, and we’re the ones that get screwed the most.”
‘I did vote for Trump’
The Rio Grande Valley has become a battleground within a battleground this election season, with Republicans eyeing Trump’s 2024 gains – in which he won 14 of the 18 counties along the US-Mexico border – as evidence of a wider red shift.
They have set their sights on flipping at least two Democratic-controlled seats along the border, currently held by Representatives Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar, while holding onto a third, held by Republican Monica de la Cruz.
Democrats, riding on Trump’s high disapproval ratings among Latinos, who account for about 40 percent of the state’s population, are hoping to elect the first member of the party to statewide office in Texas since 1994. Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is running against Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, meanwhile, is seeking to unseat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
While once considered a Democratic workhorse, the Rio Grande Valley has found itself increasingly out of step with both political parties, according to Alvaro Corral, an assistant professor of politics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.
Many have drifted away from a Democratic Party once embodied in figures like former President Bill Clinton, who captured “a mixture of traditional working-class economic platform that we associate with the Democratic Party, the New Deal Democrat sort of style, mixed with a little bit of, like, social conservatism, and being quite law-and-order focused”, Corral explained.
Some voters, in turn, found common ground in the religiously-dominated economic populism of Trump’s Republican Party, Corral said, only to find themselves alienated by his administration’s aggressive domestic immigration enforcement and a lack of pocketbook relief.
At the Alamo polling site, 40-year-old Natalie, an education worker who declined to give her last name out of professional concern, grimaced when she recounted her 2024 vote.
“I did vote for Trump,” she said. “It was immigration and the economy.”
But seeing her students grapple with family separation from Trump’s mass deportation drive, and watching the price of diesel to fuel her truck continue to tick up amid the US-Israel war on Iran, made her come to regret her vote.
“I just want people with empathy,” she said.
Voter Gabriel Ruiz pointed to the high cost of housing as a unifying issue, noting houses can cost between $400,000 and $500,000, a rate previously unheard of in the valley.
He said it has become common for voters to think beyond a party.
“It’s always going to be about the economy, job growth, being able to keep jobs here, and for the American people to flourish on their own and be able to afford housing, healthcare,” the 24-year-old said.
‘Paycheck to paycheck here’
Michael Mireles, the director of civil engagement at La Union Del Pueblo Entero (LUPE), a local organisation that works to turn out Latino voters, said 2024 was, in part, a result of Democrats failing to conduct meaningful outreach in the Rio Grande Valley.
Only about 40 percent of registered voters cast ballots that year.
“Democrats in the last cycle, they were not trying to reach new voters. They were not trying to talk to people who are typically left out of Valley politics, which I think is a huge mistake,” he said.
“Because the work that needs to happen is with the people who have not been activated politically.”
Advocates believe the region is ripe for that kind of engagement.
The poverty level in the Rio Grande Valley hovers around 21 percent, the highest rate in the state and twice the national rate. It has remained nearly unchanged for a decade. As of 2023, about 37 percent of Rio Grande Valley residents did not have health insurance.
The Rio Grande Valley also has the highest concentration of so-called “colonias” of any part of the state. Colonias began as informal settlements in the 1950s, with the majority of modern residents US citizens.
About 1,200 colonias in the area are typically unincorporated neighbourhoods, meaning they do not fall under local jurisdictions and can lack basic infrastructure.
LUPE is among the groups that do voter outreach and education in those neighbourhoods.
Speaking to Al Jazeera from her home on the Erling colonia in Donna, Texas, 36-year-old Angeles Arguelles recounted not taking her sick children to the doctor recently because she could not afford the medication. Her husband works two jobs as a dishwasher, and the family has no insurance.
Despite being a US citizen, she said she has never voted.
“It just feels corrupt,” she said. “I just keep to myself and my family.”
At a nearby colonia in the city of Edinburg, 52-year-old Mario Hernandez, a restaurant worker, said his neighbourhood has become increasingly politically engaged.
“I’m not a Republican. I’m not Democrat. But it depends on who it is,” he said.
Hernandez said he had cast his ballot for all Democrats this year, motivated in part by concerns for his neighbours without health insurance.
“A lot of elderly can’t survive on their income,” he said. “Most of us live paycheck to paycheck here.”

Have hypermarkets squeezed out small retailers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:23:07 UTC
19:23:07 KST

Author
Gergana Mancheva
Saturday 31 October 2026 11:25
Saturday, 31 October 2026, 11:25
PHOTO Pexels
Font size
The expansion of major supermarket chains into Bulgaria has pushed small grocery stores out of the market dealing a severe blow to small family-run businesses. Shopkeepers welcomed customers personally, knew their neighbors by name, and often saw people stopping by to enjoy their morning coffee and read the newspaper. Times have changed, however, and small neighborhood stores are now facing growing challenges from competition and pressure from large retail chains, which have reshaped the shopping habits of Bulgarians.
PHOTO Pexels
Large hypermarkets offer everything customers need under one roof. They use social media marketing and reach consumers directly in their homes through advertising leaflets and television commercials. Major retail chains are also expanding deeper into residential neighborhoods and are able to offer lower prices because of their economies of scale. Small shops, by contrast, purchase goods from distributors at higher prices.
It turns out that small retailers’ greatest competitive advantage lies in offering fresh, traditional Bulgarian produce.
Staff shortages are another major challenge. Labour is in short supply everywhere, while wage and social security costs are simply unaffordable for the smallest businesses. This is why every member of the family runs the small fruit and vegetable shop owned by Yuliana and Atanas Donchevi in their neighborhood. They handle every aspect of the business, from deliveries and stocking shelves to processing sales documentation and dealing with customers. The shop is open seven days a week, yet the family sees little room for growth or future prospects in the sector.
PHOTO personal archive
“It takes a lot of effort,” Atanas Donchev explains. “We focus on quality, but our prices are higher than those at the big supermarket chains. We don’t have a steady clientele; everyone shops wherever it’s most convenient for them. Since the major grocery chains entered the market, things have become much harder for us. We have children and a family to support. We have to work to make a living, but it’s getting increasingly difficult.”
Atanas’s wife, Yuliana, shares his concerns. She also works in the family shop every day, which sells produce supplied by another relative who is a farmer. This leads the conversation to the challenges facing Bulgarian agricultural producers.
PHOTO BGNES
“Atanas’s brother is a farmer, and we also sell his produce - peppers and tomatoes. The seeds of our tomatoes come from an old Bulgarian variety that my mother-in-law has preserved. People love their taste and keep coming back to us throughout the summer looking specifically for these tomatoes. We also buy plums, pears and peaches from other local growers. Bulgarian fruit tastes much better than imported produce. Inspectors constantly check our shop and always find something to pick on. They are always looking for problems, even though we comply with all the requirements. We are trying to support local producers by offering their products as well. But small farmers are disappearing too. They are being overwhelmed with bureaucracy and unnecessary requirements. My son-in-law cultivates a small plot of land in Pazardzhik. This year, officials from the Food Safety Agency visited the fields and required all the farmers to complete a training course on irrigation systems. The certificate is expensive, costing between EUR 350 and EUR 500, but it has now become compulsory. Anyone who has not completed the course faces a fine of more than EUR 1,000.”
PHOTO BGNES
Customers appreciate the efforts of small businesses to survive in a fiercely competitive market, even if they cannot always afford to shop at these stores.
“I prefer shopping at small local shops. They feel more welcoming and cozy, but there are none left in the area where I live”, Sofia resident Diana Vasileva told us in our survey.
“I used to shop at smaller stores because the people who run them depend on them to support their families. What’s more, these little shops also source goods directly from producers, including Bulgarian-grown vegetables. We need to support Bulgarian farmers. At supermarkets, I’ve noticed that the products often aren’t Bulgarian.”
PHOTO Pexels
“Even with a market share of 50–60% (the proportion of food sales in Bulgaria accounted for by major retail chains - editor’s note), the sector is still far from being a monopoly. In more developed Western European countries, this share has long exceeded 80%. Small shops tend to specialize in specific product categories or find a niche by offering different opening hours during the week. In Western Europe, major retail chains generally operate for far fewer hours than they do in Bulgaria. They close much earlier, and most do not open on Sundays at all. Over time, this has led to a certain balance in the market”, Bogomil Nikolov, Executive Director of the Bulgarian National Association Active Consumers, told Radio Bulgaria.
Bogomil Nikolov
PHOTO BNR
“Bulgaria has yet to achieve this. We are still in a transition, and what we are missing most is direct sales. Alongside small shops, consumers also need farmers’ markets where they can buy directly from producers. We have yet to achieve this essential diversity of retail formats. Beyond that, it is simple: consumers vote with their wallets when they shop. But the truth is that Bulgarian produce is becoming less available, and there are many reasons for this. Flawed agricultural policies over the past two decades have led to a sustained decline in fruit, vegetable, milk and meat production in Bulgaria. No matter how closely we examine different retail formats, we will not find the solution to increasing the supply of Bulgarian produce. Small retailers’ prospects lie not so much in their prices as in the quality of their products, the personal service they offer and the trust they can build with their customers.”
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov
This publication was created by: Kostadin Atanasov

Estonia faces a shortage of competent car repair specialists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

Estonia faces a shortage of competent car repair specialists
Car dealers are complaining that it is difficult to find good and knowledgeable specialists for repair workshops, and vocational school graduates do not fill the gaps.
Business owners say it is not easy to find competent employees for car repair workshops. While technicians and painters can still be found, the situation is much more complicated when it comes to good auto body repair specialists.
For example, in Pärnu there are five professional auto body repair specialists whom car repair workshops lure away from one another with higher pay.
"Those who have already trained and are specialists in this field really have to be searched for high and low. The young guys aren't there yet. Some are very skilled and learn the job very quickly, while for others it is exactly the opposite – somehow the profession just doesn't suit them," said Kristjan Lagern, head of Eurostauto's Pärnu dealership.
Every year, around 20 young prospective technicians start studying at Pärnu Vocational Education Center and recieve their education both in the garage and the classroom. They also learn about electric cars.
"Technology is constantly developing and everything is evolving, but the basics remain the same – a wheel is a wheel, a bearing is a bearing and an engine is an engine. It's just that more and more additional features and control systems are constantly being added. You have to be capable of learning or be diligent, because here we only learn the basics in three to four years, but you have to keep learning all the time," said Priit Auväärt, lead teacher of automotive studies at Pärnu Vocational Education Center (PARK).
But not every student has a passion for the automotive industry. Some are studying only because their parents tell them to.
Car sales company Amserv has spent years ensuring its workshops have a steady supply of enthusiastic specialists. The company supports automotive technology students at Pärnu Vocational Education Center with a scholarship. This year, the €750 scholarship was awarded for the seventh time.
"On the one hand, we certainly want to develop a new generation of employees for ourselves. On the other hand, we ourselves started out young, and this is a good opportunity to now give young people opportunities," said Ahti Aasala, head of aftersales at Amserv Group.
This time, the scholarship and an internship position went to Robin Mitt, a second-year automotive technician student, who has been interested in cars since childhood.
"With friends, there was already this kind of tinkering around with cars, and then I developed a desire and interest in it at home as well. Nowadays, all these cars are becoming full of electronics, and there are countless different electrical devices in them. You definitely need knowledge of the electrical side," Mitt said.
A modern automotive technician must be able to work under the hood, understand electronic devices and, ideally, know how to use TikTok to post informative clips for customers about problems with their cars.

Lithuania Receives Its First Thales GM200 MM/C Counter-Battery Radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:15:07 KST

The first Thales GM200 MM/C multifunctional radar system, designed to detect enemy artillery positions and drones, has arrived in Lithuania.
This was reported by the Lithuanian Ministry of Defence.
The new radars are intended to enhance the reconnaissance and counter-battery capabilities of a division currently being formed within the Lithuanian Army.
According to Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, they will also enable the detection of FPV drones and improve the safety of military personnel.
The procurement is being carried out as part of defense cooperation between Lithuania and the Netherlands. The corresponding intergovernmental agreement was signed in January 2024.
The total cost of the project is €126.7 million and covers personnel training, technical documentation, spare parts, and specialized equipment.
The Lithuanian company ELSIS TS, a subcontractor of the French firm Thales, has been engaged to carry out the contract. It will participate in the maintenance, modernization, and adaptation of the systems to the needs of the Lithuanian military.
Lithuania and the Netherlands also plan to continue their cooperation on radar maintenance and implement a program for their ongoing improvement.
The GM200 MM/C is a mobile, multifunctional radar station with an active phased array antenna.
It is capable of determining the coordinates of artillery and mortar positions based on projectile trajectories, as well as detecting air targets, including drones.
The system belongs to the Ground Master family of radars developed by the French company Thales and can be integrated with air defense systems.
Other European countries have already purchased similar systems. In particular, Militarnyi reported that Norway had ordered five such radar stations.

Interview: Namibian media executive eyes AI cooperation, stronger Global South voice at World Media Summit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:13:07 CST
19:13:07 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Global South media must unite to dismantle persistent stereotypes and adopt artificial intelligence (AI) wisely, a senior Namibian news executive has said ahead of the World Media Summit in Beijing, China.
In an interview with Xinhua recently, Confidence Musariri, Acting Manager for Editorial and Operations at the Namibia Press Agency (NAMPA), said his agency is already using AI to cut production costs, speed up delivery and widen its audience, and that Global South news agencies should share content directly with one another rather than relying on Western gatekeepers.
Musariri addressed the need for Global South media to come together to challenge and dismantle enduring stereotypes while also exploring the practical application of artificial intelligence in newsrooms.
Specifically focusing on the stereotypes surrounding Africa, Musariri highlighted how Namibia, like many other African countries, is often subject to these generalized views.
He noted that most African countries are put under the blanket as "one Africa" rather than recognized as individual sovereign nations; hence, he said this is where the issue of war, of poverty, of corruption, all these stereotypes come out from.
He said such stereotypes hurt investment and the image of a country, and that the media must evolve and embrace social media to counter that.
"I believe we must adopt the usage of social media where every content creator tells the story the way they see it. It is outside the boundaries of conventional media now. I think social media is playing a bigger role in demystifying the stereotypes and false narratives," he said.
Musariri called on the Global South to unite and embrace the emerging momentum generated by social media.
According to NAMPA, media organizations have failed to fully utilize existing political agreements and distribution channels, continuing to rely on Western news agencies to verify and gatekeep content.
"There is a need for us now to also boost the cooperative news exchange agencies. There has to be exchanges within the agencies within the Global South for us to share the content directly with one another," he noted.
Musariri said NAMPA is integrating AI and its applications to cut costs, speed up delivery of content, and expand its audience reach.
He expects to secure hands-on skills exchange that goes beyond traditional reporting training, focusing instead on educating journalists to effectively adopt and adapt to rapidly evolving AI tools in the newsroom.
The goal is to leverage the World Media Summit to learn how newsrooms can integrate and automate data processes and digital convergence, ensuring AI analytics are deployed effectively to maximize results, Musariri noted.
"We are looking forward to striking cooperation deals, cooperation agreements with different media stakeholders at the media summit, and learning also how they are adopting the new forms of media," he said.
As Namibia formulates its national AI policy, he added, newsrooms need forward-looking technology rather than outdated tools, expressing hope that the summit will help identify next-generation AI solutions designed to support journalists over the next three to five years.
Musariri, who has travelled four times to China in a professional and personal capacity, meanwhile, said the upcoming summit carries special significance because he covered the 2008 Olympic Games as a journalist.
"It's interesting that this summit is taking place in the very same district where I stayed while covering the Olympics in 2008. That's almost 18 years ago. So, I'm basically going to a place where things have changed," he noted.
Musariri said that NAMPA will use its Global South network and partner entities to report on the summit, ensuring that media colleagues across Namibia and the broader continent have direct access to its key outcomes.
The 7th World Media Summit, hosted by Xinhua News Agency under the theme "Media's Mission and Cooperative Action amid Intelligent Transformation," will be held in Beijing from Nov. 5 to Nov. 9, 2026. ■

====================================================================================================

UK PM opens door to slavery apology but rules out reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said his government is open to formally apologizing for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade but ruled out financial reparations, ahead of a Commonwealth summit where Caribbean and African leaders are expected to renew demands for historical justice.
In an article published Saturday in The Guardian, Burnham said Britain was prepared to begin a structured dialogue with countries and communities affected by slavery, acknowledging that its failure to confront the past had damaged relations within the Commonwealth.
"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery," he wrote. "By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function."
Burnham said listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state would be an important part of the proposed discussions, adding that he was open to such a step.
"The trans-Atlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people," he said, expressing sorrow and regret for the suffering of millions of enslaved Africans and acknowledging the lasting impact of slavery on the modern world.
However, the prime minister firmly rejected demands for Britain to pay reparations, arguing that people living in the country today should not be held financially responsible for historical crimes in which they had no personal involvement.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," he wrote.
His position sets the stage for potentially difficult discussions at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, scheduled for Nov. 1-4 in Antigua and Barbuda, where reparations are expected to feature prominently.
The trans-Atlantic slave trade saw at least 12.5 million Africans abducted and transported across the ocean between the 15th and 19th centuries, according to the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. Britain transported an estimated 3.2 million of them, building considerable wealth through the forced labor of enslaved people in its colonies.
Britain passed legislation abolishing the slave trade in 1807 before outlawing slavery throughout most of its empire in 1833. Successive governments have traditionally emphasized the country's role in ending the trade, while avoiding a formal acknowledgment of its responsibility for the suffering and wealth generated by slavery.
Burnham said Britain needed to recognize both sides of that history, arguing that acknowledging its participation was essential to rebuilding trust with Commonwealth members.
The issue has gained renewed attention during King Charles III's Caribbean tour, which precedes the summit. The monarch has faced calls for Britain to apologize and pay reparations for its colonial past.
Speaking in Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas, on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged "the great suffering and injustices of the past," but stopped short of issuing an apology. As a constitutional monarch, he speaks on behalf of the elected government and has traditionally been bound by its position on the issue.
The king is due to address Commonwealth leaders during the meeting in St. John's, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.
Caribbean nations have increasingly framed reparatory justice as a broader effort to address the lasting economic and social consequences of slavery. Their demands include debt relief, development financing, investment in education and health care, and assistance with climate resilience.
Burnham sought to redirect part of the discussion toward those present-day challenges, proposing a new debt-relief initiative to help vulnerable developing countries repay loans over longer periods and at lower interest rates.
He said he would work with other wealthy nations and investors to advance the proposal, with former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, a longtime advocate of debt relief for developing countries, expected to attend the Commonwealth gathering.
Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne welcomed Burnham's willingness to consider an apology and his proposals for practical assistance. However, he made clear that the Caribbean's position on reparations had not changed.
"The Caribbean's longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged," Browne wrote in a Facebook post.
Burnham's remarks also come amid growing pressure within Britain to confront its colonial legacy. In 2020, protesters in Bristol pulled down a statue of Edward Colston, a 17th-century merchant and politician who played a prominent role in the Royal African Company, which transported thousands of enslaved Africans to English colonies in the Americas.
The incident intensified debate over how Britain commemorates figures who accumulated wealth through slavery.
Some institutions and families connected to the trade have already acknowledged their historical involvement and offered apologies or compensation. The Guardian's owner, for example, has previously apologized for the newspaper's historical links to slavery.

US campaign for control of Congress enters final weekend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:11:49 UTC
19:11:49 KST

US campaign for control of Congress enters final weekend
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 31 - As the campaign for control of the US Congress reached its final weekend, the Trump administration stepped up its legal intervention in the Alaska Senate race while the number of Americans casting early ballots neared 50 million, a record for a midterm election.
The Department of Justice accelerated its criminal investigation in Alaska on Friday, following reports that aides to a Democratic Senate candidate recruited a retired schoolteacher from a remote fishing village to get on the ballot because he has the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The DOJ, acting on a civil lawsuit that President Donald Trump said he instigated, also filed further motions in an attempt to block the state of Alaska from certifying the Senate results if the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, loses a close race on a ballot that includes the nonpartisan candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
The closely contested race in Alaska is seen as crucial for the Democrats if they hope to take control of the Senate from Trump's Republicans in Tuesday's vote.
PROSECUTOR ALLEGES 'SHAM CANDIDATE' IN KEY ALASKA RACE
It is one of 35 races in the 100-member Senate that will set the tone for Trump's final two years in office. Also up for grabs are all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives.
Early voter participation this cycle has set a record. More than 49 million Americans have already cast ballots, either in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day in the last midterms, in 2022.
A Democratic victory in one or both chambers could result in congressional investigations of the Trump administration, which for two years has enjoyed largely compliant Republican majorities.
Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is not scheduled to travel on Saturday, when there will be a mash-up of American traditions: politics, Halloween and college football across the country. Trump returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
The DOJ's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article about the supposed recruitment effort had driven a "surge" of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."
The Times reported on Wednesday that aides to Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola recruited Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to run. Heyman labeled him a "sham candidate" but declined to say what crime may have been committed.
The department had already filed its civil action but, Heyman said, "when the New York Times article hit, that's additional information that accelerated what we've been doing."
Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.
ADMINISTRATION GETS INVOLVED IN RACES NATIONWIDE
The Trump administration has also sued California to try to prevent the counting of ballots cast by more than 20,000 registered voters who the administration alleged could be noncitizens. It has also sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia, seeking unredacted voter rolls, part of a pattern that has alarmed election officials.
A federal judge on Friday ordered the DOJ to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration's directives regarding alleged voting by noncitizens.
Sean Morales-Doyle, director of the voting rights and elections program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the administration’s actions parallel the tactics undertaken by election deniers in the 2020 presidential election. While the administration is unlikely to win in court, he said, the efforts could create a political atmosphere that leads to official misconduct.
“It's about creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos, hoping that you create the political circumstances in which maybe the lieutenant governor of Alaska does feel pressure to do something that they're not supposed to do. Maybe the governor does start to question things, too,” Morales-Doyle said.
Even so, a bipartisan majority of US voters trust the overall electoral process, with 76% saying they are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a September 30 to October 5 Reuters/Ipsos poll. Some 15% were not confident and the rest were not sure or did not answer the question. Confidence was about equally high among Republicans and Democrats. REUTERS

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Friday that inviting Poland to attend G20 meetings was counterproductive and broke with the diplomatic practice of seeking consensus at such gatherings, according to Russian news agencies.
“Of course, this violates the principles of diplomacy, and especially multilateral diplomacy, when members of associations such as the G20 work on the basis of consensus,” Lavrov was quoted as saying on the sidelines of a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Lavrov said Poland “contributes nothing” to the meeting. He argued that its economy was not big enough to qualify and that NATO and the EU were already well represented in the group. He added that no one had pressed Russia to accept Poland’s presence. “The Americans simply invited the Polish minister, and he came in and sat down in the chair set aside for him,” he said.
The US, which holds the rotating presidency of the G20 this year, invited Poland to take part as a full participant. It has also proposed that Poland become a full member, much like Germany or France, which are also represented through the EU.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking at a reception for the ministers at Atlanta’s Georgia Aquarium, said Poland deserved to be made a full member.
“[US] President [Donald] Trump believes their economic success and growing global influence is exactly what the G20 needs to tackle the major economic challenges we all face,” Rubio said.
Poland in Constitutional Standoff as Court Heads Suspended
Economic miracle
Poland’s economy passed $1 trillion for the first time last year, making it the world’s 21st largest, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The IMF expects it to grow 3.3% this year, well above the European average. Poland’s economy is already larger than those of G20 members such as Argentina and South Africa.
Western officials say it could take years for Poland to be accepted as a full member given Russia’s opposition and the G20’s requirement for consensual decisions.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said he welcomed the push and had discussed it with a number of G20 member countries in bilateral meetings in Atlanta. He said Britain, which will head the G20 next year, had already invited Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to attend the 2027 leaders’ summit in Manchester, England, and that Poland was working to secure invitations from the following presidencies, South Korea and Mexico. He said he did not expect “enthusiasm from Russia”.
Sikorski also called for a rapid ceasefire in the Black Sea that would allow safe passage for grain shipments from both Ukraine and Russia. He said Moscow must end its war against Ukraine before being allowed to resume energy sales to Europe, formerly its most lucrative market.
“I spoke in favor of doing something quickly because the people of the Global South need this grain,” Sikorski told reporters.
He said Ukraine must be included in any effort to end Russia’s invasion, now in its fifth year. Europe also had “cards” in the issue and should be involved, he said.
Lavrov said Russia’s position on the war was unchanged and that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s comments on maintaining strikes on Russian targets were unhelpful in preparing for new talks.
“Our position is known, but what Ukraine intends to bring to the negotiating table, I don’t know,” Lavrov said.
He said Zelensky’s frequent comments that Ukraine was acquiring more weapons to strike Russian targets made preparation for new talks difficult. “This kind of attitude doesn’t really help much in preparing for negotiations,” Lavrov said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have said they are willing to hold further three-sided talks with the US for the first time since early in the year. Zelensky said this week that he hoped a trilateral meeting would take place in Abu Dhabi between November 6 and 10, and that Kyiv wanted Europe to be involved.
On relations with Washington, Lavrov said: “Fundamental issues are not being resolved. Sanctions remain, all the sanctions from [former US President Joe] Biden are echoed by the current administration.”
He pointed to a State Department announcement on Friday that it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine.
Foreign ministers at the G20 skipped the traditional group photo in Atlanta, with some making it clear they objected to appearing with Lavrov.

Australia: Italian Technology at the Heart of a New Green Steel Hub
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:07:54 CET
19:07:54 KST

Italian technology is at the forefront of Australia’s first new steel plant in over 35 years. The project, valued at 850 million Australian dollars, will be built in Collie, Western Australia, and will be developed by the Australian company Generation Steel with the participation of two major Italian groups: Danieli and Webuild, through its subsidiary Clough.
                                    
The Italian Ambassador to Australia, Nicola Lener, accompanied by the Consul in Perth, Sergio Federico Nicolaci, and the President of SACE, Guglielmo Picchi, attended the signing ceremony for the industrial agreements on October 29.
                                    
Danieli will supply the steelmaking technologies, including an innovative electric arc furnace, while Clough will handle the design and construction planning for the facility, in preparation for the subsequent awarding of the construction contract. Powered entirely by renewable energy, the new facility will transform Australian scrap iron into 450,000 metric tons of low-emission steel annually, contributing to the country’s industrial diversification and energy transition.
                                    
During the visit, Ambassador Lener, together with Consul Nicolaci and President Picchi, also met with Vikas Rambal, President of Perdaman, to discuss the group’s major investments. These include the Ceres project for urea production in the Pilbara, valued at approximately 6.5 billion Australian dollars, carried out with the decisive contribution of Saipem and Clough (Webuild), and the proposal for a new fuel refinery, currently under study, which could offer further opportunities for Italian companies.
                                    
“These investments are concrete examples of the contribution of Italian technology and know-how to Australia’s industrial diversification, within the framework of an increasingly strategic bilateral economic partnership,” commented Ambassador Lener.
                                    
The strengthening of industrial cooperation was further solidified by the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between SACE and the Government of Western Australia, aimed at promoting new investment and collaboration opportunities across the critical minerals supply chains—from extraction to refining, through to advanced manufacturing and recycling, with a particular focus on technologies for the energy transition.
                                    
The agreement follows up on the joint declaration signed on August 6 in Perth, during the “Calcio Italiano” event, as part of the economic forum “Beyond the Pitch: Connecting Western Australia and Italy,” organized by the state government in collaboration with the Italian Consulate. The initiative, attended by Premier Roger Cook and SACE President Guglielmo Picchi, laid the groundwork for closer cooperation on critical raw materials and supply chain security.
                                    
The agreement is part of Italy’s broader strategy to diversify supply sources and strengthen industrial security—including in strategic sectors such as defense—amid growing attention to the resilience of production chains. These initiatives confirm Western Australia’s growing importance as a strategic partner for Italy in the Indo-Pacific, highlighting the complementarity between Australian resources, industrial capabilities, and Italian technologies, and translating institutional dialogue into new, concrete prospects for economic cooperation.

Rubio to host meeting of Indo-Pacific Quad, wrap up G20 gathering
WASHINGTON, Oct 31 - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will host a meeting with the foreign ministers of Australia, India and Japan on Saturday, their third meeting this year, as plans take shape for a summit of the leaders of the four countries in Manila next month.
The leaders' summit, slated to occur during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) conference in the Philippine capital November 15-18, will be the first since 2024, and the first for US President Donald Trump.
The first formal leaders' summits of the four countries known as the Quad did not begin until President Joe Biden took office in 2021. Trump was scheduled to attend a Quad summit in India in late 2025, but canceled the visit due to trade frictions and tariff disputes with New Delhi.
After the Quad ministers' meeting, Rubio will wrap up a two-day meeting of the Group of 20 major economies being held in Atlanta, after which he has invited the ministers to watch a college football game, according to the State Department schedule.
Rubio's elder son, Anthony, is a running back for the University of Florida, which will be squaring off against the higher-ranked University of Georgia team.
Rubio, speaking at a reception at the Georgia Aquarium on Friday evening, repeated his call for G20 members to cooperate where possible given today's complex economic and geopolitical challenges, including many with serious global consequences.
"Because we all face these challenges, we must all work together to address them," he said. "The future of our nations depend on our willingness to understand that while our interests may not always align, we should always seek to work together to advance them when and where they do align."
Friday's meeting revealed deep rifts in the G20 over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with organizers nixing a traditional family photo after some European members refused to be photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
Rubio, who will hold a press conference after the meetings conclude on Saturday, said he hoped the G20 foreign ministers could lay the groundwork for a successful leaders' summit December 14-15 at Trump's Doral golf resort. REUTERS

Abuse survivors to press Church on accountability during pope's trip to South America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:06:46 UTC
19:06:46 KST

Abuse survivors to press Church on accountability during pope's trip to South America
MEXICO CITY/LIMA, Oct 31 - As Pope Leo prepares to return to South America, Peruvian abuse survivor Pedro Salinas sees reason for both hope and unease in the pope’s record confronting clerical abuse.
For a decade, Salinas watched as the Catholic Church investigated Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, the Peru-founded Catholic community he helped expose. Then, in the final days of Pope Francis' papacy last year, the Vatican dissolved the group and its branches.
"What was achieved, nobody, absolutely nobody, could even have imagined. It was inconceivable. But it happened," said Salinas, 63, a journalist and former member whose reporting helped expose allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse inside the group.
Robert Prevost, as Leo was known when he was a bishop in Peru and later a Vatican cardinal, quietly worked with survivors and advocates, Salinas said, attending meetings, gathering information and communicating by WhatsApp and email.
"Without him, the needle didn't move," Salinas said.
The first US-born pope will travel through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru November 6 to 17, ending with six days in Peru, where he arrived as a missionary in the 1980s and later became a citizen and served as bishop of Chiclayo. The Vatican said he will meet clergy abuse survivors there, as he has done on other recent trips.
Survivors say they wonder whether Leo's approach in Peru, which they credit with helping bring about the rare step of dissolving a Catholic community, can translate into broader change across a Church where they say accountability is uneven.
“What is lacking are bishops everywhere in the world committed to this issue," Salinas said.
Peru is preparing for a tourism bonanza during Leo's visit. José Enrique Escardó, 56, president of a Peruvian survivors network, views the excitement from a different perspective.
While Escardó acknowledged that some survivors credit Leo with helping dissolve Sodalitium, he said the Church's actions have not delivered sufficient justice, accountability or reparations.
“Survivors have grown tired of being told things, of being promised things, but nothing being done,” Escardó said. “We feel more abandoned. We feel deceived.”
He wants survivors to become involved in shaping Church policy and wants reparations to include psychological care and education.
The Vatican did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
'TIP OF THE ICEBERG'
Francis, the first Latin American pope, left a complicated legacy, survivors say. Juan Carlos Cruz, the survivor whose case became central to Francis' 2018 reckoning with abuse in Chile, credits Francis with changes including revisions to canon law, removal of the pontifical secret — the Church's highest level of confidentiality — surrounding abuse cases and Vos Estis Lux Mundi, a Vatican framework for bishops accused of abuse or cover-up.
"We're still at the tip of the iceberg," said Cruz, whom Francis appointed in 2021 to the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors. "The commission has been working for years on universal safeguarding guidelines and those standards need to be applied around the world."
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the watchdog group BishopAccountability.org, which tracks Catholic Church abuse allegations worldwide, called Vos Estis the most significant action Francis took on abuse. But she said the Vatican rarely makes clear whether an accused bishop's resignation represents punishment.
“The public is left in the dark,” she said.
Barrett Doyle said the Vatican has not released global disciplinary data comparable with figures it provided to a United Nations committee in 2014. Her group relies on public records, media reports and investigations by prosecutors, governments and commissions to track cases.
She wants Leo to make permanent removal from ministry the universal rule for priests found under canon law to have sexually abused children, extending worldwide a policy adopted by US bishops in 2002.
"To say that no child molesters should be out to practice as priests is just such a no-brainer," she said. “It's a step that Leo could take now.”
Vatican officials have previously cited the difficulty of creating a single abuse reporting law across all countries and argued that removing priests can put them beyond Church supervision.
Angela Walker, executive director of the US-based Survivors Network of those Abused by Priests, said survivors increasingly turn to civil authorities because of the Church's "incredible failure" to police itself.
"There needs to be more transparency, more openness, and more accountability," she said. "I will believe it when I see it."
SURVIVORS' LONG WAIT
In Mexico, survivors pressed the Vatican on clerical abuse decades before it became a defining crisis across Latin America. Among the most notorious cases was that of Marcial Maciel, the Mexican priest who founded the Legion of Christ order and whose accusers took allegations to the Vatican in the 1990s. The Vatican ordered Maciel in 2006 to withdraw from public ministry. He died in 2008, without ever facing his accusers.
The scale of his abuse became clearer after his death. In 2019, the Legion reported that Maciel had abused at least 60 minors, among 175 instances of child abuse the order documented involving 33 priests over eight decades.
José de Jesús Barba Martin, 87, alleged Maciel abused him when he was studying for the priesthood in the 1950s. He recalled survivors struggling to be heard by Church and state authorities in the late 1990s and said an appeal he sent Pope John Paul II went unanswered.
Decades later, that experience has left him with little expectation that another appeal to Rome would bring change.
“The Church is made up of two types of men: good and bad, courageous and cowardly," he said. "It will take a long time, and the issue will not be addressed under this pope nor the next."
Alberto Athié, 72, a former Mexican priest who pursued clerical abuse cases from inside the Church before leaving the priesthood in 2003, sees Leo's visit as another opportunity to push for transparency.
“I do have hope,” he said. “But my hope fades just the same ... Things have to be fixed within the Church."
Abuse survivor Sebastian Cuattromo said the Argentine Church should have been “at the international forefront” of confronting abuse under Argentine Pope Francis, but fell short of what he had hoped to see.
"There is a major outstanding debt," Cuattromo said.
Argentina's Episcopal Conference declined to comment. REUTERS

Africa suffering in ‘strongmen’ era, says governance watchdog
‘If you’re an African leader and you see all those strong people rising everywhere … you say, why not me too? I can get away with it’
Democracy and rights are declining in Africa as leaders take their cues from the rise of strongmen in other parts of the world, the head of a governance monitor told AFP.
Mo Ibrahim, 80, is a Sudanese-British billionaire who made a fortune in telecoms and ploughed it into monitoring and encouraging better governance across Africa.
The Mo Ibrahim Foundation’s latest report, finds broad progress on economic opportunity and human development over the past decade, but also steep declines in security, human rights and public participation at a time when Africa has suffered multiple military coups and devastating wars.
Ibrahim highlighted elections over the past year in Tanzania, where security forces were accused of killing thousands of protesters, and Uganda, where opposition leader Bobi Wine was “hunted and physically attacked”.
