Europe's fears, Ramallah's hopes and Trump's dilemma: World braces for Israel's political deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:05:32 UTC
19:05:32 KST

Israel's election for the 26th Knesset ended without a clear winner, but the political deadlock is already drawing reactions in Washington, Europe and the Middle East. As Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot seek a path to forming a government, world leaders and diplomatic officials are assessing how the results could affect the war with Iran, the future of the Gaza Strip and relations with the Palestinians.
U.S. President Donald Trump has already indicated that he would not rule out becoming involved in efforts to establish a unity government, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas has proposed resuming peace negotiations, and Germany has warned that urgent humanitarian measures in Gaza must not be delayed until coalition talks are completed.
Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, the Jewish parties in the bloc opposed to him secured 48, while Ra'am and the Joint List together won 19 seats, an unprecedented achievement for the Arab parties. Neither bloc holds the majority needed to form a government, and President Isaac Herzog will have to task one of the candidates with doing so. In the meantime, until a new government is established, Netanyahu will continue to lead a caretaker government that may face significant security and diplomatic decisions.
Trump weighs whether to intervene
One of the leaders closely following developments in Jerusalem is President Trump, who publicly endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the election and subsequently claimed that his support helped the prime minister achieve a better-than-expected result. Although Likud remains the largest party, Netanyahu's bloc lost the majority it held in the outgoing Knesset, and his ability to remain in office now depends on negotiations with parties that ran against him.
Asked in a post-election interview with Axios whether he intended to intervene in efforts to form a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said he had not yet considered the possibility but added, "I'll look at it." Reuters noted that a broad government led by Netanyahu could serve the American interest in political stability in Israel, while stressing that neither side currently appears willing to reach such an arrangement.
The central issue for Washington is Iran. Trump and Netanyahu have recently raised the possibility of renewing strikes against the Islamic Republic amid the prolonged conflict and the prospect of further escalation after the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Reuters noted that Israel's political uncertainty comes at a sensitive time for the U.S. administration, which is also grappling with the economic consequences of the war and the stalemate in diplomatic efforts over Gaza. However, replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily bring a fundamental change in Israel's security position toward Iran. Jonathan Panikoff, a former senior U.S. intelligence official who is now a researcher at the Atlantic Council, told Reuters that a different Israeli leadership would also likely support escalation against Iran if Trump decided to resume strikes.
Meanwhile, Tehran is also preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting. A report published Friday by the French newspaper "Le Monde" said Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had instructed government ministries and executive agencies to remain on alert in light of regional developments. At the same time, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is continuing talks with mediating countries in an effort to prevent escalation. An Iranian analyst who spoke to the newspaper assessed that Tehran believes renewed strikes could serve Netanyahu's political interests, because another military confrontation could shift the public debate in Israel away from the coalition crisis and toward security issues, potentially encouraging the formation of a unity government.
Europe: 'We cannot wait for a new government'
Europe is also closely watching Israel's political developments, although reactions have varied. On Wednesday, the European Union issued a measured diplomatic statement congratulating Israeli citizens on the high voter turnout, describing it as a sign of the vitality of Israeli democracy. The EU expressed its willingness to work with the next government while maintaining open dialogue on cooperation, areas of disagreement and efforts to promote regional stability and peace.
France, meanwhile, made clear that even a change of government would not alter its policy toward Israel and the Palestinians. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot was asked in an interview with France 2 whether an Eisenkot victory could improve relations between the two countries. He replied that French policy would remain unchanged. France, he said, would continue working to ensure Israel's security while also promoting a two-state solution. Barrot also addressed the Arab parties' electoral gains, saying their increased strength in the Knesset could influence the next government's decisions. However, he stressed that Paris would not wait for political change in Jerusalem before continuing to pursue its positions, including measures to restrict trade with settlements in the West Bank.
In Germany, concerns are growing over the consequences of prolonged coalition negotiations. A report published Friday by Deutsche Welle (DW) said the government in Berlin was avoiding expressing a preference for a particular coalition but wanted to ensure that Israel's political crisis would not delay urgent measures in Gaza. German Development Minister Reem Alabali-Radovan warned that the approaching winter was likely to worsen the humanitarian situation in the territory and called for aid organizations to be allowed to expand their operations without waiting for the conclusion of political negotiations in Israel. She also addressed settler violence in the West Bank, saying it must be stopped even during the caretaker government's term.
Meanwhile, Jürgen Hardt, a foreign policy expert from Germany's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told DW that he would prefer an Israeli government closer to the political center. He said the Arab parties' electoral gains could open new coalition possibilities, including a minority government led by Eisenkot that would rely on their external support. However, he emphasized that the decision ultimately rests with Israel's elected representatives.
Concerns about the consequences of a prolonged caretaker government have also been raised by European think tanks. Beth Oppenheim, a researcher at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), warned in an analysis published Thursday that Netanyahu could exploit the period of political uncertainty to resume the military campaign against Iran or expand military operations in the West Bank. She argued that European countries should act now, together with the United States and Arab states, to prevent further escalation and advance the Gaza ceasefire plan.
Abbas proposes peace talks: 'We hope we can begin a dialogue'
The election produced a different outcome from the one some Palestinian leaders in Ramallah had hoped for. Nevertheless, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas chose to publicly express his willingness to resume negotiations. During a visit to Cyprus on Thursday, where he met President Nikos Christodoulides, Abbas expressed hope that the formation of a new Israeli government would allow the sides to return to the negotiating table.
"For many years, we have extended our hand to the Israeli side to achieve peace, so that Israel and Palestine can live in security, stability and peace," Abbas said. He added, "We hope that immediately after a new Israeli government is formed, we can open a dialogue together."
Abbas also asked Cyprus to help mediate between the sides, explaining that its good relations with both Israel and the Palestinians could enable it to play a meaningful role. The Cypriot president, for his part, expressed his willingness to help advance regional stability. It is important to note that despite Abbas' remarks, Eisenkot also opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state, although he advocates a different policy toward the Palestinian Authority and supports action against settler violence.
Arab states remain skeptical
A sharper response came from Qatar following allegations that it had interfered in the Israeli election. Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari strongly denied Thursday that Doha had financed activities intended to influence the vote. He accused political and media figures in Israel of trying to drag Qatar into the country's internal political struggles. "These accusations are both ridiculous and dangerous," Al-Ansari said. He added that if all the allegations made in recent years about Qatar's political influence in Israel were true, Doha "would already control the entire country."
The spokesperson stressed that Qatar does not interfere in Israel's political competition and would continue its role as a regional mediator. He called on the next Israeli government to respect international law, advance a resolution to the Palestinian issue and recognize the Palestinians' right to self-determination and an independent state along the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. Meanwhile, Israel's Central Elections Committee clarified that allegations of systematic election irregularities were unfounded and that the security investigation into suspected foreign interference would not change the election results.
Other Arab countries have shown little enthusiasm for the possibility of a change in Israel's leadership. An analysis published Wednesday by Germany's DW noted that even a more moderate Israeli government would be unlikely to bring a rapid change in Israel's position on Palestinian statehood or its military presence in Lebanon and Syria. However, experts interviewed by the network said a government that did not include Netanyahu's far-right partners could make it easier to advance regional security arrangements, including the possibility of renewed negotiations on a security agreement with Syria and progress in talks on an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon.
One of the region's most significant questions concerns the future of normalization with Saudi Arabia. Riyadh has repeatedly made clear that it will not move toward normalization without progress on the Palestinian issue. According to experts quoted by DW, even a change in the composition of Israel's government would not guarantee a breakthrough, although it could make it easier for Arab countries to engage in diplomatic and security talks with Jerusalem.
'Netanyahu and Eisenkot are not the same'
The debate over the significance of Israel's election has also reached the opinion pages of the European press. In an article published Friday in "Le Monde," French columnist Alain Frachon argued that despite similarities between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on several major security issues, their differences could have significant implications for Israel's future and its relations with the world. Frachon noted that both leaders oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state but emphasized their differing approaches to the Palestinian Authority, settlements, Trump's Gaza plan and the status of Israel's democratic institutions.
He argued that the outgoing government's policies had contributed to Israel's international isolation, while Eisenkot was presenting an approach that could allow for some restoration of relations with Israel's Western partners.
This analysis does not necessarily reflect the position of the French government, which, as noted, has made clear that its policy will not change according to the identity of Israel's next prime minister. It does illustrate, however, that the debate in European capitals is focused not only on who will lead the next government but also on the nature of the coalition that emerges and the policies it adopts.
For now, Israel's political deadlock has left its international partners in a state of uncertainty. Washington faces decisions concerning Iran and Gaza, Europe fears further escalation and delays in advancing humanitarian measures, and Ramallah hopes the next government might make it possible to resume negotiations. The question of who can secure 61 Knesset seats remains unanswered, but it is already clear that the political outcome in Jerusalem will shape not only Israel's future but also its relations with the world in the years ahead.

Turkey nominates former FM in race for next UN chief
Turkey has officially nominated a former foreign minister and yearslong ambassador to the United Nations for the next UN secretary-general, state-run media reported Saturday.
The next UN chief will succeed António Guterres, who has led the world body for almost 10 years. The organization is under pressure to reform as it finds itself sidelined in wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza while also facing a financial crisis that has forced major cuts to humanitarian and development programs.
Feridun Sinirlioglu, a 70-year-old former Turkish foreign minister and UN diplomat, had floated his candidacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York last month.
Sinirlioglu was Turkey's top diplomat for a few months in 2015, an interim period between elections, and its UN ambassador between 2016 and 2023. He currently serves as the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
His current three-year mandate is scheduled to end in December 2027, but the top UN job would have a Jan. 1 start date.
Ahmet Yildiz, Turkey’s current representative to the UN, told the Anadolu news agency that Sinirlioglu's name was officially submitted with backing from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Erdogan has been vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council, especially criticizing the dominance of its five permanent members. Sinirlioglu is likely to reflect the president’s agenda.
The next U.N. secretary-general will be decided by the 15-nation UN Security Council, especially its five veto-wielding members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The 193-member General Assembly must give final approval.

Tusk’s government has been trying for weeks to force out the court’s judges, who were appointed by the previous PiS government that ruled from 2015 to 2023.

Beyond Western narratives: What the Russia-Africa Media Forum delivered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:01:02 UTC
19:01:02 KST

Beyond Western narratives: What the Russia-Africa Media Forum delivered
Western broadcasters have long interpreted Africa for the world and, too often, for Africans themselves, while promoting negative portrayals of Russia, speakers at the Russia-Africa Media Forum argued.
Organized by RT in cooperation with Sputnik and TASS, the forum ran in Moscow from October 26 to 29 alongside the third Russia-Africa Summit. It brought calls for greater local control over the continent’s stories and direct exchanges that bypass Western interpretations.
More than 200 participants from 46 African countries attended the media gathering, which produced partnerships covering reporting, professional training, and broadcasting technology. The main Summit drew delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 leaders.
“In Ghana we are overly dependent on Western assessments of international affairs,” Ghana Broadcasting Corporation Director General Amin Alhassan said, explaining his organization’s cooperation with Russian media. Access to another perspective would help make its reporting more balanced, he argued.
The discussions unfolded amid competing accusations of interference. Moscow accused Western governments of obstructing its exchanges with African journalists, while France alleged that Russia was manipulating public opinion on the continent.
Who gets to tell Africa’s story?
African Union of Broadcasting Director General Grégoire Ndjaka urged Russia to support African journalists in producing their own accounts of events, including through training and cooperation on news 
content. 
“We do not want our history to be written for us and then sent back to Africa,” he told a Wednesday session examining the influence of media from countries of the global majority.
Ndjaka criticized what he described as an overwhelmingly one-way flow of information from the West to Africa. He said that the broadcasting union had established a center to produce news about the continent and wanted partnerships that would help African perspectives reach wider audiences.
Sebastian Maganga, head of content at Tanzania’s Clouds Media Group, similarly highlighted the value of exchanging stories directly. Such gatherings, he told RT, give African outlets opportunities to share their perspectives internationally while obtaining material from Russia and elsewhere.
Western media dominance under scrutiny
TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov argued that the era of Western media hegemony had ended, attributing the shift to declining trust, double standards, and the suppression of inconvenient information.
For decades, he said, a small group of Western media companies had exercised disproportionate influence over which events became international news and how countries were portrayed. African journalists were increasingly challenging that arrangement by reporting on their societies themselves.
“The world is becoming multipolar, and the information space is becoming multipolar with it,” Kondrashov said, advocating a wider range of perspectives in international reporting.
Mayya Nikolskaya, head of a research program at MGIMO University’s Institute for International Studies, accused major Western broadcasters of increasingly prioritizing criticism of Russia over coverage of development.
“They [Western media] used to focus more on development projects, now they’re talking mostly just about how Russia is bad,” she told RT.
Nikolskaya named CNN, the BBC, RFI, and France 24, arguing that African countries now had greater freedom to choose partners according to their own priorities.
Pressure and competing allegations
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told African journalists on Tuesday that Western countries were trying to obstruct direct communication between Russia and Africa. 
“We must push back against this collectively... not individually, but by acting together,” she said. Zakharova alleged that some participants had faced intimidation or been offered competing events to discourage them from traveling to Moscow. She linked this to broader efforts to restrict African cooperation with Russia, including through pressure involving financing and political support.
Separately, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot accused Russia on Tuesday of manipulating public opinion in sovereign African countries to damage French interests. He said that he would seek EU sanctions against those responsible for an alleged interference operation targeting several countries, particularly Cameroon and the Republic of Congo. Barrot accused Moscow of trying to “colonize minds.”
His allegations come as France’s influence in Africa has dwindled, particularly in the Sahel, where governments have expelled French troops, citing their failure to help combat jihadist violence. Russian media organizations have expanded partnerships with African broadcasters despite restrictions in Western countries. In March 2022, the EU suspended broadcasting by RT and Sputnik, accusing them of 
spreading disinformation and manipulating information.
In July, RT became the first international partner of Tafouk TV, the joint television channel of the Alliance of Sahel States, comprising Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. Their memorandum covers exchanges of content and expertise, alongside joint coverage of developments in Russia and the three countries.
From discussions to newsroom partnerships
The forum also produced practical cooperation commitments. RT Editor-in-Chief Margarita Simonyan said that the network signed agreements with African outlets representing Ghana, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Libya, and other countries. Cooperation would include exchanges of experience, training, skills development, and media technologies.

Examples included RT Arabic’s partnership with Mauritania’s Radio and Television Broadcasting Corporation. The Mauritanian organization said that the protocol would support exchanges of technical expertise and improvements in broadcasting operations.
TASS reported signing seven cooperation agreements on Monday with news agencies from Burundi, Guinea, Cameroon, Mali, Niger, Seychelles, and Tanzania. The agency also said it already supplied Arabic- and French-language news services free of charge to more than 300 African media outlets.
Other examples included Rossiya Segodnya’s partnerships with outlets in Algeria, Chad, Morocco, Ghana, and Zimbabwe. These covered content exchanges and expanded existing cooperation. Memorandums with Ethiopia’s Debre Markos University and Niger’s Higher School of Journalism and Communication provided for professional dialogue and joint events, with participants also highlighting training in 
artificial intelligence.
Liberation’s legacy and changing perceptions
Thursday’s RT session, “Forging Independence: Lessons from the Founders of African Nations,” brought descendants of liberation leaders into the discussion about Africa’s place in the world.
Samia Nkrumah, daughter of Ghana’s first president Kwame Nkrumah, connected their presence in Moscow to Russian support for African independence movements.
“We are the descendants of African liberation leaders and we are all here in Russia for a reason,” she said, adding: “That is because Russians helped us during our long and sometimes violent independence struggle all over the continent.”
Musata Kaunda Ndhlovu, granddaughter of Zambia’s first president Kenneth Kaunda, described liberation as an ongoing responsibility. Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of South Africa’s Nelson Mandela, recalled first meeting him through a prison window on Robben Island in 1981, aged 16.
The question of how personal experience challenges outside narratives also featured in RT’s interview with Ghanaian YouTuber Wode Maya, whose videos challenge negative narratives about Africa and reach more than two million subscribers.
Maya told RT that fears about traveling to Russia had initially made him reluctant to attend the forum. “You won’t believe that I fell for the propaganda,” he said, describing how his reception in Moscow had changed his expectations.
Maya also welcomed the opportunity for Africans to speak for themselves and challenge stereotypes about their continent.

‘Plantation tourism’: court victory signals hope in Jamaica’s fight to keep beaches public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:41 UTC
19:00:41 KST

When the Australian human rights lawyer Eva Buzo emerged from the sea on to the shores of One Man Beach in Montego Bay on Sunday after her gruelling, nearly 11-hour-long swim, the thunderous pulse of welcome drums was drowned out by the chants of “free beach” from jubilant supporters.
Here in Jamaica’s tourism capital, against a backdrop of jagged mountains and sunset-tinted clouds, Buzo – a celebrated marathon swimmer – said she was pleased to help support the important work of the Jamaica Beach Birthright Environmental Movement (Jabbem) and others fighting for free public access to Jamaica’s beaches.
“People’s rights are more important these days than ever, and people keep on trying to encroach on our fundamental freedoms,” she said, calling the privatisation of beaches a colonial legacy. But for Jabbem, her swim was not the most significant milestone this month in its fight for public access.
That came earlier in October, when Jabbem celebrated a rare victory in one of several court cases to end the 1956 Beach Control Act that had given the state ownership of the island’s foreshore and seabed. The act has allowed successive administrations to restrict access to beaches and sell off coastlines to wealthy luxury hoteliers.
In October, however, the court issued an injunction preventing the government from continuing to restrict access to Little Dunn’s River in St Ann while the case continues.
“This victory means a lot for the Jamaican people. It means that our case is strong,” said Dr Devon Taylor, an immunologist with a PhD in biochemistry, who founded Jabbem in 2020.
Wilbourn Carr, 73, who is involved in another fight for beach access in Portland parish, in Jamaica, said the temporary injunction offered hope for other cases.
“The matter of beach access is right across Jamaica. And we just had some success at Little Dunn’s River with that injunction. It gives us hope. Because the fact is that one judge now believes that Jamaicans should have access,” he said.
The Jamaican government has said it will appeal. In an interview, the environment minister, Matthew Samuda, said there was no basis for protest. He said the government was safeguarding critical tourism investment and protecting communities from crime, while improving beach access through updated legislation requiring future developments to create access points and investment in community leisure spaces.
In the case of Little Dunn’s River, Samuda said access had been restricted after a murder.
“Because of the cultural sensitivity and the love that certain residents of St Ann and those who travel far and wide to come to the facility have for the space, the government intervened and said it would put up appropriate security structures and would facilitate free access to this area on a weekend basis, Friday, Saturday and Sunday,” he said, describing this as “structured management” that also provided benefits such as lifeguards.
Describing tourism as the “largest foreign exchange earner” and the main source of income for nearly 200,000 Jamaicans, Samuda accused activists of portraying the industry as “the enemy”.
He said: “176,000 people aren’t protesting anything to do with beach access, but 176,000 people are feeding their families because of our tourism product … Let’s not put their needs and their concerns on one side.”
Taylor, however, rejected crime prevention as justification for beach closures, pointing out that “the Beach Control Act of 1956 predates the level of crime seen in Jamaica and was never a tool to control crime”. He referred to the Little Dunn’s River restrictions as an illegal “collective punishment of the Jamaican people” that had nothing to do with solving an alleged murder.
“So you could close it until forever, until you solve this murder, which you have not solved,” he said. “You present no evidence that this place was still under threat … So we refute Little Dunn’s River was closed to solve some murder or to stop more from happening, because four years later you only allow the people to use it on Saturdays and Sundays. We deserve leisure seven days a week.”
Paul Roberts, a British architect living in Jamaica and Jabbem’s St Ann community coordinator, argued that the government is creating a false impression that Jamaicans cannot be trusted.
“It’s a load of rubbish,” he said. “I’ve been coming here for 15 years now and I’ve never had any trouble. I’ve never been robbed, I’ve never been mugged and I’ve never faced any issues.”
Campaigners did not oppose hotels, Taylor said, but rather a “plantation tourism” model that disadvantaged Jamaicans.
“Cheap labour of the Jamaican people, degradation of the environment, exclusion of the Jamaican people from the foreshore, plantation tourism, untenable working conditions. Lock us out using colonial-era law. The industry is guilty of that,” he said.
“We the people do not want to be treated as second-class citizens in our country … we want fairness, equality and equity.”
Buzo described access to shared public spaces as a human rights issue, pointing to countries such as Australia, where she is from, and Barbados in the Caribbean that maintain public beach access alongside thriving tourism industries.
“There’s no reason why hotels can’t have beachfront properties that then front on to a public beach. It’s just this kind of exclusivity and segregation that small amounts of people think they need,” she said.
Samuda argued Jamaica was different because, although the country had “conquered our crime monster”, it had “spent 30 years being in the top three most murderous countries on the planet”.
Much of Jamaica’s coastline was also rocky, he said, with only a fraction considered “beach”. He argued that most of the “beachy” areas remained publicly accessible, although some carried restrictions or charges.
Jabbem is campaigning for full, free and unfettered beach access, arguing that many families are priced out by high entrance fees and forced to buy expensive on-site food and drinks owing to outside-food bans. The group’s western Jamaica community coordinator, Monique Christie, said tourists also lost out when separated from local communities.
“The product that is Jamaica is not the hotel. It’s definitely not the rooms. It’s definitely not the name of the resort. It has always been us, the people. It has always been our warmth and the desire of everyone to just come and meet us.”
Dr Theresa Rodriguez-Moodie, the chief executive of the Jamaica Environment Trust, said questions over what constitutes publicly owned space had become increasingly complex, leaving many Jamaicans feeling disenfranchised.
“I think that we need to be paying attention to what the Jamaican people are asking for, they’re talking about, and find a way to address that through changes to the law, changes to the policies.”
In March, Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, proposed a beach access and management policy supposedly intended to modernise legislation and increase access. Campaigners say it still permits unacceptable restrictions.
“The 2026 policy that was published in March was supposed to try and address some of the issues, but it really didn’t,” Rodriguez-Moodie said.
For Taylor, the fight will continue. “The people are crying out. We need a fundamental change. And they must listen to the people because we won’t stop until this law is abolished and we have fundamental rights and workers’ rights in this country. That is what our ancestors fought for,” he said.

The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized
Unknown

2026-10-31

19:00:40 KST

Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the Tesla Diner in Los Angeles, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.
Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.
Musk’s spending is a staggering example of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO’s political influence, as he seeks to help Donald Trump’s administration retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, though current polls predict Democrats achieving a majority. The contributions are at a scale that is difficult to fathom and dwarf efforts from big name megadonors like George Soros or Michael Bloomberg, setting a new precedent for how the rich and powerful attempt to shape politics.
Only last year, Musk claimed he would step away from making large scale political donations after putting nearly $300m towards Trump’s 2024 presidential election campaign. FEC data since then shows he has not only leaned back into financing campaigns, but that his spending has dramatically ramped up as election day approaches, increasing by about $200m in the final two months of campaigning.
Musk’s money has primarily flowed into several Republican-aligned Super Pacs, with his largest contribution of $216m going into his own America Pac. The Pac has targeted 43 House and Senate races across the US, blanketting voters with television commercials, digital ads, text messages and mailers.
America Pac made 839 independent expenditures in House races and 623 in Senate races in 17 states across the country. The spending varies greatly depending on the state, however, with campaigns in battlegrounds such as Michigan and Arizona receiving more of the Pac’s support.
Musk’s Pac has spent the most in his home state of Texas, where a closely fought Senate contest between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton has turned into the most expensive race of the midterms. America Pac has overall poured more than $33m into efforts to elect Paxton, while Musk also made a $168m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund which supports the Paxton campaign.
A large portion of America Pac’s output focuses on attack ads against Democratic candidates such as Talarico, often accusing them of being radical socialists or targeting them over supporting transgender rights. The Pac has spent $28m on anti-Talarico content, including between $300,000 and 350,000 in October on a single Google ad targeting the Texas Senate candidate.
“James Talarico supports parents being charged with child abuse if they do not support transitioning their children,” stated the ad, which was shown more than 10m times over an eight day period.
Musk has also reposted America Pac’s content to his more than 200m followers on X, the social media platform he owns. One of Musk’s posts in October amplified an America Pac attack ad and claimed: “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”
The nearly $446m that Musk has donated this election cycle far exceeds his contributions in the 2024 presidential race, when the tech mogul also held rallies and appeared on stage next to Trump during the campaign. While Musk has been a less visible presence in the midterms, potentially reflecting the US public’s dislike of him, behind the scenes he has greatly upped his financial support for Republicans.
Musk’s spending far outpaces all other donors in the elections, including fellow tech and finance moguls like Marc Andreessen, who also started his own Super Pac. Musk has put more money into this election cycle than what every top Silicon Valley donor, including himself, spent on the 2024 presidential election combined.
The stakes of the midterm elections are potentially high for Musk, who has closely aligned himself with the Trump administration and benefited from its lax policies toward regulating tech and artificial intelligence. SpaceX has also intertwined itself into the government more extensively, landing lucrative contracts this year for Trump’s missile defense program and the use of Musk’s Grok AI chatbot in the Pentagon.
Despite the immense and unprecedented scale of Musk’s political spending, his contributions this election are still only a tiny fraction of the centibillionaire’s overall assets.

The real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for long | Robert Hutton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:40 UTC
19:00:40 KST

You join us on a steam train in Scotland as we head to the next episode of the BBC’s hit show Political Traitors. It’s like the celebrity edition, except that everyone is less comely – politics being the practice of show business for ugly people. For this week’s task, the players have to construct a “budget” of tiny crowd-pleasing measures, carefully balanced by invisible tax rises.
What makes the show so compelling is that the players don’t know the whole story. Only those of us on the outside can see what’s really going on. While John and Andy run around shouting about how they have faithfully met their “fiscal rules” in the third year of the forecasts, on our sofas at home we know that this incantation is entirely meaningless.
But people who’ve been on the show say that when you’re in the midst of it, it feels completely real. So much so that there are ongoing questions for the producers about safeguarding. Liz, who was a sensation of chaotic energy when she briefly appeared in 2022, is the most obvious example of someone who shouldn’t have been allowed to take part. She was last heard explaining her plan to colonise Mars.
If the series has any value beyond entertainment, it’s for the insights it offers into human psychology, especially the way people convince themselves of narratives that are objectively nonsense. Take Kemi, from the current run. After the banishment of Keir earlier this year, she could be heard explaining to anyone who would listen that this was the result of her brilliant inquisitions at the roundtable.
We could all see that the other players, after debating why on earth Keir hadn’t already been stabbed in the back, had concluded that although he was 100% faithful, he was also 1000% loser.
Nevertheless, there’s something rather charming about Kemi’s total conviction that she’s a masterly player on course for triumph. It’s easy for us to laugh, but you have to remember that she doesn’t have access to the information we do, such as opinion polls and byelection results.
That information gap is the joy of the show. Several times Nigel has seemingly revealed himself to be a traitor, and his close ally Nathan was actually unmasked as one, but still no one seems able to put two and two together.
Some players adopt a strategy of trying to fly below the radar to avoid being noticed. One current player, Ed D, has been so successful that many viewers have forgotten he exists and refuse to believe he is part of the game at all, even after his triumph in the water slide task.
Each morning, the players meet over breakfast TV for a heated discussion in which they all insist that whatever has just happened proves their theory is right. Then there’s the dramatic moment of discovering who has been banished, or simply walked off the set. In one compelling episode in 2022, almost all the players quit in the hope of forcing Boris to admit he’d been lying. Even then, to viewers’ delight, he still had the support of the loyal Nadine.
In last month’s “conference” task, the players were handed the severed head of a deceased teammate and had to mimic their distinctive cry. Kemi, predictably, chose Maggie, although her impersonation looked more like pastiche. Andy, on the other hand, reckons he can do a mean Harold. He’s rejected any suggestion that he should try copying Tony, one of the game’s most successful players, but he’s failed to brush aside the lingering suspicion that he’s simply doing an impression of Keir.
The format has been sold around the world, with changes for local markets. The French edition involves a runoff vote. The Israeli version is so complicated that no one understands anything about it except that somehow Bibi keeps winning. And the American one is louder, brasher and far more expensive. It also seems to be played entirely by idiots who have failed, despite an impossible number of very clear clues, to identify their obvious traitor.
Although the players change at an alarming rate, the one constant in the British show is the host, Lindsay. With his ridiculous outfits and his catchphrases – “Order! ORDER!” and “Mr Holden, I think you need to leave” – he is fast becoming a national treasure. And now, as he says at the end of every roundtable, the time for talk is over.
I’m joking, of course. In this version of the show, the time for talk never ends.
- Robert Hutton is a journalist and author

How ‘sin bin’ for red light jumpers saves cyclists from being saddled with a fine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:39 UTC
19:00:39 KST

When Aman cycled through a red light in the City of London this week, he was surprised when the police pulled him over. He was positively shocked when, instead of giving him a fine, officers took him into a gazebo to watch a bike safety film.
Aman was one of 30 cyclists caught in the first 20 minutes that morning, as part of a new scheme by City of London police to dissuade cyclists from running red lights.
Many concerned pedestrians have celebrated the time-out zone and, perhaps more surprisingly, cyclists have too.
The new pop-up scheme, called “stop, look, listen, change”, gives offending riders the chance to view an educational film about the dangers of red light jumping. Those caught by police who do not want to pay a £50 fine are taken to a “sin bin” by the roadside, where they watch testimonies from visually impaired road users.
“It is about taking that time away,” said Rob McTaggart, media and engagement manager at City of London police. “Time they didn’t stay waiting for the light is now the time they’re having to spend watching the video. It’s a bit of instant justice in that regard.”
As cyclists continued to be corralled into the time-out zone, McTaggart said the police team had noticed no difference between the numbers of red light runners on hired e-bikes versus those on regular bicycles.
When the sin bin was first launched two weeks ago, roughly 70 people were brought in within90 minutes, McTaggart said. None of the halted riders opted to take the fine.
Watching the safety film, McTaggart said, was useful for spreading road education.
“Right now you can jump on a bike without any training whatsoever,” he said. “It’s about that understanding that just because you can go, it doesn’t mean you should go. We’re not going to enforce our way out of it.”
Sgt Stuart Ford, who helped create the scheme, said it was inspired by the Exchanging Places initiative, where cyclists are brought into large goods vehicles to understand risks like blind spots and difficulties in manoeuvring.
Ford said he was sympathetic to cyclists – “You can quote me: I like bikes” – but added that police “get more complaints than anything else in the city around cyclists jumping lights and their behaviour”. He added: “I’m afraid to say it but a lot of the time, the cyclist is the protagonist here.”
Ford collaborated with the National Federation of the Blind UK (NFBUK) to understand how vulnerable road users are affected by riders skipping lights or riding on the pavement.
Hyacinth Malcolm, who is fully blind, said: “I’m just lost for words as to why they [cyclists] are behaving the way they’re behaving.”
Malcolm said she had to rethink before going out for a daily coffee because of the risk of cyclists colliding with her.
Sarah Leadbetter, a disability activist with visual impairments, also said the footways were not safe for disabled people and that things were getting worse.
She said she relied on a cane, her guide dog and the rotating cone at pedestrian crossings – a small, unassuming plastic or metal cone which is attached to the underside of the push-button unit.
But, she said, she could not be certain of her safety because cyclists “suddenly come through the red light and go straight into you”.
McTaggart said the scheme had sparked discussions across the country and that there was a “huge appetite for what we’re doing here”. In the last week, pedestrians have complained of cyclists riding through the recently pedestrianised Oxford Street.
Sarah Gayton, street access campaign coordinator from NFBUK, commended the new education scheme, but hoped to see the fine increased to £300 and further action taken by the government. “Something has got to give,” she said. “We need designs that work for everybody.”
While some have pitted cyclists and pedestrians against each other, Tom Fyans, CEO of the charity London Cycling Campaign, said he also wanted to see more changes in London’s road designs to better suit all road users.
Standing at the busy junction of Old Street roundabout in the east of the capital, he said: “London isn’t designed for cycling, it’s getting better, but it’s designed for cars. What we need to see is far more cycle-friendly, pedestrian-friendly designs where the car is less important. Then you’ll see a much safer environment for everybody.”
On the new scheme, Fyans said his charity supported the measures over what he believed to be ineffective monetary penalties. He said: “Punishing cyclists with fines and criminal prosecutions, it doesn’t really work. But getting them to think about their impact on other road users – hearts and minds – is much better.”
Fyans said most cyclists do follow the Highway Code, but that a focus on bicycle users was “disproportionate” and a result of the rising number of bike users on London’s roads.
“I think there’s double standards quite often,” he said. “We’re not the biggest danger. It’s cars and speeding and drivers not paying attention that kill people on our roads. That’s the biggest challenge that needs addressing.”
Fyans, who works with Wheels for Wellbeing – a cycling disability group – said he understood the dangers for visually impaired pedestrians and wheelchair users.
But can relations between cyclists and pedestrians be improved? “Let’s address it, but let’s be proportionate about what the real problem is,” he said. “Cyclists are not really the main problem on the road when it comes to danger.”

Nearly 90% of voters now expect their candidate to win. The math doesn’t work.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:36 UTC
19:00:36 KST

Nearly 90 percent of American voters who name a preferred presidential candidate now expect that candidate to win, up from roughly 70 percent a few decades ago. New research published in Political Behavior suggests this surge in optimism is linked to growing hostility toward the opposing party. When those high hopes are dashed, losing voters who expected to win tend to stay more hostile toward the other side than losers who saw defeat coming.
In almost every democratic election, far more people predict that their favored candidate will win than the final vote tally can support. Political scientists call this pattern wishful electoral thinking, a phenomenon in which a person’s desire for an outcome directly shapes what they expect to happen. Optimistic predictions may help voters avoid mental discomfort and cope with an uncertain future.
Social scientists have documented how stubbornly these biases resist correction. For instance, a 1997 study of voters in a Jerusalem mayoral election found that citizens overwhelmingly predicted their favored candidate would win, even when they knew the latest polls or were offered cash for accurate forecasts. Media coverage can also shape expectations: two 2018 experiments on news consumption found that when partisan outlets covered viewers’ own party as winning the race, viewers became more likely to predict a win, and when coverage showed their side losing, they lowered their predictions.
Over the past few decades, the United States has also experienced a steep rise in partisan animosity, often called affective polarization, which refers to Democrats and Republicans viewing the opposing party with deep dislike and distrust. Some research suggests that many voters today are driven more by dislike of the other party than by affection for their own, though others dispute how common this is. Preliminary evidence from a 2022 working paper based on an online survey, which has not been peer reviewed, suggested that disliking the opposing party predicts expecting an election victory more strongly than feeling warmly toward one’s own party.
Hostility toward political opponents shapes how citizens process election results as well. For example, a survey of voters surrounding the 2020 presidential election found that while most Americans overestimated their emotional reactions to the outcome, people with deeply negative views of the opposing candidate experienced more intense emotions than anticipated. Building on this line of research, study author Seth Warner of the University of Connecticut examined whether partisan animosity has driven the surge in electoral optimism, and whether those high hopes leave losing voters more resentful when their candidate falls short.
“I think, initially, this started when I noticed how news outlets whose audiences lean left or right run stories that suggest that the ‘other side’ is about to fall apart,” Warner told PsyPost. “Reading the New York Times, for example, it sometimes seems like Donald Trump is always in trouble, Republicans are about to turn on him, or his supporters are beginning to question things. You see much the same thing in reverse in right-leaning media.”
“I know from personal experience — and it’s backed up by a lot of psychology — that people react badly when things don’t turn out the way they expect,” Warner added. “So my original thought was that when people expect their party to win and then lose, they might come away from the election feeling even more hostile toward the other side. That’s part of what I found, but the bigger discovery was just how stratospherically high Americans’ expectations of victory have become.”
In the first of two studies, Warner tracked how election predictions have changed using the American National Election Study, a long-running national survey of American adults conducted around each presidential election, drawing on its cumulative file from 1952 to 2020 plus survey data from 2024. Before each presidential election, participants answered who they thought would win in November, allowing Warner to measure whether voters predicted a victory for their preferred candidate (among the 71 percent expressing a vote intention) or for their party’s nominee. To account for objective race conditions, he matched each interview date to a seven-day rolling average of national polls from Gallup (before 2004) and RealClearPolitics (2004 to 2024).
Warner then analyzed survey waves from 1980 to 2020 to test which individual traits explained the rise in poll-adjusted optimism. He examined party loyalty in voting, party attachment strength, policy alignment, campaign news interest, living in a state and congressional district dominated by one’s party, and political knowledge (knowing which party controlled the U.S. House of Representatives). He also measured attitudes on a 0-to-100 “feeling thermometer” scale, where 0 represents very cold feelings and 100 represents very warm feelings, defining ratings above 75 for one’s own candidate as warm feelings and ratings below 25 for the opposing party as high partisan animosity.
The historical data showed that the share of voters expecting their preferred candidate to win hovered around 70 percent for decades, rose into the high 70s in the 2000s, and reached the high 80s from 2012 onward. Polls mattered: each additional percentage point of polling lead was associated with about a 7 percent increase in the odds of expecting victory. But polling could not explain the recent surge. Even after accounting for polling margins and how close each race was, the odds of expecting one’s side to win stayed within a fairly narrow band for decades and then climbed sharply from 2012 onward.
“The big takeaway is that elections these days are close, and nobody really knows in advance who’s going to win,” Warner explained. “Polling the public has gotten quite hard, and although we can usually get results within 5 percentage points, most pivotal elections these days are decided by less! You wouldn’t know that to talk to most Americans, though. In the last election, about 90% of people now expect their preferred candidate to win, so we’re seeing a big disconnect between expectations and reality.”
When Warner calculated how much each trait contributed to the 17.6-percentage-point linear rise in expectations of an in-party win between 1980 and 2020 (a statistical accounting rather than proof of cause), two factors stood out. Party loyalty in voting rose by 8 percentage points and accounted for 24.9 percent of the rise in optimistic predictions, while the share of voters with high partisan animosity jumped by 47 percentage points over those four decades and accounted for 22.0 percent of the increase.
Disliking the opposing party had almost no link to electoral optimism in 1980 but became a reliable predictor by 2020, whereas strong party identity (3.0 percent), candidate ratings (2.8 percent), and news interest (2.2 percent) explained very little of the shift. Taken together, the measured traits accounted for roughly half of the overall increase in optimism, leaving about half unexplained.
In a second study, Warner examined whether changes in an individual’s partisan hostility over time correspond with changes in their election predictions. He analyzed data from the American National Election Study’s 2016, 2020, and 2024 multi-wave panel survey, which tracked the exact same partisans and independent leaners across three presidential elections (providing over 5,100 observations). Partisan animosity was measured continuously from 0 to 100 by reversing each respondent’s feeling thermometer rating of the opposing party, and statistical models isolated changes within the same person from one election cycle to the next.
Across these within-person models, rising hostility toward the opposing party reliably predicted higher expectations of victory, though the link was stronger among Democrats; among Republicans it pointed the same way but was not statistically significant. Controlling only for polling margins, a one-standard-deviation increase in animosity (roughly the typical spread of scores on the scale) corresponded with an 8.0- to 8.9-percentage-point increase in the probability of expecting one’s party to win.
After controlling for candidate ratings, party attachment strength, ideology, news interest, and geographic sorting, a one-standard-deviation rise in animosity still corresponded with a 3.3- to 3.7-percentage-point increase in the probability of predicting a win. Warm feelings toward the in-party candidate had the largest direct relationship (a 17.4- to 18.0-percentage-point increase per standard deviation), while news interest and geographic sorting were not statistically significant.
Using a statistical technique that maps how different attitudes feed into one another over time, Warner also traced how attitudes among 1,912 panel participants in 2016 related to their views in 2020 and subsequently predicted expectations in 2024. This analysis indicated that 2016 partisan animosity was linked to 2024 victory predictions indirectly, through its connections with other attitudes measured in 2020, even though its direct link to 2024 expectations was small and not statistically significant. The model also suggested a two-way relationship: expecting a win in 2016 predicted higher animosity in 2020, though this reverse effect was weaker than the path from animosity to expectations.
Next, Warner tested what happens after Election Day when hopeful voters see their party lose. He analyzed pre- and post-election interviews with 22,313 respondents from American National Election Study surveys across presidential elections from 1996 to 2024 (excluding 2000, when post-election party ratings were omitted). Comparing pre-election feeling thermometer ratings of the opposing party with post-election like-or-dislike ratings, both rescaled from 0 to 1, he tested how pre-election predictions interacted with election loss while controlling for pre-election animosity, candidate ratings, party identity strength, ideology, demographics, and election year.
The results suggest that losing usually takes some of the edge off partisan hostility, but not for voters who expected to win. After accounting for their pre-election views, losing voters who had anticipated defeat ended up about 2 points less hostile toward the other party than winners, on a 100-point scale. Losing voters who had expected to win showed no such drop, scoring about 3.1 points higher than losers who had braced for defeat. The effect pointed the same way in every election studied and reached statistical significance in 2004, 2016, 2020, and 2024, with the largest estimates in the three elections Donald Trump contested.
Among Republicans who expected to win in 2020, the added hostility was still detectable in 2024, while Democrats’ disappointment from 2016 had faded by 2020. Warner cautions that the 2020 aftermath, which included Trump’s unfounded claims of mass voter fraud, was an unusual case, and that the 2016 result calls for caution about how long such effects typically last.
Warner sees this effect as small next to the rise in optimism itself. “The ‘dashed hopes’ effect that I found on post-election animosity is more modest, about three points on a 100-point scale,” he noted. “But it occurs at a particularly sensitive moment for democracy, when one side has to accept defeat and the other prepares to take power. Even relatively small changes in political hostility could matter at that moment.”
These findings stand in tension with an earlier study of American partisans across the 2022 midterm election cycle, which found that hostility toward the opposing party and support for democratic norm violations stayed persistently high after the election, leaving winners and losers equally polarized.
Both studies evaluated post-election partisan animosity among winners and losers, though Warner’s analysis spanned multiple presidential cycles and separated voters by their pre-election expectations, whereas the earlier study tracked overall shifts across a single midterm election without distinguishing between hopeful and realistic voters. Warner suggests his findings may help reconcile the two: if nearly everyone on the losing side expected to win, the usual post-election cooling may not show up.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Because the study relies on observational survey data rather than an experiment that randomly alters political preferences, it cannot establish strict cause and effect. Unmeasured factors could simultaneously boost both a voter’s dislike of the opposing party and their optimism, and high expectations can also feed back into greater animosity over time. In addition, pre-election animosity was measured on a 0-to-100 feeling thermometer and post-election animosity on an 11-point like-or-dislike scale, making the before-and-after comparison approximate.
National surveys are also limited in how well they can separate internal psychological desires from partisan information bubbles. Although Warner accounted for campaign news interest and geographic sorting, these measures do not capture a person’s exact media diet or social networks. Future research using experimental designs could help isolate how much of electoral optimism stems from an emotional desire to see the opposing party lose versus exposure to partisan commentators who repeatedly predict victory. Warner suggests that tempering these unrealistic expectations could help support democratic stability during post-election transitions, when unprepared voters may be especially vulnerable to anger and false claims of election fraud.
“To speak a little more normatively, it’s important for people to remember that democracy involves winning and losing,” Warner said. “In a competitive two-party system, your side is going to lose about half the time, and some degree of intellectual humility is important for democracy to work properly. That means being willing to consider what a good-faith person might find lacking in the way your side has made its case, so that parties can be self-improving, as opposed to just negatively defined by who their opponents are.”
“Of course, there are big moral issues in American politics that are genuinely difficult to find agreement on, and we shouldn’t pretend otherwise,” he added. “But there are also plenty of pragmatic issues where everybody holds a similar goal — like good jobs and schools, low crime, and national security — and it’s just the approaches that differ. For better or worse, those are often the most important ones to the swing voters who decide elections.”
The study, “Partisan Wishful Thinking in Polarized Times,” was authored by Seth Warner.

Education under fire: Gaza’s children face death on their way to school

Education under fire: Gaza’s children face death on their way to school
Children have faced Israeli bombs and sniper fire since school resumed in Gaza for the first time in years.
Gaza City— Mohammed Hamad, 14, was on his way home from school in Deir el-Balah on October 17 when an Israeli strike targeted the road he was travelling along.
He had finished classes at the makeshift school and was walking home through the al-Baraka neighbourhood with his 10-year-old brother, Abdullah. Mohammed was killed in the strike along with another man. Abdullah survived.
Mohammed was Riyad Hamad’s third child, an eighth-grade student among the top pupils in his class. His loss is difficult for the 44-year-old father to comprehend.
“He was not just my son, he was my friend,” Hamad told Al Jazeera from his family tent in Deir el-Balah. “He was doing so well. May God have mercy on him.”
The family has struggled to come to terms with the death of a boy whose schoolwork and achievements had been a source of pride.
“Mohammed used to ask me: ‘How am I with you?’ I swear, I never asked him for anything more,” he said.
The loss has also left a deep mark on Abdullah, who now fears losing his father, too.
“He has become very afraid of going to school. They used to go together every day and come back together. Now he cannot come to terms with having to go on his own,” Hamad said.
“We are living in fear. When I go out into the streets, I swear I am afraid. Even when I am walking or sitting in a car, my heart is filled with fear … Why should our children have to live with this constant fear and anxiety, even until the last moment?
“Enough is enough. The child is supposed to bury his father, not the father bury his child. They have turned the order of things upside down.”
The gradual return of children to school – even in makeshift classrooms and tents – had offered families in Gaza some hope of restoring a sense of normality after years of disruptions.
But Israeli air raids and sniper fire have continued, despite a ceasefire being established last October for Gaza. Since then, Israel has killed at least 1,574 Palestinians and injured 5,687 in Gaza, according to the enclave’s Ministry of Health.
The academic year resumed in Gaza on September 19, after nearly three years of disruptions caused by Israel’s war – and with it came more Israeli strikes.
Ten children aged from six to 16 and a teacher were killed between October 18 and 24. In a statement last Sunday, the Ministry of Education said that two girls were wounded during morning assembly at Muradiya School in Jabalia on October 21. Five students were also injured, some critically, in an attack on the Islamic University campus in Gaza City on Sunday.
The ministry called for urgent international action to protect students, schools and universities in Gaza.
The risks are particularly high for schools located near the so-called “Yellow Line”, a point that divided Gaza’s territory between Israeli and Palestinian control as part of the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. The line has moved westward to give Israel control of more than 65 percent of Gaza, according to the United Nations, up from the 53 percent agreed upon a year ago
At least 66 Palestinian children have been killed close to the Yellow Line, and pupils and teachers travelling near this zone remain in mortal danger from Israeli snipers and bombs.
On October 21, Suad Abd Rabbo, a fourth-grade student, went to school carrying her bag and books. Not long afterwards, her older sister rushed home shouting that Suad had been shot.
“I ran out barefoot,” Suad’s mother, Aliaa Abd Rabbo, recalled. “When I saw her, I was confused. I didn’t know what to do. She was bleeding, crying and screaming.”
The bullet struck Suad above the knee and lodged in a sensitive area close to her nerves and tendons. She was rushed to hospital, where doctors warned that trying to remove it could cause paralysis. They operated on Suad but were still unable to extract the bullet, which remains in her leg.
Abd Rabbo remembers when Suad came round from the anaesthesia after surgery and started reciting a passage she had been preparing for a school dictation exercise.
“‘O symbol of generosity and resilience … When I feel tired, I sit under an olive tree in the yard of our home, and feel rested after the exhaustion,” her mother recalled her saying.
Suad has since been discharged from hospital and has returned to her tent, where she remains unable to walk or move around. She needs surgery abroad to fully recover, but with Israel tightly controlling exit and entry from Gaza, her prospects of proper treatment are remote.
“Suad is now deeply frustrated. She cries and asks: ‘Why did this happen to me? Why was I targeted? What did I do?’” Abd Rabbo said.
Israeli tanks, military vehicles and cranes regularly open fire close to their tent in northern Gaza, particularly after sunset. Families often have to lie flat on the ground for hours to avoid the stray bullets that ricochet through the camp.
“My heart hurts when I send the girls to school. I told my husband I regret coming back from the south,” Abd Rabbo said about their return home to Jabalia after fleeing to Deir el-Balah during the war.
Another girl was also injured on the same day as Suad as students at Muradiya School were preparing for assembly at about 10:30am, Naim Aloush, the school’s principal, said.
“The girls had formed two lines … one suddenly screamed and fell to the ground … another girl standing nearby was struck by a bullet in her side,” she told Al Jazeera.
Teachers rushed to the girls and found that Suad had been shot while the second pupil, Amina Khader, a fifth-grade student, sustained a minor injury to her abdomen.
Aloush said the shooting sent fear through the school, with parents rushing to collect their children.
Pupils who had witnessed the incident were left terrified, and the school saw a marked increase in absenteeism in the days that followed.
The principal sees this incident as part of wider dangers facing the school in the al-Ghubari area, west of Jabalia al-Balad, consisting of 20 educational tents and serving about 1,000 pupils in the surrounding community, close to the Yellow Line.
Aloush said stray bullets or projectiles – from Israeli artillery, quadcopter drones and snipers – still regularly hit the school.
“Education is under fire, and our whole lives are under fire. At any moment, there can be gunfire. It is not light … it comes down like rain,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Every day, I come to school with my hand over my heart, afraid that one of my pupils or a member of the teaching staff might be hit.”
Amina, the other child injured along with Suad, has been left deeply traumatised by the incident, her father, Khaled Khader, said.
Khader said he rushed to the school after hearing that Amina had been injured and carried his daughter to a nearby clinic.
“There was terror, absolute terror. My daughter was in shock. She broke down, started screaming and collapsed,” Khader told Al Jazeera.
“Thank God she is safe … but the psychological impact of what happened will take years to overcome.”
Amina has since been afraid to return to school. Her family tried taking her back once, but she left early, unable to bear the sound of the gunfire.
“She is now afraid of the school itself. She keeps dreaming about her classmate lying there with blood running from her,” Khader said.
He said the incident had also left him afraid for the rest of his children and his wife, with Israeli air raids, random gunfire and shelling continuing to affect streets near the school.
“We are confused about what to do. Do we keep our children away from school and deprive them of their education, or do we send them out, knowing that they could be targeted at any moment?” Khader said. “A student needs stability to be able to learn. But we have no stability, and there are no alternatives.”

How ancient Chinese stayed cosy using gadgets found in classical literature, historic artwork
A TCM practitioner says warming baskets dispel body dampness and unblock meridians, especially when infused with herbs

Fran Luin Beijing
In ancient China, without electricity, how did people stay cosy at home during freezing winters? The answer lies in warming baskets, which have been used for more than 2,000 years.
A traditional warming basket featured a charcoal brazier beneath a bamboo cover. One of the earliest written references to the device dates back to the Qin and Han dynasties (221 BC–220).
At first, the basket served as a stove to keep a room warm. Later, people added incense to the brazier and placed a basin of water beneath the basket. This allowed it to double as a garment steamer, drying clothes while infusing them with fragrance.

An AI Agent Injected Drugs Into a Live Mouse’s Brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.
Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.
Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.
“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.
AI models are trained primarily on published scientific literature. That means they may miss important information about the research process, including failed experiments, unexpected observations, and decisions scientists make in real time. Integrating AI models with real-world experiments can make the models more reliable, Santero says.
It’s why his team decided to connect an AI agent to a custom-built surgical setup used for performing brain injections on mice. The rig included a motorized device used to immobilize a mouse and a camera that allowed the agent to observe the procedure, move an injection needle, and control the delivery of a compound. For the experiment, his team was testing a gene therapy to see whether it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.
They asked the AI model to choose a treatment from 19 options in a spreadsheet. A veterinary surgeon first performed a craniotomy on the mouse while the AI agent observed. The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.
The team initially tested Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, but it refused to guide the needle into the mouse’s brain, suggesting it might stop midway through the surgery, which could endanger the animal.
“He did the experimental planning, but when it was time to inject, he said, ‘something on my output is telling me I shouldn't do this,’” Santero says, referring to the agent. “That was very interesting.”
The team switched to using Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Opus is a heavy-reasoning intelligence specialist best for complex multistep problem-solving, according to Anthropic, while Sonnet is better suited for everyday tasks, though it may be a stretch to call mouse brain surgery a common chore. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)
Frontier labs have been planning for more widespread physical manifestations of AI, and researchers have already begun enlisting agents to do other things in the physical world. In August, Anthropic put out a framework for how its models can interact with the real world. More recently, AI engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a car to pick up lunch at In-N-Out Burger. Only one of the models succeeded.
The brain injection procedure wasn’t without hiccups either. The researchers had established safeguards, including requiring the AI to propose an injection plan for human approval and installing an emergency button a human could hit that would disconnect the rig’s motors. They also restricted the agent's access to the underlying equipment code to prevent it from modifying its own operating rules.
However, a technical glitch disrupted the equipment's coordinate system. Although the agent correctly recognized that the calculated injection position was wrong, it refused to modify the code to correct the problem because its instructions explicitly prohibited doing so.
The team resolved the issue by using a separate AI agent on Opus 5 to make the necessary code changes, but they didn’t tell the agent that a live surgery was happening. The resulting back and forth delayed the procedure, Santero says: A typical brain injection surgery like this takes about 45 minutes, while this experiment lasted slightly longer than an hour. They’re now waiting for the therapy to take effect before assessing its impact on seizures.
Despite those glitches, Santero and his team were impressed by the agent’s performance. They’re testing Grok and other models next to figure out whether one model performs better. The company is also experimenting with agent-controlled craniotomies—a much more complicated task—but wants to be absolutely sure of their safety before moving to live surgeries.
“A mistake at that stage could seriously harm the mouse,” he says.
Santero thinks AI agents will increasingly work alongside human scientists, with direct access to lab equipment. For now, he says human oversight is key, particularly when experiments involve living animals. And it’s far too soon to unleash an AI agent on a human brain.
As for the mouse, Santero reports it’s recovering well.

A historically paralyzed Congress faces its voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

A historically paralyzed Congress faces its voters
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Just 10% of Americans approve of Congress’ job performance.
- Critics say Speaker Mike Johnson has ceded congressional authority to the executive branch.
WASHINGTON — Next week’s elections are widely seen as a referendum on President Trump, his team and his party, with most voters telling pollsters they seek a check on his power. But the midterms will also serve as a reckoning for one of the least productive sessions of Congress in a century.
A stunningly low 10% of Americans approve of the job performance of Congress, which has passed fewer bills and conducted less oversight than any of its predecessors in modern history, according to scholars of the legislative branch.
The biggest achievement of unified Republican control has also become one of its biggest liabilities. Deeply unpopular when signed, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has only grown more controversial, with most Americans still unclear on what’s in it — and those who do know largely disapproving of the law, which cut taxes for businesses and billionaires while adding trillions to the national debt.
A summer Politico poll found that just 8% of Americans believe the law has improved their bottom line. The bill cut billions of dollars for food stamps and over a trillion in health programs and Medicaid.
Two veteran Republican incumbents are battling for a solidly red congressional seat in Orange and Riverside counties in an election that could be swayed by Democratic and independent voters.
Two other significant bills passed by this Congress — the Epstein Files Transparency Act and a housing reform package targeting corporate purchases of single-family homes — ultimately became law over Trump’s opposition, leaving Republicans little credit for bipartisan wins.
“It’s not a partisan statement to say that the current Congress will go down in history as one of the most ineffective in history,” said Charles Stewart III, director of the Election Data and Science Lab at MIT. “It may not be the most ineffective, but it’s down there.”
Norman Ornstein, an emeritus scholar at the conservative American Enterprise Institute, said that congressional performance can be measured by several criteria, including the quantity and quality of legislation, its oversight of the executive branch, investigations of government and private-sector failures, and its defense of congressional powers and ethical standards.
By all accounts, he said, “the 119th Congress is an abysmal failure, perhaps the worst I have seen in well over five decades of immersion in the legislative branch.”
A recent Fox News poll found that government corruption is voters’ top concern this year, surpassing even the economy. Yet the Republican-controlled Congress has failed to deliver meaningful oversight. The enrichment of Trump, his family, allies and aides has gone uninvestigated, while Senate Republicans continue to block legislation targeting insider trading by members of Congress.
It has been a running theme from Democrats working to unseat Republican incumbents, with Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York — slated to become speaker of the House if Democrats win control of the chamber — repeatedly characterizing the current session as a “do-nothing” Congress.
In Alaska, Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate, accused her GOP opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, of doing nothing to stop Trump’s tariff policies or his war with Iran. Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio has attacked the Republican incumbent Jon Husted for his procedural attempts to end debate over legislation on the Epstein files. And Democrat Adam Hamilton has targeted Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas for voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that jeopardized funding to rural hospitals.
Defending the record of his majority, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has highlighted a decline in prescription drug prices, the elimination of “wasteful spending” on various federal programs and bipartisan housing reform. Only so much can be accomplished with a razor-thin majority in the chamber, Johnson has said.
California’s general election takes place on Novemer 3. Learn about L.A.’s city and county races as well races for state office.
Trump has vowed on the campaign trail that, if kept in power, a Republican Congress would pass a $5,000 dividend to each American, despite its thin record to date.
Critics of the speaker say Johnson’s deference to Trump — and relinquishing of congressional authority to the executive branch — has unilaterally ceded power, souring voters on unified government.
But Stewart, who also co-directs a voting technology project with Caltech, said Congress’ problems run deeper than its current record.
“Not only is Congress not pushing back against the administration, or even innovating in policy, but its members also don’t seem especially interested in serving their constituents on the small-ball aspects of representation,” Stewart said.
“It’s hard to say members of this Congress are connecting with their constituents as they did in decades past,” he added. “We’ll see if that lack of constituency connection will have an impact on the results.”
