Proposed billionaire tax could impact California sports teams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Proposed billionaire tax could impact California sports teams
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The proposed billionaire tax on California’s November ballot could slap a one-time 5% levy on wealthy residents, including sports team owners, to raise healthcare funds.
- Opponents warn professional sports teams owned by wealthy Californians could face higher costs, resulting in job losses, as well as increases to the cost of tickets, parking and concessions.
- Supporters argue billionaire team owners should pay their fair share after benefiting from Trump-era tax cuts.
The billionaires targeted by the wealth tax on the November ballot include owners of some of California’s top sports teams and, among them, there will be winners and losers if voters approve the measure.
Which owners would be ensnared by the proposed tax on billionaires’ assets remains unclear, since it’s largely dependent on whether they are declared official California residents, at least for state tax purposes. And that’s before lawyers and accountants get involved, an almost certain bet if the ballot measure is approved by California voters.
So it’s possible that the majority owner of the Los Angeles Chargers, Dean Spanos, would have to pay the the wealth tax while the owner of the Los Angeles Rams, San Kroenke, would not — even though both their teams are playing on the same home field at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. It all depends on whether the state considers Spanos or Kroenke official California residents and how their assets are tallied.
Other wealthy team owners or co-owners who have residences in California and could be subject to the tax include the Golden State Warriors’ Joe Lacob and Peter Guber, the San Diego Padres’ José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones, the San Jose Sharks’ Hasso Plattner and the Anaheim Ducks’ Henry Samueli.
Among those who appear to live out of state, according to news reports, and may not be impacted: the San Francisco 49ers’ Denise DeBartolo York and John York, the Los Angeles Clippers’ Steve Ballmer, the San Francisco Giants’ Charles Johnson, the L.A. Kings’ and the L.A. Galaxy’s Philip Anschutz.
In August, embattled billionaire Mark Walter agreed to sell the L.A. Lakers to former Disney chief executive Bob Iger and venture capitalist Joshua Kushner. The proposed billionaire tax would apply to Iger, who lives in California, but not Kushner, who lives in New York. A spokesperson for Iger declined comment. Walter, who also owns the Dodgers and has been under federal investigation, told the California Post on Wednesday that he has no plans to sell the team.
There is uncertainty and disagreement about how the tax would be levied on sports team owners, and how their ownership stakes would be evaluated by the state when assessing their assets.
Representatives of the Warriors and Chargers, declined comment. Spokespeople for the Kings, Padres, Sharks and Ducks did not respond to requests for comment, nor did representatives of Kroenke or Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla, who lives in California and whose $9.6-billion purchase of the Seattle Seahawks was finalized in September.
Legendary sports agent Leigh Steinberg warned that the proposed tax would have unintended consequences. “It creates an uneven playing field,” he said. “Out-of-state owners get an advantage over in-state residents.”
Steinberg, who has represented more than 300 professional athletes including Troy Aikman, Drew Bledsoe, Michael Vick and Oscar De La Hoya, said the increased tax could be passed on to fans if voters approve Proposition 40 on Nov. 3.
“Ticket prices are high enough anyway, and somewhat prohibitive to a working person or young person attending a game live,” Steinberg said. “The last thing in the world positive for the growth of sports is passing on that surcharge.”
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on many of the assets of billionaires, including their holdings in companies. It was crafted by a healthcare union to compensate for federal healthcare cuts signed by President Trump last year that will cost California an estimated $100 billion, impacting the state’s most vulnerable residents.
David Gamage, a tax law and policy professor at the University of Missouri’s law school, countered that consumers would be far more hurt by the impacts of the impending federal healthcare funding cuts than by potentially higher prices at sporting events.
“The billionaire wealth tax would address the healthcare crisis caused by the Trump administration slashing Medicaid and other healthcare funding. Passing the billionaire wealth tax would be expected to reduce healthcare costs and thereby keep the prices of hot dogs and other consumer goods lower,” Gamage said. “Trying to fool voters by implying otherwise is shameful.”
More than 200 billionaires live in California, some of whom moved themselves or their businesses out of the state because of the proposed tax. Facebook creator Mark Zuckerberg, the chief executive of social media giant Meta, told company leaders that he planned to leave the state to avoid his control over the company being substantially diluted by being forced to sell enough stock to pay the proposed levy. Last week, the company announced the creation of a new nonvoting type of stock that would allow Zuckerberg to sell enough shares to pay the proposed tax while retaining his voting power in exchange for him agreeing to remain in the state for eight years.
Proposition 40 supporters say that billionaire sports team owners have benefited from Trump’s tax cuts — dividends they didn’t share with the fans who spend hard-earned money to bring their families to games — and that they need to pay their fair share.
Opponents argue that professional sports are among myriad California economic engines that will suffer if voters approve the proposition, in part because owners based in the state would be subject to the tax while those who reside in other parts of the country would be exempt.
The measure “will also drive up the cost of operating a sports team in California, increasing the price of tickets, concessions and merchandise,” said Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable. “This is just one of many ways Proposition 40 will cost Californians.”
A poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies released Thursdayshowed public sentiment had turned against the billionaire tax, with half of likely voters opposing it and 42% supporting it.
More than $404 million has been donated to efforts supporting and opposing the wealth tax, according to the California Secretary of State’s Office. Proponents of the ballot measure had raised $36.5 million as of Thursday, while opponents received nearly $368 million.
The upheaval underscores how L.A. franchises have become billion-dollar assets in a high-stakes arms race, in which owners chase media money, luxury arenas and global clout as fiercely as championships.
The residency of billionaires is often difficult to ascertain, given that many have multiple properties across the nation and around the world. It is not solely based on where the person is registered to vote.
Among the “facts and circumstances” the California Franchise Tax Board considers are the person’s employer, their spouse’s and childrens’ locations, where mail is delivered, and the location of doctors, accountants, lawyers, country club memberships and houses of worship. The number of days spent in California also is factored into the board’s assessment of residency.
Los Angeles Times owner Dr. Patrick Soon-Shiong, a billionaire, owns 4% of the Lakers and recently became a co-owner of a new women’s professional volleyball team in Los Angeles expected to start competing next year.
Soon-Shiong noted that it’s not only wealthy Californians who oppose the tax. Teachers, firefighters and other groups oppose Proposition 40 because of concerns about long-term impacts on the state. And, as a businessman with stakes in sports teams, he predicted bad effects on pro sports.
“It’s really, really expensive to bring a family to watch a professional game, whatever that game may be,” he said during an interview in September. “All those costs will go up, and for sure, it’ll be passed down to the cost of the ticket.”
Times Library Director Cary Schneider contributed to this report.

Vitaparcours: from a Zurich gym club to a global fitness model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Vitaparcours: from a Zurich gym club to a global fitness model
If you want to do sport in Switzerland, you don’t necessarily have to join a club, buy an expensive gym membership or struggle with a training plan. All you need to do is head to a vitaparcours (fitness trail) in the woods. This is the story of a Swiss export success.
You’ll find this almost nowhere else in Switzerland: entry is free and the facility is usually open round the clock. It isn’t located in an exclusive sports centre, but rather where many Swiss people spend part of their free time – in the woods.
The vitaparcours External linkis one of Switzerland’s most unassuming yet successful exports. There are now around 500 such facilities around the country, and thousands more like them can be found worldwide.
It all began with a men’s gymnastics club
The story begins with a Zurich gymnastics club. In the 1960s, the men of the Zurich-Wollishofen Gymnastics Club moved their weekly gymnastics session to a nearby woodland. The head coach at the time used tree trunks, branches and other natural obstacles lying around for additional exercises.
It was a practical idea. In the woods, the group could go for a run and intersperse the route with strength and agility exercises. However, the makeshift equipment regularly disappeared because forestry workers cleared away the branches and logs.
This improvised training therefore gave rise to the desire for a permanent facility. The men found support from Vita Life Insurance, a subsidiary of what is now Zurich Insurance. On May 18, 1968, the first vitaparcours was opened in Zurich-Fluntern, near the zoo.
The original audience consisted mainly of trained gymnasts and athletes. However, the target group soon changed. From 1972 onwards, the vitaparcours was explicitly aimed at families and less athletic people as well.
Five years after it opened, there were already a hundred such facilities in Switzerland. In 1990, the 500th vitaparcours was inaugurated.
More than just a woodland trail with exercise equipment
A vitaparcours is no ordinary fitness trail. It typically follows a route of around two to three kilometres through the woods or across open countryside. Along the way, there are 15 stations set up with a wide variety of exercises, each marked with a different colour.
Blue stands for endurance, red for strength and yellow for flexibility and agility. Many stations offer several different exercise options. This means that the same course can be used in different ways by walkers, families or well-trained athletes.
Such a fitness trail is surprisingly unspectacular: it requires neither grand architecture nor complicated technology. Much of it consists of wood, metal, paved paths and weatherproof signs. It is precisely this simplicity that makes the concept so robust.
This is also precisely what makes it uniquely Swiss: the vitaparcours is at once a sports facility, a local leisure amenity and a public health infrastructure.
Like the ski slopes in Switzerland, the individual courses are now categorised by difficultyExternal link: blue (flat terrain), red (hilly) and black (steep).
Why Switzerland?
People were already exercising outdoors on fitness equipment elsewhere, even before the first Swiss fitness trail was created. For example, a so-called Schweisstropfenbahn (beads of sweat track) was opened in the German city of Münster as early as 1962. However, this consisted of just seven stations along an existing running track.
Other countries also already had running tracks featuring simple fitness equipment. The decisive Swiss contribution, therefore, was that Vita Life Insurance developed a portable system.
This explains why Zurich is regarded as the birthplace of the modern outdoor fitness trail, even though similar precursors existed beforehand. And, much like with mini-golf, it was not necessarily the very first invention, but rather its successful standardisation that made the Swiss model the origin of a global trend.
More
How Switzerland became the ‘motherland of minigolf’
Switzerland therefore standardised not so much each individual bar or piece of equipment as the very concept of the trail: running, stopping, training, more running – while engaging the whole body.
From the Swiss forest to the world
In Germany, the Swiss concept was copied particularly frequently in the early 1970s. At that time, the country was swept up in a major mass participation sports campaign.
On March 16, 1970, the German Sports Federation launched the Trimm Dich durch Sport (get in shape through sport) campaign. With the mascot Trimmy, posters, and radio and television adverts, the aim was to encourage the public to be more active.
This campaign and the German Trimm-dich-Pfade (get in shape paths) were historically closely linked, although they were not the same thing in organisational terms.
The Swiss Vita insurance company exported its model to Germany, where the term Trimm-dich-Pfad became established. Some of the trails were set up by private companies and local authorities.
At their peak, there were around 1,500 such facilities in Germany. The Swiss concept was well suited to the times: people were less active in their everyday lives and were not necessarily keen on competitive sport.
In France, too, parcours de santé or parcours Vita emerged; in Austria, they are known as Waldmeilen or Forstmeilen.
In the English-speaking world, terms such as fitness trail, exercise trail and parcourse became widespread. The formats differed, but the basic principle remained similar.
SRF Archive: This is how people trained on the vitaparcours in 1969External link (German)
Adapted for all age groups
A major overhaul of the vitaparcours took place in the late 1990s in collaboration with experts from the Swiss Federal Institute of Sport in Magglingen. The exercises were organised more clearly according to endurance, strength, flexibility and agility.
This made the circuit much more varied. A fit person can complete the course at a fast pace and choose challenging variations. An older person can walk, take breaks and do easier exercises.
Since 1993, it has no longer been the life insurance company but the Vitaparcours Foundation that has been responsible for the long-term support and further development of the programme. The Foundation sees the course as a contribution to free recreational sport and family experiences in the countryside.
The publicly accessible site does not usually belong to the foundation, but to a local authority, a club or another local organisation. The foundation supports these organisations by providing guidance and equipment.
The costs of construction and maintenance are borne by the local organisation. For annual maintenance, local authorities typically budget for several thousand Swiss francs per facility. In larger municipalities, the budget can be significantly higher.
Today, the vitaparcours have also embraced digitalisation: a dedicated appExternal link offers personalised training plans, additional exercises and guidance on how to perform them correctly.

Germany’s largest industrial union launches nationwide strikes, demands pay rise for 3.7M workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:59:44 UTC
18:59:44 KST

Germany's largest industrial union on Saturday announced the launch of nationwide warning strikes in the metal and electrical sectors after rejecting employers' wage offer affecting about 3.7 million workers.
IG Metall chair Christiane Benner criticised the employers' proposal as a real-wage cut, accusing companies of provoking "incomprehension and anger" among employees amid rising prices.
"The employers want to take money away from people in the end," Benner said in a statement.
"Renunciation does not make anything better. We demand a clear commitment from the other side to the future of the factories and employees," she added.
The first work stoppages are scheduled to begin overnight into Sunday, according to the union.
IG Metall warned that strikes would intensify if further regional negotiations next week failed to produce progress.
The union is demanding a 5 percent pay increase over 12 months, along with measures to protect jobs.
Employers, however, offered a one-time payment in July 2027 equivalent to 1 percent of average annual gross pay, ranging from approximately €555 to €800 ($620 to $894), depending on the region.
Their proposal also includes a permanent 1.3 percent wage increase beginning in July 2028 under a 26-month agreement.
IG Metall rejected the offer, arguing that it would leave employees worse off as living costs continue to rise.

Top 10 plants that protect homes from negativity and misfortune
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:58:55 EET
18:58:55 KST

Top 10 plants that protect homes from negativity and misfortune
Kyiv • UNN
Aloe, basil, lavender, and other plants are believed to protect the home and bring good luck and prosperity. There is no scientific evidence for these properties.
Houseplants can make a home cozier, but in folk traditions some of them were assigned a much more special role. UNN explains more about which plants earned a reputation as natural protectors and which superstitions are associated with them.
Aloe vera
In various cultures, this plant was valued not only for its medicinal properties. The Indigenous peoples of the Americas regarded aloe with particular reverence and even called it the "heavenly staff." Over time, many protective beliefs about the plant emerged.
It was believed that aloe in the home helped ward off troubles and protected residents from accidents; the plant was also often placed above the entrance to a home as a symbol of good luck and a barrier against negative influences. In areas with a warm climate, aloe was also planted near houses in the hope of protecting them from evil spirits. Aloe also has special significance as a symbol of domestic comfort and prosperity. Its presence in the yard or near the entrance was associated with the homeowners’ desire to protect their family from troubles. Such customs were passed down from generation to generation, reinforcing belief in the plant’s protective power.
Basil
Basil is known primarily as an aromatic seasoning, but in folk traditions its significance extends far beyond cooking. The plant is believed to be capable of creating a favorable atmosphere in the home and repelling negative influences. According to popular beliefs, having basil in the house can help get rid of a bad mood and also attract love and passion. To achieve this, it is enough to grow basil at home. In addition, the location of the pot is also considered important; in particular, people believe that the northern, eastern, or southeastern parts of the home are supposedly best suited for basil.
Lavender
Lavender’s pleasant aroma has made it a popular garden plant, but in folk beliefs it is also associated with purity, love, devotion, and good luck. Lavender held a special place in ancient rituals, when it was believed to be thrown into bonfires during the celebration of St. John’s Day to drive away evil spirits and misfortune. The plant was also credited with another unusual property: superstitious people believed that its scent could help them see ghosts. However, the symbolism of lavender changed during different historical periods; for example, in the Victorian tradition, these flowers were associated with distrust.
Eucalyptus
In folk beliefs, eucalyptus is associated with prosperity and renewed strength; it is even called a kind of magnet for financial luck, as the plant supposedly helps attract abundance, promotes normal sleep, and restores energy. Its reputation as a protector of the home is no less important. According to popular beliefs, eucalyptus does not allow negative influences to enter the house and helps ward off envy and ill wishes.
Cactus
Ambiguous beliefs have also developed around this plant. In folk beliefs, cactus spines symbolize powerful energy that can affect the surrounding atmosphere. It was believed that a plant placed directly beside a person, for example on a desk, could create tension and provoke irritability. At the same time, the cactus was also credited with protective properties. In particular, in the right location it could supposedly ward off external aggression, the evil eye, and ill wishes. That is why it was placed near a window, closer to the front door, or on a balcony.
Nettle
In folk tradition, the common nettle appears not simply as a wild plant but as a means of countering unwanted magical influences. Beliefs about its special properties spread from Northern Europe and Asia, where it was credited with the ability to destroy curses and remove spells. Incidentally, this is precisely why nettles were used in the creation of protective amulets.
In addition, British accounts also mentioned other unusual properties of the plant. For example, there was a belief that placing a nettle leaf in one’s mouth could relieve toothache. Because of this, nettles were often regarded as a plant worth keeping close at hand for protection against evil forces. It was also believed that even the day on which nettles were gathered mattered; in particular, nettles picked on a Saturday were supposedly deprived of their healing properties.
Sage
Sage has long been associated with wisdom, strength, and healing. In ancient Greek mythology, this plant was considered particularly special, and its properties were even attributed to divine origins. It was also believed to have a positive effect on memory.
A separate tradition concerns the use of sage to cleanse the home. Superstitious people burned it, believing that the smoke helped dispel negative influences and protect the domestic space. The plant was also associated with a medieval belief in longevity: supposedly, daily consumption of sage could bring a person closer to immortality.
St. John’s wort
In folk legends, St. John’s wort has a reputation as a plant that helps ward off danger. Its sprigs were kept in homes, while dried parts could be placed between the pages of books. In this way, the plant was used as a kind of household talisman.
Particular attention was paid to the time of gathering. It was believed that St. John’s wort collected on the eve of summer acquired extraordinary protective power and could drive away evil spirits, demons, and even gloomy thoughts. To protect the home, the plant was placed near windows and doors, while for personal protection it was carried in a pocket.
Thyme
In many folk traditions, thyme is associated with good luck and confidence. It is considered a plant that can contribute to success in various areas of life. In France, for example, there was an interesting tradition of planting thyme in the garden to attract fairies. Those seeking professional advancement were advised to keep the plant at their workplace. It was believed that thyme helped strengthen self-confidence, improve health, and even banish nightmares.
Tradescantia
In folk beliefs, this plant is assigned an unusual function: it supposedly can signal an unfavorable atmosphere in the home. If its leaves begin to turn yellow and fall, superstitious people interpreted this as a sign of negative influence. If changing the conditions and care did not help, however, the cause was associated not with the location of the pot but with the overall atmosphere in the home. In addition, tradescantia is believed to protect its owners from gossip, envy, and the evil eye, and this plant has also been associated with protection against respiratory illnesses.
Cayenne pepper
In Central and South America, Indigenous peoples cultivated cayenne pepper, using it as a seasoning and in folk medicine; over time, however, it also became part of protective traditions. According to beliefs, this hot red pepper, like salt, can create a kind of barrier against evil. It was scattered near the entrance or in certain places around the house to prevent unwanted influence, or hung by a thread near the door to protect the home and prosperity. Pepper was also added to mixtures of herbs used to make talismans.
Protective plants are part of ancient folk beliefs in which every flower or herb has its own symbolic meaning. Some are credited with protecting against envy and curses, while others are believed to attract good luck, love, or prosperity. There is no scientific evidence that plants can absorb negative energy or drive away evil spirits, but the traditions associated with them continue to this day.

From pagan shadows to Soviet nightmares: Inside Russia’s unique thousand-year horror story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:57:39 UTC
18:57:39 KST

In Russian culture, fear has never been just an emotion – it’s a way of making sense of the world. Where Western horror often pits the individual against some invading evil – the ghost, the vampire, the creature in the dark – Russian horror sees evil as something earned, deserved, or even necessary. The monster doesn’t come from the outside. It’s sent as punishment, or reminder.
The Russian language is full of proverbs about fear: “Fear has big eyes,” “The eyes fear but the hands keep working,” “Two deaths can’t happen, but one is inevitable.” Fear, in these sayings, is not paralysis but duty – an emotion to be mastered, not escaped.
And when Russians choose to be frightened on purpose – in stories, films, or urban legends – they rarely chase the adrenaline of terror. What they seek instead is moral clarity. From pagan spirits lurking in the bathhouse to Pushkin’s cursed gamblers and modern tales of serial killers, Russian horror has always been less about screaming in the dark and more about understanding why the dark exists in the first place.
Before Russians had psychology or theology, they had the forest. And the forest had rules. Fear in ancient Rus’ wasn’t about the unknown; it was about forgetting what you were supposed to know. A farmer who worked at noon, a woman who bathed on the wrong day, a hunter who mocked the spirits – all risked punishment. The early Russian imagination didn’t invent chaos, but personified discipline.
The creatures of Slavic folklore were never purely evil. The Bannik, a hairy old man who lurked in the bathhouse, might scald you alive – but only if you broke his rules. The Poludnitsa, a pale woman with a sickle who appeared at midday, punished those who labored too long in the sun. Likho, the one-eyed hag of misfortune, followed the greedy and the proud. Even the devilish Chort could be tricked into serving a clever peasant.
Each monster embodied a kind of social control. Every story whispered the same warning: don’t be arrogant, don’t be careless, don’t try to outsmart the world. Fear, in this early form, was a survival strategy.
When Christianity took root, these creatures didn’t disappear; they were baptized into the moral order. Pagan dread merged with Christian guilt, and terror found its theology. Evil was no longer a misstep in ritual – it became sin. Yet the core remained: fear was not rebellion against the divine but recognition of it.
That is why, even today, Russian horror rarely celebrates the act of resistance. The earliest demons taught a simpler lesson: fear keeps the world from falling apart.
If the early spirits of Russian folklore punished mistakes, their successors punished intentions. The next generation of monsters acquired faces, motives, even philosophies. They no longer embodied the rage of nature – they tested the soul.
Two of them – Baba Yaga and Koschey the Deathless – survived every cultural upheaval. They’re Russia’s oldest recurring villains and, paradoxically, its first moral teachers.
Koschey, the skeletal sorcerer who hides his soul inside a needle, the needle inside an egg, the egg inside a duck, the duck inside a chest, is less a character than a warning. His elaborate chain of protection isn’t about immortality – it’s about denial. He’s the prototype of a man who thinks he can postpone judgment. In Russian folklore, that’s the ultimate sin: trying to cheat fate rather than accept it.
Baba Yaga is harder to categorize. She lives in a hut on chicken legs that spins with the wind, an image of restlessness itself. Sometimes she devours travelers; sometimes she rescues them. She scolds, tests, bargains – a trickster grandmother who decides who deserves to live. Her evil always has a reason.
Together, they form the moral spine of Slavic horror: the idea that punishment isn’t arbitrary. Even a witch obeys rules. And every curse, like every miracle, has its logic. In this world, a strange moral mechanism that rewards humility and punishes arrogance.
And as stories evolved, the monsters began to fade, leaving only the rules behind. The next figures to inherit this world were no longer witches or demons but people – heroes who suffered under the same invisible laws.
In the bylinas, the epic songs of early Rus’, terror moved from the forest into the heart.
Ilya Muromets, paralyzed for thirty three years, gains strength from holy wanderers – only to face trials that leave his loved ones dead and his faith shaken. Dunai Ivanovich, the warrior-lover, kills his own bride by accident and discovers her unborn child inside her. From his blood, the Danube begins to flow – a river born of guilt.
The moral of these stories – every gift carries its punishment. And where Western knights slayed dragons, Russian heroes struggled against inevitability.
Even the great disasters of history followed the same logic.
When the Mongol invasion burned cities and annihilated entire regions, chroniclers saw it not as chaos but as correction – a divine punishment for collective sin.
By the end of the Middle Ages, Russian fear had completed its transformation. What began as terror of the forest had become awe before the moral universe – fear not of monsters, but of meaning itself.
By the nineteenth century, Russian fear had grown up. What once punished the sinner in the bathhouse now punished him in his conscience. Horror did not live in the forest anymore, but in the mind.
The Enlightenment had promised reason and progress, but the Russian soul wasn’t so easily tamed. Rational optimism soon cracked under its own contradictions. What filled the gap was mysticism – polite, urban, and deeply anxious.
The salons of Saint Petersburg began hosting séances. Aristocrats flirted with Freemasonry and spiritualism. Even Emperor Alexander I, haunted by the chaos of the Napoleonic wars, found solace in prophecy and divine visions.
From that world of candlelit parlors and nervous faith came the first masterpieces of Russian horror. A prime example is Pushkin’s story ‘The Queen of Spades’, one of the first pieces of Russian literature that became famous in Western Europe. In the story, a card player is haunted by a ghost that reveals winning cards to him. Ultimately, he betrays the ghost’s trust and becomes insane.
The supernatural was only a mirror; the real horror was greed, isolation, the inability to stop. A striking illustration of this is Nikolay Gogol’s story ‘Viy’. In that story, three students from a seminary venture into a village, where they encounter witchcraft and evil spirits. They manage to fend off the witches but soon face Viy – a Slavic demon who cannot open his eyes on his own, but whose gaze kills. One of the students succumbs to his curiosity and looks into the demon’s eyes, dying just before the final crow of a rooster that drives away all evil. The sin is not disbelief, but the desire to see beyond belief.
‘Viy’ became very popular, embedding itself in Russian culture and inspiring multiple screen adaptations. For some time, Russian writers continued to explore themes of mysticism and evil spirits, often setting the stories in rural areas. This influence extended to music as well, exemplified by Mussorgsky’s ‘Night on Bald Mountain’, inspired by traditional witches’ sabbaths on “bald mountains.”
These stories terrified readers not because they described demons, but because they suggested that demons might be right. They blurred the line between guilt and destiny – between punishment and justice.
The shift from folklore to literature was the shift from fate to conscience.
Dostoevsky’s murderers and madmen inherit the logic of ancient Rus’: every crime carries its own retribution, every secret a sickness that must reveal itself. In his novels, there are no ghosts left to fear – only the unbearable weight of being alive.
Russian horror thus became something unique: not a genre, but a diagnosis.
The Soviet project promised to banish fear by erasing its causes. No God, no demons, no uncertainty – only progress. Officially, there was nothing left to be afraid of. The future was planned, the present under control. Horror, as a genre, simply didn’t fit.
And yet, the attempt to build a world without fear created one steeped in it. The state itself became the unseen monster: secret, omnipresent, impossible to confront. It didn’t stalk people in the dark – it rang their doorbells.
Censorship kept horror films off screens, but the atmosphere often did the job better than fiction. The whispering neighbors, the midnight knock, the vanishing of friends – these were everyday Gothic tropes dressed in bureaucratic gray.
Only in the late Soviet and post-Soviet years did the genre return – not from the studios, but from the streets. Real horror had escaped fiction. Serial killers appeared in headlines: Vladimir Ionesyan, nicknamed ‘MosGas’, tricked his way into apartments by posing as a gas worker; Sergey Golovkin, “the Fisher,” raped and murdered boys near Moscow. The last was executed in 1996 – the final death sentence in Russia’s history.
The myths changed too. When information censorship collapsed, fear turned into rumor. People whispered about AIDS-infected needles hidden in cinema seats, about alien autopsies under Moscow State University, about a secret subway system built for the Kremlin elite. If folklore once kept villagers from wandering into the forest, urban legends now kept city dwellers from touching escalator rails.
The new demons wore human faces – policemen, criminals, doctors, strangers. Their motives were senseless, their violence random. For the first time in centuries, Russians faced horror with no moral explanation, no cosmic order, no promise of redemption.
Modern Russia no longer trembles. It scrolls. The ancient monsters have become mascots and memes; witches sell herbal tea on Instagram, and Koschey stars in children’s cartoons. Fear has been commercialized, softened, stripped of transcendence.
In cinema, horror never reached blockbuster status. A few cult directors revived folk motifs, but audiences treated them as fantasy, not warning. The real horror migrated elsewhere: into true-crime documentaries, political thrillers, and nightly news.
Psychopaths replaced phantoms, and headlines replaced folklore. Yet the emotional undertone remains the same – that dread of something vast and inevitable, only now without a name or a purpose. The Russians who once feared God, fate, or history now fear the absence of all three.
Information wars have taught Russians skepticism and irony. Every rumor is suspect, every catastrophe half-believed. Fear doesn’t paralyze, it exhausts. What began a thousand years ago as superstition has ended as fatigue.
And yet, somewhere in that fatigue lies continuity. Russians may not fear demons anymore, but they still live with the feeling that the world is ruled by forces beyond them – whether cosmic, political, or digital.
The monsters have gone, but the logic remains: that fear is not chaos, but proof of order – a faint reminder that the universe is still watching.

Estonian border guards could be given additional powers to stop migrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:56:00 UTC
18:56:00 KST

Estonian border guards could be given additional powers to stop migrants
Estonian border guards could be given additional powers to stop border violators, Minister of Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) has said, after meeting with his Latvian counterpart.
At a press conference at Estonia's Piusa border guard station on Friday, the ministers said measures need to be found to stop the Belarusian government from organizing illegal migration into the Baltic states.
The pressure is expected to fall over the winter, but is likely to pick up again next spring.
"One possibility is for all these countries to close their border crossing points with Belarus for a while, because Belarus is interested in maintaining this traffic, so perhaps that would get the message across, because in Poland's case it certainly worked," Taro said.
Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava said Latvia has amended its legislation so that border guards can respond more effectively to both border violations and damage to infrastructure.
"I think that if some of them reconsider the possibility of entering Latvian territory, we have given our border guards more opportunities to use weapons against those who illegally cross the border and attempt various actions against our technological infrastructure. So I think this also works as a preventive measure," he said.
Taro said Estonian border guards also need to be given additional powers.
"We should take into account that if people are operating in the border zone and it is not clear that they are our own people, then they are probably enemies, and in that case a border guard must have complete confidence that they can use all means to stop that hostile activity there, up to and including weapons, up to and including lethal force. We are currently analyzing how our legal framework deals with this, how much room for interpretation we have and whether anything needs to be changed," the Estonian minister said.

Why Ukraine has launched a platform for citizens considering a future return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:53:16 UTC
18:53:16 KST

As millions of Ukrainians weigh what comes after displacement, a new platform aims to help people make informed decisions about returning home without telling them they should.
For Ukrainians living across Europe, the hardest part of returning may no longer be the journey itself, but deciding where to begin with sorting out documents, work, housing, local services, or finding a place where rebuilding everyday life feels realistic.
Many Ukrainians abroad have spent their time working toward stability in their host countries. Yet even as they have settled into this new reality, many continue to imagine what their lives back in Ukraine might look like in the future.
Recent research by UNHCR and the OECD points to the same shift. For many people, the question is no longer simply whether they will come back, but what returning would actually require.
Ukraine has launched a new platform called Dodomu ("Homewards") for people navigating exactly that uncertainty.
It seeks to give people planning to return to Ukraine the reliable information they need to feel confident in their decision and to understand their options, whether they are thinking about moving next month, next year, or keeping the possibility open.
Turning uncertainty into a roadmap
After completing a short questionnaire, users receive a personalized roadmap that brings together practical information relevant to their circumstances, from documents and employment to housing, health care, social support, and other services that may matter before making a decision. The platform is built on the principle that the plan should fit the person making the decision.
Finding the right place to rebuild
Coming home does not always mean going back to the same place. While some people already know where they want to live, others are still comparing places across Ukraine, trying to work out where they could settle back into daily life, be close to family and friends, or find new opportunities.
According to the International Organization for Migration, decisions about returning are shaped not only by security, but also by access to housing, employment, health care, and reliable information before departure.
That is why Dodomu is built around individual communities rather than a single national overview. The platform currently has profiles of 154 communities across Ukraine, with local information on housing, jobs, health care, education, and available services. More communities are expected to join as the platform develops.
Recent research on Ukrainian communities by the charitable foundation Rokada suggests a similar pattern. Whether a return lasts increasingly depends on local conditions, particularly on access to practical support in the place where people choose to settle, rather than on national policy.
Note: The screenshot shows an English translation of the Dodomu website (dodomu.unity.gov.ua). The original website is in Ukrainian.
A platform taking shape
Dodomu is currently in beta, and its development is meant to continue with input from users.
The creators are inviting Ukrainians abroad to help shape it now, rather than wait for a finished product. They can test key features, report technical issues, and suggest practical improvements. Users can also share any concerns that still need to be resolved before they return.
Even for people who are not planning to return anytime soon, testing the platform can help improve a resource designed for millions of Ukrainians abroad whose circumstances continue to evolve. Users can leave feedback through the platform or share their own experiences of returning or what still stands in the way.
Dodomu was developed within the YOUA project "Shaping New Paths, Building Ukraine's Future," which is implemented on behalf of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) by Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH in cooperation with the Ukrainian Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity. According to the project, no Ukrainian state budget funds were used to develop or operate the platform.
The project supports informed return decisions by improving access to reliable information while strengthening the capacity of Ukrainian national institutions and local communities to receive returning citizens and facilitate sustainable reintegration. Its activities include conducting research, developing strategic documents, expanding the Dodomu platform, working with communities to improve their readiness for return, and engaging with Ukrainians abroad to maintain long-term dialogue and connections with Ukraine.
The project provides technical assistance only and does not influence individual decisions about returning to Ukraine. Participation in its activities and use of its services are entirely voluntary for people considering return, those who have already decided to return, and those currently reintegrating after returning to Ukraine.

New EU customs duties for Swiss parcels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:52:11 UTC
18:52:11 KST

New EU customs duties for Swiss parcels
The European Union is introducing a handling fee on parcel consignments from third countries on November 1. The new €2 (CHF1.85) fee will be levied in addition to the recently introduced €3 fee on small consignments. Swiss online shops are affected by the new charge.
Online retail, primarily via Chinese platforms such as Shein and Temu, is booming. According to figures from the European Commission, just under 5.9 billion small consignments were sent to the EU in 2025. That equates to just over 16 million items per day. This volume is putting pressure on customs authorities.
From November 1, the EU will charge a processing fee of €2 on imports. According to the EU’s decision, the platforms – and not the consumers – are responsible for paying the fee and completing the other customs formalities. Violations could result in fines of up to 6% of a company’s annual import value.
The processing fee is charged per product category rather than per item. For example, a consignment of 20 T-shirts incurs a fee of €2. For a consignment of ten T-shirts, two caps and an umbrella, the fee is €6. This calculation is based on how goods are declared at customs.
The measure is part of a wider EU customs reform due to come into force next month.
Minimal impact expected for Switzerland
The fee will be levied on all parcels imported into the EU. It applies “irrespective of the free trade agreement between Switzerland and the EU”, Swiss Post said on its website.
Patrick Erny, director of the Swiss Retail Federation, estimates the impact on the sector as a whole will be “minimal”. He attributes this to the fact that the Swiss retail sector is strongly focused on the domestic market.
More
EU parcel tax ‘will not slow Chinese retailers’: Swiss Post boss
“Specialised niche retailers with many direct deliveries to consumers in the EU, as well as retailers of low-cost products with low-value shopping baskets, are likely to be more significantly affected, as the charges represent a larger proportion of their turnover,” said Erny, whose association represents both brick-and-mortar and online retailers in Switzerland.
EU introduced levy in July
The new levy is being imposed in addition to the customs duty on small consignments introduced by the EU in July. The €3 levy, which has been in force since the summer, applies only to consignments with a value of up to €150 imported into the EU from third countries such as Switzerland. The levy is valid for two years and is due to expire in July 2028.
Since the levy was introduced, imports of small consignments have fallen by 64%, the French news agency AFP recently reported. However, Brussels points out that it is still too early to draw any conclusions.
More
Fees for small parcels in EU puts pressure on Switzerland
Erny also says that the available Swiss foreign trade statistics do not yet allow any conclusions to be drawn about the consequences of the three-euro customs duty for the Swiss retail sector. He also considers the impact of this duty to be minimal.
Levy for Switzerland?
According to the director of the Swiss Retail Federation, the new levy reflects a challenge currently facing many countries: the rapid rise in direct imports via online marketplaces from third countries that do not comply with domestic product safety legislation. He reckons the key question is how Switzerland is addressing these same challenges.
More
Chinese retail platform Temu challenges consumers and retailers
To address this challenge, the Federal Council sent a revision of the Federal Act on Product Safety out for consultation in June this year. In its proposal, the Federal Council draws heavily on legal developments in the EU.
It believes that additional funding is required for more intensive and highly digitalised market surveillance in online trade. To this end, it should be possible to levy a supervisory fee on direct shipments from abroad.
The consultation period ended last September. As a next step, and provided the Federal Council continues to see a need for action, it will submit a dispatch on the revision to Parliament.

Besieged by the Houthis, Yemen’s Taiz is teetering on the edge of humanitarian catastrophe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:51:48 UTC
18:51:48 KST

The city of Taiz in southwestern Yemen is located roughly 250 km south of Houthi-controlled Sana’a, the Yemeni capital, and 200 km north of Aden, the seat of Yemen’s official, Saudi-supported government.
Taiz is Yemen’s third-largest city, with a pre-war population of around 1.2 million. There are around 800,000 people there now. The war between the Houthis and the official government erupted again in full intensity in July, with the collapse of the UN-brokered 2022 truce.
In the renewed fighting, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive southward. Taiz and the surrounding highlands matter because holding them would enable the Houthis to consolidate their gains in the areas further west near the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Cutting off the strategic Hejat al-Abd road from Taiz would also serve to isolate pro-government forces from their main center and source of supply in Aden.
As a result, the Houthis sought in their renewed offensive to cut Taiz off. They have largely succeeded in this objective. The Iran-supported Shi’ite Islamists have now cut off every primary route out of Taiz City.
After capturing the al-Safiya area, the Houthis severed the main road to Aden. They have destroyed parts of the Hejat al-Abd road across the mountains. An additional unpaved route exists, but is unusable for heavy vehicles that can bring supplies.
The predictable result is that Taiz city is now teetering on the edge of humanitarian catastrophe.
Yemen is a place of extreme poverty and deprivation. While reporting in the country last year, traveling through the remote Abyan province on the way up to Shabwa and the Saudi border, it occurred to me that in 25 years of working across the region, I had never witnessed impoverishment of a similar depth and scale.
The scenes remain vivid. African migrant families, trying to make their way to Saudi Arabia, walking along the highways through the desert in the shimmering summer heat, staying at night in tiny improvised shacks by the roadside.
The Houthis, who have reintroduced slavery to Yemen, prey on these migrants if they venture into their areas of control. But the migrants, hailing mainly from Ethiopia and Somalia, are not the only people affected.
There is widespread and documented childhood malnutrition in Abyan province (15,300 recorded cases, according to a recent study). The signs of extreme poverty and underdevelopment – uncollected refuse, lack of clean sanitation and water supply, extreme overcrowding in housing – are all apparent.
According to the World Food Program (WFP), “Across Yemen, more than 18 million people face acute food insecurity. Some 2.2 million children under the age of five are acutely malnourished, including 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition, the most life-threatening form of malnutrition.”
This underlines that the situation in Yemen is precarious also in “normal” periods, as a result of the ongoing conflict, the collapse of infrastructure, and the presence of large nomadic and refugee populations.
In Taiz, this preexisting reality is now exacerbated by the complete inaccessibility to access routes for wheat flour, water, and fuel stocks.
In a press release issued on October 14, the World Food Program stated that “WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children. Combined with communities affected by access losses on the west coast of Yemen in early September, a total of 800,000 people are now beyond WFP’s reach.”
El-Khidir Daloum, WFP’s country director in Yemen, said: “We are critically concerned about the escalating conflict, but even more so about the growing number of people we can no longer reach because of it…
“Many of the families affected have been displaced multiple times, and were already struggling to afford even basic food items. This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most.”
As of now, 12 hospitals in Taiz are hours away from running out of fuel. Should this happen, the lives of thousands of hospital patients dependent on the maintenance of the electricity supply will be under threat. Food stocks are nearly exhausted. The fuel crisis is also leading to the closure of desalination plants in and around the city, with the resultant dwindling of supplies of fresh water.
How to prevent disaster
What needs to happen to prevent the looming disaster in Taiz is easy to state, but difficult to achieve. A humanitarian corridor, or corridors, should be established into the city, and fuel needs to be transported to the city center to keep hospitals and water facilities functioning.
For this to happen, however, pressure needs to be placed on the besieging forces. Here lies the problem. As of now, the UN Security Council appears to have no interest in prioritizing the issue.
The supposed allies of Saudi Arabia and the official government, namely the countries of the newly minted “Mecca Pact” – Pakistan and Turkey – have made it clear that they have no intention of committing forces.
The US, too, has conveyed to the Saudis that when it comes to the fight against the Iran-backed forces in Yemen, they will receive only indirect assistance.
Iran and the Houthis themselves, of course, follow a way of war that involves deliberate and targeted strikes on civilian populations in enemy areas, and therefore can be relied upon to greet any international entreaties with indifference unless they are backed up by force, or the threat of force.
It goes without saying that the global “civil society,” and the furious Islamic and leftist crowds that gathered in European and American cities over the last three years to condemn Israel’s war effort in Gaza, will be absent from the streets when it comes to the 800,000 people now facing extreme hunger in Taiz.
Many among that gathering, indeed, will be openly supportive of the Houthis, precisely because of their stated desire for the destruction of Israel and hatred of Jews.
The upshot is that 800,000 people in southwest Yemen are currently staring down the wrong end of possible starvation, with no force waiting in the wings to remedy the situation, and the more or less complete indifference of the media outside of the Arabic-speaking world.
The war in Yemen has, in purely numerical terms, accounted for the great majority of war-related deaths in the Middle East over the last decade. More than 378,000 people have lost their lives in this conflict since 2015.
This has been met, for the most part, with indifference on the part of what used to be known as the “international community.” The next tragic chapter in this process is currently being written.

As thousands of dockworkers at more than 100 ports across the world took part on Friday in a protest against the use of their ports for arms shipments and the number of seafarers killed in wars, an anti-Israel group called 'No Harbour for Genocide' was praised by Hamas for taking part in organizing the protest and calling for a halt to shipments to Israel.
Dockworkers in Europe and around the world went on strike to protest the militarization of ports, with more than 100 ports affected and an estimated $2 billion lost due to the delays.
According to Reuters, strikers across 113 ports in 22 countries also called for pay rises, better working conditions and the right to have doctors on board vessels crossing war zones.
"We will not work for their wars, and we will not become food for their cannons," Apostolos Kypraios, head of the Greek union of merchant marine engineers, told Reuters during a rally at the Greek port of Piraeus.
The pro-Palestinian group NHG, which was one of the organizers of the strike, reiterated the day's slogan in a message on their website, "Dockworkers do not work for war," and claimed that the strike left more than two billion dollars worth of cargo sitting idle in ports across the world.
They also claimed that Dockworkers' unions across Europe and the Mediterranean said that "the struggle against wars, genocides, and aggression, [was] closely linked to problems of the salary, working conditions, automation projects and the security and health of all docks and ports workers."
The declaration called for "ports not to be used for the transportation of arms, ammunition, equipment or military material and troops to war zones."
"Trade unions must step up vigilance, inform workers, expose war cargoes and organize constant, collective mass resistance using all available means," they demanded.
The group also set out seven demands: "The immediate end to the genocide of Palestinian people to the recognition of an independent Palestinian state; an end to US-Israel wars of aggression in the Middle East, full solidarity with the peoples of Cuba, Venezuela and Sudan, alongside the defense of peoples’ sovereignty, territorial integrity, the right to resistance and self-determination," the unions wrote.
Calling for "an immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people," NHG demanded that "no arms, ammunition, military equipment, or troops" would be sent to war through their docks. They also asked that "no ports be turned into military bases," and finished the statement by saying "no to rearmament and the war economy."
Across Europe, the protesters held signs at major ports saying "no to war, no to armament," and "embargo on Zionism now."
Hamas support for NHG's day of action
Hamas released a statement on Friday, commending "the global labor solidarity movement with the Gaza Strip, which is being carried out by more than 25 labor unions representing workers at 113 seaports across 22 countries worldwide."
The statement upholds NHG's day of action as a prime example for groups around the world, asking them to join NHG and expand its scope of influence.
Hamas "urges them to continue acts of solidarity with our people in the Gaza Strip and to express their categorical rejection of the transfer of arms and military equipment to the occupying entity [Israel] - an entity that continues to commit acts of genocide and ethnic cleansing against our Palestinian people, in flagrant violation of humanitarian and international laws and norms."
"We extend our greetings and appreciation to the unions, syndicates, and labor groups participating in this movement," the statement added.
The No Harbour for Genocide movement
"NO FUEL. NO ARMS. NO HARBOUR FOR GENOCIDE," the NHG website's homepage exclaims. It claims to function as a resource for trade unions, port workers, legal experts, and more who are " seeking to stop the maritime transfers sustaining Israel’s genocidal war machine."
The movement claims to have tracked 315 shipments of components for Elbit Systems, which moved through 56 commercial ports in 29 countries between August 2025 and September 2026, according to the NHG website. It also says it "tracked 3,400 shipments of cargo supplying US military bases through 67 ports in 42 countries," between December 2025 and September 2026.
Its website has a database titled "What passes through this port," where dockworkers can track vessels that are " complicit in regularly supplying Israel’s ongoing genocide, apartheid, and illegal occupation of Palestine."
Ships that "exhibit a consistent pattern of involvement in supporting Israel's genocide" are split into subcategories depending on what they transport. The website encourages activists to block vessels that are not on its blacklist, that they don't know are in any way linked to Israel, if the dockworkers suspect they are " carrying military and dual use supplies to Israel."

Britain’s most powerful nuclear sub enters final build phase
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:50:31 GMT
18:50:31 KST

The Dreadnought programme has entered a phase that will take the first boat through the completion of her build, sea trials and certification before she enters service in the early 2030s, while the second submarine progresses to sea trials of her own, according to an answer given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what progress has been made on the Dreadnought programme in the context of the delivery confidence assessments for Government Major Project Portfolio defence projects.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “Good progress is being made on the Dreadnought programme. In July, we announced Delivery Phase 4 (DP4), the latest phase of the programme, which will enable the first-in-class submarine, Dreadnought, to complete her build, sea trials and certification, ahead of entering service in the early 2030s. During this phase, the second boat will progress to sea trials, while the third and fourth boats will achieve key construction milestones.”
Delivery Phase 4 is the funding and contracting step that carries the programme from construction into the trials and certification work needed before a ballistic missile submarine can take on operational patrols. Dreadnought, Valiant, Warspite and King George VI will replace the four Vanguard boats that have maintained continuous at sea deterrence since 1969, and the oldest of those, HMS Vanguard, commissioned in 1993 against a design life of twenty-five years.
Stretching the Vanguard class beyond that design life has produced the longest deterrent patrols in Royal Navy history, including a 204-day patrol completed by HMS Vanguard, and the Defence Committee has examined the strain that places on crews and on the maintenance cycle. The programme’s schedule matters for that reason as much as for the capability itself.
Construction runs at Barrow-in-Furness, where BAE Systems is expanding the yard to build Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS alongside each other, and Rolls-Royce Submarines in Derby supplies the reactor cores. Major facility upgrades needed for Dreadnought core production have been delivered, with work now focused on commissioning and manufacture.
The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, taking in the submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the infrastructure at Barrow, Derby, Faslane, Coulport and Aldermaston.

Rwanda releases 533 genocide convicts after sentences end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:47:41 UTC
18:47:41 KST

Rwanda has released at least 533 people convicted of crimes during the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi after they completed their prison sentences, the country’s foreign minister said Friday.
Olivier Nduhungirehe said the released prisoners "joined tens of thousands of others, who were discharged over the past 25 years."
Rwanda's National Unity and Civic Engagement Minister Jean Damascene Bizimana said the group underwent rehabilitation training before their release to prepare them for reintegration into society.
He warned those released against promoting genocide ideology, fueling ethnic divisions or committing other offenses that could lead to their return to prison.
Over 100,000 convicted over 1994 genocide
More than 100,000 people were convicted of crimes committed during the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda.
Over 1 million people, mainly ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were killed during the massacres, which lasted approximately 100 days.
The Rwandan government used traditional Gacaca courts to prosecute crimes committed during the genocide.
Established in 2002, approximately 12,000 grassroots tribunals operated across the country, adjudicating roughly 1.9 million cases.
The genocide followed the downing of a plane carrying Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira on April 6, 1994.
The aircraft was struck by a rocket, killing everyone on board.
The incident triggered mass killings carried out by Hutu extremists.

Massive Gen Z protests set to sweep cities across Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:47:00 UTC
18:47:00 KST

Massive Gen Z protests set to sweep cities across Germany
Published October 31, 2026last updated October 31, 2026
What you need to know
- Organizers of mass youth protests on Saturday hope that more than 170,000 people will take part in some 34 cities
- Protesters are to call for more money for schools, measures to lower the cost of living, greater social justice and more climate protection
- They will also protest at the possible reintroduction of military conscription
- The protests come as young people across Europe take a stand for their rights in several countries, notably in France
- Security authorities say they have no evidence of any planned violence, but the Interior Ministry has warned that extremists might hijack the protests
This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31, 2026:
What are the rules governing protests in Germany?
People in Germany have the fundamental right, enshrined in the constitution or Basic Law, to assemble in public provided they remains peaceful and are unarmed.
However, several states have adopted their own assembly acts, which means some of them have additional restrictions, such as a ban on protesting on highways in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Notification generally necessary
Federal law itself imposes the obligation on organizers of protests to notify the local authority entrusted with approving public assemblies at least 48 hours before they invite people publicly to take part.
This aims to allow authorities to put in place security measures and to lessen the impact of any assembly on others by, for example, instigating traffic control measures.
Spontaneous assemblies are, however, also allowed in cases where a topical issue of urgent importance is at stake, and there is no notification requirement for indoor assemblies.
Protests or other assemblies can be banned beforehand or dispersed while they are underway, but this is considered a means of last resort.
Some locations are also subject to restrictions on protests, such as the area around the Reichstag building in Berlin where the German parliament sits, and around the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.
Demonstrations around the Reichstag are, for example, permitted only when the parliament is not in session.
Germany no stranger to big protests
Post-war Germany has seen several massive demonstrations, including one in 1983, when 250,000 people — according to police estimates — gathered in the then West German capital, Bonn, to protest against the decision by NATO to station American nuclear missiles on German territory.
That was, however, surpassed in size by a protest in Berlin in 2003 against the invasion of Iraq by US-led forces, which drew a crowd of around half a million people.
There is some more detail on the law regarding the right of assembly in this DW article.
German 'Gen Z' protests set for cities across the country
Young people are to take part in demonstrations across Germany on Saturday, following the example of their peers in France and other countries who have been calling for better educational prospects and future opportunities.
In Germany, organizers said there is also to be a focus on rejecting military conscription and on demanding more protection for the climate as the Earth warms, with potentially catastrophic effects.
Saturday's protests are being called for by the youth initiative "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") through a social media campaign
The group itself will directly organize four of the protests — in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich —, with associated demonstrations to take place in some 30 other cities.
It has explicitly called for peaceful protests without the violence that marred recent demonstrations in France.
Focus on security fears
This has not stopped several conservative politicians, notably from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), from warning that similar scenes could occur.
"Gen Z regelt" has, however, criticized what it sees as a wrong focus on the possibility of violence at the protests.
"It shows that our point about not being taken seriously or being heard is right. No one wants to work with us on the issues at stake but instead always put the topic of violence on the agenda," an organizer of the Munich protest told a press conference in Cologne.
However, other lawmakers have come out in support of the protests.
The leader of the parliamentary party of the Greens, Katharina Dröge, told the DPA news agency: "Young people are rightly furious because the federal government does not take their wishes seriously enough."
The Left Party leader, Luigi Pantisano, also said it was the right time for protests as the government mulls reforms of the nursing care and pensions systems, calling them "social cruelties."
"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1997 and 2012.
France to see fresh cost-of-living protests
As Germany gears up for a day of mass youth protests, authorities in neighboring France are also bracing for new demonstrations on Saturday amid fears that the violence seen at October 17 rallies could repeat itself.
Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed to monitor around 150 protests across the country.
In recent weeks, protests by school pupils complaining about poor school conditions morphed into wider demonstrations on multiple issues, including the rising cost of living and social inequality.
On October 17 in particular, considerable violence occurred on the sidelines of mostly peaceful protests as extremists took the opportunity to plunder, riot and damage public property.
Welcome to our coverage
Young people in Germany are taking their lead from student protests in neighboring France to call for their opinions to be heard amid multiple challenges facing society.
As seen recently in France, organizers said they will be airing grievances about a perceived neglect of education but also calling for more social equality, less surveillance and measures to curb global warming.
Some politicians, in particular far-right leader Alice Weidel from the Alternative for Germany (AfD), have warned that the protests could attract violent extremists, but the organizers themselves have rejected any form of the violence that was seen occasionally in France.
Follow the protests as they unfold in some 34 cities across Germany.

Residents of Russian-controlled Ukrainian town Oleshky arrive in Belarus

AI generated
KYIV – Four planes carrying residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky landed in Belarus on Oct 31, the Belarusian Belta state news agency and a senior Ukrainian official said.
Hundreds of starving and exhausted residents left the town of Oleshky on Oct 30 during a US-backed local ceasefire, the first of its kind and the longest humanitarian pause in the war, which is nearing its fifth year.

The local ceasefire in Oleshky was reached after mediation efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump and with the Pope's involvement.

A fire broke out at the Bashneft-Novoyl oil refinery in Ufa, Russia, following an attack by Ukrainian drones on the morning of October 31.
This was reported by ASTRA.
According to preliminary data, the L-35 catalytic reforming unit is on fire at the facility.
Bashneft-Novoyl is part of the Bashneft company, which is controlled by Russia’s Rosneft. The plant produces automotive gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, and industrial lubricants.
The L-35 unit produces a high-octane gasoline component—reformat—as well as hydrogen, which is necessary for refining motor fuels.
Damage to the unit could significantly impact the refinery’s production capacity. Earlier, the Ukrainian military had already reported that this equipment had been damaged by a drone strike.
A video has also been posted online showing a strike drone in flight, which, based on its external appearance, resembles the Ukrainian An-196 Liutyi.
Two other refineries are located in Ufa’s northern industrial zone: Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim and Bashneft-UNPZ.
Together with Bashneft-Novoyl, they form one of Russia’s largest oil refining complexes, with a combined capacity of 23.5 million metric tons of feedstock per year.
According to reports in local chat rooms, two plants may have been attacked simultaneously.
As previously reported, on the morning of October 31, explosions were heard in Ufa’s industrial zone, after which thick smoke rose over the city. At that time, the exact location of the strike remained unknown.
The day before, on October 30, Ukrainian drones struck the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in Russia’s Samara Region. The strike caused a fire on the refinery’s premises.

UK prime minister open to slavery apology, rejects financial reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:42:37 UTC
18:42:37 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to a formal state apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade but rejected financial reparations.
In an opinion piece for The Guardian published ahead of next week's Commonwealth heads of government meeting, Burnham expressed "sorrow and regret" over the suffering of millions of people subjected to slavery.
"The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity," he wrote.
"They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognize the way it still shapes our world today."
Burnham, who is preparing to attend the Commonwealth summit in the Caribbean next week, said Britain would offer structured dialogue with affected countries and campaign groups.
"Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them," he wrote.
Rejects financial reparations
Despite expressing openness to a formal apology, Burnham ruled out financial compensation for Britain's historical involvement in slavery.
"I do not believe that is the right answer," he wrote.
"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, which happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part."
Instead, Burnham announced an initiative to restructure the debt of the poorest Commonwealth countries.
The initiative would be led by former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown and is expected to involve international organizations, he said.
Burnham noted that debt-servicing costs for these countries had reached their highest levels in more than 25 years.
More than 40% of the poorest Commonwealth countries now spend more on interest repayments than on health, according to the figures he cited.
"The Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave," Burnham wrote.
"We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today."
