India's roads kill quietly while crashes in the sky make headlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:41:16 UTC
18:41:16 KST

Six people were killed on Friday when a Trans Bharat Aviation helicopter flying from Badrinath to Dehradun crashed near Chai village in Uttarakhand's Chamoli district. The operator's fleet has been grounded and the cause is under investigation.The crash takes this year's toll in smaller civilian aircraft accidents to 22 deaths in six fatal accidents, the highest annual figure in a TOI compilation covering January 2021 to October 2026.Yet these deaths are a small part of India's transport toll. Roads kill more than 500 people every day. Major train accidents have fallen sharply, but thousands still die on railway tracks and premises. Scattered across individual incidents, many of these deaths receive little attention compared with major disasters.
Roads: A death every three minutes
Road accidents killed 1,83,434 people in 2025, up 3.5% from 1,77,175 in 2024, according to provisional figures the road transport ministry gave Parliament. There were 5,13,474 crashes, about 1,407 a day. On average, 503 people died every day, nearly 21 every hour. The figures come from the government's Electronic Detailed Accident Report (e-DAR) portal as of July 27, 2026.Road deaths have risen every year since 2021, when 1,53,972 people were killed.
The toll is up about 19% in four years. Crashes have also grown deadlier over the long term. Accident severity, measured as deaths per 100 reported accidents, rose from 21.6 in 2005 to 36.3 in 2024. Provisional figures indicate a slight dip to 35.7 in 2025.National highways make up only 2.1% of India's road network but accounted for 36.6% of road deaths in 2024, or 64,772 lives. Provisional figures show that highway deaths fell 4.1% to 62,122 in 2025, even as overall road fatalities rose.
India's deadly roads: Over 500 lives lost every day
Uttar Pradesh recorded the most deaths in 2025 (27,547) and Tamil Nadu the most accidents (71,195). India has committed to halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. The government has also announced a new rating system for national highways that will assess road conditions, safety and user experience.
Railways: Fewer train crashes, thousands still die on tracks
Consequential train accidents, which include collisions, derailments, fires and level-crossing accidents, fell from 135 in 2014-15 to 31 in 2024-25 and 16 in 2025-26, an 88% drop over 11 years. They killed 17 people in 2025-26, against 18 the year before.A single disaster can still be devastating. The Balasore triple-train collision in Odisha on June 2, 2023, killed 296 people and injured more than 1,200. Investigators identified signalling and interlocking lapses linked to the crash.The overall trend, however, is downward. Accidents per million train-kilometres fell from 0.11 to 0.01 between 2014-15 and 2025-26. The government credits improvements in signalling, track maintenance, rolling stock and safety technology, including the Kavach automatic train protection system. Spending and budget allocations for railway safety rose from Rs 39,200 crore in 2013-14 to Rs 1,17,693 crore in 2025-26.But far more people die around the railway network than in major train accidents.The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) recorded 22,413 deaths on railway tracks and premises in 2024, and another 1,888 at railway crossings, a total of 24,301. Of the 22,413 deaths on tracks and premises, 17,029 involved people falling from trains or being struck on the tracks. Maharashtra recorded the most deaths on railway tracks and premises in 2024 (3,587), followed by Uttar Pradesh (3,538). Separately, Government Railway Police data recorded 2,468 deaths on Mumbai's suburban railway network that year, down from 2,590 in 2023.
Aviation: 60 deaths in smaller aircraft since 2021
Air crashes kill far fewer people overall. A July 2025 parliamentary reply counted 18 accidents involving Indian-registered scheduled aircraft since 2015. But a single disaster can claim hundreds. The Air India AI171 crash in Ahmedabad on June 12, 2025, killed 260 people: 241 aboard and 19 on the ground.Smaller aircraft are counted separately. A TOI review of accident reports, government records and news reports finds at least 60 deaths in 19 fatal accidents involving smaller civilian aircraft between January 2021 and October 2026. These involved helicopters, chartered aircraft, training planes, air ambulances and small regional passenger aircraft. The compilation excludes military aircraft and large commercial airliners.The annual toll was one death in 2021, 14 in 2022, four in 2023, five in 2024, 14 in 2025 and 22 so far in 2026. Helicopters accounted for 37 of the 60 deaths and fixed-wing aircraft for 23.
22 lives lost: Small aircraft crashes hit 6-year high
This year's accidents span different kinds of operations. A passenger died after an IndiaOne Air aircraft made a forced landing near Rourkela in January. Later that month, a Learjet crash at Baramati killed five, including Maharashtra deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar.In February, seven died in an air-ambulance crash in Jharkhand's Chatra district, and another passenger died after a Pawan Hans helicopter crash near Mayabunder in the Andamans. A training-aircraft crash near Kanpur killed two in August, followed by Friday's six deaths near Joshimath.The Baramati, Chatra and Joshimath crashes alone accounted for 18 of this year's 22 deaths.
Uttarakhand's helicopter toll
Uttarakhand accounted for 21 of the 30 helicopter-accident deaths in India during the preceding five years, or 70%, according to a July 2025 government reply in the Rajya Sabha. In TOI's compilation, 27 of the 60 deaths are linked to pilgrimage helicopter flights.The AAIB's final report on the June 2025 Gaurikund crash in Uttarakhand, which killed seven, cited rapidly descending clouds, delayed flight-path decisions and limited experience in the Kedarnath valley. It recommended 50 hours of supervised hill flying before pilots undertake single-pilot operations in the valley for the first time.Nationally, the helicopter accident rate rose from 0.33 per 10,000 flying hours in 2024 to 0.53 in 2025, although four accidents in 2025 are too few to establish a sustained deterioration in safety.Investigators also found visibility below the minimum for visual flying and faded runway markings at Baramati, and inadequate flight-data-monitoring records at the Kanpur flying school.These findings point to operational weaknesses, but they do not establish that smaller aircraft are inherently more dangerous than commercial airliners.
The daily toll that draws less attention
At the 2025 average, India's roads claimed roughly as many lives every 12½ hours as the 260 people killed in the AI171 crash. A single average day's road toll was nearly 30 times the number killed in consequential train accidents in all of 2025-26. Air and train disasters bring immediate investigations and extensive coverage. Road deaths, spread across lakhs of crashes, rarely receive the same sustained attention.
The railways show that sustained investment and safety measures can coincide with a sharp fall in major operational accidents. The challenge is to bring similar attention to road safety, deaths around railway tracks and the oversight of smaller aircraft, areas where prevention rarely draws the attention that disasters do.

Multistage evacuation in Oleshky

Upon departing Oleshky, the evacuation convoys split based on destination preferences, with one contingent heading toward government-controlled Ukraine via the Anapa-Gomel air bridge and another group of evacuees traveling deeper into Russian territory.
87 hours of compliance under US-mediated armistice

The localized cessation of hostilities officially took effect at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on Tuesday, Oct. 27, two days ahead of initial projections, following direct diplomatic mediation coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump. According to Ukrainian officials, the armistice across the designated sector is scheduled to remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Under the negotiated terms, Ukrainian and Russian military commands committed to suspending combat aviation, drone interdiction, artillery fire, and offensive maneuvers across the Oleshky pocket and surrounding transport routes in Kherson region to enable de-mining teams to clear primary roadways and ensure safe transit for aid convoys.

'Atmosphere of fear': Trump moves to curtail voting rights ahead of the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:40:54 UTC
18:40:54 KST

'Atmosphere of fear': Trump moves to curtail voting rights ahead of the midterms
Americans vote on November 3 in midterm elections that could see Republicans lose control of Congress, endangering US President Donald Trump's legislative agenda. Under the US Constitution, elections are organized by the respective states – but that has not halted US President Donald Trump from trying to wield his influence ahead of the vote.
Trump has a history of challenging unfavorable election results, notably falsely blaming his 2020 defeat by former president Joe Biden on widespread voting fraud.
"The Trump administration has tried to insert the federal government into almost every aspect of the election process” in the lead-up to the 2026 vote, said Jonathan Diaz, director for voting advocacy and partnerships at the Campaign Legal Center.
Read moreGeorgia on Democrats’ minds: Powering up the Black vote to counter Trump's meddling
“The long-term risks I think are very significant, but for these midterms in particular – even if he hasn't been successful in changing the rules or in coercing state and local election officials to do what he wants – it's created an atmosphere of fear and uncertainty,” Diaz added.
In a new poll by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs, only 55 percent of Democrats said they are confident the final count after the midterm will be accurate, compared to 38 percent of Republicans.
The following are some examples of how the Trump administration has tried – and in many cases, failed – to interfere in the midterm vote.
The SAVE Act
Trump has repeatedly claimed that large numbers of noncitizens are voting in US elections, despite the actual numbers showing that this is exceedingly rare. Voting in US elections is reserved for citizens and already requires an ID; any non-citizens who attempt to vote can face stiff penalties including fines, prison or deportation.
Even think tanks that support Trump's voting restrictions have failed to find evidence of widespread fraud.
“The Heritage Foundation’s database of documented cases of voter fraud includes 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025. That is about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time,” the New York Times reported in April.
Nevertheless, Trump has been pushing lawmakers to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which would require people to present “documentary proof of United States citizenship” to vote.
The United States does not issue a national identity card to its citizens, and under the SAVE Act a driver’s license or other official form of identification would not be sufficient for voting if it does not indicate a place of birth.
Acceptable forms of ID would include a valid US passport, a military ID card, a valid government-issued photo ID showing the person was born in the United States, or a birth certificate – but only if it matches the person’s current name exactly, which could pose a problem for the 69 million women who changed their names after getting married and the trans community.
According to the Campaign Legal Center, more than 21 million Americans, or nearly 10 percent of voting-age Americans, lack access to documentary proof of citizenship, notably young people, those in lower income brackets and people of color. A 2024 report by the Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement found that 3 percent of people of color lack proof of US citizenship like a birth certificate, passport or naturalization documents.
By comparison, only 1 percent of white Americans have no such documentation.
A GOP amendment to the legislation also aimed to curtail the ability to vote by mail or online by overhauling these systems to comply with the stricter ID measures.
The legislation passed the US House of Representatives in February before languishing in the Senate due to a lack of support. Trump allies are still looking to get it passed through the budget reconciliation process.
Controversial database
Last year the Trump administration expanded a controversial federal database, the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (also known as SAVE), which exists to verify whether someone is a citizen and thus qualifies for government benefits. But the expansion allowed states to use it to verify whether someone is eligible to vote.
At least 25 states opted into the voluntary system, and it scanned 67 million registrations before a US district judge blocked it in June over privacy concerns and fears it could remove thousands of eligible voters.
Because SAVE uses historical immigration data its records are often out of date, which results in flagging people who have since become naturalized citizens. In Travis County, Texas, 97 people flagged as noncitizens – 10 percent of them, and possibly up to 21 percent – were actually US nationals, the AP reported.
But the US Supreme Court lifted the judge's block in a September ruling, allowing use of the database to go ahead.
The effects of that ruling on the midterms could be limited, however, as states cannot purge people from electoral rolls less than 90 days before an election.
“SAVE is incredibly unreliable when it comes to verifying the citizenship status of an individual person,” Diaz said, adding that this is especially true for naturalized citizens.
Read moreUS Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial voter 'verification' system
Charges and arrests
The Trump administration has also used the courts to pursue noncitizen voters. The Justice Department said in mid-October it had charged 113 people across 20 states with either voting or registration offenses in the past seven weeks. It earlier said it had charged some 90 people for election misconduct in 2026, including 50 who are suspected of having voted as noncitizens.
Jose Antonio Banuelos-Diaz, 42, has been living in the United States for 40 years. He was accused of trying to register to vote in 2007, around the time when he applied for a driver's license. California residents are prompted to register to vote at the same time they get their license.
“I have never voted because I know I can’t vote,” he told AP after his arrest, denying he tried to register. “If there was a mistake, they should have called me out right away, not 20 years later.” He has since been released but faces five years in prison if convicted.
The Trump administration also sued California election officials to try to prevent the state from counting some 20,000 mail-in ballots it says were sent by noncitizens. But a federal judge ruled the count should go ahead, saying the administration's request "violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections".
Diaz of the Campaign Legal Center said the list was inaccurate. "California looked at the list and said, well, half of these people were born in the United States, so they are citizens," he said. For the other half, "we don't have enough data in this set that you've given us to identify these people, much less verify ... what we're using".
Trump's Department of Justice sent letters to nearly all 50 states demanding unredacted copies of their voter registration rolls. At least 30 states and the District of Columbia were later sued to obtain their voter registration lists; 26 of those lawsuits were subsequently dismissed.
At least 16 states willingly handed over, or promised to provide, their lists.
Restricting mail-in voting
Trump has also been “irrationally” suspicious of mail-in voting, Diaz said, adding that one reason is that many people relied on mail-in voting in 2020 – when he lost the last election – because of Covid-19.
In March, Trump signed an executive order that created new regulations for the US postal system, the USPS, that would have imposed new standards on voter-specific data and ballot envelopes.
The US Supreme Court then blocked the measure in September.
But if it had gone through, this order could have prevented thousands from voting, disproportionately affecting Democrats, who are slightly more likely to use mail-in ballots. According to a report by the MIT Election Data & Science Lab, 37 percent of Democrats reported voting by mail in 2024, compared with 24 percent of Republicans.
Elections in the United States are held on Tuesdays, and many people choose to use mail-in voting instead of going to the polls in person to avoid missing a day of work.
While the Trump administration has appealed the Supreme Court’s decision, the court is unlikely to reinstate it ahead of the midterms.
According to Diaz, he will “certainly continue to try to make mail-in voting more difficult and to add new restrictions to it. I don't think he has much chance of success, but he will keep trying”.

Gerrymandering
The US congressional map looks very different in 2026 than it did in the 2024 election after Trump urged Republicans to redraw dozens of US House of Representatives districts to favor the party, notably in Texas.
This form of political redistricting, known as gerrymandering, has been used to disadvantage voters along class or race lines. Republicans sometimes seek to split up areas with a large Black population to lower their collective voting power since they are statistically more likely to vote Democrat.
“Redistricting is a problem much bigger than these midterm elections,” Diaz said. “It is bad for the long-term health of democracy when a majority of American voters do not have a meaningful choice in who represents them in Congress.”
After Texas lawmakers adopted a new electoral map that would give Republicans five more US House seats in the midterm elections, California held a referendum in which voters overwhelmingly approved a new congressional map that would give Democrats five more seats.
Republicans in Southern states have rushed to follow Texas’s lead.
And in a boost for GOP efforts, the Supreme Court voted in April to narrow the legal grounds for challenging maps that may be racially discriminatory under the Voting Rights Act, potentially opening the door to future redistricting.
Republicans gained an advantage in 16 districts because of this push. But a recent Reuters analysis suggests that nine of them are either too close to call or expected to go to the Democrats on November 3, largely due to Trump’s low approval ratings over the rising cost of living and the unpopular Iran war.
"The thing with gerrymandering is that you're always drawing maps based on data from the last election,” Diaz said. "So if voters change their preferences, the maps that you draw may not be as successful in securing support for your party as you thought.”

The Defence Secretary has called the Scottish National Party’s support for unilateral nuclear disarmament a white flag policy and said the party must explain how it would square that with membership of a nuclear alliance, according to remarks made to reporters in Glasgow.
Wes Streeting was asked about the First Minister’s repeated claim that the government in Westminster is leaving Scotland short of defence.

Finland orders 21 more trains from Swiss firm Stadler
Stadler Rail, the Thurgau-based train manufacturer, has a new contract to supply 21 additional trains to Finland.
The order forms part of an option provided for in the original contract that the Finnish company VR had signed with Stadler in November 2022, the group said in a press release on Friday. The agreement covered the sale of 20 trains and an option for a further 50.
The contract has been transferred to RailStock Finland Oy, the Finnish state-owned company responsible for managing the development and leasing of rail vehicles for passenger services.
“Our aim is to ensure sustainable public rail transport that does not distort competition, by providing all operators in the country with reliable, high-quality rolling stock,” said Joakim Mette, CEO of RailStock Finland Oy, cited in the statement.

Stadler Rail builds world’s first narrow-gauge hydrogen train
“Investments in new rolling stock lay the foundations for maintaining and further developing state-subsidised passenger rail transport in Finland over the coming decades,” he said.
Stadler has designed the low-floor trains, consisting of four carriages, specifically to meet the needs of the Scandinavian country: they are designed to operate reliably even in difficult weather conditions. The Flirt trains are specifically fitted with larger snow ploughs, underfloor heating and improved thermal insulation. Each train offers 340 seats and can accommodate up to 700 passengers in total. The maximum speed is 160 km/h. Production will take place at the group’s factories in Poland.

On the stock market, Stadler Rail shares are trading slightly lower this afternoon, at around CHF32. It should also be noted that when the company was first listed on the stock exchange in April 2019, the share was trading at CHF43.
Stadler Rail traces its origins back to the engineering firm founded by Ernst Stadler in Zurich in 1942. The company is now headquartered in Bussnang, canton Thurgau, and manufactures a wide range of rolling stock, from high-speed trains to regional trains, as well as trams and metro trains – vehicles that also operate on railway lines in Switzerland and Ticino. It employs 18,000 people, 6,000 of whom are based in Switzerland. In 2025, it achieved a turnover of CHF3.7 billion.

Senegal hosts Africa’s first ever Youth Olympic Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:37:07 UTC
18:37:07 KST

Senegal hosts Africa’s first ever Youth Olympic Games
The 2026 Youth Olympic Games opens with a spectacular ceremony Saturday in the Senegalese capital Dakar in the first ever Olympics to be held on African soil. It comes as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sporting competitions.
Issued on:
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Senegal is kicking off the Youth Olympic Games on Saturday, bringing an Olympic event to Africa for the first time as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sporting competitions.
About 2,700 young athletes aged 14 to 17 will compete through Nov. 13 in the capital, Dakar, the nearby city of Diamniadio and the beach resort of Saly.
Hundreds of dancers will join a spectacle celebrating Senegalese and African culture, in line with the Fames motto “Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates.”
“This is a first opportunity for Senegal and, by extension, for Africa, to discover new sports," Thomas Dieme, a Senegalese student said as Dakar prepared to host the games. "It is only natural that we should all be happy to welcome other people, other cultures,” he added.
Among the celebrities expected at Saturday's opening ceremony is French actor Omar Sy, who has Senegalese roots and stars in the Netflix series “Lupin”, as well as Senegalese Italian TikTok star Khaby Lame, both ambassadors for the games.
The mascot, Ayo, is a young lion wearing a traditional Fulani hat. Its name means “joy” in Yoruba, a language spoken in Nigeria and neighboring West African countries.
Watch moreOlympic fever grips Senegal as Dakar hosts Youth Olympic Games
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye is scheduled to declare the games open at 6:30pm local time (0830 GMT) at the Diamniadio stadium where International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry and some heads of state are expected to be present.
The Youth Olympics are a smaller competition than the Summer Olympics. Singapore hosted the first summer edition in 2010. Dakar was initially due to host in 2022, but the coronavirus pandemic delayed the games by four years.
Athletes will compete in 153 medal events across 25 sports, including athletics, swimming and 3-x-3 basketball.
Several sports will make their Youth Olympic debuts. They include Baseball5, a five-on-five version of baseball played without bats and gloves, Wushu, a Chinese martial art, that can be choreography-based or combat sport, and coastal rowing beach sprint, which combines beach runs with a head-to-head rowing race.
Beach wrestling will also feature at the Youth Olympics for the first time, a nod to Senegalese wrestling, the country’s national sport also performed on sand.
The first refugee team at a Youth Olympics will field six athletes based in Kenya and Uganda in track and field, judo and taekwondo.
The games arrive 130 years after the modern Olympics began in Athens. Coventry, a Zimbabwean swimming champion, became the IOC’s first African and first female president last year.
“It is time for Africa, time for Senegal,” Coventry told media upon arriving in Senegal on Tuesday.
South Africa hosted the continent’s first soccer FIFA World Cup in 2010. Morocco will co-host the 2030 tournament with Spain and Portugal. Rwanda hosted Africa’s first road cycling world championships last year and Formula 1 is returning to Africa with a grand prix in Rwanda starting early next decade. Botswana also staged the World Athletics Relays in May.
African countries increasingly see sport as “a weapon in diplomacy and a tool for development”, Dakar-based sports analyst Frédéric Sohoundé said.
He pointed to Morocco’s investment in sports facilities and its ability to attract repeated competitions. Senegal, though, needs reliable maintenance funding and regular events after the games to prevent its venues from becoming expensive, unused facilities, he said.
Russia’s delegation of 13 athletes is competing under its national flag for the first time at an Olympic event since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led to its suspension. Russians at the Paris Olympics of 2024 and this year’s Winter Olympics competed as neutral athletes without national symbols.
That follows a shift in the IOC’s approach under Coventry, who has said the Olympics shouldn’t “hold athletes accountable for the actions of their governments”.
It could be a trial run for a full Russian return at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
The games come as Senegal grapples with a debt crisis and public frustration over living costs.
Billions of dollars of unreported debt by the previous administration have left Senegalese authorities with little money for public spending, while layoffs and rising living costs have fueled protests in recent months.
Many Senegalese said in interviews that they're prioritizing making ends meet over attending the sporting activities.
A government-led foundation drew criticism after announcing a contribution of 500 million CFA francs (about $854,000) to buy 200,000 tickets for school children. Critics questioned the money’s source, which the president’s political movement said was from donors and benefactors.
President Faye has defended spending on the games, citing renovated sports facilities, training for young people and contracts for Senegalese businesses.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Rival US and Russian resolutions on Western Sahara fail at UN

Rival US and Russian resolutions on Western Sahara fail at UN
The UN Security Council rejected the competing proposals, leaving the peacekeeping mission without an approved extension.
The United Nations peacekeeping mission in the disputed Western Sahara faces an uncertain future after competing United States and Russian resolutions failed at the UN Security Council.
Russia vetoed the US-backed proposal on Friday, despite support from 11 members of the 15-member council.
A rival Russian draft then failed to secure the nine votes needed for adoption.
The mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) is due to expire on Saturday unless the council reaches a last-minute agreement.
Western Sahara is a former Spanish colony in northwest Africa. Morocco considers the territory its own while the Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.
The UN established MINURSO in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future, but disagreements over who could vote have prevented it from taking place.
The US draft would have extended the mission for a year while removing “referendum” from its name and making Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.
Under that plan, the territory would manage its internal affairs but remain under Moroccan sovereignty.
The council had already made the proposal a basis for negotiations last year.
US Ambassador Mike Waltz told the council in New York on Friday that the referendum had been stalled for decades.
Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.
Russia instead proposed renewing the existing mission without those changes.
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO, saying on Friday that UN personnel and equipment should leave the territory.
Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative at the UN, told reporters on Friday that he welcomed Russia’s veto because the US proposal would undermine Sahrawi self-determination.
Low-level fighting has continued since Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle in 2020.

Iran's Khamenei warns US against attacks, orders military buildup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:35:00 UTC
18:35:00 KST

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that any renewed U.S. or Israeli attack would trigger an immediate and geographically wider Iranian response, ordering the armed forces to expand their target lists, strengthen intelligence capabilities and accelerate weapons production.
In a written message following a meeting with senior military commanders Saturday, Khamenei said Iran would determine the timing and conditions for ending any future conflict if its adversaries resumed military or terrorist attacks.
He ordered the armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any threat, stressing that maintaining a high level of combat readiness was essential to deterring further aggression.
"Intelligent combat readiness for a powerful confrontation with enemies is a fundamental prerequisite for achieving maximum deterrence," he said.
Khamenei also instructed military commanders to update their target database to bring "all U.S. and Israeli assets, tangible and intangible," within striking range, signaling an effort to broaden Iran's potential targeting capabilities in the event of another confrontation.
The directives included strengthening military intelligence, developing domestic defense capabilities and adapting military doctrine and tactics to emerging threats. He also ordered increased production of ammunition and weapons for reconnaissance, logistical support and combat operations.
The meeting brought together senior military officials, including Maj. Gen. Abdollahi, chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces; Maj. Gen. Hatami, commander of the Iranian army; and Maj. Gen. Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The commanders briefed Khamenei on military readiness along the Persian Gulf coast, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, as well as along the country's northwestern and southeastern borders.
They also reported a significant increase in the production of key ammunition and various weapons systems for reconnaissance, support and combat missions. Khamenei expressed satisfaction with the preparations and asked the commanders to convey his appreciation to military personnel, police officers, Basij forces, Defense Ministry employees and their families.
Beyond military preparations, the supreme leader stressed the importance of strengthening the armed forces' ideological and spiritual foundations while addressing the welfare needs of personnel.
He also described public support as a central element of Iran's deterrence strategy, portraying continued public gatherings across the country as an extension of the national solidarity displayed during the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq War, which Tehran calls the Sacred Defense.
Khamenei praised the resilience of the so-called Resistance Front, referring to Iran-aligned groups across the region, and highlighted closer coordination among operational fronts as a factor in shaping a new political and security order in West Asia. He expressed hope that such cooperation would encourage greater unity among Muslim nations.
His latest instructions come amid continuing tensions following the U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran, which began Feb. 28 and killed then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior military commanders.
Iran retaliated with attacks against Israel and U.S. military assets across the Middle East, widening the confrontation and raising concerns about the security of regional shipping and energy supplies.
Although Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum in June following diplomatic efforts, disagreements over regional security arrangements and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz have kept tensions high.
The strategic waterway, through which a significant share of the world's oil shipments passes, has remained a major point of contention, with Iran maintaining pressure on maritime traffic as the U.S. sustains its military presence in the region and reported blockade measures affecting Iranian ports.
Regional diplomatic efforts, including mediation involving Qatar, have yet to produce a lasting resolution.
Iranian army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia reinforced Tehran's warnings Saturday, saying a renewed confrontation would spread beyond its previous geographical boundaries if U.S. President Donald Trump launched another military operation against Iran alongside Israel.
"If the U.S. president once again embarks on another military adventure in the region under pressure from and inducement by the Zionists, the flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," Akraminia wrote on X.
"And the end of the conflict will not be in his (Trump's) hands," he added.
Accusing Washington of repeatedly undermining diplomatic efforts, Akraminia said the Iranian army was continuously strengthening its combat readiness and closely monitoring U.S. military movements across the region.
His remarks came as Tehran and Washington remained at odds over the terms of any lasting settlement, particularly security arrangements and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father earlier this year, has maintained a relatively low public profile since taking office amid the conflict. His previous warnings have focused on U.S. military bases in the region, the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's conditions for ending hostilities, including demands concerning sanctions, blockades and regional security.

Keurig Alta Brewer Review: Brand-New Tech, Classically Good Coffee

Unknown Publisher

18:35:00 KST

Ahead of my virtual taste-test briefing for the new Keurig Alta brewer, it was 9:50 am and I was panicking. Pesky time zones be darned; the meeting I thought was taking place in two hours was actually in 10 minutes. That led to the first of many positive interactions with this machine—I had it fully set up, connected to my Wi-Fi, and ready to brew in less than seven minutes. That's about as intuitive a setup process as one could hope for with a first-of-its-kind coffee machine. (We won't talk about the amount of packaging scattered all over my kitchen floor during the aforementioned meeting.)
The Keurig Alta looks like something straight out of a design convention. It almost looks like spaceship decor with its curved white lines and sleek components (it also comes in black and stainless steel). Whereas some inexpensive Keurigs—the kind that sell for $50 during shopping holidays—can feel cheap and plasticky, this machine feels high-end from top to bottom. The cup holder is metal, the cup and whisk for the steam wand are magnetic, and the reservoir bin is slim and reversible. Both drip trays tuck away seamlessly without adding extra bulk.
The top of the machine has two compartments. On the right side, you'll find the standard Keurig K-Cup basket, with the typical needle at the bottom to pierce the cup. On the left, though, is a new compartment for the brand-new Keurig AltaRounds ($11 for a box of 8). These little pucks are the latest in Keurig's coffee technology and are like nothing I've seen before. The whole package comes at a high price point, but compared to in-home espresso makers, it's not unreasonable.
In Bloom
If you've ever used an espresso machine or watched a barista pull shots, you'll be familiar with the process of filling a portafilter with ground coffee and tamping it down. The Keurig AltaRounds look similar to this puck of coffee. Each puck is coated in a substance derived from seaweed, and that layer of “glue” holding the AltaRounds together allows them to bloom inside the machine. They're available in four varieties right now: dark roast, medium roast, a caramel blend, and double-shot espresso, with light-roast coffee and single-shot espresso varieties coming soon. The AltaRounds are stamped with a QR code that the machine reads in a split second when you insert them into the left touchscreen compartment.

Syria mulls joining Türkiye-Saudi-Pakistan Mecca Defence Alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:34:00 UTC
18:34:00 KST

Syria is considering joining the Mecca Defence Alliance, a NATO-style security pact linking Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Saturday, signaling Damascus' interest in deeper regional security cooperation as it seeks to rebuild its military and strengthen diplomatic ties.
"Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria's entry into the Mecca alliance," al-Shaibani said during the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) Manama Dialogue in Bahrain.
His remarks indicate that Damascus is seriously examining membership, although no formal application or final decision has been announced.
The pact was signed Aug. 7 in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Its central provision considers an armed attack against one member an attack against all three, allowing them to invoke their collective right to self-defense under Article 51 of the U.N. Charter.
The agreement also provides for intelligence sharing, joint military exercises, counterterrorism coordination and defense-industrial cooperation, including potential joint production and technology transfers.
The alliance established a Strategic Political and Defence Committee to oversee its activities and a permanent secretariat in Riyadh. Pakistan's retired Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood was appointed its first secretary-general for a three-year term. Membership is open to other countries with the unanimous approval of the founding members.
The arrangement builds on a mutual defense agreement signed by Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in September 2025. Its implementation gained momentum in October, when renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi targets prompted an emergency meeting in Riyadh. The alliance agreed to rapidly deploy previously agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia as a collective defense measure.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have completed their ratification processes, while Türkiye's domestic approval process remains underway.
Damascus first publicly acknowledged its interest in the alliance in late August, when al-Shaibani visited Islamabad. The trip marked the first visit to Pakistan by a Syrian foreign minister in nearly two decades.
At the time, he confirmed that Syria had reviewed the agreement but stressed that no decision had been made. He described the three founding countries as important regional powers and highlighted Türkiye's role as a key partner in Syria's reconstruction and security.
The issue gained renewed attention following Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's Oct. 6 visit to Riyadh for talks with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, amid efforts to strengthen Syria's relations with Arab countries.
Reports suggesting Damascus could provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia were subsequently denied by Syrian officials, who stressed that any cooperation would take place through established bilateral channels.
Syria's interest comes as its transitional leadership works to restore state institutions following the collapse of Bashar Assad's rule. The government has prioritized rebuilding the armed forces, strengthening ties with neighboring countries and reintegrating into regional diplomatic and security structures.
Speaking in Bahrain, al-Shaibani portrayed Syria as a country seeking to move beyond years of instability and contribute to regional security. He also condemned Israeli military operations on Syrian territory, citing more than 1,000 incidents since late 2024, and called for a return to pre-December 2024 positions and the reactivation of the 1974 disengagement agreement between Syria and Israel.
Joining the alliance could give Syria access to intelligence sharing, military training and defense cooperation while providing a framework for collective security commitments.
For Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Syrian membership would extend the alliance's reach into the strategically important Levant. Türkiye already maintains extensive military and security cooperation with Damascus, including efforts to rebuild Syria's armed forces.
However, Syria's military remains in the process of reconstruction and integration after years of conflict. Establishing the operational capacity and military coordination required for meaningful participation could take considerable time.
Any accession would also require unanimous approval from the three founding members and careful management of Syria's relations with other regional powers, particularly Israel and Iran.
Other countries, including Bangladesh and potentially Egypt, have expressed varying levels of interest in the framework or related security cooperation.

Israel and Thailand: A friendship built on respect and shared humanity - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:33:05 UTC
18:33:05 KST

Some relationships between countries are measured through agreements. Others acquire a face, a voice, and a smile. For Israel, Thailand is both a longstanding partner and the source of heartwarming human connections.
As the countries enter their 73rd year of diplomatic relations, it is worth looking beyond Thailand’s beautiful beaches and popular vacation destinations to recognize the depth of Israel’s relationship with a people whose culture offers an impressive lesson in respect, restraint, and hospitality.
I experienced the spirit of this friendship at a dinner hosted by Thailand’s ambassador to Israel, Boonyarit Vichienpuntu. The dinner honored Ami H Orkaby, dean of the Israeli Consular Corps, and me in my capacity as vice dean and acting dean.
Alongside the warm hospitality and excellent cuisine, the ambassador’s friendly personality stood out. During our conversation, I was impressed by his desire to become better acquainted with Israel, understand its culture and society, and strengthen relations between the two countries through personal familiarity, attentive listening, and mutual respect.
His curiosity was also evident in his interest in Israel’s electoral system and the prospects of forming a coalition between its political blocs. His questions reflected a sincere desire to understand the complexities of Israeli society and the possibilities for cooperation within a country containing many different opinions.
It was a pleasant encounter with a senior diplomat seeking to understand the people behind the headlines. Such a willingness to learn and listen provides an excellent foundation for deepening friendship between nations. This is diplomacy built patiently and through genuine interest in others.
Thai culture possesses a beauty evident in how people address one another, respect their elders, maintain their temples, practice their arts, and attend to detail.
Thai hospitality is not limited to courteous service. It allows guests to feel comfortable without embarrassing them or demanding anything in return. In a loud and impatient world, this approach reflects a human quality from which much can be learned.
One of its most beautiful expressions can be found at the dining table. At a traditional Thai meal, shared dishes are commonly placed in the center alongside each person’s rice, allowing everyone to taste a variety of flavors together.
Curries, soups, vegetables, and fish become part of a shared experience. To me, this conveys a beautiful message. A meal is an invitation to share, show consideration, offer something to another person, and receive something in return with courtesy, generosity, and affection.
Spicy, sweet, sour, and salty flavors come together in Thai cuisine with remarkable balance. Beyond the culinary skill, however, it is moving to see how food connects the people seated around the table.
What people eat matters, but so does the way they share it. A person who waits for someone else, serves that person a dish, and makes sure everyone is enjoying the meal gives real meaning to friendship. In this way, a simple meal becomes a language of closeness.
The bond between Israel and Thailand has also developed over decades in Israel’s fields, orchards, and greenhouses. Thai workers are important partners in Israeli agriculture.
Behind the general label “foreign workers” are individuals with names, families, hopes, and talents. Many have traveled far from home to provide their children with a better future. Their work supports Israeli farms and helps bring food to our tables. It deserves genuine public recognition.
On October 7, this relationship became intertwined with a tragedy: Thai workers employed in southern Israeli communities were murdered by Hamas terrorists, while others were abducted to the Gaza Strip.
People who came to Israel to earn a living found themselves confronting unimaginable cruelty far from their families. Thailand’s pain is part of the story of that day. We have a duty to remember those who were murdered, honor their families, and continue supporting the survivors after the cameras have moved on.
Protecting foreign workers
Our appreciation must find practical expression. Israel already has laws protecting foreign workers and requiring proper employment conditions, medical insurance, and suitable housing. Complementary and focused legislation is nevertheless needed to prevent exploitation, alongside firm enforcement of existing law.
Oversight must be strengthened. Complaint procedures should be made accessible in Thai. Illegal recruitment fees and improper deductions must be prevented, and workers must be able to report mistreatment without fear of retaliation.
Employers who exploit language barriers, economic dependence, or isolation must know they will be held accountable. At the same time, farmers who treat their employees with respect and provide good working conditions deserve recognition.
The requirements are simple: lawful wages, adequate rest, workplace safety, access to protection during emergencies, and humane treatment. This is a moral obligation toward people who work alongside us. It is also the appropriate way to preserve the trust of a friendly country and maintain our relationship with its citizens.
The same principle of reciprocity applies when Israelis visit Thailand. Israelis who enjoy its warm welcome must respect local laws and customs.
Raising one’s voice, shouting, and behaving aggressively are considered crude and impolite in Thailand. Even when a disagreement arises, it is possible to speak quietly, listen, and resolve the matter respectfully. A host’s smile is not permission to treat that person dismissively, and patience is not an invitation to test its limits.
The same applies to real estate. Legal options exist for purchasing apartments in Thailand, subject to conditions and restrictions, while foreign ownership of land is severely limited.
There have been reports of Israelis suspected of using nominee shareholders and corporate structures to circumvent the law. Suspicion is not a conviction, but the fundamental message is clear: anyone who purchases property in violation of the law harms both the host country and Israel’s reputation.
Friendship does not exempt anyone from the laws of the country offering its hospitality.
The misconduct of individuals must not overshadow a broad and positive relationship between people. Precisely because Thailand is so dear to many Israelis, we must cultivate respectful tourism, lawful investment, and direct relationships based on trust.
Cooperation in agriculture, innovation, medicine, and education can deepen further. Alongside official diplomatic meetings, encounters among students, artists, farmers, and families can give this friendship a living and enduring character.
Thailand deserves warm Israeli gratitude that extends beyond polite words. It deserves our efforts to learn about its culture, respect its citizens, and protect the workers who have entrusted part of their lives to us.
From a shared table in Bangkok to a greenhouse in southern Israel, a thread of hard work, generosity, and partnership connects our countries.
If we respond to Thailand’s hospitality with the same generosity and respect, we will give this friendship its most important gift: a better future for both peoples.
The writer is the CEO of Radios 100FM, an Honorary Consul and vice dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, president of the Israeli Radio Association, and previously served as a monitor for Israel Army Radio and as a television correspondent for NBC News.

Elections are over: The hard part comes when the ballots are counted the cameras are gone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:33:00 UTC
18:33:00 KST

By the time we read this week’s haftarah, Israelis will have gone to the polls to elect a new Knesset. After months of political arguments, accusations, and promises, the votes will have been cast.
But the haftarah, II Kings 4:1-37, according to Ashkenazi custom, raises a question that no election can answer: What does it really mean to be a leader?
The haftarah recounts two remarkable encounters between the prophet Elisha and women who turn to him for help.
'What can I do for you?'
The first is a widow whose husband has died, leaving her deeply in debt. A creditor is threatening to take her two sons as slaves in payment.
Desperate, she appeals to Elisha, who responds with a simple question: “What can I do for you?” (4:2).
When she tells him that all she possesses is a small jar of oil, he instructs her to borrow empty vessels from her neighbors. Miraculously, the oil continues to flow until every vessel is filled, enabling her to repay her debts and support her family.
The second account concerns a wealthy woman from Shunem, who regularly welcomes Elisha into her home. In gratitude for her hospitality, he promises that she will bear a son, even though her husband is elderly.
The promise is fulfilled, recalling the birth of Isaac to Abraham and Sarah in this week’s Torah portion.
But years later, tragedy strikes. The boy suddenly becomes ill and dies in his mother’s arms.
She hurries to Elisha, and when his servant Gehazi tries to push her away, the prophet intervenes.
“Leave her alone, for her soul is bitter within her,” he declares (4:27).
Elisha initially sends Gehazi with his staff to revive the child, but the attempt fails. The prophet then goes to the house himself, prays to God, and successfully restores the boy to life.
The miracles are extraordinary. But there is something else in these accounts that deserves our attention: the way Elisha responds to people in distress.
Elisha does not turn away the widow who fears losing her children, nor does he rebuke the Shunammite woman when she confronts him in her grief. He understands that their suffering demands more than just expressions of sympathy.
'A person must never become so engrossed that he fails to hear the cry of a child'
A well-known hassidic story about Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, the alter rebbe and founder of Chabad, makes a similar point.
His son, Rabbi Dov Ber, was once so absorbed in his Torah studies that he failed to hear his infant son crying after falling from his cradle. The alter rebbe, who was studying upstairs, heard the cries. He interrupted his learning, went downstairs, and comforted the child.
Later, he admonished his son, telling him that no matter how lofty one’s pursuits, a person must never become so engrossed in them that he fails to hear the cry of a Jewish child.
There is a lesson here for Israel’s political leaders as the country emerges from another bitterly contested vote.
Politicians have spent months declaring how deeply they care about the people and their problems. They have promised greater security, lower prices, and a better future. But campaign pledges are easy to make. The harder part comes when the election is over, and the cameras are gone.
It means hearing the concerns of parents whose children have spent countless months in reserve duty, families struggling to pay their bills, and those still living with the grief and trauma of Oct. 7.
It also means remembering that those who voted for another party are no less deserving of attention, respect, and concern.
Gehazi carried the prophet’s staff, but that was not enough. Elisha had to go himself. There are moments when a leader cannot simply send someone else to deal with a problem.
Israel’s election will determine the composition of the next Knesset. But the real test of those elected will come afterward, when the campaign slogans have faded, and the difficult decisions begin.
Elisha’s example offers a reminder that those entrusted with leadership must never lose sight of the people they are supposed to serve.
After all, winning an election is one thing. Earning the public’s trust is quite another.

Canadian police officer wounded while stopping gunman outside synagogue released from hospital

A Canadian police officer who was critically wounded while stopping a gunman outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, has been released from the hospital and is continuing his recovery at home more than a month after the attack.
Belleville police said Thursday that officer Jeff Smith was making progress in his recovery. Smith and his family were grateful for the support they had received from the community and beyond in recent weeks, the department said.
Smith was guarding B’nai Jacob synagogue on September 20 as worshippers gathered for services on the eve of Yom Kippur. The gunman, Sean Ward, 29, opened fire on him, striking him in the head and body.
Despite his injuries, Smith continued returning fire for nearly three minutes before officer Michael McCurdy arrived and joined him. Police said the two officers prevented the attacker from entering the synagogue and carrying out a mass killing. No worshippers were injured. Ward was wounded in the exchange of gunfire and died the following day.
Canada’s Jewish community and other donors have rallied around Smith and his family. A fundraising campaign launched by Derek Kreindler on behalf of the Canadian Jewish community had raised C$969,110 (nearly $700,000) through more than 8,300 donations as of Friday morning.
The funds are intended to recognize Smith’s actions in protecting the worshippers and help support him and his family during his recovery and rehabilitation.
Community rallies around Smith, McCurdy
McCurdy, who came to Smith’s aid under fire and was physically unharmed, has also received support. A separate fundraising campaign launched by Deborah Vogel on behalf of the Jewish community had raised approximately C$58,400 (little over $41,000), according to a report Friday morning.
Organizers emphasized that, alongside relief that McCurdy escaped physical injury, the psychological toll of responding to the shooting must also be recognized and his recovery supported.
Meanwhile, Canadian police are investigating suspected gunfire directed at a synagogue in the Montreal suburb of Westmount overnight between Thursday and Friday.
Police found holes Friday in several windows at Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom. Rabbi Lisa Grushcow told the National Post that the synagogue’s executive director noticed the damage when she arrived for a meeting.
Grushcow said the damage appeared to have been caused by air gun pellets. Nothing penetrated the building, and no one was injured. Police opened an investigation, but the motive remained unclear.
Synagogue previously targeted
The synagogue has been targeted before. A swastika was spray-painted on its walls in February 2025. This past June, a 38-year-old man was arrested and charged with attempting to set fire to the building.
“This is our third incident in less than two years,” Grushcow said. “We do not yet know the motive, but we cannot ignore the context of growing radicalization and rising antisemitism.”
She said the incident appeared to have deliberately targeted the synagogue. Westmount Mayor Michael Stern confirmed that police were investigating and that worshippers faced no danger.
The congregation said Shabbat services would proceed as scheduled despite the incident.

A purrfect day to vote: Taking part in the democratic process of Israel with my cat - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:32:34 UTC
18:32:34 KST

It’s that time again, when Israelis across the country flock to voting booths to make their voices heard.
And once again, I decided to take my cat, Medici – full name, HaRav Medici di Cuddlebutt Reich – along for the journey.
For those of you not in the know, in the last municipal elections, Medici and I went to cast a ballot. While Medici is a strong supporter of the Sephardi haredi party Shas, and I decidedly am not, the point back then wasn’t who he voted for. Everyone was simply charmed by his mere presence in line, meowing away and looking around with his adorable kitty eyes.
But this isn’t municipal elections. This is the big one. The Knesset. The general election. Everything is on the line. This can make or break the country’s future for the next several years – or months, if no coalition is formed.
This wasn’t time for pussyfooting around. This wasn’t time for jokes. This wasn’t time for holding back. We were going to come in full force, ready to make the hard decisions over who to vote for.
Medici shares his experience and wisdom as a voting member of the Israeli public
The stakes were high, the treats were packed, and off my spouse and I went, with Medici in his adorable kitty backpack that always makes him look like an astronaut.
Once we arrived at our polling station, we faced our first obstacle. By some cruel twist of fate, my spouse and I were not voting in the same booth. So with the two of us separated (literally right across the room, just different lines but for different rooms), we bemoaned this horrific turn of events as we sat alone.
Or rather, that is what would have happened… had I not brought my cat.
Instantly, people noticed Medici’s cries for democracy (“meow” is obviously short for “de-meow-crat-ya”) and swarmed around me, in awe at the wisdom held in his wide eyes; wisdom many may have questioned if they knew who he supported, but I digress.
The last time we took him to vote, Medici’s presence inspired some undecided voters. “If the cat can vote, so can I,” some said at the time.
This time, however, Medici focused not on inspiring undecided voters – voter turnout seems high at the time of this writing. Rather, he used his experience and wisdom to inspire the next generation.
Children brought by their parents were eager to say hi to the voting feline, and Medici’s meows in response seemed to pass on kernels of advice and valuable education to those around him.
'Meow meow meow meow meow meow'
Obviously, we lacked subtitles, so we cannot be certain as to what Medici’s exact words were. But we can also assume that he was educating them about how the elections worked, which parties had which letters on their ticket, and the importance of democracy.
These sentiments also seemed shared by many of the older Israelis around me, who looked at Medici with wistful smiles as they saw him teach the children about voting – and all without endorsing anyone in particular.
For while Medici may always support Shas in his heart, he would never want his party to win unfairly…. Right?
Certainly. Medici doesn’t steal elections, just food off the table. And, as I finish this article, he has just done so. The future of this country may be just a bit brighter because one cat went to the voting booths. However, because of that same cat, I now need to make myself a different breakfast.

Poland political crisis: Constitutional court in chaos as Nawrocki accuses government of staging power grab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:30:39 UTC
18:30:39 KST

Riot police were deployed outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal on Friday after its president was suspended, escalating a power struggle over the court.
On Friday evening, protesters and riot police faced off outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal after the court's president was suspended, the latest episode in an intensifying stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who cut short a trip to Senegal and headed back to Warsaw as the crisis unfolded, has since called for emergency talks with political leaders and has accused the government of attempting to forcibly take control of one of the country's key constitutional institutions.
The dramatic overnight events have escalated a long-running crisis surrounding Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, from which the Polish government has been trying for weeks to remove judges - who were appointed under the previous PiS government.
What had largely been a political and legal dispute over judicial appointments and the Tribunal's leadership has now spilled over into a direct confrontation at its headquarters.
The latest episode began when seven people chosen by the Sejm to serve as Constitutional Tribunal judges entered the building on Friday.
According to Tribunal spokesperson Weronika Ścibor, security guards at the Tribunal had been ordered to pack up their belongings and leave the building.
At the same time Bogdan Święczkowski, the Tribunal's incumbent president, and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański, were reportedly denied entry.
Ścibor suggested that the timing of the operation was deliberate and that it took advantage of the fact that some staff members were absent.
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska subsequently announced that she was taking over the leadership of the Tribunal and suspending Święczkowski from his duties.
The current Tribunal leadership has challenged the legality of these moves.
Nawrocki returns
In response to the unfolding situation, Nawrocki cut short a visit to Senegal and returned to Poland.
At the presidential palace, he met First President of the Supreme Court Zbigniew Kapiński before heading on to the Constitutional Tribunal's headquarters with Kapiński and a group of aides.
Footage posted on X showed scuffles break out with a group of judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, as Nawrocki attempted to gain entry.
Nawrocki accuses government of power grab
Early on Saturday morning, Nawrocki's chief of staff, Paweł Szefernaker, read out a statement from the president in front of the Tribunal, in which he described the night's events as a breach of Poland's constitutional order and a forcible takeover of a constitutional institution.
"Tonight, there has been a breach of the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional organ of the state," Szefernaker said.
"I call for the restoration of the legal order and for the forces of coercion sent there by the government to leave the Tribunal's grounds," he added.
Nawrocki said he had consulted with Kapiński and that neither of them recognised the actions of those who, in his view, are unlawfully claiming authority in the Tribunal.
He said he planned to hold emergency talks with representatives of parliamentary political groups on Saturday, saying the move was necessary due to what he described as a threat to the state's internal security and the need to stabilise the political situation.
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has also weighed in on the incident, expressing concerns about the president's behaviour.
"The president's behaviour alarmed me enormously," he said, adding that he hoped the prosecution service would take action and that it was unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way.
He argued that footage showed the president "forcing his way in and attacking the judges."
Żurek also acknowledged that talks had been held about the situation at the Tribunal, including with Bartłomiej Sochański, but that no compromise had been reached.
He stressed that the Tribunal should resume normal work and deal with citizens' outstanding cases.
Protest outside Tribunal
Protests were held around the Tribunal building, involving politicians from PiS and Confederation and right-wing supporters.
Among those present were party leader Jarosław Kaczyński, Mateusz Morawiecki, former Tribunal president Julia Przyłębska and Bogdan Święczkowski.
The PiS leader said the events were an assault on the Constitutional Tribunal. He called for protests to continue, warning that Poland risked turning into a police state.
PiS MEP Patryk Jaki, for his part, said that images from the Tribunal had already gone around the world and could damage the image of Donald Tusk's government.
