Millions embezzled in fraud scheme at Ukrainian defense firm – investigators
A former head of a state-owned Ukrainian defense company is suspected of embezzling millions of dollars through fake mediation deals, the country’s anti-corruption bodies have said.
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) announced in a statement on Friday that the scheme had cost the government 1.1 billion hryvnia (around $43 million).
The Western-backed agencies, which frequently target Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s inner-circle, didn’t name the suspect, only saying that he used to lead a subsidiary of Ukrspecexport, a state-run company with exclusive rights to export and import military hardware.
According to the investigators, the former head of the state-run firm signed a deal with a foreign company in 2015 for it to provide mediation during the sales of Ukrainian military products abroad.
However, it had been established that the Ukrainian firm had conducted all of the negotiations with a customer from a Middle Eastern country on its own, and the foreign company wasn’t involved, they said.
Despite this fact, the official signed falsified documents about mediation services being provided by the foreign company and transferred millions to it as payment, the statement read.
The actions of the suspect are being qualified as large-scale embezzlement and forgery of government papers, it added.
Ukrainskaya Pravda reported later in the day that, according to its sources, the official in question is Taras Shiyko, who now holds the positions of the deputy director of Ukroboronprom, a state-run conglomerate comprised of Ukraine’s arms makers. The fraud scheme relates to his time as the head of Progress, a state-run export and import company.
Shiyko became part of an anti-corruption case earlier this year, involving the suspected embezzlement of 32 million hryvnia (around $700,000).
Zelensky’s government has been rocked by a series of corruption scandals involving people close to him since November 2025, when NABU and SAPO accused Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of the Ukrainian leader, of masterminding a $100 million kickback scheme involving state contracts in the energy sector. Other investigations have implicated former Ukrainian ministers, diplomats, and senior officials.
NABU’s latest high-profile case targeted an alleged protection racket involving scam call centers and officials from the Prosecutor General’s Office. Although he was not personally named as a suspect, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko left Ukraine before being dismissed by parliament last month, according to Ukrainian media.
Critics accuse Zelensky of leading a sprawling corruption network which permeates his government, allegedly helping him maintain power and enriching those involved. A poll issued by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) last month suggested that the Ukrainians consider corruption to be a bigger problem for the country than the conflict with Russia.

Are Houthis using Russian satellites as Saudi Arabia fends off strikes?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:08:30 UTC
17:08:30 KST

Are Houthis using Russian satellites as Saudi Arabia fends off strikes?
Analysts say the seizure of state arsenals, external backing and extensive military evolution has enabled the Houthis to build a powerful arsenal.
An investigation has revealed that Russian satellites are assisting the Iran-aligned Houthis to strike Saudi Arabia’s military and energy infrastructure, further upending global energy markets amid the US war on Iran.
Hostilities between the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Houthis have been ongoing since July and escalated in September when the rebel group seized full control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
Last month, the Houthis also carried out a precision strike on pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s most important oil pipeline, the East-West pipeline. An investigation by Geneva-based private firm AURORAH GeoSignal Intelligence revealed that Russian satellites had been surveying the region days in advance to gather intelligence about the pipeline.
With fighting for control of Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government continuing, how significant is Russia’s support to the Houthis? Why can’t Saudi Arabia, the most powerful of the Gulf states that is backed by the US, hold back a group of rebel fighters?
Here’s what we know:
What did the investigation into the use of Russian satellites show?
As revealed by The Associated Press news agency this week, between July 1 and October 19, AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence examined 40 missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthis and, in every case, found a pattern of Russian government and military satellites observing the targeted areas both before and after the attacks.
Nawaf Obaid, founder of the geosignal intelligence firm, told Al Jazeera that by reconstructing Russia’s military reconnaissance architecture, the group had identified individual satellites, calculated their orbital trajectories and then established observation opportunities and correlated their activity with military developments across Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and Yemen.
He said the satellites they identified include Russia’s Bars-M military mapping satellites, Persona optical reconnaissance satellites, Lotos-S1 electronic intelligence satellites, Pion-NKS maritime reconnaissance systems and Kondor-FKA radar-imaging satellites. They also examined the EKS/Tundra infrared early-warning constellation.
“The critical finding was not the presence of individual Russian satellites, but the sequencing and integration of their complementary intelligence capabilities,” he said.
Obaid also confirmed to Al Jazeera that based on the findings, “Russian military geospatial and signals intelligence has supported the Iranian-led intelligence architecture assisting Houthi operations in Yemen.”
He said the strongest operational example of this has been the Houthi offensive along Yemen’s western coast towards Bab al-Mandeb, where Russian-derived intelligence, Iranian command integration and local human intelligence all contributed to “the rapid deterioration of opposing Yemeni forces’ battlefield coordination”.
“We assess that this intelligence relationship is also relevant to Houthi missile and drone targeting against Saudi Arabia. Russian military reconnaissance provides capabilities far beyond ordinary commercial satellite imagery, particularly when optical, radar and electronic intelligence are integrated,” he said.
“The September attacks against Saudi Arabia’s East-West Petroline illustrate the sophistication of the targeting problem,” he said. That was when three pumping stations – PS8 at Afif, PS9 at Al-Dhekra and PS11 at Al-Mesba’ah – were struck within the pipeline’s “critical high-elevation western section”.
“Their selection reflected an understanding of the infrastructure’s engineering vulnerabilities and strategic importance,” he explained.
How significant are these findings?
Brussels-based military analyst Elijah Magnier said AURORA’s findings don’t necessarily show the whole picture.
“Inability to intercept an intelligence transmission doesn’t establish who had access to the Russian satellite information, whether Russia deliberately shared it, or whether Iran obtained it independently,” he said, adding that for this, there are four possible scenarios.
“First, Russia could have deliberately shared information with Iran,” he said.
“The second is Iran obtained Russian satellite imagery through commercial channels… However, the Russian military’s reconnaissance imagery is generally not publicly accessible, so the commercial Russian imagery would not necessarily establish Russian government involvement,” he noted.
“The third is Iran obtained information through another intermediary, so a third party could theoretically have supplied the intelligence originated from the Russian system, and there is no currently publicly verified evidence establishing such an arrangement,” he added.
But Obaid highlighted that distinguishing a Russian-supported intelligence architecture from proof that a particular Russian satellite supplied the targeting data for an individual Houthi strike is essential.
“Our assessment establishes the wider intelligence relationship; attribution of specific satellite-derived intelligence to individual missile launches requires additional corroboration,” he said.
Three officials, including one from Saudi Arabia and another in the top ranks of the Houthis, as well as a private intelligence analyst, confirmed to The Associated Press that the Houthis and other Iranian allies have benefitted from Russian intelligence, as well as Chinese capabilities.
Last week, the Saudi Foreign Ministry’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, Rayed Krimly, told reporters that the Houthis receive intelligence from Russia and China.
“We do discuss these matters regularly with China and Russia, and we will continue to do so,” he had said.
How important is access to Russian satellites for Iran and the Houthis?
Russian officials have not yet commented on AURORAH’s findings, but in recent years, technological and military ties between Russia and Iran have deepened significantly, anchored by joint strategic agreements, space cooperation, and the exchange of defence technology.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst on Yemen at the International Crisis Group, said Moscow reportedly supporting Tehran’s allies like the Houthis is particularly significant because it would mean a shift in the trajectory of the Yemeni conflict.
“It is increasingly moving beyond its domestic dimensions and becoming intertwined with wider regional dynamics. Supporting the Houthis is no longer a matter of interest to Iran alone. We are now seeing other actors, particularly Russia, providing Iran with intelligence support and sophisticated weaponry, from which the Houthis are also benefitting,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The question is whether this support is being channelled directly to the Houthis or indirectly through Iran. I don’t think that distinction is important. The bottom line is that the Houthis are benefitting from increasingly diversified external support involving several countries,” he added.
But Nagi warned that Russian support to the Houthis has implications for both the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia.
“Russia’s role also extends into the diplomatic arena, where Moscow has taken positions at the United Nations Security Council opposing stronger international action against the Houthis. Taken together, these developments point to a broader expansion of Russian engagement with the group,” he added.
Where have the Houthis struck in Saudi Arabia?
Yemen’s Houthis have attacked multiple locations across Saudi Arabia, spanning from the eastern and western coasts to the capital and southern regions, since fighting escalated over the summer.
In a statement on X on Friday, Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed attacks have hit vital commercial and military infrastructure, which spanned Saudi Arabia from its east and west coasts to Riyadh and the southern region of Najran.
Saree said the Houthis targeted the Ras Tanura oil refinery with a ballistic missile, an Aramco facility in Abqaiq with a missile, King Khalid International airport in Riyadh with multiple missiles, King Fahd International airport in Dammam with a drone, the Rabigh oil refinery with a ballistic missile and a Saudi military headquarters in the Najran region.
There has, however, been no independent corroboration of these specific claims.
However, Houthi attacks generally have resulted in multiple deaths and injuries in Saudi Arabia. A severe strike on King Khalid International airport in Riyadh earlier this month killed at least 12 people and injured 300, according to Saudi officials. The attacks led to the airport’s temporary closure, forcing the postponement of Saudi Arabia’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.
The airport has since reopened, and flights resumed on Sunday with the Houthis warning travellers to avoid the facility, calling it a “military target”.
An October 21 attack on King Fahd International airport in Dammam also killed two people and wounded eight.
Why are the Houthis so well-armed?
Since seizing Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and swaths of northwest Yemen in 2014, the Houthis have demanded to be recognised as the legitimate governing authority in Yemen.
After taking the capital and state institutions, the Houthis gained access to large arsenals belonging to the Yemeni military and formed an alliance with forces loyal to former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
The internationally recognised government decamped to Aden.
Once regarded as an armed group without many resources, analysts say this has changed since the Houthis seized Yemen state arsenals, received external backing from Iran, and evolved their military capabilities.
Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, told Al Jazeera that besides learning the art of weapons assembly, the Houthis have scoured international black markets for components and carried out many military engagements to unearth a clandestine, but robust, market for sales, too.
“So while the Houthis have been expending their cache of weapons, they have been developing and expanding too – and we have seen that with their long-range missile attacks as far away as Israel – so targeting high-value targets in Saudi Arabia in contrast is very easy pickings for them,” he said.
When a truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition took effect in 2022 and continued until earlier this year, many within the Yemeni government expected it to pave the way for a political settlement, Nagi said.
“The Houthis, meanwhile, were preparing for the possibility that the conflict would resume. They used the relative lull to strengthen their military position. The extent of that preparation has become evident over the past few weeks. Their forces have demonstrated considerable military readiness, enabling them to advance across several areas and inflict significant setbacks on Yemeni government forces,” he said.
According to Magnier, the Houthis’ sophisticated missile propulsion and guidance technology remains heavily dependent on foreign expertise, however.
The Houthis receive substantial backing, training and weaponry from Iran. This includes Iranian-origin and-derived ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and one-way attack drones – such as the Palestine-2 and Toufan systems – although Iran officially denies supplying them.
Besides Iran, Magnier said Iran’s ally in Lebanon, Hezbollah, has also contributed with military training and organisational experience. “All the experience gathered from fighting Israel was transformed and offered to Ansar Allah [the name the Houthis are also known by] in Yemen,” he said.
“The cooperation has also extended to Iraqi armed groups, with the exchange involving military personnel and again operational experience in a vast area,” he added.
“This combination [of domestic expansion and foreign dependence] helps explain why years of Saudi-led military operation, followed by American and Israeli strikes, have failed to eliminate its military capability,” he added.
How has Saudi Arabia struck back at the Houthis?
The Saudi-led coalition has retaliated against Houthi targets in Yemen through air attacks and military operations.
On Friday, the coalition in Yemen reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region.
The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile which had targeted western Saudi Arabia.
Al-Maliki said on Monday its forces also destroyed four ballistic missile launchers and five tunnels used by the Houthis to store missiles.
In a post on X, he had said coalition forces attacked a missile depot, adding that the operation “focused on cutting off Houthi militia supply lines between areas under their control”.
The operation also targeted Houthi “fortifications, gatherings of their members, and their military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen”.
Al-Maliki said on Monday that Saudi air defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh”.
This month, Yemen’s government forces launched the “Operation Yemen Dawn” counteroffensive, aimed at recapturing territory held by the Houthis.
On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said air defences intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.
The kingdom’s civil defence agency said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, and reported damage to several buildings and vehicles.
Why are the Saudis struggling to contain the Houthis?
While high-level diplomatic talks such as recent meetings in Tehran involving Saudi and Iranian officials have aimed to de-escalate tensions, analysts say the Houthis are actively testing the limits of Saudi military restraint and air defence capabilities, transforming the Yemeni conflict into a wider national security test for Riyadh.
According to Magnier, the Saudis have been struggling because “nobody wins a war by air bombing.”
“The air bombing helps for the ground forces to capitalise on what the air force is doing and opens the road for the ground forces. If the ground forces are not sufficiently motivated to advance and offer sacrifices and accept large losses, then there is no point in wondering why the Saudis are struggling,” he said.
Crisis group’s Nagi shared a similar view. He added that the Saudi-backed Yemeni government camp has also remained fragmented, poorly organised and militarily unprepared.
“There was an expectation that quick fixes, particularly intensified air strikes, could produce rapid gains. But the government and its allies had not developed the military capabilities or organisation necessary to sustain a confrontation with the Houthis,” he said.
According to analyst Saj Ahmad, despite the billions spent on US and European weapons, the Saudis have failed to make effective use of their military capabilities.
“The Houthis have learned a great deal from Iran’s military strategists as well as those militias in and across Iraq that battled US troops for years after the fall of Saddam Hussein. And in that intervening period, the Saudi regime has made big weapon buys but has little skill in how to use or deploy them and has even less capability to effectively combat a guerrilla group like the Houthis,” he said.
“With Riyadh under siege, I would not be surprised if the Saudis eventually leave this combat zone, like the UAE did,” he added.

Voter turnout in Rahat, Israel’s largest Bedouin city, approached 80% on Election Day, up from 60.6% in the previous election, amid a surge in participation across communities in the Negev. Arab party campaign offices in the city celebrated the results as a “poke in the eye” for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Likud activists in southern Israel, meanwhile, blamed the minister for galvanizing Arab voters, arguing that his conduct had seriously damaged the right-wing bloc’s electoral prospects.
Local activists from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party said Ben-Gvir’s aggressive rhetoric and combative statements had failed to deliver electoral gains for the Right in southern Israel. Instead, they argued, he had spurred tens of thousands of Arab voters to cast their ballots.
Election observer describes palpable anger against Ben-Gvir
Rami, a veteran Likud activist who served as an election observer in Rahat, described an atmosphere of anger and tension on the streets and at polling stations.
“The anger was palpable everywhere. Almost every other word out of their mouths was ‘Ben-Gvir.’ It was simply incomprehensible. Over the years, Likud always managed to win a certain share of the Bedouin vote, but this time we were reduced to almost zero there. He simply sent them rushing out of their homes to vote against us,” they said.
Shimon Boker, a member of Likud’s central committee, also sharply criticized the minister’s conduct.
“Ben-Gvir caused serious damage to the national camp and single-handedly added seats to the Arab parties. This has never been the Likud movement’s way. Everyone understands that agricultural crime and illegal construction must be addressed firmly, but that requires action and sound policy, not provocations and unnecessary media noise. He provoked them relentlessly, and the result was that they flocked to the polls in protest,” he explained.
In Rahat, the voter turnout operation ran like a well-oiled machine. Throughout Election Day, residents organized buses and private cars to bring voters to polling stations.
Turnout surpasses mayor's ambitious goal of 75%
Rahat Mayor Talal al-Krenawi had set an ambitious turnout target of 75%, aiming to translate the Negev’s potential pool of 150,000 votes into four seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament.
After the exit polls were released, Krenawi expressed satisfaction: “We showed our strength. He wanted to show us who was in charge in Rahat. Now we have shown him.”
Residents stressed that their protest targeted the minister’s demolition policy and statements: “We have no objection in principle to Netanyahu, who has received votes in the Negev in the past. The problem is that Ben-Gvir dragged him into acting against us and damaged the fabric of life.”
Ben-Gvir’s supporters rejected the accusations and blamed Likud instead. Roy, an activist with Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party in southern Israel, argued that voters’ longstanding loyalty to Likud had drawn support away from the minister’s party.
“Many residents of outlying communities enthusiastically declared that they would vote for Ben-Gvir, but when the moment came, they hesitated and returned to the familiar Likud ballot," he pointed out. "Netanyahu’s aggressive campaign emphasizing the size of his party drew those votes back to Bibi. Beyond that, you cannot blame Ben-Gvir for Bedouin citizens exercising their right to vote. Does Likud expect us to abandon law enforcement, the removal of illegal encroachments and the fight against crime simply out of fear that they will go to the polls?”
Bedouins offered a different account. Raed Abu al-Qi’an, a resident of Hura in the Negev who had predicted high turnout before the election, said the mass mobilization reflected a sense of being under siege.
“People went out to vote because Ben-Gvir backed us into a corner, incited against us, and focused only on demolishing homes without offering any solution or planning an alternative. He talked about governance and security, but in practice crime continued, while basic needs such as healthcare and infrastructure were forgotten. He ran a political campaign at the population’s expense, and that is what prompted a civic uprising at the ballot box,” he said.

When buses stopped running on Brazil election day, 'Lula's Army' grabbed their car keys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:06:41 UTC
17:06:41 KST

When buses stopped running on Brazil election day, 'Lula's Army' grabbed their car keys
SALVADOR, Brazil, Oct 31 - When buses in the northeastern Brazilian city of Salvador inexplicably stopped running last Sunday, history teacher Martins Mafra grabbed his car keys and set off to pick up stranded voters across town.
Mafra's efforts in Salvador, the capital of Bahia state, were part of a massive get-out-the-vote drive across Brazil that helped power leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to an unprecedented fourth term.
Lula supporters, shocked by right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro's first-round lead, quickly mobilized as the prospect sank in that the Bolsonaro clan could return to power. They used innovative social media initiatives, free taxi rides and grassroots campaigning to secure the incumbent president over 10 million more votes in the runoff.
"I'm a father, and I work in education, so this was an opportunity to teach and show that we can make a difference," said Mafra, who offered rides to supporters of all stripes. "It's one thing to stay home complaining about city hall or posting videos online; it's another thing to get up, walk out the door, and actually do something."
Bolsonaro, son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, fled this week to the US, where he declared himself the legitimate "leader" of Brazil, questioning the credibility of Lula's 10 million-vote leap.
Bolsonaro also questioned a two-hour voting extension, requested by Lula's campaign and granted by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice, due to the out-of-service buses in Bahia. Bolsonaro's campaign also sought an extension due to rains in conservative-leaning southern states, and the extension had little bearing on the result, the federal electoral court said.
LULA STRONGHOLD
Bahia, a populous Lula stronghold, was the state with the highest fall in abstention rates between both rounds, with nearly 400,000 more people voting in the runoff.
Almost a quarter of those additional voters came from Salvador, a city of over 2.5 million people where Lula won 73% of runoff votes.
Salvador resident Gabriel Mercury, 41, son of Brazilian pop star Daniela Mercury, was one of those who helped orchestrate the turnaround.
The Lula voter watched with concern as the leftist underperformed in the first round, and decided to do something about it. He began by inviting undecided voters to have coffee with him and talk politics. Later, he offered cash rewards of up to 2,400 reais ($445.67) to anyone who could name a single Bolsonaro legislative proposal that had benefited workers.
Nobody took him up on the offer.
LULA OVERHAULS CAMPAIGN
After the underwhelming first round, Lula's team sought to reboot a campaign marred by infighting, mixed messaging and the complacency of incumbency, aides said.
Aware that no presidential candidate had ever been elected after trailing in the initial vote, the 81-year-old Lula bought his first ever smartphone to reach Brazilians on the platforms that increasingly shape Brazil's political debate.
Meanwhile, lawmaker Andre Janones, who helped Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, rapidly expanded a WhatsApp channel he called "Lula's Army."
By instructing followers to recruit friends and amplify Lula content online, he grew the channel from roughly 50,000 people ahead of the first round to over 10 million by the runoff.
Dharma political risk consultant Creomar de Souza said Lula's team, and particularly Janones, successfully pounced on missteps by Bolsonaro to convince voters he would threaten Brazil's democracy, reverse social advances and slash welfare payments on which millions of Brazilians depend.
As the runoff approached, polls showed Lula closing the gap on Bolsonaro. By election day, they were tied.
In Salvador, Mercury began to believe Lula could win. Then, early on Sunday, Salvador's bus network ground to a halt.
BUS FIASCO
In Brazil, public authorities are required to provide free public transport on election day.
But reports from across Salvador, where Mayor Bruno Reis supported Bolsonaro, suggested many buses were not running.
Inspectors from the Bahia consumer protection agency found 944 buses idling in Salvador depots. Jaime Barreiros Neto, the Bahia electoral court's judicial analyst, estimated at least 30% of the fleet was not operating.
Reis blamed the outage on Lula stickers that had been placed on buses in violation of electoral rules. As soon as city hall realized sticker removal efforts were causing a bottleneck, it immediately ordered the fleet released, he said in a press conference on Sunday.
Reis told Reuters he supported Bolsonaro in the runoff in accordance with his party, União Brasil. He denied detaining public transport or hindering voter mobility, saying the stickering of the buses held up the fleet.
Bahia’s electoral court ordered the arrest of Salvador’s transportation chief, Pablo Souza, over the absent buses. It revoked the order once voting had ended the following day, but demanded a probe into the incident.
Souza, who was in Paris on an official visit during the day of the vote, denied wrongdoing. He told Reuters the number of buses was the same as during the first round, and in line with electoral regulations.
MASS MOBILIZATIONS
As news of idling buses rippled through Salvador, Mercury and five friends asked their social media followers to drive people to voting stations. Some people got behind the wheel; others donated to cover fuel costs. Mercury estimated that his team moved around 600 voters on election day.
"Politics isn't just institutional politics," he said. "We make politics through our actions."
Uber drivers also stepped up, with thousands offering free rides worth up to 50 reais ($9.28) throughout the day, said Adriano de Jesus Braga dos Santos, an Uber driver and content creator, who personally offered 36 rides to passengers.
Nicole Soares, 18, waited 40 minutes for a bus, but never considered giving up. "I had the right to vote," she said, casting her ballot for Lula.
Some residents were still unable to vote.
Grecia de Jesus Nunes, a 54-year-old street vendor, said only two buses passed her hotdog stand between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. No buses were available during her brief break, and when volunteer drivers eventually reached her, she could no longer leave work.
Though unable to vote, Nunes rejoiced at Lula's victory.
"My life is Lula," she said. "I am Lula until I die." REUTERS

Chinese factory activity slips amid strong tech show

17:06:29 KST

China's manufacturing activity moderated in October, with the purchasing managers' index falling to 49.3 as the high-tech and equipment manufacturing sectors maintained expansion, official data showed on Saturday.
The overall reading was down 0.8 percentage points from September, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
Chief statistician Huo Lihui attributed the retreat to some demand being brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday this month and a complex international environment.
The production subindex stood at 49.8, down 1.9 points from September, while the new-orders subindex fell 1.1 points to 49.4, as both supply and demand moderated during the month.
The PMI for high-tech manufacturing stood at 51.3 while that for equipment manufacturing came in at 50.6, both remaining above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction.
The figures indicate that emerging industries continued to sustain growth momentum, supported by the ongoing development of new quality productive forces, Huo noted.
Manufacturing activity in several advanced industries remained robust. 
Both the production and new-orders subindexes for railway, shipbuilding and aerospace equipment manufacturing, as well as computer, communications and electronic equipment manufacturing, stood at 53 or above, pointing to relatively strong supply and demand in these sectors.
Large manufacturers continued to report expansion, with their PMI standing at 50.2, despite a slight decline of 0.4 points from the previous month. 
The PMI readings for medium-sized and small enterprises came in at 48.4 and 47.5, respectively.
On the price front, both major raw material purchasing prices and factory-gate prices remained in expansionary territory, although their growth moderated.
The purchasing price subindex stood at 56.8, down four points from September while the factory-gate price subindex eased 2.3 points to 51.7, partly reflecting recent declines in the prices of certain nonferrous metals and other commodities. (Xinhua)

Young boys confess to vandalizing over 100 graves in Saaremaa
Two young boys aged eight and 10 are responsible for vandalizing more than 100 graves at a cemetery on the island of Saaremaa over the weekend, newspaper Saarte Hääl reported.
One of the boy's parents shared a handwritten letter in the Kihelkonna community Facebook group in which the child apologizes for damaging the cemetery.
"I'm sorry for damaging the cemetery. And I regret it and I promise that I will never do it again," Saarte Hääl quoted the boy's letter as saying.
The children's parents and grandparents also addressed the community in the same group.
"As parents and grandparents, we are deeply sorry that our child has caused irreparable damage and heartache to the Kihelkonna community through his actions," they wrote.
The Prosecutor's Office, which is conducting a criminal investigation, confirmed to ERR that two boys under the age of 14 have been questioned in connection with the Kihelkonna Cemetery incident and that prosecutors believe they are involved in the incident.
Rein Rand, head of the investigation group at Kuressaare Police Station, told ERR on Friday afternoon that criminal proceedings had been launched under the section of the Penal Code concerning desecration of the memory of the deceased.
Margus Saar, who has worked as a cemetery caretaker for 21 years, told "Aktuaalne kaamera" on Tuesday that this was the first time vandalism of this scale has occurred.
"Police have now established that 105 graves were affected. Gravestones have been broken – pushed over and then shattered. Expensive grave lanterns made of granite have had their glass smashed, and flowers have been damaged. I'm inclined to think that Sunday was the day it happened, and that it was young people. There are footprints suggesting that," Saar said.
Minna Raun, head of the district policing group at Kuressaare Police Station, said vandalism on this scale had not occurred before.
"The prescribed punishment for this is a fine or imprisonment. If minors are involved, the type of punishment remains exactly the same. Vandalism on this scale is indeed taking place for the first time," said Minna Raun, head of the district policing group at Kuressaare Police Station.

- 1. Russell Brand’s evidence Brand, 51, who was in the witness box for four hours on Wednesday, told the jury the criminal case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life. He blamed his public fall from grace on 2023 media reports, including a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, about his alleged sexual misconduct. He said he had achieved “staggering fame” after his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry but that now nobody would “touch [him] with a bargepole”. The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, suggested he hadn’t been “abandoned” by everyone he knows, and noted he had millions of followers online. “This is not the case of poor Mr Brand being taken apart by the media,” she said. Brand denied her suggestion that consent had not been “uppermost” in his mind between 1999 and 2009, telling the court: “Consent is absolutely non-negotiable.” He said he was “innocent” of all the charges and added: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and, indeed, in many ways more important than sex itself.” Brand admitted he was wrong to have used his fame and success to “facilitate” sexual activity with women. “I think I was in a position of fame, a successful person who was admired, and I misused that commodity very selfishly,” he said.
- 2. Laura Brand’s evidence Brand’s wife, Laura, began her evidence on Thursday by confirming she is the TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher’s sister, and that they are the daughters of the Ryder Cup-winning golfer Bernard Gallacher. She told the court she and Brand fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian had cheated on her early in their relationship. “I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people. I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous,” Laura Brand said. They broke up in February 2007 but restarted their relationship in 2015 and married two years later. Laura Brand insisted he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”. “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage,” she said. During cross-examination by Karmy-Jones, Laura agreed that Brand has a channel on the video-sharing platform Rumble, presents at political conferences and was baptised in early 2024 after the sexual misconduct allegations emerged.
- 3. Brand’s demeanour in court Brand has remained still during the trial, but he was animated during his wife’s evidence, and could be seen smiling and laughing at times. He appeared to be mouthing words towards her as she talked about his 2024 baptism and nodding when she spoke of their friendship. He also showed more emotion during his evidence. With his hands behind his back, he began by giving confident answers in a booming voice to his barrister, Ian Winter KC. “Mr Brand, that is nice and loud,” the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, said. Brand also used florid language such as “badinage”, “loquacious” and “coquettishness”. But there was a marked shift in the comedian’s demeanour during cross-examination, which was punctuated with pauses and long spells of silence. There was a long pause after the prosecution’s first question: “You blame Dispatches, don’t you?”, and again when Karmy-Jones repeated the question.
- 4. Confronted by his own content Brand was confronted with extracts from his 2007 book, My Booky Wook, and his comments in media appearances. The first alleged rape victim had told the court she believed Brand was gay and effeminate when they first met at a 1999 Labour party conference fringe event, leading to her agreeing for him to come to her hotel room. The prosecutor pointed out that in his book, Brand used a picture of himself as a seven-year-old and wrote the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took 15 years to produce results.” Karmy-Jones read out another in which Brand wrote: “My egotism and the single-mindedness with which I pursued potentially sexual conquests could often make me uneasy company.” In another he set out: “Now if I want something – whether it’s a job or a woman – I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that’s in the way, until I possess the object of my desire.” In the book, Brand referred to himself as a “fervid, febrile mass of sexual energy” towards the end of sex, adding: “I’ll do anything. I’m demonically sexy.”
- 5. Closing speeches and next week The prosecutor gave her closing speech on Friday, telling jurors that the six women who had come forward to accuse Brand did not know one another and had nothing to gain. “There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago,” Karmy-Jones told the jury. “What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago. The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years.” Brand’s barrister is expected to make his closing speech when the trial resumes on Monday.

‘The last fortress’: historic Athens cafe closes as countercultural area gentrifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:00:37 UTC
17:00:37 KST

It has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and lawyers, radicals and revolutionaries for as long as anyone can remember. And for 44 years, Christos Vanas, the proprietor of Mouria, has let them all in.
Every day at 7am, the taciturn former waiter has been the first man to step inside the historic cafe in Exarchia, the heart of leftwing Athens. It is a ritual he has kept punctiliously, opening up the famous gathering place before he himself has had his first coffee.
“Only Saturdays are different,” says his daughter Areti, drawing on a Karelia, the aromatic Greek cigarette that, like Mouria, has been around for more than a century. “By 5am, he is here serving tsipouro and other [alcoholic] spirits to warm up the stallholders of the street market outside.”
But this weekend will be Vanas’s last. After a send-off expected to last into the small hours, the cafe’s large, iron-framed doors will shut forever on Sunday when patrons walk out of the mosaic-floored institution. It will be the closing act in a drama that began with the expiry of the premises’ lease last summer.
“It will be as if a friend died,” sighs Nontas Papayannis, a retired barrister who has frequented the cafe for the past 20 years. “Another change to Exarchia, but also another loss in a Greece that is dying before our eyes.”
Born and bred in the neighbourhood long viewed as the nerve centre of Athens’ counterculture scene, the blue-eyed septuagenarian has also kept to a regime, rocking up at his favourite watering hole “at least four times a week” within an hour of the clock striking noon.
Stelios Goutis, 83, is an actor who trod the boards for more than six decades before his fame broadened playing Papa Triantafyllos, a priest with a penchant for a tipple or two in the TV series Hara’s Cafe. He waxes lyrical about“the calming effect” of traditional eateries that have had such an outsized role in the lives of Greeks.
“A visit here is the route to relaxation,” Goutis says with thespian flair at one of Mouria’s marble-topped tables. “You stop by after work. You down a tsipouro or two, you meet friends you may or may not have arranged to meet, and all the pressures of daily life slip away. It’s a form of psychotherapy. When it goes, we’ll look back at it as a memory of good times even if it is a loss, too.”
Both men were among the 7,500 signatories of an online campaign that urged the Greek culture ministry to have the cafe declared a protected heritage site when the building’s owners announced they would not be renewing its tenancy in an area fast undergoing gentrification. The culture ministry failed to intervene.
Few districts in downtown Athens are more redolent of resistance, leftwing solidarity, radicalism and anarchist foment than Exarchia. Its spirit of anti-authoritarianism dates back to the uprising at the nearby Athens Polytechnic, an event that led to the death of dozens of students but is credited with the collapse of rightwing military rule in 1974, barely 35 years after the nation’s bitter civil war.
But with tourist numbers in the Greek capital more than doubling over the last decade, the neighbourhood of narrow, graffiti-daubed streets has also been discovered by investors, catering to the tastes and needs of foreign visitors.
“We were like the last fortress here,” says Areti, dressed in a black leather jacket and Dr Martens boots, the garb favoured by the area’s more youthful residents. “We didn’t change our menu, we didn’t raise our prices or serve Aperol spritzes and cafe lattes. It’s about nostalgia and we’ll leave with our heads held high.”
For Greeks raised in Exarchia, it was an unnerving experience to walk streets that were no longer recognisable, she lamented. “So much has changed. Everywhere you look there are new shops with signs in English and buildings turned into suites and short-term rentals. You could be anywhere.”
For many, the last straw had come when travel platforms began advertising tours of the hangouts in Exarchia patronised by hardened leftists. “There have been groups outside the cafe,” says Areti, her eyes firmly focused on her footwear. “What to say?”
Mouria is not alone. Its closure is emblematic of the decline of traditional coffee houses across Greece, even if the proliferation of third-wave and Italian-style cafes in more recent years has earned the country the reputation of having “a cafe economy”.
In villages far and wide, kafeneia once considered the life and soul of communities are vanishing, turbocharging depopulation.
But in Exarchia, among local people so fervently opposed to corporate culture, the end of the landmark coffeeshop on the corner of Charilaou Trikoupi and Kallidromiou streets is also part of a concerted effort to alter the neighbourhood’s traditional leftwing identity. Anger has similarly mounted over the construction of a metro station in Exarchia’s main square, championed by the centre-right government as a way of cleaning up a district that many conservatives regard as an affront to their own ideology. The public work, which has resulted in increased policing, has deprived residents of their one open space to gather.
“Exarchia is perhaps the only neighbourhood in Athens where the leftwing concept of the ‘revanchist city’ is applicable,” notes Nicos Souliotis, a sociologist at the National Centre for Social Research. “State policies are clearly aimed at imposing social discipline and control. The activism we have seen around Mouria is about defending the neighbourhood’s identity and established way of life.”
For Maria Tsampra, another longtime veteran of the cafe and a former employee of the defunct leftwing daily newspaper Eleftherotypia, the sociologist is spot on.
Enjoying what will be one of her last platters of mezedes at Mouria, she says the cafe’s closure is as much about “erasing memory” – because that, she adds, is also part of the neighbourhood’s “all for profit” transformation – as it is shutting down a leftwing stronghold in the heart of Athens.
“There’s this attempt at revisionism, of controlling us through the rewriting of history,” Tsampra says before breaking into a smile: “It won’t work. In Mouria we found a haven and we won’t be forgetting it anytime soon.”

Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about it | Carly Dober
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:00:37 UTC
17:00:37 KST

Ever longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, a new AI personal agent. Unlike traditional chatbots, this little AI tool will be able to fill out forms for you, organise calendars, pay bills and make reservations. Meta describes Muse as a personal agent “built for everyone”. The launch comes at a time when AI agents have been making headlines for hacking into government websites, public agencies and businesses. However, my immediate concern is a little closer to home.
I work as a psychologist, and I’m often talking to clients about lifestyle habits that lead to short-term gain but incur long-term pain. Our brains have a beautiful way of preferring the path of least resistance, of doing what is easiest to preserve our resources. And with the demands of modern life feeling so overwhelming for so many people, the urge to scroll after a long week or defer to a chatbot because you are exhausted is incredibly seducing.
Tech bros pushing their products on to us is nothing new (we all remember the metaverse, right?), but the message is now seemingly at fever pitch for mass AI adoption and how integral it is for human development. It is helpful to remind ourselves what we are being asked to give up, to whom and why, and to consider the potential risks before we hand over our precious data.
Some technology, such as large language models (LLMs) and social media that has an infinite scroll algorithm, seem to have a dose effect: too much reliance on this technology can lead to particular cognitive biases being activated, brain chemistry being depleted, moods and mental health being affected, and even neurological skills being atrophied, to name but a few of the documented risks.
Overusing artificial intelligence affects the brain and learning by bypassing the mental effort required to build deep neural connections, a process known as cognitive offloading. Frequent AI use fosters a passive acceptance of information, reducing the internal friction and inquiry that drive genuine curiosity and problem-solving. The brain depends on mental struggle and overcoming failure to rewire and strengthen our neural pathways. Bypassing that friction reduces our overall cognitive reserve over time.
Our tendency to favour or give greater credence to information supplied by technology (such as ChatGPT or Claude), and to ignore a manual source of information that provides contradictory information (a textbook, for example) even if it is correct, illustrates the phenomenon of automation bias. Automation complacency is closely linked – an overlapping concept that refers to the monitoring of technology with less frequency or vigilance because of a lower suspicion of error and a stronger belief in its accuracy, even when we know that LLMs often generate inaccurate answers.
Social media is designed to be so addictive because its business model relies on maximising user attention, while people give up their privacy because the immediate psychological rewards outweigh the abstract risk of data exposure. Most people say they value their privacy, but their behaviour says otherwise. This contradiction is known in behavioural economics as the privacy paradox.
Digital tools make life incredibly convenient – you can order a car with the touch of a button, a hot meal can be delivered to your door, and you can order and return outfits without ever exchanging a word with another person. People gladly trade their location data, contacts and browsing history in exchange for free maps, personalised shopping recommendations and seamless communication. Many individuals falsely believe that because they aren’t committing crimes, their data isn’t valuable. They don’t realise that aggregate data is used to manipulate purchasing habits, influence political votes and predict private life events.
Privacy policies are also intentionally long and confusing, and written in dense legal language that is inaccessible to the vast majority of users. Users face “consent fatigue” and simply click “Accept all” whenever the pesky window pops up while they are browsing because they feel they have no real choice.
There is a way out of the muck, though. Become more discerning about what information you share online; consider turning your location off unless you’re using navigation apps; reject cookies tracking you; hell, even start to poison your data if you really want to engage in some online anarchy. Does the online store you bought a T-shirt from once really need to know your full legal name and date of birth?
To avoid AI overreliance, you need to start introducing “friction” into your days – deliberate obstacles that break the automatic loop of seeking instant gratification. From a psychological perspective, AI is highly addictive because it eliminates this friction, offering immediate rewards with zero cognitive effort – and our brains need cognitive effort to remain sharp. Every time you try to work out a problem or read a book instead of the comments section, that is your brain doing a push-up.
If you’re struggling to rein in your social media or AI usage, a good way to start is by logging out of online sessions. Forcing yourself to manually type your credentials every time creates a massive psychological barrier. Also, try restricting your AI usage strictly to a desktop or laptop computer: removing ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini from your phone eliminates the urge to use it while walking, lying in bed or waiting in line. Scrolling on our phones or talking to a chatbot impedes much of the necessary mind-wandering time that our brains need to function at their best.
When you feel the urge to ask an AI a question or have it write something for you, force yourself to wait about 30 minutes. Use this time to brainstorm, look at a book or simply sit with the problem. Often the urge passes or you solve the problem yourself. Commit to writing the first draft of any email, letter or presentation entirely by yourself. Embrace the discomfort of maybe getting things wrong. Instead of asking an AI for a recommendation or an explanation, ask a friend or colleague, or check a reputable website. The delay in waiting for a human response builds patience, and we need to practise this skill in order to retain it.
Dedicate specific hours of your day to completely screen-free activities. Read books, write with pen and paper or go for a walk without your phone and see how differently things feel for you after six weeks of consistent effort. Intentionally building friction into the frictionless online experience is hard – but I promise that your brain will thank you for it.
- Carly Dober is a psychologist living and working in Melbourne

On a bibliographic rarity: Rembrandt’s drawings exhibited at the National Library
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

The National Library of Lithuania is currently hosting an exhibition of 150 drawings by the Dutch master Rembrandt. They are facsimiles from a rare portfolio published in 1903, only seven copies of which survive. One is owned by the Lithuanian artist and collector Vaidotas Žukas. Below, he explains the meaning and value of the Rembrandt portfolio.
The works in this exhibition first came into my possession through this very library. During the winter of 1979–1980, I worked in a department of the Republican Library headed by Aleksandras Kubilas (1928–2021), who was not only a librarian but also a collector. He visited the studio I had established in my parents’ apartment in the Scientists’ House, across from Lukiškės Prison. Kubilas acquired one of my painted portraits for 300 roubles and gave me this portfolio of Rembrandt drawings.
At the time, he also recounted the story of its provenance. The account may be partly a legend, but I know of no other version and have been unable to verify it. According to the former owner, “the portfolio was taken by the Red Army in 1945 from the Royal University Library in Berlin and transported to Moscow as a trophy of war. At Vilnius railway station, it was exchanged for a litre of moonshine.”
Rembrandt’s work has fascinated me since my youth. As a student, I visited the Hermitage in Leningrad and spent several days wandering alone through its Rembrandt galleries. Eventually, the guards were instructed to remove me, perhaps because they suspected that I was planning some mischief.
The paradoxes of the collection’s survival
It is noteworthy that Rembrandt himself assembled an extensive collection whose fate is highly revealing. We know its contents only because he fell deeply into debt and was declared bankrupt. Notaries inventoried his large Amsterdam house and its entire collection before the property was sold at an auction. In that sense, even misfortune can leave a valuable historical record.
The notarial inventory shows that Rembrandt owned dozens of turbans and hundreds of feathers, horns, and claws brought by ship from Africa, India, the Middle East, and the Far East. His home was, in effect, a storehouse of authentic props. Several items from this collection appear in the drawings exhibited here, including a two-handed sword, armour, and figures wearing turbans.
Rembrandt also collected dried marine specimens, including coral, starfish, and shells. Other curiosities such as snakes, lizards, molluscs, and unfamiliar fish were preserved in jars of alcohol. He owned taxidermized animals of various sizes, as well as an extensive collection of weapons: cannons, crossbows, helmets, and daggers. His holdings also included portrait busts of all the Roman emperors.
By comparison, the Antwerp painter Peter Paul Rubens owned original antique busts, which he later sold to English aristocrats, whereas Rembrandt was satisfied with high-quality copies. He approached the artistic heritage of earlier periods in a similar manner. Although he travelled little – he had a family and worked prolifically – his chests contained engravings after many earlier European masters, giving him a broad understanding of artistic developments in Germany, Spain, and Italy. Several original paintings by Raphael nevertheless hung in his house. He also amassed fabrics, belts, saddles, harnesses, and jewellery, including gold and pearl necklaces, brooches, rings, and bracelets.
Why did he need all those objects? I believe the answer lies in his art. He painted his wife, Saskia, seated on his lap, dressed in sumptuous velvet and wearing a jewelled diadem. In a self-portrait, Rembrandt depicts himself laughing, holding a tall glass of wine, with an ornate sword at his belt.
His biblical King Solomon, also represented in one of the drawings in this exhibition, is clothed in soft furs. In Rembrandt’s painting of a Polish horseman, now in the Frick Collection in New York, the rider wears gold-trimmed boots, red Polish trousers, and a red cap edged with sable. He carries a bow, a quiver filled with arrows, a battle axe, and several swords; the horse is fitted with elaborate bridles and precious stirrups. Such ethnographic detail appears throughout Rembrandt’s drawings, etchings, and paintings, yet it never becomes mere illustration. The master understood the restraint and distance required for art to remain art rather than descend into idle display.
A murderer from Denmark
While preparing this exhibition, I consulted numerous documents preserved in the archives of Leiden and Amsterdam, with online translation tools proving invaluable. The exhibition at the Martynas Mažvydas National Library includes two drawings in which Rembrandt depicts a woman tied to a post, perhaps still alive, perhaps already dead. They were clearly drawn from life: one shows the figure from the front and the other from the side. In both, an axe is fastened to the crossbar.
The documents later revealed that the woman was Elsje Christiaens, an eighteen-year-old from Jutland, Denmark. After arriving in Amsterdam, she found work as a domestic servant. Following a dispute with her landlady, she was killed with an axe. The case was thoroughly documented because women convicted of murder were rare in Amsterdam. Christiaens was publicly executed on Dam Square in accordance with Dutch law. Her body was then taken to a site in the wetlands north of Amsterdam known as the Gallows Field. Among the surviving records associated with Rembrandt is a receipt for a boat hired to reach that location. Other Dutch artists also depicted this execution ground and the bodies of condemned prisoners displayed there.
Earlier scholars dated Rembrandt’s drawings of the condemned woman to 1655. The Dutch historian Isabella van Eeghen (1913–1996), however, discovered records of the crime in the Amsterdam City Archives that established the later date of 1664. She wrote: “The fate of Elsje Christiaens was intended as a warning against crime; now it will serve as a warning to art historians to be cautious when dating works solely on stylistic grounds.”
Will restitution take place?
The portfolio of Rembrandt drawings currently exhibited at the National Library in Vilnius is a bibliographic treasure. It was printed in The Hague in 1903 using heliography, a rare and costly reproduction process at the time. Bearing the stamps of the Royal University Library in Berlin, the portfolio is numbered 7. Publicly available information indicates that only six comparable portfolios of Rembrandt drawings are held in the United States, all in museums and university libraries in New York and other cities.
Fifty drawings from this portfolio were exhibited ten years ago as part of the Santara–Šviesa Congress programme at the Alanta Manor Gallery, and again during the winter of 2018–2019 at the Gothic House of Perkūnas, then home to the Institute of Life and Faith. At the opening of the Alanta exhibition in 2016, Leonidas Donskis introduced the works from the portfolio.
After the event, Irena Veisaitė, Elena Bradūnaitė, and Leonidas Donskis asked what I intended to do with it. I replied that I wished to show it to the public in Vilnius and then return it to the Berlin library. All agreed, while emphasising that the return should not take place without public attention. For several years, working through the Lithuanian Embassy in Berlin, we have sought sources and documents that could substantiate the alleged theft in 1945. If such evidence is found, the restitution process can begin.

Russian forces using mercenaries form Africa and Asia in assaults on Huliaipole front – military
According to Ukrinform, the 7th Air Assault Corps of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram.
The 7th Air Assault Corps continues its defensive operation in the Huliaipole sector. Last week, Ukraine’s Defense Forces killed or wounded around 900 Russian troops, nearly 150 more than in the previous reporting period. This was also the highest figure recorded in the past two months.
Due to heavy losses on the front lines, Russian forces have been forced to regroup, rotate troops and replace units. In particular, according to available information, losses have prompted a change in the composition of Russia’s 5th Combined Arms Army, with the 57th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade being replaced by elements of the 60th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade. After replenishing their personnel, Russian forces are expected to try to restore the intensity of their assault operations.
The Russians continue to rely primarily on infiltration tactics, using small infantry groups of one to five soldiers.
At the same time, units operating within the 7th Air Assault Corps' area of responsibility have recorded the participation of not only Russian citizens but also foreign nationals in assaults. In particular, the Russian command is deploying mercenaries from African and Asian countries in combat operations in the sector.
Recruitment follows a familiar pattern: foreigners are promised civilian jobs or safe contract-based military service. Upon arrival, their documents and mobile phones are confiscated, and they are then forcibly sent to the front line after being deprived of communication, the military said.
Recently, Ukraine’s Defense Forces captured an Indonesian citizen in the Huliaipole sector who had been serving with the Russian Armed Forces’ 39th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade.
As Ukrinform reported, according to Brigadier General Dmytro Usov, secretary of the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, Russia’s Defense Ministry has signed contracts with nearly 46,000 foreign nationals from 151 countries. About half of the foreign prisoners of war interviewed by the Ukrainian side knew they would be fighting against Ukraine.

Poland in Constitutional Standoff as Court Heads Suspended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:53:00 UTC
16:53:00 KST

Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki turned back while en route to Senegal on Friday after orders were issued suspending the president of the country’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) and his deputy from their duties. Opposition politicians described the move as a “coup d’état”, while Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended efforts to restore the rule of law.
The suspension orders escalated a long-running dispute over the court’s leadership and the status of five judges elected by parliament but barred from hearing cases by the Tribunal’s president, Bogdan Święczkowski. Nawrocki has declined to receive their oaths of office. The five judges subsequently took their oaths at ceremonies in parliament, which Nawrocki and Święczkowski do not recognise as valid.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The TK, a specialist court that rules on the constitutionality of Polish laws, has been at the center of judicial controversies for years, with the previous government led by the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party accused of politicizing the institution by stacking it with loyal judges.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist coalition government, which came into power in late 2023, has consistently ignored the court’s rulings, questioning the body’s legitimacy.
On Friday, one of those five judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, issued orders suspending Święczkowski and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, from their duties for one month. Protests outside the Tribunal’s headquarters turned violent.
Poland Calls for Urgent Black Sea Ceasefire, Demands Fair Peace for Ukraine
Citing her seniority as a judge, Korwin-Piotrowska invoked Article 130 of Poland’s Law on the Organisation of Common Courts as the legal basis for the suspensions.
The provision allows a judge to be temporarily relieved of their duties if he or she “is detained after being caught in the act of committing an intentional crime, or if the nature of the act committed by the judge is such that the dignity of the court or the essential interests of the service require their immediate removal from the performance of official duties“.
Nawrocki said he was returning as “at a moment like this, the President must be in Poland.”
Nawrocki made the announcement on X after police entered the Constitutional Tribunal building in Warsaw. Demonstrators outside had begun throwing objects
The Tribunal’s X profile carried a message saying its website had been illegally taken over and that Święczkowski remained the body’s president.
Battle over the Tribunal
The court’s spokesperson said Święczkowski remained at the Constitutional Tribunal’s helm “whatever someone might think up,” and said the police intervention was planned.
“I suspect those who were skeptical about the Constitutional Tribunal president’s warning regarding a coup d’état are no longer laughing,” Weronika Ścibór told pro-opposition TV channel Republika.
Korwin-Piotrowska, who also assumed the acting presidency of the Tribunal, said her actions were justified by “overriding constitutional necessity” and accused Święczkowski of a range of improprieties including preventing the court’s General Assembly from being convened.
She also accused him of preventing five judges—whose status Święczkowski does not recognize—from adjudicating, as well as of violating the rules for appointing judges to hear cases and of sidelining cases of public importance to prioritize others for political reasons.
Political standoff
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution.
The appointment of judges to the Constitutional Tribunal has become the focal point of a standoff between Poland’s government and president.
The court’s composition and the process of appointing its judges were prominent issues in a rule-of-law dispute between the previous right-wing government and the EU.
The European Commission withheld tens of billions of euros in funding for Poland over accusations of democratic backsliding and politicization of the judiciary.
Restoring judicial impartiality became one of Tusk’s main campaign pledges in the 2023 parliamentary election that brought his coalition government to power.
Tusk said that restoring the rule of law was the government’s duty and required decisive action following years of what he described as lawlessness under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government.
“Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of lawlessness under PiS, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and requires decisive action. There is no alternative,” he wrote on X on Friday evening.
