Netanyahu survives the election, but Eisenkot holds key to replacing him - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:50:48 UTC
16:50:48 KST

On Tuesday night, Gadi Eisenkot delivered the speech of a man who could already see the Prime Minister's Office on the horizon. He was not alone. The first exit polls pointed to a clear victory for the opposition bloc and the approaching end of Benjamin Netanyahu's tenure.
In the rooms where politicians awaited the actual results, however, the picture gradually changed. Likud climbed to 27 seats, Yashar settled at 21, and the gap between the blocs narrowed. Eisenkot discovered what Shimon Peres had learned long ago: Exit polls are excellent at generating headlines, but somewhat less effective at transferring power.
Netanyahu, for his part, can breathe a sigh of relief. His party is once again the largest, and he remains prime minister. But the good news ends there. The outgoing coalition bloc holds just 53 seats, eight short of the 61 needed for a majority. The opposition bloc has 48, while Ra'am and the Joint List hold 19 between them. These are the numbers according to the latest reported vote count. Anyone looking for a government in them will need to bring something else to the table: Partners willing to sit together.
Voters weakened the outgoing coalition but did not give the opposition parties a majority that would allow them to form a government without reaching new agreements. Netanyahu can remain in office as long as no alternative government is established. Eisenkot must find a way to form one.
The incumbent prime minister's advantage is already clear: He does not need a new agreement to remain in office. While his rivals try to resolve their differences, Netanyahu can use his political connections, maintain his partners' loyalty, and examine who in the opposing camp might prefer a compromise to another election.
The equation Eisenkot must solve begins with the 48 seats held by Yashar, B'Yachad, the Democrats, and Yisrael Beytenu. Ra'am has eight seats, and the Joint List has 11. With Ra'am alone, the opposition bloc would reach 56 MKs; with both Arab factions, it would reach 67.
The arithmetic of a minority government
These are mathematical combinations, not coalition agreements. Eisenkot does not necessarily need 61 votes in favor of his government for it to be sworn in, but he does need a majority in the confidence vote. If all 48 members of the opposition bloc support the government, 53 members of Netanyahu's bloc oppose it, and all 19 members of the Arab factions abstain, the government will fail to win the Knesset's confidence.
To change that outcome, Eisenkot will have to secure additional support or ensure that some of the 53 opponents do not vote against him. Support from Ra'am, for example, could be sufficient numerically if the remaining Arab faction abstains and all 48 opposition-bloc MKs vote in favor. But that calculation depends on agreements that Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman opposed during the campaign.
Although 67 MKs do not belong to Netanyahu's bloc, they have not agreed to form a government together. They may manage to unite around certain measures in the Knesset without agreeing on the identity of the next prime minister. Netanyahu could remain at the head of the executive branch while his rivals assemble a majority against him in parliamentary votes.
For Eisenkot, the challenge is to turn agreement against Netanyahu into agreement in favor of a particular government. Those are two different political tasks.
Netanyahu ran a familiar election campaign: He placed himself at the center, relegated his partners to supporting roles, and portrayed every vote for a small right-wing party as a risk to his continued rule. Likud benefited from this approach far more than its partners did.
Otzma Yehudit won seven seats, United Torah Judaism seven, Shas six, and Religious Zionism and Zehut six. Together with them, Netanyahu reaches 53 seats, eight short of the majority he needs.
No party in the opposition bloc has pledged to join his government, and any attempt to recruit an outside partner could require concessions that anger his existing allies. Yisrael Beytenu has already made clear that even an offer allowing Liberman to serve first in a rotation arrangement would not change his refusal to join a government with Netanyahu.
Relations within the Right could also shift. During the campaign, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich had to defend their voters against Likud's efforts to draw away support. They may now have to choose between loyalty to Netanyahu and concern that a unity government could be formed without them.
Netanyahu needs them to preserve his bloc, but if he wants to form a government, he may have to seek additional partners who would not necessarily agree to sit alongside them. The more Netanyahu signals that he is exploring a broad government, the greater their incentive to make clear what they will not accept.
They could complicate his efforts precisely when he is trying to expand his room for maneuver. From their perspective, however, threatening to dissolve the partnership too early could leave them outside any new arrangement.
Eisenkot faces resistance from his own allies
For Eisenkot, the story begins with success. He entered the election as the leading candidate to replace Netanyahu, pushed Bennett into second place within the camp, and built a party that won 21 seats.
His personal success did not solve the coalition problem. The opposition parties' 48 seats provide a starting point for negotiations, but there is still a long road to swearing in a government.
The disagreements began months earlier, when Eisenkot raised the possibility of forming a minority government. Liberman publicly opposed the idea, while those close to Bennett also viewed it as an attempt by Eisenkot to draw voters away from within the bloc. All three wanted to replace Netanyahu, but they did not agree on how to establish the government that would succeed him.
Yair Golan was quick to propose a course of action. While his partners remained silent, the Democrats chairman called on them to include Ra'am and the Joint List in the calculation of the 67 MKs outside Netanyahu's bloc and to establish a government in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens.
He also criticized the distinction between Jewish and Arab votes. But his call did not produce agreement among the factions. Bennett and Liberman did not join the initiative, and support from both Arab factions for any particular government is far from guaranteed.
Mansour Abbas has already served as a coalition partner in a government headed by Bennett. The Joint List, by contrast, holds different positions on diplomatic and security issues, and cooperation with it would require Bennett and Liberman to cross a political line they have pledged not to cross.
Agreeing to rely on Ra'am does not necessarily indicate a willingness to rely on the Joint List as well. To swear in a government, the parties will have to reach agreements on the confidence vote and subsequently on the budget, security policy, and government decisions. Even outside support will require clarifying the conditions imposed by the factions asked to provide it.
Claims of "election theft" voiced in Likud circles after the polls closed already point to a possible line of attack against a government dependent on the Arab parties: Challenging its legitimacy.
Bennett and Liberman, who pledged not to rely on those factions, would be particularly vulnerable to such criticism.
Senior Yisrael Beytenu figures have spoken of "the sin of arrogance by Gadi and his people" and the "selfish campaign" he conducted. They argue that talk of a minority government supported by Arab parties drove away voters who had already moved to the opposition bloc, and accuse Eisenkot and Golan of returning approximately seven seats to Netanyahu's camp.
That anger is complicating negotiations before they have even begun. Liberman spent years building his political strength around a hard line toward the Arab parties and, ahead of the election, even sought to disqualify Ra'am.
Now, after his party blamed talk of a minority government backed by Arab parties for the loss of seats, it will be difficult for him to agree to such a move.
His refusal would not necessarily rule out every possibility of forming an alternative government, but it would leave Eisenkot without Yisrael Beytenu's seven seats and force him to find another combination.
Bennett faces a similar problem, although his political history complicates it in a different way. He has already formed a government with Ra'am and paid a political price for doing so.
He now leads a party with 12 seats, significantly smaller than Yashar's. Joining an Eisenkot-led government could give him influence, but it could also cement his position as the junior partner of the man who overtook him.
For Bennett, the decision also concerns his political future. If he joins Eisenkot's government, he will have to demonstrate to his voters why they should continue to see him as an independent alternative. If he stays outside, he risks being remembered as the politician who held the power needed to change the government but chose not to use it.
In August, Eisenkot spoke of presenting a government with 58 or 59 seats, without asking anything of the Arab parties. Now the opposition bloc holds only 48 seats.
If all 19 Arab MKs abstain and all 53 members of Netanyahu's bloc vote against the government, Eisenkot will lack a majority in the confidence vote. Conversely, support from Ra'am and abstention by the Joint List could allow a government to be sworn in with 56 votes in favor and 53 against.
Herzog's decision and the battle for the Knesset
Even before that, Eisenkot must deal with President Isaac Herzog.
The president is expected to receive the official results next week, hold consultations with the factions, and decide whom to task with forming a government. Likud is the largest faction, but the central question will be who can demonstrate a realistic chance of forming a government.
If 61 MKs unite in recommending a candidate, that will carry political significance, but recommendations do not guarantee a majority in the confidence vote.
Herzog will have to assess which MK has a chance of forming a government, in accordance with his authority under Basic Law: The Government.
A faction could recommend Eisenkot to prevent Netanyahu from receiving the mandate while still refusing to support his government. Conversely, a faction could decline to recommend him but later allow his government to be sworn in through support or abstention.
The number of recommendations will therefore be important, but it cannot substitute for establishing the agreements needed to win the confidence vote.
Herzog has already called on party leaders to approach consultations with an open mind and avoid another election.
The president can encourage compromises, hold talks, and try to identify a formula for a unity government, but he cannot impose one on the lawmakers who would have to vote for it.
The timetable also matters. Whoever receives the mandate will have 28 days to negotiate, with the possibility of an extension of up to 14 additional days. If that attempt fails, further procedures stipulated by law will become available.
Throughout this period, the outgoing government will remain in office until another is formed. Netanyahu will not be required to leave the Prime Minister's Office after 28 days, even if his rival receives the mandate.
During the mandate period, Eisenkot could try to change the parliamentary balance of power while Netanyahu still serves as caretaker prime minister.
Success in such an effort could restrict the outgoing government's ability to control the legislature and give Eisenkot a political achievement even before he reaches agreement on the composition of a government.
Netanyahu would continue to run the executive branch, but he might struggle to control the parliamentary agenda.
Eisenkot could show his voters that the majority opposed to the outgoing government can deliver results even without a coalition agreement.
To do so, he would have to bring MKs into the plenum repeatedly and ensure that they vote together. If he succeeds in replacing the Knesset speaker or advancing significant legislation, he could point to a tangible achievement and strengthen his position in coalition negotiations.
Failure in the first votes would expose his weakness precisely in the arena where he appears to enjoy a numerical advantage.
For Netanyahu, this would be a particularly uncomfortable scenario. As long as his rivals argue over forming a government, he benefits from the advantages of incumbency.
If they begin cooperating in the Knesset, he will have to contend with a majority whose effectiveness does not depend on agreement over the distribution of ministerial portfolios.
Netanyahu has a clear interest in deepening the divisions between them, particularly over cooperation with the Arab parties.
There is also a trap for Eisenkot. Bennett and Liberman may agree to act against Netanyahu in the Knesset precisely because such votes do not require them to support a minority government under Eisenkot.
Eisenkot could claim parliamentary achievements and apply pressure on the government, but those successes would not necessarily bring him closer to the Prime Minister's Office.
Netanyahu can remain in office as long as no alternative government is formed, even if he struggles to advance his parliamentary agenda.
Unity, Trump, and the possibility of another election
And what of a unity government?
The arithmetic is tempting. Likud and Yashar together hold 48 seats. With Bennett's B'Yachad, they reach 60 even before adding other partners.
But the numbers do not answer the disagreements awaiting the leaders around the negotiating table.
Who would serve first in a rotation? Would Netanyahu agree to a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7? Would Eisenkot agree to serve under him? What would happen to the military conscription law? Would Ben-Gvir and Smotrich be left out? And what would guarantee that any agreement signed would survive the first crisis?
Eisenkot and Bennett have pledged not to sit in a government with Netanyahu.
Breaking that promise would carry a heavy price, but outright refusal does not guarantee a way out of the deadlock either.
Another election could return all sides to the same position, or even give Netanyahu the eight seats he currently lacks. The leaders will have to consider that risk as well.
The political price of a unity government would not be shared equally by Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Netanyahu could present it as an expansion of his government's support base and a means of reducing his dependence on his existing partners.
Eisenkot would have to explain how joining a government headed by the man he sought to replace could be reconciled with breaking the central promise he made to voters.
The rotation question would be central to any such negotiations: Who would serve first, and what would ensure that the other side receives the position when its turn comes?
Even if Eisenkot manages to secure significant policy commitments from Netanyahu, ensuring that the agreement is honored would remain difficult, particularly if Netanyahu serves as prime minister during the first stage.
Then there is Donald Trump.
The US president supported Netanyahu before the election, and he may try to influence the formation of the next government as well.
Washington carries weight in security relations, the Iran issue, and the possibility of offering an Israeli government a shared agenda with the US administration.
If Trump proposes a significant diplomatic or security initiative to Netanyahu and Eisenkot that requires a broad government, he could change their calculations.
Netanyahu could argue that unity is necessary to seize a diplomatic opportunity, while Eisenkot would have to decide whether the opportunity justifies a partnership with Netanyahu.
American pressure could give both leaders a public explanation for a compromise they had initially resisted.
But for that argument to be convincing, a concrete American initiative would be needed, not merely Trump's desire to see a broad Israeli government.
Yet even Trump, for all his influence, does not hold the 61st seat.
Public support for Netanyahu does not turn Liberman into his coalition partner. A meeting at the White House does not resolve the question of a commission of inquiry, and Herzog's decision on whom to entrust with forming a government remains subject to Israeli law, whatever the White House's preferences.
The coming days will first reveal whether Eisenkot can assemble broad enough recommendations to the president.
It will then become clear whether that same majority can act together in the Knesset and whether either leader is prepared to pay the political price of a minority or unity government.
If no agreement is reached, another election remains a possibility.
Netanyahu will continue to head the caretaker government until an alternative government is formed.
Eisenkot, meanwhile, will have to persuade voters who have already voted for change but have not given his camp an agreed path toward achieving it.
Netanyahu can wait in the Prime Minister's Office. Eisenkot must persuade politicians who struggle to agree even on how to replace him.
This is not the result of an exit poll. It is the political outcome of the election.

====================================================================================================

Louvre heist emboldened art thiefs, leaving Europe's smaller museums on high alert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:50:21 UTC
16:50:21 KST

Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.
Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million ($10 million), to an accomplice and fled. At the museum's main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.
"Whatever could go wrong, did," said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.
The raid was one of a string of museum thefts in France, Italy and Spain since last year's heist at the Louvre in Paris, raising concerns that criminals are increasingly targeting smaller institutions with fewer resources to protect valuable collections.
"This is where we see the 'Louvre effect'," said Marc Balcells, a Barcelona-based researcher specializing in crimes against cultural heritage. "If the Louvre was so easy to rob, just imagine a tiny museum in a rural area or a smaller town."
Works by Antonello da Messina vanished from a museum in his Sicilian hometown in August, while two Renoirs were stolen from Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera the following month.
In Spain, thieves stole hundreds of historic gold coins from museums in Badajoz and Albacete and made off with a Bronze Age treasure in Villena, near Alicante.
A 2024 survey by France's Culture Ministry found only one in four cultural institutions had an emergency and risk-prevention plan, while nearly half lacked video surveillance.
Who checks when the alarm goes off?
A French parliamentary report in May said museums lacked the resources and preparation to adequately protect artworks and artifacts.
In Italy, the challenge is amplified by the way the country's cultural heritage is spread across hundreds of towns and institutions, a legacy of centuries of fragmented rule.
"That is also what makes our system distinctive: works remain in the places where they were created,” said Antonella Pinna, president of the Italian committee of the International Council of Museums. "But we need to make life harder for criminals."
The council worked with Italy's Culture Ministry and the Carabinieri on museum security guidelines published in 2015, but Pinna said technology alone was not enough.
"If an alarm goes off, someone has to make sure it is checked," she said.
In a narrow street in the Tuscan town of Sansepolcro, the civic museum displays four works by Renaissance master Piero della Francesca, born just steps away in the 15th century.
The Louvre theft "affected us deeply because cultural heritage is central to Sansepolcro's identity. It is our soul," culture councilor Francesca Mercati told Reuters.
After the Louvre raid, officers from the Carabinieri's cultural heritage protection unit recommended more cameras, longer retention of CCTV footage and tighter controls on bags and bulky clothing.
"We immediately implemented those recommendations," Mercati said.
A vast network to protect
The scale of the challenge is daunting.
Italy has more than 4,400 museums and similar institutions, according to national statistics agency ISTAT. Spain has about 1,500 museums, while France has more than 1,200 institutions carrying the official "Musees de France" designation, alongside hundreds of smaller collections.
Protecting such a broad network is particularly difficult for smaller institutions that depend on local funding.
Florence Imbert, a Paris-based security consultant for cultural institutions, said 85% of small French museums were run by local authorities with limited financial resources.
"The budget is key to winning the war," she said.
France's Culture Ministry announced a 33-point security plan in July, backed by €30 million over three years for local museums.
Recent figures suggest concern is warranted. The Carabinieri art squad recorded 17 thefts from Italian museums and galleries in 2025, up from 14 a year earlier.
Europol said in an August report that museum thefts were becoming more forceful and increasingly focused on precious metals, gemstones and other high-value artifacts.
Paintings can't earn the thief a fast buck
Unlike gold or jewelry, which can be broken up or melted down, a well-known painting is difficult to turn into quick cash.
Celebrated works such as those by Renoir can rarely be sold openly, Pinna said. Instead, stolen art is more likely to be hidden, used as leverage in ransom attempts or offered privately.
Even when works are recovered, museums can face significant costs linked to investigations, recovery efforts and upgraded security.
The recent thefts have also reignited debate about insurance.
Most major state-backed museums in Western Europe rely on government indemnity schemes rather than commercial cover, but some institutions have begun reassessing the risks, said Filippo Guerrini-Maraldi, a private wealth and fine art insurance specialist at broker Howden Specialty.
"And for the first time, really, in my 40-year career, I've seen art theft now becoming more of a major, major risk. It was always the minor risk," he said.
Insurers are also turning to technology. Beazley is exploring how AI can be used to analyze CCTV footage to identify suspicious behavior in museums and galleries, helping security staff spot threats sooner, said fine art underwriter Dishni Mahendran.
Balancing prioritizing security vs access
For museum directors and cultural officials, the challenge is how to tighten security without cutting collections off from local communities or diminishing the visitor experience.
"Ultimately, museums must remain easy to access," Imbert said. "People should be able to enter without having to pass through 50 security checks."
Julien Volper, a conservator at Belgium's Africa Museum, said particularly vulnerable treasures should only be displayed when adequate security measures are in place.
"I'm not saying that's the ultimate solution, but it seems better than displaying replicas," he said. "We're not at Disneyland."
In August, the Carabinieri recovered the three artworks stolen from the Parma museum from a cardboard box hidden in an apartment. Five Moldovan nationals were arrested in connection with the theft.
Investigators said wiretaps indicated the suspects had unsuccessfully tried to find buyers in Eastern Europe and Russia.
The works have since returned to the museum in what Roffi called a "homecoming party."
"The theft triggered an outpouring of solidarity in Italy and abroad," he said. The museum now has round-the-clock guards funded by a local cheese consortium.
"It was seen not simply as a theft from a museum, but as an attack on art as a shared cultural heritage."

Zelenskyy thanks US over deal for 500 Patriot missiles but warns delivery could take years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:46:21 UTC
16:46:21 KST

Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian missile and drone attacks. The rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.
The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.
Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.
"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's gross ocean product reached 8.5 trillion yuan (about 1.27 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of this year, up 4.9 percent year on year, according to data released by the Ministry of Natural Resources.
The marine economy maintained steady growth, with an improved structure, stronger resilience and growing momentum, moving toward innovative and high-quality development, the ministry said.
In the first three quarters, the country's offshore crude oil output rose 3.5 percent year on year, and the output of seawater aquatic products rose 4.6 percent year on year.
In terms of traditional marine industries, new shipbuilding orders, completed orders and order backlogs rose 98.5 percent, 35 percent and 41.9 percent year on year, respectively; meanwhile, China maintained its lead in global market share. Coastal port cargo throughput and container throughput rose 1.6 percent and 4.7 percent, respectively.
Emerging marine industries improved in both quality and efficiency. In particular, the value of new orders for marine engineering equipment surged 123.3 percent year on year, accounting for more than 80 percent of the global market.
The seawater desalination and comprehensive utilization industry made new progress, with the combined capacity of newly launched desalination projects this year exceeding 520,000 tonnes per day.
China's marine tourism maintained stable growth in the first three quarters, the ministry said.
Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said marine tourism is characterized by strong experiential attributes, high technological content, and extensive industry linkages. "Diversifying the Canon to Recover Humanity’s Past: The Case of Pre-colonial Andean": An Essay by Jorge Sanchez-Perez (Keywords: Erasure; Colonialism;Epistemic injustice;Indigenous Epistemologies)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:40:07 UTC
16:40:07 KST

"Diversifying the Canon to Recover Humanity’s Past: The Case of Pre-colonial Andean": An Essay by Jorge Sanchez-Perez (Keywords: Erasure; Colonialism;Epistemic injustice;Indigenous Epistemologies)
From The Philosopher, vol. 114, no. 2 ("Autumn 2026")
You can purchase a physical copy here and a digital copy of this issue and all previous issues here. If you enjoy reading this, please consider becoming a patron or making a small donation. We are unfunded and your support is greatly appreciated.
‘Avila needed the information for indoctrination and
to choose the way to extirpate idolatries.
Who and which were the gods of Huarochirí?
How were they worshipped? When and where?
Everything is spelled out in the manuscript.’
- José María Arguedas
Introduction to Dioses y Hombres de Huarochirí
A brief walk among some of the most prestigious universities in the world will allow anybody to see that demands to expand the philosophical canon beyond Western perspectives have become quite common. This demand – mostly led by students, I have to point out – has created two clear sides in the academic community. On the one hand, we have the large number of academic philosophers who claim to be on board with such an idea, on the other, we have the set of common suspects who claim that something cannot be properly conceived as philosophy unless it is somehow related to European men. For example, it was not too long ago that a reviewer suggested one of my papers be rejected because it made them uncomfortable to engage with philosophical work that does not exclude Indigenous views from philosophy from the beginning. This debate, of course, presupposes that the canon has been somehow limited and shaped by certain perspectives in what the former side might consider unfair ways, and what the latter side might consider consistent with philosophical traditions extending all the way back to Socrates. The presupposition that there might be an unfairness attached to this reality, as many can imagine, does not seem to be far off. Yet for all its rhetorical appeal, if demands to diversify the canon are meant to support real change, first they need some theoretical justification, and second, some awareness of the methodological challenges involved in this demand. I will address both points here, focusing on the colonisation of the Americas as an example of how political structures and actors at different levels develop certain views that end up affecting how something like the philosophical canon looks and what challenges arise when trying to correct that.
A good way to provide theoretical justification to the demand to diversify the canon can come from looking into the work of Peruvian sociologist Anibal Quijano. Throughout his lifetime, Quijano developed an approach known as the colonial matrix of power. This approach can be used to understand colonization, an important historical phenomenon that has shaped the last five hundred years on the planet, in a more comprehensive way. A key element this framework posits is that assuming colonisation as a one-off event is not conducive to understanding the phenomenon. Instead, we are invited to think of colonisation as a set of relations that, even if traced back to an original important historical event, still endure through time and shape different aspects of a society hundreds of years later. As an example of this, we can think of Alexander the Great’s actions in the 4th century BCE, and how they shaped Europe and Asia in a way that would make the Roman Empire possible centuries later. Similarly, we could think of how Tupac Inca Yupanqui, in the 15th century CE, unified South American trading routes in a way that a couple of centuries later would allow the Spanish Empire to control the whole Andean region.
To conceive of a reality where the effects of colonialism are no longer present would be short-sighted.
As those two examples show, although we can study some historical events alone, to conceive of them as detached from other elements would be rather naïve. In the same vein, consider European colonisation, a process which between the 16th and 20th centuries led Europeans to control about 80% of the planet. To conceive of a reality where the effects of colonialism are no longer present would be short-sighted. Another implication of the use of the colonial matrix of power as a framework is that it becomes obvious that certain ways of thinking or certain ideas have indeed been preferred over others due to the role that knowledge plays in the shaping of political projects. Knowledge production, selection, and dissemination are all elements that the colonial matrix of power invites us to reflect upon. Thus, it should not come as a surprise that political projects, such as the one known as the colonisation of the Americas, had epistemic goals or constraints attached to them. Staying with the two examples I provided above, denying that Alexander the Great had a massive impact on the Hellenisation of Europe and other parts of the world, or that Tupac Inca Yupanqui had a role in the expansion of Quechua as the dominant language and culture in South America, would be very hard to defend. Those who think that events that took place in Greece over two thousand years ago can shape the life of contemporary Europe, but events that took place only five hundred years ago in the Americas cannot shape it to this day, can be rightfully called out for suffering from a very clear case of cognitive dissonance.
If we follow that kind of reasoning, a demand to expand the philosophical canon could be framed also as a demand to understand which political choices were made in light of colonial relations of power, and how those choices could have led to the current state of affairs of the set of ideas usually referred to as the philosophical canon. That is, which ideas or ways of thinking were deemed as useful for the different political projects of colonization, and which were deemed as problematic or dangerous. By approaching the topic in this way, it becomes much more obvious that certain ways of engaging with questions around race, gender, class, nature, reality, and so on, benefited certain goals. This approach provides a very plausible explanation of why the canon looks the way it does today.
For the purposes of this essay, I want to focus on the case of the colonisation of the Andean region of South America, and particularly on pre-colonial Andean Philosophy. I consider the relative global lack of awareness of pre-colonial Andean Philosophy a core example of how the colonial matrix of power can be useful to understand how some gaps in the current canon can be explained. To make sense of this, one must first be aware of the existence of the four Alexandrine Bulls, issued in 1493 by Rodrigo Borgia, also known as Pope Alexander VI. They were titled, in order: Inter caetera, Inter caetera II, Eximiae devotionis, and Dudum siquidem. Together, these documents granted the monarchs of Spain and Portugal dominion over large parts of the Americas. The theoretical and legal position that was developed from these documents, among others, would later be known as the infamous Doctrine of Discovery. Under the doctrine of discovery, the kings of Spain and Portugal could claim any discovered land, within certain geographical boundaries, as long as such lands were not ruled by a Christian prince. In practice, this doctrine became the ultimate justification for European colonialism across the planet.
To say that Andean philosophical knowledge was simply sidestepped would be wrong.
As an important sidenote, despite what some readers might think, this doctrine was not explicitly rejected by the Catholic Church until the spring of 2023. Pope Francis rejected it only after his 2022 trip to Canada, where he visited to apologized personally for the historical and contemporary failings of the Catholic Church and its participation in practices such as the implementation and management of the residential school system – a system that effectively promoted the genocide of Indigenous peoples in the country for over a hundred years. While on the trip, Indigenous leaders and scholars demanded the explicit renunciation of the doctrine of discovery. This eventually led to the ultimate abjuration of the doctrine. I consider that this case provides us with one of the most interesting examples of how decisions made in the 15th century with the goal of justifying the seizing of Indigenous land and lives, have a lasting impact reaching our days.
Going back to the case under consideration, the right to rule these ‘new’ lands came with the obligation to exalt and disseminate the Catholic faith among their inhabitants. In this way, an insidious connection between political and religious goals took place; one in which projects to control and dominate an entire continent were intertwined with epistemic goals. The goals were connected to the elimination of local views that could oppose those projects. Since the Inquisition was meant to deal with members of the Catholic faith, and not those outside the Church, new institutions and practices were developed to deal with Indigenous peoples of the Americas – specifically, to facilitate the elimination of Indigenous views which threatened the claims of the Catholic monarchs and the Church. Among those new institutions and practices, the example of the Extirpations of Idolatries needs to be considered as central in understanding why we know so little about pre-colonial Andean Philosophy.
Any individual that claimed the title of Extirpator of Idolatries had a mandate to eradicate any religious or cultural view that could oppose the teachings of the Catholic Church. To do this, they would visit a town, communicate their authority, gather information of ‘sacred’ places or items, and then proceed to destroy them. All this while promoting the abjuration of what they considered idolatries. These views, as one can imagine, were usually held by the local knowledge keepers known in Quechua as amautas. In some cases, extreme measures would be used against Indigenous populations. From physical to psychological violence, extirpators were granted a large degree of autonomy in their pursuit of their goals. These practices took place in the span of three centuries and were, sadly, quite successful. I say successful, because they managed to effectively eradicate large swaths of knowledge that Andean civilisation had carefully accumulated for over five thousand years. Yes, in less than three hundred years, most of the knowledge that had been kept since civilisation started in that part of the world was eradicated. The reason? It was deemed as a threat to the dominant views from both the Catholic Church and the European empires.
Views about time, space, nature, gender, nature, etc., were hunted and eliminated to such a degree that discussions in most philosophical academic circles are either extremely hard or impossible to come by. To say that Andean philosophical knowledge was simply sidestepped would be wrong. At this time, we simply lack the resources to even engage with it in meaningful ways, and that, as I showed before, is by design. A colonial project was implemented in that part of the world and those in command of that project deemed certain ways of knowing the world as competition and as such, those ways had to be eliminated. This is, probably, one of the best examples of how by using the colonial matrix of power we can provide an explanation, in terms of relationships of domination and political goals, of why certain philosophical traditions simply are not part of the canon. With this reality in mind, I want to address my second point: the methodological challenges that diversifying the canon would entail.
It is not uncommon to find the usual suspects who claim that unless something is somehow related to European men, it cannot be properly conceived as philosophy.
Continuing with my example of pre-colonial Andean Philosophy, I want to focus on what demands to diversify the canon would imply. As I mentioned before, most resources that could have informed any discussion of what pre-colonial Andean Philosophy would look like, as well as the views we can attribute to different groups within that part of the world, were actively destroyed. If that is the case, then how can diversification happen? What would it entail to try to diversify the canon by including something like pre-colonial Andean Philosophy? The answer to both questions is simply more work than what many individuals might assume.
My own research is focused on trying to reconstruct pre-colonial Andean philosophy from two sources. The first one is the Huarochirí Manuscript, and the second is a set of legal cases from the 17th and 18th centuries against Indigenous people of the Andes for the crime of idolatry. The first source is, without a doubt, the most important Andean document in existence. This is a manuscript compiled in secret by Choquecasa, a local Indigenous nobleman, at the bequest of the priest Francisco de Ávila, one of the most successful extirpators of his time. In this manuscript, Choquecasa, most likely due to his position as a member of Quechua nobility, was able to secretly record creation stories, practices, and foundational myths of the central Andes region from amautas. Later on, the manuscript was used by de Avila to effectively identify which ideas, places, and individuals had to be eliminated. The manuscript, written in Quechua, was neglected for centuries after the death of de Avila and left in the archives of the Library of Madrid. Luckily for all of us, by the 1930s, Hermann Trimborn, a German expert on American Indigenous cultures, would approach the manuscript with working knowledge of Quechua and properly appreciate its relevance.
While the Huarochirí Manuscript contains a host of wonderful philosophical insights about time, space, nature, human-animal relationships, and more, I also thought it would be useful to rely on alternative sources. For that reason, I engaged with a set of legal cases from the 17th and 18th centuries that are hosted in the archives of the Archbishop of Lima. In those cases, charges of idolatry and sorcery are leveled against Indigenous people. While interesting from a purely historical perspective, the description of the crimes also serves as a relevant tool to put together practices regarding nature, medicine, agriculture, etc., which also show several philosophical views that underlie many of those practices.
I will explain some of the methodological challenges that are connected to working with these sources. First, it is important to be aware of the lack of access to regular philosophical sources like philosophy texts. As I mentioned at the beginning of this essay, it is not uncommon to find the usual suspects who claim that unless something is somehow related to European men, it cannot be properly conceived as philosophy. If we add the reality that the sources people like myself are relying on do not look like the kind of philosophical texts that are common in the Western philosophical canon, then the chances of having one’s work discarded increase as well. For my research, I rely on what philosopher James Maffie, an expert on Mesoamerican pre-colonial thought, calls triangulation, a way of finding philosophically relevant information from sources that do not resemble philosophical texts. This kind of work, however, allows for the challenge of how something like an Indigenous story could count as a philosophical source to be raised. Although I have published on this topic and developed a whole account about how philosophical sources can be identified, these kinds of methodological challenges are not rare and keep happening at every corner.
I am convinced that humanity’s future can benefit from learning from humanity’s past.
Second, it is also important to notice that many of those sources are not going to be written in English, the lingua franca of our times. So, access to “diverse” sources gets even more complex. The number of philosophy PhD holders with training in Indigenous philosophical methodologies is extremely limited, and the number of those who can work on or with an Indigenous language is also quite small. To that, we have to add the difficulties attached to accessing sources like the ones I mentioned above. What I have in mind, based on my personal experience, is the challenge of properly learning palaeography–that is, learning how to read ancient handwritten texts. Finally, and insofar as sometimes those texts are not digitised, accessing those sources involves traveling to the archives in different parts of the world.
None of the points I have raised should be understood as a rejection of the demand to diversify the canon. On the contrary, I am part of the movement of academic philosophers who actively seeks to see this demand come to fruition. I am convinced that humanity’s future can benefit from learning from humanity’s past. If we fail to put the pieces of the worldviews of our predecessors together, we might be limiting our potential to understand how to do better. The drastic loss of much Andean thought is but an example of this sad reality that we need to revert. However, I also think that we need to understand that this demand cannot be materialised unless first, we are able to make sense of why the canon might look how it does nowadays, and second, we are aware of the difficulties that diversification entails. If academic philosophers are serious about this kind of project, and I know many are, we need to do better than provide rhetorical moves and start thinking in terms that address the theoretical and methodological demands that real diversification would demand.
Jorge Sanchez-Perez is an associate professor in the University of Alberta’s Department of Philosophy. He is an academic philosopher and a trained lawyer whose research interests include social epistemology, Indigenous philosophy, early modern philosophy, and moral and legal philosophy. He is the lead researcher of the SSHRC funded project “The Indigenous Stories of Philosophy.” His first manuscript, "Indigeneity and the Mestizo Question: The Limits of Latin American Philosophy," is forthcoming in 2027. He has published in the fields of Indigenous philosophical methodologies, meta philosophical issues surrounding Latin American Philosophy, race in Early Modern Philosophy, the nature of law, and Global Justice.

Speaking in the First Iran-Africa Agricultural Cooperation meeting held in Tehran on Saturday, Iran’s Minister of Agriculture Gholamreza Nouri-Ghezeljeh stated that the $940 million worth of trade with lucrative African countries’ market is insignificant that should be developed to a great extent.
Iran and African countries have high potentials to increase and enhance their trade exchanges to a great extent and this issue must be taken into serious consideration, the minister stressed.
Emphasizing the need for a paradigm shift in economic relations, he called for the transformation of political commitments into operational projects and joint investments.
Pointing to the potential capacities of both sides, Nouri Ghezeljeh emphasized that Iran sees Africa not merely as a sales market, but as a strategic partner in production and development.
Elsewhere in his remarks, the Iranian minister of agriculture pointed to the complementary capabilities of Iran and Africa, highlighting Iran’s strengths in areas such as irrigation management, greenhouse construction, agricultural machinery, seed production, livestock and poultry farming, vaccines, and agro-processing industries/
He emphasized Africa’s immense potential regarding tropical products, fisheries, and its growing markets.
The minister also said Iran has already held technical training courses for delegations from countries such as Ghana and Senegal and had pursued economic cooperation mechanisms with Ghana, Senegal, Tanzania and Kenya. He called for greater involvement of the private sector, saying governments should facilitate cooperation while businesses take the lead in implementing joint projects.

What is the situation with electricity in Kyiv and Dnipro - morning update
Kyiv • UNN
In Kyiv, water supply has resumed normal operations after three strikes. In the Dnipropetrovsk region, two DTEK facilities were damaged, and there are extensive power outages.
Russia continues its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, and as of the morning of October 31, there are updates on the situation in Kyiv and Dnipro, reported by the capital’s mayor Vitali Klitschko and DTEK, UNN writes.
Kyiv
Energy workers and utility services worked throughout the night to eliminate the emergency situation that arose after three strikes hit one of the capital’s critical infrastructure facilities yesterday evening. At present, the water supply and wastewater systems are operating normally
On the evening of October 30, as a result of an enemy attack on energy infrastructure, some consumers in parts of Kyiv and the region were left without electricity, the Ministry of Energy reported .
DTEK reported overnight on October 31 that, due to the attack and damage to energy equipment, parts of Kyiv’s Obolonskyi, Darnytskyi, Desnianskyi, and Podilskyi districts were without electricity.
As of the morning of October 31, the DTEK Kyiv Electrical Networks website states that "by order of NEC Ukrenergo, stabilization power outages are in effect on October 31."
As for the Kyiv region, as of the morning of October 31, the DTEK Kyiv Regional Electrical Networks website reported that, due to ongoing attacks and equipment damage, electricity supplies were unavailable in the Buchanskyi, Obukhivskyi, and Fastivskyi districts. Schedules are not in effect here.
Dnipro
Dnipropetrovsk region: the enemy attacked energy facilities again. Energy equipment was seriously damaged in new attacks overnight. In particular, two facilities of DTEK Dnipro Electrical Networks were damaged. One of them was the facility where energy workers had spent nearly two days working on restoration. A significant part of Dnipro and Kamianske, as well as residents of the Dnipro and Novomoskovsk districts, remain without electricity
Energy workers throughout the region, the company noted, continue working at the damaged facilities as far as the security situation allows. "We are doing everything possible to restore electricity to homes as quickly as possible," DTEK said.
"More than a day of uninterrupted work—and energy workers restored electricity to most consumers who had been disconnected due to the massive Russian attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region. More than 200,000 subscribers in the Dnipro, Kamianske, and Novomoskovsk districts still remain without electricity. Repeated enemy strikes on energy infrastructure are complicating restoration efforts and causing new outages. Despite this, the crews continue to work," Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration, added on social media on October 31.

Kangaroos top Rugby League World Cup Pool A with 66-6 win over Cook Islands
The Kangaroos finished the group stage of the Rugby League World Cup undefeated, closing out the Pool A action with a 66-6 win over Cook Islands in Townsville.
On a sweaty night up north, the Australian men were below their best to start and briefly trailed the Islanders 6-4 before asserting their dominance with 10 unanswered tries.
Wingers Tom Trbojevic and Jack Bostock both finished with hat-tricks while Tino Fa'saumaleaui grabbed a double.
Fullback Reece Walsh was named player of the match after a try, five assists and a pair of line breaks, but his fitness is somewhat concerning.
Walsh grabbed at his foot after converting Kotoni Staggs's 27th-minute try and, despite looking untroubled while finishing off a spectacular team try on the half-hour mark, handed over goal-kicking duties.
Cameron Munster kicked goals for the rest of the game and Walsh closed out an impressive performance that will likely quiet calls for him to be replaced by James Tedesco.
The Kangaroos will play their semifinal on Sunday, November 8 at the Sydney Football Stadium, but their opponent will not be known until after the clash between Tonga and Samoa tomorrow night.

Funding deadlock derails global effort to save nature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:35:24 UTC
16:35:24 KST

Astrid Schomaker, Hambardzum Matevosyan, António Guterre, and Inger Andersen in Yerevan, Armenia on Oct. 15, 2026. | Karen Minasyan/AFP via Getty Images
YEREVAN, Armenia — Scorching wildfires, disastrous floods and the looming mass extinction of species weren’t enough to convince wealthy nations to unlock crucial funds needed to halt biodiversity loss at a global nature summit this week.
As countries around the world race against the clock to protect what’s left of the Earth’s collapsing ecosystems, global talks aimed at speeding up nature protection efforts yielded underwhelming results.
The United Nations COP17 on biodiversity ended on Saturday with a renewed promise from countries to speed up global efforts to protect nature and restore depleted ecosystems by 2030.
Advertisement
But behind that grand gesture, governments are still struggling to unlock the hundreds of billions needed to meet global biodiversity protection targets. The reason? A profound and unresolved disagreement over where that money should come from.
“If we’re mutually unhappy that’s probably the closest we can get to on these very delicate compromises,” said a member of the Swiss delegation just before the text was adopted.
After two weeks of negotiations over how to speed up efforts to protect ecosystems, nearly 200 countries secured a hard-fought agreement to "accelerate the implementation" of the global biodiversity framework "including by increased ambition in addressing the gaps, challenges and barriers related to implementation," according to a draft of the text, the final version of which was not immediately available.
Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan, who presided over the summit, said negotiators had "achieved more than we could have expected."
But in the end, governments could not agree on how to increase the number of countries currently contributing to biodiversity finance, instead only stating the obvious: that more funds would be better.
The summit exposed a growing chasm between nations over who should be held financially responsible for funding conservation measures worldwide: historically wealthy countries whose economies have caused immense damage to the environment, or newly rich states whose economies have grown exponentially in the last three decades.
Advertisement
“This COP was always going to be difficult," said Steven Guilbeault, former environment minister for Canada, adding that "COP17's real legacy will be decided far beyond these walls, when words need to translate to action."
Negotiators are leaving Yerevan with many issues left to resolve between now and the next COP in 2028 in Ecuador, including on how to attract more companies that benefit from nature to fund conservation projects via the Cali Fund, a landmark vehicle aimed at mobilizing private finance into nature established in 2024.
Governments know they are running out of time. At COP17, scientific experts reiterated that a million species are at risk of extinction, and the U.N. has identified an annual biodiversity financing gap of $700 billion.
A cleared forest slope with uprooted tree stumps, disturbed soil and construction machinery in Chablais, France on Oct. 27, 2026. | Guillaume Lambin/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
“We're not on track to stop and reverse the biodiversity loss by 2030,” said Monique Barbut, France’s environment minister, during a COP17 plenary session on Wednesday. The world needs to “mobilize all international funding sources” to make it happen, she insisted.
The talks also ran long due to disagreements over language related to the involvement of Indigenous peoples in a key decision-making body of the Convention.
The dispute
The U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity relies on the consensus that rich countries should pay more to protect nature because of the pressure their societies and economies exert on global ecosystems.
Advertisement
Since its ratification in the 1990s, a group of wealthy countries including Canada, Australia, Japan, the U.K., Switzerland, Norway and some EU members have been funding efforts to implement the Convention.
Now, those countries want other high-income nations to chip in more. “We all know that we need more resources to ensure the effective implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework,” said Jessika Roswall, the EU’s environment commissioner.
But during the negotiations, non-donor countries — which include China, Saudi Arabia, Russia and Argentina — pushed back against any kind of income-related criteria to determine who should or shouldn’t be paying.
The deadlock angered some nations set to benefit from a larger donor base. “Are you telling me that rich petro-states who are in many cases wealthier than some of the original list of donors and responsible for a ton of emissions and harmful practices that directly affect biodiversity shouldn't contribute to the fund?” said Juan Carlos Navarro, Environment Minister for Panama on Wednesday, as negotiations were ongoing.
The countries “don't want to have the same obligations as developed countries on this issue [and] bring up the argument of ecological responsibilities,” said Juliette Landry, a senior research fellow at the think tank IDDRI.
In the end, countries agreed simply to state that "contributions from more Parties would improve the mobilization of biodiversity finance" and invited others to contribute voluntarily, the draft text shows.
Some successes
Despite the divisions, many hailed the final agreement as a win for green multilateralism as governments remain committed to the overarching goal of protecting 30% of Earth’s land and sea areas and increase financing for biodiversity to $200 billion annually by 2030.
Advertisement
“In Yerevan, we saw environmental multilateralism prevail once again. Countries came together, found the spirit of compromise and allowed us to agree important decisions that will support real progress for people and for planet,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UN Environment Programme.
After two weeks of endless meetings, panels and plenary sessions, negotiators agreed to strengthen the role of cities and local governments in implementing biodiversity goals, and improve how biodiversity funding reaches them. They also adopted decisions to support capacity-building and scientific cooperation, and agreed that more needs to be done to protect marine ecosystems.
The Bobonaza River next to the village of Sarayaku, Ecuador on May 22, 2025. | Rodrigo Buendia/AFP via Getty Images
Countries also recognized the need to reduce subsidies funding economic activities that harm nature and create incentives for activities that protect it. "Incentive reform has moved from the margins to the mainstream of the biodiversity agenda," said Eva zabey, CEO of the Business for Nature coalition.
Some governments including Germany, Iceland, Uzbekistan and Spain made fresh financial commitments totalling $1.8 billion to the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund and the Global Environment Facility, the funding structures set up to implement the Convention. Under the GBF, countries have pledged to mobilize $200 billion annually by 2030.
The U.N. Environment Programme also published a report showing that nature restoration is underway at an “unprecedented scale” with over 250 million hectares of land under restoration worldwide.
Still, countries remain off track on meeting their 2030 targets.
Advertisement
In Yerevan, green groups welcomed the agreement but criticized its lack of ambition key issues.
"Political promises made in Yerevan set good intentions, but won’t remove major roadblocks to implementation such as insufficient finance, fiscal and debt constraints, the nearly empty coffers of the Cali Fund and urgent reform of harmful subsidies," said An Lambrechts, a biodiversity politics expert with Greenpeace International.
Governments have struggled to stay the course since inking the Global Biodiversity Framework in 2022. Though many countries have adopted national biodiversity strategies, financial flows to conservation projects are nowhere near where they ought to be. Geopolitical shifts and economic crises have also made it harder for governments — including the 27 EU member countries — to prioritize environmental protection.
Countries agreed to renew talks to implement the objectives of the convention in Ecuador.

Is Estonia about to have a surplus of IT specialists?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:33:00 UTC
16:33:00 KST

Is Estonia about to have a surplus of IT specialists?
For years, Estonia has talked about a shortage of programmers and IT workers, but after a huge wave of layoffs this week, is there about to be a surplus instead?
One of Estonia's success stories, Pipedrive, announced on Thursday that most of the people working at the company would lose their jobs. However, the changes brought about by artificial intelligence in the labor market are only just beginning.
Microsoft recently offered voluntary severance packages to around 60,000 employees to cover the costs of AI and data centers. Amazon has cut around 30,000 office jobs in a year, while social media giant Meta has laid off 10 percent of its employees. The International Monetary Fund warned that AI would affect around 40 percent of jobs.
Telia, located next door to Pipedrive, recently announced the elimination of 100 jobs. Business is changing and AI is doing more and more.
"If I had to be an oracle, I would rather think that we will be able to do the same work with increasingly fewer people," said Telia CEO Andre Visse.
Young people have been hit hardest by the change. In Estonia, employment among under-25s working in IT has fallen by nearly a quarter in three years.
"Obviously, we are seeing these changes here, and it is considerably more difficult for young people to enter the labor market today than it perhaps was three years ago," said Urve Mets, head of research at OSKA.
However, Sergei Anikin, who years ago grew Pipedrive's engineering department from 10 people to more than 400, believes that young people are flexible and adopt new ways of working more quickly.
"If I compare young people who had no baggage with someone who, for example, has a stable job, a family and a mortgage, and then suddenly realizes that their skills are no longer actually needed because there is a machine that can do their work better and hundreds of times faster, then I think those people will find it considerably harder to cope with this situation," Anikin said.
Could Estonia soon find itself in a situation where there is no longer a shortage of programmers, but rather a surplus?
"If around 400-500 people are laid off from the sector at once, then that will certainly have an impact on the structure of the workforce, and unemployed people will appear on the market for some time. But I think that will correct itself quite quickly," Visse said.
One distinctive feature of Estonia is that IT specialists are concentrated narrowly in the IT sector, Visse said. AI could change that.
"There is actually quite considerable room for development in bringing more technologically knowledgeable, IT-savvy workers into other sectors and helping us digitalize the entire economy and automate these processes more quickly," Visse said.
There will also be high demand for technology skills in the future, but simply writing code will no longer be enough, Mets said.
"IT knowledge alone is not enough, meaning that every young person could think a little about whether, for example, they see their future work as being more connected to technology in the medical field or perhaps in the industrial sector," Mets said.
Whereas good ideas previously went unrealized because there were not enough people to implement them, AI has eliminated that bottleneck, Anikin said.
"We joke here that no stupid idea will go unrealized, so what will actually become important is the ability to distinguish stupid ideas from good ones," Anikin said.

Almost 400 migrants have been detained by the police since July in Estonia after a surge in illegal crossings at the Latvian-Belarusian border. Scam centres relocated from Cambodia operate in Madagascar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Scam centres relocated from Cambodia operate in Madagascar
ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar – Raids against online scam centres in Madagascar have exposed ties with a criminal group that ran similar operations in Cambodia, also duping African nationals via alleged human trafficking, the authorities told AFP.
Conducting romance, cryptocurrency and investment fraud, the sites were operated mostly by Chinese nationals, 148 of whom have been extradited to China, Madagascar’s Justice Ministry said.
Thirteen Chinese-run scam compounds were taken down in operations in August and September conducted with the US Department of Justice (DOJ), it said.
About US$52 million (S$66.6 million) of cryptocurrency was seized in a single day and more than 3,200 electronic devices were processed, the US authority said in a statement.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime had warned in 2025 about the expansion of these networks, particularly into Southern Africa.
Eleven Chinese nationals arrested separately in the online scam crackdown mysteriously walked free from a Madagascar jail in August in a widely publicised scandal allegedly implicating the head of the prison service.
Several African nationals remained in custody, even though initial findings suggested they may have been victims of human trafficking, officials said.
Recruited via social media
As in scam operations in South-east Asia, the Madagascar centres allegedly lured Africans to the Indian Ocean island via social media and with promises of salaries.
In this case, around 20 nationals of Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Zimbabwe were in custody, the authorities said.
“According to their statements, they were recruited via Facebook to come work in Madagascar in the commercial sector,” the police crime unit chief Hassan Mouigni told AFP.
“But when they arrived here, most of the passports were confiscated by the boss and they were forced to scam,” he said. “They were victims of deception.”
The man charged with running one romance scam scheme was a Malaysian national, identified as Chui Kok Wa, who had installed himself in a villa in the upscale Ivato neighbourhood near the capital, Antananarivo, the US authorities said.
“From the visa in his passport, we were able to deduce that he arrived here for the first time in 2024. According to the passport, he was previously in Cambodia,” Mouigni said.
The DOJ said it believed his “criminal group with connections to Malaysia and China opened scam compounds in Madagascar in early 2025, likely having moved those operations from Cambodia after law enforcement action in that country”.
The coordinator of the cybercrime unit at Madagascar’s Communications Ministry, Tsitohaina Ralihivao, drew a connection with a 2025 crackdown on scam compounds in Cambodia near the border with Thailand, when their militaries also clashed.
“When the Thais dismantled them, they just relocated the operations. The same organisations came to Madagascar,” Ralihivao told AFP.
Relocating
An FBI court document shared by the DOJ drew a similar conclusion after questioning three Brazilian nationals who worked at a scam compound in Antananarivo.
“These individuals reported that they originally responded to work opportunities posted online, and ended up working at a compound located in Cambodia.
“Later, in part due to an armed conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, and also in response to police activity in Cambodia related to scam compounds, the witnesses were moved to Antananarivo, Madagascar, in early May 2026,” it said.
“Cyber scam centres are increasingly opening in Africa following the closure of such compounds in South-east Asia,” the FBI said.
The US authorities intervened because these centres “primarily targeted English-speaking countries”, including the United States, Canada and Pakistan, Mouigni said.
Hence the “need for nationals from English-speaking African countries”, added Ralihivao.
The arrival of scam centres has not gone unnoticed in the capital of Madagascar.
“Before they occupied villas that were a little discreet. What alerted us was that they started renting entire hotels,” Mouigni said.
The suspected head of one compound installed at the Live Hotel in the city was a Chinese national who was among those extradited to Beijing.
Like all “Chinese nationals identified as leaders”, he could not be questioned by the FBI, a US federal police said in court documents. AFP

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT Taipei mayoral candidate Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) and his DPP counterpart Puma Shen (沈伯洋) faced off over housing, childcare, and education in their televised debate Saturday.
CNA reported that the debate, hosted by TVBS and SET News, came ahead of the Nov. 28 mayoral election. Chiang is seeking a second four-year term, while Shen hopes to end KMT rule in the capital.
Chiang cited the opening of the Taipei Dome sports stadium, plans for Nvidia's overseas headquarters in Taipei, and higher birth grants as key achievements. He accused Shen of making promises without clear plans to carry them out.
Shen said voters should judge the candidates on their policies rather than who won the debate. He pledged to plant more trees, tackle child abuse, and improve school meals during his first 100 days in office.

Chiang said his administration had made progress on several long-delayed urban renewal projects, claiming the number of projects had risen to 2.4 times the previous level. Shen questioned whether the figures showed real progress, arguing that approvals meant little if projects had yet to start or finish construction.
Chiang accused Shen of failing to understand the height limits near Songshan Airport, which restrict how tall nearby buildings can be for flight safety. Shen said the city should explain such rules to residents early and help them work through obstacles to rebuilding.
Childcare was another point of dispute, with Chiang questioning whether Shen could find enough carers to provide four hours of free temporary childcare each week for children under 6. The service would allow parents to leave their children with trained carers for short periods.
Shen said the plan would begin with children under 2 and expand as more staff and childcare places became available. Chiang questioned whether the city could recruit enough carers to meet demand.
The candidates also disagreed over Shen's plan to assign two teachers to each elementary school class to share teaching duties. Chiang cited an existing teacher shortage, while Shen said the scheme could first be tested in selected grades, drawing on a similar program at a school in neighboring New Taipei.
School meals also drew attention, with Chiang highlighting free lunches and milk as ways to ease costs for families. Shen proposed raising meal funding in line with food prices and giving parents the option to pay more for higher-quality meals.
On transport, Chiang pointed to efforts to ease traffic, including the removal of the Gongguan traffic circle, a busy roundabout in southern Taipei. Shen said residents still faced damaged sidewalks and unsafe cycling routes, arguing the city needed to do more to make streets safer.
The debate was the first direct televised meeting between the two candidates after weeks of talks over its date and format. Both camps agreed to let the candidates question each other, giving voters a chance to compare their plans before the election.
