Beijing’s Taiwan blockade playbook gets test run in Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:24:34 UTC
16:24:34 KST

Pakistan reportedly barred Taiwanese airlines from its airspace on Oct. 25, forcing China Airlines and EVA Air to reroute Europe-bound flights. However, the restriction was reversed three days later, with Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority restoring overflight permissions through March 2027.
Although short-lived, the episode offered Beijing a potential real-world test of how an incremental, legally framed blockade could disrupt Taiwan’s international connectivity and how quickly other countries would respond.
Pakistan’s apparent willingness to risk diplomatic and commercial friction over Taiwan reflects its economic dependence on China. Facing persistent foreign exchange shortages, a heavy debt burden and repeated reliance on International Monetary Fund assistance, Islamabad regards Beijing as a crucial financial backer. China has repeatedly rolled over loans to help the country avoid default.
The political alignment was underscored when Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong in Islamabad to advance the second phase of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) on the day the reported airspace restriction began. Defense Minister Khawaja Asif subsequently confirmed that Pakistan followed a “one-China” policy.
On Oct. 26, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning traveled to Islamabad for the third Pakistan-China Spokespersons’ Dialogue, where she joined Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar in launching the China-Pakistan Information Corridor. Tarar reportedly said: “If CPEC connects our economies, the Information Corridor will connect our minds.”
Administered through the External Publicity Wing Secretariat of Pakistan’s Ministry of Information, the initiative is intended to deepen digital, media and economic cooperation. Its proposed activities include a trade portal to promote Chinese investment in 5G and artificial intelligence, a media coalition involving 18 organizations, including Xinhua, and a northern tourism corridor intended to attract Chinese visitors and foreign exchange.
A coordinated media network could help counter criticism of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, including allegations of debt dependency. Meanwhile, the corridor’s supporters have an interest in protecting a project that has attracted tens of billions of dollars in Chinese capital.
Salami-slicing the skies
The Pakistan episode can be viewed as part of a broader pattern of pressure on Taiwan’s international mobility. It offers Beijing an opportunity to assess the consequences of restricting commercial aviation without directly initiating a military confrontation.
The dispute over the M503 flight route illustrates the longer-running pressure. In February 2024, China’s Civil Aviation Administration unilaterally scrapped flight-offset measures for routes near the Taiwan Strait, increasing concerns in Taipei about aircraft operating closer to the median line and potentially reducing its air defense early-warning time.
A second example came earlier this year when President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) faced difficulties arranging overflight clearances for a planned state visit to Eswatini. Taiwan blamed Chinese pressure after several African countries withdrew permissions. Lai eventually traveled to Eswatini in May, following a complicated route across the southern Indian Ocean.
The Pakistan episode potentially took the strategy a step further by targeting commercial aviation networks rather than presidential travel. Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) said China had learned that restricting access to foreign airspace could be an effective way to limit Taiwan’s international connectivity.
For Beijing, the incident offered an opportunity to observe how quickly Taiwan’s diplomatic partners would intervene, what pressure they could bring to bear on Islamabad and whether a temporary restriction could achieve its objectives before an international response gathered momentum.
Legal and systemic fallout
The episode also raises questions about the separation of international aviation from political disputes. Pakistan’s reported decision to condition overflight access on adherence to the “one-China” policy risks undermining the predictable and nondiscriminatory application of international aviation rules.
The Chicago Convention establishes the framework for international civil aviation, while the International Air Services Transit Agreement provides for certain overflight rights among participating states. Using political recognition as a condition for commercial aviation access could weaken confidence in these arrangements.
The restoration of permissions through the International Air Transport Association winter schedule also illustrates how ordinary administrative procedures can become instruments of political pressure. If airlines must repeatedly seek renewed access because of diplomatic disputes, they face uncertainty over routes, costs and operational planning.
Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said the government was coordinating with domestic airlines and relevant agencies to address the situation. The transportation ministry would need to consider flight safety, operating costs and alternative routes if access to foreign airspace became unreliable.
The disruption also exposed the country’s potential dependence on Russian airspace. During the reported restriction, China Airlines and EVA Air rerouted some Europe-bound flights through Russian territory. Taiwanese carriers had generally avoided Russian airspace since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, in line with many Western and Asian airlines.
Such diversions carry financial and strategic risks. Longer routes increase fuel consumption, operating costs and travel times.
They could also leave Taiwanese carriers exposed to political pressure from Moscow, which maintains close relations with Beijing. In a cross-strait crisis, Russia could potentially use its control over its airspace to restrict Taiwanese flights or impose additional conditions on transit.
Also, the episode could have implications elsewhere. If Beijing can persuade a third country to restrict Taiwanese commercial transit, other governments may conclude that similar measures carry limited diplomatic costs. On Thursday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun dismissed international concerns, saying the “one-China” policy represented an international consensus.
Anticipating the contagion
If the international response remains muted, Beijing could seek to persuade other countries to adopt similar restrictions. Cambodia and Laos are particularly exposed because of their economic dependence on China and their participation in Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative.
Their financial relationships with China could give Beijing considerable leverage over foreign policy decisions. The strategic picture is further complicated by China’s growing military presence and influence in the region, including its involvement in facilities in Laos and the development of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base.
The broader diplomatic pattern is also visible in Africa. The African Union endorsed Beijing’s position on Taiwan in the September 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation Beijing Declaration. It reiterated its support for the “one-China” policy during the ninth China-Africa strategic dialogue in Addis Ababa on Jan. 8.
In Central Asia, countries including Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan depend heavily on China for investment, trade and transport connectivity. Their geographic positions could make them important to any effort to restrict Taiwan’s remaining aviation corridors to Europe. Djibouti, which hosts China’s first overseas military base, is another strategically significant country whose position could affect Taiwan’s international access.
The potential implications extend beyond aviation. If Beijing can encourage governments to restrict Taiwanese commercial aircraft from their airspace, it could attempt to apply similar pressure to maritime transport.
Countries hosting Chinese-operated ports, particularly those heavily dependent on Chinese investment, could face pressure to deny access to Taiwanese shipping companies such as Evergreen Marine, Yang Ming and Wan Hai. Restrictions at important ports and maritime bottlenecks in East Africa, Southeast Asia or Central America could disrupt supply chains, increase shipping costs and further isolate Taiwan’s export-dependent economy.
Such a strategy would not necessarily require a formal naval blockade. Administrative restrictions, port access decisions and selective enforcement of regulations could create substantial disruption while allowing Beijing and its partners to argue that they were exercising sovereign authority.
Imposing asymmetric costs
Taiwan cannot easily challenge Pakistan through conventional international institutions because of its exclusion from the UN, the International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Court of Justice. Even so, Chen Ming-chi said several like-minded countries had quietly assisted Taiwan in resolving the airspace dispute.
But diplomatic damage control is not a long-term strategy. Taiwan’s partners need a coordinated diplomatic, financial, economic and legal response designed to deter similar actions before they occur.
The US, Japan and EU members could challenge politically motivated restrictions through diplomatic channels and raise concerns about their compatibility with international civil aviation agreements. Formal complaints would help establish that using commercial overflight rights as a political weapon carries consequences beyond the immediate dispute.
Washington and other Group of Seven members could also consider whether future financial assistance to Islamabad should take account of its willingness to comply with international aviation norms. Pakistan’s dependence on Western-backed financial institutions, including the IMF and World Bank, provides potential leverage, although any conditions would need to be carefully designed and consistent with those institutions’ mandates.
The EU could review Pakistan’s Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus trade status, which provides preferential access to the European market, as part of a broader discussion about compliance with international commitments. The EU should be cautious about linking trade privileges directly to a bilateral aviation dispute, but the issue could form part of a wider assessment of Pakistan’s obligations.
Regional partners can also help reduce Taiwan’s vulnerability by expanding alternative transport links. India, for example, could explore additional direct flights between the two countries, strengthening commercial connections and reducing reliance on routes vulnerable to political interference.
Pakistan’s reported airspace restriction was more than a brief diplomatic dispute. It exposed how Beijing could potentially use political influence over third countries to undermine Taiwan’s international mobility without resorting to military force.
For Taiwan and its democratic partners, the lesson is clear: allowing politically motivated restrictions to pass without a meaningful response could encourage further attempts to constrain access to international air routes, ports and commercial networks. The pressure may begin in the skies, but its consequences could eventually reach the world’s sea lanes and supply chains.

$1,999 iPhone Duo is in spotlight due to cracks appearing just days after release - has Apple responded
Kyiv • UNN
Apple confirmed a screen-cracking issue affecting a small number of iPhone Duo devices. The cause may be pressure from the flexible display on the hinge. Repairs may cost $999.
Apple stores reportedly received an internal memo about cracks in the iPhone Duo's screen. UNN reports this, citing MacRumors.
Details
In an internal memo sent this week to Apple stores and authorized Apple service providers, obtained by MacRumors, Apple provided technicians with instructions on diagnosing and resolving the issue of cracking in the iPhone Duo's inner display.
MacRumors claims that the instructions for technicians are straightforward, but "the fact that Apple published an internal memo indicates that the issue is widespread enough to require official guidance."
iFixit told The Verge that the cracks may occur because the flexible screen presses against part of the hinge.
Apple confirmed this week that there is an "issue" affecting a "small number" of iPhone Duo devices.
As Fortune notes, some owners of the iPhone Duo, which went on sale only on October 23, said that Apple's $1,999 foldable iPhone cracked within hours of being unboxed.
Some early iPhone Duo buyers said that the phone's 7.6-inch inner display cracked along the hinge. On Monday, Apple told CNBC that it was "aware of an issue affecting the inner display of a small number of iPhone Duo devices" and directed affected customers to AppleCare for replacements.
Apple did not immediately say what exactly was causing the cracking or whether a fix was planned, nor did it announce a recall. Affected owners were able to receive replacements at a store, but supplies are limited, so some are waiting.
Once the phone's warranty expires, the math changes. Apple lists the cost of repairing the inner screen at $999, which is half the phone's starting price. This is significantly more than a similar repair for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which cost between $419 and $579, according to an iFixit comparison.
For now, the warranty covers expenses for early buyers. Apple's one-year warranty covers defects arising from normal use, and there is a 14-day return period, Tom's Guide notes.

Taiwan introduces mobile weather radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:24:12 UTC
16:24:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Central Weather Administration said on Friday that it plans to deploy a mobile weather radar in Hualien next year to track rainfall over the barrier lake near Mataian River, CNA reported.
The CWA commissioned the mobile weather platform alongside its fixed radar station for greater visibility. It said the radar's X/Ka frequencies can observe severe weather, such as typhoons and monsoons.
CWA Deputy Administrator Feng Chin-tzu (馮欽賜) said the fixed radar station can see up to 460 kilometers. He added there were six others across the country and noted that mobile radar can overcome terrain restrictions by covering difficult-to-reach places.
Feng said the mobile platform was previously tested at Yunlin’s Hushan Reservoir and will be redeployed to New Taipei’s Wufenshan to monitor winter low-hanging cloud patterns.
CWA Deputy Administrator Hung Ching-shan (洪景山) explained that fixed radars can see raindrops but not clouds. He noted the mobile weather system can use its Ka-wavelength to see cloud and mist droplets as well as crystals within 20 kilometers, while the X-frequency can detect raindrops and winds within 50 kilometers.
Hung said there were no rainfall measurement stations to record severe rain over Mataian and Wanli barrier lakes until earlier this year. He said the CWA would use AI to compile observation data from both radars to fill information gaps.
Hung added that the system will be redeployed to the upper Mataian River around mid-2027 to monitor rainfall over the barrier lake.

India pulls half a billion people out of poverty – faster than China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:22:33 UTC
16:22:33 KST

India pulls half a billion people out of poverty – faster than China
India has pulled nearly half a billion people out of poverty in little more than a decade, the World Bank has said. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government introduced a number of highly effective policies to help channel the benefits of the country’s rapid economic growth to the poor.
The feat is particularly impressive given that its population continued to grow during this period. It is now the most populous country on Earth, having overtaken China in 2023, and achieved poverty reduction much faster than its northern neighbor.
An estimated 496 million Indians were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, according to the World Bank’s October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief.
The number of people living in extreme poverty, with an average income of $3 or less per day – declined from 27.1% of the population to as low as 2.6% during the period.
The proportion of Indians living below the lower-middle-income poverty threshold of $4.20 per day, measured at 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP), declined from 57.7% in 2011 to 16.1% in 2023.
A 2022 report, jointly produced by the World Bank and the Chinese Finance Ministry, showed that China had lifted 800 million people out of poverty, although it took four decades to do it. Beijing kickstarted its economic reforms in 1978 and the cited poverty reduction figures are from 2020.
It is not exactly an apples-to-apples comparison, but serves to show New Delhi’s remarkable achievement as India is a much smaller economy. China’s $20.85 trillion economy is now the world’s second-largest, while the Indian economy measures only about a fifth of that, at $4.5 trillion.
Increased employment, particularly among women, and expanded food subsidies and other social benefits boosted consumption growth, which played a key role in India’s achievement.
For much of the period when poverty rates were sharply declining, Modi led the country, having become prime minister in May 2014. His signature policy measure – direct benefit transfers – ensured the money from the government actually reached the bank accounts of the poor, rather than being siphoned off through various intermediaries.
The rapid economic growth under Modi’s stewardship also helped keep job generation far ahead of population growth. In the 2017-2023 period, employment in the South Asian nation increased by about 134 million people, with the job creation rate nearly twice the growth rate of the working-age population.
Much of these gains were driven by rural women entering the paid workforce and raising the number of earners per household.
The World Bank also cited wage disparities in the South Asian nation, as median earnings among the top 10% of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023. More than 824 million people, about one in ten worldwide, were living in extreme poverty in 2024, as per latest World Bank data.

Kazakhstan and Singapore set to deepen aviation cooperation
Kazakhstan’s Aviation Administration (AAK) and the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) have signed a Statement of Intent to deepen cooperation in civil aviation, strengthen bilateral ties, and increase passenger and cargo traffic, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The document was signed during a visit by a Kazakh delegation to Singapore by AAK Chief Executive Officer Michael Daniel and CAAS Director-General Han Kok Juan.
According to the Civil Aviation Committee, Kazakhstan and Singapore are major aviation hubs in Central and Southeast Asia, respectively. Air connectivity between the two countries has expanded significantly in recent years.
Under the SoI, the two countries’ aviation authorities agreed to develop cooperation in several areas, including enhancing flight safety, introducing new technologies, promoting sustainable aviation, and providing training for aviation inspectors and other specialists.
The Statement of Intent (SOI) significantly broadens the scope of cooperation, which was previously limited to the implementation of aviation training programmes in Kazakhstan under the existing Cooperation Agreement on Training signed in 2024.
AAK and CAAS will work towards formalizing the expanded cooperation through a new Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), which is expected to be signed during a CAAS visit to Kazakhstan in the first half of 2027.
The document envisages regular cooperation between the two countries in civil aviation, including annual meetings between the heads of their aviation authorities. The meetings will be held alternately in Kazakhstan and Singapore, providing an opportunity to review joint efforts and discuss new areas of cooperation.
“Strengthening cooperation with CAAS is an important step towards further enhancing the professional expertise of our aviation specialists. We see great value in exchanging experience and best practices in risk-based oversight, flight safety and aviation security, as well as inspector training. We look forward to continue our existing partnership with CAAS, expanding opportunities for specialized training and professional development, and fostering closer cooperation to support safe, efficient and sustainable civil aviation in Kazakhstan,” said AAK Chief Executive Officer Michael Daniel.
“The signing of this Statement of Intent reflects the shared commitment of both civil aviation authorities to deepening technical cooperation, bringing our countries and regions closer together, increasing professional and business exchanges, and creating new economic opportunities. We look forward to establishing a formal framework for annual meetings that will enable our aviation sectors to build a sustainable partnership,” said CAAS Director-General Han Kok Juan.
Earlier, it was reported that Singaporean company Changi Airports International could join the construction and development of Kazakhstan's airport infrastructure.

US, South Korea, Japan call for ‘complete denuclearisation’ of North Korea
The joint statement comes as US President Donald Trump seeks a new meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
The United States, South Korea and Japan have reiterated their longstanding call for North Korea to give up its nuclear weapons, a move Pyongyang has repeatedly ruled out.
The three countries addressed the issue on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G20) meeting in the US city of Atlanta on Thursday, with their top diplomats reaffirming their “resolute commitment to the complete denuclearisation” of North Korea, according to a readout by the US Department of State.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also pledged the “full implementation” of United Nations Security Council resolutions, including a ban on supporting revenue for North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.
The statement comes despite repeated overtures to North Korea by US President Donald Trump, who held a series of historic summits with its leader, Kim Jong Un, during his first term in office and has continued to call Kim a “friend”.
Last year, Trump bucked a long-held US policy by conceding that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power”.
More recently, he has played down concerns about North Korea’s nuclear programme and expressed a desire to meet Kim again. Speculation is mounting that the two leaders could reconnect at next month’s APEC summit in China, which Trump is due to attend.
Analysts and South Korea’s spy agency say Kim may have conveyed Pyongyang’s position on potential talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.
South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung – who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions – suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North’s nuclear programme in return for sanctions relief.
Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepting North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.
Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea, which is backed by Russia and China, has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law. Pyongyang’s government has declared its atomic arsenal to be permanent and irreversible.
Pyongyang denounced a joint statement on Saturday by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementation against it, pledging that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK (North Korea) as a nuclear weapons state.”

Louvre heist puts Europe's smaller museums on alert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:18:49 UTC
16:18:49 KST

Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.
Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million ($10 million), to an accomplice and fled. At the museum's main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.
"Whatever could go wrong, did," said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.
The raid was one of a string of museum thefts in France, Italy and Spain since last year's heist at the Louvre in Paris, raising concerns that criminals are increasingly targeting smaller institutions with fewer resources to protect valuable collections.
"This is where we see the 'Louvre effect'," said Marc Balcells, a Barcelona-based researcher specialising in crimes against cultural heritage. "If the Louvre was so easy to rob, just imagine a tiny museum in a rural area or a smaller town."
Works by Antonello da Messina vanished from a museum in his Sicilian hometown in August, while two Renoirs were stolen from Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera the following month.
In Spain, thieves stole hundreds of historic gold coins from museums in Badajoz and Albacete and made off with a Bronze Age treasure in Villena, near Alicante.
A 2024 survey by France's Culture Ministry found only one in four cultural institutions had an emergency and risk-prevention plan, while nearly half lacked video surveillance.
Who checks when the alarm goes off?
A French parliamentary report in May said museums lacked the resources and preparation to adequately protect artworks and artefacts.
In Italy, the challenge is amplified by the way the country's cultural heritage is spread across hundreds of towns and institutions, a legacy of centuries of fragmented rule.
"That is also what makes our system distinctive: works remain in the places where they were created,” said Antonella Pinna, president of the Italian committee of the International Council of Museums. "But we need to make life harder for criminals."
The council worked with Italy's Culture Ministry and the Carabinieri on museum security guidelines published in 2015, but Pinna said technology alone was not enough.
"If an alarm goes off, someone has to make sure it is checked," she said.
In a narrow street in the Tuscan town of Sansepolcro, the civic museum displays four works by Renaissance master Piero della Francesca, born just steps away in the 15th century.
The Louvre theft "affected us deeply because cultural heritage is central to Sansepolcro's identity. It is our soul," culture councillor Francesca Mercati told Reuters.
After the Louvre raid, officers from the Carabinieri's cultural heritage protection unit recommended more cameras, longer retention of CCTV footage and tighter controls on bags and bulky clothing.
"We immediately implemented those recommendations," Mercati said.
A vast network to protect
The scale of the challenge is daunting.
Italy has more than 4,400 museums and similar institutions, according to national statistics agency ISTAT. Spain has about 1,500 museums, while France has more than 1,200 institutions carrying the official "Musees de France" designation, alongside hundreds of smaller collections.
Protecting such a broad network is particularly difficult for smaller institutions that depend on local funding.
Florence Imbert, a Paris-based security consultant for cultural institutions, said 85 percent of small French museums were run by local authorities with limited financial resources.
"The budget is key to winning the war," she said.
France's Culture Ministry announced a 33-point security plan in July, backed by €30 million over three years for local museums.
Recent figures suggest concern is warranted. The Carabinieri art squad recorded 17 thefts from Italian museums and galleries in 2025, up from 14 a year earlier.
Europol said in an August report that museum thefts were becoming more forceful and increasingly focused on precious metals, gemstones and other high-value artefacts.
A fast buck?
Unlike jewellery, stolen famous paintings are difficult to sell openly and are more likely to be hidden, used in ransom attempts or offered privately, art expert Pinna said.
Even recovered works can leave museums facing substantial investigation, recovery and security costs.
Recent thefts have also renewed debate over insurance, with some museums reassessing their coverage.
Insurers are meanwhile exploring AI technology to analyse CCTV footage and help identify suspicious behaviour before thefts occur.
Security vs access
Museum officials face the challenge of improving security while keeping collections accessible to the public.
Julien Volper, a Belgian conservator, said vulnerable treasures should only be displayed when adequate protection is in place.
Italian police recovered three artworks stolen from a Parma museum in August from a cardboard box hidden in an apartment.
Five Moldovan nationals were arrested over the theft. The artworks have since returned to the museum, which now has round-the-clock security funded by a local cheese consortium.

FaceTime while driving costs woman conditional loss of licence in Denmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:16:49 UTC
16:16:49 KST

A Danish court has ruled that using a correctly mounted phone can still lead to the conditional loss of a driving licence if it distracts the driver from traffic.
A 46-year-old woman has been given a conditional driving ban after using FaceTime while driving on a motorway near Copenhagen.
Although her phone was correctly mounted in the car, Glostrup District Court found that the video call distracted her to such an extent that she failed to pay sufficient attention to the traffic around her.
The case highlights an important distinction for motorists in Denmark: using a mounted or hands-free phone while driving may be legal, but drivers can still be penalised if using it causes dangerous or inattentive driving.
The woman was stopped by police on Motorring 3, Copenhagen’s western ring motorway, in Glostrup on January 13.
Before she was stopped, she had failed to react appropriately to vehicles trying to merge onto the motorway. Several motorists had to brake or accelerate to enter the traffic.
Police found that her attention had been directed towards her phone rather than the road ahead.
Glostrup District Court ruled on Wednesday that she had disregarded essential road-safety considerations.
In addition to the conditional loss of her driving licence, she was fined DKK 2,500.
She must now pass both a new theory test and a practical driving test to retain her licence, according to the prosecution service at Copenhagen Vestegn Police.
“The case emphasises how important it is to keep your focus on traffic when driving a car – even if the phone is correctly mounted,” assistant prosecutor Sabrina Berggren said.
Although the woman was not holding the phone, the FaceTime conversation affected her driving and therefore road safety, Berggren said.
Hands-free does not mean distraction-free
The Danish Road Safety Council (Rådet for Sikker Trafik) also warns motorists that hands-free calls can be distracting.
Jakob Bøving Arendt, CEO of the council, said in a written comment to Ritzau that inattention is one of the major causes of deaths on Danish roads.
Although using a hands-free phone while driving is legal, the council recommends limiting its use because conversations can reduce a driver’s mental attention, he said.

Temu drops sharply in popularity among Danish online shoppers
The Chinese-owned shopping platform has fallen from third to tenth place among Denmark’s most-used online stores, while second-hand marketplace Vinted is gaining ground.
Temu has lost significant ground among online shoppers in Denmark over the past year.
In the third quarter of 2025, the Chinese-owned platform was the third most popular online store among Danish consumers. A year later, it has fallen to tenth place, according to the latest E-commerce Tracker from the Confederation of Danish Industry (DI).
The quarterly survey, conducted by research company Epinion, asks Danish consumers where they made their most recent online purchase.
Mie Bilberg, chief consultant for e-commerce at DI, says new customs rules may help explain Temu’s decline.
Previously, Danish consumers could order very cheap products directly from China without paying customs duty on low-value packages. That advantage has now been reduced.
“You used to be able to order a pack of hair elastics directly from China and have it delivered to your home in Næstved for just a few kroner,” Bilberg said.
When extra charges are added, she said, buying the same product from a Danish retailer such as supermarket chain Føtex can become more attractive.
“It is a step towards European webshops being able to compete on more equal terms with the Chinese ones,” she said.
Under the new rules, packages worth less than 150 euros are subject to a customs charge of three euros. Many such shipments were previously exempt. From November 1, an additional handling fee of two euros will also apply.
Second-hand shopping gains ground
While Temu is losing popularity, second-hand marketplace Vinted remains Denmark’s second most-used online shopping platform.
Bilberg said the result reflects a broader shift towards buying used goods.
“This aligns with the trend we are seeing both in Denmark and globally, where consumers are buying more second-hand,” she said.
Consumers are increasingly concerned about climate, looking for unique products and trying to make their money go further as everyday expenses remain high, she added.
German fashion retailer Zalando remains the most-used online store among Danish consumers.
Danish health and beauty retailer Matas has moved into third place, replacing Temu.
Source: Ritzau
Denmark moves towards allowing wolf hunting from 2027
The Danish government hopes to allow wolf hunting as early as 2027. Researchers will now determine how large the country’s wolf population needs to be to remain viable.
Denmark is taking another step towards allowing wolves to be hunted, after EU rules protecting the species were relaxed last year.
The government has commissioned work to determine how many wolves Denmark needs to maintain a stable and viable population in the long term.
At the same time, authorities want to introduce more precise monitoring using DNA to identify individual wolves.
Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of the Social Democrats said the scientific work could pave the way for hunting as early as 2027.
“We need a population model in place. It is a step towards being able to regulate – that is, hunt wolves in Denmark,” he said.
The Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV) will put the development of the population model out to public tender. A separate tender will cover individual monitoring of wolves.
At least 49 adult wolves
Denmark does not currently have an exact count of its wolf population.
In spring 2026, researchers from the Natural History Museum Aarhus and Aarhus University estimated that there were at least 49 adult wolves in Denmark.
The government now wants a more precise assessment based on DNA, making it possible to identify individual animals.
“We need a scientific count of the wolves, and we need a model for a minimum population,” Rabjerg Madsen said.
Once that work has been completed, the government hopes it will provide the scientific basis for introducing regulated hunting.
EU rules on wolves were relaxed in 2025
Wolves remain protected under EU law, but their protection status was changed in 2025.
The species was moved from Annex IV to Annex V of the EU Habitats Directive, changing its status from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
The change gives EU countries greater flexibility to manage their wolf populations, including through hunting.
However, it does not mean Denmark can simply introduce unrestricted wolf hunting.
Any hunting or population management must be compatible with maintaining the wolf at what EU rules call a “favourable conservation status”.
Determining that status involves more than simply counting wolves. Authorities must also consider factors including the population’s geographical range, habitat and long-term prospects.
The population model being commissioned by the Danish authorities is expected to be ready during 2027.
Minister hopes for hunting in 2027
Rabjerg Madsen said his ambition is to allow wolf hunting that same year.
“It is my ambition that we can have wolf hunting in 2027, because that is when we will start getting the numbers,” he said.
“My expectation is that they will show that we have a viable wolf population and that we therefore can have hunting of the wolf.”
Asked whether he was anticipating the researchers’ conclusion before the calculations had been made, the minister said the outcome would have to remain within the scientific and international rules governing Denmark.
“I have been very careful to say that it is my assessment and hope that we have a viable wolf population, so that we can have wolf hunting within the scientific boundaries we are committed to by international rules,” he said.
Individual wolves can already be killed under certain circumstances in Denmark. This can include wolves that repeatedly attack livestock protected by approved wolf-proof fencing or animals that display an abnormal lack of fear of humans.

Denmark misses pesticide target as concerns grow over groundwater
Denmark’s pesticide load rose by 33 percent in a single year, new figures show. Part of the increase is linked to farmers stocking up on pesticides that can form the PFAS compound TFA and leach into groundwater.
Denmark has missed a key target for reducing the impact of pesticides on human health and the environment, with the country’s pesticide load instead reaching its second-highest level in 12 years.
New figures from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency show that the pesticide load indicator reached 2.29 in 2025.
The target was 1.43.
The indicator is used by Danish authorities to measure the overall impact of pesticides on human health and the environment.
The issue is particularly important in Denmark, where more than 99 percent of drinking water comes from groundwater.
TFA, a highly persistent PFAS compound, was detected in 40 percent of the Danish drinking-water wells tested between 2021 and 2024. However, the Danish Environmental Protection Agency says the concentrations currently found in drinking-water wells do not pose a risk to human health.
“It is completely unsatisfactory and simply not good enough,” Environment Minister Maria Reumert Gjerding of the Socialist People’s Party (SF) said in a statement.
Pesticide load rose 33 percent in one year
The pesticide load increased by 33 percent from 2024 to 2025.
Part of the increase was caused by farmers buying stocks of pesticides before 33 products were banned.
The products contain active substances that can break down into TFA and potentially leach into groundwater.
The European Chemicals Agency has classified TFA as harmful to unborn children and human reproductive health.
The Danish Environmental Protection Agency withdrew the 33 pesticide products as part of efforts to protect groundwater.
But stockpiling does not explain the entire increase in Denmark’s pesticide load.
If purchases of the affected pesticides are excluded, the pesticide load indicator is estimated at around 1.99 – still considerably above the 2025 target of 1.43.
The government is now preparing a new strategy aimed at reducing the impact of pesticides used in Danish agriculture.
“The figures clearly call for a new ambitious pesticide strategy that ensures the necessary initiatives to reduce the load from pesticides,” Gjerding said.
Environmental group calls it a serious setback
The Danish Society for Nature Conservation (Danmarks Naturfredningsforening) described the figures as a serious setback.
“It is a serious setback for a target that we were already far from reaching,” director Lars Midtiby said.
He also criticised farmers for stocking up on pesticides before restrictions came into force.
“When a tightening is on the way, agriculture stockpiles the pesticides affected by it, and then nature, our drinking water and the Danish population risk paying the price,” Midtiby said.
Landbrug & Fødevarer, which represents Denmark’s agriculture and food sector, defended the use of the now-phased-out pesticides.
The organisation said the products had been necessary to combat diseases, weeds and pests in crops and to maintain yields and quality.
Peter Nyegaard Nissen, the organisation’s director of plant production, said a new pesticide strategy needs to balance environmental protection with agricultural production.
“An ambitious pesticide strategy must both protect our groundwater and nature and at the same time ensure that Danish farmers can continue to produce food efficiently and competitively,” he said.

Denmark can expect a relatively calm autumn weekend, with temperatures reaching 14 degrees Celsius, occasional sunshine and rain arriving on Sunday.
According to Erik Hansen, a meteorologist at the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI), temperatures will remain around five degrees above the seasonal average.
“It’s unusually mild,” Hansen said, forecasting temperatures between 11 and 14 degrees on Friday, accompanied by light to moderate westerly and northwesterly winds.
Friday will begin with widespread clouds, haze and fog, although some areas could see the skies clear as the day progresses.
Northeastern Denmark, particularly Bornholm, is expected to enjoy the most sunshine, while the rest of the country may see only brief sunny spells.
Saturday will remain largely dry but cloudy, with patches of morning fog and haze across the country.

Sunday will also begin cloudy but mostly dry before a weak cold front brings rain into northwestern Denmark during the day.
The rain will gradually spread eastward through the afternoon and evening, eventually reaching much of the country.

The new direct connection reduces the journey to four hours and 40 minutes.

Nearly two million Danes register organ donation preferences as numbers surge
Nearly four in ten people aged over 15 in Denmark have registered their organ donation preferences, following a sharp increase over the past two years.
According to figures from the Danish Center for Organ Donation, 1,941,790 people had recorded their decision by the end of September, up from 1,404,297 in September 2024.
The increase follows changes to Denmark’s organ donation rules, under which all adults aged 18 and older are automatically registered as potential donors. However, individuals must confirm their registration on sundhed.dk to become active donors.
Helle Haubro Andersen, head of the Danish Center for Organ Donation, said direct communication encourages people to make a decision.
Following the rule changes, residents received notifications through e-Boks, Denmark’s digital mailbox service.
Most of those who responded granted full or partial consent, Andersen said.
Among people who have registered their preferences, 66 percent consented to donating all eligible organs, while 16 percent granted partial consent. Another 14 percent declined donation.
Residents can also indicate that they remain undecided.
Andersen explained that deceased organ donors generally must have suffered a severe brain injury, such as a major stroke or brain hemorrhage.
There is no upper age limit for donation. Denmark’s oldest organ donor was 92 in 2019, although kidneys and livers are generally more suitable for donation at advanced ages.
The figures come amid criticism of Rigshospitalet, which has rejected donor livers for children and adults because of capacity shortages.
Andersen declined to comment on the hospital’s situation but noted that organ transplants have increased nationally.
Last year, 455 patients received organ transplants, compared with 433 in 2024, 430 in 2023 and 338 in 2022.
Danish court rules citizenship denial to woman with disability was not discrimination
A Palestinian woman who was denied Danish citizenship because she could not meet the country’s self-support requirement has lost her discrimination case against the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court ruled Friday that the decision did not constitute unlawful indirect discrimination based on her disability, according to a statement published on the court’s website.
The woman arrived in Denmark in 1999 and was involved in a traffic accident 10 years later.
Following the accident, her reduced ability to work led to her being approved for a flexjob, a Danish employment arrangement for people with permanently reduced working capacity.
She subsequently received unemployment benefits for a period, preventing her from meeting the financial self-sufficiency requirement for Danish citizenship.
Her citizenship application was rejected in February 2023.
The woman and her lawyer argued that the refusal amounted to indirect discrimination and violated international conventions protecting people with disabilities and human rights.
However, the High Court rejected those arguments and ruled in favor of the ministry.
Her lawyer, Petra Alexandra Fokdal, argued that the rules create difficulties for people in flexjobs who become unemployed.
“Once you are referred to a flexjob, you cannot be in an unemployment fund. And if the employer no longer needs you, you receive unemployment benefits, but this makes it impossible to meet the requirement of self-support,” Fokdal said.
Because of its wider legal significance, the case was transferred directly from the district court to the High Court.
Fokdal said she intends to appeal the ruling to Denmark’s Supreme Court.
Parcels arriving from outside the EU to Denmark and other EU countries will face a new fee
Cheap goods from Chinese online shops are arriving in EU in huge numbers, raising concerns about product safety.
In 2025 alone, Danish customs registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Therefore, the European Union will introduce a permanent handling fee of 2 euros per line item in parcels arriving from outside the bloc starting Sunday, November 1, the Danish Customs Agency said Friday.
The fee, equivalent to about 15 Danish kroner, will apply regardless of a parcel’s total value. It will be added to the temporary customs duty introduced this summer on parcels worth less than 150 euros.
Items with the same commodity code count as one line item. Three cotton T-shirts, for example, would incur a handling fee of 2 euros. A cotton T-shirt and a pair of denim jeans would count as two line items, bringing the fee to 4 euros.
The existing customs duty is 3 euros per line item in parcels with a total value below 150 euros.
Christian Lützen, director of the Danish Customs Agency, said the number of low-value parcels sent to consumers from outside the EU had fallen since the customs duty took effect.
“With the handling fee, we are stepping up efforts even further to, among other things, strengthen member states’ opportunities to inspect the contents of parcels,” he said in the press release.
“There are still problems with many of the goods in relation to consumer safety, and as an authority at the border, we must take that seriously.”
When the customs duty was introduced this summer, Lützen said the agency had previously seen a sharp increase in goods arriving from Chinese online shops. He called it “a major problem across EU countries” and said the duty should help make shopping with Danish businesses more attractive.
In 2025, the agency registered 68 million line items in parcels worth less than 150 euros. A count showed that more than 90% of parcels entering Denmark contained Chinese goods.
Shein and Temu were among the 10 online shops most used by Danish consumers in the latest survey by Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, a business organization.
The two platforms sell products ranging from clothing to kitchen equipment and have faced criticism over poor quality and illegal chemicals in their products.

Denmark introduces new GP payment system to improve care for patients with greater needs
Patients in Denmark will be able to book different types of appointments with their general practitioners under a new four-year agreement aimed at improving access to medical care.
The agreement, announced Thursday, was negotiated between Praktiserende Lægers Organisation (PLO), the Danish organization representing general practitioners, and Regionernes Lønnings- og Takstnævn (RLTN), the regional body responsible for negotiating doctors’ pay and fees.
One of the main changes is a new payment system that takes patients’ medical needs into account.
Currently, clinics receive the same payment per patient regardless of whether patients are generally healthy or require extensive treatment.
Under the agreement, clinics treating patients with greater medical needs will receive higher payments.
The change is intended to improve financial conditions for practices in areas with fewer doctors, where patients with the greatest treatment needs are often found.
The agreement also introduces four appointment categories: short, regular, long and complex consultations.
These will allow doctors to address several medical concerns during a single appointment when necessary.
General practitioners will also receive separate payments for continuing education, helping them expand their skills and potentially reduce referrals to other medical services.
“It is a milestone that we now have an agreement on terms and frameworks for general practice that extends four years into the future,” PLO chairman Jørgen Skadborg said.
He added that the agreement would provide stability, allowing doctors to focus on patients and developing their clinics.
The agreement takes effect at the start of the new year, with 4.5 billion DKK allocated to general practice over four years.
By 2030, annual funding is expected to be 1.7 billion DKK higher than today.

Denmark, Greenland and Faroe Islands to jointly lead Nordic Council in 2027
Lars-Christian Brask, a member of Denmark’s parliament for Liberal Alliance, has been elected president of the Nordic Council, which brings together parliamentarians from the Nordic countries.
Brask was elected Thursday during the council’s session in Helsinki, Finland, according to a statement from Folketinget, Denmark’s parliament.
Denmark will take over the rotating presidency from Finland in 2027, sharing leadership responsibilities with Greenland and the Faroe Islands for the first time.
Brask has chaired Denmark’s delegation to the Nordic Council since 2023. He said the presidency involves leading parliamentary cooperation between the Nordic countries.
“Just like in the Folketing, we can make proposals that are voted through and then go to the Council of Ministers, which then has to implement them,” Brask told Ritzau, Denmark’s news agency.
Greenland and the Faroe Islands will share the vice presidency. Justus Hansen of Greenland’s Demokraatit party will serve during the first six months, followed by Sunnvá Dahl Høgfeldt of the Faroese Sambandsflokkurin party.
According to Folketinget, the presidency will prioritize removing barriers between Nordic countries to improve regional cooperation and competitiveness.
Children, young people, civil society, culture and understanding of Nordic languages will also feature in its agenda.
Brask said Denmark intends to focus on practical outcomes rather than formalities.
“There will be fewer ceremonial speeches and more focus on delivering concrete results,” he said.
The Nordic Council has 87 parliamentarians, with its presidency rotating annually among five Nordic countries.
Denmark last held the presidency in 2021, when Bertel Haarder of Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, served as president.
Arctic sea ice survives summer with less melting than expected despite record-low winter
Arctic sea ice has retained more of its coverage than expected this summer, thanks to unusually cool weather conditions, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI).
In a statement Thursday, DMI reported that Arctic sea ice reached a record-low winter extent earlier this year but experienced relatively limited melting during the summer months.
A large low-pressure system over the Arctic helped keep temperatures cooler, slowing the melting process and allowing more ice to survive.
Gorm Dybkjær, a climate researcher at DMI, said the development was surprising but cautioned against interpreting it as a reversal of climate change.
“It is remarkable that the sea ice in the Arctic has retained so much of its winter ice after the winter’s record-low extent. But that does not mean that climate change has released its grip on the ice,” he said.
In September, when Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum, its extent ranked as the 16th-lowest since records began in 1978.
Despite this year’s relatively favorable conditions, scientists continue to observe a long-term decline in the thickness and volume of Arctic sea ice.
Since 2007, the Arctic’s total sea ice volume has fallen by an estimated 20 percent or more.
Dybkjær warned that thinner ice is increasingly vulnerable to changing weather and ocean conditions, which could trigger sudden, substantial losses.
Researchers also monitor sea ice because of its role in regulating Earth’s temperature through the albedo effect.
This refers to how much incoming sunlight is reflected into space.
Ice and clouds reflect substantial amounts of solar radiation, while darker ocean surfaces absorb more energy, contributing to warming.

PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.

The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.

Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.

Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.

Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.

He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.

ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.

Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.

The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.

Temu drops sharply in popularity among Danish online shoppers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:16:45 UTC
16:16:45 KST

The Chinese-owned shopping platform has fallen from third to tenth place among Denmark’s most-used online stores, while second-hand marketplace Vinted is gaining ground.
Temu has lost significant ground among online shoppers in Denmark over the past year.
In the third quarter of 2025, the Chinese-owned platform was the third most popular online store among Danish consumers. A year later, it has fallen to tenth place, according to the latest E-commerce Tracker from the Confederation of Danish Industry (DI).
The quarterly survey, conducted by research company Epinion, asks Danish consumers where they made their most recent online purchase.
Mie Bilberg, chief consultant for e-commerce at DI, says new customs rules may help explain Temu’s decline.
Previously, Danish consumers could order very cheap products directly from China without paying customs duty on low-value packages. That advantage has now been reduced.
“You used to be able to order a pack of hair elastics directly from China and have it delivered to your home in Næstved for just a few kroner,” Bilberg said.
When extra charges are added, she said, buying the same product from a Danish retailer such as supermarket chain Føtex can become more attractive.
“It is a step towards European webshops being able to compete on more equal terms with the Chinese ones,” she said.
Under the new rules, packages worth less than 150 euros are subject to a customs charge of three euros. Many such shipments were previously exempt. From November 1, an additional handling fee of two euros will also apply.
Second-hand shopping gains ground
While Temu is losing popularity, second-hand marketplace Vinted remains Denmark’s second most-used online shopping platform.
Bilberg said the result reflects a broader shift towards buying used goods.
“This aligns with the trend we are seeing both in Denmark and globally, where consumers are buying more second-hand,” she said.
Consumers are increasingly concerned about climate, looking for unique products and trying to make their money go further as everyday expenses remain high, she added.
German fashion retailer Zalando remains the most-used online store among Danish consumers.
Danish health and beauty retailer Matas has moved into third place, replacing Temu.

FaceTime while driving costs woman conditional loss of licence in Denmark
A Danish court has ruled that using a correctly mounted phone can still lead to the conditional loss of a driving licence if it distracts the driver from traffic.
A 46-year-old woman has been given a conditional driving ban after using FaceTime while driving on a motorway near Copenhagen.
Although her phone was correctly mounted in the car, Glostrup District Court found that the video call distracted her to such an extent that she failed to pay sufficient attention to the traffic around her.
The case highlights an important distinction for motorists in Denmark: using a mounted or hands-free phone while driving may be legal, but drivers can still be penalised if using it causes dangerous or inattentive driving.
The woman was stopped by police on Motorring 3, Copenhagen’s western ring motorway, in Glostrup on January 13.
Before she was stopped, she had failed to react appropriately to vehicles trying to merge onto the motorway. Several motorists had to brake or accelerate to enter the traffic.
Police found that her attention had been directed towards her phone rather than the road ahead.
Glostrup District Court ruled on Wednesday that she had disregarded essential road-safety considerations.
In addition to the conditional loss of her driving licence, she was fined DKK 2,500.
She must now pass both a new theory test and a practical driving test to retain her licence, according to the prosecution service at Copenhagen Vestegn Police.
“The case emphasises how important it is to keep your focus on traffic when driving a car – even if the phone is correctly mounted,” assistant prosecutor Sabrina Berggren said.
Although the woman was not holding the phone, the FaceTime conversation affected her driving and therefore road safety, Berggren said.
Hands-free does not mean distraction-free
The Danish Road Safety Council (Rådet for Sikker Trafik) also warns motorists that hands-free calls can be distracting.
Jakob Bøving Arendt, CEO of the council, said in a written comment to Ritzau that inattention is one of the major causes of deaths on Danish roads.
Although using a hands-free phone while driving is legal, the council recommends limiting its use because conversations can reduce a driver’s mental attention, he said.
