Is AI killing art? No, but the human creative process still matters, Israeli study argues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:40:09 UTC
15:40:09 KST

For centuries, mastering an art form was inseparable from personal growth. A painter spent years learning to see the world before touching canvas, and a musician devoted decades to refining physical and emotional discipline.
Today, generative AI can produce sophisticated compositions at the click of a button, shattering that age-old connection.
But according to a new paper from Prof. Amit Zoran of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem (HUJI), this digital revolution isn’t rendering human artists obsolete; it is stripping away technical barriers so we can rediscover what made creativity meaningful in the first place.
The key question is not whether AI can generate attractive paintings or music; it is whether the process of creating something has value that cannot be captured by the finished product.
As AI becomes capable of producing sophisticated art in seconds, a new paper challenges us to rethink what makes human creativity valuable.
Zoran, who teaches and conducts research at HUJI’s The Rachel and Selim Benin School of Computer Science and Engineering, where he leads the Hybrid Design Lab, focuses on bridging the gap between emerging computational technologies (including AI, robotics, and 3D printing) and traditional human crafts, gastronomy, design, and consciousness.
He earned a bachelor’s degree in Communication Systems Engineering at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Beersheba and completed postdoctoral research at the prestigious Massachusetts Institute of Technology Media Lab, and also worked at Israel Aircraft Industries, followed by a master’s degree in industrial and product design at Jerusalem’s Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design.
He published his paper in the journal AI & Society, titled “More than we can make: Generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming.”
Instead of focusing on whether AI-generated works qualify as art, Zoran argues that the significance of creativity lies not only in the finished product but also in the experiences that shape artists, audiences, and cultures.
For centuries, producing sophisticated art required years of learning, experimentation, and personal development. A painter developed not only technical skills but also a way of seeing the world, while a musician refined both physical abilities and emotional expression. Generative AI is fundamentally changing this relationship, he insisted.
Zoran introduces what he calls the “decoupling thesis,” arguing that AI “makes it possible to produce sophisticated artistic works without undergoing the personal development traditionally required to create them. Someone can now generate detailed illustrations without learning to draw or compose music without mastering an instrument.”
“For centuries, creating art meant going through a process of learning, experimenting, and changing as a person,” he explained. “Today, AI allows us to produce sophisticated works without necessarily undergoing that journey. But this doesn’t mean that human creativity has lost its value. It means we need to rethink where that value lies.”
“The real potential of AI is not just to help us produce more music, images, or designs, but to open new possibilities for how we experience, understand, and engage with the world around us,” he told The Jerusalem Post in an interview.
Rather than eliminating creativity, Zoran argues that AI is shifting it toward new activities, including experimentation, interpretation, and collaboration with technology. Importantly, the value of art also extends beyond its creator, influencing how audiences perceive the world and how cultures develop.
Human creativity has not lost its value
The paper highlights creative projects that show how technology can enrich human experiences rather than simply generate more content. In one example, a tree becomes the center of an interactive artistic experience that combines smell, taste, visual projections, recorded sounds, and AI-generated music. Instead of merely producing digital content, technology helps participants engage with nature in new ways.
The research also raises questions about how AI tools should be designed and evaluated. While current systems are often judged by speed, realism, and output quality, Zoran suggests considering whether they encourage curiosity, exploration, and new perspectives.
“As AI makes artistic production increasingly accessible, the future of creativity may depend less on what people can make and more on what they can discover, experience, and become through the creative process. Instead of making human creativity irrelevant, AI may make it possible to rediscover what makes it meaningful,” he said.
For artists, this could mean using the time saved by AI to experiment and develop richer experiences. For educational and cultural institutions, it could mean placing greater value on the creative process rather than focusing exclusively on finished products.
Ultimately, Zoran argues that as AI makes artistic production increasingly accessible, the future of creativity may depend less on what people can make and more on what they can discover, experience, and become through the creative process.
“Instead of making human creativity irrelevant, AI may offer an opportunity to rediscover what makes it meaningful,” he concluded.
Asked if creativity is valuable because of the finished product, the process of making it, the intentions of the creator, the skills acquired, the emotions involved, or the effect on an audience, Zoran said it’s not the technical complexity but actually creating changes in the artist or the culture, not how we did it. “It doesn’t matter if I drew something myself or a computer did it – but the impact.”
Asked whether someone could use AI to experience discovery, struggle, learning, and personal growth even if the system performs much of the technical work, he responded that “the experience behind it is important. We lose the experience and the authenticity. We have to think again. When musicians started using electric guitars, some said it didn’t sound good enough. But it became interesting when a computer was able to make it.”
Does the effort itself confer value, or does the value come from what the person learns and experiences? “The effort creates maturity.” AI-generated art might provoke the same emotional response as art made entirely by a human, he continued.
“Every era changed things. The Industrial Revolution changed the world. AI is the first technological revolution,” Zoran said. “I have faith in humanity, which finds a way to proceed. If there is painting on the wall of an ancient cave, with no name, there is a high level of art without credit.
“Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: Who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Today, art is capitalist, but it’s not the end of humanity. Maybe it’s not so important exactly who writes a good book.”
While AI can bypass years of artistic training, it cannot replace the transformative experiences that give creativity its deeper meaning.
“The research suggests that the future of art may lie less in producing impressive works and more in using technology to inspire exploration, meaningful experiences, and new ways of seeing the world. For centuries, creating art meant going through a process of learning, experimenting, and changing as a person.
“Today, AI allows us to produce sophisticated works without necessarily undergoing that journey. But this doesn’t mean human creativity has lost its value. It means we need to rethink where that value lies. The real potential of AI is not simply to help us produce more images, music, or designs, but to open new possibilities for how we experience, understand, and engage with the world around us,” he concluded.

US judge orders Trump administration to stop threats to prosecute state, local election officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:39:42 UTC
15:39:42 KST

A US judge ordered the Justice Department on Friday to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration's demands related to voting by alleged non-citizens.
The ruling comes days before next week's US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Although several key races appear closely contested, polls favor Democrats to take control of the House and give them a plausible chance of a Senate majority.
In the months leading up to the midterms, President Donald Trump's administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, such as pressing states for voter-registration data, saying stricter measures are needed to ensure election security and public confidence in the vote.
But the Justice Department went too far this month when it threatened to prosecute state and county officials who do not cooperate with the Trump administration's election-related initiatives, US District Judge Trina Thompson ruled in connection with a lawsuit brought by election workers' unions and some other groups.
"Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," Thompson wrote in her temporary restraining order.
The Justice Department had no immediate comment on the ruling.
Officials fear federal interference in the elections
Critics, including political experts as well as Democratic and some Republican election officials, have viewed the Trump administration's moves as federal overreach. Some election officials have told Reuters they were preparing for potential federal interference in the midterm elections.
Thompson, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, ordered the Trump administration to refrain from demanding that local election officials remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or segregate ballots cast in the midterm elections, based on a Trump administration list of alleged non-citizen voters.
Trump has made false claims related to elections in the past, including not acknowledging his defeat in the 2020 election.

The mediators are reportedly pushing Tehran and Washington to agree on steps that could be implemented in the coming days to bring both countries back to the negotiating table for discussions on issues, including Iran’s nuclear program.
According to Axios, the Qataris are trying to sell Iran on allowing United Nations inspectors to visit nuclear sites, many of which were heavily damaged by US and Israeli strikes. The inspections could act as a confidence-building measure that the US may respond to with the relaxation of sanctions.
A US official told Axios that competing demands from both sides have stagnated progress. The US has insisted that nuclear concessions must be made before talks continue, while Iran’s demands include the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports along the Strait of Hormuz, the release of frozen funds, and the easing of sanctions before the nuclear topic can be touched.
A diplomatic source, however, said to Axios that Qatari mediators were in contact with the White House over the course of Friday’s talks and that “there was positive progress.”
“Talks are still ongoing in an effort to unlock a deal between the US and Iran,” the source added.
The discussions will reportedly resume in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday.
Washington weighing renewed strikes as midterm elections approach
Friday’s talks came as Washington is weighing the possibility of renewed strikes against Iran ahead of US midterm elections set for November 3.
According to Axios, countries like Egypt, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia have pushed for Iran to continue negotiations before the midterms.
One US official said that US President Donald Trump may be more motivated to order strikes on Iran if Republicans do poorly in the election.
"If he feels embarrassed or disenfranchised, he will do something bold. That's what everyone is telling the Iranians. Their best shot to get a deal is right now," the official told Axios.
A White House official disputed that possibility, saying that the election results will not factor into Trump’s decision about Iran.

Opposition bloc considers reviving direct elections without dissolving Knesset to end stalemate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:39:28 UTC
15:39:28 KST

Senior figures in the opposition bloc are considering a return to direct elections for prime minister without dissolving the Knesset, following the inconclusive results of Israel's 26th Knesset election, according to reports by Maariv commentator Ben Caspit and journalist Michael Hauser Tov.
The election results have left Israel's political system deadlocked, with neither bloc securing the majority needed to form a government. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 seats, the opposition bloc has 48, and the Arab parties hold 19.
Although 67 Knesset members are mathematically outside Netanyahu's bloc, disagreements among the opposition party leaders and their commitments not to rely on the Arab parties have complicated efforts to establish an alternative government.
Alongside the possibility of another Knesset election, an alternative proposal has emerged within the bloc: restoring direct elections for prime minister without dissolving parliament.
Maariv commentator Ben Caspit addressed the possibility, noting that if Netanyahu seeks to trigger another election, the electoral system could be changed to allow a direct contest for prime minister, as Israel previously practiced.
Caspit said legislation could also be advanced to limit the prime minister's tenure to two terms or eight years.
He raised the possibility that term-limit legislation could prevent Netanyahu from running again. However, such a scenario would depend on the law's wording, whether it applied to previous terms in office, and the legal and political obstacles involved.
In this context, Caspit recalled comments Netanyahu made during a 1997 interview with Dan Shilon, when he supported limiting a prime minister's tenure to two terms.
"What you can't do in the first term, you'll do in the second. And what you don't do in the second term, you won't do anymore," Netanyahu said at the time.
The model Netanyahu himself proposed in 2021
Journalist Michael Hauser Tov also reported on Ulpan Shishi that senior figures in the opposition bloc had confirmed direct prime ministerial elections were among the options being examined following the election results.
According to Hauser Tov, the bloc has dubbed the proposal the "Netanyahu 2021 direct election model," referring to an initiative Netanyahu attempted to advance following the election for the 24th Knesset.
The March 2021 election ended without a decisive outcome, with Netanyahu struggling to form a government even as Likud remained the largest party.
During coalition negotiations, the possibility of cooperation with the Ra'am party, led by Mansour Abbas, was raised. At the same time, a proposal to hold direct elections for prime minister was advanced.
In April 2021, amid the political deadlock, Netanyahu presented a plan intended to determine who would serve as prime minister without holding another Knesset election.
"Direct elections for prime minister will be held. The public will directly elect the prime minister in a snap election, without dissolving the Knesset," he declared at the time.
Now, approximately five years later, the same idea is being examined by the opposition bloc, which is seeking to bring his tenure to an end.
67 seats outside Netanyahu's bloc, but no agreement
According to Hauser Tov, one reason the proposal is being considered is the difficulty opposition party leaders face in reaching an agreement on forming a government with the support of the Arab parties.
While Democrats chairman Yair Golan has called for including the Arab parties in efforts to replace Netanyahu, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman established red lines during the election campaign regarding cooperation with them.
Legally, swearing in a government does not necessarily require the support of 61 Knesset members, but rather a majority of those participating in the confidence vote.
For example, 56 Knesset members voting in favor, 53 voting against, and the remaining 11 abstaining could be sufficient.
However, this possibility depends on political agreements that have yet to be reached, particularly the willingness of Bennett and Liberman to support such a move.
According to Hauser Tov's analysis, direct elections could offer an alternative way to determine who serves as prime minister without requiring the opposition bloc to reach a coalition agreement with the Arab parties in advance.
Nevertheless, even a directly elected prime minister would not necessarily have the parliamentary majority needed to establish and maintain a stable government.
Historical precedent and legal obstacles
Israel has held direct elections for the prime minister position in the past. The system was first implemented in 1996, when Netanyahu defeated Shimon Peres. In 1999, Ehud Barak defeated Netanyahu, and in 2001, a special election for prime minister alone was held, in which Ariel Sharon defeated Barak.
In the first two elections, voters cast two ballots, one for prime minister and another for the Knesset.
By contrast, the 2001 election was held solely to elect a prime minister, without a new Knesset election.
The system was abolished later that year, and Israel returned to a parliamentary model in which the government serves on the basis of the Knesset's confidence.
Restoring direct elections would therefore require significant legislative changes and could not be implemented under existing law.
The question of whether a directly elected prime minister could form a government without sufficient parliamentary support would also depend on the provisions established in the new legislation.
Furthermore, limiting a prime minister's tenure to two terms or eight years would require a separate legislative initiative.
Applying such a restriction retroactively to previous terms in office, in a manner that would prevent Netanyahu from running, would likely raise legal and constitutional questions concerning, among other issues, the right to stand for election and changes to electoral eligibility rules.
At this stage, these remain proposals being discussed within the political system rather than a fully developed legislative initiative agreed upon by party leaders.
As Netanyahu continues serving as caretaker prime minister and the opposition bloc struggles to present an agreed-upon coalition, the possibility of changing Israel's electoral system has returned to the political agenda.
The question is whether the parties can agree to change the rules of the electoral system, or whether this initiative will run into the same disagreements that have prevented them from forming a government.

Can AI tell when patients don't need medical tests? Israeli study puts chatbots to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:39:26 UTC
15:39:26 KST

Some Israelis are willing to undergo any available tests to see if they are healthy or if a serious but preventable disease is lurking in their future. Then some decline all medical tests, from colonoscopies to mammographies, saying, “What will be will be.”
In an era where patients and clinicians increasingly turn to artificial intelligence for medical advice, a critical question emerges: Does AI know when not to test or treat?
A new joint study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Beersheba and Clalit Health Services, the largest public health fund, reveals that leading Large Language Models (LLMs) successfully identify which medical interventions are unnecessary and when they encounter gray areas in which medical consensus itself is divided.
The peer-reviewed study was published in Annals of Internal Medicine, the flagship journal of the American College of Physicians, titled “Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.”
Patients frequently request extra tests “just to be safe,” said Prof. Guy Laban of BGU’s Department of Industrial Engineering and Management and Dr. Dean Ariel, a family physician and researcher at Clalit Health Services, who worked with Dr. Stav Endelman of Rabin Medical Center-Beilinson Hospital in Petah Tikva.
“Yet in clinical practice, more testing is not always better medicine. Unnecessary tests often uncover incidental, harmless findings that trigger cascades of anxiety, specialist referrals, invasive biopsies, and surgeries that were never needed in the first place, wasting precious healthcare resources and risking patient harm,” asserted Laban and Ariel in a joint interview with The Jerusalem Post.
“Conversely, an overly conservative diagnostic system risks missing crucial interventions when real danger lurks. A clinically safe AI tool must skillfully navigate between these two failure modes.”
The researchers evaluated six leading LLMs developed by Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI across hundreds of clinical scenarios, analyzing thousands of model responses. The scenarios were constructed around recommendations from the international Choosing Wisely campaign, a global medical initiative founded in 2012 by the American Board of Internal Medicine Foundation and active in more than 30 countries to eliminate low-value care.
They were written and designed from the clinician perspective based on 15 Choosing Wisely recommendations. For each of the 15 recommendations, 15 scenarios were developed; for each of those, 10 low-value care scenarios were designed where restraint is appropriate.
For each recommendation, five scenarios were designed for which action is appropriate. Each paired case where an intervention was redundant had closely matched controls where the same intervention was medically necessary.
A young man with acute lower back pain after lifting furniture does not require imaging. However, a woman with a history of breast cancer presenting new back pain at night does.
A common viral cold with runny nose and cough does not warrant antibiotics, but a confirmed bacterial strep throat test does. When an intervention was medically indicated, the models mistakenly recommended withholding care in only 0.6% of cases, they asserted.
When an intervention was explicitly unneeded, the models inappropriately recommended testing or treatment in just 5.4% of cases.
In eight of the 15 recommendations, the LLMs did not recommend a single unnecessary procedure. The vast majority of AI over-testing errors clustered around two notoriously ambiguous clinical practices. Models recommended unneeded electrocardiograms (EKGs) in 28.3% of responses, primarily in cases where patients mentioned palpitations, where an EKG can be a reasonable part of the workup.
They also endorsed unnecessary ultrasounds in 42.8% of responses for small, incidentally discovered nodules, mirroring a real disagreement between the American Thyroid Association and the American College of Radiology over whether such nodules should be imaged at all, the researchers continued.
Does the study demonstrate genuine clinical judgment?
“One of the hardest parts of practicing medicine is knowing when to hold back,” explained Ariel. “Patients find comfort in an extra test, but an unnecessary MRI often catches an asymptomatic disc bulge, setting off unnecessary worry and treatment.
“Language models learned medicine from human clinical literature, including our less disciplined habits. We wanted to see if they also absorbed the ability to exercise restraint. For the most part, they know when to stop, stumbling primarily where we doctors hesitate.”
“People often hear an AI chatbot speak in a single authoritative voice, as if there is a unified ‘AI consensus,’” added Laban. “Yet in gray areas where experts debate, the disparity between models was striking: on the exact same clinical cases, one model recommended an unnecessary test less than 10% of the time, while another recommended it 80% of the time.
“Furthermore, telling a patient ‘you don’t need this test’ is a delicate social act. A human physician must stand firm before an anxious patient, whereas language models tend to go along with the person in front of them. The next critical research question is whether an AI assistant will maintain the correct clinical restraint when an anxious or insistent patient pushes back.”
Laban is unusual in that he has visited more than 60 countries worldwide and has a wide variety of interests. After a bachelor’s degree at Reichman University in Herzliya, he earned a doctorate in brain sciences at Scotland’s University of Glasgow that focused on how people communicate with robots and how such robots can help people with mental health.
He was a visiting researcher at Constructor University in Germany and Tel Aviv University and completed postdoctoral studies in the computer science department at England’s University of Cambridge. He is also an amateur nature photographer.
The central issue is not simply whether AI can recognize unnecessary medical interventions, but whether the study demonstrates genuine clinical judgment or merely the ability to match established medical recommendations in carefully constructed cases.
Asked how well these results would generalize beyond the particular recommendations tested, Laban said: “This is the most central practice among medical doctors, especially primary care doctors. When clinicians or patients consult with AI, they will get output with common practice. Hopefully with new models, we will see more and more online benchmarks.”
Asked if some primary care physicians are upset when patients come in grasping AI printouts about this or that disease, Laban said: “Nobody likes to be second-guessed. It can be disruptive, even unprofessional. But some use it in primary care. Doctors can’t avoid consulting with it, including whether medications they are prescribing conflict with others.”
The models were tested only in English, Ariel commented: “We structured information that was common across studies so they could be standardized.
More work will have to be done before the results can be clinically validated and used in the doctor’s office, added Ariel, who also teaches at Tel Aviv University’s Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences.
The question of who would be accountable if an AI system advised against a necessary test and a patient got into trouble is tricky.
“Safeguards would be necessary. AI is a tool, like reading something in a book. In the end, the doctor is responsible. The model just recommends; it doesn’t tell him or her what to do,” Ariel declared. “The use of AI will have to be studied prospectively, and not only based on saving money. I’m not sure it’s cheaper than sending patients to the test it prevents.”

TIMELINE – How France’s student protests grew into nationwide unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:36:04 UTC
15:36:04 KST

France is preparing for fresh nationwide protests Saturday after student demonstrations over school conditions broadened into a movement against rising living costs and strained public services.
The government has announced education concessions and tighter security measures following weeks of demonstrations, mass arrests and clashes.
Here is a timeline of how the protests spread, the government’s response and the developments leading to Saturday’s mobilization.
School blockades over poor learning conditions took place in France’s overseas territories of Mayotte and French Guiana before similar protests emerged on the mainland.
In mid-September, students in the Paris suburbs mobilized over unfilled teaching posts, overcrowded classes, deteriorating buildings and shortages of support staff.
Students described classes of up to 36 and months without teachers in core subjects. They also demanded changes to France’s university admissions platform.
By Sept. 29, around 180 schools were affected, with the Interior Ministry reporting 164 arrests.
On Oct. 1, protest activity reached 1,027 schools, including 222 blockades. A fire broke out at Nelson-Mandela High School in Nantes, while authorities recorded 1,949 arrests during unrest nationwide.
A 15-year-old student lost a hand after a stun grenade exploded during a protest in Lens on Oct. 5. Authorities subsequently suspended the grenade model’s use at student demonstrations pending an investigation.
Justice Ministry figures showed 6,059 arrests between Sept. 28 and Oct. 5, with 5,060 people placed in police custody. Minors accounted for 87% of those detained.
On Oct. 6, the Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people demonstrated nationwide, including 56,000 in Paris. Student and university organizers put participation at 450,000. The ministry reported 488 arrests.
The movement broadened beyond education, with demonstrators also raising concerns about inequality, public spending and public services.
By Oct. 9, the number placed in custody since the movement began had exceeded 6,800, including 86% minors. Twenty-one people had been placed in pretrial detention.
Alongside the student movement, social media campaigns called for nationwide demonstrations Oct. 17 over fuel prices and living costs.
The appeals echoed the Yellow Vest protests that began in 2018, with prominent figures from that movement endorsing the mobilization, although its leadership remained unclear.
Workers, farmers, pensioners and residents of disadvantaged neighborhoods were urged to gather at roundabouts, petrol stations and toll roads.
Student groups also planned to participate, bringing overlapping grievances into the streets while retaining distinct demands and organizing structures.
The Interior Ministry estimated turnout at demonstrations nationwide at 550,000, while the CGT trade union put it at 800,000.
Many demonstrations remained peaceful, but groups clashed with police, threw projectiles, set fires and looted businesses. Police used tear gas.
In Limoges, a fire severely damaged the historic city hall. In Marseille, demonstrators broke into the city hall, while Lyon’s tourist office was set on fire. Damage and clashes were also reported in Paris and other cities.
Authorities later reported 2,628 arrests, 1,144 injured security personnel and 1,522 businesses damaged or looted.
The arrests did not all result in charges or convictions. In the Paris region, prosecutors reported 855 arrests over the weekend, resulting in 557 people being placed in police custody. Authorities reported 101 arrests in Marseille and 199 in Lyon.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu blamed radical left-wing groups and criminals, while President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence and called for prosecutions.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, the France Unbowed presidential candidate who joined the Paris march, called police command decisions at the protest “aberrant” and denied that his supporters engaged in looting or destruction.
Melenchon also urged the government to address young people’s anger.
Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally also blamed France Unbowed for fueling the violence. In a video address, she criticized Macron’s government as exhausted and disoriented, describing France as caught “between violence and powerlessness.” She called for calm and expressed support for the security forces.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez acknowledged failures to anticipate the scale of the protests and a loss of control in some areas.
Macron rejected his offer to resign and demanded an examination of intelligence and security failures. The government also prepared assistance for affected businesses.
Authorities introduced targeted curfews, including restrictions on minors, and announced 70,000 police officers and gendarmes for the scheduled Oct. 24 protests, up from 60,000 on Oct. 17.
On Oct. 23, Macron met student representatives to discuss school conditions and Parcoursup, the national web platform in France that manages pre-registration and admissions for first-year undergraduate and higher education programs.
The Interior Ministry counted 410,000 demonstrators on Oct. 24, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT estimated around 800,000 nationwide and 250,000 in the capital.
Authorities recorded 289 demonstrations, compared with 441 a week earlier.
Most marches passed without major incidents, but clashes broke out toward their end. Police used tear gas and water cannons in Paris, Nantes and Lille after some demonstrators threw projectiles. Further looting and damage were also reported.
In Paris, police reported 65 arrests and more than 3,000 identity checks.
In Lyon, where demonstrations were banned in parts of the city, authorities reported 36 arrests and 22 people injured, including 18 members of the security forces. In Nantes, six people were arrested in connection with looting, according to the Loire-Atlantique prefecture.
On Oct. 26, Nunez announced 1,435 arrests and said 267 security personnel and 150 demonstrators had been injured in that weekend’s demonstrations.
An Interior Ministry assessment recorded 75 fire-related interventions, down from 2,025 the previous Saturday.
Three protesters were seriously injured in Toulouse, Clermont-Ferrand and Reims, according to authorities. An investigation was opened into the Toulouse incident.
On Oct. 26, the government announced measures addressing concerns raised during the protests.
These include replacing Parcoursup in 2028, introducing changes for the 2027 admissions cycle and creating 15,000 additional higher education places. First-year high school classes would be capped at 28 students, starting in half of the most disadvantaged schools in 2027 and extending to all public high schools in 2028.
The government also pledged to cancel 836 planned secondary education job cuts and add 500 teaching posts.
Other commitments included €4 billion ($4.47 billion) in loans for school renovations, €1 billion in campus investment and inflation-linked increases in student grants from 2027.
Student representatives welcomed some announcements but said questions remained over university capacity and the replacement admissions system.
The group Les Lycéens! maintained its call for further action.
Further demonstrations were called for Oct. 31, while trade unions announced a nationwide day of action on Nov. 5.
Nunez announced another deployment of 70,000 police officers and gendarmes for Oct. 31, warning of a high risk of violence around Halloween.
Authorities planned restrictions on gatherings in city centers where they considered public-order risks too great, with some demonstrations directed toward outlying areas.
With France approaching its 2027 presidential election, the unrest has intensified debate over education, living costs, public services and policing.

Azmi Bishara: Arab turnout denied Netanyahu a majority in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:32:22 UTC
15:32:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Azmi Bishara: Arab turnout denied Netanyahu a majority in Israeli election
Record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel was decisive in denying Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies the parliamentary majority needed to form a government, Arab intellectual Azmi Bishara said in an interview with Al-Araby TV from Lusail, Qatar, on Friday evening.
Bishara, director general of the Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies, analysed the results of the Israeli Knesset elections and responded to what he described as a Zionist campaign against both him and Qatar following the unprecedented Arab turnout.
In Bishara's reading, that turnout prevented Netanyahu's bloc from reaching the 61 seats required to form a government. He described Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the anti-Netanyahu camp, as "less bad than Netanyahu", while arguing that his bloc "does not offer a genuine alternative to the right".
The interview also touched on next Tuesday's US midterm elections. Bishara said a Democratic "blue wave" in the House of Representatives now appeared almost certain, while the contest for the Senate remained extremely tight.
At the same time, he cautioned that any U.S. decision to go to war with Iran would not depend on the outcome of the congressional elections. He reiterated what he had told the same channel the previous Thursday: an agreement with Iran would be better for Iran and the wider region because the current oscillation between war and peace was nearing its end, with relations between Tehran and Washington moving toward either war or an agreement.
Arab turnout defeated Netanyahu
Bishara focused at length on the 80% turnout among Arab citizens in Tuesday's election, arguing that this participation denied Benjamin Netanyahu and his camp the 61 seats required to form a government.
He said the most powerful force driving Arab citizens to vote in such unprecedented numbers was the government of Netanyahu and Itamar Ben-Gvir itself. Palestinian citizens of Israel, he said, had been shocked by the war of genocide in Gaza, by the repression they faced and by attempts to prevent them from expressing their position on the massacre.
This had created fear and deep frustration, Bishara said, and Arab citizens had been waiting for the election as an opportunity to express that anger and sense of grievance.
He added that what Netanyahu's government had done in Gaza and the West Bank, against Palestinian citizens inside Israel, and through its wars and crimes abroad "left no need for anyone to convince Arabs to turn out in large numbers".
Palestinian citizens of Israel had also come to feel that their citizenship and political legitimacy were genuinely under threat, he said. Their turnout therefore became a way of asserting their presence and exercising a form of citizenship that, in his view, stands in contradiction with Zionism.
Asked whether Arab citizens were better served by running on one, two or three electoral lists, Bishara said the priority was to maximise turnout regardless of how many lists contested the election.
He pointed to the fact that Arab parties had secured 19 seats through two separate lists.
Bishara said the result had sent the Israeli right into a frenzy, "to the point that its leading figures are now openly proclaiming apartheid slogans".
He said the most immediate parliamentary issue arising from the election result would be the election of the Knesset speaker.
This mattered to Arab citizens, Bishara said, because "it will be easier for Arab MPs to work in parliament if the Knesset speaker comes from outside Netanyahu's camp", adding that Yair Lapid could potentially take the post.
He again stressed that the main priority was to prevent Netanyahu from forming a coalition.
Bishara expressed regret that some elected Arab representatives, referring to the United Arab List, which won eight seats, were openly saying they would be prepared to work with a government led by Gadi Eisenkot in return for civil and economic services.
He argued that such gains had already been secured over previous decades. Bishara himself, he noted, had been a leading advocate for political and civil rights from within the Knesset over four consecutive terms without joining governments responsible for wars or apartheid.
In this context, Bishara stressed that most Arab votes had gone to the Joint List, "which may negotiate, but does not enter government coalitions".
The campaign against Qatar and me is 'sick fantasy'
Bishara said the unprecedented Arab turnout was driven by an "entirely political" cause.
Claims that American or Jewish organisations had played a role, or that money had been paid to increase turnout, were "nonsense", he said.
He described as "sick fantasy" the campaign being waged against him and Qatar by Israeli ministers, MPs and media figures who accused both him and Doha of playing a decisive role in the election result and in pushing Arab turnout towards the 80% mark.
Although he regarded the allegations as "sick fantasy", Bishara spent several minutes of the television interview responding to them.
What struck him most, he said, was the extent to which leading figures in the campaign, including Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli, were resorting to conspiracy theories to explain their defeat.
Bishara noted that "any genuinely democratic country, meaning not Israel", regards participation in elections as something fundamentally healthy.
He added that around 22 countries make voting compulsory and fine people who fail to take part, citing Australia and Belgium as examples.
Bishara said the level of what he described as delusion had reached the point where the Israeli magazine Makor Rishon, which is close to Netanyahu, claimed on Friday that Qatar was behind the current protests and unrest in France.
He described the claim as "hallucination, obsession and an outright lie".
Bishara said he simply did not have the time to run electoral campaigns because he was occupied with research, writing and the institutions he had founded.
He summed up his position by saying: "I am, of course, with my people, but I do not have time to run campaigns. A person should not retreat from their positions because of these campaigns. The mistake would be not to take these positions, not the opposite."
Asked why he and Qatar were being grouped together in the same Zionist campaign, Bishara said the idea was a baseless fantasy.
He suggested that the main reason for the campaign against Doha was Qatar's support for the Palestinian cause.
Possible scenarios
Turning to the possible scenarios after Tuesday's election failed to produce a clear winner, Bishara repeated what he had said in his previous interview with Al-Araby TV about US pressure to form a national unity government headed by Netanyahu and joined by Eisenkot and others from his camp.
That arrangement could potentially include Avigdor Lieberman, who previously served as director of Netanyahu's office before the two fell out.
Bishara said this option, aimed at avoiding another election, was also favoured by Israeli President Isaac Herzog.
He noted that Herzog had previously been a senior figure in the Labour Party and was known for signing shells that were later fired at Lebanon and Gaza.
Bishara said both the Netanyahu and Eisenkot camps were now trying to persuade individual politicians and parties to cross over from the opposing bloc.
Another possibility was to bring the opposition into a government headed by Netanyahu, perhaps under an arrangement in which the premiership would rotate after two years.
Netanyahu, he said, was meanwhile trying to persuade individual figures from the opposing camp to join him so that he could avoid the unwelcome prospect of sharing the premiership under a rotation deal.
Bishara cited ongoing contacts with the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party, which holds seven seats, as one example. Efforts were underway to persuade it to leave Netanyahu's camp and join an Eisenkot-led alliance.
If that happened, Bishara said, Eisenkot's bloc would reach 55 seats and achieve what he described as a clear Jewish majority.
Bishara then looked back to the period before the 1999 election to illustrate what he sees as the decline of the Zionist left.
The Labour Party, which won the 1999 election, secured only four seats in 2022, he said.
Now, even after allying with the left-wing Meretz party, it had secured only eight seats.
In Bishara's analysis, aside from those eight representatives of the Zionist left, virtually everyone else in the Knesset belonged to the right.
His conclusion was that the organised Zionist left had effectively disappeared, leaving only individual figures.
"Either the left must be non-Zionist or it will disappear," he said.
Within this context, Bishara described Eisenkot as "less bad than Netanyahu".
But, he argued, like Netanyahu's other rivals on the right, Eisenkot had failed to establish a stable political party or organisational structure.
Bishara cited Benny Gantz as another example. Gantz had once been the strongest opposition leader, yet his party failed to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold in Tuesday's vote.
Bishara argued that liberal right-wing forces, which he said did not fundamentally differ from Likud on Palestine or on the question of a just political settlement, had struggled to establish stable parties or coherent ideological structures precisely because they did not offer a genuine alternative to the right.
The only areas in which they offered a fundamentally different programme, he said, concerned lifestyle issues, personal freedoms and the powers of the judiciary.
"Apart from that, all their criticism of Netanyahu is either security-related or concerns the failure to draft the ultra-Orthodox into the army," Bishara said.
What awaits the region after the election
Addressing the potential regional impact of the election result, Bishara said Netanyahu's opponents did not reject his regional policies in principle, whether towards Iran, Lebanon or Syria.
Instead, he argued, their differences were mainly over the methods and form those policies should take.
On a possible war with Iran, Bishara said there would therefore be little difference between a Netanyahu government and one formed by the camp opposed to him.
He said, however, that some figures within the opposition had criticised Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Some within Eisenkot's camp might also be more willing to engage with the Palestinian Authority, Bishara said, although not to remove settlements, establish a Palestinian state or withdraw to the 1967 borders.
In Bishara's assessment, a government emerging from the anti-Netanyahu camp might take greater account of US alliances in the region than the current Israeli government does.
Life under such a government might also be somewhat less difficult for Palestinian citizens of Israel and for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, he said.
"But at the international level, a government emerging from the anti-Netanyahu camp could be more useful to Israel," Bishara said.
He argued that such a government would present a better international image than Israel's current position of growing isolation under a far-right government containing figures he described as "terrorists", including Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

Canada Pledges €500M Toward EU’s €90B Ukraine Loan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:32:00 UTC
15:32:00 KST

Canada will commit €500 million ($550 million) as an initial contribution to the EU’s planned €90 billion loan facility for Ukraine, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on Friday, Oct. 30.
Carney confirmed the financial commitment during a joint press briefing with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa at the 21st EU-Canada summit, news agency APA reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The arrangement leverages frozen Russian sovereign assets to supply Ukraine with non-budgetary military and reconstruction financing.
“With respect to the Ukraine loan, €500 million will be our initial participation,” Carney said.
“This is a very important and effective mechanism, and I actually commend the innovation of President von der Leyen, the Commission, and President Costa in creating this, using frozen assets to provide the much-needed financing for Ukraine.”
The Canadian prime minister described Ottawa’s entry into the European financing mechanism as a practical application of Canada’s association with the EU, characterizing the bilateral partnership as a “positive alliance”.
Defense procurement and Canadian arms purchases
Canada’s integration into the loan architecture establishes an operational channel for Ukrainian military procurement, enabling Kyiv to acquire military equipment directly from Canadian defense manufacturers utilizing European financial facilities.
Europe Launches $24 Billion Round of SAFE Funding, Focus on Ukraine
According to official summit background materials released by the Canadian government, the framework expands transatlantic defense-industrial cooperation while addressing acute materiel requirements along active combat sectors. The procurement mechanism connects Ukraine’s defense needs directly to Canadian industrial output across armored vehicles, sensory equipment, and drone systems.
The bilateral agreement coincided with a separate decision announced on Friday by the European Commission to advance the remaining €45 billion tranche under the broader €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan facility, locking in predictable multi-year financing for Kyiv through 2027.
In a joint summit communique, Carney, von der Leyen, and Costa reaffirmed their unconditional commitment to Ukraine’s sovereignty, political independence, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, vowing to intensify joint sanctions pressure against Moscow and pursue legal accountability for wartime aggression.
Bridging Kyiv’s €70B shortfall
The Canadian commitment arrives as European policymakers actively lobby international partners outside the European Unio to bridge Ukraine’s projected €70 billion ($77 billion) budgetary deficit for 2027.
With the EU and its constituent member states providing approximately 80 percent of all international external assistance flowing into Ukraine, Brussels has sought to avoid bearing the financial burden exclusively through European taxpayers.
European Commission President von der Leyen warned that international partners must accelerate contributions to prevent fiscal instability in Kyiv, pointing to uncertainties surrounding long-term defense authorizations in Washington.
The EU’s baseline €90 billion loan facility covers roughly two-thirds of Kyiv’s medium-term macro-financial requirements across 2026 and 2027. European officials had initially projected that non-EU democratic allies – including Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Norway – would collectively supply another €45 billion ($50 billion) to fully close the gap, though multilateral disbursements have experienced procedural delays.
Addressing the European Parliament, European Council President Costa emphasized that allied democracies must mobilize supplemental financing, while European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis highlighted Ukraine’s 2027 financing requirements during international monetary meetings in Bangkok.

NEW DELHI: The Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC) on Saturday expelled former party general secretary Kripa Alva for six years over her alleged involvement in a sting operation targeting Congress leaders in the state. The expulsion takes immediate effect, according to an order issued by KPCC vice-president M Narayanaswamy.The order said the controversy had caused embarrassment to the party because of negative publicity and media reactions. It also cited alleged anti-party activities as the reason for the disciplinary action.
"As your name has figured in this sting operation case and your conduct in the matter amounts to anti-party activities, on the instructions of the Hon'ble KPCC President, you are hereby expelled from the party for a period of six years with immediate effect," the order stated.According to the KPCC, a show-cause notice had previously been issued to Alva seeking her explanation over the allegations. However, the party said she had not submitted any response so far.The action comes amid an ongoing police investigation into a video allegedly targeting former Karnataka chief minister Siddaramaiah.Siddaramaiah had named her behind the 'defamatory video'. The Bengaluru police said on Thursday that the sexual abuse allegation featured in the video was part of a "fabricated and deliberately constructed narrative".
"The evidence gathered so far prima facie indicates that the allegations of sexual abuse portrayed in the video are part of a fabricated and deliberately constructed narrative," the police said in a statement.The police further said that statements recorded from individuals appearing in the video and the evidence collected so far did not substantiate the allegations."Their statements and the evidence collected so far, prima facie, with regard to the allegations made or implied in the recording about any individuals mentioned in the video, is false and concocted," the statement said.Investigators said the original mobile phone allegedly used to record the video had been traced, recovered and seized. It has been sent for forensic examination, with the report awaited.According to the police, the video was allegedly recorded in 2023 and purportedly concerned an incident dating back to 2011. Investigators are examining whether the recording was staged, fabricated or manipulated and are tracing its circulation before it appeared on social media in September-October 2026.The police also said the video was uploaded through anonymous accounts using VPNs, masked IP addresses and spoofed phone numbers. A mobile phone allegedly linked to the YouTube upload was traced to a shop dealing in used and refurbished devices in Delhi.
One person connected with the procurement of the device was arrested from the National Capital Region on October 24. Police said preliminary findings suggested that he worked as a freelance social media content creator and may have links with politically connected individuals in New Delhi. These associations are being investigated.Alva had earlier appeared before the Central Crime Branch (CCB) on October 26, where she was questioned and her statement recorded. Police sources quoted by news agency ANI said she had also been questioned on previous occasions.Siddaramaiah had named Alva in connection with the alleged sting operation and obtained a court injunction restraining media organisations from airing or publishing the video. His son and minister Yathindra Siddaramaiah had also alleged the involvement of some Congress leaders.The investigation remains ongoing, with police examining the video's creation, ownership, circulation and the identities and possible motives of those involved.

France to deploy 70,000 security personnel as it prepares for Halloween protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:31:22 UTC
15:31:22 KST

Mass protests are expected to sweep across France this Saturday, coinciding with Halloween celebrations as authorities deploy a major security operation.
Authorities in France are bracing for another potentially tense day of protests, with a source close to the country's Interior Ministry warning of a "very high risk of public disorder" on Saturday.
Around 70,000 police officers have been deployed nationwide as trade unions, students and yellow vest protesters take to the streets for a third consecutive weekend to march against the cost-of-living crisis and school conditions.
This comes days after the French government presented several policies addressing student grievances on Monday, which unions have branded as insufficient.
Authorities are rolling out a ramped-up security operation, as they did on 24 October, in response to the widespread violence and looting that overshadowed otherwise peaceful demonstrations on 17 October.
The source close to the Interior Ministry warned on Friday that "calls for undeclared gatherings in public squares across France have proliferated," along with "plans for unauthorised marches towards places of power and state institutions."
On Thursday, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez declared that protests in city centres had been banned and that only those "on the outskirts of cities" would be permitted. He added that organisers had been asked to "provide guarantees" that demonstrations would occur in "good conditions."
For their part, trade unions and the yellow vest movement have criticised these measures. In a joint statement issued on Wednesday, major unions said they would explore "all possible avenues of appeal against this general and disproportionate ban on the exercise of a public freedom that is essential in a democracy."
Halloween could heighten unrest
Nuñez also said on Thursday that the fact that protests coincided with Halloween could encourage unrest, which may run into the night. He warned that gatherings seeking to pass off as Halloween celebrations would be banned, while also calling out social media posts from groups including "ultra-left circles" that have urged individuals to back a "revolution" and "insurrection."
The heightened security measures come amid as human rights groups continue to accuse French law enforcement of using excessive force against protesters.
A number of law enforcement officers who were on leave had been called back to duty across France, while others have had their rest days cancelled.
Meanwhile, Paris police imposed a curfew on Saturday and Sunday night in districts that experienced significant unrest on 17 October.
The final route for the march in Paris on Saturday has been set for the eastern outskirts of the capital, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton, after the Council of State (Conseil d'État)overturned an administrative court's decision that had authorised a demonstration between Bastille and Nation.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party, said on Saturday that he would join protesters at Porte de Bagnolet.
"We want to uphold the right to demonstrate peacefully at a time when Macron’s government is drifting towards authoritarianism and the far right seeks to hold the country to ransom with threats of attacks," he wrote in a post on X.
France's student protest movement began in mid-September, after pupils staged demonstrations against school conditions in the Parisian suburbs. The movement rapidly spread nationwide, leading unions and political forces to join.
The demonstrations - which come around six months before France's presidential elections - have since expanded into a broader social movement against the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices.

Week in Brief: President’s vision for Kazakhstan, AI ambitions and Dimash’s concert in Türkiye
This week in Astana and beyond, Qazinform News Agency presents a roundup of the top headlines that shaped the past seven days in Kazakhstan.
1. From infrastructure to AI: President Tokayev’s vision for Kazakhstan in a changing world
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's October 28 state-of-the-nation address outlined a new phase in Kazakhstan's development, combining a 6.5 trillion tenge infrastructure program with plans to strengthen energy security, develop artificial intelligence and raise living standards.
2. Tokayev and Erdoğan highlight prospects for deeper cooperation
The heads of state noted the steady development of bilateral relations in the spirit of eternal friendship and an enhanced strategic partnership. Particular attention was paid to prospects for strengthening trade, economic, investment, cultural and humanitarian cooperation.
3. Kazakhstan to train renewable energy specialists with AI skills
A key focus is on digital competencies, with the draft standards covering skills in digital monitoring, automated control systems, production data analysis, and the use of artificial intelligence tools. The initiative is being carried out in line with Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov's directive to develop and approve 100 professional standards that incorporate artificial intelligence and digital skills.
4. Tokayev: Turkic world remains united and moves confidently toward its goals
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev addressed the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Ankara, emphasizing the unity, solidarity and shared goals of Turkic nations. He highlighted the importance of respecting national sovereignty and preserving their common cultural and spiritual heritage.
5. President Tokayev suggests declaring 2027 Year of Large-scale Construction
According to the President, key priorities include the construction of roads, airports, railway stations and healthcare facilities. Special attention will also be given to rehabilitation centers for children with special needs.
6. Tokayev says Kazakhstan must become a leading logistics hub in Eurasia
President Tokayev called for accelerating the development of Kazakhstan’s transport infrastructure to make the country a leading logistics hub in Eurasia. He highlighted major railway and road projects, noting that nearly 85% of freight transported from China to Europe already passes through Kazakhstan.
7. Team Kazakhstan captures gold, silver and bronze at Asian U23 Fencing Championships
Kazakhstan’s national fencing team won three medals at the Asian U23 Fencing Championships in Manama, Bahrain. Kirill Prokhodov claimed gold, Kaisha Zhanybek took silver, and Dilyara Issabekova secured bronze.
8. Kazakh archers claim gold at Asia Cup stage
Kazakhstan’s men’s compound archery team won gold at the Asia Cup stage in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq, defeating Bangladesh 230–224 in the final. The winning team comprised Nikita Ivlev, Pavel Kuznetsov, and Islam Serikuly.
9. Two Kazakhstani freestyle wrestlers make a winning start at World Championships in Astana
Kazakhstani freestyle wrestlers Sanzhar Doszhanov and Assyl Aitakyn won their opening bouts at the World Wrestling Championships in Astana. Doszhanov defeated Kenya’s Eugine Omulule 11-0, while Aitakyn beat Kyrgyzstan’s Omurbek Asan uulu 4-0 to advance to the round of 16.
10. Dimash performs at concert hosted by the Organization of Turkic States in Türkiye
Under the baton of conductor Cemi’i Can Deliorman, the Turkish Presidential Symphony Orchestra performed celebrated masterpieces from the world’s classical repertoire. The Ankara Arena was filled with the sounds of renowned works, including Nino Rota’s Parla più piano, Brindisi from Giuseppe Verdi’s opera La Traviata, Latif Khamidi’s Bulbul, and many others.

Trainer Nick Ryan accused of having banned substance after stable inspection on Derby Day
In short:
Flemington trainer Nick Ryan had two horses withdrawn from today's Derby Day after allegations that a banned substance and syringes were found in his car.
Anglaise (Wakeful Stakes) and Doubt Time (Coolmore Stud Stakes) were pulled out of the race meet at Flemington.
What's next?
Ryan, a former champion jockey, reserved his plea and the hearing was adjourned until Monday.
Flemington trainer Nick Ryan had two runners withdrawn from today's meeting after Racing Victoria (RV) stewards charged him with alleged possession of a prohibited substance.
Ryan was charged after a stable inspection this morning by RV's Compliance Assurance Team, which resulted in the forced scratchings of Anglaise (Wakeful Stakes) and Doubt Time (Coolmore Stud Stakes).
"Mr Ryan was found to have in his possession, in the glove box of his motor vehicle, two syringes of Darbepoetin Alfa which is a prohibited substance under Prohibited List A of the Australian Rules of Racing," RV stewards reported.
Ryan, a former champion jockey, reserved his plea and the hearing was adjourned until Monday.
Zahra overcomes fall to claim first Group 1 of Melbourne Cup Carnival
Mark Zahra has bounced back from his nasty fall to pilot The Next Episode to a brilliant victory in the stallion-making Coolmore Stud Stakes (1,200m) at Flemington.
The Ciaron Maher-trained colt stamped himself as the nation's premier three-year-old sprinter, finishing a long neck clear of Chris Waller's St Gotthard in the $2 million Group 1 sprint.
Mbube was third, with Under Focus fourth.
Zahra returned to action today just two weeks after a horror Caulfield Cup fall on Half Yours.
His win in the first Group 1 event of this year's Melbourne Cup carnival comes after his dominant showing with four victories on Victoria Derby day 12 months ago.
It was Zahra's third Coolmore Stud Stakes victory and second in as many years after his win aboard Tentyris last year.
"They're very similar horses. He's a real dude now, this horse," Zahra said.
"He's so relaxed, but when you want him he just goes 'bang'. It's great to be on two magnificent colts within two years."
Zahra took a week off under doctors' orders after his Caulfield Cup fall and missed Cox Plate day, but would not be denied another shot at Flemington glory.

"Any other time of year I'm probably having a holiday in Byron or Ibiza, but this time of year you just can't do it," Zahra said.
"I just had to suck it up. It's been a tough two weeks, but this time of year is what I live for and ride for.
"Great help by the doctors and with a few Nurofen today we're bang on song."
It was Maher's first Coolmore Stud Stakes victory. The master trainer paid tribute to close friend Zahra.
"He's a super jock, Mark," Maher said.
"He had the fall the other day, and to get up and be riding at the top of his game, they're marvellous, the jocks.
"Mark's a great mate and I'm sure we'll be popping the top off a couple of champagnes tomorrow."

Waller had the quinella with Unhinged, ridden by James McDonald, finishing second ahead of Conquer The World in third.
It is the sixth time Waller has won the traditional carnival opener, and third in succession after triumphs by Aeliana (2024) and Panova (2025).
Waller also claimed the Group 2 Wakeful Stakes with De Armas, ridden by Blake Shinn.
J-Mac, Waller combine for Victoria Derby win
James "J-Mac" McDonald and Waller combined for another major victory as Stormy Marco surged home to claim the $3 million Victoria Derby (2500m) at Flemington.
The three-year-old colt charged to the lead in the straight and raced away from second-placed Cold Shower for a stunning victory under McDonald in Australia's oldest classic.
Quick Finish was third as the first filly in the race since 1990, with Murshidi fourth.
It was a fourth Derby triumph for Waller and second for McDonald.

====================================================================================================

France aims for 'responsible' 2027 budget as Fitch downgrades outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:27:11 UTC
15:27:11 KST

The US rating agency doubts France's ability to sustainably restore its public finances after the 2027 presidential election, probably followed by parliamentary elections. The government, for its part, reiterates the "absolute necessity" of having a budget adopted by the end of the year.
Equipping France with a "responsible" budget for 2027 is the goal announced by the French government as bad economic news continues to mount.
Ratings agency Fitch has kept France's sovereign debt rating at A+, but has cut its outlook from "stable" to "negative", citing weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a bigger deficit than at its previous review last August.
This verdict comes after figures published by Insee on Friday morning showed that French gross domestic product fell by 0.1% in the third quarter, after stagnating in the second quarter and shrinking by 0.2% in the first.
To justify its decision (source in French), Fitch notably highlighted that "the persistence of political fragmentation" and "a difficult social climate", with the mass protests shaking the country, "further complicate the implementation of a lasting fiscal consolidation".
France's rating is nevertheless supported by "the size, wealth and diversification of its economy, the strength of its institutions, its membership of the euro area and the resilience of its banking sector".
"The absolute need to adopt a budget"
In a statement sent to the media on Friday evening, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said he "takes note" of the US agency's decision to lower France's outlook.
"This assessment confirms the absolute need to adopt by the end of the year a responsible budget that aims to restore the public finances by reducing our deficit to 5%", he continued, adding that the government was "determined to stay on a path of fiscal consolidation".
"In an uncertain international environment, it is imperative to give economic players visibility", the finance minister concluded.
Earlier in the day, reacting to the fall in GDP on Franceinfo, Roland Lescure had described the French economy as "at a standstill". He had also warned that the country would be heading "into the wall" if the "recovery" budget were not adopted.
"I am saying it, I repeat it and I will repeat it to the end: we need a budget, we need a budget deficit of 5% or less", he hammered home.
But the chances of the text being adopted by a parliamentary vote look more than uncertain, given the lack of a majority in the National Assembly and the approaching presidential election.
49.3, ordinances: Fitch expects a push-through
The political debates taking shape six months before the vote "have not significantly increased Fitch's confidence in the possibility of a lasting reduction in the deficit that could stabilise the debt", the agency notes.
"We believe that the budget should be adopted, thanks to the constitutional mechanisms available to the government despite the lack of a parliamentary majority", the Fitch analysts say.
In the event of deadlock in Parliament, Roland Lescure has indicated that the government does not rule out resorting to article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote unless a motion of no confidence is adopted. Another option would be to use ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
Speaking to Euronews, Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University, believes that a budget adopted by ordinance could reduce uncertainty in the short term, but would not restore long-term fiscal credibility.
"Markets generally prefer a contested decision to a prolonged absence of decision. But if a budget adopted by ordinance is seen as fragile, liable to be called into question after the presidential election or as revealing a lasting inability of the political system to build majorities, the positive effect on [investor] confidence could be limited", the researcher explains.

&quot;Machines are tools&quot;: Pope Leo calls for AI disarmament
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:25:23 EET
15:25:23 KST

"Machines are tools": Pope Leo calls for AI disarmament
Kyiv • UNN
Pope Leo XIV called on the UN to ban lethal autonomous weapons. He emphasized the need for mandatory human control over AI decisions.
Pope Leo XIV stated that AI systems should be "disarmed," adding that people "are responsible for guiding, changing and, when necessary, rejecting its application." UNN reports this with reference to The Verge.
Details
In his papal address on October 30, Pope Leo called on member states of the United Nations to "take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons" during their meeting in Geneva next month.
The address reflects many of the ideas Pope Leo laid out in his first major papal document in May, which highlighted "safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence." In line with his encyclical, Pope Leo tells participants that "Machines are tools, not persons," and warns about the dangers of granting AI systems rights or legal personhood. "Decisions affecting human life, freedom, and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed, and responsible human oversight," Pope Leo says.
In 2024, Pope Francis similarly called for a ban on autonomous weapons, stating: "No machine should ever decide to take a human life." Artificial intelligence has become a popular topic for Pope Leo, who says he chose his name because he must confront the development of technology—much as Pope Leo XIII led the Church on the front lines of the Industrial Revolution.
Pope Leo closes out his address by calling for international institutions to safeguard the common good from AI-related risks, along with "shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability so that decisions concerning the development and use of AI can be examined, challenged when necessary, and accompanied by appropriate remedies for any harm caused."

After Louvre heist and string of thefts, Europe’s smaller museums are on guard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:11:41 UTC
15:11:41 KST

After Louvre heist and string of thefts, Europe’s smaller museums are on guard
PARMA, Italy – Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cezanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.
Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million (S$12.9 million), to an accomplice and fled.
At the museum’s main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.
“Whatever could go wrong, did,” said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.
The raid was one of a string of museum thefts in France, Italy and Spain since 2025’s heist at the Louvre in Paris, raising concerns that criminals are increasingly targeting smaller institutions with fewer resources to protect valuable collections.
“This is where we see the ‘Louvre effect’,” said Marc Balcells, a Barcelona-based researcher specialising in crimes against cultural heritage.
“If the Louvre was so easy to rob, just imagine a tiny museum in a rural area or a smaller town.”
Works by Antonello da Messina vanished from a museum in his Sicilian hometown in August, while two Renoirs were stolen from Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera the following month.
In Spain, thieves stole hundreds of historic gold coins from museums in Badajoz and Albacete and made off with a Bronze Age treasure in Villena, near Alicante.
A 2024 survey by France’s Culture Ministry found only one in four cultural institutions had an emergency and risk-prevention plan, while nearly half lacked video surveillance.
Who checks when the alarm goes off?
A French parliamentary report in May said museums lacked the resources and preparation to adequately protect artworks and artefacts.
In Italy, the challenge is amplified by the way the country’s cultural heritage is spread across hundreds of towns and institutions, a legacy of centuries of fragmented rule.
“That is also what makes our system distinctive: Works remain in the places where they were created,” said Antonella Pinna, president of the Italian committee of the International Council of Museums. “But we need to make life harder for criminals.”
The council worked with Italy’s Culture Ministry and the Carabinieri on museum security guidelines published in 2015, but Pinna said technology alone was not enough.
“If an alarm goes off, someone has to make sure it is checked,” she said.
In a narrow street in the Tuscan town of Sansepolcro, the civic museum displays four works by Renaissance master Piero della Francesca, born just steps away in the 15th century.
The Louvre theft “affected us deeply because cultural heritage is central to Sansepolcro’s identity. It is our soul”, culture councillor Francesca Mercati told Reuters.
After the Louvre raid, officers from the Carabinieri’s cultural heritage protection unit recommended more cameras, longer retention of CCTV footage and tighter controls on bags and bulky clothing.
“We immediately implemented those recommendations,” Mercati said.
A vast network to protect
The scale of the challenge is daunting.
Italy has more than 4,400 museums and similar institutions, according to national statistics agency ISTAT.
Spain has about 1,500 museums, while France has more than 1,200 institutions carrying the official “Musees de France” designation, alongside hundreds of smaller collections.
Protecting such a broad network is particularly difficult for smaller institutions that depend on local funding.
Florence Imbert, a Paris-based security consultant for cultural institutions, said 85% of small French museums were run by the local authorities with limited financial resources.
“The budget is key to winning the war,” she said.
France’s Culture Ministry announced a 33-point security plan in July, backed by €30 million over three years for local museums.
Recent figures suggest concern is warranted.
The Carabinieri art squad recorded 17 thefts from Italian museums and galleries in 2025, up from 14 a year earlier.
Europol said in an August report that museum thefts were becoming more forceful and increasingly focused on precious metals, gemstones and other high-value artefacts.
A fast buck?
Unlike gold or jewellery, which can be broken up or melted down, a well-known painting is difficult to turn into quick cash.
Celebrated works such as those by Renoir can rarely be sold openly, Pinna said. Instead, stolen art is more likely to be hidden, used as leverage in ransom attempts or offered privately.
Even when works are recovered, museums can face significant costs linked to investigations, recovery efforts and upgraded security.
The recent thefts have also reignited debate about insurance.
Most major state-backed museums in Western Europe rely on government indemnity schemes rather than commercial cover, but some institutions have begun reassessing the risks, said Filippo Guerrini-Maraldi, a private wealth and fine art insurance specialist at broker Howden Specialty.
“And for the first time, really, in my 40-year career, I’ve seen art theft now becoming more of a major, major risk. It was always the minor risk,” he said.
Insurers are also turning to technology.
Beazley is exploring how AI can be used to analyse CCTV footage to identify suspicious behaviour in museums and galleries, helping security staff spot threats sooner, said fine art underwriter Dishni Mahendran.
Security vs access
For museum directors and cultural officials, the challenge is how to tighten security without cutting collections off from local communities or diminishing the visitor experience.
“Ultimately, museums must remain easy to access,” Imbert said. “People should be able to enter without having to pass through 50 security checks.”
Julien Volper, a conservator at Belgium’s Africa Museum, said particularly vulnerable treasures should only be displayed when adequate security measures are in place.
“I’m not saying that’s the ultimate solution, but it seems better than displaying replicas,” he said. “We’re not at Disneyland.”
In August, the Carabinieri recovered the three artworks stolen from the Parma museum from a cardboard box hidden in an apartment. Five Moldovan nationals were arrested in connection with the theft.
Investigators said wiretaps indicated the suspects had unsuccessfully tried to find buyers in Eastern Europe and Russia.
The works have since returned to the museum in what Roffi called a “homecoming party”.
“The theft triggered an outpouring of solidarity in Italy and abroad,” he said. The museum now has round-the-clock guards funded by a local cheese consortium.
“It was seen not simply as a theft from a museum, but as an attack on art as a shared cultural heritage.” REUTERS
