Erdoğan’s Veiled Message to Aliyev Amid Growing Rift as Kazakhstan Proposes Inviting Russia Into Turkic Bloc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:51:36 UTC
12:51:36 KST

“May Almighty Allah never leave you at the mercy of the treacherous.”
With those words attributed to the legendary Dede Qorqud, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan concluded Friday’s summit of Turkic leaders in Ankara – a gathering marked by the absence of Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev amid growing tensions between two countries traditionally described as “one nation, two states.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Erdoğan, known for using public speeches to convey political messages, chose a traditional blessing from a figure deeply respected in both Turkey and Azerbaijan.
He wished that mountains would never collapse, trees would never be cut down, rivers would never run dry and swords would never break in battle.
But it was the prayer’s final line, invoking protection from the treacherous, that carried particular resonance amid the growing rift between Ankara and Baku.
Was Erdoğan indirectly warning Aliyev about the partners on whom Azerbaijan has chosen to rely?
One possible reading points to Israel, whose close military, security and energy relationship with Azerbaijan contrasts sharply with Erdoğan’s position toward the Israeli government.
Erdoğan had personally invited Aliyev to the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS). Instead, the Azerbaijani president remained in Baku to attend a FIFA youth football awards ceremony, sending Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov in his place.
Poland Calls for Urgent Black Sea Ceasefire, Demands Fair Peace for Ukraine
In his remarks, Erdoğan appealed for unity, declaring that there was no room for division or discord within the Turkic family.
A dialogue without naming names
The apparent exchange of messages began weeks earlier.
Speaking at the ruling New Azerbaijan Party’s congress on Oct. 2, Aliyev declared that his country would not tolerate outside interference.
“We need no one’s help or patronage,” he said, insisting that no country had helped Azerbaijan when it needed assistance.
He also claimed that Azerbaijan had purchased every weapon it used, sometimes paying several times the market price.
Aliyev did not name Turkey. But the remarks came amid growing criticism from Turkish political and religious circles over Azerbaijan’s restrictions on headscarves in schools.
The dispute escalated when Azerbaijan declared 31 Turkish nationals persona non grata over criticism posted on social media.
Erdoğan reportedly attempted to contain the controversy, including by dismissing an adviser who had publicly criticized Baku.
Nevertheless, Aliyev skipped the summit despite Erdoğan’s invitation.
His absence became particularly significant because Turkey was taking over the organization’s rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan.
A victory Aliyev does not want to share
The headscarf controversy may have dominated headlines, but another source of resentment lies in competing narratives surrounding Azerbaijan’s victory in Karabakh.
For Aliyev, the military victory has become the defining achievement of his presidency.
Yet Turkey’s support was crucial. Ankara provided military training, defense equipment, political backing and diplomatic support during Azerbaijan’s confrontation with Armenia.
In July 2024, Erdoğan sparked anger in Baku by invoking Turkey’s involvement in Karabakh and Libya while discussing possible action against Israel.
“Just as we entered Karabakh, just as we entered Libya,” Erdoğan said.
Azerbaijan’s Defense Ministry responded by insisting that no foreign military personnel had participated in its combat operations.
The exchange exposed an uncomfortable disagreement over who could claim credit for the victory.
Azerbaijani troops fought the war, but Turkey’s contribution went well beyond commercial arms sales.
In his Oct. 2 speech, Aliyev reinforced his preferred narrative.
“We stood alone,” he declared, adding that Azerbaijan had purchased its weapons “down to the last bullet.”
He also claimed that suppliers had sometimes charged prices several times higher than international rates.
There is, however, a difference between paying for military equipment and having an ally willing to provide it, alongside training, political backing and diplomatic support.
For many Azerbaijanis, recognizing Turkey’s role does not diminish their country’s victory.
But Aliyev’s insistence that Azerbaijan accomplished everything alone raises a political question: Is he reluctant to share the defining achievement of his presidency with Erdoğan?
A victory acknowledged as a joint strategic achievement would inevitably give Turkey a place in the historical narrative – something Aliyev’s increasingly personalized portrayal of Karabakh leaves little room for.
Why distancing Azerbaijan from Turkey is difficult
Aliyev faces a particular challenge in diminishing Turkey’s contribution: the relationship between the two peoples is older and deeper than either president.
Turkey was the first country to recognize Azerbaijan’s independence in 1991. It closed its border with Armenia in 1993 in solidarity with Baku during the first Karabakh war and maintained that position for more than three decades.
For many Azerbaijanis, Turkey’s importance is rooted in shared language, culture, history and a longstanding sense of brotherhood.
That attachment cannot easily be redefined by government messaging.
Pro-government arguments that Azerbaijan paid for Turkish weapons do not erase Ankara’s political and military support.
Nor does criticism of Aliyev from Turkey necessarily amount to hostility toward Azerbaijan.
Attempts to minimize Ankara’s contribution risk deepening the divide between the government’s narrative and Azerbaijanis who remain grateful for Turkey’s historical support.
The Karabakh victory can be both an Azerbaijani military achievement and a success made possible, in part, by Turkey’s strategic partnership. The two are not mutually exclusive.
Armenia moves closer to Turkey as Baku looks elsewhere
The growing friction comes as Armenia, Azerbaijan’s longtime adversary, is pursuing closer relations with Ankara.
Turkey and Armenia have been negotiating the reopening of their shared border, closed in 1993.
Turkey has linked normalization to progress in Armenian-Azerbaijani peace efforts. Yet the diplomatic contrast is striking: Armenia is seeking closer engagement with Turkey while Aliyev publicly distances himself from Erdoğan.
Another unexpected development came on Oct. 23, when Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Baku – the first such visit in eight years.
Aliyev personally received Jaishankar, whose country has supplied weapons to Armenia and has historically had strained relations with Azerbaijan because of Baku’s close ties with Pakistan.
The talks on expanded cooperation raise questions about Aliyev’s priorities as relations with Turkey, Azerbaijan’s closest strategic ally, grow strained.
Israel adds another layer of tension
Azerbaijan’s close partnership with Israel remains another sensitive issue.
Erdoğan has emerged as one of Israel’s fiercest critics over the war in Gaza, while Aliyev maintains extensive defense, intelligence and energy ties with Israel.
Baku insists it has the right to choose its strategic partners, regardless of Ankara’s objections. In a Jan. 5 interview, Aliyev defended his government’s position, arguing that Palestine had failed to support Azerbaijan during its conflict with Armenia.
“With all due respect and sympathy for Palestine, Palestine did not particularly protect us either,” he said.
His remarks echoed accusations in Azerbaijani political circles that Palestinian leaders had sided with Armenia.
The partnership has also given Aliyev influential allies in Washington, where pro-Israel advocacy groups have backed his government despite concerns about its human rights record.
Israeli military technology has played an important role in Azerbaijan’s military development.
Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR has also faced repeated protests in Turkey over Azerbaijani oil reaching Israel through the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline, despite Ankara’s ban on direct trade with Israel.
Russia enters the picture
Friday’s summit produced another unexpected development.
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed inviting Russia to participate in the Organization of Turkic States through its OTS+ format or as an observer.
Tokayev cited Russia’s historical ties with Turkic peoples and argued that cooperation with Moscow could strengthen the organization.
No agreement was announced, and Russian President Vladimir Putin received no formal invitation.
The proposal was particularly notable given Russia’s continuing invasion of Ukraine and Moscow’s longstanding efforts to preserve its influence across the former Soviet space.
As Turkey ties cool, Aliyev moves closer to Moscow
The growing distance between Baku and Ankara comes as Aliyev’s government appears to be rebuilding its relationship with the Kremlin, following a period of tensions over the downing of an Azerbaijani passenger aircraft by Russian air defenses on Dec. 25, 2024.
On April 15, 2026, Azerbaijan and Russia issued a joint statement declaring that they had reached a settlement over the consequences of the crash, including compensation. The two governments pledged to deepen cooperation within what they described as their allied relationship.
A more revealing development followed on Oct. 16.
Speaking at Russian Energy Week in Moscow (an event attended by Putin), Elshad Nasirov, vice president of Azerbaijan’s state energy company SOCAR, announced that Baku intended to resume purchasing natural gas from Russia’s Gazprom.
“We can proudly say that our cooperation with such a giant company as Gazprom is a very good example,” Nasirov said, according to Russia’s state-run TASS news agency.
The announcement coincided with a significant shift in Washington’s Russia sanctions policy. On the same day, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving sanctions and tariffs under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
For years, Azerbaijan has sought to establish itself as an alternative energy supplier to Europe, helping reduce the continent’s dependence on Russian gas.
The political implications extend beyond energy.
For years, Azerbaijan’s participation in the Turkic world provided Aliyev with a diplomatic alternative to Russian-led integration projects, including the Eurasian Economic Union and its customs arrangements. Baku could cultivate strong relations with Moscow without formally joining Russia-dominated economic structures.
The Organization of Turkic States offered another political center of gravity, with Turkey as Azerbaijan’s principal strategic partner.
Now, as Aliyev’s relationship with Erdoğan cools and cooperation with Moscow gains renewed momentum, that balance appears to be shifting.

US execution survivor Christa Pike says she is now in ‘constant pain’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:42:14 UTC
12:42:14 KST

US execution survivor Christa Pike says she is now in ‘constant pain’
Pike, 50, is being held in solitary confinement and faces an uncertain future after surviving a failed lethal injection.
An American woman who survived an execution in a Tennessee prison has spoken out for the first time.
In a statement released via her legal team on Friday, Christa Pike, 50, said she is now in constant pain and struggling to speak.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike said, adding that the pain is both “physical and emotional”.
“I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” Pike said.
Pike and her boyfriend tortured, stabbed and beat a 19-year-old classmate to death in 1995. As Pike was 18 at the time, she was handed the death sentence.
The victim’s mother travelled from Florida to witness Pike’s execution.
Pike said she “continues to think” about the victim’s family and the “terrible pain and loss they have endured”.
Pike’s lawyers say the two separate doses of the lethal drug phenobarbital administered to her on September 30 may have failed to kill her because the drug did not enter her bloodstream. Instead, it pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.
Pike was hospitalised and unconscious for days following the botched execution.
Despite her ordeal, Pike remains scheduled to die, and is being held in solitary confinement in the interim.
Her legal team has asked a federal judge to allow her to interact with other prisoners, saying her isolation in the wake of the failed execution has caused “significant psychological harm and trauma”.
Her legal team has also asked Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee to change her sentence to life in prison.
Last week, however, Lee told reporters that he “suspects” her sentence will be the same as before, “unless otherwise determined by the courts”.
The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.
The Tennessee governor has organised an independent review of the failed execution and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled for this year.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike’s failed execution.

Day of reflection in Bulgaria ahead of presidential runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:39:34 UTC
12:39:34 KST

Saturday 31 October 2026 05:00
Saturday, 31 October 2026, 05:00
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
October 31 is the official day of reflection ahead of the runoff in Bulgaria's presidential and vice-presidential elections. Election campaigning and the publication of opinion polls related to the vote are prohibited on this day.
Voters have just a few hours remaining to decide which of the two presidential tickets that made it to the runoff they will support. Both were nominated by initiative committees.
With voter turnout standing at 22.98% in the first round, Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev received 528,951 votes (34.76%), while Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev secured the support of 486,232 voters (31.95%). The October 25 first round saw an unprecedentedly low turnout, with only 1,525,034 of the 6,584,025 eligible voters casting their ballots in Bulgaria and abroad. There are hopes that the two presidential tickets will succeed in boosting turnout in the runoff and attracting new supporters.
The main issues concerning Bulgarian society during the election campaign were the role of the presidential institution in the country's governance, security amid the ongoing war in Ukraine, relations with Russia, and Bulgaria's policies within the EU and NATO. The incidents involving the sinking of merchant ships near the Bulgarian coast have heightened concerns over security in the Black Sea. The rising cost of living, low incomes and the 2027 state budget have also been sources of concern for voters.
Designed to serve as a mediator and balancing force between the three main branches of government - the legislative, executive and judicial - the presidency holds consultations with parliamentary groups and hands out mandates to form a government. If the parties represented in parliament fail to agree on a government, the Constitution gives the head of state a key role in forming a caretaker cabinet.
In the first round of the presidential election, a candidate ticket must receive more than half of the votes cast, provided that voter turnout exceeds 50%, to be declared the winner. In the runoff, however, the winner is the candidate who receives the highest number of votes, regardless of voter turnout.

Georgia Senate race has Jewish voters weigh Ossoff's Israel criticism, Collins' far-right ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:39:23 UTC
12:39:23 KST

Georgia Jews will choose between a Democratic politician who wants to limit arms sales to Israel and a Republican with ties to white nationalists when they head to vote Tuesday in a Senate race that will help determine which party controls the chamber.
The race pits incumbent Jewish Sen. Jon Ossoff, widely expected to be a 2028 presidential contender, against GOP Rep. Mike Collins. The Republican challenger has received a good deal of media attention, as well as attacks by his opponent, over family members’ and former employees’ far-right political views. Ossoff, meanwhile, sparked outrage among some in the Jewish community when he became one of the earliest Senate Democrats to vote to halt certain arms sales to Israel.
Collins’ son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, has invoked the Jewish Bolsheviks conspiracy theory propagated by Nazi Germany that blamed Jews for atrocities committed by the Soviet Union. He has also complained about Holocaust education and media on the subject.
“They don’t tell us the history of Germany before World War II,” Scheer said in a YouTube video last year, titled “I’m NOT a Judeo-Christian.”
He continued, “All we’re told is Germany bad, Hitler evil, don’t ask questions. Holocaust, Holocaust, Holocaust. Here’s 50 movies every year about the Holocaust and why it’s so bad.”
Collins' son-in-law promotes antisemitic conspiracy theories
In the same video, Scheer also said that “Jewish executives run the entire mainstream media complex” as well as “homosexual propaganda, they run all of the fraudulent banking systems and insurance scams. They are behind this orchestrated downfall of what was once the most prosperous nation in the world.” Israeli newspaper Haaretz has reported that Scheer apparently lives in a house built on property owned by Collins.
The Collins campaign did not return the Jewish Telegraphic Agency’s request for comment. Elsewhere, Collins has addressed Scheer’s statements, saying, “I don’t believe or support those views.”
Scheer did not respond to a request for comment.
Meanwhile, a former Collins staffer had posted Nazi imagery and an image of what appeared to be himself in KKK robes, The Washington Post reported in August. Collins replaced another staffer, his chief of staff Kip Talley, in 2024 after Slate reported that he was in a group chat with streamer Nick Fuentes, widely accused of being one of the internet’s foremost antisemites, and white supremacist Richard Spencer. Slate reported that the chat was dedicated to trying to help Charles Johnson, who has been accused of promoting Holocaust denial and was in jail at the time.
In a statement, Talley told Slate that he acted “solely in my personal capacity after hearing concerns that an acquaintance I have known for years was being mistreated in custody and denied basic medical care.”
The Georgia congressman also appeared at last year’s New York Young Republican Club gala, which drew controversy as it hosted white nationalists and a number of officials from Germany’s far-right AfD party. Fuentes said that he received an invitation that was later rescinded, and Jewish New York City Council member Inna Vernikov backed out of the event and suggested the decision was connected to antisemitism on the right.
Collins has responded to questions about his connections to these white nationalist elements by saying he condemns “all forms of antisemitism” and hate, and citing his support for Israel.
J Street targets Collins' far-right ties in $3 million campaign
J Street, the liberal Jewish Middle East advocacy group, homed in on Collins’ far-right connections in a 15-second ad released last week that ended with the message, “Mike Collins: Dangerously extreme for Georgia.”
The attack ad was the first released in J Street’s $3 million campaign this year to take down six Republican candidates who are backed by the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC. In a piece for the Atlanta Jewish Times, Collins wrote earlier this month that he supports Israel “because my faith tells me to and because it is the right policy for America.”
Ossoff, meanwhile, has long targeted Collins over his white nationalist ties, calling him a “notorious bigot, antisemite and extremist” in June. Ossoff told Collins during a debate that he “hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office.”
The quip drew some pushback. “Jon Ossoff, my advice to him is, if you start calling your political opponents Nazis, maybe it’s time to shut up,” said The Atlantic’s center-right staff writer David Brooks, during a PBS NewsHour conversation about personal attacks in this year’s US Senate races. “That’s just not what we do here in this country.”
Collins' Jewish supporters raise concerns over Ossoff's Democratic Party ties
Meanwhile, Collins’ Jewish supporters have said that Ossoff’s status as a Democrat, a party that increasingly includes strident anti-Zionist voices, is more damning than the headlines around Collins.
“At a time of rising antisemitism, at a time when Jewish Americans need friends, Mike Collins has been a friend to the Jewish community,” Sam Markstein, spokesperson for the Republican Jewish Coalition, told JTA. He said that Collins was “a friend to the Jewish community in the aftermath of Oct. 7” and pointed to his voting record on Israel.
Eric Levine, an RJC board member, said he has not been involved in this particular race but that extremes “must be condemned” on both sides.
“It is never a good thing to have ties to antisemitic/far-right figures,” he told JTA in a text. “I will also say, it is never a good thing to have ties to antisemitic/far left figures like Hasan Piker, [New York Mayor] Zohran Mamdani, [Michigan Senate candidate] Abdul el-Sayed and much of the DSA/Democratic caucus.”
Piker, an anti-Israel streamer who has campaigned with some left-wing Democratic candidates, has drawn heat for remarks about American Jews’ connection to Israel. Earlier this year, he named Ossoff positively as a “dark horse” contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. Ossoff later distanced himself from Piker and has said he will not run for president in 2028. Ossoff endorsed El-Sayed after he won the Democratic nomination in Michigan.
Ossoff faces criticism over votes to block arms sales to Israel
Ossoff has also come under fire for his decision to vote to block certain arms sales to Israel during the height of the Gaza war in November 2024, a position that he has generally stuck to since then.
In July 2025 he voted to block a sale of rifles to Israel, citing mass starvation in Gaza caused by “the policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government,” but voted against a resolution that would block an air-to-ground munitions sale.
Ossoff wrote at that time that the US “must continue to support the Israeli people, who face the persistent threat of rocket and missile attack and have been subjected to intense aerial bombardment from Iran, Lebanon, and Yemen.”
Though Ossoff called his commitment to Israel’s security “ironclad” in a Senate floor speech ahead of the arm sales vote, some Jewish voters and organizations said it rang hollow.
Michael Morris, publisher of the Atlanta Jewish Times, penned an open letter this August blasting Ossoff for “lying to me and your constituents” about his support for Israel.
Ossoff’s first vote against weapons in November 2024 spurred another critical letter from several Georgia Jewish organizations, including synagogues, Jewish schools, the local Anti-Defamation League chapter, and other groups. His vote also drew the attention of AIPAC, which released 30-second ads attacking US senators, including Ossoff, who had voted to block weapons sales.
Asked about Collins’ far-right ties, Morris told JTA he did not believe they were disqualifying.
“Most of the complaints about him are about his son-in-law who is a virulent antisemite,” Morris said in a text. “But his son-in-law does not get to vote, and as a father of 4 girls I can tell you that we do not get ANY say in who our girls marry, so from that standpoint, I am not concerned.”
Morris also said that neither President Donald Trump nor President Joe Biden condemned the most extreme among their voters, and opined that when it comes to Collins’ own extreme backers, he “can maintain their support without taking in their position.”
Jewish readers push back on Ossoff criticism, raise concerns over Collins
A number of readers disagreed with Morris’ sharp criticism of Ossoff, however, and wrote letters to the editor expressing their disapproval, as well as their concern about Collins.
“Mike Collins has peddled antisemitism. He has surrounded himself with bigotry while refusing to denounce white supremacy,” wrote a reader named Richard Mitchell, who said he is from Atlanta. “These values do not represent Georgians and are fundamental to why I will not be supporting Collins this election.”
Halie Soifer, CEO of the Jewish Democratic Council of America, which has endorsed Ossoff, wrote in a statement to JTA that her organization recognizes Ossoff’s “steadfast support for Israel’s security and future as a Jewish and democratic state.”
“Georgia voters should remember that a vote for Mike Collins is a vote for Donald Trump, and Collins is one of the most extreme candidates on the ballot,” she wrote.

'Credibility rests on even-handedness': India flags politicisation of UNHRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:35:25 UTC
12:35:25 KST

First secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, Bhavika Mangalanandan
NEW DELHI: India has said the credibility of the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) depends on “even-handedness”, warning that country-specific mandates pursued without the involvement of the concerned nation deepen divisions rather than improve human rights conditions on the ground.Addressing the United Nations General Assembly's debate on the Human Rights Council's report on Friday, First Secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, Bhavika Mangalanandan, called for dialogue, cooperation and equal treatment of all countries in addressing human rights concerns.
She said country-specific mandates pursued without the engagement of the country concerned seldom improve conditions on the ground and instead create divisions within the council.
“Credibility of the council rests on even-handedness. Country-specific mandates pursued without the engagement of the country concerned seldom improve the situation on the ground,” she said.Recalling external affairs minister S Jaishankar's remarks at the high-level segment of the 61st Human Rights Council in February, Mangalanandan said human rights should be advanced through dialogue and genuine partnerships rather than selective approaches.
Jaishankar had said that “human rights are best advanced through dialogue, capacity building and genuine partnerships, and not by politicisation, selectivity, or double standards.”Mangalanandan said such an approach was necessary for the council to speak with one voice and address allegations that human rights were being weaponised.She also identified the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), which involves cooperation and engagement with member states while treating all countries equally, as the appropriate platform for assessing human rights records.
India calls for equal emphasis on all human rights
India also stressed that economic, social and cultural rights, along with the right to development, should receive the same attention as civil and political rights.“Economic, social, and cultural rights and the right to development deserve the same attention as civil and political rights,” Mangalanandan said.She noted that poverty, debt and limited access to financing and technology remained major obstacles to the enjoyment of human rights across much of the developing world.“These call for international cooperation and not coercion,” she said.India also flagged terrorism as one of the gravest threats to human rights, particularly the fundamental right to life, and called on the council to maintain sustained attention to the issue.“We would encourage the council to give this threat the sustained attention it warrants on the basis of zero tolerance,” she said.
India raises concerns over funding and duplication of mandates
Mangalanandan said the Human Rights Council should fulfil its mandate within the resources available to it and called for transparent, member-driven rationalisation of its work.She cautioned against budgetary measures disproportionately affecting mandates dealing with development and economic, social and cultural rights.“Rationalisation should remain member-driven and transparent. It should not fall disproportionately on mandates that address development and economic, social, and cultural rights,” she said.
India also called for adequate and predictable funding for the UN's human rights pillar through the regular budget, arguing that its priorities should not be determined by earmarked voluntary contributions.Mangalanandan further flagged duplication between resolutions and initiatives taken up by the Human Rights Council and the UN General Assembly.“We should consider mechanisms that avoid resolutions and initiatives on the same topic and of similar nature, both in the Council and (General) Assembly."We see an increasing tendency for the Council to dictate reporting to the Third Committee, including reporting by Special Rapporteurs, which further undermines the need for a specialised Council,” she said.The Third Committee of the UN General Assembly deals with social, humanitarian and cultural issues.India returned to the Human Rights Council in 2026 for its seventh term, covering the 2026-28 period.

Protests erupt outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal amid leadership dispute
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:16:52 CST
12:16:52 KST

Police stand guard outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, Poland, Oct. 30, 2026. Protesters clashed with police outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw on Friday night after the court's president was suspended amid an escalating dispute between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and the opposition over control of the judiciary. (Photo by Neil Milton/Xinhua)
WARSAW, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Protesters clashed with police outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw on Friday night after the court's president was suspended amid an escalating dispute between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and the opposition over control of the judiciary.
Police detained three protesters who entered the court's premises. Several people were reportedly injured, according to local media.
Hundreds of demonstrators, including supporters of the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, gathered outside the tribunal, accusing Tusk's government of attempting to seize control of the court. PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki were among those present.
The confrontation followed months of disputes over judicial appointments. Poland's parliament, where Tusk's ruling coalition holds a majority, has elected eight judges to the tribunal this year. However, President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the opposition PiS party, accepted the oaths of office of only three.
The remaining five took their oaths at parliamentary ceremonies, but Nawrocki and the tribunal's president refused to recognize their status, preventing them from taking up their judicial duties.
On Friday evening, the tribunal's website announced that its president and vice president had been suspended for one month, with a newly elected judge whose status remains disputed assuming temporary leadership. The tribunal's leadership rejected the move, accusing those involved of illegally taking over its website and describing the action as a "coup."
Nawrocki cut short his trip to Senegal and returned to Poland, where he held an emergency meeting with judicial officials late Friday. Shortly after midnight, he visited the Constitutional Tribunal and entered the court building. ■

California governor announces "strike team" to coordinate 2028 Olympics preparations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:16:22 CST
12:16:22 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom announced Friday that he had signed an executive order creating a state coordination team to oversee preparations for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Los Angeles.
The governor appointed Jamie Callahan, his deputy chief of staff and senior counselor on infrastructure, to serve as executive director of the Games' delivery and coordination "strike team."
The team will bring together more than a dozen state agencies and departments to strengthen statewide planning and readiness ahead of the Games, the governor's office said in a statement. The team will also support regional efforts to expand workforce and economic opportunities, it added.
"California knows how to deliver on the world stage," Newsom said. "With the Olympics and Paralympics coming to Los Angeles in 2028, we're making sure our state is ready to meet the moment."
The Games are projected to cost 7.2 billion U.S. dollars, the Los Angeles Times reported, adding that the city is responsible for upgrading its transportation infrastructure to accommodate the influx of visitors.
According to the governor's office, California has already taken steps to support Los Angeles in preparing to host the world, including infrastructure investments to strengthen the region's transportation networks and modernize major venues.
State officials described the projects as investments intended to continue to benefit residents after the competitions end, not solely to accommodate visitors during the Games.
Security planning also involves multiple levels of government. The California Office of Emergency Services will help coordinate police assistance from across California and the western United States, while the U.S. Secret Service has ultimate security authority, the Los Angeles Times reported.
The announcement follows legislation Newsom signed in September to strengthen public safety coordination and address operational needs of the Games.
The Los Angeles Olympics are scheduled for July 14-30, 2028, followed by the Paralympics on Aug. 15-27, according to the Olympics' official website. Los Angeles previously hosted the Olympics twice, in 1932 and 1984. ■

Judge orders Trump administration to cease threats to prosecute election officials
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:11:58 CET
12:11:58 KST

By Kanishka Singh
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - A US judge ordered the Justice Department on Friday to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration’s demands related to voting by alleged non-citizens.
The ruling comes days before next week’s US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Although several key races appear closely contested, polls favor Democrats to take control of the House and give them a plausible chance of a Senate majority.
In the months leading up to the midterms, President Donald Trump’s administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, such as pressing states for voter-registration data, saying stricter measures are needed to ensure election security and public confidence in the vote.
But the Justice Department went too far this month when it threatened to prosecute state and county officials who do not cooperate with the Trump administration’s election-related initiatives, US District Judge Trina Thompson ruled in connection with a lawsuit brought by election workers’ unions and some other groups.
“Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the Elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs’ favor,” Thompson wrote in her temporary restraining order.
The Justice Department had no immediate comment on the ruling.
Critics, including political experts as well as Democratic and some Republican election officials, have viewed the Trump administration’s moves as federal overreach. Some election officials have told Reuters they were preparing for potential federal interference in the midterm elections.
Thompson, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, ordered the Trump administration to refrain from demanding that local election officials remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or segregate ballots cast in the midterm elections, based on a Trump administration list of alleged non-citizen voters.
Trump has made false claims related to elections in the past, including not acknowledging his defeat in the 2020 election.
(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Tom Hogue)

WOVEN BAMBOO pairs with CROCHETED TEXTILES IN CHAIR SCULPTURE
Designed by Peiyang (Camille) Li, She Blooms in the Dark is a glowing seating sculpture that examines emotional vulnerability and protective spatial thresholds. The project pairs hand-crocheted textile craft with traditional bent-wood furniture techniques, mounting an array of individual blossoms across the open-lattice framework of an oversized, woven bamboo armchair.
SHE BLOOMS IN THE DARK: Day Time View | all images ©Kexin Liu
UV-REACTIVE YARN BLOOMS STORE DAYLIGHT TO EMIT AMBIENT GLOW
The sculptural seat by designer Peiyang (Camille) Li functions simultaneously as a functional chair and a semi-enclosed personal retreat, utilizing a curved, basket-like silhouette to delineate an intimate interior microclimate for solitary reflection. Each floral element is crocheted by hand using phosphorescent, UV-reactive yarn engineered to absorb daylight and emit a soft, low-intensity glow in dark environments. By forgoing high-output electric fixtures in favor of photoluminescent fibers, the textile piece activates after dark, transforming the structural bamboo envelope into an illuminated shelter where soft woven media counterbalance the rigid natural framework.

From Guinness World Records to ancient ruins: eight facts about Kazakhstan’s cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:04:59 UTC
12:04:59 KST

From Guinness World Records to ancient ruins: eight facts about Kazakhstan’s cities
A Guinness World Record-breaking structure in Astana, a nuclear reactor that once helped turn seawater into drinking water in Aktau, and an ancient city discovered beneath a modern market in Taraz - Kazakhstan’s cities have stories that go far beyond their familiar landmarks. To mark World Cities Day on October 31, Qazinform News Agency explores 8 fascinating facts about cities across the country
1. Astana: A giant tent with a Guinness World Record
A tropical beach might be the last thing visitors expect to find in a city known for its freezing winters. Yet Astana has one, tucked inside a giant tent-shaped building.
Standing 150 meters tall, Khan Shatyr holds the Guinness World Record for the world’s tallest tensile structure. Designed by British architect Norman Foster, the entertainment center opened in July 2010.
Its transparent, climate-controlled enclosure spans more than 100,000 square meters, housing shops, restaurants and entertainment facilities, including an indoor beach where visitors can escape the cold without leaving the capital.
2. Almaty: A UNESCO City of Music with a record-breaking ice rink
Almaty has earned international recognition in two seemingly unrelated fields: music and winter sports.
In 2017, it joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Music, recognizing the role of music in the city’s cultural life.
Meanwhile, high in the mountains, the Medeu skating rink has witnessed hundreds of world speed skating records. Situated 1,691 meters above sea level, the venue has long been associated with international skating achievements.
On January 18, 2014, Medeu added another distinction when 523 people participated in a skating lesson that earned a Guinness World Record for the largest ice skating lesson.
3. Aktau: The city that used nuclear power to produce drinking water
Nuclear energy is usually associated with electricity generation. But in Aktau, on the Caspian Sea, it once served another purpose: producing fresh water.
The city’s BN-350 nuclear reactor began commercial operation in 1973, supplying electricity and supporting a desalination system that converted seawater into drinking water.
According to the World Nuclear Association, the facility produced up to 80,000 cubic meters of potable water per day, demonstrating the potential of nuclear technology to address water shortages.
The reactor was permanently shut down in April 1999, ending a distinctive chapter in the history of nuclear-powered desalination.
4. Turkestan: A UNESCO masterpiece left unfinished for more than 600 years
Some of the world’s most remarkable monuments were never completed. The Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi in Turkestan is one of them.
Construction began in 1389 under Timur, also known as Tamerlane, who commissioned the monumental complex in honor of the 12th-century Sufi teacher and poet.
But work stopped following Timur’s death in 1405, leaving the main entrance and parts of the interior unfinished.
Rather than diminishing its historical value, those incomplete sections have provided researchers with evidence of medieval building techniques.
According to UNESCO, architectural innovations developed during its construction later influenced major buildings in Samarkand. The mausoleum was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2003.
5. Taraz: An ancient city hidden beneath a modern market
For years, shoppers at Taraz’s central market walked above the remains of an ancient city.
Archaeological excavations beneath the market site uncovered parts of the historic citadel, once home to the city’s rulers and other prominent figures.
Further discoveries revealed stone-paved streets, public baths, ceramic water pipes and evidence of coin production.
These findings offered a glimpse into a sophisticated medieval urban settlement, complete with infrastructure that had remained hidden beneath the modern city.
6. Shymkent: A 2,200-year-old city recognized by UNESCO
Modern Shymkent stands on layers of history stretching back more than two millennia.
Archaeological excavations in its historic center uncovered evidence of an ancient settlement, leading researchers to establish an estimated age of at least 2,200 years.
The discovery gained international recognition in 2019, when UNESCO’s General Conference included Shymkent’s 2,200th anniversary in its calendar of commemorations for 2020-2021.
Today, the Shym Qala historical complex preserves and presents parts of the ancient settlement within the modern city, offering a glimpse into urban life long before the rise of contemporary Kazakhstan.
7. Karaganda: A museum 15 meters underground
While most museums display industrial history in exhibition halls, one in Karaganda takes visitors beneath the surface.
Located at the Karaganda Mining and Industrial College, the museum occupies a training mine approximately 15 meters underground.
Its tunnels feature mining equipment, conveyor systems, mine carts and reinforced passages that recreate the environment in which coal miners work.
The unusual exhibition offers visitors a closer look at the industry that shaped Karaganda’s development into one of Kazakhstan's major industrial cities.
8. Semey: A city of writers, poets and philosophers
Few cities in Kazakhstan have such a rich literary heritage as Semey, formerly known as Semipalatinsk. Over the centuries, the city has been associated with some of the most influential figures in Kazakh and Russian literature.
Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky lived here from 1854 to 1859 following his imprisonment in Siberia. A house where he once stayed has been preserved as part of a literary memorial museum.
Semey also played an important role in the life of Abai Kunanbaiuly, the renowned Kazakh poet and philosopher who studied in the city. Other prominent figures connected to its literary history include Shakarim Kudaiberdiuly, a Kazakh poet and thinker, and Mukhtar Auezov, whose celebrated novel The Path of Abai introduced generations of readers to Abai’s life and legacy.
Together, these figures have made Semey an important center of Kazakhstan’s literary and intellectual heritage.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency highlighted seven fascinating facts about Astana that may surprise first-time visitors.

Thousands march through Taipei for transgender equality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:03:43 UTC
12:03:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Organizers said around 3,800 people took part in Taiwan's eighth transgender pride march in Taipei on Friday.
CNA reported the march began at 228 Peace Memorial Park on Friday and was organized by the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association, a group advocating for sexual and gender minority rights. More than 61 local and international rights groups took part, calling for an end to discrimination against transgender people.
The association's spokesperson, known as Pan (盤), said the march aimed to bring people together across gender and national boundaries. Transgender rights faced growing threats at home and abroad, he warned.
Pan said online debates over transgender issues had become more divided in recent years. Such debates, he said, often reduced the issue to support or opposition, leaving little room for people to learn from one another.
Organizers also drew attention to problems transgender people face at school, work, and in healthcare. They said strict rules on changing legal gender records and social prejudice continued to create barriers, per the association's press release.
The group said the legalization of same-sex marriage in 2019 did not mean the fight for sexual and gender minorities' rights was over. Issues involving transgender rights, people living with HIV, marriage, and family life still needed attention.
The transgender march is held each year ahead of Taiwan's larger gay pride parade, which takes place in Taipei on Saturday. Organizers said the separate event aims to draw greater attention to transgender rights and issues often overlooked by the wider public.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) and her DPP counterpart Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) sparred over party loyalty, government funding, and the city's future during a televised debate Friday.
CNA reported that the two accused each other of putting party interests ahead of Kaohsiung. Ko called for a leadership change, while Lai defended the record of past DPP mayors and pledged to build on their work.
Lai accused Ko of backing changes to the revenue-sharing law that he said had reduced Kaohsiung's share of government funds. The DPP candidate said Ko had followed the KMT's position in the legislature instead of fighting for the city, a claim he had raised earlier in the campaign.
The law determines how tax revenue is shared between the central and local governments. Ko rejected Lai's claim, saying the final version did not include a KMT proposal to give Taipei more funds, and questioned his own record in the legislature.
The candidates also clashed over plans for a former military site in Kaohsiung. Lai questioned Ko's proposal to move City Hall and the city council there, while Ko said the site could become a major business district and criticized Lai's plans as unclear.
Ko accused Lai of having close ties to a powerful faction within the DPP and warned against letting party interests shape city policy. Lai rejected the claim and pledged to oppose any party decision that went against Kaohsiung's interests.
The KMT candidate also said she would not let senior KMT figures control City Hall if elected. She argued that a change in power would strengthen oversight and help uncover problems left unresolved under DPP rule.
Turning to the city's economy, Ko said many residents had yet to benefit from its growing high-tech sector. She said Kaohsiung's population had fallen by 62,000 over six years, while wages and life expectancy remained below those in Taipei.
Ko pledged to set up an office to address bullying in schools and workplaces within her first month as mayor. She also proposed an office to improve healthcare, transport, and tourism in the former Kaohsiung County, which merged with the city in 2010.
Ko said she would help traditional businesses adopt new technology and create better-paid jobs for young people. Her plans also include new roads, metro lines, expanded airport services, and a new business and housing district.
Lai pledged to raise birth grants to NT$50,000 (US$1,600) per child and expand public child care. He also proposed more aid for young families, short-term child care, and better health services for older residents.
Lai said he would expand affordable rental housing and build more homes near metro stations. Ko, meanwhile, has pledged to build 5,000 public housing units and encourage private investment to ease housing costs.
Lai also pledged to help traditional industries adopt new technology and expand Kaohsiung's role in artificial intelligence and chip production. He proposed better transport links and airport upgrades as the city attracts more investment in its semiconductor sector.
Lai credited Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁) and past DPP mayors with helping turn Kaohsiung into a major industrial and high-tech center. He pledged to build on their work over the next decade, while Ko argued that the city needed stronger oversight and new leadership.

'It's like being in an unlisted war' — Economy turns US midterms into a patience test for voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:00:38 UTC
12:00:38 KST

Washington, DC — "It takes $100 a day just to be a human being."
This is how Alfie Murphy, a mid-20s resident of New York, described the economic squeeze driven by high inflation and low wages in the US as the country heads to the midterms.
He says many people of his generation don't want to sacrifice time to work a dead-end job when they have knowledge and know what's going on in the world.
"It makes everything seem finite in the end. We just want to live. The dream of working until a certain retirement age is outdated in our eyes," Murphy tells TRT World.
Murphy, who used to live in Washington, DC, says that the food stamps in the capital used to be close to $300, but "that is now barely enough to cover weeks' worth of groceries."
"For my generation, it's always like being in an unlisted war. We are stressed out of our minds about the future, and most of it has to do with what we're exposed to… It can be a lot, especially when you don't see much change."
Murphy isn't the only one who shares this view.
According to Pew Research Center, the economy is ranked the single highest priority concern for voters, with 84 percent of all registered voters rating it as "very important".
Ongoing financial strains — compounded by high food prices, energy costs, and elevated borrowing rates — have left a strong majority of the electorate seeking substantial political change.
Young Americans, working-class, and retirees
This economic squeeze affects most Americans, though the impact can vary by class.
Working-class families are fearing the worst because jobs, while not falling, are not providing the necessary increase in income to beat or at least match the increase in prices.
Young Americans, however, are arguably suffering the most, as they struggle to secure jobs, which creates additional issues.
According to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, the FRED Youth Unemployment Rate (Ages 16–24) sat at 9.9 percent, which is more than double the national general unemployment rate of 4.2 percent.
While the broader US economy is not experiencing mass layoffs, companies have shifted into a highly competitive "low-hire, low-fire" cycle.
This lack of natural corporate turnover, paired with automated AI screening filters and an ongoing drop in entry-level listings, has made finding work unusually difficult and impersonal for young adults.
The impact on retirees, by contrast, could be starkly different.
Eugenio Aleman, Chief Economist at Raymond James, says retirees — especially those who managed to save for retirement — could see an advantage.
"Retirees, especially if they have saved for retirement, are doing much better because returns on equity have been very strong, and now fixed income is also starting to be a good place to put their savings," Aleman tells TRT World.
"Since baby boomers have accumulated the largest amount of wealth of any generation, their relative position is better than previous generations."
Those who didn't save for retirement could be disadvantaged, he says.
Disillusioned supporters
The economic strain has left a sour taste in President Donald Trump supporters' mouths, with many of them now holding a negative view of the GOP.
"Every poll is showing that trend," Aleman says.
"However, how much that will translate into a defeat for Republicans is not that clear," he adds.
The widespread disillusionment does not necessarily mean all of these voters are switching to Democrats; instead, it is creating a severe voter enthusiasm deficit for Republicans.
As many Americans reel under the pressure of inflation and economic uncertainty, the economy could be the most decisive issue in the midterms.
"Because there are lots of unfulfilled promises and people are upset about higher prices. This is affecting Republicans particularly hard because many of these issues are affecting their constituents the most," Aleman says.
"The economy is going to be the decisive factor in swing districts."
The economic picture, however, is not entirely straightforward.
Figures released just days before the election showed the US economy growing at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter, but consumer prices also accelerated to 3.6 percent year over year in September.
The contrast captures the political problem facing the administration: strong growth figures may offer reassurance, but they do not necessarily translate into relief for households still struggling with high prices, fuel costs and borrowing expenses.
For voters facing expensive groceries, housing and healthcare, national economic statistics can feel distant from the realities of the monthly budget.
For candidates across the country, the challenge is to convince voters that they understand these pressures and have a plan to address them.
They now have only three days to do so.

The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:00:31 UTC
12:00:31 KST

The idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.
The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further than Cambodia.
The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024 with an explicit offer: Donald Trump had been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.
For $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.
It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.
The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.
At 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.
On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.
“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”
The Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.
“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”
Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.
One couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube, including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.
“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.
Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.
The next day, the couple posted an update showing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.
“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.
Another passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.
The company has not provided financial aid, passengers said, or even supplied a list of hotels in Cambodia. It later offered tickets for a charter flight to the US, although many passengers had already left. The company has been contacted for comment.
Kit and Randy Cassingham, now in a hotel in Cambodia, reflected on how life changed on the ship once the Iran war began, with ominous signs that the company was running out of money. The food quality began to deteriorate, and there was less of it; there were fewer excursions on shore, they said.
“I realised as soon as the strait of Hormuz incident came along, the energy of the ship changed,” Kit said. “I think it was because the ship management realised how much more this was going to cost. And then they were starting to do cutbacks that we weren’t aware of yet.”
Far from being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil. “I watched the world, and I don’t even pay attention to the news, but I’ve watched it just kind of crumble and shatter,” said Kit. “And I’m thinking, ‘it’s going to be difficult no matter what’.”
Randy said the writing had long been on the wall. They were, after all, on a ship that “drinks petrol by the metric tonne”. “You know, literally they’re buying 150 metric tonnes of fuel at a time,” he said. “We’re talking about $800,000 if we tried to get a full tank.”
While docked in Singapore in August, passengers had already been told the company did not have enough money to continue cruising, and several of the residents had contributed their own funds to get it moving again.
“Very few expect to get any money back because we know that they [the company] have been in terrible money problems from the beginning,” said Randy. Passengers had also passed a jar around for money for the crew, who are also stuck in Cambodia, he said.
Will the story of the Odyssey put people off cruises? It is unlikely, said Prof Andrew Coggins, an industry analyst, who pointed to an unprecedented boom since the end of the Covid pandemic, with global passengers reaching a historical high of 37.2 million in 2025.
Those numbers were in part because of “pent up demand” from those who had been unable to enjoy a cruise during the pandemic years, he said. But it was also the case, he said, that a cruise could offer good value for money. “You get to be pampered, you pack and unpack once, but you see different places, you eat better food than you would get at home, and then you have the romance of going to sea,” he said.
Residential ships such as the Odyssey were, though, in a very small category of their own, Coggins added. “The World is the only other one I know about and I think there are a couple that are trying to start up,” he said. But the finances are notoriously difficult. In 2023, a three-year cruise offered by Miray Cruises, with fares starting at $30,000 per person per year, including accommodation, food, drinks, laundry and even health care, was cancelled weeks before its due departure date owing to an inability to make the sums add up.
To survive choppy world markets, charges to the passengers have to be high, necessitating a concomitant level of luxury. “The World was actually built as a residential ship,” Coggins said. “The cabins or the state rooms are much bigger.”
Speaking earlier in the week, Mikael Petterson, who launched Villa Vie Residences in 2023, accepted that he was the “villain in the story” but said he was doing everything he could to help the stranded passengers. “Nobody that’s tried residential cruising has succeeded and we have gone further than anyone else,” he said. “But I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war.”
Back in Cambodia, Randy has been blogging to keep people updated while they work out what to do next. But he isn’t bitter. For all the promises, he said, all good things must come to an end. “Our message is that we’re not saying ‘poor me’. We know that people are having trouble, that they’re trying to put fuel in their cars, food in their mouths. And we’re very lucky. We’re not crying in our soup. So we are completely aware that we’re very lucky and that we’re going to land on our feet and be OK.”
Kit, a transformation coach, agreed. “This isn’t a pity party for us,” she said. “We actually want to say to people: ‘Live your dreams. Go for the gusto. Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out’.”

‘Don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into’: Delhi women reclaim the outdoors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:00:30 UTC
12:00:30 KST

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

From Assad to Lieberman: The Israelization of the Druze in the Golan reached the polls
The election results in the Druze communities of the Golan Heights marked a double shift: decades after declaring allegiance to Syria, thousands turned out to vote in an Israeli election for the first time, while Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the right-wing opposition party Yisrael Beiteinu, won a majority of the vote.
The residents of Majdal Shams, Buqata, Masade and Ein Qiniyye had for decades declared their allegiance to Syria. The shift toward Israel began more than a decade ago, but the latest election marked a milestone, with thousands of residents who acquired Israeli citizenship in the past two years casting ballots for the first time.
Mossad to assist Shin Bet in probe of potential election interference by countries other than Qatar
The Mossad will assist the Shin Bet security service in investigating suspected foreign interference in Israel's election, including the possible involvement of countries other than Qatar.
A source familiar with the investigation told Haaretz on Friday that security agencies are examining suspicions that foreign funds were transferred to political figures in Israel and used to finance voter mobilization efforts through various platforms.
However, the source assessed that the affair was limited in scope and that its impact, if any, was far less significant than some accounts have suggested.
The Shin Bet, which is responsible for identifying and thwarting foreign interference in Israel, is leading the investigation. Until Thursday, the Mossad had maintained that it had no role to play in the probe, but on Friday it agreed to a Shin Bet request to assist with specific aspects of the investigation involving suspected foreign involvement.
If Netanyahu stays, even his voters will feel it in their pockets | Analysis
Tuesday's election cost Netanyahu's coalition its majority, yet the opposition may still be unable to replace him. The frustration of its voters does not augur the demise of the state. But there is a real danger that the decline will continue, even accelerate, a process that began with Netanyahu and Likud's relatively surprising victory in 2015 (then too, contrary to the polls and even the exit polls).
In retrospect, this was the moment the prime minister's self-confidence swelled and when he became more immersed in the three criminal affairs in which he was charged in 2019. His investigation and subsequent prosecution brought on a holy war against the judiciary, a series of closely spaced general elections amid political instability, his close alliance with the far-right parties and, finally, his absolute shirking of responsibility for the failures that made possible the October 7 massacre.
In recent years, Netanyahu resembled a driver who was determined to smash the Zionist project into a wall, indifferent to the outcries of the passengers who were stuck behind him and had no way of extricating themselves.
For many in the change bloc, the hope for an exceptional showing by Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party on Tuesday represented the last off-ramp from the expressway to hell. So far, that hasn't happened. The power of tribal-religious identity politics and fanning the fear of the Arabs played into Netanyahu's hands, even though his bloc is 11 Knesset seats smaller than after the 2022 election. In that one, too, a year before the massacre, he played on the same sentiments.
The Democrats doubled their Knesset seats, but alienated Arab voters along the way
The Democrats ultimately won eight seats: short of expectations, but double the representation of Labor in the outgoing Knesset. In the 2022 election, Labor and Meretz – the two parties that later merged to form the Democrats – ran separately. Labor won only four seats, while Meretz failed to cross the electoral threshold.
Still, the party appears to have fallen short in reaching voters it had neglected, particularly Arab citizens. During the Knesset term, Democrats lawmakers Naama Lazimi, Efrat Rayten and Gilad Kariv stood out for their parliamentary work, while during the campaign the party's candidates traveled extensively around the country. Kariv was particularly active in reaching Arab communities, and the party recruited a large volunteer network.
But Soumaya Bashir, the party's representative from the Arab community, finished only 10th in the primary, and the Democrats won only small shares of the vote in many of Israel's larger Arab localities.
Issawi Frej, a former Meretz minister and lawmaker, does not consider the Democrats' result a significant achievement. "The Democrats were never genuinely interested in partnership with Arab society. It was a pretense," he charged.
At Shin Bet's request, Mossad to assist in probe into suspected foreign election interference
Mossad has agreed to a request from the Shin Bet security service to assist in its investigation into suspected foreign interference in Israel's elections.
The move comes after Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet chief David Zini to investigate what he described as "serious suspicions" of improper foreign influence on the election through foreign funding. Sohlberg clarified in the letter that he could not "attest to the nature of the suspicions."
According to a source on the committee, claims were raised, among others, that Qatar had invested money to increase voter turnout in the Arab community. The Shin Bet said it was conducting an investigation but declined to provide further details.
Qatar, for its part, denies interfering in Israel's elections.
PM's son says Israeli Arabs are Israel's 'greatest threat' after nuclear Iran
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's son Yair said Friday that Israeli Arabs are the "greatest threat to the survival of the State of Israel, apart from the Iranian nuclear threat."
The prime minister's son wrote in a post on X that Arab citizens of Israel pose a greater threat than "their Palestinian brethren in the West Bank and Gaza, more than Turkey, and more than the surging antisemitism in the West." He added that Israel cannot survive "when 20 percent of its population identifies with its enemies and wants to see its destruction."

US judge orders Trump administration to cease threats to prosecute election officials
WASHINGTON – A US judge ordered the Justice Department on Oct 30 to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration’s demands related to voting by alleged non-citizens.
The ruling comes days before the US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
Although several key races appear closely contested, polls favour Democrats to take control of the House and give them a plausible chance of a Senate majority.
In the months leading up to the midterms, US President Donald Trump’s administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, such as pressing states for voter-registration data, saying stricter measures are needed to ensure election security and public confidence in the vote.
But the Justice Department went too far in October when it threatened to prosecute state and county officials who do not cooperate with the Trump administration’s election-related initiatives, US District Judge Trina Thompson ruled in connection with a lawsuit brought by election workers’ unions and some other groups.
“Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in plaintiffs’ favour,” Thompson wrote in her temporary restraining order.
The Justice Department had no immediate comment on the ruling.
Critics, including political experts as well as Democratic and some Republican election officials, have viewed the Trump administration’s moves as federal overreach. Some election officials have told Reuters they were preparing for potential federal interference in the midterm elections.
Thompson, who was appointed by former president Joe Biden, ordered the Trump administration to refrain from demanding that local election officials remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or segregate ballots cast in the midterm elections, based on a Trump administration list of alleged non-citizen voters.
Trump has made false claims related to elections in the past, including not acknowledging his defeat in the 2020 election. REUTERS

Ebola death toll in DR Congo passes 5,000
Unknown

2026-10-31
