Ebola death toll in DR Congo passes 5,000
Authorities are struggling to find a way to control the outbreak, with no approved treatments or vaccines.
The death toll from Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has surpassed 5,000, government data show, with authorities yet to find a way to control the country’s deadliest outbreak of the virus on record.
The latest death toll was announced on Friday.
Ebola has infected more than 10,000 people in the DRC since the outbreak was declared in May.
There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, responsible for the ongoing outbreak.
Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have helped the virus spread more rapidly than in past outbreaks, reaching eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces to date.
The virus has spread to neighbouring countries as well.
Last week, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case, extending the outbreak’s geographic spread to West Africa. East African countries Kenya and Uganda have also reported cases.
This year’s Ebola outbreak is the second-largest ever, behind only the 2014-2016 epidemic that infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000 people across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Some governments have been restricting travel to affected countries or quarantining travellers who have recently visited or transited through them.
On Friday, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and entry from Kenya, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
The measures include suspending travel by Saudi citizens to Kenya and a pause on issuing all types of visas to travellers from the country.
The kingdom is also prohibiting entry to travellers arriving from Kenya, including those transiting through third countries who have stayed in Kenya or other Ebola-affected countries within the previous 21 days.
In June, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and entry from the DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan.

Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defences after Binance heist
Unknown

Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defences after Binance heist
SAN FRANCISCO – Crypto exchanges are taking quick action to bolster their defences and urging greater industry-wide information-sharing after a record US$6.3 billion hack of Binance exposed their vulnerability just as they become more embedded in mainstream finance.
Coinbase said it had made adjustments to its systems that store cryptocurrency keys offline “solely out of an abundance of caution”, while Kraken said it was monitoring industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its defences.
But the industry will need to move urgently, analysts and industry executives said, as US President Donald Trump’s regulators promote deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, raising the stakes for an industry with a history of big hacks.
“For crypto to reach its full potential, the security situation must be addressed immediately,” said Chris Perkins, Franklin Templeton’s head of crypto.
Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, halted withdrawals after the Oct 29 attack – which analysts blamed on North Korea – and said it would use company funds to cover the losses.
Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said on X that the “complex attack” may have begun with a compromised software engineer’s laptop, giving hackers access to systems used to process withdrawals.
The company later found additional breaches, while software designed to erase traces of the attack hampered the investigation.
On Oct 30, rival crypto exchanges moved quickly to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers that their tokens were safe
“Full-time teams at Kraken look for potential vulnerabilities every day,” a Kraken spokesperson said.
Still, even as the industry reeled from the biggest cryptocurrency heist of all time, executives expressed confidence that Binance had sufficient resources to cover the losses and that the hack would not have broader financial repercussions.
Bitcoin fell more than 4% on Oct 29 while ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5%, although both tokens recovered some of that ground on Oct 30.
“Our expectation is the industry writ large will actually not suffer material losses, even though Binance is obviously going to have to deal with the exploit directly,” said Josh Riezman, chief legal and strategy officer at crypto firm GSR.
The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes late on Oct 29 and bore similarities to previous attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
North Korea routinely denies involvement in cryptocurrency thefts, and its mission in Geneva did not respond to requests for comment.
Hack involves social engineering, money laundering
While much remains unclear, social engineering, a common tactic in which hackers trick victims into revealing sensitive information or granting access to systems, may have been involved in compromising the laptop, security experts said.
Harry Donnelly, CEO of Circuit, a crypto risk infrastructure company, said companies are planning more employee training to guard against social engineering attacks.
In such attacks, hackers race to launder the funds before the exchange detects the breach and token issuers freeze assets.
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly US$1.57 billion linked to Binance, while Circle said it froze US$800 million.
Bitcoin and Ether cannot be frozen because no single entity controls the coins.
Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using sophisticated laundering patterns it had not seen before.
On Oct 30, some crypto exchange executives called for the industry to develop a coordinated hack detection system.
“We need a real-time alert system that allows participants to share information immediately when a hack occurs, coordinate a rapid response, and temporarily freeze suspected stolen funds,” said Star Xu, CEO of crypto exchange OKX, in a post on X.
GSR’s Riezman added that the Binance hack could spur the industry to act: “As we’re at this kind of confluence moment for traditional finance and digital assets, I think it’s obviously important that we continue to improve, and I think this, if anything, will be a catalyst for that.” REUTERS

‘Grit’ made her famous. Now Angela Duckworth says it isn't enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:46:53 UTC
11:46:53 KST

For years, University of Pennsylvania psychologist Angela Duckworth searched for the secret to success. What separates people who achieve extraordinary things from everyone else? Is there a particular quality that allows some people to reach the highest levels of performance?
About a decade ago, after years of extensive field research, she challenged the widespread assumption that exceptional achievement is primarily a matter of innate talent. Her bestselling book Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance introduced the idea that a combination of deep passion and relentless persistence was one of the most important characteristics distinguishing high achievers from others.
Duckworth's approach soon became enormously influential in management, education and personal development. But as interest in grit grew, so did criticism. Was success really determined by what happened inside a person's mind? Didn't life circumstances also shape the chances of achieving one's goals? And how fair was it to demand that people rely entirely on their own inner resources?
Duckworth did not dig in her heels. Instead, with the determination that had become her trademark, she continued investigating.
In her new book, Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best, she does not abandon her belief in perseverance. Rather, she adds another essential ingredient: Success also depends on how we choose and shape the situations in which we operate.
Grit remains important, but realizing its full potential requires a supportive environment. And, Duckworth argues, we can do a great deal to create one.
"After examining what goes on inside the heads of successful people, I began to wonder what might also be special about their surroundings," she writes in the book.
What kinds of situations allow people to succeed, regardless of how talented and determined they may be?
Gradually, Duckworth realized that grit was necessary for success but not sufficient. The circumstances in which we find ourselves matter far more than we tend to assume. Instead of constantly telling ourselves to work harder, she argues, we should look for the right mentors, supportive colleagues, physical spaces that help us thrive and cultures that inspire us.
Through in-depth interviews with successful people from different fields, Duckworth identified ways to proactively shape our surroundings so that our determination can translate into meaningful results. Her findings offer four practical lessons, including some surprisingly simple changes that may make success easier to achieve.
1. Willpower may be the least effective tool
For years, much of the research on behavior change focused on willpower: our ability to resist temptation, overcome distractions and force ourselves to do what we know is good for us.
Researchers even explored whether willpower could be trained like a muscle, with repeated exposure to difficult tasks gradually strengthening our capacity for self-control.
In Grit, Duckworth demonstrated the importance of long-term perseverance when connected to passion and a meaningful goal. But her more recent research led her toward an unexpected question: Perhaps what matters is not simply how much willpower we have, but how often we need to use it in the first place.
In a 2016 academic paper written with psychologists James Gross and Tamar Szabó Gendler, Duckworth argued that self-control does not have to begin at the moment temptation appears.
Instead, we can intervene earlier, by changing the situation itself.
For example, we can move our phones out of reach, avoid bringing tempting foods into the house or choose a location that makes concentration easier.
Later research by Duckworth and her colleagues found that students who used such strategies tended to spend more time practicing and achieve better academic results than those who relied mainly on willpower.
This leads to one of her most provocative arguments in Situated: Willpower may be the least effective way to change our behavior.
Not because it has no value, but because relying on willpower requires us to win the same battle repeatedly.
Instead of asking, "How can I strengthen my willpower?" Duckworth suggests asking a different question: "How can I create a situation in which I need less of it?"
The distinction is fundamental. Rather than constantly fighting distractions and temptations, we can organize our lives to make the behavior we want easier and more automatic.
2. The space around you matters more than you think
According to Duckworth, one of the most significant things we can do to improve our chances of success is to examine the immediate physical space around us and redesign it.
Everything within our field of vision and arm's reach can have a disproportionate influence on what we think about and, consequently, what we do.
The goal is to reduce friction when making desirable choices and make unwanted temptations less accessible. That might mean moving unhealthy snacks out of sight, removing distracting objects from a workspace or arranging our environment so the next productive action is the easiest one to take.
In her research, Duckworth examined students' study habits and asked where they placed their phones while working.
The students were offered five possible answers, ranging from keeping the phone right beside them with the screen and notifications active to leaving it in an entirely different room.
The results revealed a clear relationship: The farther away the phone was, the better the students' academic performance tended to be.
The lesson is not simply that smartphones are distracting. It is that small differences in our surroundings can influence the choices we make without requiring any deliberate struggle.
Duckworth illustrates the importance of personal space using Leonardo da Vinci's famous drawing, Vitruvian Man, which depicts a human figure at the center of a circle representing the space around the body.
She argues that the area we can see and reach should be treated as an integral part of our everyday decision-making process.
Our immediate environment is not neutral scenery. It actively participates in shaping our lives.
And because we can change it, we can also make it work in our favor.
3. Become a magnet for different kinds of mentors
Successful people are also proactive about the mentoring they receive.
We often assume that finding a mentor is largely a matter of luck, Duckworth writes. But research suggests that many people never establish such relationships at all. A Gallup finding cited in the report indicates that approximately 60% of employed American college graduates say they do not have even one mentor at work. Other studies suggest that far more people consider workplace mentoring important than actually have access to it.
In her research, Duckworth found that high achievers take responsibility for bringing mentors into their lives.
They do not necessarily pursue wealthy, famous or exceptionally accomplished people. Instead, they often seek ordinary individuals with whom they can build meaningful connections and share experiences.
Duckworth describes successful people as "mentor magnets," and explains that they benefit from three different types of relationships.
The first involves mentors for a particular moment, such as someone who offers guidance at an important decision-making crossroads.
The second consists of mentors for a particular period, who accompany us through a specific project, challenge or stage in our professional development.
The third includes mentors for life, who maintain relationships with us over many years, get to know us deeply and continue supporting our personal and professional growth.
But how do we attract people willing to invest their time and experience in us?
According to Duckworth, mentors are not particularly drawn to people who simply ask them for something. They respond to curiosity, preparation and gratitude, and especially to people who demonstrate that they have benefited from the relationship.
Someone who arrives at a meeting prepared, asks thoughtful questions, listens carefully and expresses appreciation is already sending a positive signal.
But the most important step often comes afterward.
Returning a few weeks later to explain how you acted on the advice you received shows the mentor that the time and experience they invested were worthwhile.
In effect, becoming a mentor magnet means turning the help you receive into something valuable for both sides.
Another powerful way to attract mentors is to mentor other people yourself.
Helping others does more than expand your professional network. It makes you part of a community in which people learn, develop and pass knowledge forward.
In other words, if you want people who are willing to help you succeed, start by becoming someone who helps others succeed.
4. Create the right conditions for other people, too
There is another dimension to Duckworth's argument. Creating favorable circumstances for ourselves is essential, but we can take the idea further by creating those conditions for other people.
She describes this as a form of situational responsibility, particularly important when helping people who cannot yet shape their surroundings independently.
Parenting offers a powerful example.
It is easy to tell a child to concentrate harder, put in more effort, persevere or exercise greater self-control.
But young children cannot choose most of the conditions that surround them. Good parenting, therefore, is not simply about asking children to become certain kinds of people. It is about placing them in situations that encourage those qualities to emerge.
Duckworth points to American swimming legend and former world record holder Michael Phelps.
His mother, Debbie Phelps, recognized that her son behaved differently in the swimming pool. In the water, he found interest, concentration and confidence. He could direct his energy toward something at which he excelled.
Rather than insisting that he adapt himself to an environment that did not suit him, she helped him find one that matched his abilities. From there, she helped create conditions in which those abilities could flourish.
When we take responsibility for helping other people succeed, Duckworth explains, we are also shaping the world in which we ourselves operate.
The principle extends far beyond parenting.
A manager who creates conditions in which her employees can thrive is not merely helping them. She is also building a more capable, committed and independent team.
A woman who helps a friend identify her strengths and find opportunities to use them is also strengthening her own support network.
Ultimately, a situation that benefits other people can also become a better situation for ourselves.
Self-assessment: How well is your environment working for you?
Duckworth's approach can also be used to evaluate the circumstances of our own lives. The following questionnaire examines four areas: personal space, colleagues, mentors and organizational culture.
Consider each statement and decide whether it accurately describes your current situation.
Personal space
I keep temptations, such as junk food or my phone, out of sight and out of reach.
I arrange my personal surroundings so the choices I want to make, such as exercising, reading or going to bed on time, are easy, accessible and appealing.
Colleagues and peers
I have colleagues who hold me accountable for my goals, and I do the same for them.
The people around me know things I do not know, and together we are smarter.
There are people who depend on me, and I know that my presence and commitment matter to them.
Mentors
When I don't know what to do, I have at least two people I can turn to for advice.
I am working on a project with someone who is more experienced or skilled than I am and from whom I can learn.
I have at least one mentor with whom I intend to maintain a long-term relationship.
Organizational culture
The organization where I work challenges me while also supporting me.
I live and work in an environment that allows me to pursue my goals and interests.
How to calculate your score
Give yourself one point for every statement that applies to you, for a maximum of 10 points.
The closer your score is to 10, the more your environment is working in your favor.
Examine the areas where your score is lower and consider what you could change to create better conditions for yourself.
Why determination alone couldn't save her marriage
Duckworth, 56, does not limit her new approach to examples from other people's lives. In Situated, she also writes with unusual openness about a crisis in her marriage to real estate entrepreneur Jason Duckworth.
After years of what she describes as a storybook romance and the birth of their two children, the couple faced a major challenge during the 2008 financial crisis, when Jason's business ran into difficulties.
Both responded in the way that came most naturally to them.
They worked harder.
They got up earlier, stayed awake later and tried to solve their problems by putting in even more effort.
But their strategy failed. Instead, both became increasingly exhausted, and their marriage entered a profound crisis.
Eventually, Duckworth writes, they realized that they had been trying to solve the problem by changing themselves rather than examining the situation in which they were living.
The breakthrough came when they expanded their perspective beyond the two of them.
They sought help from individual therapists and a couples therapist. Jason established an advisory board and began connecting with fellow entrepreneurs through a professional organization. Duckworth also started approaching her work as a more collaborative endeavor.
Gradually, rather than relying exclusively on their own internal resources, they began changing the external conditions surrounding their lives.
They created a more supportive environment, and their marriage survived.
For Duckworth, this experience captures the central message of her new book.
Sometimes the problem is not that we are failing to try hard enough. It is that the circumstances in which we are trying to succeed are not giving us enough support.
Whether in love or at work, grit still matters. But even the most determined people need circumstances in which their perseverance can translate into progress.
And that means learning to shape the environment around us, including the objects, people and places that can help bring out our best.

Three children were killed in a road accident in Khmelnytskyi region. Their bodies were found in a car that was pulled from a body of water near the village of Humentsi, Kamianets-Podilskyi district. This was reported by the press service of the Khmelnytskyi region police, according to UNN.
Details
It is reported that a local resident contacted the police to report his 13-year-old daughter missing. She had gone to a friend's birthday party the previous evening and never returned. The man also reported that two other boys, aged 15 and 16, who had also been at the celebration, had disappeared along with the girl.
Law enforcement officers immediately launched a search: they examined the community's territory and issued an alert to all police patrols. During the initial measures, it was preliminarily established that shortly before their disappearance, the children had been traveling in a "VAZ 21099" car. At around 4:00 p.m., police officers found the vehicle in a river in a neighboring village. The bodies of the three missing children were inside the vehicle
It is noted that law enforcement officers are currently establishing all the circumstances and causes of the tragedy. The investigation is ongoing.

NMC invites applications to empanel 17 standing counsels across Supreme Court, 16 High Court positions

The National Medical Commission is seeking applications for standing counsels aimed at bolstering its legal expertise.
New Delhi: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has invited applications from advocates to empanel 17 standing counsels to represent it before the Supreme Court, High Courts and their benches across the country, with preference for lawyers experienced in medical institution and medical negligence cases.According to an Expression of Interest (EOI) issued on October 30, the commission is seeking one standing counsel for the Supreme Court and 16 positions across various High Courts. These include two positions each at the Delhi High Court and Himachal Pradesh High Court, and one each at the Karnataka High Court's Bengaluru, Dharwad and Kalaburagi benches, Uttarakhand High Court at Nainital, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh High Court's Srinagar and Jammu benches, Rajasthan High Court's Jodhpur bench, Bombay High Court's Nagpur and Goa benches, Gauhati High Court's Kohima and Aizawl benches, and Jharkhand High Court at Ranchi.The eligibility criteria require applicants to be between 35 and 70 years of age as on November 1, 2026, registered with the concerned State Bar Council and to have completed at least 100 appearances before the Supreme Court or a High Court in the preceding three years. Applicants must also have a minimum of 10 years' experience handling constitutional, civil, criminal or educational institution matters before High Courts.
For the Supreme Court position, applicants must be Advocates-on-Record with at least 10 years of experience.The NMC has said preference will be given to advocates with experience in medical institution and medical negligence cases, as well as those who have handled cases involving government organisations, institutions, departments and public sector undertakings.The empanelled advocates will represent the commission in court, draft petitions, counter-affidavits and other legal documents, conduct legal research, provide legal opinions and coordinate with government departments. They will also be required to keep the commission updated on important developments and hearing dates and submit monthly and annual statements of cases handled and their outcomes.The empanelment will be for three years or until further orders, whichever is earlier, and may be extended based on performance. There will be no fixed retainer fee, with payments governed by the revised fee structure prescribed by the Department of Legal Affairs, Union law ministry.
Applications must be submitted in the prescribed format by November 30, 2026. The commission will scrutinise applications through a screening committee, followed by interviews of shortlisted candidates, either physically or virtually.

NEW DELHI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched its next-generation navigation satellite NVS-03 aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket to boost the country's independent navigation system, Navigation with Indian Constellation, it confirmed on Saturday.
The launch took place at 11:51 p.m. local time on Friday from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in the Sriharikota area of the southern state of Andhra Pradesh.
"GSLV-F18 has successfully placed NVS-03 in the intended orbit. Congratulations," stated ISRO in a post on X.
Congratulating ISRO scientists on the feat, the country's Science and Technology Minister Jitendra Singh said in a post on X that this achievement reflects India's growing prowess in space technology and its unwavering commitment to strengthening sovereign indigenous navigation capabilities.
According to ISRO, the GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of India's Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle. The third satellite in the next-generation navigation satellite system, the NVS-03, is envisaged to provide continuity of navigation services for the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System series. ■

World Bank calls for translating African urbanization into growth, jobs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:24:34 CST
11:24:34 KST

ABIDJAN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The World Bank (WB) has called on countries in sub-Saharan Africa to turn the region's rapid urbanization into a powerful engine of economic growth and job creation.
The region's urban population grew from 170 million in 1975 to 913 million in 2025 and is projected to reach 1.7 billion by 2050, the international financial institution said in a report, adding that around 15 million young people enter the region's labor market each year.
Sustained population growth in particular underscores the need for creating more jobs correspondingly for youth while expanding access to productive, better-paying employment, according to the report titled "Africa's Urban Awakening: Catalyzing Economic Growth and Job Creation," which was published Wednesday.
The Bank recommends better planning for urban expansion, targeted investment in infrastructure and transport, and stronger regulatory frameworks and land governance. It also calls for greater mobilization of private capital to finance urban facilities and services.
Marie-Chantal Uwanyiligira, WB division director for Cote d'Ivoire, Benin, Guinea and Togo, noted that currently in the region, "productivity gains remain limited, incomes have grown slowly, and too many jobs remain informal and poorly paid."
In Cote d'Ivoire, official data showed it had 17.84 million urban residents out of an estimated total population of 32.8 million last year. The number of localities with more than 100,000 inhabitants increased from eight in 1998 to 17 in 2021.
The West African country has prioritized urban development, mobility and improvements in people's living conditions in its 2026-2030 national development plan. ■

WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration plans to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan, a US official and a coalition of veterans and advocacy groups said on Friday.

• A US official said deportations would be via Pakistan. Washington cannot directly arrange deportations to Afghanistan as it lacks diplomatic ties with the Taliban.
• Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive aim to improve domestic security.
• Rights advocates say the crackdown violates due process and free speech and has created an unsafe environment for minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
• The Homeland Security Department said it would not confirm future removal operations, citing operational security.
• VanDiver urged Congress to pass legislation granting Afghans in the US temporary protected status to protect them from deportation.
• Pakistan has expelled over 2 million Afghan nationals to Afghanistan since 2023.

Trump, Milei under pressure to explain Bolsonaro flight from Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump, Milei under pressure to explain Bolsonaro flight from Brazil
BRASILIA – US President Donald Trump and Argentina’s Javier Milei faced mounting pressure on Oct 30 to explain the role their countries played in helping Flavio Bolsonaro flee Brazil after he had his passports cancelled.
The 45-year-old Brazilian senator bolted his country two days after being defeated by incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a presidential election on Oct 25.
He had been ordered to surrender all his passports due to an ongoing investigation into him on suspicion of money-laundering.
However, he left the country in a cloak-and-dagger operation via Argentina and Ecuador, and landed in Florida on Oct 28, where he declared himself the rightful “leader” of Brazil.
Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat after his loss, which came as a shock after he won a first-round election and had been seen as the narrow favourite.
According to the Argentine migration authority, Bolsonaro boarded a private plane on the evening of Oct 27 in north-eastern Puerto Iguazu, 40 minutes after entering Argentina by land.
While Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passport and diplomatic passport had been cancelled, he also holds an Italian passport, which he used to board a private jet in Argentina, according to a flight document seen by AFP.
A Brazilian diplomatic source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Argentina’s diplomatic representative had been summoned for a “routine meeting” to “provide explanations” on Oct 29.
Brasilia recalled its ambassador and downgraded diplomatic ties with Buenos Aires in August after repeated insults from Milei, who called Lula “a thief” and “corrupt”.
Argentina’s Foreign Minister on Oct 30 denied that Brazil had asked Buenos Aires to explain its role in Bolsonaro’s flight.
“False. There was no request for information,” Pablo Quirno wrote on social media platform X.
Outliers in not accepting result
Bolsonaro thanked Milei and Trump in his first statement after fleeing the country.
Milei has not recognised Lula’s election victory and Trump said the poll was a “disgrace” and “very strange”.
However, Lula’s victory has been recognised by global leaders from across the political spectrum, Brazil’s electoral court, Bolsonaro’s own party – which holds a majority in Congress – and other right-wing allies.
In the United States, Democrat lawmakers wrote a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio to request “an immediate accounting” of his department’s role in helping Bolsonaro leave Brazil.
Luis Grande, head of the Baires Fly airline that carried Bolsonaro, told AFP on Oct 29 that he had been hired by a broker “who lives in the United States”.
Some US media, including The New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, have reported that the plane was chartered by Jason Miller, an adviser to Trump.
The White House has not commented on the matter.
‘Difficult times’
Bolsonaro, who is the son of former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro, has found himself isolated and the object of ridicule at home, after his departure and proclamation that he would lead the opposition from abroad.
Speculation has switched almost immediately to who would lead the right with Flavio out of the country, and the future of the Bolsonaro movement.
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup against Lula after his 2022 election loss.
His wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was just elected senator, released a statement on Instagram on Oct 30 referring to Jair Bolsonaro as “our leader”.
“We are living through difficult times. We need to reflect and only then act,” she wrote.
“My husband stresses that this is a time for unity, not for looking for people to blame,” she said. AFP

Inside fraternities and why they are so important to US colleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:15:56 UTC
11:15:56 KST

What are frats and why is one at the centre of rape allegations at Cornell University?
New York state police have announced they will take charge of future sexual assault investigations at Cornell University in the latest fallout over the university's handling of an alleged gang rape on campus.
It comes as the university's faculty undertook a vote of no confidence in the school's administration over how it handled the allegation, with the results expected on November 6.
The alleged Cornell University incident in 2024 is not isolated, with the Associated Press reporting police were investigating allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity party at the University of Chicago on October 11.
A female student at the University of Arizona alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house on August 26, according to AP.
A few weeks later, on October 8, the University of Arizona suspended fraternity activity after reports of hazing and sexual misconduct.
According to the AP, previous hazing at the university's fraternities included forcing new members to consume large quantities of alcohol, as well as live goldfish.
Australian attitudes to fraternities, also known as frats, have been mostly shaped by popular culture, but what are fraternities really? And why are they so ingrained in higher education in the US?
What are fraternities?
Social fraternities or sororities are exclusive clubs for undergraduate students who can live together, socialise together and participate in traditions, usually in a same-sex environment.
Kimberly Davis, data analyst at Pennsylvania State University's Piazza Centre for Fraternity and Sorority Research, said fraternities were "often built around a shared identity" and members could maintain fraternity relationships "long after graduation".
"For some students, that level of connection is especially appealing during a period of life that can feel uncertain and transitional,"
Dr Davis said.
The first fraternity-like organisation was founded in 1776 at the College of William and Mary in Virginia, but they became much more popular across the US by the mid 1800s, according to Dr Davis.
Why are fraternities so important to US universities?
Dr Davis said on a practical level, fraternities provided additional residential options for university campuses.
She said fraternities were also "valuable partners" for universities to foster leadership development, student involvement in community activities, service and philanthropy.
"The friendships and communities that fraternities create also offer benefits for universities," she said.
"Alumni who have favourable fraternity experiences often associate their experiences with the university, which in turn encourages alumni to stay connected to the institution through alumni mentor ship and financial donations."
What are the problems with frats?
Loading...
According to a 2019 survey by the Association of American Universities, 10 per cent of undergraduate women who reported being raped said the incident occurred at a fraternity house, and 20 per cent of women reporting unwanted sexual touching said it occurred in a fraternity house.
6.4 per cent of men and 6.7 per cent of transgender, gender queer or questioning students who reported being raped said the incident occurred in a fraternity house, and just under 10 per cent of men and 12.6 per cent queer students reported unwanted sexual touching.
Dr Davis said fraternities did not contribute to a culture of sexual violence by design, but "that does not mean that fraternity environments cannot contribute to risk".
"Some organisational environments can normalise attitudes and behaviours that increase the risk of sexual violence," she said.
"A chapter that prioritises accountability, healthy relationships, and intervention can create a very different environment from one that normalises excessive alcohol use or tolerates harmful behaviour."
As well as sexual assault allegations, fraternities are also often associated with hazing.
The University of Colorado defines hazing as any activity that humiliates, degrades, abuses, or endangers someone, regardless of consent, as condition for entering an organisation.
The Pennsylvania State University Piazza Centre is named after student Timothy Piazza, who died as the result of a hazing incident at the university's Beta Theta Pi fraternity.
Mr Piazza was given at least 18 drinks in 82 minutes, according to prosecutors, and fell down the fraternity house stairs, becoming unconscious.
He later died from a head injury after a delayed response by bystanders.
"Timothy Piazza was one of four IFC fraternity men who died in hazing incidents in 2017 alone; that was an especially deadly year and the catalyst for many revised state hazing laws,"
Dr Davis said
Hazing prevention organisation HazingInfo's database indicates about five deaths per year have been reported in the US since 2000.
Do we have anything like them in Australia?
In Australia, the frat niche is filled by residential colleges, which provide accommodation, meals, academic support and social activities for residents.
Southern Cross University professor Elizabeth Mackinlay said instances of sexual harassment, assault and violence persisted at Australian residential colleges.
She said under-reporting continued at a concerning level, because students feared potential consequences for them and those responsible.
Professor Mackinlay said what Australian residential colleges and US fraternities had in common was hazing.
Hazing, abuse and misogyny have been reported at some residential colleges, including at Sydney University when, in 2018, allegations emerged of sexual assault, excessive alcohol consumption and other incidents.
In 2024, the City of Sydney council recommended the abolition of the University of Sydney's Residential Colleges after an incident at St Paul's College "where 6 students were expelled and a further 21 suspended after engaging in acts of 'serious humiliation' and sexual violence against a student".
Professor Mackinlay said the issues reported at Cornell University, the University of Arizona and St Paul's College she experienced herself during her time at university in the late 80s and 90s.
"The alcohol abuse, the degradation, rape, everything happened," she said.
"Nobody reported it. Leadership in the student group took part."
Professor Mackinlay said the culture of hazing and alcohol abuse had to change and "cultural norms around respectful relationships have to be in place and reinforced".
"If there's gender-based violence, there's a good chance that you're going to have to sit at the breakfast table in halls the next morning with the perpetrator there," she said.

French economy ‘headed straight for a wall’ – finance minister
France is “headed straight for a wall” unless it reins in its budget deficit, Finance Minister Roland Lescure has warned, as the country’s economy contracts and inflation accelerates.
Gross domestic product fell by 0.1% in the third quarter, following stagnation in the previous three months and a 0.2% decline at the start of the year, the national statistics agency reported on Friday. Annual inflation climbed to 3.4% in October from 3.1% in September, its highest level since January 2024.
Lescure also described the economy as being “at a standstill,” underscoring the mounting financial challenges facing President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The downturn extended across key sectors. Exports dropped 1.7%, largely due to weaker overseas aerospace sales, while investment fell 0.6%. Manufacturing output declined 1.4%, with automobile production shrinking for the fourth consecutive quarter.
France is also struggling with public debt equivalent to roughly 119% of GDP and a substantial budget deficit. Government borrowing costs climbed following Friday’s figures, with yields on ten-year bonds approaching 5%, raising concerns about the cost of servicing the country’s debt.
The deteriorating outlook has increased pressure on Macron, whose government is pursuing spending cuts while boosting military expenditure and weapons deliveries to Kiev. France increased its 2026 military budget by €6.7 billion ($7.5 billion) despite its mounting debt.
The government’s austerity policies have also fueled nationwide unrest that began in September with protests over staff shortages and deteriorating conditions at a high school near Paris. The demonstrations quickly spread, with thousands of students demanding more education funding and accusing the authorities of prioritizing weapons over schools.
The unrest escalated into violence, with rioters looting shops, setting vehicles ablaze and damaging the historic city hall in Limoges. Thousands were arrested and hundreds injured.
The protests have drawn comparisons with the 2018 Yellow Vest movement, which challenged Macron’s economic policies. Activists, students and trade unions have called for fresh demonstrations on Saturday, prompting authorities to mobilize 70,000 security personnel nationwide. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder.
Macron has blamed the purchasing-power crisis on the US-Israeli war against Iran, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and surging fuel prices. He has also accused social media platforms of “damaging democracy” by circulating footage of protests and riots.
With the 2027 presidential election approaching, the economic downturn and continuing unrest have further weakened Macron’s position, complicating efforts to secure parliamentary approval for a deficit-cutting budget.

Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising. Here's how to protect yourself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:13:29 UTC
11:13:29 KST

Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising in Victoria and NSW. Here's how to protect yourself
It starts as a small, painless lump on the skin that is easy to ignore.
But under the seemingly innocuous lump, flesh-eating bacteria are burrowing through fat and muscle.
Warning: Readers are advised that this article includes an image of an open wound.
The skin over the lump then dies, turns black and eventually becomes an open sore that, if untreated, grows.
This is a typical case of Buruli ulcer, a condition that until recently was primarily found in West Africa.
Victoria is now considered the Buruli ulcer centre of the world, with a record 426 confirmed cases last year.
Buruli ulcer is typically acquired in summer and autumn.
It is endemic in the Mornington Peninsula, Bellarine Peninsula, Geelong and some Melbourne suburbs.
It is also found in other parts of Australia: pockets of coastal Queensland, where it is sometimes called Daintree ulcer, and around Darwin.
Most recently, cases have popped up on the New South Wales south coast around Batemans Bay.
Visitors to these popular tourism areas might unknowingly get infected, go home and, months later, develop a Buruli ulcer where local doctors may not be aware of the condition.
So, coming into summer holidays, how can you protect yourself from the disease?
What causes Buruli ulcer?
Buruli ulcer is caused by the microbe Mycobacterium ulcerans.
It can be transmitted to humans via mosquitoes, so ulcers usually appear in areas near bites, such as on arms and legs.
Loading...
Once in the skin, the bacteria secrete a cocktail of molecules that numb the area, slowly kill surrounding tissues and suppress the immune system.
"These things make it quite an impressive pathogen, and often, it's been there for a while before people actually know they've got it," Daniel O'Brien, an infectious diseases physician at Barwon Health in Geelong and Royal Melbourne Hospital, says.
The progression of lump to ulcer happens in about 90 per cent of Buruli ulcer cases he sees.
In less than 1 per cent of cases, the bacteria reach bone.
How is Buruli ulcer diagnosed and treated?
Buruli ulcer advances so slowly that the first symptoms usually are not noticed until five or six months after the infection.
It is diagnosed by sending a swab off for PCR testing to see whether the ulcer contains M. ulcerans bacteria.
Treatment starts with a six-to-eight-week course of antibiotics, but the drugs themselves can be problematic. They interact with many other medications and produce side effects so awful that about 20 per cent of patients cannot finish the whole course.
Dr O'Brien is leading a team trialling a new antibiotic that can be taken over just 10 days, which he says is less harsh on the body, yet still effective against M. ulcerans.
For most people, antibiotics will be enough, but if there is too much tissue damage or the wound is not healing properly, surgery is needed.
Even with treatment and good wound care, it can take months — even a year — for an ulcer to fully heal.
Dr O'Brien says outcomes for patients are generally better if the ulcer is diagnosed early.
For that reason, he recommends getting a health practitioner to look at any suspicious lumps sooner rather than later, especially if you live or holidayed in an area known to have the bacterium, and to specifically ask about Buruli ulcer.
How can I protect myself from Buruli ulcer?
While Buruli ulcer prevalence is rising, Dr O'Brien says it is important to remember that the disease is still uncommon in humans.
"If you protect yourself from the environment … you really minimise your risk of acquisition."
While mosquitoes are a main source of Buruli ulcers, they are not the only one.
Brushtail and ringtail possums are also known to get infected, and can develop nasty ulcers on their paws, face and tail.
A 2025 study found that analysing the poo of possums could help predict regions where Buruli ulcer might crop up next, with human cases usually appearing up to three years after the first positive possum poo test.
That is because possums shed the bacteria in droppings, introducing it to the soil, which can then get into cuts in our skin.
Dr O'Brien's advice is to:
- cover up as much as possible
- wear mosquito repellent on exposed skin
- cover any wounds while handling soil, and if you injure yourself, wash it immediately with soap and water, then apply antiseptic
- avoid handling sick or injured possums
A recent study found reducing mosquito numbers in Buruli ulcer areas also lowered human case numbers, so it is a good idea to tip out standing water where mosquitoes breed and put out mosquito traps.
It is also important to note that research shows not all possums in Buruli-endemic areas carry the bacteria, and it is illegal to trap, relocate or cull possums without a licence.
And, in good news for ringtails and bushies, an edible possum vaccine in the works could help reduce infections and ulcers in the future.
Hear more about Buruli ulcer on Outbreaks, a special series on Science Friction.

Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:09:38 UTC
11:09:38 KST

Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- Brookhaven National Laboratory
- Summary:
- Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.
- Share:
New findings from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) suggest that scientists can recreate an extraordinary form of matter from the earliest moments of the universe using surprisingly small atomic collisions. By smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light, researchers have uncovered strong evidence of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang.
The findings, published in Physical Review Letters, reveal that high-energy streams of particles lose energy as they travel through the material created by these collisions. This effect, called jet quenching, provides an important clue that quark-gluon plasma has formed.
Scientists have previously observed jet quenching in collisions involving much larger atomic nuclei at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science User Facility that operated at Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 until 2026. The same effect has also been detected in oxygen collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the European Particle Physics Laboratory.
What makes the new RHIC findings especially significant is that the oxygen collisions occurred at substantially lower energies. The results establish a new lower boundary for the conditions known to produce quark-gluon plasma in this small collision system, helping scientists narrow down what it takes to create matter resembling that of the infant universe.
"The QGP is believed to be the form of matter that filled the early universe -- before the protons and neutrons that make up today's atoms formed. Understanding its properties is essential for uncovering how the early universe evolved in its first microseconds," said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University who oversaw the STAR analysis.
"One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear -- and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off," she said.
Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab, explained why investigating smaller collisions is so valuable.
"This analysis is pushing the boundaries to an extreme case to help us learn something about this jet quenching phenomenon and the conditions needed to generate a QGP."
How Scientists Recreate Matter From the Early Universe
RHIC was designed specifically to produce and investigate quark-gluon plasma. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by accelerating gold nuclei to enormous speeds and crashing them into one another.
Each gold nucleus contains 79 protons and 118 neutrons. When two such nuclei collide with sufficient energy, the boundaries of their protons and neutrons effectively break down, releasing the quarks and gluons inside them. The tremendous energy of the impact also generates thousands of additional quarks and gluons through the conversion of energy into matter, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E=mc2.
The result is a fleeting droplet of primordial matter. It is smaller than an atomic nucleus and survives for less than a billionth of a billionth of a second. Almost immediately, the quarks and gluons recombine into more familiar particles.
Because this exotic substance disappears so quickly, scientists cannot examine it directly. Instead, they use enormous instruments such as the STAR detector to analyze the particles that emerge from the collision.
One particularly revealing clue comes from particles that escape with less energy than expected. Their reduced energy suggests they interacted with the dense mixture of quarks and gluons before escaping.
Researchers pay special attention to jets, which are narrow sprays of extremely energetic particles. These often originate when a quark or gluon from one nucleus strikes a quark or gluon from another, sending two particle jets traveling in opposite directions.
If these paired jets, known as "di-jets," form near the edge of the collision region, one may have to travel farther through the plasma than the other. Comparing their behavior allows scientists to investigate how the surrounding material drains energy from particles passing through it.
Yi offered a familiar comparison to explain the process.
"You can think of it like shooting a bullet through, say, water," Yi said. "Because of the resistance, the bullet will slow down. It's the same thing with these high-energy particles. When they go through the QGP, they will lose energy."
The Telltale Signs of Quark-Gluon Plasma
For decades, RHIC experiments have provided clear evidence of jet quenching in collisions between gold nuclei. The effect is especially noticeable in jets that travel longer distances through the newly created matter.
Scientists believe these particles lose more energy because they encounter more quarks and gluons before escaping. Jets originating closer to the outer boundary generally pass through less material and experience fewer interactions.
These measurements helped establish that RHIC was successfully producing quark-gluon plasma. Additional evidence came from several other experiments, including an unexpected discovery about how the resulting matter behaves.
Scientists observed that relatively low-energy particles emerging from gold collisions moved collectively, following coordinated patterns. This behavior indicated that the plasma flowed almost like a perfect liquid, with extraordinarily little viscosity or internal resistance.
The discovery was a major surprise when researchers first identified it. Collective flow has since become another important "smoking gun" signature of quark-gluon plasma.
Can Tiny Atomic Collisions Create Primordial Matter?
After establishing these signatures in collisions involving large nuclei, physicists began finding similar collective motion in much smaller systems.
Experiments at the LHC, followed by studies at RHIC, detected collective flow when tiny projectiles such as protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei struck much larger gold or lead nuclei. Researchers at the LHC even observed comparable flow patterns in collisions between individual protons.
These results raised a major question. Did the coordinated particle motion mean that these much smaller collisions were also producing quark-gluon plasma, or could another mechanism explain the observations?
Scientists needed a more definitive sign.
"The next natural question is: Can you see jet quenching, the other key signature that QGP is formed, in these very small collision systems?" asked Brookhaven's Ma. "We haven't seen any unambiguous signal, so it's still kind of under debate in these small systems. We want to search for the smallest system where we can still see an unambiguous jet-quenching signal," he said.
To investigate, researchers turned to collisions between oxygen nuclei.
An oxygen nucleus contains just eight protons and eight neutrons, making it far smaller than the gold nuclei typically used in RHIC experiments. Oxygen nuclei also have a relatively symmetrical, spherical shape, which makes the geometry of their collisions easier to analyze.
"That means we can more easily look for signs of asymmetric quenching of di-jets produced close to the edge of the circular interaction region in head-on collisions," said Maowu Nie, an associate professor at Shandong University who contributed to the research.
The scientists could also examine how the outcome changed depending on whether the oxygen nuclei collided directly or merely grazed one another.
"We can also compare how jets behave in head-on central collisions -- those that produce the most particles and therefore have the highest likelihood of making a QGP -- with collisions where the two oxygen nuclei barely strike each other, which aren't expected to generate a QGP."
Nie explained that these grazing collisions are recognizable because they generate far fewer particles than direct impacts.
Oxygen Collisions Reveal a 20% Suppression
To search for jet quenching, the researchers developed an analysis that identifies concentrated streams of high-energy particles and measures how many emerge above a selected energy threshold.
"Our measurements are essentially counting experiments," said Sijie Zhang, who conducted the research for her master's thesis under Yi and Nie at Shandong University and is now pursuing a Ph.D. at Yale University.
"We have an algorithm that finds the collimated groups of high-energy particles, the jets, and we count how many of these particles above a certain energy threshold come out."
Yang He, a former Ph.D. student at Shandong University who developed the analysis framework and now studies oxygen collisions at the LHC, described how the team used different collision types to identify energy loss.
"We compare what we see in back-to-back jets produced near the edge of the system, and we compare what we see in head-on collisions with the counts in non-central collisions where we don't expect to see quenching."
The team analyzed STAR measurements from oxygen collisions conducted at RHIC in 2021, at a collision energy of 200 billion electron volts (GeV).
The results revealed a 20% suppression of high-energy particles associated with jet quenching.
Although this suppression was smaller than what physicists typically measure in gold collisions, that difference was expected because oxygen collisions generate much smaller systems.
Crucially, the observed effect was still strong enough to provide clear evidence that quark-gluon plasma had formed.
Comparing Big Bang Matter at Different Energies
Oxygen offers scientists another important advantage. Apart from proton-proton collisions, it is the only nuclear species that has been investigated in collisions at both RHIC and the LHC.
That gives researchers an unusual opportunity to make an "apples-to-apples" comparison between two facilities operating at very different collision energies.
The LHC carried out its first oxygen collisions in 2025. According to results reported by CERN, those experiments revealed both collective flow and jet quenching, providing additional indications that quark-gluon plasma can form in relatively small nuclear collisions.
However, the LHC operated at collision energies exceeding 5,000 GeV, far above the 200 GeV used in the RHIC measurements.
"With a higher energy collision, it's more likely to create more and more quarks and gluons and a hotter, denser QGP system," Yi said. "That means the jet quenching signal, if it's there, should be bigger at LHC compared to RHIC."
While higher energies make it easier to create the hot, dense conditions needed for quark-gluon plasma, lower-energy experiments may be more useful for determining precisely when those conditions are no longer sufficient.
By reducing the collision energy and using smaller nuclei, physicists can approach the threshold at which the distinctive signatures of primordial matter disappear.
"We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies -- and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That's a unique feature of our measurement," Ma said.
New Experiments Could Reveal the Limits of Primordial Matter
Although RHIC has now completed its operations, scientists still have additional oxygen collision data to investigate.
During the collider's final experimental run, researchers collected measurements using both STAR and sPHENIX, RHIC's newest detector. The facility concluded its operations with oxygen collisions recorded by both instruments on February 6, 2026.
These remaining datasets could provide further insights into how small a collision system can become, and how low its energy can fall, before quark-gluon plasma can no longer form.
Understanding those limits may help physicists piece together the behavior of matter during the first microseconds of the universe, when quarks and gluons had not yet combined into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary atoms today.
The research received financial support from the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and additional international agencies and organizations identified in the scientific publication.
The researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which receives direct support from NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science User Facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Pentagon Says Ukraine’s Patriot Missile Production Request Requires ‘Further Review’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:04:48 UTC
11:04:48 KST

Ukraine’s efforts to manufacture American-made Patriot interceptor missiles domestically have encountered another obstacle, with the Pentagon opting for “further review” rather than granting the licensing authorization Kyiv has been seeking.
The response leaves Ukraine without a confirmed agreement or timetable for producing the critical air defense interceptors on its own territory, even as Russia continues its missile attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The development follows Washington’s approval Friday, Oct. 30, of a proposed $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptors to Ukraine.
But President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that the newly approved missiles might not begin arriving for several years, highlighting the widening gap between Ukraine’s immediate defensive requirements and Western weapons production schedules.
“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelensky wrote on X.
He urged Washington and European allies to release interceptors from their existing inventories, with newly manufactured missiles replacing them later.
The Pentagon’s decision to keep the licensing request under review raises a separate question: whether Ukraine will eventually be allowed to manufacture the weapons itself rather than remain dependent on overseas production and deliveries.
Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Jet-Powered Shahed Drone, Injuring 3, Damaging 10 Homes
No authorization or timeline for production in Ukraine
Ukraine has repeatedly sought to expand domestic weapons production as part of its broader effort to reduce dependence on foreign military assistance.
Manufacturing Patriot interceptors domestically would be a significant step toward that objective, potentially allowing Kyiv to build a more sustainable supply of missiles needed to counter Russian ballistic attacks.
However, the Pentagon’s response of “further review” does not constitute approval, nor does it establish when a decision might be made.
Production would require more than political authorization. It would involve licensing agreements, technology-transfer arrangements, industrial investment and the participation of the American companies responsible for manufacturing the interceptors and their components.
The PAC-3 MSE is produced by Lockheed Martin, while Boeing manufactures its advanced seeker components.
Even if Washington approved Ukrainian production, building the necessary manufacturing capabilities would take time and would not immediately resolve the country’s current shortage.
Lockheed Martin confirms ‘deep’ talks on overseas production
Lockheed Martin has acknowledged that it is exploring international manufacturing partnerships as demand for Patriot interceptors rises sharply.
In an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post, Dan Tenney, Lockheed Martin’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, revealed that the company was engaged in advanced discussions with several countries about expanding production overseas.
“We are in pretty deep discussions on this,” Tenney said when asked about the prospect of international production partnerships.
He declined to identify the countries involved or confirm whether Ukraine was among them.
The company has outlined plans to expand annual PAC-3 MSE production capacity to approximately 2,000 interceptors by the end of 2030, compared with roughly 600 annually at the beginning of the expansion effort.

'Dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists': PM Modi hails ISRO after successful GSLV-F18 launch carrying NVS-03
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:04:02 UTC
11:04:02 KST

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday congratulated Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) scientists and engineers following the successful launch of the GSLV-F18 mission carrying the NVS-03 navigation satellite, saying the mission would strengthen India's indigenous satellite navigation system, NavIC.In a post on X, PM Modi said, "Congratulations to our scientists and engineers at ISRO on the successful launch of GSLV-F18 carrying NVS-03.
Also read: Success launch of navigation sat NVS-03 with desi atomic clock will make NaVIC up & running, and give military strategic independenceThis mission marks an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system. Equipped with enhanced capabilities, NVS-03 will further our pursuit of self-reliance in critical technologies and support navigation services that benefit our people.The dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud."
The successful launch is expected to strengthen India's strategic autonomy by helping restore the operational capabilities of NavIC, India's indigenous alternative to global navigation systems such as the US-operated GPS and Russia's GLONASS.The NVS-03 satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock, alongside imported atomic clocks, marking an important step towards reducing India's dependence on foreign technologies for satellite-based navigation.
Atomic clocks provide highly precise time signals that are essential for determining location, navigation and timing.NavIC, which was originally designed around a seven-satellite constellation, had been operating with only three active satellites, below the minimum requirement of four satellites for standalone positioning services. This had limited its use for critical applications, including military navigation, precision positioning and coordination of naval assets.An operational NavIC constellation is particularly important for India's armed forces, which require reliable Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals for missile guidance, precision-guided weapons, troop movement, combat aircraft and naval operations.Dependence on foreign navigation networks can pose strategic vulnerabilities during conflicts, as access to such services could potentially be restricted or disrupted. India experienced the limitations of relying on foreign satellite navigation systems during the 1999 Kargil war.With NVS-03, India aims to strengthen the availability of indigenous navigation services for both civilian and strategic applications. NavIC is designed to provide coverage across India and up to 1,500 km beyond its geographical boundaries.
The original NavIC constellation comprised seven satellites supported by a network of ground stations operating round the clock. Three satellites were placed in geostationary orbit, while four were placed in inclined geosynchronous orbits.However, the constellation's operational strength declined over time as ageing satellites could not be replaced as planned. The launch of NVS-02 on January 29, 2025, also failed to deliver the intended results after a pyro valve signal loss in the engine prevented the satellite from reaching its designated orbit.The successful deployment of NVS-03 is expected to address some of these operational limitations and strengthen India's efforts to establish an independent satellite navigation capability.

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson could make a final bid for freedom. What are the prospects of a high court appeal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:02:04 UTC
11:02:04 KST

After losing her bid for a retrial, the mushroom murderer Erin Patterson could take her fight to the highest court in Australia.
But her prospects of success are far from rosy, a legal expert says.
Patterson woke up at the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre on Saturday knowing she is unlikely to see beyond the four walls of the prison ever again.
Her appeal against her murder and attempted murder convictions failed on Friday as the Victorian court of appeal instead increased her sentence to life without parole, in line with a prosecution appeal.
Her offending was so shocking, the court said her 33-year non-parole period was inappropriate.
Removing a parole period was a rare move for an appeal court, the criminology and justice expert Brianna Chesser says.
“It really speaks to the gravity of the offending,” the RMIT associate professor says. “I was expecting the non-parole period to be raised, maybe to 37 years. But to remove it altogether was definitely a shock.”
Patterson will have 28 days to lodge an application for special leave to appeal to the high court of Australia. If she is granted special leave, she will then have a formal appeal hearing. But 90% of cases do not even cross that first special leave hurdle, Chesser says.
The Victorian court’s dismissal does not automatically give Patterson the right to challenge in the high court, Chesser says.
“The court only deals with cases that shape national law,” she says. “This case would be of particular importance because of the fact that it’s high profile. But you’d be looking for some sort of egregious procedural irregularity, some sort of human rights violation – something really serious.”
Chesser does not believe Patterson’s case falls into any of the categories the high court usually considers.
But she still expects the convicted killer to try.
“It would make sense that she’d run it to the very end and exhaust all possible avenues,” Chesser says.
Patterson deliberately served deadly beef wellingtons to her former in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, 70, and Gail’s sister Heather Wilkinson, 66, in July 2023.
The three guests died after the meal at Patterson’s Leongatha home, in regional Victoria, while Heather’s husband, Ian, fell seriously ill but survived.
She fought to quash her convictions, arguing she suffered a substantial miscarriage of justice and she should have a retrial.
“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” the court of appeal judges said on Friday.
Patterson is only the second woman in Australia to be sentenced to life behind bars without parole.
The first was NSW woman Katherine Knight, who was jailed in 2001 after stabbing her de facto husband to death, skinning him and then trying to serve his cooked flesh to his children.

Hackers are sending fake DTEK emails to gain access to computers — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
UAC-0050 is sending emails about electricity debts with dangerous links. The CPD urges people not to open attachments and to verify bills through official channels.
The UAC-0050 hacker group, linked to russia’s law enforcement agencies, is sending emails about "settling electricity arrears," allegedly on behalf of an accountant at DTEK Energy. The Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD) reports, according to UNN.

This attack is particularly dangerous amid enemy shelling of the energy system and power outages. Its aim is to gain hidden access to the computers of government institutions and complicate the operation of network monitoring systems

European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:56:00 UTC
10:56:00 KST

European diplomats shun Russia at G20 gathering in the US
October 31, 2026
A Group of 20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US city of Atlanta got off to a rocky start on Friday after top diplomats from European nations refused to take a "family photo" along with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the gathering, decided to scrap the photo before the meeting got underway because Washington didn't want it to become a spectacle or distraction.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters before the first session on Friday that there wouldn't "be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia."
The two-day gathering of the G20 grouping, which includes the EU, Russia, Germany, India, China, Brazil and other major countries, is meant to be a precursor to a G20 leaders summit later this December.
That G20 leaders meeting in December is set to be hosted by US President Donald Trump at his golf club in Miami.
Rubio stresses unity despite fractures
Rubio still opened the talks by stressing unity on major issues, telling his counterparts that they were in a "critical moment."
"We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he said.
He pointed to disruptions to global energy and trade and said many were posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order."
But several countries, including the United States and Russia, are involved in separate wars. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have resulted in a spike in food prices for people around the world.
While the message is about unity and finding solutions to problems like freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz during the G20 meeting, the reality is that finding common ground will likely be much tougher.
Given a renewed momentum to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine, there was also interest in getting Lavrov to talk about Russia's stance on future talks with Kyiv.
Russia willing to meet Zelenskyy in Moscow, Lavrov tells DW
The US has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 meeting in Miami, but it's unclear whether Russia has accepted the invitation.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously said that he would be open to traveling to Miami to hold talks with Putin if he were also there.
The Kremlin has so far declined direct meetings with Zelenskyy, with Russia's Sergey Lavrov telling DW on the sidelines of the meeting that Putin is willing to meet with the Ukrainian leader if he travels to Moscow.
"President Putin said if he [Zelenskyy] is willing to meet, let him come to Moscow," Lavrov said. "We will guarantee his safety."
Lavrov declined to say whether Putin will attend the G20 summit this December.
Putin has not attended a G20 leaders meeting since 2019 and only attended a session virtually in 2023.
Russia has also continued with its attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, stepping up drone strikes on water and energy infrastructure.
EU top diplomat calls out Lavrov's 'lies'
The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said ministers at the G20 meeting were able to call out Lavrov for his "lies" at the table.
"We were talking about the big geopolitical crises, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head-on with this," Kallas said on the sidelines of the meeting.
"Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke," she said.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also called out Lavrov, saying, "If we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine."
Lavrov says no easing of ties with US, 'no illusions' about diesel deal
Lavrov, who is under international sanctions for Russia's war in Ukraine, was invited to the US at a time when the two countries have appeared to have fostered warmer ties.
Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia earlier this month and also waived new sanctions on Russia's energy. The US announced the move just weeks away from the midterm elections on November 3.
Lavrov said on Friday that despite those efforts, "in practice, no real progress in relations with the US has so far been seen."
South Africa, a founding member of G20, excluded from US meeting
The Trump administration has been embroiled in disputes with South Africa, having imposed visa restrictions on South Africanswho it said were complicit in discriminating against white people.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year because US officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group.
But US officials didn't extend that invite to South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group.
"We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.
With this many issues on the table, it appeared less likely that there would be a joint consensus at the end of the talks.
Instead of a final declaration, the AFP news agency reported, the meeting is expected to end on Saturday with a chair summary drafted by the US.
Additional reporting from Benjamin Alvarez Gruber.

President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans are battling to maintain majorities in both chambers.
Here is an explanation of the legal issues at play and why the Justice Department will face challenges in its civil lawsuit or any criminal case.

Alaska’s ranked-choice ballot will feature Sullivan, Peltola, a retired teacher whose name is also Daniel Sullivan, and another long-shot candidate.
