A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:59:52 UTC
09:59:52 KST

A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- Mass General Brigham
- Summary:
- A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.
- Share:
A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.
The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.
The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?
Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance
To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.
At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.
The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.
Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.
Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.
A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans
One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.
The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).
This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.
"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."
Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.
Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.
One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.
"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."
There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.
In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.
Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?
The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.
Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.
Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.
For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.
"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."
Authorship: In addition to Sperling and Buckley, Mass General Brigham authors include Diana L. Townsend, Colin J. Birkenbihl, Madison Cuppels, Gillian T. Coughlan, Mabel T. Seto, Jane A. Brown, Michael J. Properzi, Merle C. Hönig, Annie Li, Aaron P. Papp, and Keith A. Johnson. Additional authors include Bryan D. James, Sid O'Bryant, Robert A. Rissman, Melissa Petersen, Jessica Z. K. Caldwell, Tobey Betthauser, Julie Elisabeth Oomens, Maria Carrigan, Sterling C. Johnson, Oliver Langford, Ron Brookmeyer, Timothy J. Hohman, Michael Donohue, and Paul S. Aisen.

Polish opposition party calls for protest outside Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:59:18 UTC
09:59:18 KST

Merve Aydogan
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Poland's opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party's Krakow district organization has urged supporters to gather outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, accusing authorities of attempting to remove its leadership.
In an appeal titled "In Defense of the Constitutional Tribunal," the party's District No. 13 organization said recent developments surrounding the tribunal required a firm response from citizens.
The appeal said the attempt to remove the tribunal's leadership, accompanied by police presence on its premises, raised concerns about the functioning of state institutions and respect for legal procedures.
"In our assessment, these actions may bear the hallmarks of an attempted coup d'etat and require urgent examination by the relevant state authorities," said the statement.
It also cited the First President of the Supreme Court Zbigniew Kapinski, who it said firmly condemned the actions, warning that allowing one institution to be taken over arbitrarily could open the door to similar actions against others.
The party urged those able to travel to Warsaw to gather outside the tribunal's headquarters, asking supporters to help arrange transportation and share the appeal.
"Today, let us demonstrate that strength through our collective, peaceful presence," it said.

The Justice Department’s legal actions in Alaska and California, where the Trump administration is trying to prevent some ballots from being counted, represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution.

McDonald’s must face lawsuit over McRib, US judge rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:46:00 UTC
09:46:00 KST

McDonald’s must face lawsuit over McRib, US judge rules
CHICAGO - A federal judge on Oct 30 rejected McDonald’s request to dismiss a proposed class action accusing it of defrauding consumers about the content of its McRib sandwich.
The plaintiffs accused McDonald’s of intentionally shaping McRib patties with ridges to resemble pork ribs and make diners believe the sandwich contains rib meat, an expensive cut known for its higher fat content and rich flavour.
Consumers said McDonald’s actual use of lower-grade pork products including shoulder, heart, tripe or stomach caused them to overpay for the McRib, one of its most expensive menu items.
While dismissing some claims, US District Judge April Perry in McDonald’s hometown of Chicago called it premature to accept the company’s argument that no reasonable consumer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat.
She said McDonald’s website describes the sandwich only as containing pork, and reasonable consumers need not do research before buying a US$7 (S$8.95) fast-food sandwich.
The judge also said ads highlighting the meat’s rib-like shape could support a claim of intent to defraud, though further proof was needed.
“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.
McDonald’s has sold the McRib periodically since 1981.
It contended that distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers, and the plaintiffs’ preference for a certain cut of pork “doesn’t turn McDonald’s truthful marketing into consumer fraud.”
In a statement, McDonald’s maintained that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach in the McRib, and has always been transparent about its ingredients. “This lawsuit distorts the facts and the claims are meritless,” it added.
Thiago Coelho, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said his clients will continue seeking accountability for deceptive marketing.
Fast-food chains have faced other lawsuits over product depictions in ads and on menu boards.
These include cases accusing McDonald’s, Burger King and Wendy’s of making burgers appear larger than they actually are. REUTERS

Binance seeks to shore up confidence after record US$6.3 billion heist; Trump weighs in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:45:00 UTC
09:45:00 KST

Binance seeks to shore up confidence after record US$6.3 billion heist; Trump weighs in
BOSTON/SINGAPORE/PARIS – Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, worked on Oct 31 to shore up public confidence after a record US$6.3 billion (S$8 billion) hack of its platform, promising it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on news of the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time. The publicly traded stocks of crypto-related firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood slid.
Binance said customer funds were safe and it was working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about US$3 billion located so far. It did not mention the status of the remaining US$3.3 billion, but Binance co-chief executive Yi He said in a post on X that US$3 billion represented only about 2% of the company’s total user assets and public reserves.
The exchange also said on Oct 31 that its technical team was targeting a resumption of withdrawal services within approximately 34 hours. Binance said it was conducting a full security review and planned an initial proof-of-reserves snapshot in 12 hours, with the results expected to be available by Nov 2.
Binance said it has set aside around US$6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a US$1 billion Bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than US$1 billion.
Binance’s other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach was a “complex attack” that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, “making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate”.
The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called “hot” wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, he said.
“Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust,” Teng wrote.
Crypto prices fell broadly but losses were contained. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of US$76,368, and Ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of US$2,178 before markets stabilised. Bitcoin last stood at US$76,447 and Ether at US$2,226. Binance’s BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at US$696.
‘Largest known theft’
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. In 2025, attackers stole US$2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
“This incident is almost certainly the single largest known theft of any kind,” British blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said.
The bulk of the Binance heist unfolded in around 20 minutes, beginning late on Oct 29, and it bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
TRM Labs said the attackers were able to order Binance wallets to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed to North Korea.
North Korea has for years used state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue, according to US and South Korean authorities as well as cybersecurity experts.
North Korea denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
Trump weighs in
US President Donald Trump, asked on Oct 30 whether North Korean hackers were behind the theft, said he did not know but his administration is looking into it.
“It was a hack. That’s the problem. You know the old-fashioned way when you used to sign a cheque, take it out. These are different. People never see the money any more. So I’ve always felt it was a little bit dangerous,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he thought any of the stolen funds could be retrieved. “But no, they (Binance) say they have it pretty much under control.”
Binance is working with the FBI and the US Secret Service, according to a person familiar with the situation.
The FBI said it is “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps”.
The Secret Service said that its investigators “are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday”.
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it froze nearly US$1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than US$800 million.
Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which issued Binance’s main operating licence, said it is “engaging closely with Binance and monitoring the incident”. Abu Dhabi-backed investment group MGX declined to comment. It became a minority investor in Binance in 2025.
Security implications
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which already was under pressure due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges,” said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group.
Investor Michael Saylor, among Bitcoin’s most prominent supporters, said in a post on X that he expects Binance to “deliver” on ensuring no customers suffered losses.
“Our industry will learn from this incident, strengthen security and emerge stronger and more resilient,” Saylor wrote on Oct 30.
335 million registered users
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about US$162.8 billion in assets under custody as at its 2025 annual report.
The heist at Binance drew a relatively measured response from crypto enthusiasts online.
On social media platform Reddit, discussions about the breach featured a mix of humour, confidence in the exchange’s financial resources, and questions about how such an enormous theft could have occurred.
The reaction stood in contrast to the panic surrounding the collapse of FTX in November 2022, when mounting doubts about the exchange’s ability to repay customer funds triggered outrage online.
“Looking at all past data, we find that hot wallet hacks – even large ones – have historically not had a meaningful impact on future crypto returns,” said Matt Hougan, chief investment officer at Bitwise Asset Management. “Investors tend to treat them as ‘one-off events’.” REUTERS

France braces for fresh unrest, government vows tough response
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:36:48 CET
09:36:48 KST

By Dominique Vidalon and Noemie Olive
PARIS, Oct 31 (Reuters) - France deployed a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Saturday in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.
“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying “a very high risk” of unrest.
France’s top administrative court confirmed on Saturday a march between the emblematic Paris squares of Republique and Bastille will be banned, rejecting a challenge by unions. Demonstrations will instead have to be held on boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, away from the main shopping areas in central Paris.
Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
Some 150 gatherings were planned across France, the interior ministry said.
The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.
The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron’s minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for manoeuvre.
Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair, have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent “Yellow Vest” movement demanding action on the cost of living.
PROTESTS SPREAD ACROSS EUROPE
The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
The French government’s promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.
“When I was little, I was told young people were the future,” said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
“Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing.”
The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Friday showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double that when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.
Along Paris’ main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry.
The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest.
(Reporting by Noemie Olive, Dominique Vidalon, Alessandro Parodi, Inti Landauro, Michel Rose; Writing by Mark John; Editing by Ros Russell and Susan Fenton)

By Miranda Murray
BERLIN, Oct 31 (Reuters) - More than 160,000 people across Germany are expected to join demonstrations on Saturday, organisers say, as a youth-led movement inspired by protests elsewhere in Europe takes to the streets to demand better education and lower living costs.
The protests follow a wave of Gen Z-led demonstrations across Europe this year. In Serbia, student-led activism helped unseat the country’s long-time leader at the ballot box, while protests in France have descended into rioting and looting.
The German protests, organised by campaign group Gen Z regelt (Gen Z takes charge), are planned in 34 cities including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich. The group says it opposes compulsory military service and wants greater investment in education as many young Germans struggle with rising costs.
German authorities say they expect Saturday’s demonstrations, which coincide with Halloween festivities, to be largely peaceful but have warned of attempts by extremist groups to exploit the movement.
Parts of Germany’s far-left extremist scene and some groups linked to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilise support, according to the federal interior ministry.
“We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, whose capital is Germany’s financial hub, Frankfurt.
“France must not be held up as a model in this regard.”
In Berlin, some businesses along the luxury Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard boarded up windows and planned early closures ahead of the demonstrations amid concerns about possible unrest.
GEN Z TAKES CHARGE
For organisers, however, the focus is on what they see as the growing pressure on younger generations in Europe’s largest economy.
“The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us,” said Steve, an 18-year-old due to speak at a rally in Munich, addressing Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We will continue to exercise our fundamental right to assemble until you stop ignoring us.”
The protests come as Germany struggles to revive economic growth while facing growing pressure on pensions and public services as baby boomers retire and the working-age population shrinks.
But questions have been raised about who is driving the campaign and whether it is genuinely youth-led, given the broad mix of political and civil society groups involved.
Germany’s national school student umbrella organisation, BSK, has distanced itself from the initiative and plans to hold a separate day of protest on November 20.
“We are distancing ourselves from ‘Gen Z regelt,’ but not from the students themselves, who have legitimate concerns,” said BSK secretary-general Amy Kirchhoff on Thursday.

“When you go inside and enter the rooms, it looks like an abandoned building,” he told Reuters. ”Yet this is where we’re expected to study on a regular basis.”

Earlier on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal’s president and an appointee of Tusk’s far-right predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.
Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the tribunal late on Friday amid a heavy police presence, while right-wing politicians addressed the crowd accusing Tusk’s government of carrying out a coup against the court.

NEW DRAMA IN LONG-RUNNING CONFLICT OVER COURT
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognise appointees put forward by the other side.
Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors — the Law and Justice Party — of subverting.
“This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he said.
The dispute dates back to 2015, when the nationalist Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.
Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.
After Tusk’s coalition took office in 2023 it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
Last month, the parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government’s stated goal of restoring checks and balances.

Rubio urges G20 cooperation amid rifts over wars in Ukraine, Middle East
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:36:09 CET
09:36:09 KST

By Andrea Shalal
ATLANTA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged fellow G20 foreign ministers on Friday to work together for greater geopolitical stability and economic prosperity, warning that a series of crises posed serious threats to the global economic order.
But Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov’s participation in the two-day gathering in Atlanta - at Rubio’s invitation - has roiled many G20 ministers, aggravating deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East during a meeting that is expected to end without a joint declaration. Such statements require consensus that has been elusive if not impossible since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband addressed Lavrov directly during the meeting, telling him: “Only yesterday your drones attacked and killed 15 people. And there are countless examples like this of you killing innocent civilians throughout this war. We all know you are the aggressor.”
Lavrov later told reporters that Moscow’s position on the Ukraine conflict was unchanged, and Russia could not accept Ukraine as a “military threat to the lawful security interests of the Russian Federation,” according to Russian news agencies.
US officials said they skipped a traditional G20 family photo after European officials refused to be photographed with Lavrov. One US official said Washington wanted to avoid a “spectacle” that could overshadow the meeting. A third of members objected, including Australia and Canada, a Western diplomat said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters a photograph with Lavrov was unacceptable because “there is no normalcy with Russia.” Lavrov himself acknowledged that there had been “concerns” about the family photo, drawing head nods from many in the room, one participant said.
Rubio, saying the world faced interconnected crises that threatened global energy and food supply, trade and the freedom of navigation, urged his counterparts to find areas of agreement during the final ministerial meeting before a leaders summit in Miami, Florida, from December 14 to 16.
“We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together … to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests,” he said. “We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle.”
Two Western officials said G20 members were in broad agreement about the severity of the economic challenges facing nearly every country as a result of the war in the Middle East. Many participants worried that renewed US strikes on Iran would send oil prices sharply higher, deepening the pain, they said.
“The possibility for a new military operation in Iran is on everybody’s mind,” said one of the officials, who spoken on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. “Everybody is under deep pressure.”
The foreign ministers’ meeting was expected to end with a chair’s statement, with the bigger effort focused on hammering out a joint declaration that could be signed by G20 leaders at their summit in December, Western officials said. It remains unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the December gathering.
With G20 members Russia, China and middle powers such as Brazil and India trying to navigate US-China strategic competition, you have “much more of a split than we’ve ever had,” said Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who was chief economist at the State Department during the Obama administration.
Over the past decade or so, G7 countries would at least “have agreed a coordinated platform before they came to the G20, but now we don’t even really have that,” she added.
Ministers are expected to discuss supply chain issues and challenges in procuring the critical minerals needed to produce advanced technologies during their discussion on Saturday.
Rubio has championed the Pax Silica initiative, aimed at uniting G20 countries concerned about China’s dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals.
But any movement on that front will probably come afterwards, experts said, pointing to a US-led statement on excess industrial capacity that some G20 trade ministers signed after the group failed to reach consensus.
Elaine Dezenski of the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies said such statements by ad hoc groups could offer a way forward in the current difficult environment.
“The right test is whether the US can build cooperation with partners when all-member consensus appears to be out of reach,” she said. She noted the Quad — a security grouping of the US, India, Japan and Australia — would also meet in Atlanta on Saturday, on the sidelines of the G20 gathering.
US President Donald Trump’s recent decisions on Russia, including a deal to buy diesel and waiving some sanctions, formed a challenging backdrop for the talks, along with Ukraine’s problems with its Starshield satellite services, participants said. Ukraine was not invited to attend.
Washington announced a multibillion-dollar sale of Patriot interceptors late on Friday, offering some good news to Kyiv.
Before the meeting, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she would call for increased support for Ukraine, while pushing for progress on accountability measures through the Special Tribunal and Claims Commission.
“Russia must be accountable,” she wrote on X.
(Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Additional reporting by Simon Lewis; Editing by Don Durfee, Kate Mayberry, Sanjeev Miglani and Tom Hogue)

Poland’s Sikorski calls for rapid ceasefire in Black Sea to allow food shipments
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:36:06 CET
09:36:06 KST

By Andrea Shalal
ATLANTA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski on Friday called for a rapid ceasefire in the Black Sea that would allow safe passage for grain shipments from both Ukraine and Russia and said Moscow must end its war against Ukraine before being allowed to resume energy sales to Europe.
“I spoke in favor of doing something quickly because the people of the Global South need this grain,” Sikorski told reporters during a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 20 major economies in Atlanta.
Sikorski, invited to attend the meeting by the US host nation, said that Ukraine must be included in any effort to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Europe also had “cards” in the issue and should be involved, he said.
He also called for a “fair end” to the war in Ukraine before Russia was able to sell its energy products once again to Europe, formerly its most lucrative market.
The United States, which holds the rotating presidency of the G20 this year, has proposed that Poland become a full member, much like Germany or France, which are also represented through the European Union.
Sikorski said he welcomed the push and had discussed it with a number of G20 member countries in bilateral meetings in Atlanta.
Western officials say it could take years for Poland to be accepted as a full member given Russia’s opposition and the G20’s requirement for consensual decisions.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told reporters that inviting Poland to attend G20 meetings was counterproductive and broke with diplomatic practice of seeking consensus at such gatherings, according to Russian news agencies.
“Of course, this violates the principles of diplomacy, and especially multilateral diplomacy, when members of associations such as the G20 work on the basis of consensus,” Lavrov was quoted as saying.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking at a reception for the ministers at Atlanta’s Georgia Aquarium, said Poland deserved to be made a full member.
“President (Donald) Trump believes their economic success and growing global influence is exactly what the G20 needs to tackle the major economic challenges we all face,” Rubio said.
Sikorski told reporters that Britain, which will head the G20 next year, had already invited Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to attend the 2027 leaders summit in Manchester, England.
(Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by Tom Hogue)

Lavrov urges Japan to abandon unfriendly policy to resume full-fledged dialogue with Russia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:33:23 CST
09:33:23 KST

MOSCOW, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told his Japanese counterpart, Toshimitsu Motegi, on Friday that Tokyo needs to abandon its unfriendly policy toward Moscow to resume full-fledged bilateral dialogue, the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
The two foreign ministers met at the request of the Japanese side on the sidelines of a Group of 20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, the United States.
Japan has joined Western sanctions against Russia and stepped up criticism of Moscow since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
The last formal meeting between Lavrov and Motegi took place in September 2021 on the sidelines of the 76th session of the UN General Assembly in New York. ■

US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:29:28 UTC
09:29:28 KST

The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

Polish president holds emergency meeting with Supreme Court chief amid court crisis

MOSCOW, October 31. /TASS/. Polish President Karol Nawrocki is holding an emergency meeting, following his return to Warsaw, with First President of the Supreme Court Zbigniew Kapinski and Bogdan Swieczkowski, who was previously reported to have been suspended from his duties as acting president of the Constitutional Court, the Onet news portal reports.
According to the news portal, Nawrocki met with the judges immediately after arriving at the presidential palace in Warsaw. The Polish leader decided to turn his plane around while en route to Senegal and return to the capital after Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek filed a motion to strip Swieczkowski of his immunity.
In recent weeks, opposition protests have been held outside the Constitutional Court over Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s decision to appoint Maciej Berek, a former minister in his government, as a judge on the court. On October 30, Zurek filed a motion to suspend Swieczkowski from his duties and strip him of his immunity. Swieczkowski was suspended from his duties for one month. Additional police forces were deployed to guard the court premises. Protesters attempted to break through the barriers surrounding the court.

Saudi Arabian surgeons successfully separate Tanzanian conjoined twins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:26:57 UTC
09:26:57 KST

Saudi Arabian surgeons successfully separate Tanzanian conjoined twins
The medical and surgical team of the Saudi Conjoined Twins Programme has successfully separated Tanzanian conjoined twins Laityness and Loveness in a 14.5-hour operation in Riyadh, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Saudi Press Agency.
The operation was performed at King Abdullah Specialist Children’s Hospital in King Abdulaziz Medical City, affiliated with the Ministry of National Guard.
Dr. Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al Rabeeah, head of the programme’s medical and surgical team, said the operation was completed in nine stages.
A total of 44 consultants, specialists, nurses and technical staff from various medical disciplines took part in the procedure to ensure precision and safety at every stage.
The twins, aged two years and two months, were joined at the pelvis and hips and shared the lower part of the intestines, the spinal column, lumbar vertebrae and spinal cord. They had four lower limbs.
According to Dr. Al Rabeeah, this was the fourth successful separation of conjoined twins from Tanzania and the 75th operation conducted under the Saudi Conjoined Twins Programme.
Over more than 35 years, the programme has assessed 160 cases from 29 countries, highlighting Saudi Arabia’s role in humanitarian and medical care.
The programme receives direct support from the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud.
Earlier, a team of Saudi surgeons successfully separated Moroccan conjoined twins Saja and Doha during a six-hour operation.

Meta settles, leaving Snap sole defendant in new social media trial

- Lawyers said the plaintiffs, SJ and KDB, claim they were exposed to “addictive and problematic” apps at ages 13 and 15.
- The settlement avoids trial costs and witness testimony, while Meta and other firms face wider child safety lawsuits and big penalties.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO - Meta reached a settlement in a landmark case over the alleged harms of social media, the plaintiffs’ lawyers said on Oct 30, leaving Snap as the only defendant in a trial set to open in Los Angeles next week.
“We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client,” Emily Jeffcott, a lawyer representing one of the young women suing both companies, said in a statement.
Jury selection began on Oct 28, and opening statements are scheduled for Nov 4.
The terms of the agreement are confidential, but sources close to Meta told AFP the company decided to settle for business reasons.
“Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception,” a Meta spokesperson said, referring to the series of test cases against the company being tried in Los Angeles.
If Snap does not settle, the trial will go ahead next week.
Snap did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
TikTok and YouTube were also named as defendants in the case, but both had already reached settlements with the plaintiffs, known by their initials SJ and KDB, their lawyers said.
Meta had also previously settled with SJ.
A California state judge consolidated the two cases into a single trial.
Snap, which makes Snapchat, will defend itself against the claims of both SJ and KDB.
Lawyers for SJ and KDB will argue that their clients were exposed to “addictive and problematic” social media apps when they started using them at ages 13 and 15, respectively, according to court documents.
“We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement earlier this week.
Avoiding trial
Thousands of lawsuits have been filed in recent years in local, state and federal courtrooms across the country with various claims about alleged harms to children and teenagers caused by social media companies.
The cases – the first of which went to trial earlier in 2026 in Los Angeles – have taken twists and turns.
Meta and YouTube lost the first so-called bellwether case earlier in 2026, when a jury found them collectively liable for harming a young user known by the initials KGM, and ordered the tech companies to pay a combined US$6 million (S$7.67 million) penalty.
Snap and TikTok settled with KGM ahead of that trial.
Months later, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled another case that was set to go to trial in August; that plaintiff, known as RKC, then withdrew their remaining claims against Meta, allowing the Instagram and Facebook maker to avoid trial without a settlement.
By settling before a trial kicks off, the social media companies contain costs from lawyer fees and potential penalties; another benefit is that it shields their executives from testifying in court.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri were expected to be called as key witnesses in the upcoming Los Angeles trial.
Snap CEO Evan Spiegel is expected to testify if the trial proceeds without another settlement.
In August, Meta agreed to pay more than US$18 billion in penalties, in addition to making changes to Instagram and Facebook for teens, when it settled with 52 attorneys general several days into a trial held in California.
That settlement came just a day after Mosseri testified, and before Zuckerberg had been called to the stand.
Meta has faced other trials, though.
Earlier in October, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case where the company was found liable for deceiving users in the state about how their data was used in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
A New Mexico jury also found the social media giant liable for harms to children, leading to a combined penalty of US$942 million earlier in 2026. AFP

Germany and France are preparing for potential protests over the weekend that could coincide with Halloween festivities.

Police plan to deploy thousands of additional officers across the country. Some luxury jewellery shops and clothing stores have boarded up windows to protect against potential looting or violence.
Protests in Germany are led by a group dubbed “GenZ regelt!”, which translates to “Gen Z has got this!”.

France braces again
Many of those grievances mirror those of the youth-led protests that have convulsed French cities and towns for three consecutive weekends.
Shops and businesses in Paris and other cities were boarding up windows on Friday.

Authorities have also said face-covering masks will not be allowed at the demonstrations.
France’s interior minister has warned of a “very high risk” of disorder over the weekend.
Two weeks ago, widespread unrest broke out in cities and towns across France as demonstrations against the cost of living and conditions in schools descended into large-scale looting and riots.
Since then, French authorities have sought to clamp down on violent protests, but last weekend saw further demonstrations across the country, including intermittent clashes with the police.

Halloween “is not helping matters”, he said, “because we’re going to have people wearing masks”.

In New Zealand’s bellwether seat, what are locals thinking as a knife-edge poll looms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:15:27 UTC
09:15:27 KST

It’s a hot spring day in the Auckland suburb of Onehunga, and the main strip is starting to hum with life. Builders slip into a bakery for a snack, retirees chat over coffee outside cafes and a shoeless man zips by on a scooter.
There are few signs New Zealand’s general election is looming along this shopping strip but Onehunga and neighbouring suburbs that make up the electorate Maungakiekie, will be closely watched when New Zealand heads to the polls on 7 November.
Over the past two elections, the Maungakiekie electorate has proven to be an “extraordinary” bellwether seat, accurately reflecting the mood of the nation.
In 2020, when Labour won 50% of the national vote, a near-identical 50.3% of Maungakiekie’s voters backed the party. Three years later, when Labour’s vote plunged to 26.9%, so too did Maungakiekie’s support for the party, falling to just 27.1%.
“[Maungakiekie] tracked the national number with extraordinary precision both times,” says Dr Michael Swanson, an honorary research fellow in politics at the University of Otago.
This year’s election is on a knife-edge. With voters frustrated by a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, polls indicate neither the left nor right blocs will win an outright majority. Support for mainstream parties, National and Labour, is slipping in favour of minor parties – one of which, Opportunity, could decide who will next govern New Zealand.
Maungakiekie defies easy categorisation. Some parts are affluent – home to leafy streets and multimillion dollar homes. Others, such as Onehunga, were working class, but have been gentrified. The seat is ethnically diverse and home to a younger demographic than the Auckland average.
Maungakiekie is “a really interesting and relatively accurate” representation of modern New Zealand, Swanson says, and has been a consistently reliable barometer for which way support is leaning for parties.
When the Guardian visits the electorate in October, two key themes emerge: a grudging fealty to the National party – which has led the centre-right coalition government since 2023 – and growing support for minor parties.
Jemimah Fifita, a 25-year-old student who works at a local cafe, is about to ditch a family tradition of voting Labour.
“I’m very mindful of who I think I should vote for,” she says, “especially as a young person, because we are struggling” – nodding to high rates of youth unemployment and the rising costs of living.
Fifita is yet to decide who will get her vote, but the centrist Opportunity party has caught her attention. Opportunity has been consistently polling above the 5% threshold of seats needed to enter parliament, but it remains to be seen if that support translates into votes next Saturday.
Across the road, sitting outside a bakery are longtime Onehunga residents, Nigel Higgins and Lance Polmear. Higgins has not voted since the 1980s because he believes “all governments are oppressive”. But Polmear, who works in construction, says he will again vote for National, despite being unhappy with some of its policies, such as immigration.
At a cafe further up the street, retiree Margôt Phillipps reckons the government has been “shocking” this term, so she will be voting for the Green party, for its environmental stance and its policy of redistributing wealth.
In Ellerslie, a more affluent and less diverse suburb than Onehunga, locals are largely sticking with the status quo: the National-led coalition with the right-wing Act party and populist New Zealand First.
Kerry McCullough, a florist on the main street, is “very much against Labour” and will vote National even though she thinks party leader Christopher Luxon is “not very appealing”.
Across the road, butcher David Parsons is weighing cuts of meat for customers. He is switching his party vote from National to New Zealand First, led by Winston Peters, a politician who entered parliament in 1978 with National.
“It’s not something I ever thought I would do – my family has a long history of voting National – but its come to the point where I see a bit more eye-to-eye with Winston Peters,” Parsons says, adding he has become more concerned about immigration and believes the country should boost mining to grow the economy, issues that New Zealand First has campaigned on.
A mood of disillusionment could spell bad news for Luxon and National, who face the possibility of being the first one-term National-led government since the party was founded in 1936.
Polling in recent months has shown just a few points separating the winning and losing blocs. A RNZ-Reid Research poll released on Thursday shows National slumping under 25%, and Labour in a position to form a government alongside the Greens and Opportunity. A 1News-Verian poll released two days earlier had National slightly ahead and returning to power.
Support appears strong for the right-leaning coalition in Maungakiekie, but recent changes to the electorate’s boundary lines could alter the political landscape.
The new boundary lines add nearly 10,000 voters from a left-leaning suburb, but cut about 2,200 voters from a right-leaning suburb. The seat could inflate support for Labour compared with the national result and upset its bellwether status, Swanson says.
Regardless, Maungakiekie will remain one of the most closely watched seats when results roll in on election night, he says.
“They have earned, across several elections, the right to be taken seriously as a signal.”

What is celebrated on October 31 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:15:13 EET
09:15:13 KST

What is celebrated on October 31 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 31 marks the international days of cities, savings, and the Black Sea, as well as Halloween and Reformation Day. Believers honor the Apostles Stachys and Luke.
On October 31, under the auspices of the UN and international organizations, the world marks World Cities Day, World Savings Day, and World Awareness Day, as well as celebrating Halloween and International Black Sea Day. According to the new calendar, the church calendar honors the holy Apostle of the Seventy Stachys, Amplias, and others, while according to the old calendar it commemorates the holy Apostle and Evangelist Luke, UNN writes.
World Cities Day
An official UN international observance established by the General Assembly in 2013. The event aims to draw the global community's attention to worldwide urbanization, promote cooperation between countries in addressing urban development challenges, and implement sustainable urban planning concepts.
The day emphasizes the importance of creating an inclusive, safe, environmentally sustainable, and livable urban environment amid climate change and population growth.
World Savings Day
Established in 1924 during the First International Congress of Savings Banks in Milan. The event is dedicated to promoting a culture of saving, improving financial literacy among the population, fostering investment awareness, and explaining the role of savings institutions in the stability of national economies.
International Black Sea Day
A regional environmental observance established in 1996, when six Black Sea countries signed the Strategic Action Plan for the Protection and Rehabilitation of the Black Sea.
The event is intended to draw attention to preserving the unique marine ecosystem, combating pollution by petroleum products and plastic, protecting biodiversity, and addressing the problem of overfishing.
Halloween
A traditional holiday originating from the ancient Celtic pagan festival of Samhain, which marked the end of the harvest and the beginning of the "dark half of the year."
In modern popular culture, Halloween has become a global entertainment holiday featuring pumpkin lantern carving, costume parties, children collecting candy, and horror- and mysticism-themed events.
Reformation Day
An official public and religious holiday in many regions of Germany, Slovenia, numerous Swiss cantons, and Protestant communities around the world.
The date was established to commemorate October 31, 1517, when German theologian Martin Luther nailed his famous "95 Theses" to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg. This act sharply exposed the Catholic Church's abuses involving the sale of indulgences and marked the beginning of the Reformation in Europe and the emergence of Protestantism.
Pope Leo apologized for the Catholic Church's role in slavery26.05.26, 03:57 • 5192 views
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the holy Apostles of the Seventy: Stachys, Amplias, Urbanus, Narcissus, Apelles, and Aristobulus - disciples of the Chief Apostles Peter and Paul, who ordained them as bishops and preached the Gospel in various parts of the Roman Empire.
Saint Stachys was the first bishop of Byzantium, appointed by the Apostle Andrew the First-Called, and together with his companions endured numerous hardships and tortures for the faith.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the holy Apostle and Evangelist Luke - one of Christ's seventy disciples, a companion of the Apostle Paul, a physician, and the author of one of the four Gospels and the Book of Acts of the Apostles. According to church tradition, Saint Luke was the first icon painter and painted the first images of the Mother of God.

====================================================================================================

The True Story of Tragedy and Perseverance Behind Everest: The Other Side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:09:18 UTC
09:09:18 KST

Mount Everest is the largest mountain in the world. It’s estimated that more than 7,500 people have stood on its peak, reaching an astonishing 29,031 feet above sea level in Nepal, typically climbing up the mountain’s south side. But Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s documentary Everest: The Other Side shifts focus to the mountain’s north face. It is here that two people, ski mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson, attempted to do something that no human being had done before.
Morrison and Nelson met in 2015 on an expedition to Makalu, the world’s fifth-highest mountain, in the Mahalangur Himalayas. The pair developed a friendship before beginning a romantic relationship in 2017, bonding over their shared sense of adventure. “There’s a connection I don’t feel anywhere else…I love how it makes me feel alive,” Nelson says about ski mountaineering in the new film, which hit theaters on Oct. 30 following its premiere at the Venice Film Festival. Together, Morrison and Nelson conceived a plan: They would climb to the top of Everest’s north face, and once they’d reached the summit, become the first to ski down it. It was the ultimate proposal for a pair of adventurous thrill-seekers, but one wrong move could result in disaster. They never got the chance to take the risk together, though: Disaster struck before they embarked on the journey, a tragedy the directors capture in devastating detail in the new film.
Vasarhelyi and Chin are drawn to stories of people who accomplish extraordinary things, and they set out to capture them in a manner that fully captures their feats, like in Free Solo, Meru, and The Rescue. Everest: The Other Side is playing in both regular format and IMAX cinemas, the latter of which takes particular advantage of the breathtaking shots the filmmakers were able to capture, offering a sense of how epic Everest is, and how dangerous.
Though most people don’t participate in extreme sports, Vasarhelyi believes there’s something inherently relatable about these feats. “I think it’s fundamental to the human paradox, which is this ability to dream audaciously, and then the mentality, psychology, mania—whatever you want to call it—to actually have the grit, determination, and diligence to get it done. I think everyone can identify with that,” she tells TIME.
A tragedy changes everything
Vasarhelyi and Chin intended for Everest: The Other Side to capture Morrison and Nelson’s historic feat. But on Sept. 26, 2022, tragedy struck. Nelson and Morrison were climbing nearby Mount Manaslu in Nepal when an avalanche swept down the slope, killing Nelson. It was a devastating moment captured on camera, one that had both the filmmakers and Morrison questioning whether they should continue with their journey, and the film, at all.
“We always knew we were making a film about Jim and Hilaree and their attempt to ski and climb the direct north face, but these films for us always had to have something deeper. The part that stayed true throughout was this extraordinary love story,” says Chin. 
Morrison had experienced tragic loss before. In 2011, he lost his wife Katie and their two children in a plane crash. “I knew about Jim’s history and the loss that he’d been through, and how he had moved through that loss and found the strength and courage to fall in love again with Hilaree. That was extremely moving to me,” says Chin. “When we lost Hilaree, we saw that again in real time. We were living it with him.”
Together, they decided that Chin, a longtime friend of the couple and an experienced climber, would step in as Morrison’s climbing partner, replacing Nelson.
“Jimmy and I fundamentally see this differently," says Vasarhelyi of whether they would continue making the film. “It was such a tragedy when Hilaree passed, and real life has to be lived in that moment. With the decision of Jimmy stepping in as Jim’s only climbing partner, my professional interest came into direct conflict with my personal responsibilities.” At the time of filming, Vasarhelyi and Chin were married with two children. The couple divorced in 2025.
“The question was, ‘Do you want to make that film?’ It was going to be heavier. It had to be very candid, which all our films are, but this was requiring us to go one step further in this investigation. There was also the reality of, how do you wrangle the story that was conceived one way into something that could both honor her legacy as well as honor this incredible journey that Jim would go on?” says Vasarhelyi.
Ultimately, it was Morrison who made the decision to continue filming. “In the beginning, I didn’t want to keep going to the mountains. I was devastated by the loss of Hilaree,” he says. Initially, it looked like the quest to ski mountaineer the north face of Everest was over, and there was a seven-month break in filming. “Over time,” Morrison explains, “the inner fire and the passion for this project Hilaree and I shared together became a driving force in my life. I began to call [Chai and Jimmy] to say, ‘I’m going to go back into the mountains. I’m going to go on another expedition and push myself to complete this goal for us and for her legacy and her story.”
With Chin as his climbing partner and Vasarhelyi and Chin continuing to document the adventure, Everest: The Other Side would go on. Instead of a story of a couple facing this incredible physical feat together, it became a story of processing grief and overcoming tragedy.
The two expeditions
The expedition on Everest’s north face occurred in 2024. Chin explains why the north side of Everest, the more challenging route up the mountain and an extremely steep, 9,000-ft. face, holds such appeal. “In terms of pure technical difficulty, it’s really challenging. Because of those challenges and because it’s a direct line, it’s really appealing to climbers.” He continues: “When you’ve spent a lifetime in the mountains, you build experience to take on more and more difficult climbs, and as a ski mountaineer, more challenging ski descents. This is the ultimate line on the tallest mountain on Earth that literally splits the biggest face on Everest.”
The 2024 expedition involved dozens of people, including climbers, camp managers, cooks, and cinematographers. The set-up involved three different camps. The climb would start at 20,000 ft. and go up 9,000 ft. to the top of the mountain. An advanced basecamp would be established at 18,100 ft., as well as three additional camps, with one right below the entrance of the Hornbein Couloir, the most challenging and steepest part of the climb.
To accomplish such a challenging climb, the climbers would do rotations, going up the mountain and back down, in an effort to build up red blood cells and acclimatize themselves to the changes in altitude as well as to bring equipment up the mountain. The process involves pushing the body to its limits, over and over again, before returning to base camp and going again. “It’s hard to sleep at 18,000 ft., so it becomes this game of acclimatizing and getting all your equipment, the rope and all the oxygen cylinders and the sherpa up the mountain,” says Morrison.
Unfortunately, one of the climbers on the expedition, Yukta Gurung, broke his leg on the journey up Everest. With that injury and the uneasy weather conditions, the decision was made to call the expedition off. “It felt like we were walking away, and we weren’t coming back,” recalls Morrisson. Chin didn’t see it that way. “Walking through the airport terminal with Jimmy, he was like, ‘Of course you’re going to go back.’”
Chin was right. In September 2025, Morrison, Chin, and a team of 12 climbers, including a healed Gurung, returned to Everest. The expedition took seven weeks, and this time there were no injuries or unforeseen weather circumstances. On Oct. 15, 2025, they arrived at the peak. Jim Morrison, Jimmy Chin, and their team of climbers—Carla Perez, Esteban Mena Yanez, Pasang Sona Sherpa, Pemba Sherpa, Roberto Morales, Erich Reopke, Nigma Tenjing Sherpa, Pemba Gelje Sherpa, Pur Bahadur “Yukta” Gurung, and Tenging Gyaljen Sherpa—reached the summit. It wasn’t over yet: Morrison still intended to be the first person to ski down Everest’s north face.
“We got to the summit about 2 p.m.,” recalls Morrison. “We spent about 45 minutes on top. I connected with Hilaree and spread some of her ashes. There were a lot of hugs and a lot of tears. Then I started transitioning to skiing, which might take five to 10 minutes normally, but takes a lot longer on top of a mountain. Just buckling your boots at 29,000 ft. Every couple of buckles, you have to stand up and take a break to get hold of your breath. Everything becomes laborious. Then I looked over at Jimmy and my other teammates on the summit and said ‘OK, here we go.’” Any mistake, Morrison reminded his teammates, and himself, could prove catastrophic.
The epic descent
Then came what Morrison describes as “the greatest run of my life—the hardest, longest, deepest, scariest, most dramatic ski run.” It took four hours and five minutes to ski down the north face of Everest. “It wasn’t four hours straight skiing,” says Morrison. “You take it one step at a time, one turn at a time, and there’s a lot of stopping.” He compares it to running to the end of the street as fast as you can, over and over. Going down at least means more access to oxygen. “As I went further down the mountain, I was able to recover a lot quicker, and as my physical endurance wore away, I got into a more oxygen-rich environment, which helped keep me going and able to achieve this.”
Morrison explains his feelings as he reached safety as “a tidal wave of emotions.” He recalls: “I just totally broke down. I’m crying and yelling at the sky. I’m all by myself in this glacier, and it was just a tremendous overwhelming feeling that we did it,” referring to himself and Hilaree. “I felt like we did it together, and we accomplished it. It starts with Hilaree and I, but it reverberates to the other 11 people that were on the summit with me, everyone that’s below me in base camp or in camp one, and everyone across the planet pushing their energy for us to accomplish and achieve it.”
He looks back on the scale and scope of what they all accomplished together. “I felt like it was a tremendous team effort and something that humanity helped me do.”

Gen Z protests reach Germany as over 160,000 expected at Halloween rallies
BERLIN – More than 160,000 people across Germany are expected to join demonstrations on Oct 31, organisers say, as a youth-led movement inspired by protests elsewhere in Europe takes to the streets to demand better education and lower living costs.
The protests follow a wave of Gen Z-led demonstrations across Europe in 2026.
In Serbia, student-led activism helped unseat the country’s long-time leader at the ballot box, while protests in France have descended into rioting and looting.
The German protests, organised by campaign group Gen Z regelt (Gen Z takes charge), are planned in 34 cities including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich. The group says it opposes compulsory military service and wants greater investment in education as many young Germans struggle with rising costs.
The German authorities say they expect the demonstrations on Oct 31, which coincide with Halloween festivities, to be largely peaceful but have warned of attempts by extremist groups to exploit the movement.
Parts of Germany’s far-left extremist scene and some groups linked to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilise support, according to the federal interior ministry.
“We all have those images from France in our minds – looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, whose capital is Germany’s financial hub, Frankfurt.
“France must not be held up as a model in this regard.”
In Berlin, some businesses along the luxury Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard boarded up windows and planned early closures ahead of the demonstrations amid concerns about possible unrest.
Gen Z takes charge
For organisers, however, the focus is on what they see as the growing pressure on younger generations in Europe’s largest economy.
“The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us,” said Steve, an 18-year-old due to speak at a rally in Munich, addressing Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We will continue to exercise our fundamental right to assemble until you stop ignoring us.”
The protests come as Germany struggles to revive economic growth while facing growing pressure on pensions and public services as baby boomers retire and the working-age population shrinks.
But questions have been raised about who is driving the campaign and whether it is genuinely youth-led, given the broad mix of political and civil society groups involved.
Germany’s national school student umbrella organisation, BSK, has distanced itself from the initiative and plans to hold a separate day of protest on Nov 20.
“We are distancing ourselves from ‘Gen Z regelt’, but not from the students themselves, who have legitimate concerns,” said BSK secretary-general Amy Kirchhoff on Oct 29.
Sean Baker, a student at the Technical University of Berlin, said he would join the protests on Oct 31 to call attention to the poor state of buildings on campus.
“When you go inside and enter the rooms, it looks like an abandoned building,” he told Reuters. “Yet this is where we’re expected to study on a regular basis.” REUTERS

France braces itself for fresh unrest, government vows tough response
PARIS – France will deploy a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Oct 31 in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The nationwide demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.
“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying “a very high risk” of unrest.
The authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.
The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.
The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron’s minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for manoeuvre.
Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent “Yellow Vest” movement demanding action on the cost of living.
Protests spread across Europe
The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Oct 31.
The French government’s promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.
“When I was little, I was told young people were the future,” said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne, who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
“Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing.”
The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Oct 30 showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion (S$1.43 billion). Other estimates put the total at double when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.
Along Paris’ main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry.
The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest. REUTERS
