‘We’re not freaks’: police raid sparks concern for Taiwan’s LGBT-friendly image
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:05:27 UTC
09:05:27 KST

Josh was having a drink at Commander D, a popular gay bar in Taipei, on a Saturday afternoon when several police officers suddenly burst in. “Squat down and don’t move,” they shouted. Bewildered, he looked around to see the bar owner being handcuffed and forced to his knees.
The 28-year-old was among 51 customers to be rounded up and taken away for questioning over suspected breaches of public decency rules.
“I didn’t expect something like this to still happen these days. It definitely made me feel a lot less safe,” says Josh, a gay man from Taiwan whose name has been changed due to the sensitivity of the incident. The police operation was criticised by rights groups as heavy-handed, and has unsettled LGBTQ+ communities in Taiwan.
On Saturday the island hosts one of the region’s largest Pride parades, and some say the police operation is emblematic of a persistent, wider stigma that risks jeopardising its global image as a LGBTQ-friendly destination.
‘Will it be safe to hold hands in the street?’
The raid took place on 3 October at a bar that is billed as Taipei’s first and only BDSM-themed bar and features in several international travel guides. Commander D has operated for more than a decade in the Ximending area – a hub for LGBTQ+ tourists where gay bars and sex shops can be easily spotted.
The bar’s owner was arrested and referred to prosecutors on suspicion of profiting from facilitating sexual or indecent acts, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison.
In the days after the raid, the police department said that it had received 13 complaints this year alleging public decency violations at the bar.
In an interview with Taiwanese media on 7 October, the bar owner accused the police of using excessive force and said that any intimate encounters between customers were a matter of personal choice. He has not yet been formally charged with any offences. His lawyer declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing investigation.
Videos posted on social media showed the police mocking a disabled customer and preventing some people from putting their clothes back on. Some had taken their shirts off because it was a warm day. Police said they had reviewed 41 body cam recordings and acknowledged inappropriate language had been used by its officers.
“There was an element of sexual humiliation,” says Victoria Hsu, a human rights lawyer specialising in LGBTQ+ rights. As police refused to let the patrons get dressed, “they weren’t allowed to go to the police station with dignity”.
The police department said their actions were intended to bring the scene under control and the court-authorised search had not targeted any particular group or sexual orientation. Yet after a strong public backlash, Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an apologised and six police officers were disciplined for inappropriate remarks and failing to supervise their juniors properly. Rights groups are calling for an independent investigation.
Wanhua police division said rights groups filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors on 7 October. “The matter has entered the judicial process, and we await the outcome of the investigation and any subsequent court proceedings.”
Midnight Poonkasetwattana, executive director of the Bangkok-based LGBTQ+ advocacy network APCOM, told Taiwan’s Central news agency that the raid “could undermine the gay-friendly image Taiwan has built”.
Hung Yan-an, a gay man living in Taipei, says he received messages from overseas friends about the incident. “A gay friend of mine in Spain has been asking me: ‘Is everything OK? If I visit, will it be safe to hold hands with my partner in the street?’”
Persistent stigma
The episode stands in stark contrast to a recent survey that found public support for gay marriage has increased from 42% to 54% since Taiwan legalised same-sex marriage in 2019, the first place in Asia to do so.
“But inclusion is not only about marriage equality, Pride or international recognition. It is also about how public institutions treat LGBTQI+ people when exercising state power,” Poonkasetwattana said in a formal letter of protest to Taiwan’s representative in Thailand over the decision to raid Commander D.
Local campaigners say the raid exposes a persistent stigma around queer venues, as well as “homophobia, discrimination and abuse of power that have long been embedded in the police system”.
A spokesperson for the Wanhua police division did not directly address the allegations of longstanding institutional homophobia but said it “fully respects social and cultural diversity and people’s rights” and would continue to combat crime and enforce the law to maintain public order.
Other gay venues have also faced scrutiny. In April, a gay bathhouse in the central city of Taichung closed after a police raid over suspected public-decency offences and subsequent inspections. In a Facebook statement announcing the closure, its owner accused police of discriminatory treatment. A gay gym in Taipei, which closed in 2021, had reportedly been inspected 186 times over three years.
“Some police officers assume that gay people are more likely to have drugs on them,” lawyer Hsu says. “I’ve had quite a few LGBTQ+ people come to me for legal advice, for example, some of them were subjected to improper police searches.”
‘A subtle sense of discomfort’
For Chien Shih-han, a Taiwanese drag queen who performs as Hannah, discrimination is not always easy to identify. He recalls gay venues facing repeated noise complaints and a pre-booked taxi driving away after the driver saw a friend in drag.
“It could all come down to this subtle sense of discomfort or anxiety towards sexual minorities,” Chien says.
In his view, gay venues such as Commander D have offered a refuge to people who do not fit the mainstream, even within the LGBTQ+ community. “It was a kind of safety net,” Chien says. “Now it feels as though someone is setting fire to that net.”
Weeks later, Josh says he still feels “a little scared” when thinking back to the raid, but that it would not stop him taking to the streets for Taiwan Pride.
“I want to express my anger at being taken to the police station that day,” he says, “I want to go with the message that we’re not strange, we’re not freaks.”

The three-day pantry: A UK push with a reminder for Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:04:47 UTC
09:04:47 KST

IN BRIEF:
- The UK has warned its citizens to prepare a three-day emergency stockpile.
- Australia's emergency preparedness advice is issued at the state and territory level.
The UK government is urging Britons to stock up on essential supplies to last three days, in the face of looming threats that range from "severe weather to cyber attacks".
Experts say Australians have a fairly adequate level of preparedness for emergencies but could do better, as many report feeling unprepared.
A recent report from the Red Cross found that while 83 per cent of Australians expected to be affected by an emergency in the next five years, 33 per cent said they didn't feel confident that they knew what to do when disaster strikes.
The survey, published in September this year, also found that 12.5 per cent of people Australia who experienced a disaster in the past year took no steps to prepare, while the most common forms of preparation were passive actions such as thinking about risks (36 per cent) or considering a plan (also 36 per cent).
"When people take time to prepare ahead of an emergency, they're often better placed to make informed decisions and navigate challenges should they arise. This directly correlates to the recovery process after the emergency as well," Australian Red Cross director of recovery and resilience Nichola Krey said in a statement.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham assured the public his government's "Be Ready" program, which advised British residents to stock up on three days' worth of supplies, was "just about being prepared and having a sensible amount of supplies in the cupboard".
The country's defence secretary Wes Streeting was more emphatic, stating the advice was about preparing for "state-sponsored terrorism" from Russia, warning Britons to prepare for war within 1,000 days.
"In the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real ... we must ask households and businesses: are they prepared? Are they ready?" he asked.
Emergency planning advice is not unique to the UK, with governments across Europe, as well as in the United States and Asia, prescribing similar action plans.
Australia's emergency advice ranges from three days' emergency supply stock to up to two weeks, depending on your location.
While the federal government can declare a state of emergency, there are no national guidelines in place.
University of New South Wales professor of architecture David Sanderson said that compared with Australia, Britain was "just catching up" on emergency preparedness.
"I would suggest Australia is a lot more advanced than the UK on this and has a lot to share with the UK," he told SBS News.
Sanderson, who leads How We Survive, a research and advocacy initiative aimed at reshaping disaster recovery, said that, "sadly", Australia's experience with natural disasters including drought and bushfires meant that it had a "lot of expertise" in disaster management.
"I think our country is actually very good at this. Efforts are made. The updated bushfire systems are much better than they used to be."
"That said, there's always a better way, and more messaging with simplicity and clarity would be great."
How should Australians prepare, and what for?
While the UK is preparing for supply-chain shortages, services disrupted by cyber attacks, and the ongoing impacts from the current El Niño event, Australia's emergency preparedness advice is largely focused on bushfires, droughts, floods and other weather-related catastrophes.
Australia has had successive national action plans, articulated by the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) but specific emergency response management is left largely to the states and territories.
A NEMA spokesperson said that Australia’s risk profile differs from the United Kingdom and other countries, and that "bushfires, floods, tropical cyclones, severe storms, heatwaves and drought affect regions differently, while overlapping disasters place sustained pressure on resources".
"Nationally consistent preparedness advice must therefore remain relevant to local conditions and the needs of regional, remote and culturally diverse communities."
Sanderson said Australia's decentralised approach was a credit, adding that "a lot of the strength lies at the state level".
While Australia's emergency response wasn't "bad", he said that for a "rich, wealthy country with a good democracy, we should be a lot better at it than we are right now".
Emergency advice for households differs by state and territory
NSW recommends residents plan for a 14-day stay at home, with a lengthy pantry list that includes recommendations for canned, long-life and bottled food, water, toiletries, cleaning products, pet foods and medications.
The advice, last updated in March 2023, suggests residents should prepare for emergencies including bushfire, flood, influenza pandemic, cyclone, storms, earthquake and utility failure.
Most other states and territories have similar advice though the length of time residents should stockpile for varies.
The NT's advice includes a section on crocodiles.
A NEMA spokesperson said the body was working with Queensland on a national approach to disaster preparedness that reflects local risks and responsibilities to consistent, practical, year-round messaging tailored to local hazards.
"Preparedness messaging should be clear, practical and proportionate," the spokesperson said.
"It should help people understand local hazards and take simple steps, such as making an emergency plan, preparing a kit and knowing where to find trusted warnings."
The spokesperson said that while Australia has well-established emergency management arrangements and world-leading emergency services, preparedness remained "a shared responsibility".
"While governments undertake year-round activities to prepare, our message to the community is to do the same at the household level. As disasters become more frequent, intense and complex, strong community awareness, practical preparation and coordination remain essential."
Sanderson said it would be "naïve" to think that preparedness wasn't also at the household level, adding that individual preparation "had to be a part" of action in Australia.
"Heaven forbid, get your grab bag ready, get your exit plans ready, especially as we're coming into a very hot period," he said.
But for people concerned about their supply shelf, Sanderson cautioned against irrational buying.
"When it comes to stockpiling, you don't need to buy the toilet rolls," he said.
"Leave the toilet rolls in Coles. Be ready, but don't be terrified."

Brazil summons Argentinian diplomat over Bolsonaro’s flight to US
The move threatens to further strain relations between Brazilian President Lula and his Argentinian counterpart, Milei.
Brazil has summoned Argentina’s top diplomat in the country to answer questions about right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who fled first to Argentina, then to the United States, after losing Sunday’s presidential election.
On Thursday, Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called in Argentina’s charge d’affaires, Maria Emilia Cortes, sources inside the government told the news agency Reuters.
Argentina’s Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, however, has denied on social media that his government received a formal request for explanations regarding Bolsonaro’s decision to flee into Argentina late on Tuesday.
The circumstances surrounding Bolsonaro’s departure threaten to further strain relations between Brazil’s recently re-elected President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his Argentinian counterpart, libertarian Javier Milei.
After Sunday’s election, Bolsonaro was given a deadline to surrender his passports. Officials ordered him to remain in the country as part of a legal case.
He is part of an ongoing investigation into a money-laundering scheme, known as the Banco Master scandal.
Investigators are probing a multimillion-dollar payment Bolsonaro received from Banco Master’s former head, Daniel Vorcaro, allegedly to finance a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The younger Bolsonaro has denied any wrongdoing and called the case politically motivated.
In an Instagram livestream on Friday, he claimed to be the victim of “persecution” back home.
“I didn’t leave Brazil, I left for Brazil,” Flavio said, alleging that Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had made false accusations against him.
He also suggested there were irregularities in the run-off, comparing them to illegal football goals that were not disallowed. He did not provide details on what those irregularities might have been.
A senator since 2019, Bolsonaro ran this year as the right-wing presidential candidate for his father’s political movement, the Liberal Party.
But after advancing to the run-off, the senator fell short by more than 4 million votes. Lula won Sunday’s race with 51.8 percent of the vote, securing a historic fourth non-consecutive term.
Bolsonaro, however, has refused to concede, though the Liberal Party has acknowledged Lula’s victory.
Instead, he made an unsubstantiated allegation of electoral malfeasance, pointing to a Supreme Court decision to extend voting hours on Sunday.
Both candidates’ campaigns had requested extensions, though for different reasons: Bolsonaro’s camp pointed to inclement weather delaying voters in parts of Brazil, while Lula’s party raised concerns about efforts to restrict public transport on election day.
But Bolsonaro argued that the last-minute extension had disadvantaged voters in regions considered right-wing strongholds.
After arriving in Miami on Wednesday, he declared himself the “legitimate president-elect” of Brazil.
He, his wife and two daughters had travelled from Brazil through northern Argentina, before boarding a chartered aircraft that passed through Ecuador to reach the US.
US President Donald Trump and Milei, both right-wing leaders, have been openly supportive of the Bolsonaro family.
The Brazilian senator later thanked Milei for his assistance, although he did not provide details about the nature of the help. A spokesperson for the Argentinian president described the journey as a rescue.
Bolsonaro, the spokesperson said, had escaped “from the claws of communism, which seeks to imprison all opposition figures”.
Trump, too, has suggested that Sunday’s election was “rigged”, though he declined to “take sides” after the result was announced.
The US president has previously issued sanctions and tariffs in response to the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro, after the former Brazilian president denied his defeat in the 2022 election. He was convicted in 2024 of plotting a coup to prevent Lula from taking power and sentenced to 27 years in prison.
Relations between Lula and Milei have been strained since the Argentinian leader took office in 2023. Milei has repeatedly criticised Lula.
The diplomatic dispute follows an earlier deterioration in relations, with the South American countries each recalling their ambassadors in August after a series of public disagreements.

The Israeli army declared the Ain Deir Baha neighborhood in Hebron, in the southern occupied West Bank, a closed military zone late Friday as troops carried out raids and detained several young Palestinians.
The move came as an Israeli military offensive in Hebron entered its eighth day, displacing thousands of civilians, detaining dozens and demolishing Palestinian homes and structures.
Witnesses told Anadolu that Israeli military vehicles entered the neighborhood and announced over loudspeakers that the area had been designated a closed military zone, prohibiting residents from entering or moving within it.
Videos circulated by local media outlets showed Israeli troops deployed in the neighborhood, warning residents that remaining in the area had become dangerous.
Other footage shared on social media, including by the Quds News Network, showed Israeli soldiers detaining a group of Palestinians.
The detainees were forced to place their hands on their heads before being escorted under heavy guard to an unknown location.
The Israeli army launched its offensive in Hebron on Oct. 23 following a shooting attack by two Palestinians that killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three others. The army later killed the two attackers.
Israeli forces have since imposed a military closure on Hebron and surrounding villages, seizing Palestinian homes in the Jalda and Ain Deir Baha neighborhoods and converting them into military barracks.
The Hebron Municipality said Tuesday that 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families had been displaced by the operation.
During the first days of the offensive, Israeli forces carried out forced displacement operations, demolished homes, commercial establishments and other structures, and destroyed infrastructure.
Troops also converted Palestinian homes into military barracks and raised Israeli flags above them.
The Palestinian Prisoners Club said Israeli forces detained 110 Palestinians in the Hebron governorate between Friday and Wednesday.
The military siege and closures have also disrupted education at 66 schools, affecting 2,872 students.
Of those, 2,198 students remain under direct siege, while another 674 have been forcibly displaced and are unable to reach their schools.
Displaced Palestinians have demanded an end to the military closure and the lifting of restrictions on their residential areas to allow them to return home and resume their lives.

Türkiye puts forward Feridun Sinirlioglu for top UN post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:00:50 UTC
09:00:50 KST

Türkiye has formally nominated Feridun Sinirlioglu, secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), as a candidate for UN secretary general, Turkish foreign ministry sources told Anadolu Agency.
Friday's decision followed an impasse in the selection process, with the latest straw poll at the UN Security Council ending inconclusively.
In a letter to the presidents of the UN General Assembly and the Security Council, Türkiye's UN envoy Ahmet Yildiz transmitted President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's nomination letter, in line with the UN Charter and a General Assembly resolution.
Sinirlioglu is a veteran Turkish diplomat who has served as Secretary General of the OSCE since December 2024.
He holds a master's degree and a PhD in political science and international relations from Bogazici University.
Sinirlioglu began his diplomatic career at Türkiye's Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1982.
He subsequently held postings at Turkish embassies in The Hague and Beirut and served as Türkiye's political counsellor at the United Nations in New York (1992–1996).
He served as Türkiye's foreign minister in 2015.
From 2016 to 2023, he was Türkiye's permanent representative to the United Nations.
In April 2023, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres appointed him special coordinator for the independent assessment of Afghanistan mandated by the Security Council.
In December 2024, he became the first Turkish national appointed OSCE secretary-general.
The election
A candidate needs at least nine votes in the Security Council to secure the required support, while any of the five permanent members, the US, China, France, Russia and the UK, can block a candidate with a veto.
The eventual nominee must be appointed by the General Assembly, with that step generally considered a formality once the Security Council has reached an agreement.
Current Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term ends on December 31.
Eight candidates have so far been nominated: Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi of Argentina, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, Guyana’s UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, former UN General Assembly President Maria Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador, former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, Ugandan politician and diplomat Olara Otunnu and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.
The next secretary-general is expected to begin a five-year term next January 1.
The Security Council straw poll was devised in the early 1980s in an attempt to break a deadlock between two candidates shut down by vetoes.
The informal mechanism has persisted, in various forms, despite criticism from countries opposed to the opaque process.
Each of the 15 Security Council members must anonymously assign each candidate one of three labels: "encourage", "discourage", or "no opinion".

Independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta shuts under Kremlin pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:56:00 UTC
08:56:00 KST

Independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta shuts under Kremlin pressure
- Novaya Gazeta said it is closing after years of Kremlin pressure, calling the shutdown a result of state repression and a wider campaign against dissent.
- The paper was one of Russia’s last open critics of the Ukraine war. It lost its media licence, faced searches, detentions and the “foreign agent” label.
- Rights groups and the Nobel Prize Committee condemned the move. They warned it is a major blow to free speech, independent media and the public’s right to know.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russia’s flagship independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announced on Oct 30 that it was closing, saying it had been “killed” by state pressure after years of repression targeting its journalists whose reporting was critical of the Kremlin and its Ukraine war.
The closure of Novaya Gazeta – one of the last outlets to openly criticise Russia’s offensive – marks the latest outcome of Moscow’s campaign against dissenting voices, which intensified after the Kremlin sent troops into its neighbour in 2022.
Since then, the newspaper, long considered a bastion of independent journalism, has seen its media licence revoked and its journalists and editors questioned, detained and their homes searched.
It was also branded a “foreign agent” – a label reminiscent of Soviet-era repression used to stifle dissent.
The paper’s Nobel Prize-winning founder, Dmitry Muratov, told AFP the closure was “part of a giant military campaign being waged by the Russian Federation”.
“We are fierce opponents of war in all its forms. And we are a part that needed to be destroyed,” said Muratov, the paper’s former editor-in-chief.
Novaya Gazeta’s current editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a statement published on YouTube on the morning of Oct 30 that the paper was “ending its existence”.
“The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work,” Sokolov said in the emotional video.
Founded in 1993 after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Novaya Gazeta was one of Russia’s most reputable and renowned organisations reporting and documenting human rights abuses.
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, donated some of his Nobel Peace Prize money to help set up the paper.
Rights groups condemned the move.
The newspaper’s closure was “yet another devastating blow for remaining independent media in the Russian Federation”, United Nations rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.
Reporters Without Borders chief Thibaut Bruttin said: “Novaya Gazeta will remain the symbol of free, pluralistic, independent and rigorous journalism – a model for the entire profession around the world.”
Amnesty International said the closure was a “devastating loss for everyone in Russia who turns to independent, investigative journalism to uncover the truth”.
Several Novaya Gazeta reporters have been murdered in killings widely seen as retribution for their work.
They include Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia’s military during its campaigns in Chechnya.
She was found dead in her apartment block on President Vladimir Putin’s birthday in October 2006.
Muratov, who was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his work, had to step down as editor-in-chief two years later after being declared a “foreign agent”.
‘In a kill zone’
The Norwegian Nobel Committee on Oct 30 called on the Russian authorities to “end their repression of independent media”.
“The closure is a grave blow to freedom of expression and the public’s right to information,” committee president Jorgen Watne Frydnes told AFP in an e-mail.
Sokolov, in his video statement, said that Novaya Gazeta for nearly five years of war “managed to operate while completely surrounded by intelligence services. But now, that’s it. We’ve ended up in a kill zone.”
“This isn’t just our own private story – it’s the story of a country and a society that are being finished off in exactly the same way.”
The paper, which used to be published several times a week, cut down production inside the country after the war began, but its online version was still available despite court orders.
“Human rights and freedoms have been abolished, and their defence has been equated with a crime,” Sokolov said in the video statement. “Beliefs have become state treason.
“The murder of Novaya Gazeta is yet another piece of evidence. All these years we wrote precisely about this, for as long as we could. Thank you to everyone who listened to us. And the final issue will come out.”
In recent months, the Russian authorities have searched the home of Sokolov and earlier in 2026 arrested one of its journalists, Oleg Roldugin. AFP

EU, Canada Vow More Pressure on Russia as Ottawa Moves to Join €90 Billion Ukraine Defense Loan

The European Union and Canada pledged to intensify pressure on Russia and maintain long-term military, financial and diplomatic support for Ukraine, as Ottawa announced plans to join a €90 billion ($105 billion approximately) European loan program that would allow Kyiv to purchase Canadian-made military equipment using EU funds.
The commitments emerged from the 21st EU–Canada summit in Montreal on Friday, Oct. 30, attended by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In a joint statement, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders, while promising to increase pressure on Moscow and pursue accountability for crimes committed during Russia’s invasion.
The summit also produced a potentially significant development for Ukraine’s military procurement: Canada’s intention to participate in the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan for 2026–2027.
According to the Canadian government’s official summit backgrounder, the arrangement would enable Ukraine to buy military equipment from Canadian defense companies using European financing, helping Kyiv address urgent battlefield needs while expanding transatlantic defense-industrial cooperation.
EU advances €45 billion in additional funding for 2027
The announcement coincided with a separate European Commission decision on Friday to advance the remaining €45 billion under the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, providing another source of predictable financing for Kyiv in 2027.
Canada and EU Launch New Alliance Covering Ukraine, Critical Minerals and AI
Of that amount, €31.7 billion is earmarked for Ukraine’s defense industrial capacity, while up to €13.3 billion would support the state budget through the Ukraine Facility and macro-financial assistance.
The Commission’s proposal, which still requires approval from the Council of the EU, would make the remaining funding available by Dec. 31, 2027.
Von der Leyen described the measure as essential to ensuring Ukraine can continue maintaining public services and defending itself against Russia’s invasion.
“Together with our allies, we must also do everything in our power to mount pressure on Russia to stop its barbaric war of aggression,” she said.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius emphasized Ukraine’s immediate military requirements, including drone interceptors, ammunition, missiles and air defense radars.
The Commission said it would continue working to accelerate European defense production and timely deliveries to Ukraine.
Canada’s proposed participation would complement that effort by potentially making Canadian defense manufacturers an additional source of equipment under the EU-financed procurement framework. Ottawa has not announced a finalized participation agreement or a specific Canadian financial contribution.
EU and Canada pledge stronger pressure on Russia
In their joint declaration, the EU and Canada promised to continue providing Ukraine with comprehensive political, financial, economic, energy, humanitarian, military and diplomatic assistance.
“We will further increase pressure on Russia and seek its accountability for the crimes committed in and against Ukraine,” the leaders said.
The statement did not announce a specific new sanctions package but reaffirmed a shared commitment to holding Moscow responsible for its actions.
The leaders also endorsed a comprehensive, just and lasting peace based on international law and the UN Charter, explicitly supporting Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.
They pledged to continue efforts to secure the immediate and safe return of Ukrainian prisoners of war, detained civilians and children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred by Russia.
The declaration specifically highlighted the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, an initiative in which Canada has played a leading diplomatic role.
Ahead of the summit, von der Leyen also addressed the human consequences of Russia’s invasion during a speech in Montreal, noting Canada’s longstanding support for Ukraine and its efforts to help return children taken by Russia.
She emphasized that the partnership was rooted in the principle that nations must be free to determine their own future.
Beyond immediate military needs, the summit statement reaffirmed support for Ukraine’s long-term reconstruction, institutional reforms and Euro-Atlantic integration.
The EU and Canada said they would continue supporting reforms intended to strengthen Ukraine’s institutions and prepare the country for closer integration with European and transatlantic structures.

Oct 30 (Reuters) - Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov was cited as saying on Friday that Russia’s position on the Ukraine conflict was unchanged and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s comments on maintaining strikes on Russian targets were unhelpful in preparing for new talks.
Lavrov, addressing reporters on the sidelines of a G20 meeting in Atlanta, also said fundamental issues in relations between the US and Russia were unresolved as sanctions on Moscow remained in force and arms were still being provided for Kyiv.
“Our position is known, but what Ukraine intends to bring to the negotiating table, I don’t know,” said Lavrov, quoted by Russian news agencies.
He said Zelenskiy’s frequent comments that Ukraine was acquiring more weapons to strike Russian targets made preparation for new talks difficult.
“This kind of attitude doesn’t really help much in preparing for negotiations,” Lavrov said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have said they are willing to hold further three-sided talks with the US for the first time since early in the year.
Zelenskiy said this week that he hoped that a trilateral meeting with peace negotiators would take place in Abu Dhabi between November 6 and 10. He said Kyiv also wanted Europe to be involved in the talks on how to end the war.
Lavrov said Russia’s position on the conflict “was unchanged from the very start of the special military operation,” as Moscow calls its military campaign in Ukraine.
Moscow, he said, could not accept Ukraine as a “military threat to the lawful security interests of the Russian Federation”.
On relations with Washington, Lavrov said: “Fundamental issues are not being resolved. Sanctions remain, all the sanctions from (former President Joe) Biden are echoed by the current administration.”
He said US cooperation in sharing intelligence with Ukraine had grown, while arms supplies were continuing, pointing to a State Department announcement on Friday that it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine.
Foreign ministers at the G20 have skipped the traditional group photo in Atlanta, with some making it clear they objected to appearing with Lavrov.

Oct 30 (Reuters) - Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov was quoted as saying on Friday that inviting Poland to attend G20 meetings was counter-productive and broke with diplomatic practice of seeking consensus at such gatherings.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski told reporters in Atlanta that the US had made a motion to make Poland a permanent G20 member and Warsaw was lobbying for that.
“Of course, this violates the principles of diplomacy, and especially multilateral diplomacy, when members of associations such as the G20 work on the basis of consensus,” Lavrov told reporters on the sidelines of a G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, according to Russian news agencies.
“This concerns the agenda and it concerns extending invitations to new participants,” he said.
Poland, Lavrov said, “adds nothing” to the meeting.
He said Warsaw failed to qualify for attendance at the meeting as its economy was not big enough.
And its description as a representative of “eastern Europe” was erroneous as there was already sufficient representation from NATO and the European Union.
Lavrov said Russia had been subjected to no pressure in terms of Poland being invited to the Atlanta meeting.
“The Americans simply invited the Polish minister, he came and sat in the chair that was provided for him,” Lavrov was quoted as saying.
Sikorski, in his comments to reporters, also called for a rapid ceasefire in the Black Sea that would allow safe passage for grain shipments from both Ukraine and Russia.

Russia, US veto rival UN Western Sahara resolutions, leaving peacekeeping mission in limbo
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:45:41 CET
08:45:41 KST

By Antoni Slodkowski
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Russia and the United States vetoed rival resolutions on Western Sahara at the Security Council on Friday, leaving the UN peacekeeping mission there without a renewed mandate just a day before it expires.
The unusual showdown threatens the future of a mission the council has routinely renewed for decades and deepens a dispute over the territory, most of which is controlled by Morocco but claimed by the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks an independent state.
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the mission, saying its personnel and equipment should leave Western Sahara in the coming days. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire in the territory.
The US-drafted resolution would have extended the mission for another year while cementing Morocco’s autonomy plan as the only basis for talks to settle the half-century-old conflict and scaling back its military component.
Russia vetoed the resolution. The United States then vetoed a Russian draft that would have extended the mission’s mandate for another year without those changes.
Unless the Security Council agrees to a last-minute extension, the mandate for the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, will expire on October 31.
Oxfam warned that losing the mission could put refugees at risk. Hostilities have persisted at low levels since Polisario said in November 2020 that it was resuming “armed struggle”.
Last year, the Security Council dealt a blow to Polisario’s ambitions when it backed Morocco’s autonomy proposal as a basis for resolving the conflict and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.
The failed US resolution would have gone further, removing the reference to a referendum from the mission’s name, renaming it the United Nations Mission in Western Sahara, or MINUSO.
Following the vote, US Ambassador Michael Waltz said a referendum had never taken place because of longstanding disagreements over voter eligibility.
“UN officials have been telling us this reality for 30 years,” he said.
“Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter ‘R’ for referendum in the mission’s name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades,” he added.
France, the UK, the two other permanent Security Council members, along with 9 non-permanent members backed the US resolution and Morocco’s autonomy plan.
MISSION AT RISK
Russia said the US draft went too far in endorsing Morocco’s position on the disputed territory. “We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty,” Russia’s UN envoy Vassily Nebenzia said.
“The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of the draft,” he said.
Nebenzia called the US veto “the political murder of the mission.”
With 155 military personnel, the mission, tasked with organizing a referendum as part of a UN-brokered ceasefire, is set to cost $62 million in the fiscal year that started in June this year, according to a UN Secretary General report.
“The loss of MINURSO’s monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability, with serious consequences to civilians and prospects of a peaceful resolution,” Oxfam said in reaction to the vote.
While most Sahrawis live in Morocco-ruled Western Sahara, tens of thousands are estimated to be living in Polisario-run refugee camps in Algeria.
The vetoed US resolution called for a census of the refugees.
UNITY DAY
Morocco’s royal palace said the non-renewal of the mission was a “significant development” and that it meant the Western Sahara issue should be withdrawn from consideration by the Security Council.
“The non-renewal of MINURSO’s mandate clearly means that the presence of the mission in the Kingdom’s southern provinces, including its personnel, vehicles, equipment and symbols, should come to an end in the coming days,” the palace said in a statement.
In Laayoune, the largest city in Western Sahara, streets were decorated with Moroccan flags and lights to prepare to celebrate “Unity Day”, a holiday the government declared last year to commemorate last year’s UN Security Council vote on October 31.
On Wednesday, the Polisario staged a rally at the Smara camp near the town of Tindouf, in southern Algeria.
A couple hundred men and women, waving flags of the Polisario’s self-proclaimed Sahrawi Arab Republic, gathered near Polisario fighters in military fatigues, waving signs with slogans such as, “No to Morocco’s autonomy plan. Yes to the right to self-determination”.
(Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski and Ahmed El Jechtimi; additional reporting by Dina Sakr and Abdelaziz Boumzar; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

Armed group shuts crude pipeline linking western Libya’s Hamada field to Zawiya refinery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:43:06 UTC
08:43:06 KST

Lina Altawell
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) said Friday that an armed group shut a valve on the main crude oil pipeline linking the western Hamada field to the Zawiya refinery, and it warned that a prolonged closure could result in the loss of 15,000 barrels per day.
The NOC said it received a report that an armed group had closed the main Hamada pipeline valve in the Riyayna area.
The 18-inch pipeline is one of the main lines supplying crude oil to the Zawiya refinery and connects the Hamada fields, as well as the Tahara field, to the refinery.
It said the sudden and forced closure caused a sharp increase in operating pressure, forcing technical teams to halt pumping through the pipeline at 12.30 am (1030GMT Thursday) to protect the line and production facilities.
As a result, crude oil supplies from the fields connected to the pipeline were suspended.
The NOC warned that if the closure continues, 15,000 barrels per day of crude destined for the Zawiya refinery would be lost.
The disruption also poses a direct threat to oil facilities and the continuity of crude supplies to the refinery, with potential repercussions for Libya’s economy, it added.
The NOC condemned the closure and urged relevant authorities, particularly the Petroleum Facilities Guard, to secure the pipeline, reopen the valve and allow pumping to resume as soon as possible.
It also urged authorities to protect oil installations and transportation lines from attacks that could threaten production stability and Libya’s oil resources.
The incident follows a similar closure on Oct. 22, when the NOC said armed men shut a valve on the Hamada-Zawiya crude pipeline, which carries oil produced from the Hamada and Tahara fields.
On Sept. 21, the corporation said armed members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard closed a crude oil valve at the Sharara field in southwestern Libya, causing a sharp decline in production at one of the country’s major oil fields.
The NOC later said the disruption at Sharara resulted in $95 million in losses.
Petroleum facility guards have long demanded higher monthly salaries amid similar protests by workers in several sectors in Libya.

U.S. stocks tumble amid Big Tech earnings misses, AI spending fears
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:41:09 CST
08:41:09 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks fell sharply on Friday, suffering a second consecutive day of steep losses, as disappointing quarterly reports from tech giants Amazon and Alphabet renewed anxieties over the sustainability of massive artificial intelligence capital expenditures.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 points, or 1.09 percent, to 51,770.31. The benchmark S&P 500 sank 140.32 points, or 1.82 percent, to 7,580.07, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 747.73 points, or 2.86 percent, finishing at 25,437.
Six of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors closed in positive territory, with energy and consumer staples leading the advancers by climbing 1.91 percent and 1.38 percent, respectively. Technology paced the decliners by a wide margin, tumbling 4.24 percent, followed by industrials, which lost 1.57 percent.
Technology equities endured severe selling pressure after rare earnings misses from mega-cap bellwethers shook investor confidence in the AI boom. Amazon shares declined 1.41 percent, while Alphabet extended a sharp downward trajectory after recording its steepest single-day percentage drop in more than two decades.
The rout extended into the semiconductor and hardware spaces. Intel plummeted 28.58 percent after the chipmaker delivered a fourth-quarter revenue outlook that fell well short of Wall Street estimates. Concurrently, data storage firm SanDisk plunged 13.47 percent despite beating first-quarter earnings forecasts, as investors looked past its announcement of an eight-for-one forward stock split.
Commodity markets added fresh headwinds to broader sentiment as crude oil futures gained over 2 percent. International benchmark Brent crude jumped to 117.64 U.S. dollars per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude climbed to 104.12 dollars per barrel, stoking persistent headline inflation worries.
Monetary policy anxieties were reinforced by hawkish commentary from central bank policymakers following Wednesday's rate-pause decision. Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President Alberto Musalem warned that inflation remains excessively high and broad-based, emphasizing that the central bank needs to act soon to prevent elevated prices from becoming entrenched.
Concurrently, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Tom Barkin signaled that monetary policy remains pointed toward higher borrowing costs to rein in persistent inflation against the backdrop of firm demand. He noted that the key question facing the Fed is the pace and extent of future rate increases. ■

EU climate funding hits €41.6 billion: Where is the money going?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:37:16 UTC
08:37:16 KST

EU climate funding hits €41.6 billion: Where is the money going?
The European Union and its members provided €32.3 billion in public climate finance in 2025. They also mobilized €9.3 billion in private funding for developing countries, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the Council of the EU, the funding helps countries cut emissions and adapt to climate change.
The Council released the figures ahead of the COP31 UN climate conference. Türkiye’s Antalya will host the talks from November 9 to 20.
European Commission data show 48% of public funding supported adaptation or projects also addressing emissions. Grants accounted for 41% of the EU and its 27 member states’ public contribution.
The public total included €4.3 billion from the EU budget, including the European Development Fund. Another €2.7 billion came from the European Investment Bank.
Public interventions helped attract the additional €9.3 billion in private finance. These included guarantees, syndicated loans, direct investments in companies and credit lines. The private total excludes public money used to mobilize those investments.
The Council said the figures reaffirmed the EU’s commitment to international climate finance. It highlighted developed countries’ collective goal of mobilizing $100 billion annually.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that human-induced warming caused over half of estimated heat-related deaths across 854 European cities.

31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said Friday that the US tabled a proposal to make Poland a permanent member of the G20, adding that he is lobbying other countries to support the move.
Speaking at a news conference on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in the US city of Atlanta, Sikorski thanked Washington for inviting Poland to participate under its presidency.
"We're very grateful to the United States for having issued the invitation during their presidency," he said.
He said the UK, which will hold the next G20 presidency, had also invited Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to attend next year's gathering in Manchester.
Sikorski said he discussed possible joint initiatives with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio during the meeting.
"I was pleased to be sitting next to secretary Rubio, and therefore we were able to exchange not only views but also ideas on common projects. I can't publicly say all of it, but expect more Polish American initiative on the international scene," he said.
Turning to the war in Ukraine, Sikorski urged a ceasefire in the Black Sea to allow grain shipments from Ukraine and Russia to reach countries in need, including Egypt.
Sikorski also emphasized the importance of protecting international waterways, including the Strait of Hormuz, as a shared interest of the international community.
Poland is participating in this year's G20 activities as a full participant following an invitation from the US. Warsaw is seeking permanent membership in the group.

31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
US Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose urged restraint on Friday amid a confrontation at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, warning that the situation was "very serious."
"We appear to be witnessing an unprecedented confrontation over the government’s use of state power and the independence and authority of a constitutional institution," Rose wrote on US social media company X.
He said both sides offered sharply different accounts of what happened and why, and that thousands of people gathering outside the tribunal made an already dangerous situation more combustible.
"The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse," he said.
The envoy said the US is on Poland's side, but it has no right to judge or interfere in the country’s internal affairs.
He added that Washington's concern is for the stability, security and democratic future of a country it considers a friend and ally.
Rose urged government officials, law enforcement and demonstrators to "take a deep breath" and avoid any action that could provoke violence or further escalation.
"Poland’s strength ultimately must come from within," he said, citing its people, institutions and shared commitment to the rule of law.
Rose added that Poland has come too far and accomplished too much to let political differences put that progress at risk.

====================================================================================================

How hackers steal crypto - and what they do with it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

How hackers steal crypto – and what they do with it
SAN FRANCISCO - The biggest cryptocurrency hack on record has raised fresh questions about the industry’s ability to protect digital assets and become part of mainstream financial infrastructure. 
Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, suspended withdrawals from its platform after a security breach affected an estimated US$6.3 billion worth of funds. 
Crypto exchanges have long been lucrative targets for hackers because they control huge pools of digital assets that can be transferred around the world rapidly, typically with a measure of anonymity. 
A barrage of cyber attacks has exposed decentralisation – once touted as one of crypto’s greatest strengths – as a vulnerability.
Without central authorities to safeguard assets and absorb losses, crypto users are dependent on fragmented infrastructure that malicious actors keep finding ways to attack. 
Increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence models are supercharging the ability of hackers to discover weaknesses to exploit.
How common are crypto attacks?
Crypto-related hacks have been getting larger and more frequent. 
Roughly US$1.2 billion was lost across 255 attacks from July to September, compared with US$822 million in 222 incidents from April to June, according to blockchain security firm CertiK. 
Before the Binance heist, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost US$1.5 billion in tokens.
How do hackers target crypto?
Some attacks rely on simple social engineering, where hackers trick humans into giving them access to private systems. They can gain entry through compromised accounts, stolen credentials or malware.
Binance initially said the October incident may have involved a software developer’s compromised laptop, although it later flagged “additional points of breach”.
Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic have all pointed to North Korea as likely being behind the heist.
There are more technologically sophisticated crypto attacks beyond social engineering. 
Hackers target weaknesses in the technology surrounding a blockchain – a digital ledger of transactions stored across a vast network of computers. This includes software flaws that let hackers get around security controls and weaknesses in bridges that connect different blockchains.
A common method used by hackers is to steal cryptographic keys that authorise transactions, allowing attackers to move funds out of exchange wallets. 
Another weak point they target is so-called hot wallets – digital wallets that are connected to the internet and used for transactions. These are more vulnerable to cyberattacks than cold wallets, which keep the keys controlling crypto transactions offline.
Cold wallets were once considered to be impregnable by criminals but they, too, are now being targeted. 
Attackers have tampered with hardware associated with these wallets, while software flaws in the devices have also exposed users to theft. 
In late July, hackers absconded with more than US$100 million worth of Bitcoin from thousands of wallets secured by hardware devices made by Canada-based Coinkite Inc. 
The attack exploited a software flaw that made it possible for hackers to figure out the private keys protecting the crypto.
How do hacks on decentralised platforms happen?
The Binance hack targeted a centralised exchange where a platform is acting as an intermediary for transactions. 
But crypto also has a decentralised-finance, or DeFi, ecosystem. This is essentially a network of blockchain-based protocols that employ self-executing code known as smart contracts to let users move crypto assets without relying on centralised intermediaries.
DeFi creates a different set of vulnerabilities. 
Hackers can exploit flaws in the smart contracts’ code to manipulate prices or drain assets. 
They can also target private keys, cross-chain bridges and the infrastructure surrounding a protocol.
The US$320 million hack of Liquid Network, a network connected to Bitcoin that allows faster transactions and settlement, was among the major crypto security breaches this year. 
Separate attacks on DeFi protocols KelpDAO and Drift Protocol in April together accounted for US$577 million in losses. 
Cross-chain links are a critical component of DeFi, enabling assets and information to move between separate blockchains. 
But a proliferation of cross-chain projects and a limited capacity for cybersecurity vetting has raised additional points of vulnerability.
Can stolen funds be tracked, frozen and returned?
Crypto can often be tracked surprisingly well.
Transactions on public blockchains are permanently recorded, allowing investigators to follow stolen funds as hackers move them between wallets, cryptocurrencies and, increasingly, different blockchains.
But tracking the money does not necessarily mean it can be stopped. 
Bitcoin and Ether, for example, do not have a central issuer that can simply freeze an attacker’s wallet. 
Centralised exchanges can block assets deposited on their platforms. 
And issuers of some stablecoins – crypto pegged to another asset such as the US dollar – have the ability to freeze tokens held at specified addresses. This includes Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC. 
But freezing has to be done quickly as attackers may try to swop assets that can be frozen for ones that cannot and move them across blockchains.
Frozen does not mean recovered. 
Returning assets to their original owner may require cooperation from exchanges or token issuers, as well as potentially lengthy legal and law-enforcement processes. In some cases, hackers themselves have returned stolen assets, sometimes after negotiating a bounty.
What was affected in the Binance hack?
The funds drained included Bitcoin, Ether, dollar-backed stablecoins USDT and USDC, and a range of smaller tokens.
Binance said that “user funds remain safe”. 
It pledged to cover all losses and said it has reserved more than $6.3 billion of company funds to do so. 
Some $5 billion is already held in the exact tokens that were impacted and the exchange is in the process of buying the remaining tokens from the market. 
Binance also said that around $3 billion of affected assets had been frozen on-chain and that it was working with law enforcement and partners to freeze and recover additional funds.
While this is crypto’s biggest known hack, the amount involved is still relatively small compared with Binance’s overall size. 
Binance has about US$137 billion in on-chain assets, as tracked by analytics platform DefiLlama, nearly five times the roughly US$29 billion held by second-largest exchange OKX.
Is it easy to turn stolen crypto into cash?
Turning stolen crypto into fiat cash is often the hardest part, especially after a large public hack, because blockchain transactions can be traced and regulated exchanges can identify or freeze suspicious deposits.
But hackers do not necessarily need to cash out immediately.
Criminals increasingly use stolen crypto as a store of value or payment method, layering transactions through other services before attempting to reach an exchange, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. 
In the case of KelpDAO, the infiltrators used most of the crypto as collateral for borrowing on Aave, the biggest DeFi lending protocol. 
Hackers can also split stolen assets among numerous wallets, move them across different blockchains or send them through crypto mixers, which pool transactions to make the flow of funds harder to follow.
Eventually, some may try to convert the assets into cash through exchanges or other intermediaries.
What role does AI play in crypto hacking?
Cyber criminals are getting better at scanning software for weaknesses and rapidly designing a mode of attack, which experts say likely reflects the help of widely available AI models.
As AI becomes more sophisticated, it’s increasingly able to discover serious cybersecurity vulnerabilities. 
This has lowered the barrier to entry for would-be crypto thieves and enabled skilled attackers to find and take advantage of loopholes more quickly.
AI isn’t just a useful tool for hackers to engage in sophisticated code exploits. It can also allow the more mundane social-engineering side of crypto hacking to be conducted at a larger scale, producing convincing phishing messages, impersonations and other material used to steal credentials or obtain access. US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine for $2.1 bln — State Department

WASHINGTON, October 31. /TASS/. The United States has approved the sale to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 missiles for the American-made Patriot PAC-3 air defense system, along with related equipment, for $2.1 billion.
The US Department of State and the Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA), a Pentagon agency responsible for foreign military sales under government-to-government agreements, announced the decision.
The statement noted that the purchase would be "funded entirely by partners and allies." The delivery will include "PAC-3 MSE classified and unclassified spare parts; and other related elements of logistics and program support."
According to Washington, "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe."
US authorities said Ukraine would pay for the missiles with funds provided by Canada, Germany and Norway, as well as through an EU loan. "No US funds are involved in this sale," the statement said. The US authorities also said that "the proposed sale will improve Ukraine's capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capability."
The missiles will be supplied to Ukraine by Lockheed Martin, one of the Pentagon’s key contractors. The statement said that implementing the deal "will not require the assignment of any additional US Government or contractor representatives to Ukraine," and that there will be no adverse impact on US defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale.
The US administration has already notified Congress of the decision. Lawmakers now have 30 days to review the agreement and potentially block it.

Etsy cracks down on AI-copying issues but some users still sceptical
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:28:26 UTC
08:28:26 KST

Etsy cracks down on AI with new guidelines but some craft sellers still sceptical
In short:
Online marketplace Etsy, known for handmade products, updates its policies to restrict AI use, following criticism from its community.
Etsy users are cautious about the changes, with some saying AI-copying issues persist.
What's next?
Etsy says these changes are merely a "starting point" and will be periodically re-evaluated.
Global online marketplace Etsy has updated its artificial intelligence policies following widespread criticism from users faced with AI-generated products.
Etsy recently sent an email to sellers, informing them of the changes, and published the new policy online.
"We recognise we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted," it said.
"AI is threatening [buyer] trust, and we have a responsibility to protect it."
The statement provided a list of policy updates to set clearer restrictions on AI use.
One requires sellers to include at least one unedited photo of their item against a real background, with exceptions for some products.
"Some digital items, like audio files, don't have visual elements. For those listings, you may use representative imagery, including AI-generated images, as long as it doesn't mislead buyers about what they're purchasing," it said.
Photo-editing tools, such as exposure, crop and background adjustments, including AI, are still allowed for other listing images "as long as those edits don't make the item appear different".
Etsy said that if the item received by buyers is "materially different" from the listing images, the seller may be responsible for a refund.
Another update banned AI-generated functional guides like recipes and crochet patterns.
Listings for these items that aren't AI-generated must also provide an image of a real result.
New features are also being introduced, such as a specific "misleading AI-generated images" reporting option and guidance for listing photos.
However, at this stage, the reports are only to help Etsy "better understand how members perceive potential AI misuse and won't result in immediate enforcement action".
It's unclear if the guidance for listing photos has been implemented.
AI-generated art, like prints, are still permitted "when sellers play a clear creative role in what they create and are transparent about their process".
'Bit of a laugh', seller says
Earlier this month the ABC spoke with Lucy Cooper, a Hobart-based crochet artist known for her 90s-surf-wear-inspired spiral beanie design.
Ms Cooper said she had discovered an Etsy store selling an AI-generated version of her crochet beanie pattern, with AI-generated images.
Etsy's new AI policy changes suggest it will prevent experiences like hers from occurring.
However, it has since happened again.
Ms Cooper found another Etsy store selling an AI-generated version of her beanie pattern, and all eight product images were generated by AI.
The listing was published on October 28, six days after Etsy announced its policy update.
"It's good that they're actually doing something, but I think that it's a little bit of a laugh," Ms Cooper said.
"They're addressing the problem, but they're not actually really doing anything about it."
Ms Cooper said she felt the changes relied too heavily on sellers doing the right thing.
"The problem is people aren't being honest," she said.
"If you're the platform owner, you have to do something to make it so that this can't happen."
Etsy's community has mixed feelings
Following Etsy's announcement, users across the globe took to social media to voice their opinions on the changes.
In an Instagram post, Jade, a seamstress, said, "It seemed like [Etsy] didn't want to demonise AI usage, but I think that's going to alienate a large part of their database — buyers and sellers alike — who are truly anti-AI."
In the comments, one user said: "They are trying to serve a larger group of people and shops. Banning AI entirely would mean a lot of shops would close.
"I am a visual and web designer, photographer and … wood artisan. I create physical and digital crafts. There is a place for AI, and banning it would really make some parts of the design process unnecessarily slow.
"Just because so many create AI slop does not mean the entire use of AI should be banned. It just needs more guidance."
In another post, Molly, a crochet artist, asked, "is Etsy going to take a proactive approach to finding [AI-generated pattern listings]? I think that these are positive changes … I'll believe it when I see it."
Some are frustrated by Etsy's decision to not immediately remove listings that are reported for AI misuse.
"I think [the new reporting feature is] really good. But if you're not going to do anything about it, what's the point of it being there?" Ms Cooper said.
"When you report an item, and you say it's AI-generated or this pattern doesn't work or it's copyright or it's plagiarism, it should immediately get taken down, or they should notify you what's happening with it."
Changes just a 'starting point', Etsy says
Etsy says it is aware there is more to address as AI continues to evolve, and that it will keep making improvements as it listens to its community and learns what it needs.
"We recognise we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted," the company said.
"It's changing fast, and like many of you, we're thinking seriously about what it means for Etsy, what's allowed on our marketplace, and how it impacts running a creative business.
"We are closely monitoring developments in this rapidly evolving area, listening to feedback from our community, and periodically re-evaluating our policies.
"These changes are our starting point, not the finish line."

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Omer Asur Cuhada and Sahin Demir
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
The United Arab Emirates announced Friday that it contained an oil spill from a tanker involved in an incident in its territorial waters, while efforts continued to address marine pollution affecting several coastal areas.
The Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure said it was coordinating with the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, the National Emergency Crisis and Disaster Management Authority, and other agencies to secure the oil tanker GEM NO. 2 and minimize potential risks, according to the state news agency WAM.
The ministry said technical teams were continuing repairs to damaged sections of the tanker, restoring some operational systems and assessing the vessel’s structural integrity to determine the safest way to handle it.
No new oil leakage has been detected from the tanker, while maritime and aerial monitoring, supported by satellite imagery, continues, according to the latest field assessments,
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said its teams were continuing efforts to contain marine pollution caused by the spill, including field surveys, monitoring and cleanup operations in affected coastal areas.
It stressed that public safety remained its top priority, WAM reported.
Satellite imagery available as of Friday shows the oil slick was concentrated off the coast of Umm Al Quwain, extending partially toward coastal areas of Ras Al Khaimah, Ajman and Sharjah.
The ministry said the concentration of pollution had declined significantly, while efforts continued to contain the spill and address its environmental impact.
It added that cleanup operations primarily relied on mechanical recovery methods, alongside chemical dispersants used in accordance with international standards and approved technical guidelines.
The ministry said the temporary closure of several beaches and coastal areas was precautionary.
It clarified that the closures did not necessarily mean contamination had been detected at every affected location, but were intended to protect public health and the marine environment while cleanup operations continued.
Meanwhile, Etihad Water and Electricity said drinking water remained safe, adding that it had implemented precautionary measures to monitor seawater quality and test produced and distributed water without disrupting supplies to consumers.
Authorities did not disclose the nature or cause of the tanker incident, nor did they say when it occurred.
On Oct. 23, the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment announced the temporary closure of all beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain after detecting marine pollution caused by an oil spill from a tanker.

Russia, US veto rival UN Western Sahara resolutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:24:32 UTC
08:24:32 KST

Breadcrumb
Russia, US veto rival UN Western Sahara resolutions, leaving peacekeeping mission in limbo
Russia and the United States vetoed each other's Western Sahara resolutions at the Security Council on Friday in a dispute over Morocco's autonomy plan that leaves the UN peacekeeping mission there without a renewal a day before its mandate expires.
The two vetoes mean the Security Council has not renewed a mission it has extended routinely each year. They also block a US push to go further than last year's council endorsement of Morocco's autonomy plan. Oxfam warned that losing the mission could put civilians at risk.
The US-drafted resolution would have cemented Morocco's autonomy plan as the only basis for talks to settle the half-century-old conflict and scaled back the military component of the peacekeeping mission there.
The votes followed an unusual showdown among major powers over the mission's annual renewal, long considered procedurally routine at the Security Council.
Polisario, an armed group based in neighbouring Algeria, has sought an independent state in Morocco-controlled Western Sahara since former colonial power Spain withdrew from the territory in 1976.
Morocco says it has historical rights to the territory, which it calls its "southern provinces", and where it has invested heavily in infrastructure and public services.
Last year, the Security Council dealt a blow to Polisario's ambitions when it backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as a basis for resolving the conflict and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.
The failed US resolution, which would have extended the mission's mandate for another year, would have removed a reference to a referendum from the mission's name, renaming it the United Nations Mission in Western Sahara, or MINUSO.
Following the vote on the US draft, US Ambassador Michael Waltz said a referendum had never taken place because of longstanding disagreements over voter eligibility.
"UN officials have been telling us this reality for 30 years," he said.
"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," he added.
France, the UK, the two other permanent Security Council members, backed the US resolution and Morocco's autonomy plan.
"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty,” Russia's UN envoy Vassily Nebenzia said.
“The security council must not give a blessing to such a one sided approach therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of the draft," he said.
The United States then vetoed a Russian-drafted resolution that would have extended the mission's mandate for another year without changes. Eleven members voted against it.
“The political murder of the mission,” Nebenzia said.
With 155 military personnel, the mission, tasked with organizing a referendum as part of a UN-brokered ceasefire, is set to cost $62 million in the fiscal year that started in June this year, according to a UN Secretary General report.
"The loss of MINURSO’s monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability, with serious consequences to civilians and prospects of a peaceful resolution," Oxfam said in reaction to the vote.
While most Sahrawis live in Morocco-ruled Western Sahara, tens of thousands are estimated to be living in Polisario-run refugee camps in Algeria.
The vetoed US-resolution would have urged the UN refugee agency to conduct a census of the refugees in the camps.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
