Following the 1975 Madrid Accords, Spain transferred administrative responsibilities for Western Sahara to Morocco and Mauritania before withdrawing from the territory in 1976. When Mauritania, under pressure from Polisario guerrillas, abandoned all claims to its portion in August 1979, Morocco subsequently took control of the areas vacated by Mauritania and has since controlled most of the territory. Fighting broke out between Morocco and the Polisario Front, which is fighting for the independence of Western Sahara.
A cease-fire was signed in 1991. The UN mission was deployed that year to monitor the cease-fire and to organize, if possible, a referendum on self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Visiting Kew through lens of biodiversity conservation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:48:35 CST
07:48:35 KST

People visit Kew's Palm House in London, Britain, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Feng)
by Zhang Feng and Larry Neild
LONDON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Inside the Princess of Wales Conservatory at the Royal Botanic Gardens, also named Kew, a dark blue tile captured the attention of visitors.
In 1985, British naturalist David Attenborough buried a time capsule beneath it, containing seeds of endangered plant species.
According to the plan, the capsule was to be opened in 2085. By then, scientists fear, some of the plants whose seeds lay inside might have disappeared from the wild.
The urgency of biodiversity protection was underscored at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital of Yerevan.
How can biodiversity be safeguarded and humanity's relationship with nature restored? And how can the world achieve the goal of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 and living in harmony with nature by 2050?
Recent visits to Kew offered some clues.
"LIVING RAINFOREST IN LONDON"
Originally the private gardens of King George II, Kew started botanical collections in 1759. Today, Kew is home to some 17,000 plant species and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003.
As autumn set in and temperatures began to fall, plants outside Kew's Palm House have been cleared away, making room for species better suited to colder weather.
Yet stepping inside, visitors were greeted by warmth and lush greenery. Nicknamed "living rainforest in London," the Palm House opened in 1848 and housed more than 1,000 tropical and subtropical plant species, including Eastern Cape giant cycad from South Africa and Australia's pandanus tree whose above-ground roots rose to human height.
Staff member Leaf said that to conserve the tropical plants from around the world, the Palm House maintained consistently high temperatures and humidity levels of around 80 percent.
However, the historic structure itself faced considerable challenges. Rust could be seen on the building's framework, with large patches of its surface coating peeling off.
Despite two major restoration projects in the 20th century, the Victorian-era greenhouse continued to suffer from structural deterioration, posing grave challenges to its plant collections.
Leaf said the Palm House was scheduled to close for renovation starting next year, with the project expected to take three to five years.
CONSERVATION BEYOND BORDERS
In 2021, Kew received Guinness World Records recognition for the "largest collection of living plants at a single-site botanic garden."
Alexandre Antonelli, executive director of science at Kew, said that protecting biodiversity called for cross-border efforts. "Kew has a long history of engagement with China," said Antonelli in an exclusive interview with Xinhua.
He noted that Kew maintained long-standing cooperation with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, expanding collaboration in areas such as joint postgraduate training and exchange of scientific research findings.
"Kew supports China's broad goals of ecological civilization, where people and nature thrive together," said Antonelli.
In Kew's Temperate House, sunlight streamed through an enormous glass roof, illuminating elegant architectural curves and towering plants from temperate regions worldwide.
Among them, a Chinese gooseberry, or kiwi fruit plant stood out. The information board nearby unveiled a lesser-known story of the plant's global journey. Contrary to popular belief, kiwifruit did not originate in New Zealand but was native to China, where it has been cultivated for centuries.
In the early 20th century, Mary Fraser, a New Zealand school principal, brought kiwifruit seeds back home after returning from a visit to China's Hubei Province.
Nathan, an exchange student from New Zealand, was much delighted by the discovery. He said that kiwi fruit was commonplace back home, where growers often built fences to support the climbing vines. The English word "kiwi" also became a familiar nickname for New Zealanders.
Learning that the plant was being jointly protected by China and New Zealand, he exclaimed, "That's so cool!"
ENGAGING THE PUBLIC IN CONSERVATION
Antonelli said that preserving biological diversity required not only "world-leading scientific research" but also "public education through exhibitions, interpretation, events, and schools programs."
For many people, the desire to protect biodiversity began with a sense of wonder at the beauty and stunning characteristics of plants.
Inside Kew's the Princess of Wales Conservatory, crowds gather around a pool of giant waterlily, competing to photograph the remarkable plants.
In 2023, Kew took part in the inaugural Giant Waterlily Weigh-Off and claimed first place with a load-bearing capacity of 43.5 kilograms, prompting visitors to reconsider what these seemingly delicate aquatic plants were capable of.
Not far from the pool, curious visitors gravitated towards a cluster of sundews. The slender leaves were covered with countless tiny hairs. At the tips of these hairs, droplets of liquid glistened in the sunlight, resembling morning dew.
But the sparkling droplets concealed an incredible hunting mechanism. Once an insect landed on the leaf, the sundews' trapping mechanism was triggered. Sticky droplets ensnared the prey, while the leaf gradually curled around it, drawing the unfortunate insect into the plant's grasp.
In addition, Kew's annual orchid festival was another important bridge between science and the public. The 30th edition of the festival this year chose China as its theme for the first time. The exhibition area featured a giant dragon made from plant materials, resembling colorful wooden dragons on Kew's Chinese-style Great Pagoda.
Kew Director Richard Deverell said the Orchid Festival was not simply an opportunity to admire beautiful flowers, but also a platform for educating the public about the importance of plant conservation.
China was selected as this year's theme "because it's one of the most biodiverse countries in the world," he explained.
AN INSURANCE POLICY FOR PLANTS
In a report published by Kew in 2020, it was estimated that approximately two-fifths of the world's plant species were at risk of extinction.
To help safeguard plant diversity, Kew established the Millennium Seed Bank around 2000. Located in West Sussex, the facility had stored more than 2.4 billion seeds representing over 40,000 species as of July 1 this year.
Volunteer Simon working there described the seed bank as an "insurance policy" for plants. With global plant diversity facing mounting threats, he said, preserving seeds provided a vital safeguard for restoring species in the future.
In 2020, after months of extreme heat and drought, devastating bushfires swept across Australia, burning more than 10 million hectares of land. Among the plants severely affected was clover glycine, a nationally vulnerable pea endemic to southeast Australia.
Fortunately, more than 1,000 seeds collected in 2007 were safely stored at the Millennium Seed Bank. Some 250 of them were swiftly shipped to Australia for propagation and ecological restoration.
The idea of "insurance policy" resonated with the Germplasm Bank of Wild Species in southwest China's Yunnan Province. The facility conserved a wide range of wild rare and endangered plants, important agricultural crops, and newly discovered species.
Together with the Millennium Seed Bank in Britain and the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway, it formed part of an international network at the forefront of global biodiversity conservation.
In May this year, Attenborough, who placed the time capsule in 1985, celebrated his 100th birthday. Over the decades, he has narrated acclaimed nature documentaries such as The Blue Planet and Planet Earth.
In Kew's documentary Kingdom of Plants, he offered a heartfelt reflection: "Not only do plants give the world much of its beauty, they are indeed the very basis of all life on earth."
For humanity as a whole, ensuring that life in the natural world continues to flourish in all its diversity is a challenge that we must address indefinitely. ■

OTTAWA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The two-day 21st Canada-European Union Summit concluded Friday in Montreal, Canada, with the launch of an alliance to bolster collective strength, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is working toward becoming the EU's first "associate member."
According to a joint statement issued Friday, Canada and the EU launched the "Alliance for the Future" aiming to deliver ambitious cooperation in the following areas: trade and regulatory cooperation; digital, research and communications technologies; critical raw materials and energy; financial services and markets; security and preparedness; and people-to-people.
The prime minister's office said in a news release that the alliance is a new partnership of nations that will leverage the strategic capabilities of Canada, the EU, and a variable geometry of like-minded nations to address common issues.
Together, Canada and the EU will deliver more choice and lower costs for families, new export markets for businesses, and greater opportunities for young people to live, work, and study where they want, in Canada or the EU, according to the release.
In closing remarks, Carney said that the two sides are working toward the deepest possible partnership, short of accession, with Canada becoming the EU's first associate member.
"Over the coming months, we will determine the substance, scale and scope of this form of membership," Carney said.
The joint statement noted that the two sides are working to define by the 2027 EU-Canada Summit the concept of an "ever-closer association" of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself.
During the Canada-EU summit, the two sides unveiled more than 20 new initiatives and announced the conclusion of negotiations for the Canada-EU Digital Trade Agreement. As Canada's first agreement dedicated entirely to digital trade, it aims to reduce frictions in online trade and make it easier for businesses to sell goods and services. ■

Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:42:26 UTC
07:42:26 KST

Meta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.
The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.
Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.
The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process.
Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."
A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision.
"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."
Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.
The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.
S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies that the country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles - three weeks after offering the country such a right.

EXPLAINER - Police deployed after head of top court suspended, president cuts trip short: What's happening in Poland?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:17:46 UTC
07:17:46 KST

Burak Bir
31 October 2026•Update: 31 October 2026
- 'This is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,' says Prime Minister Donald Tusk
- Polish envoy to China resigns following developments, says he 'can no longer serve'
Polish President Karol Nawrocki cut short a trip to Senegal on Friday to return to Warsaw as riot police were deployed to the top court and its president was suspended amid an escalating constitutional crisis.
The crisis surrounding Poland's top court, the Constitutional Tribunal, escalated after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and Nawrocki have been locked in a dispute over the tribunal's composition.
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska issued orders suspending Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice President Bartlomiej Sochanski from their duties.
Korwin-Piotrowska accused the leadership of obstructing the work of judges elected by the parliamentary majority, violating judicial procedures and preventing the proper functioning of the tribunal.
But the tribunal rejected the orders, saying on its website that Swieczkowski "remains the president of the Constitutional Tribunal and Sochanski remains the vice president."
It wrote on US social media company X: "All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'état."
Following the announcement, protesters gathered outside the tribunal building as tensions escalated, with some reportedly climbing over the fence and throwing objects at police.
Reactions
Following the developments, Nawrocki said he was cutting short his trip to Senegal and returning to Poland.
"At such a moment, the President must be in Poland," he wrote on X.
Tusk said: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty."
"After years of PiS (party)-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added.
Meanwhile, Polish Ambassador to China Jakub Kumoch resigned following the developments.
"In light of the events in the country, I have concluded that it is no longer possible for me to continue serving as the Ambassador of the Republic of Poland. As of today, I have submitted my resignation and a request for recall," he wrote on X.
Police said they had not entered the court building and denied claims that officers had stormed it.
Law and Justice (PiS) party leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski and other opposition politicians arrived outside the court and accused the government of trying to seize control of the institution.
Kaczynski described the events as a "coup against the Constitutional Tribunal" and urged Nawrocki to intervene.
Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, in the US city of Atlanta for a G20 meeting, said measures concerning the Constitutional Tribunal aimed to restore the court's functioning after "politicization under the previous government."
Long-running legal dispute
The crisis began after the PiS-led government took office in 2015, as the PiS majority in parliament quickly moved to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority, since the court can decide the legality of legislation.
The European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that the PiS majority had improperly elected three judges because they duplicated positions that the previous parliament had validly filled.
The European courts ruled that Poland's Constitutional Tribunal was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal."
Tusk's government has used the rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
When he took office in 2023, Tusk vowed to depoliticize the judiciary, but he partially failed because Nawrocki and his predecessor, Andrzej Duda, used their presidential vetoes to block the attempts.
PiS and Nawrocki accused the government of using the rule-of-law campaign to remove political opponents from key state institutions.
Nawrocki was expected in Warsaw late Friday evening as the standoff continued and was set to meet the first president of the Supreme Court, Zbigniew Kapinski.

This early Black Friday sale means you don’t have to wait until the late-November holiday to score the worthwhile discount—and we recommend you don’t. Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store are all offering the 25 percent off deal, but I don’t know for how much longer. In other words, now is a great time to score this smartwatch for less.
A Record-Low Price
The Pixel Watch 5 is one of the best smartwatches available for Android users. "This govt is committed to uphold the constitutionally guaranteed rights to freedom and expression". Section 7 says that "the personal data of a data principal may be processed by a data fiduciary (a) for the specified purpose for which the Data Principal has voluntarily provided her personal data... and in respect of which she has not indicated... that she does not consent to the use of her personal data."

====================================================================================================

People high in neuroticism report sleeping less, but wrist monitors tell a different story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:00:58 UTC
07:00:58 KST

Young adults who scored higher in neuroticism reported sleeping less, but a wrist-worn sleep monitor did not show that they actually slept less, according to a study published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Neuroticism is a personality trait associated with a greater tendency to experience negative emotions, such as worry and distress. Previous research has found that people with higher neuroticism often report shorter sleep. But studies using actigraphy, which relies on a wearable device to estimate sleep from movement, have generally not found the same relationship.
To examine this discrepancy, Derick M. DeCamp and Elizabeth J. Pantesco of Villanova University looked at both kinds of sleep measures in the same group of people. The study included 134 undergraduate students (average age 19; 95 women) without diagnosed sleep disorders.
Participants wore a wrist actigraph for five nights, including two weekend nights, and completed questionnaires about their personality, sleep, and symptoms of depression and anxiety. The researchers measured reported sleep over the past month in two ways: participants directly estimated how many hours of actual sleep they usually got, and the team calculated sleep duration from participants’ usual bedtime, wake time, and time taken to fall asleep.
Higher neuroticism was linked to shorter sleep on both self-report measures, but not to sleep duration as estimated by the actigraph. The differences were modest: each one-point increase in neuroticism on a five-point scale was associated with roughly 15 to 20 fewer minutes of reported sleep. The connection between neuroticism and self-reported sleep remained after the researchers accounted for actigraphy-estimated sleep, demographic characteristics, body mass index, depression and anxiety symptoms, night-to-night sleep regularity, and other personality traits.
The study’s average sleep estimates illustrate how measurement methods can differ. Participants reported 6.74 hours of sleep on the direct question, while the actigraph estimated 6.70 hours, and the calculated self-report estimate was higher, at 7.40 hours. Compared with the actigraph, participants higher in neuroticism tended to underestimate their sleep on the direct question and to overestimate it less on the calculated measure.
Symptoms of depression and anxiety were closely related to neuroticism but were not themselves linked to how long participants slept or reported sleeping, and accounting for them did not weaken the association. The authors suggest this points to a role for the stable personality trait rather than temporary distress.
The authors wrote that their findings are “consistent with the possibility that neuroticism is more strongly related to how individuals perceive, recall, and report their sleep duration than to actigraphy-assessed sleep duration.” They suggested that people higher in neuroticism might recall or interpret their sleep more negatively, or that worry before bed might make it feel as though falling asleep takes longer. These explanations remain speculative, as the researchers did not directly measure recall errors or reporting bias.
The authors also noted other possibilities. People higher in neuroticism might spend more time lying still but awake in bed, which an actigraph can mistake for sleep, and because both neuroticism and habitual sleep were self-reported, part of the association may reflect shared reporting tendencies.
Some limitations should be noted. The questionnaires asked about sleep during the previous month, while the actigraph recorded only five nights, which may not be enough to reliably capture typical sleep; the mismatch also makes direct comparisons harder. Participants may also have altered their sleep because they knew it was being monitored, and the sample consisted of college students, most of them women, from a single private university.
The study, “Neuroticism is associated with self-reported, but not actigraphy-assessed, sleep duration,” was authored by Derick M. DeCamp and Elizabeth J. Pantesco.

German inflation eases to 2.8 pct in October as energy price rises slow
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:57 CST
07:00:57 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Germany's inflation rate eased to 2.8 percent in October after rising for three consecutive months, official data showed Friday, as energy price increases slowed following the introduction of temporary fuel tax cuts.
The decline came after inflation reached 3.3 percent in September, its highest level in nearly three years, driven largely by a sharp rise in energy costs, according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
Energy prices rose 12.2 percent year-on-year in October, easing from a 14.9-percent surge in September, the sharpest rise since February 2023.
The slowdown in energy price increases followed the introduction of temporary fuel tax cuts by the German government on Oct. 1, with the measures set to expire at the end of the year. Analysts had previously estimated that the tax cuts would lower Germany's October inflation rate by 0.3 percentage points.
Despite the easing in inflation, economists warned that price pressures could intensify again in the coming months as elevated energy costs continued to weigh on Europe's largest economy.
A survey released Friday by the Munich-based ifo Institute showed more German companies were planning to raise prices, with its price expectations index climbing to 25.9 points in October from 23 points in September.
"Companies are responding to the sharp increase in prices for crude oil and natural gas, which reached their highest level in the second half of October since 2022," said Timo Wollmershaeuser, head of forecasts at ifo, who warned both producer and consumer price inflation would rise further in the coming months.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, said that the start of the winter heating season, combined with low gas storage levels in Germany, was likely to push up gas prices further in the coming weeks.
Brzeski expected headline inflation to rise again and remain above 3 percent towards the end of this year and in early 2027.
The German government also expects inflationary pressures to persist. In its autumn forecast released earlier this month, it projected an average inflation of 2.7 percent in 2026, up from 2.2 percent in 2025, before rising to 3 percent in 2027. ■

====================================================================================================

British business confidence drops following Budget 2026: IoD
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:53 CST
07:00:53 KST

LONDON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Confidence of British business leaders fell remarkably after the government unveiled its 2026 budget, according to a poll released Friday by the Institute of Directors (IoD).
Ahead of the budget announcement, entrepreneurs' expectations for business revenue increased from 21 in September to 28 in October, the highest level since July 2024. But the figure plummeted to 8 after the budget release, marking its lowest level since December 2025, the IoD said.
The index of investment intentions also climbed from minus 8 in September to 1 ahead of the budget announcement, hitting the highest level since August 2024, before dropping to minus 9 afterward.
A similar trend was seen in employment expectations, with the index falling from 2, its highest level since April 2025, to minus 6 after the budget announcement.
"Our post-Budget snap poll suggests the budget has done little to encourage business leaders to take their investment and recruitment plans out of mothballs," IoD Chief Economist Anna Leach said. Revenue expectations fell sharply to their weakest in 10 months, while investment and hiring intentions also deteriorated, she added.
Ahead of the budget release, business leaders made clear that they wanted the government to address the deterioration in public finances. In its 2026 budget, the government introduced a package to either freeze in real terms, reduce or cut to zero the business rates for all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England. It also took around 70,000 more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses out of business rates by increasing the Small Business Rates Relief threshold.
However, Leach said the budget has allowed fiscal headroom to fall substantially, leaving the public finances with relatively little protection against further shocks.
"With difficult decisions on spending still ahead and limited fiscal headroom, businesses will be concerned that the risk of further tax increases has not gone away," she said.
After two years of weak business confidence, the priority remains to provide a more stable and supportive environment for firms to invest, recruit and grow, she added. ■

Artillery shelling also struck areas around Kfar Shuba in the Arqoub region, the outskirts of Hadatha in the Bint Jbeil district and Wadi Zibqin in the Tyre district.

US-brokered talks

====================================================================================================

Feature: Chinese pianist performs Chopin underground in Polish salt mine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:43 CST
07:00:43 KST

Chinese pianist Rao Hao performs works by Chopin at the Wieliczka Salt Mine in Wieliczka, Poland, Oct. 27, 2026. (Wieliczka Salt Mine/Handout via Xinhua)
by Xinhua writers Yue Yuanyuan, Du Zhiqian
WIELICZKA, Poland, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Some 135 meters beneath the surface of the earth, even the softest touch of the piano keys can be clearly heard, resonating through the chamber in the Wieliczka Salt Mine, near Krakow.
For Chinese pianist Rao Hao, the venue was unexpectedly intimate: the audience sat close by while delicate musical details floated through the space. It felt, the pianist said, like a small musical salon.
Rao gave the underground Chopin recital as part of his October concert schedule in Poland. At Wieliczka, Chopin's music was met with a landscape shaped by centuries of mining.
For a musician accustomed to theaters and concert halls, the setting of a subterranean chamber carved from rock salt was inviting.
"It was a very new experience for me," Rao told Xinhua before the performance. "We chose works by Chopin to better express my own feelings and my understanding of Polish musical culture."
Around him was an underground hall connected to chapels in the mine. On the walls of the chambers, sculptures feature generations of miners working to extract salt.
Mining activities here date back to the 13th century and Wieliczka was among the first sites inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1978. Its underground spaces preserve both the history of mining and the artistic imagination of those who worked there.
For Rao, however, the main discovery was acoustic. The chamber responded to even the quietest playing, allowing subtle changes in pressure to be heard by the audience, he said.
The short distance between performer and public also made the experience more relaxed, the musician said, providing an ideal setting to convey a powerful Chopin of courage, pride and longing -- qualities he feels can be overlooked in the composer's music.
Chopin was often portrayed as fragile or melancholy, but Rao said: "He was a composer with backbone and courage, and he was full of homesickness."
His program included Chopin's four scherzos and the "Heroic" Polonaise. "This time, I want to bring out his strong side," Rao said.
Rao was 17 when he received an honorable mention at the 2021 International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw, an experience that introduced him to a wider international audience.
Now 22, he hopes to demonstrate his growth as a performer. He said his personal connection with the music has deepened, as have his reflections on Polish and Chinese cultures.
For the mine's hosts, the recital also carries special significance.
Barbara Zieba-Godula, president of the management board of the Wieliczka Salt Mine Tourism Company, said Chopin's music is appreciated in both Poland and China, and the concert also showed visitors another way to experience the mine: enjoy an evening listening and explore history at the same time.
Zieba-Godula added that she hoped Rao's visit would encourage more Chinese artists to perform at the mine and create further opportunities for cultural exchange.
For the occasion, the organizers invited representatives of the Chinese embassy, classical music festivals, musical institutions and tourism organizations.
Among the guests was Tomasz Chabowski, who runs a local Chinese kung fu school. With about 30 people in the audience, the concert was "exceptionally intimate," he said, and the setting made it all the more memorable.
"I'm no Chopin expert, but this concert reminded me how moving his music can be," said Chabowski, praising Rao's masterful playing and choice of repertoire. ■
Chinese pianist Rao Hao performs works by Chopin at the Wieliczka Salt Mine in Wieliczka, Poland, Oct. 27, 2026. (Wieliczka Salt Mine/Handout via Xinhua)

====================================================================================================

British people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:00:25 UTC
07:00:25 KST

On 28 October 1787, Thomas Clarkson pushed through the crowds to reach the pulpit of Manchester Cathedral. A campaigner for abolishing slavery, he spoke urgently about the horrors of the slave trade and the humanity of enslaved people. “He drinks the cup of sorrow,” Clarkson said. “And he drinks it at our hands.”
During Black History Month, these are the stories it is important to remember. They show us the complicated truth of our history. Thousands of people in Manchester signed a petition against slavery after Clarkson’s sermon. And yet Manchester’s cotton industry was built on the labour of enslaved people. There are similar stories up and down the nation. We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives.
The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths. I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.
Our history is intertwined with countries that are now our allies, particularly in the Commonwealth. Next week, I will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm). In an increasingly divided and dangerous world, our family of nations in the Commonwealth is vital to our interests: a beacon of stability, strength and security. Together we can face down shared challenges. We can seize opportunities for trade and economic collaboration. We can strengthen our respective countries and share our values to build a safer world for us all.
But facing a changing world together requires us to stand on firm foundations. To meet those challenges of the future, we need to face up to the past. For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.
Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.
So we are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.
Some have called for financial reparations for the slave trade. I do not believe that is the right answer. I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.
My focus is on building a future where people at home and abroad live in greater peace and prosperity.
So we will bring to the Chogm our determination to tackle the issues that affect people across our Commonwealth family and beyond.
Today, debt-servicing costs in the poorest and most vulnerable countries are at their highest in more than 25 years. More than 40% of these countries spend more on interest repayments than on health. I want to launch a new drive on debt, working with our global partners to help those countries repay over a longer time period and with better rates. That is why the chancellor, foreign secretary and I have asked Gordon Brown, who will join us at the Chogm, to help with this work.
We will also support the energy transition in the face of the climate crisis. And we will build on the incredible work being done to educate women and girls, give smaller countries a louder voice on the world stage, and end global poverty and inequality.
I want us to build stronger relationships with each other and renew the relevance of the Commonwealth in a new era. We do that by facing our past together and focusing on a future where every person living within it has equality, security and hope.
We stand on the shoulders of those such as Thomas Clarkson and the many ordinary people who spoke out for justice and humanity.
In 1862, at the height of the American civil war, Manchester was the cotton capital of the world. In a vote at the Free Trade Hall, the humble cotton workers resolved that they would no longer handle slave-picked cotton. Their actions helped end the civil war, prompting Abraham Lincoln to write to them praising their “sublime Christian heroism”.
It is so often the case in British history that huge injustices ignored by the powers-that-be are eventually overturned by ordinary people. Those Manchester cotton workers represent that proud British tradition, and I will take inspiration from them as we go forward into our new dialogue.
- Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

====================================================================================================

Andy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
22:00:24 UTC
07:00:24 KST

Andy Burnham has gone further than any previous prime minister towards offering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, in a Guardian article ahead of a Commonwealth leaders’ summit where the subject is expected to dominate.
As he prepares to fly to the Caribbean next week, the prime minister said he was open to calls for an official apology on behalf of the state and offered formal talks to those affected, including individual countries and campaign groups at home and abroad.
Burnham wrote: “The Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”
While any formal statement will depend on that dialogue, Burnham gave what amounted to a personal apology, saying he wanted to share his “sorrow and regret” for the pain and suffering of millions of people, and to recognise the way the slave trade still shapes the world now.
However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries and campaigners for the UK to pay financial reparations for its role in the slave trade, maintaining the position of successive governments that British people today could not be held liable for the past.
He wrote that reparations were not the “right answer”, adding: “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, which happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”
Instead, Burnham said he would launch a new drive to restructure debt for the poorest Commonwealth countries – led by former prime minister Gordon Brown and expected to eventually include organisations such as the IMF – helping them repay debt over a longer period and with better interest rates.
Debt servicing costs for the poorest and most vulnerable Commonwealth countries are at their highest in more than 25 years, he added, with more than 40% of those spending more on interest repayments than on health.
Burnham’s intervention follows years of pressure from Caribbean states, backed by some African countries, for European nations including the UK, France and Spain to offer reparations – including monetary compensation, a full formal apology, support for health and education and debt cancellation.
As recently as last week, the Commonwealth secretary general, Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey, said a formal apology for slavery from King Charles, who will attend the heads of government summit, “wouldn’t hurt” and the “time has come” for a serious conversation on reparations.
Writing for the Guardian, Burnham said: “The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths.
“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.”
He added: “We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.”
Burnham’s intervention received a cautious welcome from leading figures in the Caribbean. Dorbrene O’Marde, the chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations support commission, said his organisation welcomed the statement as “a movement in the correct direction in the interest of reparatory justice and humanity generally”.
But, he added: “We reject the decision that financial reparations will not be on the table.”
Ralph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the Repair campaign, told the Guardian that an apology was the first point in the Caribbean community’s 10-point reparations plan but “though necessary, is insufficient”.
He added: “We are pleased to hear that [the UK] comes into a conversation. But it can’t be a conversation about nothing. It has to be a conversation about something. If they are not going to entertain reparations, what is the conversation about? Nothing.”
Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caricom reparations commission, said he believed Burnham “is carrying the broad middle of British opinion on this matter”.
He said the call for financial reparations need not be a stumbling block to progress: “There are much broader issues that can occupy that dialogue. So you don’t know what you will emerge out until you have a conversation of decency.
“I think the prime minister will find that Caribbean leaders are very reasonable people on the matter of developing a new Anglo-Caribbean bond … words are important, but the spirit of collaboration is more important.”
Caribbean leaders have been reacting to Bunham’s announcement. In a statement, the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground” but said she and the UK government “are not yet on the same page on every element”.
“On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully. Honest disagreement on some questions should not hold back progress on the many others where we can readily agree.
“An apology, a commitment to eradicate a mindset that is anchored in Afrophobia and against all things “black”, investment in health and education, development partnership that fights systemic poverty and institutionalised inequality, and fairer terms on debt for vulnerable states, as called for by the Bridgetown Initiative, are a few of the areas where we believe understanding can be reached and settled,” her statement said.
“I thank prime minister Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, for breaking new ground and recognising that this is the right thing, and the moral thing, to do by ensuring that we move to the next stage of engagement on this difficult and emotional issue,” it added.
Antigua and Barbuda’s prime minister Gaston Browne, who is hosting this year’s CHOGM, welcomed particularly Burnham’s offer to assist with debt restructuring and a transition to renewable energy.
“The Caribbean’s longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged. Differences over financial compensation should be addressed through dialogue, but they need not prevent progress in areas where agreement is possible,” he said in a statement.
Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also welcomed Burnham’s willingness to discuss a formal apology. In September, Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to the king seeking legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March.
“We have always been open to having full and meaningful dialogue on this important issue. We welcome this development, coming in the wake of our legal petition which is now before the privy council,” Holness said in a statement.
Similarly, the Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, commended Burnham’s decision to agree to a dialogue and consider an apology. “The Bahamas approaches this dialogue with a clear understanding that the issue is not simply one of historical remembrance. It concerns the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress for the generations of Africans and their descendants who continue to live with its legacy,” he said.
The UK government has taken a cautious approach to the issue amid pressure from leftwing MPs to offer a formal apology and engage in reparatory justice, alongside concerns over the potential fiscal and electoral impact, with polls suggesting most voters are opposed to financial compensation.
The Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), which King Charles will also attend, runs from Sunday 1 November until Wednesday 4 November.
At the previous Chogm summit in Samoa two years ago, Britain’s former colonies agreed “the time has come” for a dialogue about reparations – even though then-prime minister Keir Starmer said it would not be on the agenda.
Some inside the UK government had questioned whether Burnham should even attend after the reparations row dominated the 2024 gathering. But his decision to address the issue head-on is likely to be welcomed in Antigua and Barbuda.
Campaigners see the summit as the culmination of decades of advocacy from Caribbean leaders for a deeper acknowledgment of the UK’s historic responsibility for the enslavement of millions of Africans.
Advocates say the UK had been under increasing pressure to act after a UN resolution in March which described the trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.
The UK was among the 52 countries that abstained, saying that while it recognised the gravity of the issue, it disagreed with the fundamental proposition of the text which it said risked creating a hierarchy of historical atrocities.
In June, Mottley, announced a new manifesto from Caribbean leaders asserting the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations over damage caused by hundreds of years of enslavement.
The 10-point plan argued that repair could include international debt cancellation and that climate justice and slavery reparations were “inextricably linked”.
Burnham also referred to the history of Manchester as “the cotton capital of the world” which grew in part thanks to cotton picked by enslaved people.
In 2023 the owner of the Guardian apologised for the role the newspaper’s founders had in the transatlantic slave trade, and launched the Cotton Capital series and a 10-year programme of restorative justice.

He added that air defenses were engaging drones over key government institutions in Aden following the missile strikes.
Casualties and damage were not immediately known.

Aden International Airport has also come under repeated attacks in recent days. On Wednesday, explosions were reported near the airport after the Houthis warned people to evacuate the facility, claiming a Saudi military cargo aircraft there was transporting weapons.
On Friday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement posted on X that Saudi forces had carried out 93 air and missile strikes over the past 24 hours in Sanaa and several Yemeni provinces. The figures could not be independently verified.
Also on Friday, Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported that seven people were killed and a child was wounded in Saudi airstrikes on residential houses in Yemen's southwestern province of Taiz.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition announced in separate statements that it had intercepted and destroyed three drones and two missiles targeting different regions of the kingdom, including the Saudi capital Riyadh and the regions of Mecca and Medina.
Sarea denied carrying out any attack deep inside Saudi Arabia, disputing Saudi claims that drones had been intercepted over both Mecca and Medina. Sarea said the Houthis had "not carried out any operation toward the Saudi interior" and described the reported interception as a "fabricated claim," without providing further evidence.
Recent weeks have seen escalating cross-border hostilities between the two sides, with Saudi strikes hitting Houthi-held areas in Yemen and the Houthis launching missiles and drones toward Saudi Arabia.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. ■

Azerbaijan approves draft law to reward corruption whistleblowers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:21 CST
07:00:21 KST

BAKU, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Azerbaijan's parliament on Friday approved a draft law in the first reading that offers financial rewards to individuals who report corruption-related offenses, local media reported.
Under the draft law, whistleblowers whose information is confirmed would be eligible for a tax-exempt reward of up to 25 times the national minimum monthly wage. The reward would be paid within 10 working days and funded from the budget of the organization concerned.
In criminal cases resulting in a conviction or another final ruling, informants would also receive 5 percent of the funds recovered for the state, including through the special confiscation of assets and compensation for damage, after prescribed expenses are deducted.
The reward amount would depend on the nature of the offense, the number of cases involved, the value of the information in exposing the offense, the extent of the damage caused and the value of assets recovered.
In criminal proceedings, decisions on reward payments would be made by an investigator with the prosecutor's consent during the pretrial investigation stage, and by the court during trial.
The draft law also proposes amendments to the Tax Code to exempt such rewards from income tax. ■

Explainer: What is Canada's EU "associate member"? Why is it disputed?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:15 CST
07:00:15 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The European Union (EU) and Canada on Friday launched "Alliance for the Future" and opted for "ever-closer association" instead of using the name "associate member" in their summit joint statement.
Meeting in Montreal in eastern Canada, the two sides pledged to define the closer relationship, short of full EU membership, by their 2027 summit.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, nevertheless, continued to advocate associate membership, saying after the summit that the idea had been a main point of discussion.
WHAT IS AN "ASSOCIATE MEMBER"?
The proposed status remains undefined. In her statement following the summit, von der Leyen described the idea as "association without accession." She said EU treaties prevented a country outside Europe from joining, but envisaged a partnership closer to membership than any previous arrangement.
The joint statement establishes no new membership category. It provides for closer political engagement through summits, ministerial exchanges and cooperation committees, while leaving the broader concept for further negotiation.
"We will work to define the concept of an ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy," it said.
WHAT COULD CANADA GAIN, AND WHAT WOULD IT CONTRIBUTE?
Von der Leyen outlined closer policy consultations, expanded research cooperation and deeper Canadian participation in EU programs.
The joint statement announced the conclusion of substantive negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement and welcomed Canada's participation in the European High-Performance Computing Joint Undertaking. Negotiations will also pursue deeper participation in Erasmus+, the EU's education and youth program.
According to the Canadian prime minister's office, Canada intends to participate in the EU's 90 billion euro (100 billion U.S. dollars) Ukraine Support Loan.
WHY HAVE SOME EU COUNTRIES QUESTIONED THE LABEL?
Ahead of the summit, Germany, France, Italy and Greece had objected to mentioning associate membership in the draft declaration, according to a report of POLITICO.
At a government briefing in September, German spokesperson Stefan Kornelius welcomed a particularly close partnership and new models of cooperation, but said the proposed title of "associate member" should be reconsidered.
Analysts said that governments feared the designation could complicate the relations with Ukraine, which seeks full membership of the bloc, and with Norway and Switzerland, which already have special arrangements with the EU.
The Commission acknowledged that member states were making efforts over the wording at a news briefing on Thursday. The final statement leaves the title aside while preserving an extensive cooperation agenda.
WHY ARE THE TWO SIDES MOVING CLOSER NOW?
The joint statement cites geopolitical tensions, economic fragmentation, climate change and technological transformation as reasons for a deeper relationship.
Analysts described the summit as part of efforts by both sides to reduce their dependence on the United States, and to search for new alliances amid international tensions.
The joint statement also expressed regret over U.S. sanctions against the International Criminal Court, illustrating shared differences with Washington.
Von der Leyen argued that acting together would strengthen their ability to respond to a changing world, though she said the partnership was not directed against anyone else.
WHAT'S NEXT?
The joint statement sets the 2027 EU-Canada summit as the target for defining the closer association.
Von der Leyen also announced a meeting between the Canadian government and the full European Commission in spring.
Meanwhile, the two sides will pursue negotiations on deeper Erasmus+ participation and a framework for Canadian access to Galileo services, alongside discussions on mobility and professional qualifications.
These processes will determine how the summit's political commitments translate into practical access responsibilities and opportunities for citizens and businesses. ■

UN Security Council holds 7th straw poll on secretary-general candidates
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:14 CST
07:00:14 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The UN Security Council on Friday held its seventh straw poll on candidates vying to become the next UN secretary-general.
"The seventh round of straw polls has taken place," said Aglaia Balta, Greece's permanent representative to the United Nations, whose country holds the rotating presidency of the Security Council for the month of October.
Each candidate will be informed of the results through the permanent representatives of nominating member states. The president of the UN General Assembly will also be informed that the poll has been conducted, Balta told reporters after the secret vote.
Security Council straw polls on secretary-general candidates are informal closed-door ballots used to determine the viability of the candidates. Their results are not officially released.
Through the polls, the Security Council selects a candidate to recommend to the General Assembly for appointment as the next UN secretary-general.
Council members are believed to receive one ballot for each candidate, containing the candidate's name followed by three options: "encouraged," "discouraged" and "no opinion expressed."
To win the council's recommendation, a candidate needs at least nine "encouraged" votes and no "discouraged" votes from any of the five permanent members of the council.
In the sixth straw poll held on Oct. 16, ballots were color-coded to distinguish the votes of permanent and non-permanent members. However, in the seventh straw poll, the council members switched back to undifferentiated ballots following the entry of a new candidate into the race.
Lana Nusseibeh, a diplomat from the United Arab Emirates and the country's former permanent representative to the United Nations, entered the race on Oct. 21. Macky Sall, a former president of Senegal, announced his withdrawal on Oct. 17.
In addition to Nusseibeh, six candidates participated in the seventh straw poll: Ivonne A-Baki, a former Ecuadoran minister and diplomat; Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a former president of the UN General Assembly and former foreign minister and defense minister of Ecuador; Rafael Grossi of Argentina, the current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency; Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice president of Costa Rica and current secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development; Olara Otunnu of Uganda, a former UN under-secretary-general; and Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Guyana's permanent representative to the United Nations.
According to leaked results, Grynspan topped Friday's poll with 11 "encouraged" votes and four "discouraged" votes. She was followed by Grossi, who received nine "encouraged" votes, four "discouraged" votes and two "no opinion expressed" votes.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term expires at the end of this year. His successor is scheduled to take office on Jan. 1, 2027. ■

'Social Media on Steroids.' Advocates for Children Call for Guardrails Around AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:49:22 UTC
06:49:22 KST

“We are living through the greatest transformation that we have seen in our lifetimes, and likely for a significant time before that,” two-time Surgeon General Vivek Murthy told an audience at New York City’s flagship public library on Oct. 28, comparing the advent of artificial intelligence to the advent of nuclear weaponry in terms of the need for carefully thought out safety standards. “We're at a branch point,” he added. “What should the future really look like, what are we trying to protect and preserve?”
Murthy was not alone in sounding the alarm. Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of Common Sense Media, the organizer of the conference, told the mostly supportive crowd that recent history had proved that the industry leaders or, as he called them “tech broligarchs,” could not be relied upon to create digital information systems that were safe or healthy for children. “We did not get out in front of social media in time,” he told the gathering. “This is the moment. AI is a bigger deal. It's basically social media on steroids.”
New York’s governor Kathy Hochul seemed to underscore the point when she made an unscheduled stop at the daylong summit to announce new regulations around chatbots interactions with children. The bill was designed to ensure that AI agents do not impersonate humans or communicate in a way that suggests they have a relationship with a child. “It's happening so quickly,” said Hochul of the technological changes. “It's almost impossible for parents to know what's going on, for elected officials to stay ahead of it, and we certainly have learned the lesson that we can't count on the companies to put out products that are responsible and that put children first.”
Specifically, the new law, which goes into effect in January, will ban chatbots from encouraging suicide, self-harm, secrecy, or isolation and from discouraging children to seek help from other humans. They will also be banned from engaging in sexually explicit interactions and restricted from using a child’s past personal or health information in later conversations.
For the attendees and speakers at the summit, who ranged from Chelsea Clinton and Columbia law professor Tim Wu (onstage) to Uma Thurman (in the audience), the announcement was a good start, although many bemoaned the lack of federal regulation, around both AI and social media. “To this day, 2026, our federal government and Congress has still—nearly a quarter century after the advent of social media—failed to announce anything to protect our kids,” said Murthy, who is now chair of the advisory board of Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute, which studies, tests, and rates AI platforms for children.
Panelists called for a range of protective and preventative remedies for what they described as the coming tsunami of AI, including requiring more data transparency from tech companies by enabling regulatory agencies and researchers to get more access to the information they’re holding, using consumer-protection laws to ensure that AI models have been rigorously tested for potential negative outcomes, adopting the European model of not allowing AI companies to deploy their platforms until they have proved they are safe, or even instituting criminal penalties for AI companies who unleash unsafe technologies. “As a former prosecutor, I can tell you one thing,” said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who earlier this month won a $25 billion judgment against Meta. “When you bring out handcuffs, suddenly everything changes.”
Not all the issues around AI can be solved by the law, however. One concern is the socialization of very young children by AI, including via voice-activated assistants like Alexa or very agreeable AI-enabled toys. “What do kids start to learn to expect from social practice? Do they expect someone to always agree with them? Is it always easy? Is it always like a transaction?” asked Dana Suskind, an early-childhood expert and professor at the University of Chicago. Human relationships are a lot messier, she noted. “They're chaotic, and that sort of mess is where a lot of learning happens.” Parents, who were caught off-guard by the influence of social media and digital devices, need to be educated about AI and encouraged that their imperfect parenting, as well as other human interaction, is vastly more beneficial to children than an AI companion, she said.
The summit also touched on the enormous implications AI is having on education and students’ ability to work and learn, when answers are in such ready supply. “MIT just did a report saying every assignment at MIT could be done by generative AI,” said John King, a former U.S. Secretary of Education and current chancellor of State University in New York. King is considering major changes to student assessment. “We have to make sure we are seeing the students do the work, and we have to make sure they're getting those foundational skills,” he said. “It literally means every faculty member reassessing what they assign and how they measure student learning.” And, as Clinton pointed out, this is an equity issue too. “We know that in families with less than $30,000 of household income, teenagers are three times more likely to either largely or entirely do their homework through artificial intelligence than those households with family incomes of $75,000 or more,” she said.
At the same time, students need to be prepared to enter a workforce in which AI skills are not optional. For those who have mastered them, the future is very bright. “The people coming in learn much more rapidly because AI gives them more capacity than they've had before,” said Gene Sykes, chairman of global mergers and acquisitions at Goldman Sachs of the banking giant’s new recruits. “So somebody, within a month, can be doing incredibly productive work.” If good education in AI is distributed unevenly, some graduates will be vastly better prepared for a career than others, further exacerbating wealth inequities.
While there was little consensus on the immediate steps to take as AI arrives, there was no argument that it will be consequential for children, families, and generations to come. “As we go into this age of transformation,” Murthy noted, “the question forced upon us is the following: What aspects of human existence do we want to protect and preserve at all costs?”

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski on Friday defended police action at the Constitutional Tribunal, saying it aimed to allow duly elected judges to resume the court's work.
Speaking at a news conference on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in the US city of Atlanta, Sikorski said the tribunal had been "politicized under the previous government," and the current leadership dispute had prevented the court from functioning properly.
He said a majority of judges elected by the new parliament during the last two years had been unable to carry out their duties because the outgoing court president had not convened the tribunal's council.
As a result, the court had been unable to issue judgments, interpret laws or even approve its budget for the coming year, said Sikorski.
"So, action had to be taken to enable the tribunal to function again," he said.
The comments came after police entered the premises of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal on Friday, while the court announced that its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, had been suspended.
Police said officers entered the premises following incidents outside the court, including the throwing of dangerous objects at police.
The developments also prompted President Karol Nawrocki to cut short his trip to Senegal and return to Poland.
"At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," Nawrocki said on US social media company X.

8 things we learned at the EU-Canada summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:43:34 UTC
06:43:34 KST

Ursula von der Leyen, António Costa and Mark Carney hammered out the contours of a new partnership during a whirlwind 48 hours in Montreal. Here’s everything you need to know.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrive during the welcome ceremony at the 21st EU-Canada summit in Montreal, on Oct. 30, 2026. | Alexis Aubin/AFP via Getty Images
MONTREAL — Prime Minister Mark Carney wanted the landmark EU-Canada summit to be about much more than “nomenclature.” He got what he craved.
Over a whirlwind 48 hours in Montreal, top officials from Brussels and Ottawa huddled to pursue agreements on critical minerals, super computers and defense cooperation.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Carney gathered as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to upend the global order and Chinese dominance of critical markets squeezes middle powers.
Advertisement
Those challenges have pushed the EU and Canada into a rapidly developing partnership that eclipses anything attempted by Brussels with a non-member country since the bloc was formed.
Here are all the key things POLITICO learned during the EU-Canada meetings.
Carney finally embraced ‘associate membership’
Initially reluctant, the Canadian prime minister came around by the end of the summit to endorse von der Leyen’s controversial label for the global alliance the EU and Canada are building.
Carney set a six-month deadline to firm up the ground rules of what “associate membership” is, trialing an induction process that could be a model for other non-European countries.
“With Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member, in the coming months we will determine the full substance, scale and scope of this new form of membership,” he said Friday.
Carney added he will meet periodically with von der Leyen to track progress, including a return trip for the College of European Commissioners to meet with their Canadian counterparts in March.
Advertisement
Got minerals
Both Canadian and EU officials are walking away from the summit with at least one major win: the framework agreement signed between the European Investment Bank and Canada that will open up the bloc’s lending arm to Canadian critical minerals crucial for future tech.
That means batteries, circuit boards and semiconductors, which all require lithium, nickel, cobalt and other critical raw materials that, as of now, the EU is largely dependent on China to score.
The deal helps wean the Europeans off a politically volatile critical minerals dealer, for a more reliable Canadian supplier.
The agreement does not immediately unlock funding for specific projects, but it supports pathways for future investments in Canadian mining and helps link the bloc’s supply chains with Canada’s.
Canada’s energy ambitions still point east
Critical minerals aren’t the only Canadian natural resource on the menu for Europeans.
Carney has said he wants to make Canada an “energy superpower” and leverage huge stores of oil and liquefied natural gas in his country for export. The only problem: Most of it is in the western province of Alberta, far from Europe.
Advertisement
But the summit concluded with a commitment by both sides to a “long-term feasibility study” on exporting LNG to Europe via the east coast or Arctic ports closer to the bloc.
“There's also a huge opportunity in terms of bringing some of the fossils and gas from Canada to the EU,” said a Commission official, who was granted anonymity to talk about sensitive diplomatic negotiations. “The old infrastructure in Canada was built north-south for historical reasons, but now there is talk of starting to build east-west.”
Making nice with Washington? Don’t hold your breath.
As Europeans and Canadians preached deeper ties, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) was there doing damage control.
Welch, whose state is a little over an hour’s drive south of Montreal, spent Thursday reassuring business leaders that U.S. relations with Canada and beyond can, some day, get back to normal. When exactly, he couldn’t say for sure.
During his trip, Welch met with Quebec Chief Trade Negotiator Pascal Paradis, tourism industry leaders, businesses and manufacturers nailed by tariffs, and hit up a Eurasia Group lunch.
Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections could offer a waypoint to warmer relations. But Welch loaded his optimism about Democratic Party fortunes with caveats.
Advertisement
“I think we’ll be successful, but you’ll still have a president who abuses his authority and acts in arbitrary ways,” he said. “It’s not like I can give any assurance that things are going to change.”
Unspoken in the communiqué: China
Canada and the EU pledged deeper cooperation on pumping more European money into the mining, production and refining of critical minerals, a response to China’s dominance of the global market for those minerals. But the final summit communiqué steers clear of naming specific countries.
Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty was more candid.
“China has been vacuuming up as many critical minerals as they can throughout the world, particularly in the African continent, cutting deals, usually infrastructure for critical mineral deals. That could be a soccer stadium, for example. It could be a light rail system,” McGuinty told POLITICO at the summit Friday.
“It turns out that Canada's got a huge amount of critical minerals, and basically all 10 of the 10 critical minerals on the short list for NATO, which the United States is also aware of. We're going to not only exploit, but we intend to move to transform,” he said.
The common language: Sovereignty
Outside the summit, many Montrealers were oblivious to the landmark meeting taking place in the city. Inside, the vibe was existential.
Advertisement
The trio of leaders — Carney, von der Leyen and Costa — invoked individual and collective sovereignty as reasons to pursue a closer alliance to weather “new storms” stoked by climate change, challenges to democratic norms and the weaponization of trade. Carney has notably claimed concerns about encroachment on Canada’s sovereignty as a reason to walk away from trade talks with the Trump administration.
“Today is about sovereignty,” Carney said. “We're building the industries and infrastructure that underwrite our collective security.”
Quebec wanted a seat at the table
The summit came to Montreal weeks after Quebec — the French-speaking province in Canada that hosted the summit — elected a separatist government. Quebec shares powers with Ottawa and had its own seat in the CETA trade talks with the EU over a decade ago; and it had sought a similar role at this summit.
But Ottawa refused to let new Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon address the summit, so he boycotted it, complaining he was being asked to “serve shrimp cocktail.”
Carney accused him of leaving “an empty chair.” It stayed empty, even though six former Quebec premiers came to dinner.
The Europeans did not escape unscathed. The Quebec press panned von der Leyen’s English-only speech on the opening day as a faux pas in Canada’s largest francophone metropolis. Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera did little better, telling Radio-Canada in French that, for Brussels, summits like this are between national governments.
Bagel diplomacy
In a town where the original heated rivalry persists between two bagel shops, von der Leyen couldn't resist picking a side with a photo-op at St-Viateur.

Strikes blamed on Houthis target Yemen presidential palace
Yemen's Houthis targeted the presidential palace in Aden on Friday with two missiles, a police official told AFP, hours after Saudi forces said they had intercepted an attack by the group on the Gulf kingdom.
Aden, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government, has been targeted repeatedly since Yemen's dormant civil war reignited in July.
Two eyewitnesses told AFP they saw ambulances entering the palace in Aden, a large compound made up of several buildings including facilities used by government and Saudi-led coalition forces, after the incident.
Shortly before, residents and an AFP journalist said they heard two blasts in the city.
The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa to the north, most recently struck the perimeter of Aden's airport on Wednesday after saying they had targeted a naval base and a military camp last week.
The coalition, which is fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, said on Friday it had intercepted and destroyed a drone near the Saudi capital of Riyadh, as well as a missile fired towards the country's southern region.
In two posts on X, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said forces had destroyed the drone in Riyadh province as well as "a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the southern region".
Earlier on Friday, the coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone in the Mecca region, with the group denying it targeted Islam's holiest city.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," Malki wrote in a post on X.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree called the Saudi statement "a massive and egregious fabrication".
Hours later, Malki reported another drone interception, this time over the Medina region, home to Islam's second holiest city.
Yemen's war began in 2014, with Saudi Arabia entering the conflict in support of the government the following year.
A ceasefire in 2022 brought relative peace until this summer, when the conflict reignited.
More than a decade of warfare has created a humanitarian catastrophe in one of the world's poorest countries, which the UN estimates is home to 42 million people.
