Russia, US veto rival UN Western Sahara resolutions, leaving peacekeeping mission in limbo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:41:24 UTC
06:41:24 KST

Competing US, Russia resolutions on Western Sahara defeated in UN Security Council
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 30 - Russia vetoed a US-drafted resolution on Western Sahara at the Security Council on Friday, leaving the UN peacekeeping mission there without a renewed mandate just a day before it expires.
The resolution would have extended the mission for another year while cementing Morocco's autonomy plan as the only basis for talks to settle the half-century-old conflict and scaling back its military component.
The council then defeated a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission for a year. That draft got three votes in favor and one against, with 11 abstentions, failing to get the nine affirmative votes needed to pass.
The showdown threatens the future of a mission the council has routinely renewed for decades and deepens a dispute over the territory, most of which is controlled by Morocco but claimed by the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks an independent state.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the mission, saying its personnel and equipment should leave Western Sahara in the coming days. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire in the territory. Polisario representative Sidi Omar thanked Russia for vetoing the US-backed resolution, which he said would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and "threaten regional and international peace".
Unless the Security Council agrees to a last-minute extension, the mandate for the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, will expire on October 31.
Oxfam warned that losing the mission could put refugees at risk. Hostilities have persisted at low levels since Polisario said in November 2020 that it was resuming "armed struggle".
Last year, the Security Council dealt a blow to Polisario's ambitions when it backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as a basis for resolving the conflict and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.
The failed US resolution would have gone further, removing the reference to a referendum from the mission's name, renaming it the United Nations Mission in Western Sahara, or MINUSO.
Following the vote, US Ambassador Michael Waltz said a referendum had never taken place because of longstanding disagreements over voter eligibility.
"UN officials have been telling us this reality for 30 years," he said.
"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," he added.
France and the UK - the two other permanent Security Council members - along with eight non-permanent members, backed the US resolution and Morocco's autonomy plan.
MISSION AT RISK
Russia said the US draft went too far in endorsing Morocco's position on the disputed territory.
"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's UN envoy Vassily Nebenzia said.
"The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of the draft," he said.
With 155 military personnel, the mission, tasked with organizing a referendum as part of a UN-brokered ceasefire, is set to cost $62 million in the fiscal year that started in June this year, according to a UN Secretary-General report.
"The loss of MINURSO’s monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability, with serious consequences to civilians and prospects of a peaceful resolution," Oxfam said in reaction to the vote.
While most Sahrawis live in Morocco-ruled Western Sahara, tens of thousands are estimated to be living in Polisario-run refugee camps in Algeria.
The vetoed US resolution called for a census of the refugees.
UNITY DAY
Morocco's royal palace said the non-renewal of the mission was a "significant development" and that it meant the Western Sahara issue should be withdrawn from consideration by the Security Council.
"The non-renewal of MINURSO's mandate clearly means that the presence of the mission in the Kingdom's southern provinces, including its personnel, vehicles, equipment and symbols, should come to an end in the coming days," the palace said in a statement.
In Laayoune, the largest city in Western Sahara, streets were decorated with Moroccan flags and lights to prepare to celebrate “Unity Day”, a holiday the palace declared to commemorate last year’s UN Security Council vote on October 31.
On Wednesday, the Polisario staged a rally at the Smara camp near the town of Tindouf, in southern Algeria.
A couple hundred men and women, waving flags of the Polisario's self-proclaimed Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, gathered near Polisario fighters in military fatigues, waving signs with slogans such as "No to Morocco's autonomy plan. Yes to the right to self-determination". REUTERS

Mbappé apologises for remarks as financial backlash hits Real Madrid and La Liga
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
23:36:06 EET
06:36:06 KST

French football star Kylian Mbappé has triggered a commercial crisis for himself, Real Madrid and Spain’s La Liga after describing China’s revolutionary leader Mao Zedong as a dictator during an interview. Chinese companies have terminated sponsorship agreements reportedly worth millions of euros, while broadcasters have suspended Spanish football coverage, placing television contracts worth hundreds of millions at risk.
The controversy has also raised questions about cultural sensitivity, historical understanding and the different standards applied to political leaders in Western countries and elsewhere.
The dispute began when a clip from Mbappé’s appearance on the French programme The Bridge resurfaced on social media on 26 October.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Asked about his favourite internet meme, the Real Madrid forward referred to an image showing his face superimposed on that of Mao Zedong, the founder of the People’s Republic of China.
He described the person in the image as “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.
The remark spread across Chinese social media, where football supporters criticised the player for referring to a figure associated with China’s revolution, national independence and modernisation in such terms.
Within days, the controversy had developed into a commercial dispute involving Chinese companies, Spanish football’s broadcasting arrangements and Real Madrid’s business interests.
According to French newspaper Le Monde, Mbappé’s sponsorship agreements with Chinese companies were worth an estimated 50 million yuan, equivalent to approximately €6.7 million.
Three companies, Dongpeng Beverage Group, Mengniu Dairy and Milkground, announced the termination of their relationships with the French international.
The companies did not disclose the individual value of their agreements or how much money had already been paid. The €6.7 million figure represents an estimate of the combined sponsorship arrangements rather than a confirmed financial loss.
The commercial consequences extended to international brands. According to Le Monde, Dior and Swiss sportswear company On removed promotional material featuring Mbappé from their Chinese social media accounts. Reports indicated that watchmaker Hublot had taken similar action.
Mbappé’s accounts on Weibo and Xiaohongshu also faced restrictions, limiting his access to Chinese supporters and consumers.
Forbes estimated his earnings for the 2026 season at approximately $100 million, including $30 million from endorsements and other business activities. The full effect of the Chinese sponsorship dispute on those earnings remains undisclosed.
La Liga faces a separate financial challenge.
China Media Group, which operates state broadcaster CCTV, suspended Spanish league coverage and removed advertising and video material featuring Mbappé.
The decision affected the league’s television exposure in a market where European football generates revenue through broadcasting, sponsorship and merchandise sales.
The larger concern involves La Liga’s broadcasting agreement with China Mobile and its Migu streaming platform.
The agreement, signed in August 2026, grants Migu exclusive digital broadcasting rights in mainland China through the 2029–30 season and covers all 380 league matches each season.
According to Spanish newspaper Mundo Deportivo, citing market estimates reported by Vozpópuli, La Liga’s Chinese television rights business has been valued at up to €400 million through 2030.
That figure represents the estimated value of the business at stake, not money already lost. The contractual terms remain confidential, and Migu had not announced a complete suspension of its La Liga coverage as of 29 October.
Real Madrid also has commercial interests in China, where Le Monde estimates the club has approximately 97 million supporters.
Its income from merchandise, sponsorship agreements and digital content depends partly on maintaining relationships with those supporters.
The financial implications prompted responses from Spanish football authorities.
La Liga president Javier Tebas apologised to Chinese supporters and sought to distance the league from Mbappé’s remarks. He also met China’s ambassador to Spain as the dispute developed.
Real Madrid issued its own apology on 28 October after Chinese media and football organisations criticised the club’s initial response.
Mbappé had apologised the previous day in French, Chinese and English, describing his words as “ill-judged” and expressing “deep respect for the Chinese people and their history”.
China’s Foreign Ministry said it took the apology seriously. The government did not announce a formal ban on the player, although broadcasters and commercial partners imposed their own restrictions.
Beyond the financial consequences, the dispute has brought attention to cultural sensitivity and the responsibilities of public figures whose audiences extend across national and political boundaries.
Footballers occupy a position in international popular culture that reaches beyond sport. Their words travel through social media, television, advertising and commercial partnerships to audiences with different histories and political experiences.
A remark made during an informal interview in France therefore reaches people who interpret it through their own understanding of national identity and historical memory. In China, Mao occupies a place in national history that differs from the image often presented in Western political debate.
Mao led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in 1949 after decades of civil conflict, foreign intervention and Japanese occupation. His government established the People’s Republic of China and pursued programmes of industrialisation, literacy, public health and infrastructure development.
China expanded its industrial capacity during the Mao period, while improvements in healthcare and disease prevention contributed to substantial increases in life expectancy. These developments formed part of the economic and institutional foundations inherited by the reform government that followed Mao’s death in 1976.
For many Chinese citizens, Mao remains associated with national sovereignty, the end of foreign domination and the establishment of a unified state.
His portrait continues to occupy a central position at Tiananmen Gate in Beijing, and his image appears on Chinese currency. Mbappé’s description did not acknowledge that historical context. The distinction between historical criticism and cultural insensitivity is important.
Calling Mao a dictator reflects an assessment of his authoritarian rule. Historians and political commentators have examined that aspect of his leadership for decades. Yet discussing a historical figure through a casual joke, without recognising the significance attached to that figure by another society, raises a different question.
The issue concerns not only the accuracy of a political description but also the circumstances in which it is used and the audience receiving it.
A historical assessment involves evidence, context and an understanding of the period concerned. A remark about an internet meme provides none of those elements.
Cultural sensitivity does not require agreement with a government’s interpretation of history. Nor does it place political leaders beyond criticism.
It involves recognising that historical events and national figures hold meanings shaped by experiences that differ across societies.
For Chinese citizens whose families lived through foreign occupation, civil war and the establishment of the People’s Republic, Mao’s place in history extends beyond the political terminology used to describe his government.
The same consideration applies to historical figures in Western countries.
Public discussion of national leaders often distinguishes between their achievements, their failures and the historical circumstances in which they governed.
Figures associated with national independence, state formation or major political changes frequently retain public recognition despite controversy surrounding their policies.
Such distinctions form part of how societies preserve and debate their histories.
International athletes and entertainers encounter these differences whenever they refer to national symbols, political leaders, religious traditions or historical events outside their own countries.
The responsibility extends to the arts, where films, music, comedy and other forms of expression regularly draw upon historical subjects.
Artistic freedom includes the right to criticise political leaders and challenge established interpretations of history.
Cultural sensitivity concerns the manner in which those subjects are represented, particularly when an artist or performer has limited knowledge of the society involved.
Satire based on historical research differs from a casual reference that reduces a figure associated with another country’s national identity to a single political label.
The distinction does not depend on avoiding controversial subjects. It depends on understanding the subject and recognising the experiences of the people concerned.
In international sport, cultural awareness has an additional dimension because athletes represent institutions with supporters from different countries.
Real Madrid and La Liga have spent years developing relationships with Chinese audiences through broadcasting agreements, sponsorships, promotional campaigns and merchandise sales.
Those relationships involve more than financial transactions.
Chinese supporters follow European clubs, identify with their players and participate in the international football community.
Their engagement also brings expectations that clubs and athletes will treat their country’s history and cultural identity with consideration.
The same expectations arise when European clubs visit countries in Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.
Supporters in those regions do not necessarily share Western interpretations of political history or international relations.
For an athlete with a worldwide audience, understanding those differences forms part of communicating across cultures.
The controversy surrounding Mbappé also raises questions about Western exceptionalism and the different standards used to describe political leaders.
Western political debate frequently applies terms such as dictator and authoritarian to leaders of non-allied states, while political figures in Western democracies are generally discussed within the framework of electoral competition and constitutional institutions.
Differences between political systems help explain that distinction. Elections, judicial independence, civil liberties and constitutional limits provide criteria for assessing how governments exercise power.
Yet those criteria also apply to Western leaders.
The fact that a leader holds office through an electoral process does not place that leader’s conduct beyond examination.
Questions concerning executive authority, political accountability, treatment of opponents and conflicts of interest remain relevant regardless of nationality or political system.
US President Donald Trump offers a contemporary example of this debate.
Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 following his election victory, but his approach to presidential authority has drawn criticism from constitutional scholars, human rights organisations and democracy researchers.
Human Rights Watch warned in February 2026 that his administration had attacked institutions of American democracy, citing immigration enforcement, threats to voting rights and other government policies.
The International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance also documented concerns over executive power, restrictions affecting civil society and pressure on democratic institutions.
Trump’s administration has been described by critics as one of the most corrupt in American history, amid allegations that the president and his family have profited from political power.
According to Forbes, Trump’s personal fortune increased by approximately $2.7 billion between the 2024 election and September 2026, reaching an estimated $7 billion.
Forbes attributed much of the increase to cryptocurrency ventures and overseas business arrangements.
A Reuters investigation published in June 2026 found that Trump and his sons had generated at least $2.3 billion in profits from their principal cryptocurrency ventures since his return to the White House.
Reuters also reported that Trump’s financial disclosures showed more than $1.4 billion in income from family cryptocurrency activities during 2025.
The findings prompted questions about conflicts of interest involving presidential authority, financial regulation and private business arrangements. The figures document financial gains but do not, by themselves, establish criminal corruption.
When Western public figures describe foreign leaders through terms associated with authoritarian rule, the same scrutiny of political power, accountability and personal financial interests also belongs in discussions of leaders within Western democracies.
The competing interpretations reflect differences in political interests, but they also demonstrate how the language used to describe government conduct changes according to the position of the observer.
Cultural sensitivity requires awareness of those differences without demanding agreement with every political or historical interpretation.
Public figures increasingly address audiences whose historical experiences and national identities differ from their own.
A statement that attracts little attention in one country sometimes becomes a source of controversy elsewhere because the subject holds a different place in public memory.
The Mbappé dispute demonstrates how quickly such differences affect international sporting relationships.
Real Madrid and La Liga apologised after Chinese companies ended sponsorship agreements and state television suspended coverage.
The Chinese Football Association demanded apologies from the player and his club, while state media criticised Real Madrid’s initial response.
Chinese football platform Dongqiudi also reportedly removed Mbappé’s name from its 2026 Ballon d’Or ranking.
The controversy continued after the apologies.
On 29 October, France 24 reported that Mbappé, Real Madrid and La Liga faced difficulties restoring their relationships with Chinese supporters and commercial partners.
The immediate financial consequences included sponsorship agreements estimated at €6.7 million and the suspension of La Liga coverage on Chinese state television.
The wider financial exposure concerned broadcasting agreements whose combined market value has been estimated at up to €400 million through 2030, although no loss approaching that amount had been confirmed.
Real Madrid also faced uncertainty over merchandise sales and commercial partnerships in a country where its supporters number in the tens of millions.
As of 29 October, the terminated sponsorship agreements had not been reinstated, and the restrictions on television broadcasts and promotional content had not been fully reversed.

we drove volvo’s electric EX60 to russel wright’s modernist woodland home at manitoga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:35:59 UTC
06:35:59 KST

we drove volvo’s electric EX60 to russel wright’s modernist woodland home at manitoga
from seasonal color studies to an interior that projects leaves onto its seats, volvo’s electric EX60 draws design inspiration from nature.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
an autumn drive into the hudson highlands
Volvo‘s new all-electric EX60 took us from Manhattan to Manitoga, the woodland home of American industrial designer Russel Wright in Garrison, New York. The drive north brought us out of the city and into the tree-lined roads of the Hudson Valley, glowing with autumn color, where the Swedish automaker had organized a design experience around its newest electric SUV.
During the mid-twentieth century, Wright spent decades transforming a former quarry into a 75-acre woodland estate. The experimental and iconic modernist home incorporates the surrounding forest into its architecture, with the resulting space feeling like an architect’s fairytale.
Volvo’s designers have been exploring similar ideas for the EX60, studying natural materials and the changing colors of the landscape to shape the experience inside the car.
the all-electric ex60
The EX60 translates the familiar proportions of Volvo’s popular XC60 into a fully electric SUV. Its low front end and gently sloping roofline contribute to a drag coefficient of just 0.26, while beneath the body sits the company’s new SPA3 electric architecture.
The platform introduces megacasting and cell-to-body battery integration to reduce weight and improve efficiency. For the U.S. market, the P10 AWD offers 503 horsepower and up to 330 miles of EPA-estimated range, with charging from 10 to 80 percent taking as little as 16 minutes under optimal conditions.
material and color choices
Inside, the EX60 introduces a 15-inch curved OLED center display with Google Gemini integrated into the infotainment system. The cabin has a fairly simple layout, with tactile finishes and natural textures softening the presence of its digital technology.
Once we arrived at Manitoga, we met Sara Erichsen Susnjar, Volvo Cars’ Senior Color & Material Design Manager, who has spent twenty years with the company and oversees color and material design for its midsize models.
Presenting a palette of materials, Susnjar drew our attention to the EX60’s available tailored wool-blend upholstery. Wool, she explained, naturally responds to body temperature, remaining comfortable through changes in weather. Its breathability is especially useful when returning to a parked car on a hot day. The material comes with challenges around production costs and customer expectations, although its practical qualities make a compelling case. ‘I think it’s a little bit brave, but also it has a function,‘ she told us.
The conversation soon turned to color. Susnjar explained that developing a new automotive finish can involve an entire year of evaluation, with painted vehicles taken outdoors in different seasons to observe how their colors respond to changing light.
‘We have to check all the light,‘ she explained. This means moving between controlled lighting environments and outdoor settings, from warm summer sunlight to the colder light of winter.
russel wright’s manitoga is a house shaped by the forest
There was an interesting historical parallel waiting inside Manitoga. Wright approached color as something that should respond to the seasons, changing elements of his home’s interior throughout the year. Warmer colors appeared during winter, while cooler tones were introduced for summer. Best known for his American Modern dinnerware, introduced in 1939, Wright had long been interested in how design could make domestic environments more comfortable and enjoyable.
In 1942, Wright and his wife Mary purchased the former quarry and logging property in Garrison. The estate would eventually become home to Dragon Rock, completed in 1961 with architect David Leavitt. Touring the house, we found interiors filled with unusual handmade experiments.
Large boulders extend into the rooms, while actual pine needles are embedded in green plaster walls. Wright even pressed butterfly wings or wildflowers between sheets of translucent plastic to creating decorative screens from materials gathered in nature.
immersed in wild nature
Outside, a waterfall drops into the former quarry pool, while trails wind through the surrounding woodland. Our guide explained how Wright encouraged native moss to spread by removing competing plants to gradually transforming the forest floor.
Today, Manitoga is a National Historic Landmark, designated in 2006, and is maintained by the nonprofit Russel Wright Design Center, which continues to preserve and restore the house and landscape.
bringing the forest into the electric cabin
One of the EX60’s more unusual interior features is its Forest Light ambient lighting system, which projects a pattern of leaves onto the rear seats and center console. Susnjar described the feature during our visit, explaining that the design team wanted to bring some of the experience of nature into the vehicle. As the presentation took place during the day, we could only get a partial impression of the effect, which is designed to be experienced in darkness.
After exploring Dragon Rock, Wright experimented extensively with lighting. Large expanses of glass bring the changing woodland into view from almost every room. His home responds directly to its surroundings, with natural materials appearing throughout the architecture. Volvo takes a different approach, using contemporary technology to introduce an impression of the forest into the enclosed space of a car.

company: Volvo | @volvocarusa
estate: Manitoga / The Russel Wright Design Center | @visitmanitoga
architecture: Russel Wright with David Leavitt, Dragon Rock, completed 1961

‘The killer was never punished’: The forgotten Egypt terror attack and its tragic fifth victim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:35:38 UTC
06:35:38 KST

Mor Shamli, 35, the widow of Alon Shamli, who was murdered before her eyes in Egypt on October 8, 2023, became the fifth victim of the shooting attack Friday, after dying following more than three years of psychological anguish.
The shooting took place in Alexandria one day after the Hamas massacre of October 7, as Israelis were still struggling to comprehend the scale of the atrocities and eliminate the remaining terrorists in communities near the Gaza Strip. An Egyptian police officer opened fire with his weapon at a group of Israeli tourists near Pompey's Pillar, a Roman triumphal column considered one of the best-known tourist attractions in Alexandria, Egypt's second-largest city. 
Alon Shamli and Amnon Bezalel were pronounced dead at the scene, while Hagai Efrat died of his wounds about 10 days later. Egyptian tour guide Sayed Kamel al-Khawalqa was also killed in the attack. Alon's widow later said: "My life ended there in Egypt on October 8, 2023, when they murdered us. The bullet that struck Alon's heart struck mine too."
Alon Shamli, who was 34 when he was killed, coached a youth team at Hapoel Tel Aviv soccer club. He also worked as a physical education teacher at Rishonim School in Bat Yam. Following his death, Hapoel Tel Aviv said Alon "was highly regarded in the youth department. His players said he always devoted himself to them and pushed them to improve."
Amnon Bezalel, 64, of Bat Yam, served in the Israel Police for about 40 years. He was known as a diligent and respected officer and spent much of his career with the Holon police. His final position was technology coordinator in the Ayalon police region.
Hagai Efrat, 83, of Rishon LeZion, whose death was confirmed about 10 days after the attack, played soccer for Hapoel Haifa in his youth and managed Hapoel Jerusalem's soccer club during the 1970s and 1980s.
Friends of Egyptian tour guide Sayed Kamel al-Khawalqa said he was highly educated and possessed extensive knowledge, which helped him in his work as a tour guide. According to Egyptian media reports, he was also accompanying another group of tourists on the day of the attack and was caught in the gunman's line of fire.
But the attack, which received relatively little attention because it occurred so soon after the October 7 massacre, had another victim: Mor Shamli, who never recovered from what happened. In January, she announced to her Instagram followers that she intended to end her life through medically assisted suicide in Switzerland. 
The announcement sparked a wave of false rumors that the procedure had already taken place and that she had died. In Instagram Stories posted that month, she explained the painful decision she had made and the feelings that had accompanied her since the attack, which occurred just one day after the massacre in Israeli communities near the Gaza Strip.
"The pain is unbearable. You wouldn't believe how many tears the heart and eyes can produce," she wrote in January. "I am not alive, but not entirely dead either. I exist as though I am floating above life. Here, but not here. I am sorry that I am hurting everyone, that the suffering is being passed on to you. There are no words that can express how sorry I am. I hope you can understand and forgive me. I wish that every day of your lives could be like the life Alon and I shared together, full of love and happiness. Please try to remember me as I was before that terrible day. And do not hold anger in your hearts. Now I am no longer suffering. Now I am happy and at peace."
Mor's parents, Ilan and Shoshi Cohen, said Friday evening in grief: "Mor was murdered along with Alon in Egypt. She continued living, but she could not bear the pain and the loss of her husband, Alon. She had no desire to live. She was simply living but dead, until today, when she is no longer with us."
Three years without justice
The shooter's name has never been officially released, although several Arabic-language reports identified him as Mohammed Abdel-Magid. Since the October 7 massacre and the war that followed, diplomatic relations with Egypt have deteriorated significantly. Israel has no ambassador stationed in the country, and Israeli diplomats travel to Cairo from time to time for several days but are not permanently based there. 
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi refuses to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Recently, reports emerged that three Israelis, Ahmed al-Dougi, Bilal Salem Abu Aish and Bilal Masoudin, were taken into Egyptian intelligence vehicles in Sharm el-Sheikh and disappeared. Their whereabouts remain unknown.
Against the backdrop of the current diplomatic climate with Egypt, which has hardly distinguished itself by holding accountable terrorists who leave its territory to carry out attacks in Israel, justice has still not been served for those murdered, even three years after the attack. Reports about the gunman are almost impossible to find, and he has yet to stand trial for his actions.
In an interview this past July with Kan's Reshet Bet radio station, Mor Shamli said: "So much time has passed, and every time they give me different answers. The bottom line is that there are no answers. The killer who was caught that day still hasn't been punished. At first, I was told he was awaiting sentencing. Now I've been told his trial will only take place in another three months. It really feels like they're making a mockery of us."
Mor also described her struggle to retrieve Alon's clothes from Egypt. "I kept asking, and at first the Foreign Ministry told me: 'Listen, this takes time.' Then they told me: 'Too much time has passed. They no longer have them. They've already thrown them away.' The Foreign Ministry is basically telling me: 'We're just passing along the Egyptians' answers.' As if they're merely a go-between for me and the Egyptians."
Doubts that the attacker will ever face justice are further heightened by Arabic-language reports published after the shooting that avoided describing it as a terror attack. Al Jazeera, for example, claimed a day after the killings that the shooting had been preceded by "provocations" by the Israeli tourists, who supposedly "insisted on taking photographs with an Israeli flag." 
According to the unsupported account, the police officer asked the Israelis to stop, an argument developed and he eventually opened fire. Israelis who were present at the scene categorically denied the allegations, saying they had actually tried to avoid drawing attention to their Israeli nationality, particularly in light of the October 7 massacre the previous day.
Several months before the Alexandria attack, another deadly attack occurred along the Israel-Egypt border, also carried out by an Egyptian police officer. On June 3, 2023, Egyptian security officer Mohammed Salah infiltrated Israel and killed Staff Sgt. Ori Yitzhak Ilouz and Sgt. Lia Ben-Nun, both serving in the Bardelas Battalion, at a guard post. Later, during searches and an exchange of fire inside Israeli territory, a third soldier, Staff Sgt. Ohad Dahan of the Caracal Battalion, was killed. The terrorist was subsequently shot dead.

UAH 294.8 million will be allocated for shelters in 84 maternity hospitals, and another UAH 59.8 million for the protection of hospitals. The funds will be redistributed within the budget of the Ministry of Health.
The government has allocated UAH 354.6 million to repair shelters in maternity hospitals and strengthen the protection of hospitals. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, UNN informs.
Details
According to him, UAH 294.8 million will go toward repairing shelters at 84 facilities where births are delivered. The shelters will be equipped taking into account the needs of pregnant women, women in labor and newborns, so that they have heating, lighting, water and ventilation.
It is important that women who have difficulty moving around can get there safely. Medical workers will be able to deliver babies and care for mothers and children even during air raid alerts
He specified that another UAH 59.8 million will go toward strengthening the protection of healthcare facilities under the management of the Ministry of Health that have inpatient departments.
These include operating rooms, intensive care units, neonatal intensive care units, delivery rooms and more. Gabions, metal roller shutters and impact-resistant protective film on windows will be installed for this purpose
He added that the funds would be reallocated within the Ministry of Health's budget, so this would not require additional expenditures.
Recall
The Cabinet of Ministers is preparing changes to the rules under which Ukrainian enterprises may continue operating during a yellow-level air raid alert. Businesses are promised more time to equip shelters, will be allowed to use protective structures nearby, and the requirements will be linked to the number of people at the facility.

US Formally Approves $2.1B Sale of 500 Patriot Missiles to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:30:44 UTC
06:30:44 KST

The US has approved a $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine, but President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Friday, Oct. 30, that deliveries could take years – potentially leaving Kyiv without the urgently needed weapons as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
The Trump administration’s decision authorizes the sale of Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptors, among the few weapons Ukraine has capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But the announcement comes with a major caveat: the missiles are part of a new procurement arrangement, not an immediate transfer from existing American stockpiles.
“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelensky wrote on X late Friday, responding to the US State Department’s announcement.
The president welcomed the approval as a significant step but urged Washington to find a way to provide the interceptors immediately rather than leaving Ukraine waiting for future production.
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelensky said.
He suggested that the US and European allies transfer missiles already held in their arsenals, then replenish those stockpiles using newly manufactured interceptors covered by the approved purchase.
Erdoğan’s Veiled Message to Aliyev as Kazakhstan Proposes Inviting Russia Into Turkic Bloc
Ukraine wants 500 missiles now, not years from now
Zelensky stressed that 500 interceptors could provide substantial protection for Ukraine during the coming months, particularly as Russia escalates its strikes against the country’s electricity network.
The president said Kyiv had requested a winter package providing 100 PAC-3 interceptors per month, potentially giving its air defenses a more reliable supply of missiles against Russian ballistic attacks.
He warned that Russia was striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure daily, making the delivery schedule just as important as the number of missiles approved.
In the final two weeks of October alone, Russia carried out more than 30 attacks against critical electricity infrastructure, according to Zelensky.
The president argued that Western partners already possess the missiles Kyiv needs and could provide them now without waiting for additional manufacturing capacity.
Such an arrangement would allow countries contributing to Ukraine’s defense to receive replacement interceptors later, while helping Ukraine defend its population against Russia’s continuing attacks this winter.
The proposal reflects an increasingly urgent problem for Kyiv: Western governments continue approving major military purchases, but the production and delivery timetables often extend far beyond Ukraine’s immediate battlefield requirements.
US approval still requires congressional review
The State Department’s notification authorizes a possible Foreign Military Sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles, together with spare parts and logistical support, at an estimated cost of $2.1 billion.
The proposed sale is subject to congressional review, and the State Department did not provide a delivery timetable.
“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the department said.
The package will be funded by Ukraine’s Western partners, including Canada, Germany and Norway through the US JUMPSTART program, as well as Ukrainian national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan.
No US funds will be used for the purchase, according to the State Department.
Lockheed Martin will serve as the principal contractor.
The company is working to expand PAC-3 MSE production amid growing global demand, with plans to increase annual capacity to approximately 2,000 missiles by 2030.
However, expanded manufacturing capacity does not necessarily translate into immediate deliveries, particularly as existing orders from the United States and other customers compete for production slots.
Lockheed Martin in ‘deep’ talks to expand Patriot production overseas
Lockheed Martin, the principal contractor for the newly approved missile sale, is already in advanced negotiations with allied countries to establish PAC-3 production outside the US, as global demand for the interceptors surges.
In an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post on Oct. 1, Dan Tenney, Lockheed Martin’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, revealed that the company was investing up to $9 billion through 2030 to expand production, strengthen supply chains and establish new manufacturing facilities.
“We have historic demand for the PAC-3 around the world,” Tenney said. “We have seen a tripling of the demand.”
Asked by Kyiv Post whether Ukraine could become part of the company’s overseas production plans, Tenney confirmed that negotiations with several countries were already well advanced, although he declined to identify potential partners.
“We are in pretty deep discussions on this,” he said.
The company plans to expand annual PAC-3 MSE production capacity from approximately 600 to 2,000 missiles by the end of 2030, while investing in at least 20 US facilities.
But Tenney acknowledged that increasing production would take time.
“Really, it’s just time,” he told Kyiv Post, referring to the challenge of building new factories to meet surging global demand.
Kyiv presses Washington over delayed interceptors
The latest US announcement comes after weeks of complaints about delays in receiving American-made air defense missiles already financed by European partners.
On Oct. 26, Zelensky said Kyiv had been waiting nearly a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to authorize additional supplies for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.
Zelensky also said Ukraine had received an average of only 12 Patriot interceptors per month this year, despite needing far more to defend against Russia’s ballistic missile campaign.
The situation has become particularly urgent as Russia steps up attacks on Ukraine’s electricity generation, heating and other critical infrastructure.
The weapons approval also follows a period of strained relations between Washington and Kyiv, including disagreements over US policy toward Russia, reported interruptions in intelligence sharing and restrictions affecting satellite communications used by Ukraine.
Those tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on Oct. 20.
Despite the delivery concerns, Zelensky thanked President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the State Department for authorizing the purchase.
But in his Friday statement on Telegram, he emphasized that Kyiv needed decisions that would protect civilians when the missiles were urgently required, rather than years later.

NEW DELHI: Cabinet secretary T V Somanathan has directed secretaries of ministries and departments to identify cases that can be withdrawn following decriminalisation of several offences under Jan Vishwas Act and removal of obsolete legal provisions. They have been asked to complete the exercise by the end of this month.The move is part of govt's efforts to reduce its litigation burden and avoid pursuing cases that may have lost their relevance following changes in the legal framework. Officials said some ministries, including road transport, defence and telecommunications, may have fewer pending cases, but the financial implications of these litigations are likely to be substantially higher.
In two rounds under Jan Vishwas legislations, in 2023 and 2026, several sections of different central laws have been decriminalised and rationalised by introducing compliance provisions.TOI has learnt that while chairing a meeting of all secretaries, Somanathan informed them that a dedicated "litigation management portal" will be launched in Nov to monitor the functioning of litigation management cells, review of legacy litigations and appeals, mediation and screening of cases. Ministries and departments will have to regularly update the status of cases.

Census 2027 population enumeration to span up to 50 days, with 40 questions including caste, Aadhaar and voter ID details

The census exercise in the state was put on hold after demands from various sections within the state that the National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise be conducted first.A notification issued by the Union home ministry Friday declared that a nationwide census of population shall be undertaken - except in Manipur (till further declaration); poll-bound states of Goa, UP, Punjab and Uttarakhand, where it was preponed in view of the impending assembly elections early next year; and UT of Ladakh and snow-bound, non-synchronous areas of Himachal Pradesh and UT of Jammu & Kashmir, where it has already been completed - from Jan 25 to Feb 27, 2027.
This shall be preceded by a window of self-enumeration from Jan 10-24. While the reference date for Census 2027 has already been declared as March 1, 2027, a revisional round will be conducted from March 1-5, 2027.The new fields to be captured in Phase-2 of Census include, apart from caste, spouse's name and mother and father's particulars, the respondent's nationality as declared, permanent address, place of Covid-19 vaccination, total number of bank accounts, mobile number, Aadhaar number, voter ID number, passport number and availability of driving licence.While the mobile number, Aadhaar and voter ID may be shared if available, the passport number is required only from an Indian passport holder.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

Five Great Reads: Elections, eugenics and high school reunions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:21:44 UTC
06:21:44 KST

Hello and welcome to the weekend. It’s been a big week around the world, with results of three major elections taking many people by surprise. And away from the news cycle, our journalists have been asking some big questions – about birth, death, cocaine and why on earth anyone wants to go to a high school reunion.
1. Seven lessons for the planet from Lula’s win
At a time when populist leaders and the far right appear to be on the rise, Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s extraordinary victory on Sunday offered more than a glimmer of hope. As Jonathan Watts writes: it “should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections”.
So what do we do? Many analysts have put Lula’s win down to galvanising the streets and social media, and that campaign group – in particular the WhatsApp group ‘“Lula’s Army” – gathered up about 8% of the electorate by voting day. But that’s far from the only mechanism – political messaging, challenging tech giants, standing up for the environment and sheer determination are among some of the big takeaways here.
Notable quote: “Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action.”
How long will it take to read: Just under three minutes.
Further reading: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback; In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely.
2. How cocaine conquered the UK
You may have noticed it – at the pub, with friends at dinner, or maybe even brazenly, out in the open – people shamelessly snorting cocaine. Journalist Robyn Vinter had been observing the uptick in drug use for some time and wanted to know “how did cocaine conquer Britain?” Here, she lays out some sobering findings.
From the middle class to the far right: “It is just staggering the amount and the accessibility of it,” a West Ham pub owner says. Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25, a rise of 26% since 2021. And the class A drug, once firmly associated with middle classes, has moved around the demographics, including now appearing to be a drug of choice for the far right.
Fuelling crime: The Guardian’s investigation found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019, and Home Office figures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.
How long will it take to read: Three and a quarter minutes.
Further reading: ‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuse.
3. Memento mori
Most people do their best to avoid talking about death. But as of now, science has yet to find a cure for the affliction that comes for us all. So why the social taboo? In the final instalment of the Guardian’s series about death – Memento mori – Meaghan O’Connell documents the journey her mother took after deciding she wanted to donate her body to science. O’Connell wasn’t prepared for what came next but says, “In some ways, it was absolutely perfect”.
Why would you donate your body to science? Demand for medical cadavers far outstrips supply. More than 25,000 Americans donate their bodies for research purposes after their death but, according to Tamara Ostervoss, director of Oregon Health & Science University’s (OHSU) body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice”. For medical students, the ability to practise procedures on the real thing versus a human model is like “the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane”.
The emotional cost: Not knowing exactly what happened to her mother’s body weighed on O’Connell’s mind. But she says going down the donation route also offered an element of simplicity. No being upsold by funeral directors, no grief-stricken decisions about embalming, or what goes on the gravestone. Just a quick phone call and a short physical assessment, then “voilà, off my mom went to fulfil her destiny”, O’Connell says.
Notable quote: “Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath”? – O’Connell, after learning her mother’s body was accepted as a medical cadaver.
A memorial of sorts: After fulfilling her mother’s posthumous wishes, O’Connell was invited to a “body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students from OHSU memorialise body donors and their families. Two students offered their thanks through an aerial yoga routine; others sang Taylor Swift. O’Connell was looking for closure but all this offered was amusement.
How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.
Further reading: More from the Guardian’s Memento mori series.
4. Liberal eugenics and the troubling quest for human perfection
It may be Greek for “good birth” but the term eugenics has, for the past century at least, been seen as a racist and repulsive movement. But whether you like it or not, eugenics is back in a new guise, this time by companies offering prospective parents the problematic promise of delivering the “best baby”. Jan Grue, who has a form of spinal muscular atrophy, considers the ethical implications.
What is ‘the best’? Adverts on the New York City subway offer embryo scans for every genetic disorder under the sun, eye and hair colour, and for traits ranging from strength and longevity to insomnia and male pattern baldness. Whether the promises are credible is one thing but a more important one might be: what is “valuable and worthless in a human life?”
Notable quote: “I think it is crucial to acknowledge disability as part of human variation. In treating ever more traits and qualities as things to be measured, ranked and diagnosed, we are doing the opposite – turning variation itself into something like disability.”
How long will it take to read: Eight minutes.
Further reading: The girl with a will to live: the love, hope and pain of raising Elsie – my one in 163 million daughter.
5. Why – and how – people get through their high school reunions
High school reunions are notoriously awkward; just ask Romy and Michele. While some look forward to reconnecting with friends, others see reliving the past as “a potential hellscape”. But can you go in prepared? The Guardian asked a mix of experts and reunion-goers for their advice on tackling one of life’s most fraught social situations.
Should you even go? Psychologist and author Amberley Meredith says it is normal to ruminate over reunions, and you should expect to not be the only one with existential questions about your place in life. If you are on the fence, experts say avoid making a pros and cons list – instead, just focus on the potential positives.
The dos and don’ts: Still feeling nervous before the big day? Etiquette expert Jodie Bache-Mclean says you can come prepared with a few conversation starters and a bit of background on your past classmates, but while “a little homework is helpful; a full social media investigation is not”. What about alcohol? Should you drink to calm your nerves? “A glass of wine may help, four may not!” Bache-Mclean says.
How long will it take to read: Just under four minutes.
Further reading: Why are class reunions so terrifying? And are they even good for us?

Series set for epic finale as Aussie batters must stand up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:21:19 UTC
06:21:19 KST

Although doubts have been expressed in the last few days that the Cape Town speed gun is operating with flawless accuracy, late on day four of the third Test there appeared to be some validity to its claim that Mitchell Starc had breached the 150km/h barrier.
Soon after, one couldn't help thinking of that speedometer figure — illegal in a car, faintly alarming in a sporting arena — and wince. One of Starc's typically brutish bouncers had spat up off the Newlands pitch and was rearing towards a Proteas batsman.
In the split second it took him to realise his gloves would soon be in the ball's path, and having prized his wicket all day, Ryan Rickelton got his hands out of the way on the understanding the ball would cannon into his ribs with that horrifying thud only a rare breed of cricketer accepts as his duty. And boy did it thud.
There was a time not long ago when the done thing in such situations was to grit one's teeth and pretend it hadn't happened. Think David Boon's thousand-yard stare, or Justin Langer grinning sans tooth. Not Rickelton.
He was on 92 by that point, hours into a game-turning innings, and knew that if a nasty bruise was blossoming, there was no point in pretending it wasn't so. Up came his shirt and sure enough, the mark was already ranking high on the Brian Close scale.
Rickelton showed it off to Travis Head at short leg, either for confirmation or possibly approval of its nastiness. Head seemed to offer both.
It is one of those unspoken paradoxes of Test cricket: the more two teams respect each other, the more they try to hurt each other, and vice versa. As they had the previous evening, and for the telling first two-thirds of the fourth day, Australia's bowlers had been throwing everything at Rickelton and none of it was working.
In the end, it took a run-out to remove him — moments after he brought up a century that slowly but surely ruined Australia's hopes of a quick kill. Rickelton already has a Test double century to his name.
He is a world champion. But here was the sort of high-stakes, backs-to-the-wall performance that can define a career.
As a result, from 4-140 at the start of the day, South Africa piled on 387 to convincingly rebut suggestions they'd roll over. For the third time in the series, a Test between these two proud cricket nations will go down to the fifth day.
The pressure is now all on Australia, who will need to chase down 288 runs to win and retain the status of world number one, with Kagiso Rabada, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer licking their lips at the prospect of series-winning wickets.
That Australia's task is so onerous is mostly a result of Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder's 154-run partnership for the sixth wicket, which stretched across 53 overs after Matthew Breetzke's dismissal for a spiky, counterpunching 43 in the morning.
Mulder was no second fiddle. After Rickelton departed for a brave and controlled 101 from 219 deliveries, Mulder carried on with a faltering tail, scattering fielders and clubbing sixes to reach a superb 115 of his own.
The above numbers should not give the impression the Australian attack misfired, per se, nor that Australia lacked intent. Until the last minute of the day, they fielded with great gusto to create pressure and affect run-outs to make up for the lack of help from the pitch.
All day, Nathan Lyon bowled with guile and control, jagging the ball at right angles.
It was just that for almost as long, Rickelton and Mulder defied him with the disciplined application of a solid plan: put your ego to one side, get back and across, don't hit against the spin, concede Lyon's end in the knowledge that the quicks at the other end would not get as much help from the surface.
Of the latter, Starc, in particular, gave everything of himself and more, and as late as the final half-hour of play was literally bowling himself off his feet to try and take South Africa's final wicket.
His nine dismissals for the game on a pitch that has offered him little represented a superhuman endeavour.
Where Australia can be faulted, perhaps, is for squandering the second new ball. South Africa was 5-222 when it arrived and there was no repeat of Starc's first-innings clean-up job.
In a day of thankless toil, skipper Pat Cummins broke his wicket drought but otherwise rarely threatened, only claiming his second when Mulder holed out in the final over of the day.
Again, there were industrial quantities of interpersonal drama, although nothing that crossed the line. Hyped up and a little uncoordinated between the wickets, Breetzke tangled with Lyon and spoiled for battles with every other bowler, including a prolonged one-way conversation with Starc.
Loading Twitter content
After taking the bails to run out Rickelton, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted down the pitch like a terrier in the Crufts dog show to let Mulder know it was his fault.
Of course, Labuschagne and others will need their bats to do the talking on the final day, and there is a sense that Rabada will not miss out twice in one game, even without his muse Steve Smith around to get his blood boiling.
A week ago, one might have asked: who will be Australia's Rickelton and Mulder? But all of a sudden, there are a few more convincing answers.
So, a gripping Test series — worthy in every way of its billing as a de facto world title — will now get its fitting conclusion.

Hypersonic Missile Interceptors for Patriot: USA Allocates $660 Million to Develop PAC-3 Edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:15:51 UTC
06:15:51 KST

The U.S. Army has signed an agreement with Lockheed Martin to support the development of new missiles for the Patriot systems, the PAC-3 Edge, designed to intercept hypersonic targets as part of the Future Interceptor program.
This was reported by the U.S. Army Public Affairs Office.
The total estimated cost of the project is $1.08 billion, of which $660.4 million is government funding and $423 million will be raised by the company itself as part of a co-funding arrangement.
The Future Interceptor is being developed to counter modern, ever-changing air and missile threats by increasing interception range and altitude, boosting speed, and improving maneuverability.
Under the terms of the agreement, the U.S. Army, in collaboration with Lockheed Martin, will continue to develop prototypes and conduct testing and evaluation to determine whether the system’s performance meets established operational requirements.
Further decisions regarding development and production will be made based on the actual performance of the prototypes, operational requirements, available resources, and relevant procurement procedures.
Lockheed Martin clarified in its press release that these funds will be directed specifically toward the development of the PAC-3 Edge anti-aircraft missiles.
The new interceptor was developed as a further evolution of the PAC-3 MSE anti-aircraft missiles. The missile features a new multi-pulse solid-fuel rocket motor manufactured by Northrop Grumman and an improved guidance system.
One of the key components of the PAC-3 Edge will be a new homing seeker, which is being developed at Lockheed Martin’s Strigo Product Center.
The company notes that it has invested $250 million in this center to implement new homing technologies designed to improve the accuracy and maneuverability of the interceptors.
Testing of the PAC-3 Edge is scheduled to begin in 2027. The interceptor is expected to be ready for deployment by 2031.
The new interceptor missile is intended to integrate with the U.S. Army’s existing and future integrated air and missile defense systems, including the IBCS combat command system, the M903 launcher, containerized launchers, and HIMARS Flex.

UK govt announces new ‘safe and legal’ routes for refugees in India to resettle in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:15:21 UTC
06:15:21 KST

UK announces three new refugee resettlement routes for people in India and six other countries, allowing sponsorship through charities, employers and universities.
TOI correspondent from London: In a bid to dissuade asylum-seekers from arriving in Britain on the backs of lorries or via small boats, the UK home office has announced three new “safe and legal” sponsorship routes for refugees in India and six other countries to come to the UK and claim asylum.The new routes are initially targeted at refugees who have sought protection in India, Bangladesh, Egypt, Kenya, Malaysia, Pakistan and Uganda.To be eligible, the refugees will need to be outside their country of nationality, to have been verified by the UNHCR as meeting the definition of refugee and to have registered with the UNHCR or relevant authorities in one of these seven countries before Oct 1. So, in India’s case, it could be Tibetans, Sri Lankan Tamils, Afghans, Rohingya and others from Myanmar, who could be eligible for these routes, but not Indian nationals residing in India, nor internally displaced people.
The refugee sponsorship routes, modelled on a similar programme in Canada, allow sponsors in the UK to identify refugees they wish to sponsor. The new routes are named community sponsorship, which enables UK charities to identify refugees they wish to sponsor; refugee work, which enables UK employers to sponsor and provide refugees jobs; and refugee study, which enables UK universities to sponsor refugees to study in the UK.
Once resettled, the refugees will have an immediate right to work, study and to access welfare benefits in Britain and be placed on a five-year path to permanent resettlement.Sponsors will have to finance and provide their accommodation, the aim being to reduce the amount UK’s govt spends on asylum hotels.Applications to be sponsors for the community and study route have opened and the first arrivals are expected in autumn 2027. Applications under the work route will open in spring 2027.Both Reform UK and the Conservatives vowed to shut the scheme if they come to power. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said until illegal migration is stopped, “we should not be creating new routes into the UK for asylum claimants”.

Tusk-Nawrocki battle escalates as chief judge is ousted from Poland’s top court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:12:50 UTC
06:12:50 KST

Poland’s constitutional court descended into turmoil Friday evening as judges barred from hearing cases moved to oust the institution’s nationalist-linked leadership, sparking accusations of a coup and tense protests.
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge with the court, ordered its president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy to be suspended for a month and announced she was taking charge. Święczkowski rejected her authority, accusing those involved of a “coup d’état,” while his deputy was turned away at the building’s gates.
The showdown marks an escalation in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s struggle to undo the judicial overhaul carried out by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) former government. During its eight years in power, PiS filled the Constitutional Tribunal with its appointees, including Święczkowski and his deputy, placing it at the heart of Poland’s confrontation with Brussels over the rule of law.
Advertisement
Outside the tribunal, protesters clashed with police, who said objects had been thrown at officers and three people detained after climbing over the court’s fence. Police said they had deployed to maintain security following warnings of threats to judges and staff, but had not entered the building.
PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński took part in the protest and tried to force his way into the court building. He accused Tusk of staging a “coup” against the court and turning Poland into a “police state,” and demanded presidential intervention.
President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally and rival of Tusk, interrupted his official trip to Senegal, declaring, “At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland.”
Tusk was defiant. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote on X. “After years of PiS lawlessness, it’s a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
But efforts to change the court’s makeup have met resistance. Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority. They took their oaths in parliament instead, but Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.
Advertisement
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek blamed the turmoil on Święczkowski, who he accused of turning the institution into his “private fiefdom” and preventing newly elected judges from doing their jobs.
“And now the judges have spoken,” Żurek told POLITICO.
Żurek, who also serves as Poland’s prosecutor general, said he submitted five requests to lift the immunity of Święczkowski and his deputy, backed by 50 volumes of case files. He defended Korwin-Piotrowska’s move as a decision by a legally appointed judge, insisting that the government had nothing to do with it.

Iran reports three tanker mine strikes in Hormuz; U.S. disputes claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:12:25 UTC
06:12:25 KST

Iran reports three tanker mine strikes in Hormuz; U.S. disputes claims
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Friday that three oil tankers, including a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, had struck naval mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, claims disputed by the United States and not independently verified, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to the IRGC Navy, the supertanker struck a mine while traveling along a southern shipping route that Tehran considers unauthorized. The resulting explosion reportedly set the vessel ablaze, forcing its abandonment near the entrance to the strait. Iranian authorities described it as the third tanker to suffer an explosion on Friday while attempting to transit routes not approved by Tehran.
Earlier in the day, the IRGC Navy reported that two other tankers had caught fire after allegedly striking mines in the waterway. It claimed the vessels had disabled their navigation and positioning systems and ignored repeated radio warnings before the incidents. Iranian authorities did not identify the ships, their operators or flag states, and provided no information about the crews. The reported mine strikes have not been independently confirmed.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) rejected Iranian claims that commercial vessels were striking naval mines, maintaining that American forces had cleared all internationally recognized primary transit routes through the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military said those routes remained free of sea mines and continued to be used by commercial shipping.
Oman’s Maritime Security Center reported that the Royal Navy of Oman had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel following an attack that caused a fire off the coast of Musandam Governorate. The crew members received medical care following their evacuation. Omani authorities did not identify those responsible for the attack or provide details about the vessel’s condition. It remains unclear whether the incident was connected to any of the tanker fires reported by Iran.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) also reported that a tanker traveling through the Strait of Hormuz was attacked Thursday, approximately 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. A small boat reportedly approached the vessel and attached two explosive devices to its hull, triggering blasts that caused an engine-room fire and temporarily disabled the tanker. UKMTO subsequently reported that the fire had been extinguished, all crew members were safe and the vessel had resumed its journey. No environmental damage was reported.
The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global oil and gas shipments and has faced mounting security threats since the United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran on February 28. Tehran has repeatedly warned that vessels attempting to cross the waterway without its authorization could face attacks, while Washington maintains that internationally recognized shipping routes remain navigable.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that several oil tankers had caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after reportedly striking naval mines three weeks ago.

Bhutan GLOF creates new lake downstream, raises fears of secondary hazards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:11:49 UTC
06:11:49 KST

Bengal spared Bhutan GLOF impact, water of Sankosh recedes
DEHRADUN/KOLKATA/GUWAHATI: A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) originating in Bhutan, which prompted an alert across parts of Assam and West Bengal on Friday, has led to the formation of a new temporary lake downstream, raising concerns about a possible secondary hazard.Bhutan’s National Centre for Hydrology and Meteorology (NCHM) confirmed that the outburst had led to the creation of a new artificial lake at Taktsemakhang, situated at the confluence of Sintaphu Chhu and Lungu Chhu, also known as Gangchen Tag Chhu. The newly formed body of water is being monitored for any potential secondary flood hazard, with NCHM advising residents in the Mochhu and Punatsangchhu river valleys to remain vigilant and avoid riverbanks and low-lying areas.The Oct 29 GLOF originated from Shintaphu glacial lake which, according to International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) estimates, contained 6 to 7 million cubic metres of water, equivalent to approximately 2,400-2,800 Olympic-size swimming pools, before the breach. The volume of water released remains under assessment. India’s Central Water Commission (CWC) subsequently issued a special flood advisory for West Bengal and Assam, warning that water levels in Alipurduar and Dhubri districts could rise sharply as floodwaters moved downstream through the Sankosh river system.
West Bengal had issued a high alert across north Bengal but the GLOF has had little or no impact in the state. On Friday morning, as water from the Bhutan hills came downstream, the Sankosh river rose 1.5 metres from its normal level but began receding soon. By Friday afternoon it appeared the crisis was over and people who had taken refuge in flood centres returned to their homes. No damage was reported. The Alipurduar district administration had opened 18 flood shelters in Kumargramduar block on Thursday night and around 10,000 people living along the banks of the Sankosh in Kumargram tea estate, Kumargram forest village, Pakriguri and Bholka had taken refuge in these shelters along with a couple of thousand from Assam.Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said the state was closely monitoring the possible impact of the glacial lake outburst across all vulnerable revenue circles of Dhubri and Kokrajhar districts. “Our teams … are ready to respond if needed. Residents are requested to stay alert, follow official updates and cooperate with officials,” he said.According to Bhutan’s national daily “Kuensel”, the GLOF sent floodwaters down the Mochhu river, damaging roads, bridges and public infrastructure in Gasa and Punakha. No casualties have been reported. Floodwaters washed away facilities at Gasa Tshachu, damaged sections of the Punakha-Gasa Secondary National Highway and the Gasa-Laya road, and swept away a Bailey bridge in Punakha built in 2022 with Indian support.Ashim Sattar, a glacial hazard expert at IIT Bhubaneswar, told TOI that the formation of temporary lakes downstream is a known risk during such disasters. “During GLOFs, powerful floodwaters erode river valleys and carry large amounts of debris, which can temporarily block river channels and form new lakes. Such lakes generally drain naturally, but they can also become secondary flood hazards if not regularly monitored,” Sattar said.He explained that Shintaphu was a medium-sized glacial lake located close to the Lunana glacial lake complex, a cluster of four lakes, including Thorthormi, considered one of Bhutan’s most hazardous.According to NCHM, the flood crossed Taktsemakhang around 8.27 pm on Thursday. Warning sirens along Mochhu and downstream Punatsangchhu were activated as monitoring stations recorded a sharp rise in river levels. At Yebesa, the water level peaked at 6.7 m at 11 pm before receding to a normal level of 2.84 m around 12.30 am on Friday, a drop of 3.86 m within 90 minutes.Sattar noted that timely activation of the regional early-warning network prevented loss of life.
The incident highlights the growing threat of cascading disasters in the Himalayas, where an initial glacial breach can trigger secondary hazards downstream through valley erosion, sediment deposition and temporary river blockages.Previous assessments by ICIMOD and UNDP identified 47 major potentially dangerous glacial lakes (PDGLs) across the transboundary Koshi, Gandaki and Karnali river basins. Current estimates show that 388 GLOFs have been documented across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, including Karakoram and the central and eastern Himalayas.In 2015, a GLOF in the headwaters of the Mo Chuu river, where Sintaphu lake is located, prompted Bhutanese authorities to work with the SERVIR-Himalaya initiative to assess glacial lake risks in the catchment, according to experts at ICIMOD.

Russia’s diplomatic victories
Four years of unprecedented sanctions and an active conflict didn’t deter four dozen African nations from sending delegations to Moscow for the third Russia-Africa Summit this week. Forty-eight out of Africa’s 54 countries were represented at the summit, 21 of them by their heads of state.
More than 140 bilateral and multilateral agreements were signed, including a Russia-Africa Action Plan for 2027-2029, and a joint declaration opposing unilateral sanctions and the unlawful seizure of civilian shipping, pledging deeper counter-terrorism cooperation, and supporting increased African representation on the UN Security Council. RT covered the summit minute-by minute, and broke down Putin’s plan to help bring about the “second awakening” of Africa.
Before he welcomed the African delegations to Moscow, Putin held a rare phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb – a figure repeatedly floated as a potential EU envoy to Russia – and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. Putin later said that Russia welcomes “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations,” and while the call brought the Russia/Ukraine conflict no closer to an end, Russian analyst Sergey Strokan noted that it should serve as a warning to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky that “metal fatigue is setting in across Europe’s political machinery – and that time is running out for the regime in Kiev.”
With the EU nowhere to be seen, and Stubb and Store incurring the wrath of their fellow European leaders for even daring to speak to Putin, the tone in the US could not be more different. There, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov touched down in Atlanta for a meeting of G20 foreign ministers on Friday. Sanctions on Russian diesel exports have been lifted, trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev, and Washington are slated for next month, and Putin has been invited to the G20 leaders’ meeting in Florida in December. However, the most tangible result of Russian-American diplomacy came 5,000 miles away from Washington, in the besieged town of Alyoshki.
The Alyoshki breakthrough
Moscow and Kiev agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region last Friday, with both sides agreeing to suspend all military operations to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for civilian evacuations.
The Kremlin confirmed this week that the ceasefire was coordinated by US First Lady Melania Trump, who said she was moved by the plight of Alyoshki’s “elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.”

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva narrowly defeated right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday, in the first of three major elections this week. After a first-round loss to Bolsonaro, whose father was jailed last year Brazil’s Lula-aligned Supreme Federal Court, Lula won the runoff election by a margin of 51.79% to 48.21%, securing a fourth term in office.
The drama did not end when the votes were counted. Bolsonaro was ordered by the court to surrender his passports the following day, but he instead fled Brazil to the US, with the help of Argentina’s right-wing government. After landing in Florida, Bolsonaro accused Lula of fraud, declared himself “the leader of Brazil,” and pledged to “lead the opposition” from abroad.
US President Donald Trump is a close ally of Bolsonaro, and it remains unclear whether Washington will turn up the diplomatic pressure on Lula in the wake of the election.
Hours after Lula claimed victory in Brazil, former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic lost his bid to extend his party’s decade in power. Serbia’s Student List defeated Vucic’s SNS party by 53.03% to 38.97%, and despite accusing the students of doing the “dirty work” of “various European countries and the American deep state,” Vucic conceded and congratulated his opponents.
Although the Student List entered politics as an outgrowth of youth-led protests, its base is broader than similar pro-Western movements in the region. However, the Student List has not yet chosen a candidate for prime minister, and Vucic has claimed that the party will walk back these promises in the coming months.

Spain’s train tragedy
The collision of two high-speed trains near the Spanish city of Toledo on Wednesday was the country’s deadliest railway disaster in more than a decade. At least 69 people were killed and 179 injured when a high-speed Renfe AVE train struck a stationary Iryo train on the Madrid–Seville line.
The crash happened at a time of political crisis in Spain, after weeks of anti-government protests over housing and inflation. Fires were set outside the Spanish Transport Ministry in Madrid on Wednesday night, at a protest organized by the far-right Falange and Revuelta groups. “How many more people have to die before we throw these murderers and traitors out of our institutions?” Falange spokesman Federico Campanero said in a speech.
