The FBI has arrested a former North Carolina government contractor for allegedly leaking classified national defense information on social media.
James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, was taken into custody after charges that he shared top-secret safety data online, unlawfully stored national defense materials at his residence and stole night-vision equipment from the US army special operations command.
He faces federal counts of unauthorized transmission of national defense information, unlawful retention of defense records and theft of government property, prosecutors said.
According to a press release from the justice department, Ashbacher “photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site.”
The statement further alleges that, in a private direct message, Ashbacher had urged a social media user to take down several uploaded materials, explaining that he was “trying to do some damage control”.
Federal agents conducting a subsequent search of his home discovered a classified military award nomination containing sensitive national defense information – as well as a specialized night-vision goggle system that had previously been reported missing from an army special operations command unit.
Ashbacher worked for a contractor providing security and emergency management services to the US army at North Carolina’s Fort Bragg, where he held a top secret clearance with sensitive compartmented information (SCI) access.
His arrest came nearly two years after a federal judge sentenced a Massachusetts air national guard member to 15 years in prison in connection with his pleading guilty to leaking highly classified military documents about Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Jack Teixeira admitted that he illegally collected those secrets and shared them with other users on the social media platform Discord.
Ashbacher’s case is being investigated by the FBI Charlotte’s field office in coordination with the US Department of the Army’s criminal investigation division.

Iran targeted USS Abraham Lincoln with cruise missile, Navy Cmdr. says
TEHRAN - Iran's Navy targeted the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier with a strategic cruise missile during the 40-day Ramadan War, the Iranian Navy's deputy coordinator has said, noting that the force carried out more than 20 operations against U.S. warships and around 300 operations against American interests in various locations.
Rear Admiral Jalil Moghadam said Iranian forces identified the carrier during the first two days of the conflict, using visual observation and available surveillance systems to track its position.
Speaking to the IRNA news agency, Moghadam said the Navy launched the missile after locating the carrier. He added that the vessel halted flight operations for three days following the strike before moving farther away from Iran's coastline.
According to the official, Iranian naval forces concluded that the carrier had been hit after examining a series of developments following the operation.
Moghadam said aircraft operating from the carrier attacked Iran's second and third naval regions on the third day of the war. He noted that the carrier conducted no launches or flights for three days after Iran's operation.
He added that, on the day of the attack or that night, the carrier requested assistance from a coastal country and reported having injured personnel.
"Later, it was announced that the carrier had caught fire," Moghadam said, adding that images released from the site of the damage did not, in his assessment, correspond to an ordinary fire.
He said the images showed ruptures in the hull and deformation of the structure, which he interpreted as evidence of a missile strike.
 
Iran Navy rejects claims of destruction
Moghadam also rejected U.S. claims that Iran's naval forces had been destroyed, arguing that developments during and after the war demonstrated that the force remained operational.
He said U.S. and Israeli forces had refrained from approaching Iran's coastline, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, and questioned why they had remained hundreds of kilometers away if Iran's naval capabilities had been eliminated.
The official mentioned that Iranian naval forces had continued to inflict damage on U.S. and Israeli interests during the 40-day conflict and after the ceasefire.
He added that the Navy had reviewed its military doctrine following the conflict, incorporating lessons from the war and reassessing its equipment and operational priorities.
Moghadam said that, in the event of another war, Iran's naval operations would extend beyond the scope of the previous conflict, citing improvements in the force's equipment and capabilities.
He also described the Strait of Hormuz as a strategic advantage for Iran, arguing that regional maritime security would not return to its desired state while U.S. forces remained in the region.
The Iranian Navy official's remarks come amid continued tensions between Tehran and Washington over regional security and the strategic waterway, through which a significant share of global oil shipments passes.

The leadership of Poland’s top court said that the court’s website had been "unlawfully taken over."
"Bogdan Swieczkowski remains president of the Constitutional Tribunal, and Bartlomiej Sochanski remains vice president," the tribunal said on its official X account.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government has been trying for weeks to force out the court's judges, who were appointed by the previous PiS government that ruled from 2015 to 2023.
The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over European Union law, and the EU accused Poland's highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time.
Tusk vowed to end the dispute with Brussels after winning the 2023 election. 
But the country's president, a right-wing independent, has blocked his nominations to the court.
Former PiS prime minister Jaroslaw Kaczynski addressed the demonstration and called for Nawrocki to act.
The president said he had called off an official trip to Senegal mid-flight and ordered it back to Warsaw.
He was to go to the court from the airport, media reports said.

Legal immunity

"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," he said.
"After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way."
The constitutional court's official website was not accessible on Friday evening.

Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. State Department has approved the possible sale of 500 PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine. The $2.1 billion deal will be financed by partners and allies.
The U.S. Department of State has approved a decision authorizing the possible sale to Ukraine of 500 missiles for Patriot air defense systems worth $2.1 billion. This is stated on the website of the U.S. Department of State, reports UNN.
Details
The U.S. Department of State has approved a decision authorizing a possible foreign military sale to the Government of Ukraine for the procurement of Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement missiles and related equipment. The total estimated cost is $2.1 billion, fully funded by partners and allies
According to the Department of State, the Government of Ukraine requested the purchase of 500 PAC-3 missiles. The delivery will also include the following non-major defense equipment: classified and unclassified spare parts for PAC-3 MSE, as well as other related logistics and software support elements.
This proposed sale will support U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives by improving the security of a partner country that is a driving force for political and economic stability in Europe. Ukraine will pay for this procurement with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway under the JUMPSTART program, as well as national funds financed through a European Union loan to support Ukraine. No U.S. funds are involved in this transaction. The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s ability to counter current and future threats by enhancing its integrated air and missile defense capabilities. This sale will support existing Patriot system operations against current air threats. Ukraine will have no difficulty integrating these goods and services into its armed forces

Five children among seven dead in eastern Syria floods
Seven people, including five children, have died and seven others were injured after torrential rains triggered flash floods in eastern Syria, authorities said on Friday.
Four people remain missing and rescue teams are continuing to search flooded areas, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said in a statement on X.
The five children drowned in pools of water formed by the floods, while another person died in a traffic accident, Saleh said, without providing details of the seventh death.
Flooding has hit the eastern provinces of Raqqa, Deir Ezzor and Hasakah, as well as parts of Aleppo, damaging infrastructure, cutting off roads and forcing families to leave their homes.
Syria's civil defence teams have carried out more than 550 emergency operations since the storms began, rescuing 60 people trapped by floodwater and responding to more than 900 distress calls, Saleh said.
Emergency crews evacuated more than 350 students from two schools and helped 375 families leave camps in Raqqa province. Teams also responded to flooding at camps in rural Aleppo and Idlib, and pumped water from around 250 homes and public buildings.
In Deir Ezzor, the floods damaged roads and telecommunications infrastructure, disrupting transport and communications, state news agency SANA reported. Heavy rainfall also caused seven culverts to collapse, cutting off access to several areas.
Authorities suspended classes in Raqqa, Hasakah and Deir Ezzour on Thursday, while forecasters warned unsettled weather could continue into Saturday.

Iran reports destruction of US drone and three tanker incidents in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:49:19 UTC
04:49:19 KST

Iran reports destruction of US drone and three tanker incidents in Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN – Iran’s armed forces have reported the destruction of two different American unmanned platforms and incidents involving three oil tankers attempting to navigate unauthorized routes through the Strait of Hormuz, as the country maintains restrictions on maritime traffic through the strategic waterway.
In separate announcements on Thursday and Friday, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) Navy and the Iranian Army Navy reported the interception of an American MQ-1 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), the destruction of an enemy unmanned surface vessel (USV), and incidents involving three oil tankers accused of disregarding Iranian navigation regulations and safety warnings.
The announcements underscore Iran’s continued emphasis on enforcing its maritime security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz and preventing unauthorized movements through designated shipping routes.
Three oil tankers involved in incidents
In a statement issued on Friday, the IRGC Navy announced that two oil tankers attempting to pass through unauthorized routes in the eastern and western sections of the Strait of Hormuz had encountered incidents and were stopped in the southern waters of the strategic waterway.
According to the statement, both vessels had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and attempted to leave the strait through unauthorized routes with the support of the US military.
The IRGC Navy said the tankers had ignored repeated radio warnings, entered areas designated as unsafe, and subsequently encountered incidents before being halted.
The force attributed the incidents and fires aboard the vessels to 'hostile actions by the US military,' as well as the tankers’ disregard for Iranian regulations governing navigation through the strait.
In a separate announcement, the IRGC Navy reported that a supertanker had exploded after striking a naval mine while attempting to navigate an unauthorized route through the waterway.
The vessel, which was carrying more than two million barrels of oil, was left burning near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, according to the statement.
The IRGC Navy described the supertanker as the third oil tanker to have suffered an explosion and caught fire on Friday after attempting to use unauthorized routes.
The announcements did not identify the vessels or disclose their flags, ownership, or the precise circumstances of the incident.
Iranian Navy destroys unmanned surface vessel
Separately, the Iranian Army Navy announced that its forces had destroyed an enemy unmanned surface vessel operating in the eastern Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Friday.
According to the Navy's public relations office, the remotely operated vessel was struck and destroyed while moving and conducting operations within the area monitored by Iranian naval forces.
The Navy also reported that two enemy oil tankers had sustained damage and caught fire after striking naval mines while navigating restricted and unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz with their tracking systems switched off.
It said the vessels had disregarded previously issued warnings and maritime regulations, adding that their owners would bear full responsibility for the consequences of unauthorized navigation and failure to observe safety instructions.
The Navy warned that any hostile movement, infiltration or provocative action in areas monitored by Iran's armed forces would be met with a firm and proportionate response.
IRGC downs American MQ-1 drone
In a separate development announced on Thursday, the IRGC reported that its Aerospace Division had intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-1 unmanned aerial vehicle over the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
According to a statement published on the IRGC's official website, the drone was brought down by an advanced air defense system operating within Iran's integrated air defense network.
 
The IRGC described the aircraft as the 14th advanced MQ-1 drone intercepted and destroyed.
The aerial drone incident is distinct from the Iranian Army Navy's announcement concerning the destruction of an unmanned surface vessel. The two statements refer to different platforms and separate military operations.
Iran emphasizes control over maritime traffic
Iran has repeatedly warned commercial vessels against using navigation routes that have not been authorized by its maritime authorities, emphasizing that compliance with designated corridors and safety instructions is essential to preventing incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.
Since the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran began on February 28, 2026, Tehran has introduced new arrangements governing maritime traffic through the strait, citing security considerations and the need to protect its territorial waters and national interests.
The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Indian Ocean, is one of the world's most strategically important maritime passages. A substantial share of internationally traded crude oil and petroleum products passes through this waterway, making maritime security and uninterrupted commercial navigation there a matter of international economic importance.
Iran maintains that safe passage through the strait requires vessels to observe the regulations established by the coastal authorities and refrain from unauthorized movements, particularly amid heightened regional tensions.
The latest announcements by the IRGC Navy and the Iranian Army Navy reinforce Tehran's warning that vessels operating in the area must comply with its maritime security instructions and that unauthorized navigation in designated restricted zones carries serious risks.

U.S. clears sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:48:14 UTC
04:48:14 KST

- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.1 billion sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors to Ukraine on Oct. 30.
- Canada, Germany and Norway are funding part of the sale through JUMPSTART, with the rest financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors to Ukraine for its Patriot air defense systems, a package worth an estimated $2.1 billion that will be paid for entirely by Ukraine’s allies and partners. The department notified Congress of the decision on Oct. 30.
Canada, Germany and Norway are contributing donations through JUMPSTART, a U.S. Foreign Military Sales mechanism for donor-funded Ukraine purchases, and Ukraine will cover the rest with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan. No U.S. funds are involved. Besides the missiles, the package includes classified and unclassified PAC-3 MSE spare parts and logistics and program support. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor.
The notification is not a contract. It opens a congressional review period, after which Ukraine and the U.S. government can sign a letter of offer and acceptance and the U.S. Army can place the order with Lockheed Martin. The State Department gave no delivery schedule, and it did not say how the cost will be split among the three donors and the EU-financed share. Divided evenly, the total comes to about $4.2 million per missile, but that figure also covers spares and support.
The State Department said the missiles will help Ukraine sustain its existing Patriot operations against ongoing aerial threats, and that Ukraine will have no difficulty absorbing them into its armed forces. The sale will not require any additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine.
The approval comes days after Ukrainian officials publicly pressed Washington on interceptor supplies. On Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS systems, including transfers from allied stocks that require U.S. approval. A day later, he told journalists that Ukraine had received an average of 12 Patriot interceptors a month from the United States in 2026, while Russia launches about 150 ballistic missiles a month that Ukraine needs to intercept.
PAC-3 MSE is the Patriot system’s main weapon against ballistic missiles. Unlike the older PAC-2 interceptors, which detonate a blast-fragmentation warhead near the target, the PAC-3 family destroys targets by direct impact, a method known as hit-to-kill. The Missile Segment Enhancement version adds a larger two-pulse solid rocket motor, with the second pulse firing late in the flight to extend range and altitude against maneuvering threats. That makes it the interceptor Ukraine relies on against Russian Iskander ballistic missiles and Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched missiles. Ukrainian officials have described PAC-3 as their only effective defense against Russian ballistic missiles.
Ukraine received its first Patriot battery in April 2023, and in May of that year Ukrainian crews shot down a Kinzhal over Kyiv, the first publicly confirmed combat interception of the missile. Ukraine has since received further batteries from the United States, Germany, the Netherlands and Romania, and in July 2025 Germany and Norway agreed to pay for three more systems to be bought from the U.S. manufacturer. Interceptor supply has been a tighter constraint than launchers. In February 2026, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius offered five PAC-3 rounds from German stocks if other allies together supplied 30 more, and in July, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said it was using about $1 billion from the EU loan to buy roughly 100 Patriot missiles.
The financing reflects how Ukraine’s air defense is now paid for. The U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency describes JUMPSTART as a channel that lets allies and partners finance Ukraine’s Foreign Military Sales cases with their own donations. Norway reported routing about NOK 10 billion through the mechanism in 2025, much of it for F-16 support. In September 2026, Canada said it would put about C$350 million toward air defense interceptors for Ukraine through JUMPSTART. Separately, NATO allies buy U.S. weapons for Ukraine through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL.
EU governments agreed in early 2026 on a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, with €60 billion set aside for defense, and the first disbursements went out in June 2026. The loan gives priority to weapons built in Ukraine, the EU and the European Economic Area, but allows purchases elsewhere when no European alternative exists. Patriot interceptors are one case where none does.
Production is the main limit on how fast the missiles can arrive. Lockheed Martin delivered 620 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in 2025, a company record. In January 2026, the company and the U.S. Department of War signed a seven-year framework agreement to raise annual output from about 600 to roughly 2,000. In April, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a $4.76 billion PAC-3 MSE contract, most of it funded through Foreign Military Sales customers. Demand has also climbed since the United States drew on its own Patriot inventory during this year’s conflict with Iran.
At 2025 production rates, the 500 missiles approved for Ukraine equal about 10 months of Lockheed’s output. Where Ukraine’s order falls in the production queue, and when the first missiles from this sale will reach Patriot batteries in Ukraine, has not been disclosed.

The EU and Canada announced an alliance on Friday, Oct. 30, aimed at cementing their own relations in the face of President Donald Trump’s moves to tear up US ties with its old partners.
Canada agreed to contribute to a €90 billion ($103 billion) support loan for Ukraine and work closer with Brussels on anything from critical minerals to artificial intelligence, after a two-day summit in Montreal.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The world’s becoming more dangerous and divided. Our societies are being shaken by new storms,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told a press conference, mentioning eroding democratic norms and “the weaponization of trade.”
“Together, Canada and the European Union are anchoring the ground. Anchoring our ground to uphold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can all thrive,” he said after talks with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.
Already sharing a free trade agreement, Canada and the EU have sought to move closer together since Trump’s shock return to power.
Both Canada and the EU have been hit with US tariffs and territorial threats.
In Montreal, they sketched out a two-tier partnership that von der Leyen, the European Commission president, stressed was “not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
But the plan was partially overshadowed by an intra-EU squabble over what the new relationship should be called, which led to some mixed messaging at the summit.
Pope Leo XIV Votes in US Elections: First Time for a Pontiff
Unable to fully join the bloc, Canada would become its first “associate member,” von der Leyen, said doubling down on a term opposed by Germany and a handful of other EU states.
The group had successfully pushed to have the label dropped from a joint summit statement, arguing it doesn’t exist in EU treaties and needed defining.
Von der Leyen was, however, backed by Carney who also used the title as he addressed journalists after the talks, adding its “substance” would be determined in the coming months.
In Brussels’ view, the term defines the unique partnership the EU has with Canada and entails aligning policies, such as on climate and artificial intelligence, Canada joining some EU programs, and creating a stable governance framework.
Broader alliance
As part of this Canada will have a more stable presence at the EU table.
Carney will take part in an EU leaders summit in June and European commissioners and Canadian ministers would hold a separate meeting in the spring, Costa, the European Council president, said.
More broadly, Canada and the EU would form the “nucleus” of a larger “alliance for the future” open to other partners, von der Leyen said.
This “will focus on increasing our collective sovereignty and resilience in areas such as AI, energy, critical minerals, quantum, and beyond,” Carney said.
A senior EU official explained a key part of it would be coordinating economic security measures, like tariffs, so that they do not inadvertently harm members of the group.
To kick off work, Brussels and Ottawa signed a digital trade deal and a separate pact allowing the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
Canada is rich in rare earths and critical minerals Europe currently sources mostly from China but needs massive infrastructure investment to jump-start its mining industry.
The allies agreed to deepen cooperation on satellite connectivity and navigation and artificial intelligence – a field where they are playing catch-up with the US and China.
They also launched work towards Canada’s participation in EU initiatives like the Erasmus program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad, and the Galileo satellite program – an alternative to the American Global Positioning System (GPS).
Europe opened its supercomputing infrastructure to Canadian researchers, industry and start-ups.
Finally, Carney said Canada will join the EU’s 90-billion-euro support loan for Ukraine with an initial participation of 500 million euros, in what von der Leyen described as “a powerful message” of support to Kyiv.
Brussels has been looking for help to plug gaps in Kyiv’s finances, as Russia’s war of invasion grinds on.

Border guards deny that "call from Kyiv" enabled Kravchenko to leave Ukraine

Unknown Publisher

Border guards deny that "call from Kyiv" enabled Kravchenko to leave Ukraine
Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, has denied claims that former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko was allowed to cross the border following a "call from Kyiv".
Source: Demchenko in comments to Ukrinform
Details: According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, Kravchenko, who was prosecutor general at the time, was initially refused permission to enter Poland through the Shehyni checkpoint because of a flag in the database entered by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO). However, he was later allowed through following a call from Kyiv.
Quote: "Ruslan Kravchenko, who was prosecutor general at the time, crossed the border on the night of 13-14 September 2026. He travelled through the Shehyni checkpoint in Lviv Oblast. During border control procedures, Kravchenko presented documents confirming he was on an official business trip, which entitled him to leave Ukraine."
Details: Demchenko said that during the processing of his documents, an instruction issued by an authorised state body, marked index I (notification), was triggered in the database. According to the spokesperson, this meant that the relevant state authorities had to be informed of the person's departure.
"Under the established procedure, the body that had issued the instruction was immediately notified by telephone that this person had left Ukraine. I would also like to point out that this instruction did not prohibit the person from leaving the country; it merely required the initiating body to be informed. The body that issued the instruction did not raise any objections to Kravchenko's departure. No other instructions restricting this person's departure from Ukraine were issued to the State Border Guard Service by the authorised state bodies," Demchenko explained.
He also said that the authorised state bodies clearly understand the procedures followed by border guards when they receive different types of instructions from the State Border Guard Service. These include travel bans, wanted-person notices and requests for additional checks to establish whether there are legal grounds for someone to cross the state border.
"In this case, there was no ban, and the border guards acted accordingly. When restrictions imposed by authorised bodies are entered into the system, the person is not allowed to leave the country," Demchenko stressed.
Background:
- Kravchenko left Ukraine on the night of 13-14 September. Under an order he had signed himself, he was due to spend five days in Paris, allegedly attending hearings on Ukrainian children under the auspices of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. However, his name did not appear on the list of participants in the discussion.
- His official business trip ended on 18 September. According to Mariana Haivovska, spokesperson for the Prosecutor General's Office, Kravchenko had not returned to work by 21 September.

‘Nobody Wants This’ season 3 is charming enough to forget the Adam Brody controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:43:26 UTC
04:43:26 KST

The new season of the popular Netflix series, Nobody Wants This, about a character the Internet has dubbed the Hot Rabbi and his romance with a gentile woman, just started streaming, and the timing of its release brings to mind that old joke, “Other than that, Mrs. Lincoln, how did you enjoy the play?”
That’s because a recent political controversy involving the show’s cast threatened to obscure everything enjoyable about it. Up until now, the series has been a truly charming and funny look at upscale Jewish life in Los Angeles, with a well-rounded portrait of two quirky families, one Jewish and one, to quote an Aaron Sorkin line, “incredibly not.”
It’s also been a way to spend time with American Jewish characters that the series creator, Erin Foster, who based the series on her own conversion and her life, designed as a kind of respite from rising antisemitism and controversies over support for Israel.
Engaging third season
It functioned well as witty (and sometimes silly) escapism, with an overarching affection for Jewish tradition. But obviously it’s hard to keep reality at bay forever.
So when Adam Brody, who plays Noah, the rabbi on the series, recently made a comment accusing Israel of genocide in words that were inane and annoying even by the very low bar of political statements by Hollywood actors, it seemed that it might no longer be possible to enjoy it.
The first season’s rabbi advisor, Steve Leder, called Brody’s comments “flippant” and “disgusting,” and Tovah Feldshuh, who plays Noah’s mother, fired back as well, calling the genocide accusation “wild” and “right out of Hitler’s playbook.”
It was with trepidation that some fans, myself included, tuned in to the new season. But the good news is that Foster, her cast, and crew have made season three engaging enough that you can forget the controversy while watching it.
I still had fun spending time with these very attractive, sweet characters, and enjoyed the eye candy and real estate porn that goes along with their lifestyles.
The new season is increasingly predictable, but that doesn’t really matter, since sitcoms are almost always predictable – and that is part of what is soothing about them.
Joanne (Kristin Bell) is busy taking a Judaism class at the temple where Noah used to be the rabbi to prepare for her conversion, and her blunt teacher is played by Sarah Silverman, a welcome addition to the cast. Noah is trying to find a way to get his old job back, and the two are living together for the first time, which provides The Odd Couple-fodder.
But it’s the supporting characters who are especially appealing this season, with a lot of will-they/won’t-they drama involving Joanne’s sister, Morgan (Justine Lupe), and Noah’s brother, Sasha (Timothy Simons). Sasha’s estranged wife, Esther (Jackie Tohn, GLOW), is also around, and it’s still nice to see a character named Esther who isn’t 90 or haredi (ultra-Orthodox).
There is also an unexpectedly touching backstory about how Joanne and Morgan started their sex/lifestyle podcast. Fans will binge this season quickly and will eagerly await the fourth season, hoping that there will be no more idiotic statements by anyone involved to cloud its arrival.
Israel will soon be able to See Everything
A new documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of a blood-testing start-up currently serving a prison term for fraud, called You Can See Everything, has achieved a very difficult feat: it has gotten a lot of people excited about going to the movies.
There is even a lot of buzz that it may be the first documentary to win a Best Picture Oscar. The movie, by Nathan Fielder, creator of the HBO docu-comedy show The Rehearsal, is set to open in Israel at the end of November. But while you’re waiting, there is some Holmes-related content currently available here.
Disney+ offers The Dropout, a miniseries about Holmes and the investigation by Wall Street Journal reporter John Carreyrou (Ebon Moss-Bachrach, The Bear) that brought her down. It’s well-made and entertaining, although Amanda Seyfried and Naveen Andrews, who play Holmes and her former romantic and professional partner, Sunny Balwani, who is also behind bars, are a little too movie-star good-looking to be completely convincing in their roles.
I think the fascination with Holmes is not so much that she is a criminal but that she is creepy. The strange, Steve Jobs-adjacent persona she created for herself, with her fixed stare, black turtlenecks, and bizarrely deep voice, seduced investors, including Rupert Murdoch, former US secretary of state George Schultz, and much of the media into backing her long after the initial fraud allegations came to light.
Seyfried is much softer, and as television usually does, the series wants us to feel for the heroine, portraying her as someone galvanized into choosing her path of fakery and self-promotion because her father was laid off from his job.
But it details how she tried to stonewall Carreyrou and investigators, and how she ruthlessly threatened employees who raised questions about the technology. It ends with her finding romance with her new partner, which is the starting point for You Can See Everything.
If a miniseries seems like too much of a commitment, a movie by master documentary director Alex Gibney, called The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, is available on HBO Max.
The Walk-In, which is currently available on Hot VOD and Next TV, is an excellent British series that is very difficult to watch because it deals with neo-Nazis and far-right extremist groups in the UK about 10 years ago.
There is some violence shown, of course, but what makes it a tough watch is how sad and twisted these racists and antisemites are, and how they lure lonely and confused young men into joining their ranks.
The main character is a real person, Matthew Collins (Stephen Graham, the father on Adolescence), a journalist and researcher who was once a neo-Nazi himself and who gradually awakened to the fact that this was an evil cause. He has since devoted himself to spreading the word about the virulence of this movement, meaning he and his family are constantly threatened and have had to move over and over again.
In a parallel story, a quiet, underemployed young man, Robbie (Andrew Ellis), who lost his father to cancer, finds himself drawn to the zeal and certainty of members of the National Action group, and starts spouting conspiracy theories about how Jews have concealed the cure for cancer so they can make money off useless treatments.
While Collins works tirelessly to combat these groups, it seems that there will never be an end to the cycle of hateful antisemites manipulating lost young men like Robbie into joining them.

Mystery at the Jerusalem YMCA pool drives Yehoram Gaon’s first film in nearly a decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:43:24 UTC
04:43:24 KST

Amichai Greenberg’s Love, Statistically Speaking, which opened in theaters around Israel on Thursday, features iconic singer and actor Yehoram Gaon as a recently widowed actuary, obsessed with life expectancy statistics, whose outlook is transformed when he teams up with his granddaughter, an aspiring content creator played by rising star Meshi Kleinstein, to solve a mystery.
Watching these two bring out the best in each other, despite some initial misunderstandings as they bridge the generation gap, is at the heart of this enjoyable comedy, which is set in and around the Jerusalem YMCA, where the Gaon character’s late wife was an enthusiastic swimmer.
The plot revolves around how Reuven (Gaon) and Eden (Kleinstein) try to find out who stole a huge amount of cash from a locker at the pool that Reuven’s wife wanted to leave to Eden – and don’t ask why Reuven brought the money there in the first place. It’s also driven by Reuven’s terror that he is about to die soon, because according to the statistics that have ruled his thinking for decades, he has just seven months to live after losing his wife.
For Greenberg, whose previous feature, The Testament, dealt with a very different kind of investigation – it was about a son who learns a secret about his mother’s Holocaust survival story – making audiences laugh and also touching their hearts was a challenge he wanted to take on.
“I understood that it’s a real challenge to make a comedy like this here in Israel. There is this barrier: either you do the artistic film, or you do broad comedy, and it doesn’t mix. But I wanted to create something that could carry a message but would still be light. For me, as a creator, it was a challenge to explore those territories… I decided, Let’s not aim here for festivals. Let’s aim for the audience. Let’s do something that could speak to people.”
Greenberg, the rare Israeli director who lives in Jerusalem and comes from a Modern Orthodox background, said he came up with the story a few years after the deaths of his parents, while at the same time, he was the father to a 12-year-old.
“The film explores this process of deciphering life, of distinguishing what truly matters from what does not… When the end of the ‘movie’ of your life comes into sharp focus, life takes on a new perspective, and what we see as significant shifts dramatically. It’s a lot like in a swimming pool: we discover that things that look beautiful and serene above the surface are, in fact, making absurd, frantic movements beneath it.”
This idea is illustrated beautifully by footage of a synchronized swim team in a pool that is shown under the opening credits.
Greenberg, who swims every day, was intrigued by the sense of community that develops among swimmers, all of which is heightened by the sometimes absurd situation of seeing each other nearly naked on a daily basis.
The idea of making Reuven an actuary came to the director by chance. When he was stuck in traffic once, Greenberg heard an actuary speaking on the radio and was struck by the implications of a profession that uses numbers to predict what might happen to people.
“It’s like a modern prophet, but just with numbers,” he said. “I wanted two people who are afraid of the unknowns of life. She is at the beginning of her story; he is nearing the end. Each conceals that fear differently, and their defenses initially keep them apart.”
Greenberg said he could identify with their conflict because his father was an engineer, while he went to film school, the Ma’aleh School of Film and Television in Jerusalem, and he often found himself questioning his own choice.
“It’s this thing of me asking myself, am I really doing something?” he said.
One of his day jobs while he established himself in the movie business was as a computer programmer, which he discovered was more creative and satisfying than he would have imagined before he tried it. As he created Reuven, he looked back on this work to give him an insight into the character.
The story began to come into focus more sharply when he cast Gaon in the lead. He said he likes to send potential collaborators his script and hear their ideas before completely formulating his own. When casting director Amira Buzaglo suggested Gaon for the lead, the director was taken aback.
“I was completely floored,” he said. “I thought it would be brilliant.”
Greenberg was surprised and grateful when Gaon signed on to appear in the film, his first in almost a decade. He took a similar approach to the other roles, and the cast includes Chelli Goldenberg, originally a model and the glamor girl of 1970s Israeli cinema, one-time children’s TV star Michal Yannai, and Shmuel Levy, who was in Schindler’s List, who brought even more nostalgic associations to the movie.
The cast also features some of Israel’s most interesting character actors, among them Loai Nofi and Danna Semo, in key roles.
Finding a young actress to play against Gaon’s legendary star power was more challenging. Greenberg wanted someone funny, but who could also convey vulnerability. The character of the granddaughter is working as a waitress abroad, hoping to hit it big as a content creator, and bases her look on Amy Winehouse.
But at first, her grandfather can only see her as someone who lacks focus. She rejects his criticism of her life choices, which makes their gradual bonding all the more satisfying to watch.
“You need the chemistry,” Greenberg said. With Gaon and Kleinstein, he could see it immediately. “They really were happy with each other.”
Challenges and moving forward
Greenberg cited Woody Allen’s Manhattan Murder Mystery as an inspiration for Love, Statistically Speaking. “I wanted that kind of domestic investigation. She suspects their neighbor of killing his wife, but it’s really the story of their marriage. I liked the idea of a domestic investigation that represents a gap in relationships. It’s the same idea here. The story isn’t the money. The story is the relationship.”
Writing during the COVID restrictions, Greenberg found he was inspired by these restrictions. “I took it as a creative challenge. I said: I’ll only shoot in locations within 300 meters of my home. I was living in the middle of Ben Maimon Street, near Adraba, the bookstore. All the locations in the film are within 300 meters of my previous apartment.”
He is currently working on a prequel to the film. “It’s set five years earlier, when his wife is alive. It’s their story. She wants a divorce. There’s a flower shop in a small neighborhood shopping center, and he’s in touch with the florist. Suddenly the florist disappears. He thinks something has happened to him. Everyone thinks he’s distracting himself from the fact that his wife wants a divorce, but the florist really has disappeared.”
He said he was also working on a more personal story, about a yeshiva student who is inspired to help a woman thousands of miles away, which was inspired by a real incident in his life. “It sets him off on a journey through Israeli society: the army, South America, coming back. He tries to find God in reality. It’s a story of faith and the cracks along the way.”
In a strange way, it sounds like it could also be a description of Love, Statistically Speaking.

What to know about the MLB offseason
Mazel tov to the Milwaukee Brewers on winning their first World Series title in franchise history! Team Israel alum Colton Gordon made one appearance for the Brewers this season – making him eligible to receive a championship ring – and was in the dugout on Wednesday as Milwaukee toppled the Tampa Bay Rays.
And the Brewers would not be where they are without former owner and MLB commissioner emeritus Bud Selig, whose statue stands outside American Family Field in Milwaukee.
With the end of the World Series comes the beginning of the baseball offseason. Even before the possible lockout, there will be awards handed out and (possibly) some free-agent contracts signed.
Here’s a quick Jewish guide to the next month in the baseball world:
Awards
Chicago Cubs star Alex Bregman is a finalist for the National League Gold Glove Award at third base. He won the American League award with Houston in 2024. Max Fried, who has won the award four times, did not make the cut this season.
Bregman could also be a candidate for the NL Silver Slugger Award, given to the best offensive player at each position. Despite his slow start, the 32-year-old had 19 homers and 52 RBIs after the All-Star break, which could also garner him some down-ballot votes for NL MVP.
Perhaps more of a long shot, but Texas Rangers DH Joc Pederson could be a candidate for AL Comeback Player of the Year. After an abysmal 2025, Pederson clubbed 26 homers in 2026, his most since 2019, with an .816 OPS.
Free agency
Pederson has a mutual option with the Rangers for $18.5 million. If either side declines, he becomes a free agent. And Rowdy Tellez, who spent most of 2026 in Triple-A before appearing in three playoff games with the Atlanta Braves, is also a free agent.
Halftime report
The St. Louis Blues condemned the display of signs at a game last week that read “Israel Kills” and “Free America from Israel.” The fans were ejected from the arena, and Blues owner Tom Stillman called the signs “vile messages of hate” that were “unfortunate and unforgivable.”

Davidson College men’s basketball coach Matt McKillop and two of his players spoke to Rabbi Erez Sherman of Sinai Temple in Los Angeles this week about their recent team trip to Berlin, where they learned about the Holocaust. Check out their conversation on the latest episode of Sherman’s “Rabbi on the Sidelines” show.

Brazil summons Argentine diplomat over role in Bolsonaro's flight to US, sources say
BRASILIA, Oct 30 - Brazil called in Argentina's highest diplomat in Brasilia to explain the Argentine government's role in the departure of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro to the US after losing the presidential election, two sources in the Brazilian government said on Friday, as Argentina denied the summoning.
Brazil's foreign ministry summoned the charge d'affaires at Argentina's embassy, Maria Emilia Cortes, on Thursday, the sources said. Cortes was received by the ministry's South America Department director, Joao Marcelo de Queiroz, one of the sources added.
It marks the latest diplomatic tension between the neighboring countries after Brazil downgraded ties with Argentina in August following insults from President Javier Milei towards his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Argentina's Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno, commenting on a media report about Brazil's move, wrote on X that "there was no request for explanation." The Brazilian foreign ministry declined to comment.
Senator Bolsonaro, son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, arrived in the US on Wednesday morning after leaving Brazil.
Argentine authorities said that Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters crossed a bridge into northern Argentina on Tuesday evening before boarding a chartered aircraft. Bolsonaro and his family then flew to Miami via Ecuador.
In a letter released on Wednesday, in which Bolsonaro said he was Brazil's rightful "leader", the senator thanked Milei for his assistance, without providing further details.
Milei traveled to Brazil for the launch of Bolsonaro's presidential campaign earlier this year, and has repeatedly insulted Lula, calling him a "thief" and "corrupt" in a media interview. The comments prompted Brasilia to permanently recall its ambassador to Argentina.
Bolsonaro was defeated by Lula in Sunday's runoff election.
His departure from Brazil violated a Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports and remain in Brazil as part of a money-laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing. Bolsonaro has said he is a victim of judicial persecution. REUTERS

The US canceled the traditional group “family” photograph at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on Friday, Oct. 30, after several European diplomats declined to pose alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Two officials confirmed this to BBC News, with a diplomatic source naming the UK among the countries that refused to take part. “The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that,” a British official told the broadcaster.
Meanwhile, Ukraine was not invited to the gathering that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting through Oct. 30-31.
According to US officials, the decision reflected a policy of limiting invitations to formal members, even though Kyiv had attended previous meetings as a guest.
The discussions took place the same day that Kyiv requested an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council, after Russia’s strikes left at least 25 civilians dead and 110 wounded nationwide.
Washington avoids ‘diplomatic distraction’
According to a US official, the photo was scrapped once it became clear that several delegations would not participate.
To prevent “a ceremonial photo opportunity” from turning into “a diplomatic distraction,” Washington chose to drop the photograph altogether, the official said, adding that the focus would remain on the substantive talks.
Ukraine Requests Emergency UN Security Council Meeting Over Russian Strikes
Lavrov, who has been under US sanctions since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, arrived in Atlanta earlier on Friday, despite calls from US lawmakers to bar him from the country.
“Lavrov should not be allowed in the country. As long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is waging war against Ukraine and bombing cities, Russian leaders should not be welcomed in any of these forums. They lead a pariah state,” Republican Rep. Don Bacon wrote in a statement on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, sharply criticized US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.
“Donald Trump needs to wake up,” Shaheen said in an Oct. 8 CNN interview. “He needs to understand that courting favor with Vladimir Putin is not good for America.”
Shaheen, who joined 13 bipartisan senators in calling for Putin and other sanctioned Russian officials to be barred from G20 events on US soil, called on Washington to increase pressure on Moscow rather than reward it.
The criticism came ahead of the US midterm elections, which are scheduled for Nov. 3.
The elections come as Trump faces severe pressure over record-high diesel prices, for which he has previously blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries rather than the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Pope Leo XIV, who has repeatedly clashed with Trump’s administration over the US-Israeli war with Iran and immigration, cast his ballot in the US midterm elections by mail, officially becoming the first pontiff to do so.
“I have no fear of the Trump administration or speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel,” the pontiff said during his papal flight to Algeria earlier in April.
Russia expected to challenge sanctions
Lavrov is expected to use his appearance at the G20 to argue against economic sanctions and other trade restrictions on Moscow, portraying them as instruments of pressure.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck an abrupt diesel deal with Putin, after which the US Treasury authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
Although the deal has drawn scrutiny from Washington, Kyiv and Europe, Trump’s administration has continued easing sanctions on Russia.
The New York Times reported on Oct. 27 that the Russian Direct Investment Fund, which helped arrange the diesel shipments, is now seeking the removal of US sanctions against it.
The fund’s chief, Kirill Dmitriev, has become Moscow’s main economic channel to Trump’s team, working directly with senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
On Oct. 21, Witkoff publicly confirmed that Washington and Moscow are discussing future economic and trade cooperation, while revealing that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Dmitriev.
The visit comes as Washington prepares new trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine and Russia, expected in November in Abu Dhabi, which the European side is not expected to attend.

The US State Department has ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group, the US Embassy said Friday, Anadolu reports.
In a security alert, the US Mission to Saudi Arabia said the departure order took effect on Oct. 23 due to safety risks.
The mission warned that Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure had caused casualties and major travel disruptions, adding that hostilities could escalate rapidly.
US government employees must obtain special authorization to use airports in Saudi Arabia following recent missile and drone attacks, the statement said.
The embassy said Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport had partially reopened, while airports in Jeddah and Dammam remained operational with some delays and cancellations.
It also urged US citizens to exercise extreme caution when traveling by air and warned against photographing missile interceptions or attack sites, citing Saudi regulations.
The alert comes amid intensified Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.
On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition announced that its air defenses had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh.
On Friday, the coalition reported intercepting a Houthi cruise missile targeting western Saudi Arabia, as well as a drone in the Riyadh region.
The Houthis have also claimed attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports in recent days.
The Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in March 2015 to support the internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa since September 2014.

What to know about California’s midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:38:49 UTC
04:38:49 KST

What to know about California’s midterm elections
Redistricting in California, the most populous US state, could flip control of US House from Republican to Democrat.
As voters across the United States head to the polls for the midterm elections – widely seen as a referendum on President Donald Trump’s second term in office – the state of California is set to play an important role.
Several races across the country’s most populous state could help determine whether the Democratic Party takes control of the US House of Representatives, where Trump’s Republican Party currently holds a slim majority.
California’s ballot initiatives – or policy decisions made by voters – have also received national attention.
Perhaps the biggest difference in this year’s elections, however, is the introduction of new congressional district maps drawn up through a partisan redistricting initiative approved by California voters last year.
That initiative aims to net at least five additional Democratic Party seats in the House, where Republicans have a four-seat majority.
Which California races are competitive, who are the main candidates and how has the state’s redistricting push changed the electoral landscape?
When is election day?
The election will be held on Tuesday, November 3. California polls will be open from 7am (15:00 GMT) to 8pm (04:00 GMT Wednesday). Mail ballots must be postmarked by election day.
What is partisan redistricting?
The House is divided into 435 districts, each represented by one member of Congress elected by their constituents. While congressional districts are populated equally, their boundaries are set by states and can shift.
Partisan redistricting involves states drawing those district maps in a way that advantages candidates from one party over another.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat and Trump critic, first proposed a one-time statewide redistricting effort in response to seven Republican-led states redrawing their maps in an attempt to secure seats for Republicans. Although California had banned partisan redistricting, Newsom pitched the idea as an unfortunate but necessary retaliatory measure.
California voters approved the redistricting plan in a 2025 ballot measure – Proposition 50 – that temporarily suspended the state’s nonpartisan redistricting commission until 2030. California then drew new maps to make several Republican strongholds more competitive for Democratic challengers.
As a result, the handful of districts previously seen as favourable terrain for Republicans have instead become hotly-contested races between the two parties.
What races are being watched?
California has 52 members in the House of Representatives – the most of any state – with Republicans holding just eight of the seats. There are several closely watched state races in the Democratic Party’s effort to secure a majority in the House, the lower chamber of the US Congress.
One is the 22nd congressional district, located in California’s agriculture-rich Central Valley. The district map was redrawn under Proposition 50, setting up one of the state’s most contentious races in a former Republican stronghold.
Incumbent Republican Representative David Valadao is locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Randy Villegas. Valadao has portrayed himself as a moderate, while Villegas has hammered him over issues such as the rising cost of living, healthcare and Trump’s immigration crackdowns – a key issue for the area’s immigrant farm-working communities.
California’s 48th district, a traditionally Republican stronghold which includes parts of San Diego County near the border with Mexico, is also considered highly competitive after its boundaries were redrawn. The district’s longtime representative, Republican Darrell Issa, decided to retire after the redistricting, with two local officials – Republican Jim Desmond and Democratic San Diego Councilmember Marni von Wilpert – now vying for the seat.
While California’s redistricting aimed to make historically reliable Republican districts more competitive for Democrats, the process has also had some unexpected impacts: Two Republican members of Congress, Representatives Ken Calvert and Young Kim, have found themselves locked in a bitter race against each other after redrawn maps put them in the same district.
Who is running for governor?
Vying to replace Governor Newsom are Republican political commentator Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra. Becerra is a former California attorney general and secretary of health and human services during former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Hilton has blasted Becerra for rising crime and homelessness as well as high fuel prices in California, where a gallon (3.78 litres) of petrol costs $5.95 compared with $4.22 nationally, according to the American Automobile Association. Heavily favoured in the Democratic stronghold state, Becerra has sought to associate Hilton with Trump, who is deeply unpopular among Californians.
Polls show Becerra with a strong lead over the Republican challenger. A recent Emerson poll suggested that he was ahead by 27 points.
What ballot initiatives are voters deciding on?
California voters will also weigh in on a handful of policy questions, including a tax on billionaires and whether the state should adopt mandatory voter ID.
Perhaps the most contentious is Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare and education. The measure is one of three impacting the state’s ultra-wealthy residents, with the referendums dubbed the “billionaire battle”.
The tax would apply to about 200 of the wealthiest people in California, according to the news website CalMatters. The proposition is opposed by powerful industries and tech titans, who have poured more than $152m into fighting the ballot measure compared with $33m raised in support of the tax, a California public radio station KQED reports.
The measure has drawn opposition from figures such as Google cofounder Sergey Brin, who has given more than $102m to defeat the referendum, as well as Hilton, Becerra and Newsom. Despite being supported by the Democratic Party, Proposition 40 is also being fought by some progressive groups opposed to the one-time tax.
Other progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Ro Khanna, a wealthy member of Congress from California’s Silicon Valley, support the referendum.
Two other ballot measures, Propositions 41 and 42, would effectively nullify Proposition 40 if approved by voters.
Another measure, Proposition 39, has also been the subject of fierce debate. If passed, it would require Californians to show government-issued IDs in order to vote.
While supporters say mandatory IDs will bolster confidence in elections by countering voter fraud, studies have found that fraudulent voting is nearly nonexistent in the US.
Critics say that voter ID laws add obstacles to voting by requiring government-issued documents, such as a driver’s licence, that not all citizens hold. They argue that strong safeguards ensuring only eligible voters cast ballots are already in place.

Iran condemns Canada, UAE for reiterating territorial claims over three Persian Gulf Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Iran condemns Canada, UAE for reiterating territorial claims over three Persian Gulf Islands
TEHRAN– Iran has strongly condemned Canada and the United Arab Emirates for reiterating territorial claims over Abu Musa, the Greater Tunb and the Lesser Tunb, reaffirming that the three islands are inseparable and eternal parts of Iranian territory.
Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Thursday denounced the UAE’s “brazen and interventionist” claims and Canada’s decision to endorse them in a joint statement issued following a meeting between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Ottawa.
Baqaei stressed that the islands’ established geographical, historical and legal status could not be altered by political statements or the repetition of 'baseless territorial claims.'
“The islands of Abu Musa, the Greater Tunb and the Lesser Tunb are inseparable and eternal parts of Iran’s territorial domain, and the repetition of baseless and unfounded claims about them will not change the established geographical, historical and legal realities,” he said.
Tehran denounces Ottawa’s intervention
The Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman particularly criticized Canada's decision to endorse the UAE's position, describing Ottawa's move as short-sighted and contrary to the fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter and international law.
He said Canada's involvement in the territorial dispute was especially objectionable given that the country itself faces territorial assertions by the US administration.
Baqaei stressed that endorsing another country's territorial claims against Iran carries international responsibility for the Canadian government.
He also called on Abu Dhabi to respect the principles of good-neighborliness rather than repeatedly raising territorial claims against a major neighboring country, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect and respect for national sovereignty in relations between regional states.
Canada's position is not new. Ottawa had previously endorsed the UAE's claim in a joint statement issued during Carney's visit to the Emirates in November 2025, in which the two countries likewise called for an end to what they described as the occupation of the three islands.
The latest statement, however, comes as Canada and the UAE move to elevate their bilateral relations to a strategic partnership, expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy, defence and security, advanced technology and diplomacy.
Iran has consistently maintained that Abu Musa, the Greater Tunb and the Lesser Tunb are integral parts of its national territory and rejects any foreign government's endorsement of competing claims over them.
Tehran has also repeatedly stressed that relations with neighboring countries should be founded on mutual respect, respect for territorial integrity and the principles of good-neighborliness, rather than political alignments with extra-regional powers.

Before captain, a king: The dramatic life of Patrick Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:36:59 UTC
04:36:59 KST

Long before he trekked aboard the USS Enterprise, Sir Patrick Stewart trod the boards on stages across the globe.
"The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time," Stewart wrote in his memoir.
The Royal Shakespeare Company wrote a tribute to Stewart, who died yesterday aged 86, calling him one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation.
"Despite being one of the most recognisable Shakespearean performers in the world, Sir Patrick remained deeply connected to Stratford-upon-Avon and the RSC throughout his career," the company said.
The Royal Shakespeare Company said his contribution was "beyond measure", with his knighthood for services to drama and his star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame as markers of a career that spanned 70 years.
But before he was a household name, a young Stewart cut his teeth as an ensemble member touring Australia.
Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorised Shakespeare for fun as a teenager.
He would go on to win a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching his career as a character actor.
Theatre programs archived at the National Library of Australia show that a 21-year-old Stewart toured with the Old Vic company across 1961 and 1962.
Stewart had ensemble roles in Twelfth Night and The Lady of the Camellias, both directed by Robert Helpmann and starring Vivien Leigh.
ABC archives show that reporters made sure to capture the moment Leigh and Helpmann landed on the tarmac in Australia to be greeted by adoring fans, but likely didn't know that just out of frame was a star-to-be in young Stewart.
Loading...
From the Young Vic, Stewart went on to join the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing roles including Mark Antony, Henry IV, Shylock and Oberon.
In 1975, he would return to Australia to play Ejlert Løvborg in Hedda Gabler with the company.
From royal crowns to the captain's chair
Although often revered as a classical actor, Stewart denied this title, saying: "I was not a trained classical actor, I just had a training".
"What I did happen to do was spend a huge number of years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, but doing just as much modern drama as I was doing blank verse," he told the ABC in 1995.
After joining Star Trek, he found himself frustrated at the implication from reporters that doing a syndicated television show must have meant he was "slumming it".
Stewart had a very different point of view.
"All of those years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, all of those years sitting in the throne of England, all of those years wearing those crowns and speaking that blank verse was nothing but a preparation for sitting in the captain's chair of the Enterprise," he said.
It was Stewart's understanding of profession that made him so versatile, that every prior piece of work in an artist's portfolio contributes to the next, regardless of the piece being set in futuristic space or written in Elizabethan England.
Always returned to theatre
Star Trek may have been Stewart's launch into the broader global audience, particularly in America, but he continued to return to the stage, often rehearsing shows while filming.
In 1988, Stewart premiered his one-man adaptation of A Christmas Carol.
The performance started as a three-hour rendition, performed in a church in Yorkshire.
Several years later, it would make its Broadway debut.
The revised version would be staged time and time again, nabbing a Laurence Olivier Award for Best Entertainment in 1994.
In 2007, Stewart played the role he'd waited 50 years for — Macbeth.
The Times of London said his performance was "an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humour".
"I learned it when I was 14. I memorised all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great," Stewart told The Associated Press.
"And they stuck, so I didn't have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.
"Nearly 50 years I've waited."
In 2009, Stewart starred with his dear friend Sir Ian McKellen in Waiting for Godot.
McKellen wrote of his friend on social media, retelling the moment Stewart told him about taking a role on Star Trek.
"'But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?'" McKellen said he asked at the time.
"Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did."
Audiences will feel lucky to have seen Patrick Stewart deliver time and time again.
But in his own words, he felt just as lucky to see them too.
"I enjoy what I do so much that I do actually feel sucked into it, particularly the live theatre, the performing side of it," he told the ABC in 1995.
"I'm one of those really fortunate individuals, I do feel blessed in this, who ended up doing as a profession what I would've done for nothing."
