Washington’s Midterm Letter Game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:34:49 UTC
04:34:49 KST

Washington’s Midterm Letter Game
From Carter to Vance, US messages have failed to break Iranian resistance
TEHRAN — The disclosure of a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei has triggered a wave of contradictory narratives in Washington, speculative reporting in American media, and a calm, conditional response in Tehran.
The story broke on Oct. 28 when The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, reported that Vance had written to Rezaei, Iran’s top security official and former commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps, to explore a framework for restarting negotiations and averting a new round of US strikes. The report said the outreach was made at President Donald Trump’s direction.
Hours later, Trump himself undercut that account. Asked by reporters whether he had directed Vance to restart peace talks, he said “No,” and claimed the contact was about helping Iran obtain “medical supplies and various things.”
“Basically, it’s getting supplies in to help people that are not well,” Trump said.
The semi-official Tasnim news agency confirmed on Oct. 29 that Tehran had received the letter but had not yet responded. Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, one of
Tehran’s negotiators, wrote on X that “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly communicated to the mediators” and that “the carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran.”
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi added that while Iran’s Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the homeland, Iran “continues to give diplomacy a chance.”
Beyond those confirmed facts — a letter was sent via Qatari mediators, delivered on Sunday, acknowledged in Tehran, with no published text and no formal reply — almost everything else published in the past 48 hours is speculation and cannot be verified.
A routine channel, not a breakthrough
Viewed in historical perspective, the letter is anything but unprecedented. Writing to Iranian leaders has been a standard American practice since the victory of the Islamic Revolution in 1979, and at least 20 letters, messages and written contacts have been publicly disclosed so far.
The list begins with President Jimmy Carter’s Nov. 6, 1979 letter to Imam Khomeini carried — but never delivered — by Ramsey Clark and William Miller after the takeover of the US Embassy. It continued with President Ronald Reagan’s signed Bible inscribed on Oct. 3, 1986 with the verse Galatians 3:8, handed to Iranian intermediaries in the Iran-Contra affair, along with the earlier McFarlane mission carrying a key-shaped cake.
President Bill Clinton sent messages through the Swiss ambassador in 1997 proposing direct government-to-government talks after Mohammad Khatami’s election, repeated the offer via Vice President Al Gore through Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah in May 1998, and wrote the detailed June 1999 letter on the Khobar Towers bombing while insisting the US had “no hostile intentions” toward the Islamic Republic.
President Barack Obama wrote at least four letters to Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei — in May 2009, September 2009, January 2012 on the Strait of Hormuz as a “red line,” and mid-October 2014 linking cooperation against ISIS to a nuclear deal — plus the exchange of letters with President Hassan Rouhani in August-September 2013 that led to their historic phone call, not to mention six Nowruz messages.
President Donald Trump sent a letter via late Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in June 2019, which was publicly rejected, then relied on the Swiss encrypted fax channel in January 2020 after the assassination of General Qassem Soleimani to warn against escalation, and sent the March 5, 2025 letter delivered on March 12 by Emirati diplomat Anwar Gargash, setting a 60-day deadline that led to five rounds of indirect Steve Witkoff-Abbas Araghchi talks in Oman and Rome before the June war.
From this standpoint, a message from a US vice president to the SNSC secretary is a routine and conventional step, not a turning point. Washington writes when pressure fails. Tehran listens, measures, and decides on the basis of interests, not envelopes.
No one knows what is inside
No official text of Vance’s letter has been published by either side, and every claim about its content comes from anonymous “officials familiar with the matter.”
The Journal said it contained “no specific peace plan” but focused on a framework for negotiations. Axios, citing a US official, added that Vance stressed any talks to head off strikes “require discussions on the nuclear issue,” and called it the most senior-level US outreach in months. The New York Times, citing a US official and an Iranian official, claimed the letter proposed an early meeting led by Vance himself, possibly as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey, technically “without preconditions.”
Washington Post columnist David Ignatius, citing a US official, went further, writing that Vance offered to meet Rezaei personally in Istanbul or Doha, defined America’s interest as ensuring Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon and Iran’s interest as rebuilding its war-ravaged economy and preserving sovereignty, and demanded “representatives who are empowered to discuss the nuclear issues.” He portrayed Rezaei as “the essential point of contact in Tehran and the only person who could build a consensus.”
None of this has been confirmed by Tehran or by any published document. Iranian media have treated all of it as guesswork. Until a text is released or an official reply is issued, responsible journalism requires treating these versions as competing American leaks aimed at shaping expectations, not as facts.
Midterm panic at the pump
The timing, however, is revealing. The United States is days away from midterm elections on Nov. 3, and all signs point to a very difficult contest for Republicans. The eight-month war with Iran has become the administration’s Achilles’ heel.
Despite repeated threats to “finish the job,” Trump has failed to control domestic gasoline prices, which have surged on the back of disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices above $110, damaged tankers, and a US naval blockade that has raised insurance and shipping costs globally rather than forcing Iranian submission.
Washington has tried everything to calm the pump before the vote, from emergency releases and arrangements with Russia to stabilize the fuel market to the highly controversial authorization for the use of cheaper red-dyed diesel, yet prices remain politically toxic. A short, sharp new war would send them even higher; a televised diplomatic “process” would, in the White House calculation, create a positive shock and allow Trump to claim the situation is under control.
That is why the same administration that warns Gulf allies to “prepare” for post-midterm strikes simultaneously leaks a peace letter. The goal is not peace but performance: to stage a show of agreement-seeking before the elections and inject artificial calm into the Republican camp at a moment when it is in no good shape at all.
Seven conditions, no retreat
Tehran’s answer to such theater has been consistent and public. Iran has announced seven conditions for ending the current state of war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz to free navigation, centered on a region-wide ceasefire, lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting sanctions on oil exports, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, and guarantees against renewed aggression.
Rezaei himself drew the line on Oct. 21: “Not a single ounce of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran,” and negotiations are possible only if Iran’s demands are met. Tasnim stressed on Oct. 29 that “any position that undermines this firm framework is unacceptable.”
This firmness is not rhetorical. It reflects the assessment of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, who in his recent meeting with Rezaei described the SNSC and its Secretariat as the “crossroads of policymaking,” stressed safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control over the Strait of Hormuz, and insisted on pursuing the rights of the Iranian nation and the Resistance Front by ensuring the country’s conditions for ending the war are met and bringing the state of “neither war nor peace” to an end.
Most importantly for the present episode, the Leader said sound and well-grounded decisions require a roadmap based on a comprehensive understanding of each undertaking, from its starting point to its conclusion. In other words, Tehran will not enter a process whose end is pre-scripted in Washington.
Open door, not open eyes
Iran has not closed the doors of diplomacy. The quadrilateral meeting hosted by Tehran on Monday with senior officials from Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia, the continued Qatari mediation — with Qatari envoys returning to Tehran on Friday — and Rezaei’s own statement that security in West Asia must originate from within the region show that Tehran prefers a regional, endogenous order to foreign dictation.
But openness does not mean naivety. Tehran remembers too well the March 2025 Trump letter to Ayatollah Khamenei, the five rounds of Witkoff-Araghchi talks, and then the Israeli attack of June 13 and the 12-day war. It remembers four Obama letters followed by maximum pressure, and a signed JCPOA abandoned unilaterally.
Iran will not walk blindfolded and wishfully into a negotiation so that Trump can exploit the mere image of talks for electoral gain, freeze the battlefield in his favor, pocket a nuclear concession upfront, and postpone sanctions relief, unblocking and guarantees to an indefinite “later.” Sequencing matters: Washington demands nuclear-first, relief-later; Tehran demands simultaneous, verifiable steps. Without that, there is no roadmap from start to finish, only a photo opportunity.
Desperation after failure
Behind the letter is a serious American impasse. Neither eight months of direct strikes and Israeli operations, nor the naval blockade of ports, economic warfare, cyber operations and threats of regime change, have forced Iran to surrender its enrichment, its missile program, or its control over Hormuz. The economy, though wounded, has not collapsed; the Armed Forces have not fractured; regional partners have not defected — they came to Tehran.
A new round of war will not bring Iran to its knees. It will only deepen American costs: higher energy prices before and after the midterms, wider regional escalation that Qatar, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia openly fear, further exposure of US bases and warships that Leader Khamenei’s commanders have explicitly vowed to target, and a deeper reputational defeat when a superpower cannot dictate terms to a nation it has sanctioned for 47 years.
Washington now acknowledges, in its own leaks, that it must talk to the hard core of Iranian power — the SNSC secretary with direct access to the Leader and the trust of the IRGC — because no imposed settlement is possible. That is an admission of failure, not a gesture of goodwill.
The ball is in the US court. If Washington wants more than an election show, it must trade the logic of imposed agreement for balanced agreement: end the blockade, release Iran’s frozen assets, lift oil sanctions, accept verification in exchange for guarantees, and let West Asia’s security be built within the region. Otherwise, the letter from Vance will join the long archive of American letters since 1979 — received, read, measured against Iran’s roadmap, and answered not with surrender but with resistance.

Time for a trip to New Zealand? Why Australian travellers now have an advantage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:30:49 UTC
04:30:49 KST

While the prospect of higher interest rates could leave borrowers with less money to spend, it has come as good news for the Australian dollar.
The Aussie surged above NZ$1.25 this week for the first time in more than 13 years, making holidays across the Tasman more affordable for Australians.
Our currency has gained more than 10 per cent against the New Zealand dollar over the past year, giving Australian travellers greater purchasing power.
Two contrasting economic developments helped drive the latest move.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Wednesday's stronger-than-expected inflation report pushed the market-implied probability of a Melbourne Cup Day interest rate rise by the Reserve Bank of Australia above 80 per cent, supporting the Australian dollar.
Across the Tasman, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets by leaving interest rates on hold.
Like Australia, New Zealand is also grappling with inflation above its central bank's target, with annual consumer prices rising 3.7 per cent.
Differences in interest rate expectations between the two countries have helped push the Australian dollar higher, potentially making a New Zealand getaway better value.
Major discounts coming for Australian shoppers
Bigger discounts could be on the way during Black Friday and the Christmas period as many Australian retailers battle for shoppers amid slow sales growth.
The sluggish growth in sales could be a sign that consumers are holding back from spending big during the sales, or that cost of living pressures and the prospect of higher interest rates are weighing on household budgets.
Woolworths CEO Amanda Bardwell told shareholders at the company's annual general meeting (AGM) this week that four in 10 Australians say they often struggle to make ends meet. The supermarket giant estimates groceries account for 10 per cent of household spending among borrowers.
But that hasn't stopped Woolworths from making what its CEO described as a good start to the financial year, with food sales rising nearly 7 per cent in the three months to September. It's doing better than Coles, which reported slower sales growth over the same period at 3.6 per cent, still topping $10 billion in revenue.
It seems that even in tough times, people have to eat — who would have thought?
Betashares investment strategist Hugh Lam told the SBS On the Money podcast that shares in the consumer staples sector have risen about 20 per cent so far this year.
"A lot of companies within there, like Woollies, Coles and even Bega Cheese, are benefiting because these are sectors of the market where people are still going to be spending despite where we are in the economic cycle," Lam said.
For retailers selling more discretionary items, however, the picture isn't as rosy.
This week, Super Retail Group, which owns Rebel, Supercheap Auto, BCF and Macpac, said weaker consumer confidence and pressure on discretionary spending had weighed on its business.
It specifically pointed to higher petrol prices as a factor behind the decline in quarterly like-for-like sales at outdoor retailers BCF and Macpac.
JB Hi-Fi, which also operates The Good Guys and kitchen and bathroom retailer e&s, reported negative comparable sales growth across its Australian businesses.
It highlights the pressures many businesses in the discretionary sector — selling wants rather than needs — are facing in this economic climate.
"I think what this means … is potential discounting from these retailers which is of course going to hit margins," Lam said.
"And that's because higher interest rates mean that there's less discretionary money everyday Australians can spend on."
Even Bunnings, owned by Wesfarmers, has seen sales growth moderate, according to Wesfarmers CEO Rob Scott at the company's AGM.
But he said the group's Kmart business was performing well as shoppers increasingly sought value.
For consumers, that could mean more bargains during Black Friday and Christmas sales, as retailers compete harder for every dollar.
Will you have to pay for Claude and its competitors?
AI chatbot Claude's owner, Anthropic, lodged its prospectus this week as it prepares to list on the US sharemarket.
The filing offered investors a detailed look at the company's extraordinary revenue growth, mounting expenses and the risks associated with developing increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.
Among the most serious risks identified were "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such (AI) systems were misused, replicated, weaponized [sic], or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Loftus Peak chief investment officer Alex Pollack told the SBS On the Money podcast that other potentially catastrophic threats already exist, including nuclear and cyber risks.
"But the question you’ve got to ask yourself is, what is the probability of those risks happening?" Pollack said.
But buried among the warnings was another risk with more immediate implications for the millions of people using AI chatbots for free.
Anthropic warned that its marketing strategies, including free trials and free subscription tiers, might fail to deliver sufficient financial benefits.
"If the costs of supporting free users exceed the value we derive from their eventual conversion or other benefits such as network effects and word-of-mouth referrals, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected."
Could that eventually mean an end to free access?
The prospectus doesn't suggest Anthropic has made such a decision, but it does highlight the financial challenge of offering expensive AI services at no cost.
Anthropic reported revenue of US$16.28 billion ($23.12 billion) in the six months to the end of June 2026, compared with US$1.16 billion ($1.65 billion) in the same period a year earlier.
But that extraordinary growth comes with enormous costs.
The company spent nearly US$9 billion ($12.78 billion) on computing and infrastructure over those six months, accounting for more than half its total operating expenses.
It's a reminder that while AI chatbots might be free for many people today, the technology powering them is anything but cheap.

This Week’s New Movies: Seven Premieres Worth Seeing on the Big Screen
Kyiv • UNN
From November 2 to 8, cinemas will show nine premieres — from animation to biographical dramas and a concert film. They include films about Kafka, George Michael, and The Cat in the Hat.
Next week, viewers can look forward to stories to suit every taste. UNN will provide more details about which premieres will appear in cinemas from November 2 to 8.
The Cat in the Hat
Premiere: November 5
The familiar troublemaker returns with a new mission. This time, the Cat in the Hat is tasked with entertaining children who are forced to adjust to life in a new city. The task proves difficult: if the hero fails, he will lose his main magical artifact forever. Viewers can expect fantastic adventures, unexpected antics, and plenty of humor. The Cat will have to use all his ingenuity to turn a challenging period for the children into a real adventure. Will he be able to carry out his assignment and preserve what is most precious to him?
The Iron Curtain
Premiere: November 5
The film is set in Warsaw in 1981, when the Polish authorities suppress youth protests and impose martial law. British professor Joan Andrews arrives in the city to give a lecture, but her trip unexpectedly turns into a fight for her life. The woman witnesses a political assassination, after which she finds herself in the sights of the security services. Now she must not only save herself, but also tell the world the truth about what is happening. The film is an adaptation of a story by Polish writer and Nobel Prize laureate Olga Tokarczuk.
Wild Horse Number Nine
Premiere: November 5
Chile, 1973. Two CIA agents, Chris and Lee, head to Easter Island, where a secret assignment awaits them. Among the mysterious stone statues, the heroes find themselves at the center of dangerous events linked to conspiracies and their own past. The situation becomes even more complicated when Chris grows close to a group of female students who oppose the authorities. This connection could ruin the agents’ plans and jeopardize the entire operation. Against the backdrop of political upheaval, the heroes will have to confront not only external threats, but also their own secrets.
A New Dawn
Premiere: November 5
In a small Japanese coastal town, the Obinata family has been making fireworks for more than three centuries. However, the family craft is threatened with extinction, and the factory site is slated to be cleared for the construction of a highway. Keitaro, the younger member of the family, refuses to accept such a future. He has settled in the abandoned factory and continues to create fireworks on his own. At the same time, the boy is trying to uncover the mystery of Shuhari, a special firework conceived by his father before his mysterious disappearance. "A New Dawn" is the directorial debut of Yoshitoshi Shinomiya, an artist and animator who worked on renowned Japanese films. The film combines traditional artistic techniques with an unusual animation style. It also became the only animated film in this year’s Berlinale competition program and received the jury prize in the Contrechamp section at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival.
George Michael: The Faith Tour (in the original language)
Premiere: November 5
Fans of George Michael will have the opportunity to see the artist again during one of the most brilliant periods of his career. Cinemas will screen a concert recording of his 1988 performance in Paris, restored using original footage on 35mm film. In addition to the concert, viewers will be shown rare personal material belonging to the musician, as well as previously unreleased audio. The program will also include a short film by Mary McCartney, created from archival recordings from 1986–1988—the period when the album Faith was taking shape.
The California Scheme
Premiere: November 5
In the late 1990s, musicians Gavin Bain and Billy Boyd decide that their dreams of the big stage should not remain merely dreams. After being mocked for their accents, they come up with an unusual way to break into the music industry: they reinvent themselves as rappers from California. The duo changes the sound of their compositions, invents a new backstory, and convinces those around them that they are well-known figures on the American rap scene and longtime friends of Eminem. The plan works better than they expected: the musicians secure a contract, a large advance, and the opportunity to perform on MTV. However, maintaining their fabricated image becomes increasingly difficult, and the deception gradually begins to unravel.
Franz. Kafka’s Story
Premiere: November 5
The film offers a look at Franz Kafka not only as an outstanding writer but also as a person with fears, doubts, and complicated relationships with the world around him. The story spans his life from childhood to his final days. The protagonist tries to find his place, experiences complicated romantic relationships, fears intimacy, and at the same time feels a constant need to write. His desire to live an ordinary life conflicts with the expectations of others and his inner struggles. The film became Poland’s official submission for the Academy Award in the Best International Feature Film category. The film is voiced in Ukrainian: the translation is played over the actors’ original language.
The Woven Man
Premiere: November 5
A lonely fisherwoman from a small coastal town has long been accustomed to mockery and contempt from the local residents. Tired of unsuccessful attempts to find a close companion among men, she decides to take an unusual step and orders a partner made from willow branches. Soon, her unusual creation comes to life. The willow man proves attentive and devoted—qualities the heroine could not find in ordinary relationships. But the appearance of such a companion sparks a wave of outrage and envy in the town. The story becomes an unusual tale about loneliness, acceptance, and a person’s right to decide for themselves where to seek happiness.

Iran’s nuclear doctrine debate reflects national demand for stronger deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

04:27:55 KST

Iran’s nuclear doctrine debate reflects national demand for stronger deterrence
TEHRAN — Tehran’s interim Friday prayer leader, Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, has described calls to review Iran’s nuclear doctrine as a growing national demand rooted in the Iranian people’s experience of Western conduct, heightened security concerns and the need to strengthen the country’s deterrence capabilities.
Addressing worshippers during Friday prayers in the Iranian capital on October 30, Haj Ali Akbari said the debate over a possible revision of the country’s nuclear doctrine should not be dismissed as an emotional reaction or attributed to a particular political faction. Rather, he argued, it reflects a broader public reassessment of the security requirements facing Iran following years of confrontation, unfulfilled commitments and hostile actions by its adversaries.
His remarks come amid renewed public discussion in Iran about the country’s nuclear policy and the relationship between its established positions, national security requirements and the evolving regional and international environment.
A debate shaped by security concerns
Haj Ali Akbari said Iran’s adversaries had crossed the nation’s red lines, pointing to the assassination of the martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, and 'repeated failures' to honor commitments and agreements.
He argued that the Iranian people’s accumulated experience had prompted a more considered debate about the country’s deterrence requirements, including whether its nuclear doctrine should be reviewed in light of the security challenges it faces.
According to the cleric, the proposal is rooted in the Iranian nation’s right to live in dignity and security. He stressed that the discussion should be understood as a matter of national concern rather than an initiative belonging to any single political group or current.
Haj Ali Akbari also said that some people had reacted angrily to the proposal but maintained that the public discussion surrounding it reflected a broader demand that policymakers should examine seriously.
Citing previous surveys, he said more than 70 percent of respondents in some polls had supported reviewing Iran’s nuclear doctrine.
He added that calls for reconsideration had subsequently emerged from a range of social and professional groups, including university students, school students, academics, intellectuals and professional associations.
The cleric urged universities, researchers, security specialists and other experts to contribute to the debate by conducting substantive studies and developing policy proposals. He also called on the relevant authorities to undertake further assessments, with the aim of submitting the resulting recommendations to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei.
He emphasized that the final decision rested with the Leader and said that any decision he made would be followed.
Negotiations and the question of vigilance
Alongside the nuclear doctrine debate, Haj Ali Akbari cautioned against interpreting US calls for negotiations, diplomatic correspondence, or the involvement of intermediaries as grounds for relaxing Iran’s vigilance.
Drawing on Iran’s experience of dealings with Washington, he argued that diplomatic overtures should be assessed in the context of the other side’s conduct and actions, rather than its statements alone.
He warned that, in some circumstances, US messages and proposals for negotiations could coincide with more serious threats than those conveyed through explicit declarations of hostility. His remarks underscored the importance of maintaining vigilance while assessing diplomatic initiatives.
The comments reflect a central concern in Iranian political and security discourse: that diplomatic engagement must be evaluated alongside practical guarantees, respect for commitments, and the broader security environment.
For Tehran, the question is not simply whether negotiations are proposed, but whether the process can produce credible and lasting commitments while safeguarding Iran’s national interests.
From public debate to policy assessment
Haj Ali Akbari’s remarks place the nuclear doctrine debate within a wider discussion about deterrence, national sovereignty and the country's response to changing security conditions.
 
By calling for contributions from universities, professional bodies and relevant specialists, he presented the issue as one requiring sustained examination rather than a decision driven by immediate political pressures.
The distinction is significant: a public demand for a review does not, in itself, constitute a formal change in national policy. Any revision would require consideration by the competent authorities and a decision through the country's established institutional framework.
Iran's nuclear policy has long been a subject of international debate, particularly in relation to its stated position against nuclear weapons, its nuclear program and the country's security concerns. A discussion about revising the doctrine therefore raises questions that extend beyond technical nuclear policy to include deterrence, strategic calculations and the country's assessment of the international environment.
Haj Ali Akbari called for the debate to be informed by expert analysis and national considerations, while reaffirming that the Leader would make the final decision.
His remarks signal that calls for a reassessment of Iran's nuclear doctrine have become an issue of public and political discussion, with supporters framing the debate around national security, deterrence and the lessons drawn from past confrontations. Whether that discussion results in any change in policy remains a matter for the country's competent decision-making authorities.

In a papal first, Pope Leo XIV casts ballot in US midterm elections
Leo XIV has reportedly become the first pope to vote in an American election, and likely the first to vote in a democratic, secular election, Qazinform News Agency cited Anadolu Agency.
Pope Leo XIV has cast his ballot for next week’s US midterm elections, reportedly becoming the first sitting pontiff to vote in a secular, democratic election, the Vatican announced Friday.
The first American pope "has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago," the Vatican said in a statement.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the statement added.
As a US citizen, Leo is registered to vote in New Lenox, a Chicago suburb where his brother, John, lives, according to voter records.
Voting early and by mail is common in US elections, depending on the local laws, as US elections are run by states, not the federal government in Washington.
Before becoming Pope Leo in May 2025, the man born Robert Francis Prevost took part in both Republican and Democratic party primaries and voted in the 2024 US presidential election, according to official records.
As reported earlier, Pope Leo XIV's postoperative recovery was showing steady improvement, according to doctors treating him at Rome's Gemelli Hospital.

US approves $2.6 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
- The US approved a US$2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine, with funding from Canada, Germany, Norway and EU-backed loans.
- The deal comes after delays that angered Kyiv, as President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for critical missile supplies while Russian attacks intensified.
- Lockheed Martin will build the missiles, and the US is pushing contractors to speed up output as it worries about air defence stockpiles and future winter needs.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US State Department said on Oct 30 it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated US$2.1 billion (S$2.6 billion), in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.
Delayed missile deliveries added to Ukraine's tensions with the US after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country.
The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Oct 30, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelensky said on Oct 26 that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will likely not receive the missile interceptors quickly.
Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence is encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the defensive interceptor missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through the US JUMPSTART programme, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
The JUMPSTART programme was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth US$825 million made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.
In July, the US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to US$58.6 billion (S$748 billion) to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200.
Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier in 2026 at the centre of efforts to increase missile output. REUTERS

Fact check: Inside Russia's campaign to undermine France's pro-Ukraine candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:25:23 UTC
04:25:23 KST

Fact check: Inside Russia's campaign to undermine France's pro-Ukraine candidates
Le Havre Mayor Edouard Philippe (R) and French President Emmanuel Macron (L) in Le Havre, France, on Sept. 12, 2024. (Benoit Tessier / Pool / AFP via Getty Images)
With the French presidential election months away, Russia's disinformation machine works to ensure no pro-Ukraine candidate enters the Elysee Palace.
Viginum, the French agency that counters foreign interference, has already detected hundreds of disinformation operations targeting the vote, whose outcome will have major ramifications for Ukraine and Europe.
Moscow-linked campaigns have spread false claims that center-left Raphael Glucksmann helped set up torture prisons in Ukraine, that President Emmanuel Macron's protege Gabriel Attal inherited a drug empire, or that the centrist candidate Edouard Philippe suffers from dementia.
A victory by one of these three candidates would signal that Paris will stay on its pro-Ukraine, pro-European course — making them a primary target for Russia.
Undermining them ahead of the April 2027 election could pave the way for a runoff between far-right Marine Le Pen and far-left Jean-Luc Melenchon.
Smearing France's pro-Ukraine candidates
Glucksmann, the co-leader of the center-left Place Publique (PP) party, ranks among the most decisively pro-Ukraine voices on the French political scene.
The social democratic MEP lambasted European leaders for not doing enough to help Kyiv and urged the seizure of immobilized Russian assets.
It comes as little surprise that he found himself one of the primary targets of Russian-backed disinformation.
In the summer, a fake story impersonating the French investigative outlet Blast claimed — even using AI-generated voices — that Glucksmann's partner, Lea Salame, tried to bribe the media into publishing positive stories about the candidate.
Blast journalists denied ever publishing the story, while Glucksmann denounced it as a Russian military intelligence (GRU) operation.
The attacks did not stop there.
VT Foreign Policy, a self-described "alternative media" outlet amplifying pro-Kremlin narratives, published a fake story on Aug. 29 alleging that Glucksmann has helped set up torture prisons in Georgia while working as an advisor to then-President Mikheil Saakashvili.
The fake story went on to allege that the French politician then used his experience to establish similar operations in Ukraine after the EuroMaidan Revolution, working with a military officer, now Ukraine's commander-in-chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi.
The site cited one source for the allegations: the Foundation to Battle Injustice, a front founded by the late Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin, which the EU has sanctioned as a Russian influence operations group.
Philippe, a former prime minister and the mayor of Le Havre who met Zelensky in Kyiv in May, was also targeted, with fake reports masquerading as the news channel BFM TV claiming he suffers from dementia.
Similar tactics were deployed to falsely claim that Attal, who served as prime minister under Macron, inherited a drug empire from his father.
The campaigns also sought to exploit domestic tensions. Fake reports detected by Bot Blocker on X alleged both that Attal supported the recent wave of student protests and that he accused Russia of orchestrating them.
Disinformation monitors say the method and apparent intent squarely point to Russia as the culprit.
Inside Russia's disinformation machine
Two notorious Russian-linked campaigns have targeted French elections.
Matryoshka, which pushes out a dozen false reports a day while posing as established media outlets or experts, is the most prolific, says Chine Labbe, the senior vice-president for partnerships and managing editor for Europe at NewsGuard.
"As of mid-October 2026, we had counted 89 fake Matryoshka reports targeting French presidential candidates."
The other is Storm-1516, a more sophisticated campaign linked to the GRU that uses generative AI to set up whole new websites.
"Since this summer, we have counted seven claims from this operation targeting French candidates, three of which imitated real news outlets," Labbe told the Kyiv Independent.
According to Viginum, the fake news stories targeting Philippe and Glucksmann in the summer were carried out by Storm-1516.
The same operation was behind more recent false reports — posing as the French environmental news site Reporterre — that Glucksmann spent over 2 million euros ($2.2 million) on private jet flights, the independent Gnida Project reported.
The fact that the three centrist, pro-Kyiv candidates are the main target of these operations is also a clear clue of Russian involvement.
"The false claims typically portray them as mentally unstable, corrupt, and generally unfit for office, echoing the Russian-backed false claims that have targeted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in recent years," Labbe said.
Paris has emerged as one of Kyiv's key military allies since Russia launched its full-scale war, providing long-range missiles, fighter jets, artillery, and more.
Macron has also played a leading role in the Coalition of the Willing, a group of nations committed to providing aid and post-war security guarantees to Ukraine. A victory by far-right or far-left candidates would likely call this role into question.
But support for Ukraine is far from the only issue that Russian disinformation seeks to exploit.
Amelie Jaques-Apke, a disinformation and foreign influence expert at Sciences Po's CEVIPOF research center, identifies the erosion of trust in French democratic institutions as the chief goal.
"Damaging individual candidates is the visible tactic. The more durable objective is to make whatever result emerges look illegitimate," Jaques-Apke told the Kyiv Independent.
However, the actual impact of these campaigns on French voters is more difficult to gauge. Viginum described the operations as "mediocre" and "lacking visibility."
"The real risk lies in amplification," Jaques-Apke says.
"These fakes gain reach when they are picked up by Russian officials or state media, by pro-Russian figures in the West, or when politicians denounce them loudly and unintentionally spread them further."
Furthermore, Russian disinformation continues to evolve, deploying generative AI to produce more convincing fakes, professionalizing its operations, and monetizing divisive content, the expert warns.
"(The campaigns') limited impact so far is therefore no guarantee for April."

Pakistan military 'cautiously optimistic' on Iran-US mediation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:24:05 UTC
04:24:05 KST

Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his first interview since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir – Pakistan's chief mediator in its efforts to de-escalate the now eight-month-old Iran war – has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
Pact does not bar new members
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
There were still "powerful spoilers and detractors," who believed conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan's armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the United States had backed the trip.
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defense pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. "We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict," he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi terror group has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.
Home front
On the home front, the federal government suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), on October 11 and detained Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.
The government had accused the provincial administration of failing to tackle militancy. The PTI rejected the allegations and said its government took part in counter-terrorism efforts. PTI leaders called the move a pretext to crush protests.
Asked if there would now be larger military-led campaigns in the province, Chaudhry said that was not how the army conducted counter-terrorism.
"Our counter-terrorism operations are based on what we call IBOs, intelligence-based operations... The tempo of the freedom of action of (those) IBOs will further increase," he said.
Independents backed by Khan’s PTI won the most directly elected seats in the February 2024 election but fell short of a majority. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was the only province controlled by Khan’s party.
Khan has been in jail since 2023, and his supporters see the military behind his imprisonment and the dismantling of the PTI. The army denies involvement in politics.

'A bullying atmosphere': UN's Israel obsession sidelines atrocities elsewhere, ex-UN official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:24:03 UTC
04:24:03 KST

In December 2024, More than a year after Hamas terrorists stormed the Gaza border area, killing civilians in their homes, Dr. Alice Jill Edwards, who then served as the UN special rapporteur on torture, toured the kibbutzim where the massacre occurred.
“It was a very eerie experience,” Edwards recalls.
“It was more than a year after that great suffering. And yet some of the flowers had started to emerge out of the rubble. That is one of the images that stays with me very profoundly.
“The other thing that I can’t forget was the amount of bullet holes in ordinary people’s houses,” she says. “I walked into houses where the microwave oven had been shot to pieces or the fridge. These were civilians.”
Her conclusion is blunt: “I think if you can’t have empathy for this, then I worry about people’s general humanity.”
For Edwards, who served as the UN special rapporteur on torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment from 2022 to 2026, the visit was an opportunity to see the consequences of the October 7, 2023, massacre for herself. It also reinforced a conviction that would increasingly put her at odds with colleagues within the international organization.
“This is entirely unlawful under international law,” she says of attacks against civilians. “There are no excuses or exceptions. There are no rights under international law for this type of attack against civilians.”
Edwards is no longer serving as the UN’s torture rapporteur. That distance from the institution, she says, has allowed her to speak more openly about what she considers a deeply troubling failure in the international response to October 7.
“Look, we just had the third anniversary of the attacks, and there was still no investigation or documentation or report on those events by two of my colleagues, yet we have also quite a number of reports, rightly, in relation to Israel’s actions,” she says.
Her accusation is not that Israel should be exempt from scrutiny. On the contrary, Edwards insists that alleged violations by Israeli forces must be investigated. Her objection is that the same standards should apply when the victims are Israeli, and the perpetrators are Hamas or other Palestinian armed groups.
Edwards did produce a report in the months after October 7, as did UN Special Representative on Sexual Violence in Conflict Pramila Patten. But what followed, in Edwards’s assessment, was a prolonged period in which the issue received insufficient attention.
“After that time, there’s been a very long lag,” she says. “There have been occasional references to Hamas activities in Gaza, but very few and often buried within reports about Israel’s activities.”
'No real excuses'
She identifies two colleagues in particular: the UN special rapporteur on violence against women and the special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories. In her view, both failed to engage adequately with the October 7 atrocities despite opportunities to do so.
“And I think that was deliberate,” Edwards says. “And I still think it is deliberate. There’s no real excuses for not having done so.”
Asked whether she had seen her colleagues attempt to interview survivors of sexual violence or other people who experienced the October 7 atrocities, Edwards answers simply: No.
“They had all the opportunities,” Edwards says of her colleagues’ responsibilities. “They are required to produce reports. They are required to engage in communications.”
One explanation offered for the lack of engagement, she says, was that Israel had not provided access. Edwards disputes that argument, noting that she herself was criticized for relying on Israeli information, even though she says her findings were based on independent sources rather than Israeli government material.
“It’s kind of a contradictory statement to say the reason we haven’t done it is because Israel wouldn’t give us the information and then to criticize me for relying on Israeli information,” she says.
For Edwards, the consequences of October 7 extend beyond the people murdered, wounded, or taken captive during the attack. They also include the families who were left wondering whether their loved ones were alive, where they were being held, and whether they would ever return home.
“Across all the many circumstances, including the very large-scale taking of 251 hostages on October the 7th, the family members themselves suddenly are launched into a situation of not knowing where their loved ones are, not having information about them,” she says. “That torment and distress is exactly what torture also is, psychological torture.”
'Obsession'
Her meetings with hostage families in Tel Aviv made that argument especially personal.
“It was very compelling to me when I was in Tel Aviv and met with some of the hostage families and the children of these hostages... four-year-olds who don’t know where their father is or their mother is, when they’re coming home, if they’re dead or alive; they can’t sleep at night.
“These are very traumatic experiences which can rise to the level of psychological torture,” she adds.
Her criticism of the UN extends beyond the handling of October 7. She believes the organization devotes disproportionate attention to Israel while failing to give comparable scrutiny to other conflicts in which civilians experience mass violence and abuse.
Asked about her use of the word “obsession” to describe the pattern, she defends the term.
“Yes, and I say it like this because every time Israel takes a step, does anything, there is a response,” she says.
She points to conflicts in Sudan, Yemen, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, arguing that grave violations elsewhere deserve much greater international attention.
“Do you know that there were 90,000 rapes in the DRC last year alone, documented and verified by the United Nations?” she asks.
According to the numbers she provides, there had been approximately 50 communications concerning Israel since October 7, compared with around 10 concerning Sudan. She says communications related to the war itself between Russia and Ukraine numbered in the mid-teens.
For Edwards, the figures raise a question about how international attention is distributed.
“Yes, we should be calling out governments; we should be calling out Israel for violations,” she says. “But we should also be making sure that we are being independent and impartial.”
The most troubling aspect, Edwards says, may be the atmosphere in which international human rights officials carry out their work.
She describes efforts by colleagues to soften the language of communications concerning October 7, followed by further attempts to prevent others from endorsing them.
“There were times when my colleagues, especially in the investigation on October the 7th, attempted to water down the language,” she says. “There were many, many efforts to change the language.”
Even after adjustments had been made, she says, there were efforts to ensure that other officials would not sign on.
“There was, and there is still, I think, an atmosphere of bullying and intimidation that you have one view only, and you cannot and should not be seeing the other side in the Israel-Palestine conflict,” Edwards says.
She believes that kind of environment undermines the very principles the UN is supposed to uphold.
“We should be able to do our work without feeling like if we speak out, there will be repercussions, there will be retaliation, that there will be consequences,” she says. “The atmosphere is such that it is very frightening to speak out.”
She describes a situation in which professionals may be excluded from events or sidelined in their work if they are perceived as holding the wrong position.
“Since I put out the article, I’ve had many lovely emails from people thanking me for speaking out,” Edwards says.
Some people, she adds, told her they had left the United Nations because they felt unable to perform their work in an atmosphere they believed should be grounded in human rights.
“We are in a dark space, I think,” she says.
A line of integrity
Edwards does not place primary responsibility for the situation on Secretary-General António Guterres. She says his influence over the conduct of individual rapporteurs was limited, although she believes stronger leadership would have been welcome.
“He’s also said it’s not his call. It would have been good to have more leadership,” she says.
She argues that the next secretary-general should make peacemaking and conflict prevention central priorities, alongside efforts to ensure that ceasefires and political settlements lead to a more secure future for people living through war.
The consequences of the dispute go beyond the UN’s human rights machinery. If Israel and other countries lose confidence in the organization’s impartiality, its ability to serve as a credible mediator in international conflicts may suffer.
“It’s regrettable the United Nations has been sidelined in the Middle East and in the Russia-Ukraine war,” she says. “That needs to be repaired with the new secretary-general.”
Yet Edwards also believes Israel has a role to play in restoring international confidence. She expresses disappointment at the lack of international observers in Gaza and at the absence of international access to prisons. She also suggests that Israel consider allowing international judges to participate in relevant judicial proceedings, without transferring the cases to an international court.
“It would be even better if that could be somehow adjusted to allow for international judges,” she says, suggesting that two international judges could participate.
“I think the reputation of Israel is also at an all-time low, and that needs to be improved so that they have the opening to be able to engage in a peace process,” she says.
She rejects the idea that her criticism of the UN should be understood as support for one side against another. Her work, she says, has involved investigating allegations against Israeli authorities over their treatment of Palestinian prisoners as well as examining abuses in other conflicts.
“In all the conflicts I deal with, we’re dealing with people, human beings who have families, who are living in communities,” she says.
“We must walk what I call a line of integrity, that when we see something, we investigate, we call it out when we can, we engage in quiet diplomacy or other strategies, and likewise if we see other violations.”
Her message is not that the organization should abandon its scrutiny of Israel. It is that the same commitment to evidence, empathy, and accountability must extend to every victim.
“I’m not biased towards one side or another side,” she says. “I want things to be fair.”

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:23:29 UTC
04:23:29 KST

A 23-person multinational delegation aiming to meet Palestinians in the West Bank during olive harvest season has been banned from entering the territory, The Guardian reported on Tuesday.
The group of French, Spanish, Luxembourgish, Swiss, Greek, Danish, Irish, and American delegates planned to attend Progressive International’s Second Ramallah Congress in November, hosted in partnership with Birzeit University.
According to the congress’s website, the program has participants “hear expert testimony, deliberate the economic and legal dimensions of occupation, and prepare a collective roadmap for urgent international action.”
British parliament member Sam Tarry, formerly with Labour, told The Guardian the group thought they had a “genuine chance of going across” the Allenby crossing with Jordan into the West Bank. However, authorities stopped and held the group for about nine hours before refusing them entry, without explaining why.
“They made a political decision very clearly based on the fact they didn’t want people to witness what’s been going on in the West Bank, especially ahead of the elections,” Tarry continued.
Labour Party parliament member Clive Lewis told The Guardian: “We were detained, taken aside and then interrogated. People were shouted at. We were asked why we were going in, what was happening, why our stories were one way or the other. The bottom line was it was a deeply unpleasant experience.”
'Turned away at the border with no reason'
UK Member of Parliament Lara Bird, who was among those detained and barred from entering the West Bank on Tuesday, said in a statement that she "came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away at the border with no reason given."
"It is more important now than ever that we bear witness and show our solidarity. But we were prevented from doing so," the statement read.
The Guardian reported they contacted the Israeli embassy for comment.
The prohibition came after Defense Minister Israel Katz instructed officials at the beginning of October to pursue administrative removal orders against activists whose activities were believed to threaten public order or security in the West Bank, following a request from Yesha Council chairman Yisrael Ganz.
In one incident following Katz's order, the IDF detained nearly 90 US, Israeli, and British volunteers aiming to help Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem in the West Bank, including New York congressional candidate Brad Lander. The IDF and Foreign ministry claimed that the group of volunteers did not coordinate their visit and activities ahead of time and were in a prohibited zone.
However, The Jerusalem Post received a copy of a letter sent by the organizers to coordinate their visit with the IDF nearly two months before the incident.
Increase in settler violence
Extreme Israeli nationalist attacks in the West Bank have been on the rise as the seasonal olive harvest has flared confrontations.
Earlier this month, the United Nations aid coordination office (OCHA) recorded at least 160 attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers in the West Bank during the first two weeks of the olive harvest. The UN report also claimed that the IDF and Israeli border police protected settlers and even participated in attacks on Palestinians.
The Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture claimed that attacks on olive trees and harvesters have resulted in $157 million in losses and the destruction of roughly 286,000 olive trees since he start of the war with Hamas in October 2023.
Amichai Stein and Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

Texas grand jury indicts ICE officer accused of running over man in Houston
The officer faces charges after allegedly striking a fleeing construction worker with an SUV during an immigration raid.
A grand jury in Texas has indicted a United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of deliberately running over a Mexican construction worker during an operation in Houston this month.
ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales faces charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for the October 10 incident, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced on Friday.
Criminal charges against federal immigration officers have been rare during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, although several encounters involving officers have prompted investigations.
Morales is accused of striking 48-year-old Miguel Parra-Hernandez, an immigrant who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years. Teare said that Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record.
Parra-Hernandez was running away from federal agents when an unmarked black Jeep Cherokee struck him in a car park near Clay Road and Highway 6, according to investigators. He suffered multiple fractures to his right leg and an ankle injury which required surgery.
The indictment follows a dispute between local prosecutors and federal authorities over what happened. ICE has maintained that Parra-Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, dismissing the allegations that the officer intentionally struck him as “reckless and false.”
But Teare has said surveillance video contradicts the agency’s account.
It shows the SUV crossing a median and pursuing Parra-Hernandez as he runs away. Although another vehicle obscures the moment of impact, the video shows the man on the ground moments later.
Authorities also released body-camera footage on Friday. In the recording, Morales can be heard acknowledging that he struck Parra-Hernandez with his vehicle.
Teare also accused federal authorities of failing to cooperate with the investigation, including by removing the Jeep before local investigators could examine it for potential evidence.
A search warrant obtained by local media shows investigators had not been granted access to the vehicle as of October 23.
The case has also raised questions about the operation’s intended target. ICE said agents were searching for a man identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, whom they believed to be travelling with Parra-Hernandez.
But Mendoza-Cervantes’s daughter told The New York Times that her father died in 2017. Parra-Hernandez’s family has disputed that the two men knew each other.
The Morales indictment comes as the Harris County District Attorney’s Office continues investigating the fatal shooting of another Mexican, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, on July 7.
An ICE officer, Gregory Feathers, has been accused of firing at the vehicle Salgado Araujo was driving on his way to work in Houston.
Federal authorities said the officer acted in self-defence, a claim the surviving passengers in the vehicle dispute.

Costa Rica’s Grynspan extends lead in informal UN chief poll, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
20:15:39 CET
04:15:39 KST

By Antoni Slodkowski
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Friday showed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan extended her lead as frontrunner in the race to become the 10th UN secretary-general, two people close to the process said.
Grynspan got 11 votes in favor and 4 against on the 15-member council, marking her strongest showing in seven closed-door ballots conducted in recent months to replace Antonio Guterres as he finishes his second five-year term this year.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in US contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body’s declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
Securing the council’s recommendation will require a formal vote, expected once one candidate shows a strong chance of prevailing, with at least nine positive votes and no “discourage” votes from the five permanent members — France, Britain, the US, Russia and China. Friday’s ballot did not show how those five members voted.
Five of six polls in recent months showed Grynspan, 70, narrowly ahead, with one poll in August placing Guyana’s UN ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett in the top spot.
On Friday, Rodrigues-Birkett received eight votes in favor, coming in third, while Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, the director general of the UN nuclear watchdog, came in second with nine “encourage” votes.
Friday also marked the first poll since United Arab Emirates diplomat Lana Nusseibeh entered the race, but the Middle Eastern contender and former ambassador to the UN came in fourth with seven votes in favor, six against and two marked as “no opinion.”
When Guterres was chosen in October 2016, it took six straw polls for the council to reach agreement.
In the more than 80-year history of the UN, there has never been a female secretary-general.
In an interview earlier this month, the Costa Rican economist told Reuters that the UN has become too risk-averse and its next leader must be prepared to bear the cost of diplomatic failure and to try again.
(Reporting by Antoni Slodkowski; Editing by Edmund Klamann)

Authorities suspended classes in Raqqa, Hasakah and Deir al-Zor on Thursday, while forecasters warned unsettled weather could continue into Saturday.

Sanctioned Tankers Carry Russian Diesel Toward US Under Trump-Putin Deal

Sanctioned Tankers Carry Russian Diesel Toward US Under Trump-Putin Deal
Six tankers carrying approximately 288,000 tons of Russian diesel fuel are heading to the United States, marking the first shipments under an agreement reached between US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin on October 9, according to Greenpeace Ukraine.
The environmental organization identified the vessels and published their locations on a new interactive map, allowing the public to monitor their movements in real time.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Greenpeace warned that the shipments violate European sanctions and are illegal under US law, calling for the tankers to change course.
According to the organization, the deliveries are taking place amid increased secrecy surrounding Russia’s energy exports following a decree signed by Putin on September 28, 2026.
The decree restricts the publication and use of detailed information about Russian oil and energy exports, including prices, trading partners, transportation routes, terminals, storage facilities, and customs data.
Greenpeace argued that the restrictions are intended to conceal shipments and help Russia circumvent international sanctions designed to limit the revenue Moscow uses to finance its war against Ukraine.
“Every shipment of Russian diesel comes at a price—human lives. Every dollar that flows into Russia can finance new attacks, new destruction, and new deaths. These shipments also undermine the international sanctions regime and send a dangerous message: business with Russia can continue as usual, despite its war against Ukraine. Human lives must matter more than fossil fuel profits!” said Polina Kolodiazhna, an energy campaigner at Greenpeace Ukraine.
To increase transparency, Greenpeace launched a tracking platform displaying information about vessels transporting Russian diesel, with additional shipments to be added as new data becomes available.
The organization identified six tankers currently being tracked: Taurus, Agioi Fanendes, Talisman, Leruo, Iblea, and Primorye. Three of them—Talisman, Leruo, and Primorye—are subject to sanctions imposed by several countries, with Talisman having been under US restrictions since January 2025.
However, the organization cautioned that Russian tankers operating under sanctions frequently provide inaccurate shipping information or change their declared destinations during voyages.
According to Greenpeace, the shipments are the first deliveries under an agreement reached between Trump and Putin on October 9.
The reported agreement provides for the supply of 300,000 tons of Russian diesel, equivalent to approximately 2.25 million barrels, to US and global markets. Further deliveries are reportedly planned, including an additional 500,000 tons in November 2026, followed by another 1 million tons.
The reported shipments have also drawn criticism in the United States, with New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill considering measures to prevent Russian diesel from entering a port in her state.
As KYW Newsradio reported on October 29, Sherrill is weighing the possibility of blocking one of the shipments, criticizing the Trump administration’s fuel agreement with Russia over its failure to reduce energy costs for American consumers.
“Donald Trump isn’t doing anything to bring down gas prices, diesel prices, or costs,” Sherrill stated. “Instead, he is lining Vladimir Putin’s pockets at the expense of American consumers and our democratic ally Ukraine.”

Mark Carney puts deadline on EU ‘associate membership’ push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:11:14 UTC
04:11:14 KST

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney arrives to a roundtable event at the EU-Canada summit in Montreal, on Oct. 29, 2026. | Pool photo by Christopher Katsarov/ AFP via Getty Images
MONTREAL — Canada embraced the European Union’s offer of “associate membership” after a two-day summit at which Brussels and Ottawa gave themselves until next June to work out what their new relationship will look like.
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s endorsement of the proposal by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen followed weeks of hesitation, a hostile response from U.S. President Donald Trump and pushback from EU heavyweight Germany.
“In the coming months, we will determine the full substance, scale, and scope of this new form of membership,” Carney told a press conference on Friday at the end of the two-day summit at the Port of Montreal.
Advertisement
“Today, we move towards associate membership for Canada,” Carney said, describing it as “the deepest possible partnership short of accession.”
The two sides have set a June 2027 deadline to determine the terms and boundaries of their intensifying relationship — an alliance that comes with a payment schedule. Carney danced around a question pressing him on how much associate membership will cost the Canadian public.
“We don’t view this as paying, personally,” Carney said, stressing the alliance as a “positive” project.
Von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa, standing either side of Carney, presented the experiment as a necessary survival strategy to thrive in an increasingly dangerous world.
“The concept of an associate member is uncharted territory but we have the ambition, trust and creativity to shape it together,” Von der Leyen told reporters. “To be crystal clear, this is not a partnership against anybody, but for our common strength.”
Canadian government officials who spoke to reporters after the press conference confirmed legislation won’t be necessary to legitimize Canada’s EU associate membership status.
Advertisement
“Our relationship is so special that we want to create something new — to go beyond a simple association, everything short of a full EU membership,” said Costa, pitching a new model for non-European countries to integrate more closely with the bloc. “Our association will be the closest, deepest and most unique of its kind.”
Irritants persist
Despite the upbeat rhetoric, some longstanding trade disputes remained unresolved after the summit.
The issue remains part of ongoing trade discussions, one official said, noting progress in addressing what Canada views as flaws in the legislation. The officials were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic and trade negotiations.
Another irritant has been whether Canada would qualify for “Made in Europe” status under the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act, a landmark measure that would seek to channel public procurement spending in sectors ranging from green energy to automotive toward locally produced goods.
Von der Leyen said the regulation proposed earlier this year by the Commission foresaw including Canada as a free-trade partner, but added that it was now subject to review by EU lawmakers and governments.
Advertisement
“The Industrial Accelerator Act has been proposed by the Commission to include all countries with whom we have free-trade agreements. So automatically Canada would be in,” she said in response to a question.
“Of course now the proposal has to go through the co-legislative process. But our proposal is very clear in including Canada.”
Despite months of preparations, the summit itself was chaotic, with agenda details confirmed at short notice and bilateral meetings split between two locations. The informal arrangements were intended to encourage more face time between EU commissioners and Canadian ministers, who are set to see much more of each other.
Canadian ministers have been invited to attend more meetings with their EU counterparts as part of a plan to deepen political alignment. Recent participation by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu in informal EU meetings has served as a trial run.
Carney himself is expected in Dublin in two weeks, having accepted Costa’s invitation to join an informal European Council meeting.

Evacuation convoys from Russian-occupied Oleshky split toward Ukraine and Russia, officials say
Evacuation convoys carrying residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast have separated, with some heading toward Ukrainian-controlled territory and others toward Russia, Ukrainian and Russian officials said on Oct. 30.
Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said he was continuing to personally coordinate the humanitarian mission and was heading back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Earlier, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova said that buses carrying evacuees had reached Armiansk in Russian-occupied Crimea, where they were to split into two convoys.
The Ukrainian delegation had traveled to Oleshky via Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, from where they reportedly flew to Belarus before continuing by bus to Ukrainian-controlled territory, David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary faction, said earlier on Oct. 30.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Despite efforts by the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and even Pope Leo XIV, a ceasefire agreement has only come about since the intervention of Melania Trump.
Twenty-five buses with a combined capacity of 750 passengers, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility, had been prepared to evacuate residents from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Lubinets said.
Lubinets's statement came amid reports that Russia had begun evacuating residents ahead of the agreed date.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," Lubinets said.
Lubinets and Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova held a joint press briefing in Armiansk, Russian-occupied Crimea, ahead of the evacuation from Oleshky.
Lubinets said the Ukrainian and Russian delegations were accompanied by media representatives from three countries. However, photos published by Ukraine's Ombudsman's Office show predominantly Russian media outlets.
Around 11:30 a.m. Kyiv time, the Ukrainian delegation had safely reached Oleshky, and the ceasefire had been in effect for 80 hours and was still holding, Lubinets said.
Lubinets added that he was speaking with local residents to hear about their needs and understand what kind of assistance they required most.
Arakhamia said around noon that humanitarian aid had been delivered to Oleshky and that "technical support" was being provided to those wishing to evacuate.
Lantratova also confirmed on social media that the evacuation from Oleshky had begun, with people gradually boarding buses. She added that some residents wanted to travel to Russia, while others wished to go to Ukrainian-controlled territory, without specifying how many people were in each group.
Following the separation of the convoys, Lubinets proposed making humanitarian missions coordinated by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump a regular initiative, saying the operation in Oleshky demonstrated that such agreements could help civilians.
