Russia has damaged more than 800 Ukrainian energy assets since September
Russia has carried out more than 350 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since September, damaging more than 800 pieces of equipment, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said on Friday.
The strikes are increasing pressure on the country’s power system as the heating season approaches. Ukraine is stepping up efforts to protect energy facilities while expanding generation capacity to reduce the impact of further attacks on an already crippled system after years of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Speaking during a question-and-answer session with the government in parliament, Shmyhal said the damaged equipment included facilities at substations and power generation sites.
He said a second level of physical protection had been built for 235 transformers. According to the minister, only one piece of protected equipment had been hit by a ballistic missile over the past six months.
"Without this protection, restoring energy facilities under the current intensity of Russian attacks would take months," Shmyhal said.
Alongside protecting existing infrastructure, Ukraine is working to expand its electricity generation capacity through smaller, decentralized power plants.
On Oct. 29, the government approved the mechanism and terms for providing almost Hr 939 million ($20 million) in loan financing from the Finnish-Ukrainian Investment Fund to state-owned energy company Ukrnafta.
The funding will support four projects to install gas-engine power plants in the western Ivano-Frankivsk and Lviv oblasts, adding around 60 megawatts of capacity to Ukraine’s power system, Shmyhal reported.
The money will cover the purchase of the power plants and related equipment, as well as installation, testing and commissioning. The loans were raised for Ukraine’s state budget under a framework agreement between the Ukrainian and Finnish governments signed in November 2024.
The projects are part of broader efforts to develop distributed generation, spreading electricity production across multiple locations rather than relying solely on large power plants.

Can Russia’s independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta rise from the ashes a third time? Editor Sergey Sokolov discusses what comes next.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
19:10:31 UTC
04:10:31 KST

Can Russia’s independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta rise from the ashes a third time? Editor Sergey Sokolov discusses what comes next.
On the morning of October 30, Novaya Gazeta said it was closing. The day before, its journalists said the newspaper was being evicted from its office on Potapovsky Lane in central Moscow, where it had been based for 29 years. In recent years, Novaya Gazeta had somehow managed to keep working inside Russia despite searches, website blocks, the revocation of its newspaper registration, a show trial of investigative reporter Oleg Roldugin, and the newspaper itself being labeled a “foreign agent.”
Novaya Gazeta’s editor-in-chief, Sergey Sokolov, has worked at the newspaper since its founding in 1993. In an interview with the outlet Bereg, he spoke about how the staff had weathered the past few years, what the final straw was, and what the journalists plan to do next. Meduza is publishing the interview in full.
‘Novaya Gazeta has already shut down twice. I’ve grown a thick skin by now’
— As I understand it, you and your colleagues decided to close Novaya Gazeta on October 26. What have the past few days been like for you?
— I couldn’t tell you exactly when we made that decision. It’s all a blur. Yes, we made that decision because right now we have absolutely no idea how we’re going to get by, or what we’re going to live on.
We’re being given a month to move out — they’re threatening to seal off our floor if we don’t get out in time. We’ve been here for 29 years and built up collections of books donated by our readers, archives, keepsakes, the Politkovskaya museum, and the Novaya Gazeta museum. Now we’re rushing to move everything out and find somewhere else to set up shop.
On top of that, they cut off our access to the donation platform we depended on. That left us with no way to support ourselves at all. All of this happened essentially in a single day. There’s no doubt this is a coordinated effort to destroy Novaya Gazeta once and for all. The current government and the security services have destroyed it.
That’s why we announced that Novaya Gazeta is no more. We’re working until November 9 — fulfilling our last obligation to our readers. Then we’re shutting down the servers and heading out into the street, with nowhere to go.
— What have you been through since you realized you were closing?
— Novaya Gazeta has already shut down twice. I’ve been at this newspaper since its earliest days, so personally, I’ve grown a thick skin by now. Every time Novaya Gazeta has shut down, it has eventually come back. We’ve risen from the ashes before.
The question is when it [the relaunch] will happen — in a month or in years. We can’t say. But we have the most important thing, something nobody can take away: our team, even though circumstances have scattered us across different countries. We have our convictions. We have our memories, our history. Nobody can seal those off. So when it becomes possible, we’ll try to bring Novaya Gazeta back.
— How’s the staff doing right now?
— Running ourselves ragged. We’re still publishing stories and posting on YouTube and Telegram. At the same time, we’re packing up everything we can to save it and move it out.
— I’d like to ask about the circumstances of the closure…
— The circumstances are very simple. We got together, weighed all the factors, and made the decision as a group. We don’t make decisions in secret — it was all done openly. When the online publication Novaya Gazeta was labeled a “foreign agent,” we knew perfectly well this might come up.
Even then, we said [among ourselves] that if the state escalated things any further, we wouldn’t survive. That’s what happened — they took away our office and our means of supporting ourselves. And we didn’t survive. After that, it became impossible to work.
‘Our banks do as they’re told, because today you’re a banker, and tomorrow you’re on a prison bunk’
— The Economist reported that unidentified people entered Novaya Gazeta’s office overnight on October 25–26, and that the next morning, you and Dmitry Muratov gathered the staff in the basement of a neighboring building and asked them to leave their phones outside. Muratov then said Novaya Gazeta could be designated an extremist organization, and the journalists collectively decided it was time to close the publication. Is that how it happened?
— You know, I’m not prepared to comment on other media outlets’ reporting. It’s true that we met away from the office. A lot was said there, and I can’t remember it all now. People shared a wide range of views and information. In any case, the completely reliable information is what’s in our statement.
— Did unidentified people enter Novaya Gazeta’s office?
— I won’t comment on that.
— How likely did you think it was that Novaya Gazeta would be designated an extremist organization?
— I won’t comment on that. As I said, that’s another media outlet’s report, and I won’t comment on it. As for whether someone said that in the heat of the discussion, I don’t remember.
— What other risks did you see for the staff if the publication kept working?
— I don’t want to answer that question, because the answer would give the people persecuting us a cheat sheet. Let them figure it out themselves.
— Did you or your colleagues get any indication from the authorities that this was definitely the end?
— No, we haven’t had any dealings with the authorities for quite some time. We’re toxic to them, and the feeling is mutual. We received an official letter terminating our lease and notices from the banks saying they would no longer work with us. That was the extent of the official contact.
— How did the landlord explain the decision to terminate the lease?
— The explanation was simple: They have the right to terminate the lease, and they’re terminating it. The thing is, the building isn’t privately owned. It belongs to Moscow City Hall. I’m not prepared to interpret the details of the contracts, because I’m not a lawyer.
— Could you tell me a little more about the donation system being cut off — who cut it off, and what explanation did they give?
— They cited some internal corporate rules. I know perfectly well these aren’t internal corporate rules — they’re rules imposed from outside. They were told to do it. Our banks do as they’re told, because today you’re a banker, and tomorrow you’re on a prison bunk. I assume they simply saluted and obeyed orders from people in uniform. Other banks and payment-processing platforms we approached also refused to work with us, citing the same thing. That tells me all organizations of this kind were told not to work with us.
I don’t want to name the particular people who turned us down, because it’s not their fault — it’s their misfortune. Everyone in the Russian Federation is in the same predicament. And holding them responsible would, if you’ll forgive the repetition, be irresponsible.
— Am I right that, under the current circumstances, you can’t launch any kind of fundraiser?
— Yes, we don’t have the technical means to do that. The only option is for people to send payments directly using our bank details. But that’s unlikely to work for long or on a regular basis.
— So there’s no normal way to keep this going inside Russia anymore.
— It’s impossible to work, and foreign banking services don’t operate in the Russian Federation.
‘The hardest part was being unable to cover the central tragedy unfolding before our eyes’
— After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, many independent journalists left Russia. Why did Novaya Gazeta decide to stay at that point?
— We were thinking about what to do next. We held a staff meeting, and opinions were divided. Some people thought we couldn’t keep working under the censorship that had been imposed right away. Others thought we could.
We didn’t know what to do, so we asked our readers. Because we have people who are in this with us — the people who gave us money, our core audience. We asked them what we should do. More than 90% wrote back saying we needed to keep working, because there were lots of things they couldn’t live without knowing. They wanted to stay informed.
So those [staff members] who felt they couldn’t work here left the country and are involved in all kinds of projects. Those who felt it was possible to keep working here stayed.
We’ve worked throughout these years of war, trying to comply with every law of the Russian Federation, even the monstrous ones, so we could keep our readers informed and fulfill our professional duty.
— It’s impossible to imagine the pressure you kept working under all this time. How did it affect the publication’s work — what did you feel personally?
— It’s hard for me to sort out my own feelings. It was truly grueling, exhausting work. It was creative work, so it was interesting. We did a lot. I’m not ashamed of a single article or a single film.
We did what we could to fill the gap in coverage, because nobody knows what’s actually happening in Russia.
— What was the hardest part for the staff during that time?
— Our newsroom is full of strong personalities, so everyone would probably have a different answer to that question. My answer is this: For me, the hardest part was that we can’t cover the central tragedy unfolding before our eyes.
— But you covered its consequences quite successfully, I think.
— We certainly cover the consequences for the country and the world. That’s what we had a duty to do, and that’s what we did.
— Do you believe it’s still possible to practice independent journalism inside Russia today?
— You can count the independent media outlets left in Russia on one hand — both national and regional. They’re hanging on for now. And I wish them every success. We’ll give them all the help we can.
But I think the aim is to destroy the entire information landscape, so that the surviving outlets paint a picture of a country completely unlike the Russia people actually live in.
‘The search of my apartment turned up nothing but dust’
— What will happen to Novaya Gazeta’s archive?
— We’re moving it. The archive will be preserved.
— You’re not saying where yet?
— Why would I? It’ll be stored somewhere.
— A memorial plaque honoring Anna Politkovskaya has been on the facade of your office for 13 years. Aren’t you afraid it’ll be taken down?
— First of all, we’re not afraid of anything — they’ve trained that feeling out of us.
And second, Anna Politkovskaya’s memorial plaque was installed following a decision by Moscow City Hall. Removing it would also require a decision by City Hall. No one else can intervene in that process. So that’s a question for the Moscow city government, not us.
— Is there anything in the office that’s especially precious to you, something you can save and take with you despite the closure?
— Everything we’re moving out now: our archives, both our museums, our collection of back issues, and gifts from readers. It’s not the desks we’re worried about.
— Is there perhaps one object that symbolizes the newspaper for you?
— For me, the people symbolize the newspaper. Keeping our team together will be our first priority. Even keepsakes are just things.
— How many people work at Novaya Gazeta now?
— About 50 staff members, plus a sizable number of freelancers and contributors.
— Do you know what will happen to them after the closure?
— We don’t know the answer to that yet. Right now, we’re dealing with an urgent move. Then we’ll sit down and think. What’s clear is that work under the Novaya Gazeta name has stopped.
— In October, you were questioned in connection with the case against your colleague Oleg Roldugin, and your home was searched. Aren’t you concerned about facing criminal prosecution?
— My home was searched in connection with a case being handled by the Interior Ministry’s Investigative Committee. I’m a witness in that case. It directly concerns Oleg Roldugin, who worked under me.
It was only to be expected that I’d be questioned in this case. I have no concerns about it, because I gave a full account in my testimony. The search of my apartment turned up nothing but dust. So I don’t see anything out of the ordinary about it.
— Would you consider leaving the country?
— As I said, we’re not making plans yet — there are immediate tasks we need to deal with. We don’t know what we’ll do next, because we don’t know what’s going to happen in this country. I suspect nobody does.

retro cocktail bar with multi-chrome lighting and curved steel hides behind barcelona focacceria
behind a neighborhood focacceria storefront on barcelona's carrer tuset, designer isern serra completes focacha, a speakeasy cocktail lounge inspired by space age and verner panton's visiona.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ISERN SERRA CONCEALS RETRO COCKTAIL BAR BEHIND FOCACCERIA
Designed by Isern Serra for hospitality group Grupo La Confitería (led by Lito Baldovinos and Enric Rebordosa), Focacha is a speakeasy cocktail bar situated at Carrer Tuset 17 in Barcelona. The venue pays programmatic and aesthetic homage to the city’s 1960s and 1970s intellectual counterculture, the ‘gauche divine,’ and night-life figure Oriol Regàs, founder of the historic Bocaccio club. Concealed behind a traditional focacceria storefront designed by Pichy Glass, patrons access the venue through an operable refrigerator door, transitioning from a vernacular culinary retail interior into an immersive two-zone lounge modeled after Verner Panton’s 1968 Visiona installation.
CHROMATIC bar interiors PAY HOMAGE TO VERNER PANTON’S VISIONA
The interior layout, developed by designer Isern Serra, divides into two distinct spatial volumes. The initial bar area is wrapped in continuous carpeting across the floor, walls, and ceiling, establishing a monomaterial envelope referencing Verner Panton’s 1968 Visiona installation. At the center of the room, a curved stainless-steel bar features rounded edge profiles that catch and redistribute ambient reflections. Surrounding the counter, seven distinct seating modules transition across a calibrated chromatic gradient from yellow to crimson and deep blue. Along the perimeter, curvilinear niches recessed into the upholstered walls accommodate both functional back-bar bottle shelving and secluded, low-slung banquette seating. Multi-Lite pendants by GUBI suspend directly overhead, illuminating the metallic work surfaces while highlighting the contrast between the reflective steel counter and the dense, sound-dampening textile surfaces.
DOMED DJ LOUNGE INTEGRATES SCENOGRAPHIC LIGHTING design
The second spatial volume hosts the DJ room, creating a Retro-Futuristic setting. A circular portal cuts through the carpeted wall plane, transitioning into the adjoining music and DJ lounge. Centered under an organic vaulted dome, the volume explores Space Age aesthetics through fluid geometry and enveloping surfaces. Scenographic lighting systems are concealed within circular ceiling apertures and perimeter wall openings, allowing the light temperature and color spectrum to shift dynamically in response to musical tempo. Period-specific luminaires anchor the perimeter seating arrangements, including Louis Poulsen Panthella floor lamps, &Tradition Flowerpot VP2 pendants, and Wire Stool VP11 units, while a central Dana lamp by Tacchini acts as a sculptural focal point beneath the plaster canopy.

Influenza vaccination in Ukraine is delayed — the Ministry of Health cited the reasons
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
21:06:13 EET
04:06:13 KST

Influenza vaccination in Ukraine is delayed — the Ministry of Health cited the reasons
Kyiv • UNN
The supply of influenza vaccines is delayed due to the switch to trivalent vaccines and production difficulties. The Ministry of Health expects them in November 2026.
As of the end of October, the supply of influenza vaccines to Ukrainian pharmacies has been delayed due to the global transition to trivalent vaccines following WHO recommendations. At the same time, the Ministry of Health assured that as of October 30 there was no shortage of other vaccines. This was stated in the Ministry of Health's response to a request from UNN.
Details
The Ministry of Health reported that as of October 30, influenza vaccination in the 2026–2027 epidemic season had not yet begun.
According to information from manufacturers' representatives, the start of vaccine deliveries to Ukraine's retail network is expected in November 2026. The delivery timelines were affected by the transition from quadrivalent to trivalent vaccines in accordance with updated recommendations from the World Health Organization, the later availability of materials and reagents for quality control, as well as production difficulties involving certain vaccines
At the same time, the ministry noted that similar changes to delivery schedules are also being observed in a number of other European countries. Measures are currently being taken to facilitate the fastest possible arrival of vaccines in Ukraine.
The agency also assured that as of October 30, stocks of other vaccines included in the mandatory vaccination schedule were sufficient. Vaccination is carried out according to age.
The ministry said that during the same period last year — by the 43rd week of 2025 — 6,123 people had been vaccinated against influenza. During 2025, 20,000 doses of influenza vaccine were supplied through humanitarian aid programs. This figure covers the entire year of 2025 and does not reflect the total volume of supplies through all channels for the comparable period in question.
In addition, the Ministry of Health said that supplies of medical immunobiological products for preventive vaccinations included in the Schedule are funded from the State Budget of Ukraine, while vaccinations based on epidemic indications are funded from local budgets and other sources not prohibited by law.
Influenza vaccinations are recommended. At the same time, the Schedule provides for their administration based on health status and epidemic indications. Vaccinations based on health status are mandatory as part of the medical care of patients with the diseases and conditions specified in the Schedule. Currently, centralized procurement of seasonal influenza vaccines using funds from the State Budget of Ukraine is not carried out. Vaccines are supplied to the Ukrainian market on a commercial basis and may be purchased by citizens themselves, using funds from local budgets and other sources not prohibited by law. Local executive authorities and local self-government bodies, within their powers, may provide for the purchase of influenza vaccines and vaccination of designated target groups under the relevant local programs. The volumes and timelines of commercial vaccine supplies to Ukraine, including additional batches, are determined by importers in accordance with market demand, orders from pharmacy chains and healthcare facilities, and manufacturers' capabilities. Vaccines are distributed among regions by suppliers in accordance with the orders received
The ministry also said that influenza vaccination is primarily recommended for people at increased risk of severe disease and complications: young children starting at six months of age, older people, pregnant women, women planning to become pregnant during the epidemic season, patients with chronic diseases, as well as healthcare workers and other people at increased occupational risk of infection.

An explosion occurred at a Spanish plant producing shells for Ukraine – media
Kyiv • UNN
A waste incineration area exploded at a gunpowder plant in Granada. Two people suffered minor injuries, while a trade union reports three injured.
An explosion occurred at a plant in Granada, Spain, in the morning of October 30. The plant produces ammunition supplied to Ukraine. This is reported by ABC, according to UNN.
Details
The incident occurred at around nine o’clock in the morning on Friday, October 30, and, according to preliminary data, no one sustained serious injuries. The 112 emergency service reported that, based on the initial information they had received, the matter concerned the provision of medical assistance for minor injuries in any event. Sources in the National Police, for their part, do not currently know the cause of the explosion
In particular, the 112 service reported that the first of “numerous reports” arrived at around nine in the morning and warned of a “powerful explosion” in the area. It was soon confirmed that the explosion had occurred at a gunpowder plant, specifically in the waste-incineration area.
In addition, emergency services arrived at the scene and launched an emergency rescue operation there. However, sources contacted by the publication emphasize that they have not yet received any information indicating that anyone suffered serious injuries as a result of the explosion.
The National Police later confirmed that two people sustained minor injuries as a result of the explosion, including hearing damage. The UGT trade union, however, claims that there were three injured people.
As the publication writes, since the invasion of Ukraine, one of the main activities of the enterprise located in Granada has been the production of ammunition of various sizes and rocket components for supply to Ukraine.

In Germany, three construction machines burned down overnight into Friday at the construction site of defense company Rheinmetall near “Kassel-Calden” Airport.

J&K HC asks Rajouri admin to report on Pakistan-born teen's return to Indian father

IN BRIEF: How humanitarian mission in Alyoshki went
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:59:26 UTC
03:59:26 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Some residents of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region travelled freely towards Russia, while the others travelled to Ukraine, said Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova.
TASS has compiled the key facts about the humanitarian mission.
Lantratova's statements
- Lantratova said that Alyoshki residents thanked all parties for carrying out the humanitarian mission: "It's very important that people waited, they thank both sides."
- According to her, some of the residents travelled "absolutely unhindered" towards Russia, the others to Ukraine: "People gathered, families with children, the elderly, and buses were organized."
- She said that the residents took their pets with them.
- Humanitarian aid was provided to those who were unable to leave the town due to various circumstances.
- Lantratova said that everything was going on normally: "Both offices of the ombudspersons are monitoring the situation."
- She noted the contribution of the First Lady of the United States Melania Trump to the organization of the humanitarian mission: "This is very important to us, and we thank the First Lady for helping people, for saving lives."
Statements by the Ukrainian ombudsman
- Ukraine’s Ombudsman Dmitry Lubinets declared full observance of the silence regime in the Kherson direction and the absence of any violations from the moment of its establishment: "We came to Alyoshki as safely as was possible in the current conditions. The silence regime is fully respected. I emphasize that there have been no violations since the establishment of the silence regime."
- He said that residents of the city who did not have time to submit an evacuation request can still leave the town: " "There are already cases when people who did not sign up came - they were also given the opportunity: ‘Please, come in if you want to leave Alyoshki’."
Lubinets highly appreciated the work of Lantratova's team in Alyoshki, noting high professionalism of the staff: "Yana Valeryevna's staff, together with my staff, have worked out a very systematic approach. And today we are really here, on the ground, seeing how everything works. This is why I rate the organization of the work as very professional, for which I am especially grateful to Yana Valeryevna."
Preparation of the humanitarian corridor
- On the evening of October 29, the Russian military completed the clearance of routes for the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- The Dnepr battlegroup neutralized the roads adjacent to the town from unexploded ordnance, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- Two people, including a field engineer, were killed while demining to ensure the safe passage of a humanitarian mission, Lantratova said.
- According to the ministry, field engineer of the 98th Guards Airborne Division, Sergeant Andrey Vedernikov was killed.
- Earlier, the Defense Ministry said that Ukraine was remotely mining access roads with drones to prevent the evacuation of civilians and block the delivery of food, medicines and socially important goods to the town.
On conducting a humanitarian operation
- The humanitarian mission in Alyoshki is taking place in full compliance with the agreements between Russia and Ukraine, Melania Trump said.
- In the town, Lantratova and Lubinets coordinated the implementation of the agreements reached with the assistance of the First Lady of the United States.
- The Alyoshki residents who decided to leave the settlement could do so before 2:00 p.m. Moscow time (11:00 a.m. GMT).
- The distribution of humanitarian aid was scheduled for after 2:30 p.m. Moscow time (11:30 a.m. GMT)..
- All security measures were taken.
- According to Lantratova, several dozen tons of humanitarian aid were distributed to the residents of Alyoshki - food, hygiene products, fuel for generators and other necessary things. The list of what is needed was compiled at the request of the residents.
- She noted that it is important for those who decided to stay in the settlement.
- Lantratova said that the ombudspersons of Russia and Ukraine are considering regular delivery of humanitarian aid to Alyoshki.
- Chairman of the Russian Red Cross Pavel Savchuk said that the RCC provided humanitarian aid to the people in Alyoshki. The cargo was delivered by the office of Russia’s ombudsman as part of a humanitarian mission.
Evacuation of the people
- A humanitarian aid convoy was sent to the central district hospital.
- It consisted of 25 buses, Lantratova said.
- Special buses for bedridden people with 30 seats and nine ambulances were also prepared.
- A separate bus was also organized for people with pets.
- On the afternoon of October 30, Lantratova said that all those who expressed the desire to leave Alyoshki were placed on the evacuation buses.
- According to her, people traveled to both Russia and Ukraine.
- On October 26, Lantratova called Kiev's statements about the forced removal of children from Alyoshki unacceptable.
- The ombudswoman called on Ukraine to give the residents of Alyoshki the opportunity to make an informed decision, let them live in peace and order their military to stop the daily shelling of the town and mining roads.
The work of journalists
- According to Lantratova, more than 50 journalists from different countries arrived in the Kherson Region to cover the operation.
- As the ombudswoman noted, all of them will be able to personally communicate with the residents of Alyoshki.
- The humanitarian mission in the city was documented, among others, by Newsmax journalists.
- Melania Trump said they act as neutral observers, will independently film and document the progress of the mission.
- One of the American journalists from the mission, John Chay, said that he was in touch with the first lady of the United States.
Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he considers the presence of Russian, not foreign, journalists to be the key to covering the humanitarian mission.
Coordination of the humanitarian operation in Alyoshki
- According to Lantratova, the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki has been prepared since May.
- As previously reported by Russia’s Chief of the General Staff, Army General Valery Gerasimov, Russian troops will introduce a ceasefire regime in the Kherson direction from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 for the humanitarian operation.
- Ukraine’s General Staff also said it was complying with the ceasefire from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27.
- Lantratova later said that the temporary ceasefire in the Kherson direction would last until 10:59 p.m. Moscow time (7:59 p.m. GMT) on November 1.
- Since the beginning of the silence regime, she has been reporting daily on its observance by both sides.
Reaction to the announcement of the ceasefire
- Lantratova thanked Melania Trump and all the participants of the negotiating group for their cooperation in organizing a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed the agreement, his official representative Stephane Dujarric said in a statement.
- White House Communications Director Steven Cheung called the agreements an important step towards resolving the Ukrainian conflict.
The situation in Alyoshki
- On September 21, Peskov called the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki critical.
- It was impossible to bring food or medicines to the town due to shelling and drone attacks from Kiev.
- On September 1, a determined attempt was made to break the blockade of Alyosha to deliver humanitarian aid to the people, but Ukrainian militants fired at a convoy of vehicles and almost completely destroyed the cargo, said Rodion Miroshnik, Ambassador-at-large of the Russian Foreign Ministry for crimes of the Kiev regime.
- A little more than 1,000 people remain in Alyoshki, he informed.
- Miroshnik noted that the situation has worsened in the last four to five months.
- Residents of nearby settlements on the left bank of the Dnepr River tried to deliver food to Alyoshki, but Ukraine prevented this, evacuated resident Svetlana Popova told TASS.
- According to her, the civilian population of the city did not receive humanitarian aid from Ukraine, all reports about this are lies.

Defense forces use drones to destroy Russian Mi-8 helicopter in Luhansk region
According to Ukrinform, the Third Army Corps reported this on Telegram.
“During a raid on enemy logistics, a crew operating a ‘Hornet’ kamikaze UAV from the SKYFOM strike wing platoon of the Unmanned Systems Battalion detected an enemy Mi-8 and flew out to intercept it. The enemy was forced to change course in the air,” the statement reads.
Since the Russian helicopter’s cruising speed exceeded that of the attack drones, the soldiers waited for it to land. They then struck the area around the fuel tanks, and a second “Hornet” drone confirmed that the target had been destroyed.
“As a result of the attack, the military helicopter—which the Russian Armed Forces use to transport personnel and cargo, conduct evacuations, and provide fire support—was completely destroyed—and we welcome this outcome,” the Third Army Corps emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers at the “Marinovka” airfield in the Volgograd region of the Russian Federation.

“Shto mi e milo i drago” by Dobri Hristov: A benchmark of Bulgarian Choral Music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:57:47 UTC
03:57:47 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
Article
Highlights of Bulgarian musical culture
“Shto mi e milo i drago” by Dobri Hristov: A benchmark of Bulgarian Choral Music
Friday 30 October 2026 20:00
Friday, 30 October 2026, 20:00
Dobri Hristov (1875 – 1941)
PHOTO Archives State Agency
Font size
Dobri Hristov, one of the great creative figures of the first generation of Bulgarian composers, holds an exceptional place in the country’s cultural history. His work as an outstanding conductor, inspiring teacher, perceptive scholar and active leader of leading musical institutions helped lay the foundations of professional music in Bulgaria. His contribution to the collection and study of Bulgarian folklore is immense, as is his role in creating classical examples of choral and solo song and in shaping the aesthetic and creative principles of the country’s second generation of composers. Among his pupils were such eminent figures as Pancho Vladigerov, Veselin Stoyanov, Philip Koutev and Marin Goleminov.
Hristov’s choral output, which brought together authentic Bulgarian folk music and Orthodox Church Slavonic chant with the principles of classical harmony, made a fundamental contribution to Bulgaria’s classical music. Drawing on folk songs from different regions of the country, he composed dozens of works for mixed, male and children’s choirs. Many of the texts in these vivid miniatures retain their original dialect features, allowing Hristov to blur, to a considerable extent, the boundary between his own artistic creation and the folk tradition.
Although he began his musical journey as a self-taught, albeit exceptionally gifted, musician in his native city Varna, Hristov composed two choral suites, Lilyana, the Beautiful Maiden and The Girls of Zheravna, before he had even turned 20. He submitted them to a competition for a scholarship to study abroad. His rejection by the selection committee was regarded as an affront by the people of Varna, who raised funds to send the young musician to the Prague Conservatory, where he studied under Antonín Dvořák.
His three years in Prague broadened Hristov’s understanding of the standards and values underpinning national musical art.
The cover of the collection "Madeconian Songs" from 1923
PHOTO Archive
After returning to Bulgaria in 1903, Dobri Hristov began arranging folk songs from the region of Macedonia, which he considered particularly well suited to artistic treatment using the techniques of classical harmony.
Most of these arrangements, written for male choir, were published in 1923 in the collection Macedonian Songs. Among the best-loved and most frequently performed is Shto mi e milo i drago (“How Dear and Precious It Is to Me”), in which a young man sings of his longing to own a shop in the town of Struga, sit outside it and watch the beautiful young women on their way to fetch water from the local springs.
In recent decades, this folk song from the Struga region, a picturesque town in present-day North Macedonia on the northern shore of Lake Ohrid, has become particularly popular in the interpretation of the celebrated Bulgarian folk singer Kostadin Gugov. Bulgarian choirs also favour and frequently perform the arrangement by Petko Staynov, a distinguished composer of the country’s second generation. Yet it was the great master Dobri Hristov who created the first choral arrangement. His version, scored exclusively for male voices, has been performed by numerous ensembles.
Mihail Milkov (1923 – 2003)
PHOTO archives.bnr.bg
One of the most remarkable interpretations dates from the early 1990s and features the male singers of the Bulgarian National Radio Mixed Choir under the baton of conductor Mihail Milkov (1923–2003).
A leading authority on Bulgarian choral performance, Mihail Milkov founded the BNR Mixed Choir in 1952 and led it for more than four decades, leaving the Radio archives a legacy of over 500 recordings. The choir’s landmark international tours and its collaborations with some of the world’s greatest conductors, including Herbert von Karajan, Claudio Abbado and Riccardo Muti, remain particularly noteworthy.
The performance of the song Shto mi e milo i drago conducted by Mihail Milkov is striking for its expressive power, the richness and beauty of its vocal timbres, and its remarkably balanced, cohesive ensemble sound.
You can find more installments in Radio Bulgaria's running series "Highlights of Bulgarian Musical Culture" HERE.
Photos: Archives State Agency, archives.bnr.bg, archive
Editor: Elena Karkalanova
English version: R. Petkova

Fire Devastated a Mongolian Nature Reserve. Who’s to Blame?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:57:00 UTC
03:57:00 KST

On October 8, a massive fire broke out in Numrug, a nature reserve in Khakhgol soum, Dornod aimag (province), Mongolia. The flames were not completely extinguished until October 16.
According to statistics from the Ministry of Natural Environment and Climate Change of Mongolia released on October 28, the total area burned by the fire amounted to 504,960.4 hectares, approximately 5,050 square kilometers or 1.2 million acres. That’s more than twice the area of Tokyo, Japan’s capital. Nearly all of the damaged land – 448,993.6 hectares – was in the Numrug Strictly Protested Area. Over three-quarters (76.4 percent) of the nature reserve’s total area was affected by the fire.
According to preliminary investigations by Mongolian authorities, the fire was directly caused by a vehicle convoy belonging to Mongolian mobile communication operator Mobicom, which is 98.8 percent controlled by Japanese telecommunications giant KDDI. The chassis of one vehicle became wrapped in dry plants, and prolonged driving caused friction and heat to ignite the grasses. That set off the larger fire.
The fire was located in an area adjacent to the China-Mongolia border, and the issue was compounded by the involvement of a Japanese firm and disputes over border communication infrastructure. Thus it quickly escalated from an ecological event to a geopolitical issue affecting Mongolia, China, and Japan, becoming a landmark sample for observing the logic of cross-border environmental governance and capital regulation in Northeast Asia.
Shortcomings in Ecological Governance
The Numrug Strictly Protected Area is located in the transitional zone between the western foothills of the Greater Khingan Range and the eastern grasslands of Mongolia. It is an important source of biological diversity and an ecological security barrier in Northeast Asia, inhabited by various rare species listed in both the IUCN Red List and Mongolian Red Book, such as the Ussuri moose, black billed capercaillie, and Far Eastern taimen fish, as well as more than 250 species of birds.
The impact of high-intensity burning in autumn on the ecosystem is long-term and irreversible. The organic matter on the surface of the soil is completely carbonized, and the soil’s ability to retain water and nutrients has been greatly diminished. When strong winds arrive in spring and autumn, the risk of regional desertification and sandstorms will significantly increase.
The native vegetation seed bank has also suffered a devastating blow. According to ecological observation data from cold and arid grasslands, it will take at least 20 to 100 years for the native community in this area to fully recover, and permanent species replacement may occur in some areas.
The fire points to an alarming structural failure of environmental governance in Mongolia, even within a protected nature reserve. On the one hand, the government is known for “heavy approval, light supervision” and “heavy firefighting, light prevention.” During autumn, the high-risk period for fires, the core protected areas are still open to commercial vehicles. There is a complete lack of environmental risk assessments and fire prevention verification before human activities.
On the other hand, there is a lack of ecological monitoring and emergency response capabilities. Minister of Natural Environment and Climate Change Sandag-Ochir Tsend admitted that due to the complex terrain and logistical conditions, it is difficult to carry out on-site assessments after disasters. Mongolia’s remote areas have long relied on satellite remote sensing monitoring, and there are obvious shortcomings in the logistics support capabilities for ground verification and emergency response.
Cross-border Ecological Risk and Geopolitical Implications
The fire line approached the Mongolia-China border, directly triggering a cross-border emergency response. According to the 1999 agreement between China and Mongolia on Forest and Grassland Fire Prevention in Border Areas, more than 3,400 professional firefighting and emergency forces were quickly mobilized in Inner Mongolia, China. China was able to keep the fire from crossing the national border, while keeping a passage open for wild animals escaping across the border.
Liu Zhiyan, a researcher at the Institute of Ecological Civilization of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, pointed out that the grasslands in eastern Mongolia are highly interconnected with ecology in northern China. If the fire spreads across borders, it will not only cause huge economic losses, but may also trigger serious diplomatic disputes. Viewed in this light, Mongolia’s passive approach has given it the image of an “ecological risk exporting country.”
The Chinese side invested a large amount of manpower and material resources to intercept the fire. Now China is demanding that it be compensated for the effort – not by Mongolia, but by Japan.
The illegal entry of Japanese companies into the core protected area and the resulting catastrophe have directly undermined Japan’s long-standing image as a responsible green investor in Mongolia.
According to the Japanese embassy in Mongolia, Japan’s official development assistance (ODA) to Mongolia from 1977 to 2021 has accumulated to 364.107 billion yen, covering multiple fields such as infrastructure, energy, and communication. Mobicom was once a benchmark project for Japan Mongolia economic and trade cooperation. Now public anger is running high.
Early on, Mobicom sought to avoid responsibility, saying it had followed “complete legal procedures.” It only publicly apologized and promised to cooperate with the investigation after the public opinion pressure escalated. While Mobicom has now agreed to provide compensation, after a joint working group assesses the loss and damage, the company still insists that it had the proper permits and took necessary precautions.
Mobicom stated that its vehicles entered the protected area to conduct 4G network communication tests, but the project is located adjacent to the Mongolia-China Sumber-Rashaan Border Port, and its technical and economic rationality has been widely questioned by the Mongolian public. According to the 2010 Sino-Mongolian Treaty on the Management of the Border Regime, both sides must give prior notice of major border projects and wireless facilities construction. Thus Mobicom’s presence in the border area also could have an impact on mutual trust in border security between Mongolia and China. Some analysts in Chinese media have raised concerns about information security regarding Japanese communication projects in sensitive border areas, but these claims have not been officially confirmed.
Adding to the discontent, Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru did not make an official statement until October 26, two weeks after the fire broke out. He then only mentioned Japan’s willingness to assist Mongolia in ecological restoration, with no mention of the impact on China. This further exacerbated the geopolitical rift.
On October 29, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae held 10-minute telephone call with Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor, marking the highest‑level bilateral exchange since the disaster. During the call, Takaichi stated that the government of Japan “takes seriously the scale of the damage caused” by the fire, “and extended her heartfelt sympathies to the people of Mongolia.”
She said that Japan “intends to provide a package of cooperation that contributes to the recovery of the affected areas, including the provision of necessary equipment to Mongolia and human resource development in the fields of recovery from the wild fires and environmental restoration.” The package will be based on an on‑site assessment from Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) experts in forestry and natural environment conservation dispatched on October 27. Takaichi pledged “close communication” with the Mongolian government through the assessment and compensation process.
In response, Uchral briefed Takaichi on the full extent of the disaster damage. He expressed deep gratitude for Japan’s sympathy and support offer, and welcomed Japan’s “science‑based approach” to advancing “ecological restoration in a phased and effective manner,” adding that Mongolia stands ready to cooperate closely with Japan on all recovery efforts. The two leaders also agreed to further strengthen bilateral friendly relations and practical cooperation ahead of the 55th anniversary of the establishment of Japan‑Mongolia diplomatic relations in 2027.
According to the official readouts released by both governments, the brief conversation focused exclusively on Japan‑Mongolia bilateral relief and diplomatic agenda. No reference was made to China’s large‑scale firefighting deployment along the border, nor to the cross‑border spillover risks the fire had posed to Chinese territory.
Three Countries, Three Positions
The incident has caused strong reactions in the political, academic, and public opinion circles of Mongolia, China, and Japan, with clear differences in interests and positions among all parties.
In Mongolia, the fire raised questions of sovereignty, accountability, and internal reflection. Uchral classified it as a “serious ecological incident” at a Cabinet meeting. He stated clearly that “foreign investors have no privilege above Mongolian law,” and demanded a thorough investigation of the process of granting access permits to protected areas. He vowed to hold the companies and officials involved accountable according to law, via a comprehensive ecological loss assessment and compensation procedure.
Member of Parliament Altangerel Oyunsaikhan, part of the opposition Democratic Party, has put forward a more radical demand for accountability. He demanded that the judiciary freeze all of Mobicom’s assets and financial accounts in Mongolia as collateral for ecological compensation.
Former sumo wrestler Yokozuna Asashoryu (Dagvadorj Dolgorsuren in Mongolia), who has broad social influence, took a different view. He pointed the finger at Mongolia’s internal governance and bluntly stated that “blindly condemning the Japanese side is one-sided.” He called on the media to thoroughly investigate the officials who issued the permits for Mobicom’s entrance into Numrug, suggesting local regulatory corruption.
Asashoryu’s intervention may have pushed regional border officials and political networks, including Dornod MP Otgonbayar Ukhnaa, brother of President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, into a fierce media storm over who approved the convoy. However, Otgonbayar firmly denied any involvement in this matter, claiming that the questions were a politically motivated smear campaign.
At the Japanese level, there is anxiety over both corporate responsibility and national image. Shimba Kazuya , the secretary general of Japan’s Democratic Party for the People (DPFP), publicly criticized the incident as far beyond the scope of corporate civil liability. He demanded that the government intervene at the national level to demonstrate the sincerity of Mongolia in assuming responsibility.
Domestic public opinion in Japan generally accuses the government of a slow response and double standards. Japan’s government is highly sensitive to minor environmental damage, while Japanese companies have caused world-class ecological damage. Kihara’s delayed statement has been criticized by opposition parties and the media as diplomatic incompetence and corporate protectionism. Some called the two-week silence from Tokyo a “national shame.”
Voices across Japan’s ruling and opposition camps have converged on the need for accountability, though with differing strategic priorities. Within the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), former State Minister for Foreign Affairs Nakayama Yasuhide argued on ABEMA News that while corporate giant KDDI and its subsidiary Mobicom must assume absolute civil, financial, and moral liability, this isolated operational failure must be strictly decoupled from Japan’s sovereign alignment with Mongolia.
Given Ulaanbaatar’s historical value as an irreplaceable diplomatic mediator in resolving the existential national security issue of North Korean abductions, Nakayama stressed that the bilateral strategic bond is far too critical to be compromised by a single corporate incident. He emphasized that the sensitive geographical positioning of this infrastructure along the China-Mongolia and Russia-Mongolia frontiers poses a direct geopolitical signal intelligence risk, meaning that any erosion of Japan’s “third neighbor” status would directly compromise regional security networks.
Concurrently, LDP lawmaker Nagashima Akihisa, chairperson of the Japan-Mongolia Parliamentary Friendship League, fortified the legal defense by highlighting that the Mobicom convoy entered under explicit administrative approval and was actively escorted by Mongolian border port authorities. Consequently, Nagashima condemned premature external judgments. Alongside Nakayama, he flatly rejected Chinese state media demands for a formal apology to Beijing, dismissing them as an unverified cross-border political distortion designed to manufacture leverage.
This unified realist defense has allowed Takaichi to execute her own response. By initiating a direct call with Uchral and deploying a state-backed JICA Environmental Revitalization Expert Group, Takaichi is masterfully deploying sovereign “green diplomacy” to absorb the recovery portfolio, effectively shielding and isolating Japan’s strategic footprint and critical infrastructure map in Mongolia from third-party regional intervention.
Environmental Governance
Beyond the geopolitical implications, the Numrug fire stands as a stark example of the limits of corporate Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) commitments, which too often exist only on paper. KDDI, a leading telecommunications giant in Japan, enforces exceptionally stringent environmental and production safety standards domestically, yet its overseas operations reveal a troubling double standard. By sending a vehicle convoy deep into the core zone of a strictly protected nature reserve during the highest-risk wildfire season, Mobicom exposed a severe discrepancy in risk management. The company’s ability to navigate local regulations via special administrative clearances underscores a systemic exploitation of gaps in host-country environmental oversight.
The lackluster on-site emergency response capabilities further confirmed a catastrophic failure of risk control. Reports indicate that the corporate management team was completely unequipped with professional firefighting tools suitable for open grassland suppression. That’s why the initial fire could not be contained and spread to such a large scale. This critical deficiency pierces the superficial narrative of polished ESG reporting. For many multinational enterprises, complex risk-management and environmental emergency blueprints serve primarily as public relations assets for capital market ratings; when put to a real-world test on the frontlines of a disaster, these theoretical systems fall apart completely.
The ecological cost to Numrug provides a profound warning for cross-border environmental governance in Northeast Asia. To prevent another disaster on this level, there are steps that must be taken by Mongolia specifically and the region collectively.
First, Mongolia should improve the environmental responsibility system for foreign investment. That means promoting the introduction of specialized ecological responsibility regulations for foreign-invested enterprises. High-risk foreign-invested enterprises should be required to set aside environmental safety and quality deposits, as a certain proportion based on their total investment amount, which should be deposited into the central bank’s special account for ecological restoration after accidents.
At the same time, the United Nations ecosystem service valuation standards should be used to calculate the total damages. The U.N. standards include soil carbon sink loss, biodiversity damage, and the costs of managing secondary disasters, thereby significantly increasing the cost of environmental non-compliance.
In terms of technical capabilities, it is necessary to establish an integrated air-ground environmental monitoring network and deploy automated infrared drone patrol systems to enable precise, minute-level early warning of fires during high-risk periods. Furthermore, the equipment and operational authority of the protected area’s law enforcement teams should be upgraded to strengthen the verification of personnel and equipment entering from outside the borders, thereby preventing unauthorized activities conducted under the guise of commercial operations.
Regarding regional cooperation, efforts should be made to upgrade the border fire prevention and control agreement between Mongolia and China, explore the establishment of a green channel for cross-border emergency firefighting within a certain range of the border, and simplify the approval process for cross-border rescue in major fire situations. At the same time, we can promote the establishment of a transnational environmental infringement liability recovery mechanism, and the United Nations Environment Program can promote the establishment of a long-term ecological trust fund supported by the responsible enterprises, specifically for regional ecological restoration and biodiversity protection. This would create a closed-loop system encompassing incident response, compensation, and long-term management.
The ashes that have replaced three-quarters of the Numrug grasslands are a painful reflection of the backwardness of the cross-border environmental governance system in Northeast Asia. In the context of the interweaving of climate change and geopolitical games, environmental governance is no longer the internal affair of a single country, but a core issue related to national sovereignty, regional security, and multilateral trust. Only by constraining the environmental responsibility of transnational capital with rigid systems and filling the blind spots in border governance through multilateral cooperation can we truly build a resilient ecological security barrier for Northeast Asia.

Five children among seven dead in eastern Syria floods
Oct 30 - Seven people, including five children, have died and seven others were injured after torrential rains triggered flash floods in eastern Syria, authorities said on Friday.
Four people remain missing and rescue teams are continuing to search flooded areas, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said in a statement on X.
The five children drowned in pools of water formed by the floods, while another person died in a traffic accident, Saleh said, without providing details of the seventh death.
Flooding has hit the eastern provinces of Raqqa, Deir al-Zor and Hasakah, as well as parts of Aleppo, damaging infrastructure, cutting off roads and forcing families to leave their homes.
Syria's civil defence teams have carried out more than 550 emergency operations since the storms began, rescuing 60 people trapped by floodwater and responding to more than 900 distress calls, Saleh said.
Emergency crews evacuated more than 350 students from two schools and helped 375 families leave camps in Raqqa province. Teams also responded to flooding at camps in rural Aleppo and Idlib, and pumped water from around 250 homes and public buildings.
In Deir al-Zor, the floods damaged roads and telecommunications infrastructure, disrupting transport and communications, state news agency SANA reported. Heavy rainfall also caused seven culverts to collapse, cutting off access to several areas.
Authorities suspended classes in Raqqa, Hasakah and Deir al-Zor on Thursday, while forecasters warned unsettled weather could continue into Saturday. REUTERS

Pakistan army ‘cautiously optimistic’ about US-Iran mediation efforts

Pakistan army ‘cautiously optimistic’ about US-Iran mediation efforts
Pakistan’s military spokesman warns of ‘powerful spoilers and detractors’ who still believe the conflict serves them.
Pakistan’s army is “cautiously optimistic” about mediation efforts between Iran and the United States as regional countries seek to revive a ceasefire in the eight-month-old war.
Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, spokesman for Pakistan’s military, suggested on Friday that there were positive signs in attempts to de-escalate the conflict. His comments to the Reuters news agency were the first since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief mediator, has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday, alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
He also warned that there are parties seeking to obstruct mediation between the US and Iran.
There are still “powerful spoilers and detractors” who believe conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan’s armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed in Tehran or whether the US had backed the trip.
His comments on Friday came as Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran in another apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the June ceasefire that collapsed months later.
Mecca defence pact
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Pakistan’s Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. “We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict,” he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.

‘Deepest possible partnership’: Canada and EU announce new alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:54:51 UTC
03:54:51 KST

Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.
Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.
“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.
As they concluded their two-day summit, Canada agreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.
While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.
Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.
Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.
Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.
“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.
Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.
In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.
“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.
“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.
The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.
“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.
European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.
Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.
Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.
“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.
He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

Putin’s African ties: Military cooperation, “history” wars, and sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:50:50 UTC
03:50:50 KST

Russia and a range of African countries have adopted declarations on political and economic cooperation following the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow. In the outcome documents, the parties agreed to counter the “rewriting of history,” the blocking of sovereign assets, and the politicization of international justice while working to foster cooperation in security, space, mineral extraction, and AI. Vladimir Putin said that Russia already has agreements on military and military-technical cooperation with 45 African nations. The Insider has compiled the main statements and agreements of the two-day summit.
The third Russia–Africa summit took place in Moscow on Oct. 28–29, with delegations from 48 of the continent’s 54 countries in attendance. Two dozen states were represented by high-level officials, with sessions co-chaired by Putin and Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who currently heads the African Union.
As a result of the gathering, the parties adopted three main documents: the final declaration of the summit, a declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of AI, and the action plan of the Russia–Africa partnership forum for 2027–2029. In addition, more than 60 official agreements were signed at the summit and at the parallel economic and humanitarian forum, Russian presidential adviser Anton Kobyakov announced via Telegram.
Countering sanctions, “rewriting of history,” and colonial legacies
A significant part of the final declaration is devoted to international politics. Russia and the African states in attendance agreed to oppose the blocking and seizure of sovereign assets, as well as to resist outside political and economic pressure. The parties intend to coordinate their positions when it comes to sanctions against African countries.
The summit participants also agreed to counter attempts at “rewriting and falsifying history.” These and other provisions are included in the final declaration, which consists of 101 points.
Another area will be assessing the damage “inflicted on African states during the colonial period.” Russian scientists are already developing a methodology for such assessment jointly with African colleagues. Preliminary results should be presented in 2027, and a special research laboratory is expected to open in Uganda in November 2026.
In his speech on Oct. 28, Vladimir Putin accused Western countries of trying to preserve Africa’s economic dependence and impose new debt obligations on it. The Russian president claimed that Moscow is ready to transfer technology and foster production on the continent.
African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf stressed in his speech that African states are interested in developing local industry and gaining access to international capital. He also called for reforming the U.N. Security Council by expanding African representation.
Military cooperation and fight against terrorism
Putin stated that Russia has intergovernmental agreements on military and military-technical cooperation in effect with 45 African states, noting that Moscow trains African servicemen and law enforcement officers at Russian educational institutions.
In the final statements, the parties reaffirmed their intention to expand cooperation in the fight against terrorism and extremism, counter the use of new technologies by terrorist organizations, and develop joint security mechanisms.
Special attention was paid to the Sahel states: Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger. Commenting on the statement of Assimi Goïta, the head of Mali’s military government, Putin stressed the global importance of resolving the situation in the Sahel.
Russia’s military presence in the region has expanded in recent years. After the Wagner Group wound down its activities following the death of founder Yevgeny Prigozhin in August 2023, Russia's state-run Africa Corps stepped in to take over the role in several African states. Russian military units currently operate in Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, and the Central African Republic.
Two days ahead of the summit, African branches of Amnesty International appealed to its participants with a call to demand that Moscow stop the deceptive and coercive recruitment of citizens of African states to take part in the war against Ukraine. Human rights activists claim that Russia recruits foreigners under the guise of employment and then sends them to the front.
AI, space, and control over technology
The summit participants devoted a separate declaration to cooperation in AI — to promote equal and fair access to safe AI technologies, the development of joint educational programs, and capacity-building efforts. Satellite communications and the use of space were discussed separately.
According to Putin, approximately 40,000 students from African countries are studying in Russia, and Moscow is expanding training programs for foreign civil servants, including in the digitalization of public administration. Putin also characterized Russia as being one of three countries with full digital sovereignty — a claim The Insider has examined in its Antifake section.
Precious metals, nuclear power plants, and trade
The economic part of the summit focused on energy, transportation, agriculture, and the mining and processing of minerals.
Russia’s Rusal and the state-owned Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation agreed to create two joint ventures in Ghana. The companies plan to develop the Nyinahini deposit with annual output of up to 5 million metric tons of bauxite and build an alumina refinery with a capacity of 1.2 million metric tons per year, with Rusal receiving controlling stakes in both ventures. Reuters notes that the company is seeking to reduce its dependence on external suppliers of raw materials after losing part of its supplies from Ukraine and Australia in 2022.
Ghana’s President John Dramani Mahama also announced the start of negotiations with Rosatom on building the country’s first nuclear power plant.
According to Putin, Russia’s trade with African countries reached $27 billion in 2025, and since 2023 Moscow has opened eight new embassies on the continent. In the near future, Botswana, Seychelles, and Togo intend to open diplomatic missions of their own in the Russian capital.
Putin also said that in the first nine months of 2026, Russia had supplied African countries with 13 million tons of agricultural products. Deliveries of mineral fertilizers, he said, exceeded 2.2 million tons this year, compared with 1.5 million tons for all of last year.
Trade with Africa remains significantly below the level promised by Putin
Despite claims of successful cooperation, Russia’s trade with Africa has not yet reached the level that Putin promised at the first summit in 2019. As Chatham House notes, the Russian leader set a goal of bringing trade turnover to $40 billion; however, in 2025, it totaled only $27 billion. For comparison, also according to data cited by Chatham House, China’s trade with African countries reached $348 billion in 2025, and the European Union’s was about $395 billion.
At the same time, Russia continues to expand its political and military presence on the continent. Earlier, The Insider described how Moscow uses cooperation with African governments to gain access to natural resources and strengthen its influence in international organizations.
Six days before the current summit, The Insider identified a GRU officer who in April 2025 infiltrated the diplomatic residence of the African Union in Ethiopia. He turned out to be Alexander Dubikov, who worked undercover as an assistant to the Russian military attaché and is linked to hackers from the Sandworm group. The incident occurred at a compound used by the current chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, who also took part in the Moscow summit.
Dialogue with Europe, possible war, and situation in the Baltic Sea
At the press conference following the summit, Putin took questions about relations with Europe. Commenting on his Oct. 27 phone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Putin said the European leaders themselves initiated the call, stressing that they were acting in their national capacity, not on behalf of the European Union. Despite being critical of his counterparts, Putin called the conversation the right step and supported attempts to restore dialogue with European countries.
Nevertheless, Putin said that Russia is ready for war with Europe, even if it does not seek one. He criticized statements by European politicians about the need to prepare for a possible military conflict by 2030 and expressed confidence that Russia cannot be dealt a strategic defeat. “If it goes too far, there will be no winner at all,” he commented, adding that Russia remembers the lessons of the First and Second World Wars and is doing everything it can to prevent reliving them.
Finally, Putin touched on the situation in the Baltic Sea, which he had discussed with the leaders of Finland and Norway. According to Putin, his Nordic interlocutors had invoked the need to comply with international maritime law. Putin supported their position but warned that a situation similar to what is happening in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz could develop in the Baltic. Russia, according to him, does not want such a development but is ready to respond to any challenge.

Serhiy Prytula’s Foundation has, for the first time, delivered 45 Black Betty loitering munitions — a new, cost-effective variant of the RAM-2X — to the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
The foundation told Militarnyi that the drone is designed for high-precision strikes against enemy logistics.
They were part of a batch of reconnaissance and strike assets with a total value of UAH 69.8 million, which was distributed to seven units as part of the “Shchelypy” fundraising campaign.
In total, the military received 45 Black Betty systems, 14 Shark-M systems, and nine systems equipped with RAM-2X loitering munitions.
The equipment was received by the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade, the 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 65th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the Intelligence Command Center, the 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Systems Forces, the 98th Special Operations Reconnaissance Center, as well as units of the Security Service of Ukraine.
Black Betty is a new, cost-reduced variant of the RAM-2X developed by Ukrspecsystems.
It is designed for mass production and intended for high-precision strikes against enemy logistics, particularly moving targets.
The Shark-M and loitering munitions operate in tandem. The Shark-M can remain airborne for up to seven hours, cover a distance of up to 180 km, and relay signals to operational-tactical-level kamikaze drones. The first drone detects the target, and the second strikes it.
In September, it was reported that RAM-2X strike drones had already hit over 450 targets.
The RAM-2X loitering munition operates at the operational-tactical level and has a range of up to 180 km. The drone is designed to strike enemy targets and can remain airborne for over two hours.
The drone is equipped with a warhead containing a 2.7- or 3.5-kg strike core and supports the integration of artificial intelligence systems. The system is characterized by a high degree of automation and a variety of communication channels.
The drone can operate via multiple radio frequency bands as well as through a Starlink terminal.
