analysis
Politics is an image game, and the government needs to find better visuals
Politics at its most visceral is visual, which is why governments and oppositions spend so much time crafting the perfect image. Burnishing and beavering away to dispel the dismal, disguise the dishonest and nudge the narrative.
When it gets really fun is when the unexpected happens. Like a purposeful set-up that backfires, embarrassing the participants. Awks, as the kids might say.
There have been many examples over the years, but there was something in the air this week that rekindled memories of a 2015 photograph of then-prime minister Tony Abbott and his treasurer, Joe Hockey.
Taken in the prime minister's office on the eve of that year's budget, the photograph captured the two men side-by-side. Abbott leans to his left and puts a pastoral hand on Hockey's bare forearm.
Hockey looks miserable. Forlorn. Like a man beaten. Which it turned out he was. As was Abbott.
The photo was taken 12 months after what was regarded at the time as one of the least popular budgets in history: the notorious 2014 edition with all its broken-promise spending cuts.
A year later, still in its first term but with an eye on the coming election in 2016, the Coalition released its second budget at a time of deep poll trouble.
Hemmed in by the Senate and a popular backlash against the cuts, a politically battered and bruised Hockey was forced to shelve his ambitions for big reform that began when he declared an end to the "age of entitlement".
Instead, his second budget was a plodding affair full of cash handouts that spent almost every dollar saved. It was panned by the economic commentariat as a do-little effort that left the country drifting sideways.
Having Abbott sit with Hockey was intended to demonstrate unity and resolve. Instead, it produced snickering.
Four months later, almost to the day, both men were out of their jobs, rolled by Malcolm Turnbull who cited the fact Abbott had lost 30 straight NewsPolls to Labor.
What's the relevance of this?
Towards the end of Question Time on Wednesday — a day of bleak news on the economy, with rising inflation and interest rate worries — the prime minister got a question from the opposition about when he plans to replace Jim Chalmers with cabinet secretary Andrew Charlton.
The question was a political shit stir, designed to highlight the bad blood between the prime minister and treasurer.
Albanese used his answer to pump up the treasurer, who has made no secret in recent weeks of his frustration at being seen as the locus of blame for everything wrong with the government.
"This treasurer produced back-to-back surpluses," the prime minister began, before laying it on thick.
"This treasurer returned 75 per cent of revenue upgrades to the bottom line. He's one of only nine treasurers of finance ministers around the world to have a AAA credit rating from all of the agencies."
As he sat listening, Chalmers had the air of a man who wasn't entirely over the moon about the praise. How helpful it was, given tensions in the air, is debatable.
It certainly reminded those who saw it of the pressure Chalmers is under, which is looking more and more like an uncontrolled pile-on.
Going through some things
The risk when prime ministers have to defend their treasurers in a performative manner is that it sets tongues wagging.
Why now? What's the goal? Who is he trying to convince?
"If Jim could have flipped Albanese the bird in the middle of it, he would have," said one Labor observer.
A cynical interpretation is that the prime minister was also reminding the public that it's the treasurer who owns the government's economic story.
Which — as Donald Trump once said of an ill-fated US ambassador to Ukraine — is "going to go through some things".
Next week will almost certainly be brutal for the government, given the likelihood of another Reserve Bank rate hike on Tuesday, the fifth this year.
The prime minister will be in the Caribbean for a Commonwealth Heads Of Government Meeting (CHOGM), leaving Chalmers to face the music.
Like a rogue wave bouncing off a seawall, a story then appeared on Friday in the Sydney Morning Herald citing "government sources", suggesting Chalmers is a victim rather than villain of the government's deteriorating economic story.
The Herald quoted people saying that Chalmers' push for spending discipline was obstructed by the prime minister's razor gang in the lead-up to the May budget. And that his heroic fiscal rectitude was undermined by the prime minister's inner cabal of spendy left-faction ministers, led by Katy Gallagher, Mark Butler, Penny Wong and Tim Ayres.
This columnist has heard similar tales.
Alarmingly for the government more broadly, it hints at a shift in the underlying ecosystem of the government. It is far from irretrievable or terminal — and old hands speak of the current tensions as nothing compared to the Gillard-Rudd years. But the change is noticeable.
People are getting jittery, looking sideways. The easy confidence of key figures in the government is dwindling.
Loading
The souring reality
This week — like workers returning to the office on a Monday to discover the fridge stopped working over the weekend — drove home the sense that things that used to be certain have gone off.
Next to the soured milk sits the slightly whiffy items of the government's thus-far successful operating model — like the notion that cabinet stability is an unquestionable virtue. The government is in its fifth year, and many ministers have been in their portfolios since 2019.
As this columnist noted in February, some of Labor's frontbench is starting to look tired.
Nearly eight months on and that hasn't changed. Too many are carrying baggage. Punters have tired of them. Their lines resonate a little less each day.
One view is that it's also strange that Labor is not making opportunities for its next generation of leaders. The backbench is full of talent, some of whom are reduced to nodding for the Question Time camera.
Another souring reality is that Labor can no longer blame the previous government for all of today's problems, even if that were true.
Finally, on the war against Iran, it's not clear voters are as forgiving of the consequences as they were in March, April and May, when the government scrambled to secure fuel supplies. Back then, voters blamed Donald Trump.
Today's mood — as reflected in the polls, social media comments and political observers — suggests voters are blaming the government for rising transport costs.
It might be time for some better visuals.
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

Students use 'rage bait' and AI bots to sway fictional election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

University students attempt to manipulate fictional election in 'Kingstonia' using AI bots
Computer engineering student Kaira Dumasia has an unusual university assignment — using AI bots to interfere in an election.
"I am really going to try to rage bait everybody," she said.
Fortunately for democracy, the election — and the voters she hopes to influence — are not real.
Kaira is part of a competition led by researchers at the University of New South Wales, which pits teams against one another to manipulate social media to win a simulated vote.
They're allowed to build AI bots to post, like, share and reply on a made-up social media platform. Points are awarded for grabbing attention, changing voters' views and spotting rival teams' bots.
The aim is to help students understand how AI can conduct in-authentic behaviour online by experimenting with controlling it themselves.
UNSW computer science senior lecturer, Hammond Pearce, said it helped students recognise the signs of manipulation, and functioned as a Petri dish for academics hoping to study AI electoral interference.
"We're trying to expose that tech… to students in a safe environment so they can learn both what the attackers are doing by doing it themselves and also what the defenders need to do in order to try and catch that kind of attack," he said.
A vote on dolphin flu
This year, the competition is set in Kingstonia, a fictional island nation that is having a referendum on whether proof of vaccination against dolphin flu should be required to enter public spaces.
Teams campaign for their chosen side on a platform called Legit Social. The AI-powered citizens read posts, interact and change their views over the month-long competition.
Kaira's strategy has been inspired by real life. Her plan is to make people angry enough to comment, boosting her posts and earning more points.
"I see a lot of it is rage bait content, engagement bait content,"
she said.
But there is a countervailing force: rival teams can report posts they suspect have been sent by other bots, and not simulated citizens.
Correctly identifying this AI bot activity also earns points for a team.
Dr Pearce said they built Legit Social specifically for the competition to have a safe place to practise their manipulation and detection skills under the watchful eyes of the organisers.
Beyond the game
The fictional vote is taking place in the lead-up to the US midterm elections and shortly after Australia's election watchdog warned about AI's role in amplifying existing election integrity threats.
Earlier this month, Australian Electoral Commissioner Jeff Pope told parliament's joint committee inquiry into AI that includes misinformation, influence operations and foreign interference, as well as physical security risks through harassment and impacts on social cohesion.
Researchers also use the game to study how participants build AI bot networks and identify other bot activity.
A preliminary academic paper published online about last year's competition examined the techniques used by competitors to win.
It found some participants turned to high-volume posting because the scoring rewarded engagement.
Kaira, who was a moderator in last year's competition, said the competition helped her recognise more AI-generated, bot-like posts.
She also recognises how easily attention-grabbing content can work on her.
"Yes, my strategy does come from a lot of posts that I see on social media. And I often find myself falling to rage bait and then I'm like, whoa, take a step back."

How a 'kickstart' gift helped a Victorian man escape homelessness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

'Kickstart' gift helps Victorian man escape homelessness
By the time he met Dorothy Maafu, Jake Dell'Aquila had been sleeping in a tent on a Melbourne beach for months.
Every evening, he would unpack his things and settle in with his German shepherd dog on the Rosebud foreshore.
Every morning, he would pack them up again.
He had been unhoused for more than a year.
Loading...
"I'd tried everything," he told Mornings with Raf Epstein on 774 ABC Melbourne this week.
"I'd tried all the resources. I'd tried the Salvation Army. I'd tried everything and nothing had worked.
"I was so desperate for help and there [was] no help through … any of these programs because I've got a dog, [and] there's the housing crisis."
It was on those cold mornings that Ms Maafu, a nearby resident, started to see him as she walked her own dog.
The pair started talking. After a while, the polite chat turned into an invitation to come visit Dorothy's home for some meals and a shower.
"I wanted to understand what it was that drove him to the streets," she said.
"From my own experience, homelessness isn't always about someone needing a roof over their head for one night.
"It's about giving people stability, dignity, and a chance to just get their lives back on track."
'Just one person can make a difference'
For Mr Dell'Aquila, the path to that Rosebud beach involved cutting off his family and friends, escaping dysfunction and abuse.
"I seemed to be doing circles and things had not been working out the best for me," he said.
"At times it was very hard. But I never gave up."
Sometime after those first few shared meals and moments of connection, Ms Maafu took a further step.
She purchased a second-hand caravan, and booked Mr Dell'Aquila into caravan parks for the next six months.
"I haven't been able to solve everything, but knowing he has shelter rather than a broken tent means a lot to me," she said.
"It was a tough road for both of us in just getting him stable.
"But I would do it all over again for another Mr Dell'Aquila on the street because it just breaks my heart to see these people, the situations they get into.
"My friends and family couldn't believe what I did. But if I don't do it, who else is going to do it?
"Just one person can make a difference in someone's life."
The stability meant Mr Dell'Aquila has been able to find work, and to find a spot in a safe rental property.
Ms Maafu, he said, would remain a lifelong friend.
"Everyone just needs a little bit of a helping hand," he said.
"I wasn't being approached by anyone the way Dorothy approached me, and it was so moving and so powerful and so life-changing what she's done.
"I may not be in the situation I'm in now with my own house and stability and paying bills if it wasn't for that little kickstart that Dorothy helped me with."
Homelessness 'rapidly' increasing across Australia
The Mornington Peninsula Shire, where Ms Maafu and Mr Dell'Aquila were located at the time, had the highest number of people sleeping rough out of any Victorian local government area as of mid-2025.
In June last year, there were 110 people in the area recorded as homeless, with the majority of them sleeping rough "in tents, cars, and on foreshore reserves".
Almost 1,000 people in the area sought homelessness services in the 2024-25 financial year.
There were 2,624 applicants waiting for public housing in March 2025.
A report by the Mornington Peninsula Shire at that time blamed a lack of appropriate affordable housing.
"Homelessness is rapidly increasing, and is likely to worsen without action,"
the report said.
According to Homelessness Australia, there were 122,494 people experiencing homelessness nationwide on Census night in 2021.
Just 6.2 per cent of them would be sleeping rough, with the rest experiencing "hidden" homelessness: staying in crisis accommodation, insecure housing, or couch surfing.
Almost 289,000 people were being assisted by specialist homelessness services in 2024-2025, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).
A further 370,000 requests for assistance either went unanswered or were turned away in the same time period, with services stretched to breaking point.

The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:56:11 UTC
02:56:11 KST

Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action.
Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal.From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.
These are structural changes that will transform the relationship between local government and a notoriously overly centralised state. They have so far failed to generate anything like the coverage that accompanied the Conservatives’ levelling-up programme, which degenerated into a tawdry pork barrel exercise for “red wall” Tory MPs. But it is on this municipal terrain that Mr Burnham’s aspiration to rebalance the country, reduce regional inequality and “roll back” the 80s will be played out.
Replacing government grants with guaranteed income streams will give strategic authorities more certainty over future revenue – against which they will be able to borrow – and the ability to plan flexibly according to locally set priorities. The devil will be in details to be announced in next year’s spending review, in particular regarding mechanisms to ensure poorer areas with a smaller tax base do not lose out. But the roadmap is a first move towards restoring proper agency to local authorities struggling to cope with the disastrous twin legacy of deindustrialisation and austerity.
Further steps will need to be taken if, as the prime minister intends, local government is to drive “good growth” that improves general living standards and prospects throughout communities. As the Local Government Association pointed out, cash-strapped councils on the frontline face a £7bn funding gap by 2028-29, and are in a perennial struggle merely to meet their statutory obligations on social care. Strategic authorities need to be given the capacity to gradually reassume control of priorities in sectors such as care, housing and the utilities. That will take time and investment at scale in forms of community provision that can offer an alternative to a model in which services have been outsourced and profits offshored.
Devolution will not of itself reduce inequalities or restore a degraded public realm. But this week’s budget measures began the necessary process of rewiring British politics. Mr Burnham’s core conviction is that radical devolution can redistribute power to those who know their own community best, and allow councils to rebalance the relationship between the public and the private sector. After decades in which the latter has profited hugely from calling nearly all the shots, that is very much the right direction of travel. The starting gun has been fired in a process that can lead to a genuine renaissance of municipal England.

Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:55:51 UTC
02:55:51 KST

Trade, sovereignty and reform: key Russia-Africa Summit 2026 takeaways
Russia and African countries have agreed to deepen economic cooperation, strengthen political coordination, and push for reforms of global institutions, Russian President Vladimir Putin and African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye said in a joint press statement on Thursday.
Speaking at the conclusion of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, the two leaders outlined the results of the October 28–29 gathering, which brought together senior delegations from 48 African countries, including 21 led by heads of state.
The gathering resulted in the adoption of three documents: the Declaration of the 3rd Russia-Africa Summit, the Declaration of Cooperation in the Civilian Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies, and the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum Action Plan for 2027–2029.
Turning political solidarity into economic cooperation
Ndayishimiye said African countries are seeking to diversify their international partnerships and strengthen their sovereignty, with Russia playing a role in accelerating economic development and regional integration.
Speaking about the summit’s three-year action plan, he said that the leaders “outlined priorities, financing mechanisms, implementation schedules and areas of responsibility, and set dates by which expect to see results.”
The African Union chair called for greater Russian investment to help African countries create added value locally. He also stressed that African youth expected tangible results, including more scholarships, reliable energy supplies, and digital solutions.
Expanding trade and financial independence
Putin said Russia-Africa trade currently stood at $27 billion but remained well below its potential, and called to double it.
The Russian president noted national currencies, including the ruble, now accounted for 85% of settlements in commercial transactions between Russia and African countries.
Reducing technological dependence
Ndayishimiye called for reducing Africa’s technological dependence. He stressed the summit had adopted a separate declaration on artificial intelligence, advocating equitable international cooperation with a central role for the United Nations.
Putin said Russia and African countries had signed agreements aimed at introducing Russian digital solutions, including AI-based technologies, in African economies and public administration.
Africa must choose its own partners
Asked whether Africa risked becoming an arena for competition between major powers, Putin rejected the suggestion that Moscow viewed African countries as objects of geopolitical rivalry.
“We have not pursued any colonial policies. It is the opposite: we helped them to liberate themselves from the neo-colonial yoke,” he stated.
Ndayishimiye similarly stressed that African nations were no longer in a position where outside powers could determine their partnerships.
Reforming global institutions
Putin backed permanent African representation on the UN Security Council. “I am absolutely convinced that Africa must be represented there on a permanent basis, including in the Security Council,” he said.
Ndayishimiye reaffirmed Africa’s position on UN reform, while calling for greater representation in global financial institutions and closer cooperation with BRICS.
Strengthening security and humanitarian cooperation
Putin said Russia would continue consultations with parties involved in African conflicts and expressed hope that Moscow’s diplomatic efforts could help prevent further escalation.
He also pledged to expand cooperation in healthcare and education, including medicine supplies, mobile laboratories, and training for African students.
Russia’s epidemic-control assistance program for African countries has been extended through 2029, Putin said, adding that African partners supported expanding Russian university branches and educational centers on the continent.
Moscow Declaration sets out common political positions
The 101-point declaration, adopted in Moscow on October 29, is divided into five sections covering political and legal cooperation, security, economic ties, humanitarian cooperation, and environmental protection and climate issues. Here are its key points.
- Maritime security: Oppose the unjustified detention, seizure or arrest of civilian vessels, including African-flagged ships, in violation of international law. The document warns that such actions against commercial vessels turn maritime trade into “a tool of economic and political pressure.”
- Sanctions: Oppose unilateral coercive measures that violate international law, including measures imposed outside the UN Security Council, and strengthen coordination to reduce their impact on trade, energy, healthcare and food security.
- Sovereign assets: Oppose the freezing and attempted confiscation of sovereign assets, as well as political and economic coercion against sovereign states.
- Colonial reparations: Pursue legal mechanisms to assess and compensate for damage inflicted on African countries during the colonial era, alongside efforts to complete the continent’s decolonization.
- International justice: Counter the politicization and misuse of international criminal justice mechanisms, including their use to exert neocolonial pressure on African states, and strengthen cooperation to ensure the independence and impartiality of international courts.
- UN reform: Work toward reforming the Security Council to increase African representation, taking into account the continent’s common position under the Ezulwini Consensus and the 2005 Sirte Declaration.
- Counterterrorism: Strengthen cooperation against terrorist groups’ use of drones, encrypted platforms, and digital finance, while also addressing terrorist financing, organized crime, and maritime piracy.
- Arms control: Oppose the politicization of international arms control, disarmament, and nuclear nonproliferation mechanisms, and support compliance with existing treaties governing nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons.
- IMF and World Bank: Push for reforms to give African countries greater representation in the leadership of both institutions and more influence over decision-making.
- G20: Call for South Africa’s full and active participation in the group to be restored as soon as possible, while strengthening the voice of African countries and the wider Global South.
- Cultural heritage: Support the return of cultural objects and historical artifacts removed from African countries during colonial rule, alongside efforts to protect cultural heritage from illicit trafficking.
- Space cooperation: Expand cooperation in peaceful space exploration, satellite communications, Earth observation, and joint research, including spacecraft technologies and equipment.
- Trade and infrastructure: Expand cooperation in precious metals, strengthen industrial value chains, and develop maritime, river, road, rail, and aviation infrastructure. Remove trade barriers, increase African exports of value-added products and establish reliable financial settlement mechanisms to support trade and investment.
- Energy cooperation: Expand cooperation across oil and gas, nuclear, hydropower, hydrogen, and renewable energy to strengthen energy security and improve access to electricity.
- Education and healthcare: Expand academic exchanges, Russian-language education and joint research, while strengthening healthcare systems through medical training, laboratory development, and epidemic preparedness.
- Media cooperation: Strengthen ties between Russian and African media through the opening of representative offices, journalist training, information exchanges, and joint media projects.
- Climate policy: Oppose discriminatory protectionist measures introduced under the pretext of combating climate change, while expanding cooperation on climate adaptation and environmental projects that take national priorities into account.
- Sovereignty: Counter neocolonial practices that undermine states’ independence, restrict their decision-making, or facilitate the exploitation of natural resources, while upholding countries’ right to determine their own development paths.
- Conflict resolution: Support African-led efforts to resolve and prevent conflicts on the continent, guided by the principle of “African solutions to African problems.”

French economy stalls as budget deadlock fuels concerns over public finances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:55:18 UTC
02:55:18 KST

France has recorded no growth since the start of the year, while GDP fell 0.1% between July and September. The government is urging political forces to adopt the 2027 budget, as the country's ability to reassure markets is in doubt.
A setback. France's GDP fell by 0.1 % in the third quarter, the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) announced on Friday, after stagnating in the second quarter and a 0.2% decline in the first.
It is another blow for the government, with France's borrowing costs having climbed above 5% on the financial markets last week and the social climate still highly volatile, on the eve of a new nationwide day of mobilisation against the high cost of living and in support of young people's demands.
While household consumption is accelerating (+0.4 %), the fall in output is one of the main drivers of the contraction in French GDP. It is particularly sharp in transport equipment (-3.5%), dragged down by aerospace (-4.5 %) and automotive (-1.5 %). Activity is also declining in the agri-food sector (-1.5%), which is suffering from the impact of poor summer harvests.
This drop effectively leaves the eurozone's second-largest economy on the brink of recession. At the same time, inflation has picked up again, reaching 3.4% year on year in October, compared with 3.1% in September. According to Insee, this is its highest level since January 2024.
The poor figures do not come as a surprise to experts, given the particularly unfavourable macroeconomic environment. "France is highly likely to experience a technical recession over the coming quarters", says Jérémie Peloso, chief strategist for Europe at BCA Research, speaking to Euronews.
"This scenario was already conceivable before the recent budgetary turmoil and the rout on the bond market", he adds.
"We will hit the wall"
The government has been shaken by the news and is stressing the need to secure adoption of the 2027 budget on time, in a parliament where it has no majority.
Speaking on Franceinfo, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure described the French economy as "at a standstill". He also warned that the country "will hit the wall" if the "recovery" budget is not adopted.
If parliamentary talks fail, the government is not ruling out using article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote, unless a motion of no confidence is carried. Another possibility is to resort to ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
According to Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University and author of the blog "La finance au cœur de nos vies," adopting a budget is not "decisive" in itself, as it would not, "through any kind of leverage effect, miraculously revive activity in the short term".
"On the contrary, a fiscal adjustment plan generally tends to weigh on growth in the immediate future". The researcher points out that the issue is not just getting the government's bill through but giving investors medium and long-term visibility over the trajectory of France's public finances.
France is borrowing at increasingly high cost on the markets. "Each rise in interest rates gradually feeds through into the state budget, reduces future room for manoeuvre and ultimately weighs on private investment", Jérôme Mathis reminds us. Budget uncertainty can also become a drag on activity, he warns. "Companies postpone some investments, households defer some spending and the markets demand a higher risk premium".
As of Friday, the yield on 10-year French government bonds stands at 4.9%, 0.17 percentage points below the peak reached on 22 October. The Franco-German spread, which measures the gap between the two countries' borrowing rates, is hovering at around 1.55 percentage points.
"Yesterday's ECB meeting, which was relatively free of surprises, certainly contributed to this easing, even though its president, Christine Lagarde, refused to comment on the French situation", notes a strategy paper written by Jérémie Peloso for BCA clients and seen by Euronews.
"The main risk to the French economy is not the absence of a budget. It is the absence of visibility over the trajectory of public finances", insists Jérôme Mathis. In this context, "the main economic cost of the current deadlock lies less in the content of the measures that would not be voted than in the prolongation of uncertainty".
Ordinances: what signal?
As for a possible adoption of the budget by ordinance, the professor does not see it as "an obvious economic solution". In his view, investors do attach importance to the speed of political decisions, but also to their "legitimacy" and their "durability". A budget adopted by ordinance may reduce uncertainty in the short term, but is not enough to restore long-term fiscal credibility, he warns.
"Markets generally prefer a contested decision to a prolonged lack of decision. But if a budget adopted by ordinance is seen as fragile, liable to be overturned after the presidential election or indicative of a lasting inability of the political system to build majorities, the positive impact on confidence could be limited", explains Jérôme Mathis.
In his view, this is precisely what distinguishes the current situation from "more classic" budget crises: markets are not questioning France's technical ability to raise taxes or repay its debt. "They are more doubtful about its ability to slow their increase".
"As long as this question remains, pressure on interest rates is likely to persist, whatever institutional vehicle is chosen to pass the budget," he concludes.

French economy on brink of recession amid GDP fall, rising borrowing costs and budget deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:55:18 UTC
02:55:18 KST

France has recorded no growth since the start of the year, while GDP fell 0.1% between July and September. The government is urging political forces to adopt the 2027 budget, as the country's ability to reassure markets is in doubt.
A setback. France's GDP fell by 0.1 % in the third quarter, the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) announced on Friday, after stagnating in the second quarter and a 0.2% decline in the first.
It is another blow for the government, with France's borrowing costs having climbed above 5% on the financial markets last week and the social climate still highly volatile, on the eve of a new nationwide day of mobilisation against the high cost of living and in support of young people's demands.
While household consumption is accelerating (+0.4 %), the fall in output is one of the main drivers of the contraction in French GDP. It is particularly sharp in transport equipment (-3.5%), dragged down by aerospace (-4.5 %) and automotive (-1.5 %). Activity is also declining in the agri-food sector (-1.5%), which is suffering from the impact of poor summer harvests.
This drop effectively leaves the eurozone's second-largest economy on the brink of recession. At the same time, inflation has picked up again, reaching 3.4% year on year in October, compared with 3.1% in September. According to Insee, this is its highest level since January 2024.
The poor figures do not come as a surprise to experts, given the particularly unfavourable macroeconomic environment. "France is highly likely to experience a technical recession over the coming quarters", says Jérémie Peloso, chief strategist for Europe at BCA Research, speaking to Euronews.
"This scenario was already conceivable before the recent budgetary turmoil and the rout on the bond market", he adds.
"We will hit the wall"
The government has been shaken by the news and is stressing the need to secure adoption of the 2027 budget on time, in a parliament where it has no majority.
Speaking on Franceinfo, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure described the French economy as "at a standstill". He also warned that the country "will hit the wall" if the "recovery" budget is not adopted.
If parliamentary talks fail, the government is not ruling out using article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote, unless a motion of no confidence is carried. Another possibility is to resort to ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
According to Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University and author of the blog "La finance au cœur de nos vies," adopting a budget is not "decisive" in itself, as it would not, "through any kind of leverage effect, miraculously revive activity in the short term".

Local devolution decisions rest solely with Scotland and Wales, first ministers tell Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:53:51 UTC
02:53:51 KST

Scotland and Wales’s first ministers have told Andy Burnham that decisions on local devolution rest solely with their parliaments, in response to the prime minister’s push to extend English-style regional powers across the UK.
After Burnham held discussions in Glasgow with John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth about localised employment and reindustrialisation powers, Downing Street characterised the talks as constructive.
However, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, caused friction before the summit by criticising Swinney’s government for hoarding powers it acquired from Westminster rather than devolving them further.
Streeting told BBC Scotland: “One of the critiques we have … is that for the Scottish government, devolution is often about transferring power, responsibility, resources from Westminster to Holyrood and the challenge Andy Burnham is setting out is: ‘What about devolving more power also from Holyrood to local government across Scotland?’”
Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, had also been due at the talks, but did not attend after a political row between Sinn Féin and the DUP. Burnham said it was “disappointing” she was not there.
The prime minister said he hoped to have all four UK nations moving at the same pace on devolution, particularly on efforts outlined in Wednesday’s budget to give mayors in England more powers over tax revenues.
“There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind,” Burnham said. “I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also, crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.”
Ap Iorwerth said he had pushed Burnham on his wish to have more powers for his government.
He added: “I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd.”
Swinney’s comments after the summit took a similar line, saying he would “work constructively and collaboratively” in devolving more powers to his government, while adding that Burnham had assured him “that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour”.
Despite the emollient tone, tensions remain. Shortly before the summit, ap Iorwerth said Burnham’s first budget, which the Welsh government said amounted to a real-terms funding cut for the country, showed the prime minister was “not serious about Wales”.
Plaid Cymru, which won May’s Senedd elections, putting nationalists in office in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, has already formally asked Burnham to give Wales the same devolved powers as Scotland.
The SNP-led government is frequently irritated by comments such as those by Streeting, characterised by one Scottish official as “lecturing us on devolution”.
Separately, Lee Waters, who was a minister in the Labour-led Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until the elections in May, told the Guardian that Burnham, who was the Greater Manchester mayor before becoming prime minister, should not try to impose an English-style mayoral model on Wales, as “we are not comparing like with like”.
He said: “The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas.
“Transposing an English mayoral worldview on to a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends.
“Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government.”

US woman who survived botched execution says she’s in constant pain
- Christa Pike said she is in “constant pain” after surviving a botched execution in Tennessee, and still struggles to speak.
- Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital on 30 September, was taken to hospital in critical condition, and later returned to prison.
- Her lawyers want Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison, while he has suspended executions pending an independent investigation.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Convicted murderer Christa Pike said on Oct 30 that she is in constant pain, a month after surviving a botched execution attempt in the US state of Tennessee.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike said, in a statement released by her lawyers.
“My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts,” she said.
“I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”
Pike, 50, was given two doses of the drug pentobarbital at a state prison on Sept 30 – a usually fatal dose that nevertheless failed to kill her.
She was transported to hospital in critical condition and returned to prison after receiving medical treatment.
Pike is the only inmate to ever survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre.
Pike was sentenced to death in Tennessee after she and her boyfriend beat and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp. Pike was 18 at the time of the murder.
In her statement, Pike said she is recovering “but healing is not the same as being okay.”
“I don’t know why I survived that night,” she said. “I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time.”
Since the botched execution, Pike’s lawyers have repeatedly called on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison.
Lee, a Republican, has suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation.
Asked by reporters this week about Pike’s fate, Lee said: “I suspect her sentence will be the same as it was before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
There have been 32 executions in the United States this year, all by lethal injection.
The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others – California, Oregon and Pennsylvania – have moratoriums in place. AFP

RAWALPINDI, Pakistan, Oct 30 - Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his first interview since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.
Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir — Pakistan's chief mediator in its efforts to de-escalate the now eight-month-old Iran war — has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.
“Why would the Field Marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.
PACT DOES NOT BAR NEW MEMBERS
“The word that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.
There were still "powerful spoilers and detractors," who believed conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan's armed forces are headquartered, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the United States had backed the trip.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin joined Munir in Tehran on Monday.
Their two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will be treated as an attack on all.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.
While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.
After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional countries without foreign intervention.
The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.
“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. "We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict," he added.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.
HOME FRONT
On the home front, the federal government suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), on October 11 and detained Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.
The government had accused the provincial administration of failing to tackle militancy. The PTI rejected the allegations and says its government took part in counter-terrorism efforts. PTI leaders called the move a pretext to crush protests.
Asked if there would now be larger military-led campaigns in the province, Chaudhry said that was not how the army conducted counter-terrorism.
"Our counter-terrorism operations are based on what we call IBOs, intelligence-based operations... The tempo of the freedom of action of (those) IBOs will further increase," he said.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:48:38 UTC
02:48:38 KST

Russia has fired more than 925,000 shells at Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast since late 2022 and now sends up to 6,500 drone attacks against it every week. Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration, set out the toll at the Council of Europe’s Congress of Local and Regional Authorities in Strasbourg.
Approximately 70% of Kherson Oblast remains under Russian military occupation, primarily across the left (east) bank of the Dnipro River, while Ukrainian forces control and have liberated the right bank, including the regional center of Kherson city.
“Everything except nuclear weapons”: the toll Kherson carried to Strasbourg
Prokudin told European partners that his region has spent nearly five years at the epicenter of the war, a few kilometers from Russian positions.
“It used everything except nuclear weapons. A separate danger is the ‘drone safari,’ today up to 6,500 drone attacks a week. This is deliberate, targeted terror against civilians, children, medics and rescuers. But we stayed, adapted and learned to counter this terror,” Prokudin said.
What nine European countries are now coming to learn
The region has answers that are already keeping 140,000 residents alive, he said: coordination among local authorities, the military, emergency services and volunteers; underground schools and hospitals; the pace of demining in deoccupied areas; and anti-drone defenses that let Ukraine’s forces bring down most of the incoming UAVs.
“We paid an extremely high price for this knowledge. That is why our unique experience of civil-military administration is already being studied by nine European countries, from the Baltics and Scandinavia to Germany and Poland,” he stressed.
His central message, he added, was that a large-scale crisis leaves no time to prepare, and that Europe must ready its communities, energy, medicine and local government, not only its armies, while it still holds the one thing Ukrainians lacked in February 2022, which is time.
“Our pain must gain meaning, and our lessons must save thousands of lives,” Prokudin added.
He thanked the Council of Europe and international partners for their solidarity with the region.

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Security Council on Friday adopted a resolution to extend the mandate of the UN Verification Mission in Colombia for another year, until Oct. 31, 2027.
Resolution 2833 decides that the mission's mandate will be focused on its primary function only: the reincorporation of former combatants of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and personal and collective security guarantees.
The Colombian government and the FARC struck a peace deal in August 2016 after four years of negotiations in Havana, Cuba. The UN Security Council in July 2017 approved the establishment of the Verification Mission to verify the political, economic and social reintegration of former FARC combatants as well as security guarantees.
The mandate of the mission was later expanded to include monitoring the implementation of the 2016 peace agreement's comprehensive rural reform and ethnic chapters. Friday's resolution retained only the primary tasks of the mission. ■

Ethiopia's bike-sharing service grows popular
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:46:39 CST
02:46:39 KST

Bicycles of Addis Bike are seen at a docking station in Addis Ababa, capital of Ethiopia, Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Michael Tewelde/Xinhua)
ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Sitting in his office in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, Yeabsera Yismashewa monitors bicycles being rolled out along the city's newly constructed bike lanes.
Yismashewa works as chief technical officer for Addis Bike, the country's first station-to-station bike-sharing operator. Launched in August 2024 with a fleet of 20 mechanical bikes, Addis Bike has now deployed 100 bikes, offering service along selected routes and designated bike lanes in the city.
"We have seen a growing number of people using the bike-sharing service in the city," Yismashewa said, adding that the public's awareness of and interest in using the service is surprisingly improving.
Yismashewa attributes the launch of the new transport service to government-led expansion of the infrastructure network for non-motorized vehicles, prompting demand for the biking service.
"We recognized that many daily journeys in the city cover relatively short distances, yet people often spend considerable time and money to reach their destinations. We want to offer an alternative transportation service that combines convenience, technology, and environmental friendliness," he told Xinhua in a recent interview.
The service mainly addresses transportation challenges faced by government employees, who may find it difficult to get a taxi or bus while going to the office during morning hours, said Yismashewa.
Since the fleet's launch in 2024, Addis Bike has reported over 35,311 sign-ups and 51,720 trips, with an average ride lasting 30 minutes. Riders are charged per minute, with a 30-minute ride costing 95 Ethiopian birr (about 0.6 U.S. dollars).
However, established travel habits, low public awareness, and insufficient parking and docking stations remain a challenge to the business, said the company.
Eyoas Girma is one of the many students who often use the bike-sharing service to commute between home and school.
"These days, it is very difficult to get a taxi during morning hours. I prefer to ride the bike to school," Girma said, noting that he finds the service more "flexible and economical."
Addis Bike's operating model incorporates digital fleet management, including Global Positioning System tracking and a smart-lock system, to help trace the bikes on the road, determine their status, and take appropriate follow-up action in case of misuse.
Other residents share similar sentiments. "I am happy the bike-sharing service is launched in Ethiopia. I have been enjoying the service since six months ago," Etsub Getahun said. "I ride the bikes to keep me strong and fit."
Since 2020, the government of Ethiopia, through the Addis Ababa City Administration, has been building bicycle lanes and pedestrian walkways as part of its corridor development project, aiming to slash greenhouse emissions and promote green mobility.
Accordingly, the government banned imports of petrol and diesel vehicles in 2024, while reducing taxes on electric vehicles (EVs), a policy that helped increase the adoption of EVs nationwide. The transition also aims to ensure energy sovereignty by saving foreign currency spent on fuel imports. ■

A man rides a bicycle of Addis Bike in Addis Ababa, capital of Ethiopia, Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Michael Tewelde/Xinhua)

UN Security Council renews authorization of EU-led stabilization force in Bosnia and Herzegovina
China
Unknown Publisher

01:46:35 CST
02:46:35 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The UN Security Council on Friday renewed the authorization of an EU-led stabilization force in Bosnia and Herzegovina for another 12 months.
The 15-member council unanimously adopted Resolution 2834, which re-authorizes European Union Force Althea (EUFOR ALTHEA) and the NATO presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a further period of 12 months, starting from the date of the adoption of the resolution.
EUFOR ALTHEA, a successor to a NATO-led stabilization force, has a mission to ensure continued compliance with the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, which put an end to the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
The resolution authorizes UN member states to take all necessary measures, upon request, in defense of EUFOR ALTHEA or the NATO presence respectively, and to assist both organizations in carrying out their missions.
It recognizes the right of both EUFOR ALTHEA and the NATO presence to take all necessary measures to defend themselves from attack or threat of attack. ■

This aerial drone photo taken on July 20, 2026 shows the historic markets and surrounding buildings in the Old City of Aleppo, northern Syria. (Photo by Monsef Memari/Xinhua)
by Hummam Sheikh Ali
ALEPPO, Syria, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Abdul Qader al-Qusaib, who owns a roastery in Aleppo's Old City, remembers a time when the souks bustled with merchants and customers, and the sounds of trade filled the narrow passageways.
The hustle and bustle came to an abrupt end when fighting engulfed the historic marketplace in northern Syria. Shops were damaged or shuttered, commercial activity ground to a halt, and merchants lost not only their workplaces but also the livelihoods they had built over the years.
When restoration began, al-Qusaib closely followed the work and witnessed the changes firsthand.
Initially, some shopkeepers were reluctant to reopen while nearby markets remained damaged and customer numbers were low.
Gradually, the situation began to change. As more sections were restored, merchants reopened their shops, customers returned and the once-disconnected markets began functioning again. Al-Qusaib eventually reopened his own shop.
Al-Qusaib's return reflects a broader revival taking place across the historic marketplace.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1986, Aleppo's historic souks had long been a vibrant trading hub along the Silk Road. Once the largest covered market in the world, the 13-km labyrinth through the old city was devastated during some of the fiercest fighting of Syria's civil war.
A massive fire in 2012 swept through large sections of the souks, destroying hundreds of shops and damaging centuries-old structures. Shelling and fighting between 2012 and 2016 further devastated the area, forcing traders to abandon shops passed down for generations.
In 2017, restoration projects began reconnecting parts of the marketplace after the fighting subsided. Rehabilitation has been completed in several markets, including Souk al-Hibal, while work has continued in other sections of the old city.
Yet those involved in the recovery say preserving the markets requires more than reconstructing their historic appearance.
Firas Qasmo, involved in the old city's rehabilitation efforts, stressed the importance of bringing economic activity back alongside physical restoration, including supporting traditional trades and creating opportunities for younger generations.
For Osama Rostom, who runs a handicrafts and art shop in Souk al-Hibal, this means bringing life back to the souks and repairing their historic structures.
Having witnessed the market's destruction and rehabilitation, Rostom remembers how wartime damage left parts of the historic commercial district empty and disrupted trades associated with its specialized souks for generations.
Rostom reopened his shop in 2023 and gradually saw other businesses follow. As more shopkeepers returned, visitors began walking through the restored lanes again, bringing activity back to streets that had once stood largely deserted.
For Rostom, the recovery means more than just revenue.
He said that Aleppo's traditional markets are not simply collections of historic buildings. Their identity is closely connected to the crafts, skills and commercial practices passed down through generations.
Therefore, the reopening of neighboring souks has become an important part of his own business's recovery, drawing more visitors into the wider commercial district and improving the prospects of merchants who have already returned, he added.
In the old city, physical reconstruction and economic recovery are closely linked: restored streets allow shops to reopen, returning merchants help attract customers, and growing commercial activity encourages more shopkeepers to return.
"We hope everything will come back, but little by little, as the rest of the markets are restored," al-Qusaib said. ■
Workers conduct restoration work inside one of the historic markets in the Old City of Aleppo, northern Syria, July 20, 2026. (Photo by Monsef Memari/Xinhua)
A worker conducts restoration work inside one of the historic markets in the Old City of Aleppo, northern Syria, July 20, 2026. (Photo by Monsef Memari/Xinhua)

How cuts under Colombia’s de la Espriella threaten a key human rights court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:43:21 UTC
02:43:21 KST

Bogota, Colombia – Angela Cordon was only a teenager when her father and uncle disappeared.
They were among a string of farmers and merchants to go missing in the southwestern department of Huila in Colombia.
First came her uncle Reynaldo Cordon Herrera's kidnapping. A grocer by trade, he had been travelling by truck on January 22, 2003, when he went missing.
The next month, Guillermo Cordon Herrera — Angela's father — set out to discover what happened to his brother, tracing his whereabouts through rural Colombia.
Guillermo called home one night with news: He had made contact with the rebel fighters he believed to be responsible for his brother's abduction.
It was the last time his family would ever hear from him. His body was never found, nor was his brother's.
Angela's father and uncle are among the more than 450,664 people killed as part of Colombia's six-decade-long internal armed conflict.
In the 23 years since their disappearance, Angela and her family have sought any information they could find about their loved ones' last days. "I have dedicated my life to this search," she told Al Jazeera.
She credits one institution in particular with helping her find answers: Colombia's Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), a transitional justice court.
Set up in 2016 as part of a peace deal between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's largest rebel group at the time, the court handles the prosecution and investigation of crimes committed during the conflict.
But victims, their loved ones and even some former fighters fear that budget cuts could gut JEP, leaving the court unable to fulfil its mission.
This month, the administration of right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it would enact a 2027 budget with dramatic reductions for government bodies like JEP.
The total cuts to JEP were valued at around 181 billion Colombian pesos, or roughly $57m.
On Wednesday, a Senate committee also advanced a bill to eliminate JEP altogether by March 2028, with a proposal to transfer its functions to the general court system.
Angela, however, credits JEP with offering closure that the criminal justice system was never able to provide. She worries that slashing the court's funding — much less shuttering it entirely — could derail its work.
Through JEP, Angela learned about her father and uncle's time in captivity, as well as the site of their execution. JEP has also worked with former FARC members to try to locate their remains.
"Fewer resources mean fewer missions to the field to find answers, less humanitarian personnel," Angela said, bracing for the cuts.
"It probably means that we will never be able to return to the site."
A 'duty to manage spending'
De la Espriella has framed the budget reduction as necessary to combat Colombia's rising public debt, which exceeds $370bn.
"It is my duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the government's limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone," de la Espriella wrote in a September statement, defending his decision to trim JEP's funding.
He estimated that its payroll budget alone was north of 404 billion pesos, or $127m, in 2026.
Critics, however, have questioned whether austerity is the motive for the downsizing.
At around 634 trillion pesos or $200bn, de la Espriella's 2027 budget increases spending overall.
Passed by presidential decree, the budget is considered the largest spending package in the history of the country.
But de la Espriella has targeted JEP for reasons beyond its cost. He has repeatedly criticised JEP as slow and ineffective, failing to deliver on its promises of justice.
He has also slammed the court's investigations as biased against military members — and too lenient on rebels.
In an interview with the radio show Recap Blu, he accused JEP of "persecuting the heroes of the homeland" while "washing the hands of the guerrillas who committed crimes against humanity".
'Disastrous for victims'
But many victims' rights advocates dispute that assessment.
Ana Maria Rodriguez, a lawyer who represents victims of Colombia's conflict, described the accusation of bias as "patently false".
She pointed out that JEP has convicted some of the top leadership in the FARC, the rebel group that disarmed as part of the 2016 peace deal.
“It hasn’t been perfect or complete,” Rodriguez said of the JEP's work. "But the peace process here has become a model studied by other countries around the world. We have to keep this process functional.”
She believes that cuts to the court's budget will lead to fewer convictions, furthering impunity rather than preventing it.
“Many of the [perpetrators] have never faced any justice mechanisms outside of the JEP,” Rodriguez said.
In its effort to close unsolved cases, the court has offered leniency to soldiers, rebels and other fighters in exchange for cooperation with ongoing investigations.
Those cases typically result in rehabilitation work instead of a prison sentence, with defendants asked to engage in community service.
Those kinds of sentences have fuelled some of the criticism against JEP. But Rodriguez feels such trade-offs are necessary to offer resolution to victims' families.
After all, more than 100,000 people have been reported missing in Colombia's conflict. Their fate remains unknown.
“It isn’t clear how cases will be able to proceed without witness cooperation programmes," Rodriguez said.
She predicted that shrinking JEP's funding will be "absolutely disastrous for victims".
A fear of jeopardising investigations
Ahead of the anticipated cuts to JEP this month, more than 20 Colombian Congress members signed an open letter to the International Criminal Court (ICC), asking for help.
The ICC shares a similar mandate as JEP, as both are charged with investigating and prosecuting war crimes.
The international court was also supportive of the 2016 peace deal that gave rise to JEP's creation.
"We are concerned that [the budget's] approval will jeopardise investigations, trials and the execution of sentences for crimes under the court's jurisdiction," the lawmakers wrote to the ICC, in a request for support.
Alberto Yepes, a spokesman for the Colombia-Europe-United States Coordination Group, a human rights coalition, is among those rallying against the JEP cuts.
He sees a connection between the attacks on JEP and de la Espriella's heavy-handed approach to law enforcement.
De la Espriella, he explained, has modelled his security platform on hardline programmes in countries like El Salvador and Ecuador, where police and soldiers have been granted expanded powers.
Yepes believes that, by weakening JEP, the president may seek to prevent the future prosecution of military leaders in cases involving state crimes.
"These policies accompany aggressive new security measures, and combined, I think it seems very clear that this government is seeking impunity for the military," Yepes said.
In addition to reducing JEP's funding, de la Espriella's government is reportedly weighing a 116-page "counterterrorism" bill that would increase penalties for certain offences, criminalise some forms of protest, and make it more difficult to suspend military operations.
In Yepes's view, the ultimate goal is to shield law enforcement from accountability.
"De la Espriella is making decisions for a minority of the people that will benefit from these policies," he said.

Liberal Zionists are trying to distance themselves from the reality that Israeli voters overwhelmingly want genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:42:34 UTC
02:42:34 KST

The recent Israeli elections brought the terrifying views of Israeli youth into full view. Videos of young Israelis calling for the mass slaughter of Palestinians or expressing their desire for the new Israeli government to go even further to the right than it already has have been making waves online, and while it’s no surprise that these soundbites go viral on social media, it is important to understand just how pervasive these views are. It is not just one or two fanatics who were taken out of context online. It is a whole new generation of Israeli youth who, in the wake of October 7 and the genocide in Gaza, are fully embracing fascism.
This is not typical internationally, where younger generations are often less nationalist-conservative than older ones. A poll from this year, conducted by Israeli Channel 12, shows that among 18- to 21-year-olds who hadn’t voted in the 2022 elections, the share identifying as right-wing rose to 75%, up from 68% in the older population. This segment, consisting of about half a million potential new voters, formed in their teens by genocide, is simply more genocidal than ever, and this obviously played a part in the elections this week.
With votes in Israel now fully counted, it is clear that the Israeli public still voted overwhelmingly right. Netanyahu’s Likud leads with 27 seats (the big opposition party Yashar, headed by ret. general Gadi Eisenkot, mastermind of the murderous ‘Dahiya Doctrine’, comes in second with 21). Although Netanyahu’s current government bloc hasn’t got a majority (it has 53 and one needs a 61 majority), the opposition bloc still contains right-wing parties like Yashar, as well as Avigdor Lieberman’s further-right Yisrael Beitenu (7), Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s Together (12), and even The Democrats led by ret. general Yair Golan (8) don’t want to talk about two states anymore. The left that is not Zionist is represented by the Palestinian-representative Joint List, with a surprising 11 seats (the conservative Palestinian Ra’am got 8) – but the Jewish Zionist bloc by and large refuses to touch them. So the ‘opposition bloc’ without the Palestinian parties has 48 seats, and while the Democrats have started considering cooperation, it is contentious. Zionist racism is the overall frame of this picture.
Perhaps one of the best ways to understand the views of this new generation of Israeli voters, and how Israeli “liberal” Zionists are trying to distance themselves from the current reality — in a futile attempt to restore a fictional version of the liberal Israeli “democracy” they cherish — is with a popular video series that veteran TV host and comedian Lior Schleien made this year.
The series followed Schleien, a proud “liberal Zionist,” as he toured schools across the country, engaging in debates with Israeli youth on topics related to the “conflict” with the Palestinians, Middle East geopolitics, and other national and religious issues.
Brace yourselves: the views of the Israeli youth, and Schleien’s misguided attempts to sway them to more “liberal” views, reveal a grim picture of the state of the Israeli political landscape, and how the genocidal apartheid state is only getting more genocidal.
Confronting extremism…to a point
In his tours of schools around the country, Schleien confronts explicitly genocidal youths and films his encounters. In one video, which has since been removed by request of the student’s parents, one student tells him, “Every Arab in the world should die, whether he is good or not good… I have no problem killing fifty Arabs and dying – Arabs, terrorists, I don’t care which.”
Schleien asks whether there is a difference between a terrorist and an Arab – the student answers “no, every Arab should be in the grave, that’s it”.
That’s clearly way too far for Schleien – he asks whether such a thing is “possible,” that is, to kill every Arab.
So Schleien seeks dialogue with this ‘extremist’ youth, because as he told Haaretz in an interview, “Israel is still a democracy, and there’s only one way to change things in a democracy, and that’s by persuading people to see things your way.”
In another encounter, Schleien argues with a right-wing settler-student that she and her peers are “not human shields,” in response to her claim that Israeli settlements are strategic. Instead, he argues for ethnic “separation.” So he proposes pragmatic solutions, based on the Zionist apartheid logic, that speak to the fears of these upcoming voters:
“If Israel annexes the West Bank and grants all the Palestinians citizenship and the right to vote, they would soon have a majority in the Knesset, and you all would lose this Jewish state that is so important to you. And if you prefer to deny them citizenship and the right to vote, then prepare yourselves for Israel to be boycotted by most of the world.”
In another video with the “Hilltop Youth“, Schleien tries to persuade them not to “bother Palestinians, or beat them up, or rob them”, since that will “not convince 3 million people to get up and leave their home, even if their life sucks” (in the West Bank). “It won’t happen,” he emphasizes, “I’m not telling you it’s not moral, or not legal – it’s not gonna happen.” Schleien is countered by a teenager who says that “here in Judea and Samaria” (biblical names for the West Bank, which Schleien also uses), “we have deterrence. Every Arab here experiences deterrence by a Jew; when he sees a Jew, he fears that Jew more than in Tel Aviv or any other place, and I think that in general, deterrence is our victory.”
Schleien’s argument about “ain’t gonna happen” doesn’t seem to harmonize with the witnessed experience of ethnic cleansing, and also genocide. These youths see what their state is doing. “Bothering Palestinians” is an understatement, and it’s not just the “Hilltop Youth” doing it; it’s the state.
The liberal Zionist fight against the right and the left
The increasingly extremist views of Israeli youth are no doubt disturbing. However, as an Israeli myself, who has been documenting this racist and genocidal society and its views for a long time, what stood out to me more than the views of the youth was the attempts of Schleien to push back against them in pursuit of his vision for an Israel that does not, and has never existed.
In the context of the elections, Israel’s supposedly liberal Zionist opposition to Netanyahu is struggling to make itself relevant. Although no Zionist party advocates the elusive ‘two-state solution,’ there are those who still struggle to portray it as liberal – perhaps mostly for the sake of their own self-view.
Schleien is one of the main representatives of this effort. He seeks to fight Netanyahu, while simultaneously fighting the growing isolation of Israel through boycotts, divestment, and sanctions (BDS).
Schleien’s series is not just about confronting the right-wing views of Israeli youth. Simultaneously, he also charges American liberals, and particularly Jews, with being too extreme on Israel – chiding them for supposedly doing the same thing Netanyahu is doing to the liberal Zionists, just from the left (by, for example, boycotting Israeli academia).
Schleien thus seeks to position himself in the middle of all that – precisely as a proud ‘liberal Zionist’.
“Because of the catastrophic mistakes of this government we elected – and I’m obviously using the royal ‘we’ here – we are in danger of losing this beloved country of ours,” he says, cited by Haaretz. “We elected a government that is dismantling this country and will continue to do so if it remains in power. So, before our haters ‘free Palestine from the river to the sea,’ we Israelis need to free Israel from this government that is pushing us to the brink.”
Schleien’s portrayal of this as a fight between the Zionist left and the Zionist right is betrayed by a reality wherein both are fighting a similar fight against Palestinians. As the former head of the Kibbutz Movement, Nir Meir, said in his interview to Haaretz in 2024, the right-wing settlers are “correct”, in that this “is the way to seize and hold land, and their claim that, any place we Israelis leave, the Arabs will come in our place, is correct”. Meir also noted that the settlers “learned from us how to settle and seize land”. And Meir is correct about this being a cardinal Zionist view. The supposedly leftist kibbutzniks, who have had a major inciting role in the genocide of Gaza, are arguing with the right-wing settlers about location and speed, not principle.
So Schleien has taken up a balancing act.
Zionist gaslighting
Lior Schleien is thus seeking to advocate for the ‘good Zionism.’ His is open to dialogue with the extremists, much in the nature of the late author Amos Oz, who was also a major propagandist for Zionism. While calling the settlers ‘zealots,’ Oz also mocked Palestinians for their ‘illness’ in seeking their right to return, opining that one needed a “big stick” to deal with them.
Schleien professes to be apolitical, as it were. “I’m not a campaigner, and I don’t tell them which party to support,” he tells Haaretz. “All I tell them is that they need to formulate their political positions based on facts rather than fallacies, that they need to think critically, and I present a non-apologetic liberal democratic worldview.”
But that worldview is limited by Zionism, in which apartheid is central. So he seeks to make an ultra-nationalist ideology relevant in liberal thinking, portraying himself as the moderate in debating the extremists – both for the personal image, but also for the international one. Yet it is doubtful whether Schleien will be able to convince the world that Israel can heal itself from within, and that external pressures must be fended off for that to happen. Many have just stopped consuming that ‘liberal-Zionist’ gaslighting.
It is not yet clear how the recent elections will end up in terms of government. The unwillingness to involve Palestinians in governance may result in another forever-elections cycle like the one experienced in 2019-2022, with five elections taking place within less than four years. But any result will be a manifestation of Israel’s increasingly explicit right-wing turn, and the youth indicate that this tide is only growing.
Some, like Schleien, seek hope through internal Zionist discussions. But those of us who know better know that Zionism’s settler-colonialist vein is ultra-nationalist, so it’s natural for it to go that way. If one wants a more serious solution to this problem, then this will require outside pressure. Any other talk is just naiveté or hypocrisy. Schleien seeks to stem precisely that pressure, which is why his effort amounts to window-dressing at best.

Drone strikes on Ethiopia displacement camp kill at least 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:42:09 UTC
02:42:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Drone strikes on Ethiopia displacement camp kill at least 15, sources say
At least 15 people, several of them children, died in a series of drone strikes that hit a camp for displaced civilians in Ethiopia's Amhara region, two sources involved in a rescue operation said on Friday.
It was not clear why the camp was targeted or who was behind the attack, but the strikes highlight continuing clashes in the area despite a lull in the heavy fighting that erupted last month between an alliance of rebels from northern Tigray region and the government in Addis Ababa.
"There were around five explosions. Then ... we started collecting bodies," a community representative involved in the burials told Reuters, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The representative said they helped bury 13 people at the camp, which is known as Jari 2 and is home to more than 1,700 people who fled previous violence.
Two of the injured later died at a hospital in Hayk, a town 17 km (10 miles) away.
A spokesperson for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A local official said they were aware of the incident and were helping get medical treatment to 36 people who had been injured.
A man who lost a family member described seeing a drone circling overhead on Wednesday and then returning on Thursday.
“Then finally it hit the camp … three times,” the relative told Reuters. “Their body parts were scattered everywhere. We collected and buried pieces of their body parts.”
A resident of Hayk who was helping provide shelter to survivors also said 15 people had been killed. "Those from the camp are now sheltering in a school," the resident said.
The dead included five children, according to the two sources involved in the rescue.
The relative of one of the victims said they had seen at least 10 injured children under the aged of five receiving treatment.
All three sources said there had been no fighting in the area when the strike took place, but members of the Amhara Fano National Movement, which is part of the rebel alliance spearheaded by fighters from Tigray, had been nearby.
Government troops have driven back the rebel alliance since their offensive was launched on 23 September.
They retook the capital of Tigray region earlier this month and advanced towards the border with Eritrea, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebellion by sending troops over the border.
Eritrea denies the accusation and says Addis Ababa's allegations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a "declaration of war".
Given the web of interconnected conflicts in the Horn of Africa, with neighbouring countries and powers further afield backing their respective proxies, experts have warned that war in Ethiopia could trigger a broader conflict in the region.
