Russia Spent Decades Modernizing One Giant Cruiser—Now Its Flagship Is Headed for Scrap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:56 UTC
01:47:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Spent Decades Modernizing One Giant Cruiser—Now Its Flagship Is Headed for Scrap
Russia’s flagship nuclear-powered battlecruiser Pyotr Velikiy is no longer considered worth repairing or modernizing after years of accumulated wear, according to a preliminary assessment by a special commission.
Vladimir Maltsev, head of the All-Russian Fleet Support Movement, told Russian state media agency TASS that specialists had concluded the massive warship could not realistically be restored to service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The cruiser cannot be restored. The ship has a certain degree of wear,” Maltsev said on the sidelines of the “330 Years of the Russian Fleet” forum.
He stressed that the finding remains preliminary and that a final decision will be announced later.
According to a TASS source in Russia’s defense industry, Moscow had originally planned to begin modernizing Pyotr Velikiy immediately after completing work on its sister ship, Admiral Nakhimov. The idea was to ensure that the Russian Navy always retained at least one nuclear-powered cruiser of the class.
That plan fell apart as work on Admiral Nakhimov dragged on eight years beyond the original schedule. By the time the overhaul was finally nearing completion, Pyotr Velikiy had reportedly exhausted its remaining service life.
The cruiser serves as the flagship of Russia’s Northern Fleet and is the last active ship of the Soviet-designed Orlan nuclear-powered cruiser family.
Russian sources have long described it as the Navy’s most heavily armed surface strike vessel and one of the world’s largest surface combatants outside the aircraft-carrier category.
Four ships of the class were built at the Baltic Shipyard between 1977 and 1996. Two—Admiral Ushakov and Admiral Lazarev—have already been retired.
The modernization of Admiral Nakhimov, meanwhile, stretched across decades and was completed this summer. The cruiser is currently undergoing trials and is expected to return to the Northern Fleet before the end of 2026.
Sevmash, the Severodvinsk shipyard responsible for the overhaul program, has capacity to accommodate only one cruiser of the class at a time.
Work on Admiral Nakhimov had originally been expected to finish in 2018, but repeated delays pushed the program far beyond schedule. Its reported cost more than doubled during the process, eventually exceeding 200 billion rubles.
If Pyotr Velikiy is retired, Admiral Nakhimov will become Russia’s principal heavy surface combatant of the type.
The modernized ship is expected to carry Fort-M and Pantsir-M air-defense systems, Paket-NK and Otvet anti-submarine weapons, and universal vertical launch cells capable of holding as many as 80 Kalibr, Oniks, and Zircon missiles.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia was preparing to retire its only aircraft carrier, Admiral Kuznetsov, effectively shutting down its fixed-wing carrier aviation.

Ukraine’s FPV Drone Hits Loaded Russian Grad and Sets Off Massive Explosion, Video
Russian BM-21 Grad multiple-launch rocket system was hit by a powerful blast after being struck by an FPV drone while still positioned for firing, according to footage released by the Signum Battalion of Ukraine’s 59th Unmanned Systems Brigade.
The Russian crew reportedly managed to fire only two ranging rockets before the Ukrainian drone reached the launcher.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The forecast says the hail is canceled. SIGNUM fighters hunted down a Russian BM-21 Grad multiple-launch rocket system right on its firing position,” the unit said.
Footage of the strike shows the launcher erupting after impact, with the remaining rockets apparently contributing to the violent secondary detonation.
The Signum operators also struck several other Russian vehicles used to move personnel and supplies toward the front.
According to the unit, the additional targets included a pickup truck from which Russian troops were seen jumping out, an ATV, a camouflaged vehicle, and other logistics equipment.
The BM-21 Grad remains one of Russia’s most widely used multiple-launch rocket systems in its war of aggression against Ukraine.
Developed in the early 1960s and introduced into Soviet service in 1963, the system is mounted on a Ural truck chassis and carries 40 launch tubes for 122mm rockets.
A Grad can fire its full load in roughly 20 seconds, saturating an area of up to about 14.5 hectares, or 36 acres.
Depending on the ammunition used, the system can strike targets at distances of up to roughly 40 kilometers, or 25 miles, making it particularly dangerous against troop concentrations, defensive positions, and infrastructure.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces tracked down and destroyed a Russian BM-30 Smerch multiple launch rocket system (MLRS) and its accompanying reloading vehicle hidden approximately 60 kilometers behind the frontline.

Binance hack losses exceed total market theft over past two years — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:37 UTC
01:47:37 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. The scale of the hacker attack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, which resulted in the withdrawal of approximately $6.3 billion, has exceeded the combined losses suffered by the crypto market from hacks over the previous two years, Olga Goncharova, head of the Digital Financial Assets and Digital Currencies Expert Center of the Association of Banks of Russia, told TASS.
"The bulk of the funds was siphoned off in just 20 minutes – more was taken from the exchange than hackers stole from the entire crypto market over the last two years. This is a classic 'black swan' – an event no one anticipated that has instantly rewritten the industry's entire statistics. Hundreds of minor incidents occur over the years, and then one single event happens that overshadows years of data. You cannot prepare for this based on average figures. Security must be built with the worst-case scenario in mind," she noted.
According to the expert, despite the scale of the attack, it is premature to speak of critical flaws in Binance’s security system. "I know Binance from the inside. Their security team has always been one of the strongest in the industry, so I wouldn't call it a critical error just yet. It is more likely a case of social engineering," Goncharova explained.
Earlier, the Binance press office stated that the attackers may have gained access to the exchange’s internal infrastructure via a compromised work laptop belonging to one of its engineers. The exchange estimated the scale of the incident at approximately $6.3 billion and announced plans to compensate all losses using its SAFU insurance fund and corporate resources.

Israel’s final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.
The results released early yesterday showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.
Photo: AP
“Now comes the truly hard part,” centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: “If you want to know if something’s happening behind the silence you’re hearing now, the answer is yes.”
Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?
Much of Israel yesterday started winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them.
“There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties,” said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv.
The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president on Wednesday, then Israeli President Isaac Herzog would task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.
If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he would do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.
In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20 percent of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahu’s far-right allies such as Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats.
In Netanyahu’s first public comment yesterday, he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties.
The head of Israel’s election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims, but asked the agency to investigate.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”
As it announced results, the election committee said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Central Elections Committee Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the investigation had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.

China expels record number of officials from CCP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:22 UTC
01:47:22 KST

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25 percent of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
Photo: EPA
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia (張又俠), the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui (馬興瑞), the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society think tank, said in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. However, in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey.”
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi and the military’s anti-graft czar, Zhang Shengmin (張升民).
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of next year. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of communist China since Mao Zedong (毛澤東).
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo would be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Ministry approves first carbon sequestration exploration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:21 UTC
01:47:21 KST

The Ministry of Environment yesterday said it has approved the nation’s first carbon sequestration geological exploration plan, marking a shift from policy to practice in Taiwan’s carbon sequestration efforts.
The plan was proposed by Formosa Petrochemical Corp (FPC, 台塑石化), based in Yunlin County’s Mailiao Township (麥寮).
Last month, media reports said that Formosa Plastics Group (FPG, 台塑集團), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) and US oil giant Exxon Mobil Corp were jointly planning and evaluating a carbon capture and storage project in deep waters off the township. The project is expected to help TSMC acquire low-carbon electricity in line with its net zero target.
Photo: Taipei Times
The ministry yesterday said that FPC proposed the geological exploration plan last month in accordance with the Regulations for the Management of Carbon Dioxide Capture and Storage (二氧化碳補捉後封存管理辦法), which were promulgated in August.
The project is to conduct a geological exploration of a 2,500km2 area that covers the FPG-run Mailiao Industrial Park and offshore waters, the ministry said.
The exploration work includes onshore and offshore seismic surveys, exploratory well drilling, well testing, petrophysical and core mechanics analysis, monitoring facility and model evaluation, it said.
The goal is to assess whether the area has reservoir stratum and caprock at 1,000m to 1,800m below ground level to ensure the safety of the sequestration site, it said.
Geological exploration is critical to selecting a carbon storage site, which must have a storage reservoir that is thick, continuous and topped by a compact, intact caprock layer to serve as a reliable sealing barrier, it said.
Such geological conditions and potential leakage pathways must be examined based on field measured data obtained through seismic surveys and hydrocarbon exploration, the ministry said.
FPC may start geological exploration after the ministry approved the plan on Thursday, but it may not apply for carbon storage at the site until its carbon sequestration project has completed an environmental impact assessment, it added.
The ministry held two meetings with authorities and experts to review the plan, it said.
They approved the exploration methods proposed by FPC as well as the plan’s scope of implementation and duration from Thursday to Dec. 31, 2031, it said.
No carbon dioxide injection test is allowed in future evaluation of the site’s injection reservoir, the ministry said.
Approving the exploration does not mean the site’s sequestration potential has become exclusionary, nor does it guarantee that the company’s future application for carbon storage would be prioritized, it said.
The plan’s reviewers have asked the company to do an environmental base line survey and take environmental protection measures before it starts drilling exploratory wells, the ministry said, urging the company to conduct environmental impact assessments based on exploration results.

Indigenous ancestry travel book launched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:21 UTC
01:47:21 KST

A book written by a Bunun man about his journey through an abandoned hunting path in search of “tears of the moon” has been launched in Taipei, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Nantou branch said on Wednesday.
Titled Mudadadan — meaning “go on foot” in the Bunun language — the book documents ancestry trips taken by a group of young Bunun people of Tumpu Village (東埔部落) in Nantou County’s Sinyi Township (信義).
The trips began with a Bunun tale that author Ibi Takiludun Takisbisazuan’s father used to tell him, in which a sun was shot down by an arrow and turned into the moon with its tears left on a rock.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Nantou Branch
Takisbisazuan on Wednesday told a news conference that he used to be scared of the dark when he was little.
“However, I realized when I grew older that what scares me more is the gradual loss of people who can lead me out of the dark,” he said.
Bunun mythology is rooted in the village’s surrounding topographic landscapes, Takisbisazuan said, adding that he learned about such stories while staying with village elders.
“Bunun hunters of younger generations lack the environment for them to become a cultured hunter,” he said, adding that a hunter is educated through experiences in the mountains rather than classroom learning or secondhand stories.
Takisbisazuan also encouraged younger Bunun people returning to their hometowns to learn more about elders’ traditional wisdom with a humble attitude.
Village members performed two songs at the news conference, Pasibutbut and Pislahi.
Pastor Supina said Pasibutbut is a prayer for a good millet harvest where each singer imitates sounds of everything in nature, such as sounds of winds, streams, waterfalls, bees and cicadas.
The resonant voices integrate into one melody echoing through the sky, she said, adding that the beautiful resonance is considered worthy of God’s blessing.
Pislahi is a song that Bunun hunting groups would chant before they enter the mountains to hunt for food, Supina said.
It prepares hunters with a godly mindset about their hunting trip when they sing to invite different animals to their hunting guns, she said.
“Muntjac, please come to my gun. Sambar deer, please come to my gun,” Supina said, reciting the lyrics.
“The song reflects Bunun people’s outlook on hunting,” she said. “Hunting while walking in the woods is not slaughter, plunder or brutal conquest, but to accept God’s blessings and arrangements.”
Hunters invite the animals to their guns and accept them with a reverent and grateful mind, she added.
Forestry agency Director-General Lin Hwa-ching (林華慶) said the book originated from forestry authorities’ collaborations with local indigenous people in indigenous hunting self-management.
Traditional indigenous hunting is not just about food; it has deep significance, he said.
That includes how indigenous people safeguard their land and resources, as well as their understanding of the land and nature after generations of migration, Lin said.
The book is expected to help the public understand the significance of traditional indigenous hunting and how indigenous people’s traditional wisdom can benefit today’s sustainable governance of natural and wildlife resources, he said.
Indigenous hunting self-management is not only about setting guidelines or a convention, but to help the government work with indigenous communities to apply their wisdom to forestry conservation, Lin said, adding that such a vision has been achieved with Tumpu Village.
Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute Director Yang Jia-dong (楊嘉棟) said cultural diversity is often overlooked in biodiversity conservation.
Tumpu Village has long been assisting the institute in biodiversity investigations and ecological conservation, he said, adding that the book helps readers understand Bunun people’s culture and emotional bond with the land.
Council of Indigenous Peoples Deputy Minister Qucung Qalavangan, who is also a Bunun member from the township, thanked the forestry agency and the branch for closely collaborating with the village.
The collaboration marks the start of reconciliation between the government and indigenous people since they were forced out of their traditional territories, he said.

‘Star Trek,’ Shakespeare actor Patrick Stewart dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:20 UTC
01:47:20 KST

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died on Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed.
“We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today,” Hugh Jackman, a frequent Stewart costar in the X-Men universe, said on social media. “And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”
Photo: Reuters
While best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation series and professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of A Christmas Carol and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land and Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot in repertory with buddy Ian McKellen.
He won three Olivier Awards, including one for playing Claudius in Hamlet opposite David Tennant. He also had a Grammy — in 1996 for best spoken word album for his recording of Peter and the Wolf.
He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England’s Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London’s West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008.
Stewart’s performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor.”
The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in “a truly great performance” and the New York Times said it was “a must-see.”
Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working-class corner of northern England, the future 24th-century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor.
He had been bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family.
His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”
In his memoir, Making It So, Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother, Trevor, braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother.
“Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head.”
The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims.
Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon.
“People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?’” he said. “Telly?”
Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film Excalibur. He had just done a production of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? in 1987 when an interesting offer came along.
“I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail,” he wrote.
It did not, of course. Thanks to Stewart’s rich baritone and noble bearing, the Star Trek franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan “Make it so.”
His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander.
“There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in Henry IV, which is about brave men,” Stewart wrote in his memoir.
Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another Star Trek icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969.
“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk in the franchise, wrote on Instagram. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did.”

Advocates criticize handling of river silt buildup issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:18 UTC
01:47:18 KST

Environmental advocates yesterday questioned the government’s handling of a river siltation problem in northern Tainan in which NT$1.3 billion (US$40 million) was allocated for bridge rebuilding without taking any action against allegedly illegal upstream land clearing.
The advocates convened a news conference in Taipei where they presented aerial photos showing that patches of woodland in Baihe District (白河) had been cleared, mostly within Baihe Reservoir’s water source quality protection area.
They said illegal land clearing has caused the build up of silt not only in downstream rivers such as the Jishuei River (急水溪), but also across local farmland.
Photo: CNA
Farmer Chang Ling-teng (張令騰) said he has eight hectares of farmland near the river and the Chianan Irrigation Canal (嘉南大圳), which faces serious siltation issues, especially following typhoons.
The silt erodes cultivation areas and can build up to 2m on the farmland, he said.
“Our fields are flooded with silt whenever Baihe Reservoir releases water during typhoons,” Chang said, adding that Typhoon Gaemi in 2024 caused the most severe agricultural losses.
Siltation issues forced Chang to abandon six hectares of green bamboo cultivation, he said.
Taiwan Water Resources Conservation Union chair Chen Jiau-hua (陳椒華) said the government has built Baihe Reservoir sediment bypass tunnels, which brings sediment into the Jishuei River.
Downstream siltation worsened around the Jishueisi Bridge (急水溪橋) — which spans the river’s main stream — as well as Cingye Bridge (青葉橋) and Baihe Bridge, which cross the river’s tributaries, she said.
Union executive director Wu Li-hui (吳麗慧) said that the government allocated NT$1.3 billion to reconstructing the three bridges, including NT$100 million for Baihe Bridge, NT$350 million for Cingye Bridge and NT$850 million for Jishueisi Bridge.
Combined with the Forward-Looking Infrastructure Development Program’s NT$1.75 billion budget invested in the reservoir sediment bypass project, the government has spent a great amount to solve the issue, she said.
However, it failed to stop upstream illegal land clearing and more than 10,000 tonnes of sediment continues to be discharged into the Jishuei River whenever heavy rainfall occurs, Wu said.
The Tainan Water Resources Bureau said that operators have been penalized for illegal land development in accordance with the Soil and Water Conservation Act (水土保持法).
Removing vegetation without changing the terrain is not punishable by the act, it said.
Regarding which agency is responsible for inspecting such land clearing, it was agreed that the Ministry of Agriculture’s Irrigation Agency is responsible.
However, the broader water source quality protection area requires coordination between the Irrigation Agency’s Chianan Management Office and the city government, the Water Resources Agency said.

In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. CEC head Michael You apologizes for national ID leak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:11 UTC
01:47:11 KST

The head of the Central Election Commission (CEC) on Thursday apologized after the national ID numbers of more than 1,500 candidates running for office, including those of top politicians, were reportedly exposed on its Web site for 11 days.
“This kind of thing should not have happened,” CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said during a news conference, blaming the lapse on “negligent” handling by a third-party contractor.
The issue came to light on Wednesday, when an alliance of smaller political parties said the ID numbers of 1,573 candidates running for mayor, commissioner or councilor in the Nov. 28 local elections had been publicly accessible on a CEC financial disclosures database.
Photo: Chang Chia-ming, Taipei Times
The alliance, known as Taiwan Go Go, consists of the New Power Party (NPP), the Taiwan Obasang Political Equality Party, the Taiwan Statebuilding Party and the Green Party Taiwan.
NPP Chairwoman Claire Wang (王婉諭) said that while compiling a “civil society version” of the official election bulletin, her team accessed the candidate asset declaration Web site made public by the CEC on Oct. 16.
On Tuesday, her team found that, although the site’s public-facing interface displayed only basic personal information, using a browser’s built-in developer tools (such as by pressing the F12 key) freely allowed people to retrieve data such as national ID numbers, she said.
The CEC on Wednesday said an external contractor had inadvertently exposed the ID numbers, but that the text in the files was “scrambled” and “indecipherable” to the general public.
Wang in a post on Facebook wrote that the “scrambled” text was due to “character encoding” settings, which could be rendered into Chinese characters using a browser’s developer tools.
Moreover, national ID numbers are composed of English letters and numbers, and were not scrambled in the files, she said.
You on Thursday said the CEC was notified of the leak on Tuesday evening and fixed the issue within two hours.
So far, the evidence points toward the exposure being an inadvertent oversight by an external contractor, Acer E-Enabling Service Business, which is owned by Acer Inc, he said.
You said his first reaction upon hearing of the leak was that it was “unbelievable” and “unacceptable.”
He acknowledged the “unease” it had caused among candidates and the public, and, along with the other CEC officials present, bowed in apology for the lapse.
Asked if the data leak would affect preparations for elections next month, You said it would not.
Only 32 IP addresses visited the CEC financial disclosures database during the 11 days the sensitive data was accessible, none of which were from overseas, he said.
As for whether the personal data had been copied by those who accessed it, You said the CEC could not be sure, as that information would only be on those users’ computers.
Asked if the commission would seek compensation from the contractor, CEC ethics office head Huang Shang-hsiang (黃尚香) said it would do so following an investigation and in accordance with their contract.
After two days of deliberation on the issue and ways to prevent any recurrence, You said his provisional solution was to “strictly implement the four-eyes principle.”
When the government outsources or commissions a project, the work should be checked by another team, and then verified again by the government itself, he said.

Plenum could formalize Xi’s extended rule: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:11 UTC
01:47:11 KST

The latest Chinese Communist Party plenum could help institutionalize Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) prolonged rule while preparing a new generation of officials without identifying a successor, experts said at a forum in Taipei yesterday.
The four-day plenum — the fifth of the party’s 20th Central Committee — concluded in Beijing on Thursday and adopted a measure on sustaining efforts to bolster party discipline and governance, an official communique published by Xinhua showed.
It also confirmed earlier decisions to expel 33 officials from the party, including former senior military leaders Zhang Youxia (張又俠) and Liu Zhenli (劉振立).
Photo: AP
That left what the Guardian described as “an unprecedented number of empty seats” at the plenum, “indicating the scale of purges under Xi.”
Of the 376 Central Committee full and alternate members named in 2022, only 279 attended this week’s gathering, the Guardian said.
The plenum also elevated Central Military Commission Vice Chairman Zhang Shengmin (張升民) to the politburo and promoted 10 alternate Central Committee members to full membership.
National Chengchi University Institute of International Relations associate research fellow Tzeng Wei-feng (曾偉?) said the plenum elevated Xi’s thinking on party building, and established standards for training, selecting and supervising officials loyal to his vision.
“It is using the language of institutions to carry personal authority,” Tzeng said at the institute’s forum examining the meeting.
The process was a “succession without a successor,” he said, referring to generational turnover within the leadership rather than a transfer of power from Xi to a designated heir.
Tzeng suggested Xi’s thinking on party building could be incorporated into the party constitution at next year’s 21st party congress, potentially followed by changes to supervisory institutions and cadre assessment.
Party supervision could place greater emphasis on officials’ performance and conduct, extending beyond corruption and criminal wrongdoing, Tzeng said, adding that those standards could guide a substantial leadership reshuffle, bringing forward younger officials whom Xi considered capable and trustworthy.
Tzeng said his interpretation remained preliminary pending an examination of all of the measures adopted at the plenum.
Chihlee University of Technology Department of International Trade professor Chang Hung-yuan (張弘遠) said disciplinary purges should increasingly be seen as a lasting feature of the party’s governance rather than a temporary campaign.
“In the past, we treated the anti-corruption drive as a campaign. Now it appears to be part of the system,” Chang said.
The promotion of officials with disciplinary inspection and regulatory backgrounds reflected greater emphasis on supervision and ideological control ahead of the next congress, he said.
However, tighter discipline also risked discouraging officials from taking action, Chang said, adding that Xi needed cadres to implement policies and address economic problems while remaining obedient, creating tension between strict control and administrative flexibility.
CY Cergy Paris University Chinese Studies professor Zhang Lun (張倫) offered a distinction between formal institutions and the exercise of power.
Party plenums often confirmed agendas and personnel arrangements already largely settled, providing procedural legitimacy, he said, adding that some earlier meetings had allowed substantive discussion.
Under Xi, actual authority was concentrated in him, despite the party’s formal organizational hierarchy, Zhang Lun said.
The latest plenum was transitional, with purges and personnel selection still underway, he said.
Vacancies did not necessarily require immediate replacement, and some arrangements might become clearer at the next plenum as Xi consolidates control over the leadership lineup, he added.
This week’s plenum decided to hold the next party congress in the second half of next year.
Zhang Lun said he expected a “sixth plenum” of the Central Committee to take place before then.

01:47:11 KST

Shares in Taiwan plunged by just under 2.5 percent yesterday, led by major artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks, after tech stocks on US markets saw heavy losses overnight amid growing concerns that massive AI investments would not deliver comparable returns, analysts said.
The TAIEX closed down 1,156.50 points, or 2.49 percent, at 45,211.83 on turnover of NT$877.730 billion (US$27.03 billion).
“After the latest earnings reports by major American cloud service providers, worries over AI spending came back to haunt investor sentiment,” Concord Capital Management Corp (康和投顧) analyst Lu Chin-wei (呂晉維) said.
Photo: Kelson Wang, Taipei Times
Alphabet’s disappointing sales renewed AI concerns, sending its shares plunging overnight, while Amazon.com shares also slumped on its soaring AI spending.
“Tech stocks had gained substantially since the beginning of this year, so such disappointing earnings reports simply prompted investors to trim their holdings and pocket gains,” Lu said.
After the tech-heavy NASDAQ fell 1.38 percent on Thursday, the electronics index in Taiwan fell 2.90 percent yesterday.
Contract chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), which accounts for more than 40 percent of total market value, lost 1.86 percent to close at NT$2,370, contributing about 360 points to the TAIEX’s decline.
Among other semiconductor stocks, smartphone integrated circuit designer MediaTek Inc (聯發科) shed 3.21 percent to close at NT$3,915, while IC packaging and testing firm ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控) closed down 2.20 percent at NT$668.
Application-specific IC designer Alchip Technologies (世芯) shed 6.93 percent to close at NT$3,425.
Elsewhere in the tech sector, iPhone assembler and AI server maker Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) slid 1.01 percent to close at NT$245.50, while Quanta Computer Inc (廣達), another AI server supplier, was unchanged at NT$318.
Investors rushed to park their money in select safe havens, with Chunghwa Telecom Co (中華電信) up 1.27 percent to close at NT$160 and Far EasTone Telecommunications Co (遠傳電信) closing 0.88 percent higher at NT$114.
“The financial sector also appeared resilient. I suspect government-led funds stood on the buy side,” Lu said.
The financial index dropped 0.16 percent, with CTBC Financial Holding Co (中信金控) closing up 0.66 percent at NT$75.80, E. Sun Financial Holding Co (玉山金控) up 0.10 percent at NT$49.05 and Fubon Financial Holding Co (富邦金控) falling 0.31 percent to NT$161.50.
Among safe havens in the old-economy sector, food brand Uni-President Enterprises Corp (統一企業) closed up 1.52 percent at NT$80.20 and Wei Chuan Foods Corp (味全食品) rose 9.72 percent to NT$13.55.
“Turnover shrank further, indicating many investors were reluctant to buy on the dip as they feared uncertainty ahead of the mid-term elections in the United States,” Lu said. “As the TAIEX fell below the technical resistance ahead of 45,300 points, the 120-day moving average, more losses are possible.”
Foreign institutional investors sold a net NT$112.47 billion on the market yesterday, Taiwan Stock Exchange data showed.

China’s new export curbs draw a line around its AI crown jewels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:10 UTC
01:47:10 KST

China’s proposed artificial intelligence (AI) export curbs will push a business model favored by Beijing and the industry’s biggest players: keeping valuable technology at home while selling access to it abroad as rivalry with the US intensifies.
The draft rules, released on Oct. 16, distinguish between foreign customers using Chinese AI services and foreign companies obtaining the models, data or expertise needed to operate or reproduce them independently.
“The structure the leadership prefers, with IP [intellectual property] and R&D [research and development] kept onshore, and operations and access sold abroad, is the one the market was already converging on,” Ankura managing director Alfredo Montufar-Helu said.
The new rules would broadly allow overseas users to access Chinese AI through Web sites and cloud platforms while subjecting some transfers of underlying technology or deployments overseas to government approval.
That distinction matters for developers that rely on computing facilities abroad, where they can gain access to powerful chips constrained by US export restrictions on China.
The broader regulatory oversight adds to the already uncertain macroenvironment facing China’s tech giants and start-ups, who are wrestling with a meltdown of Chinese AI and semiconductor stocks.
China is expected to adopt the proposals by the end of the year and issue guidelines on implementation later, a source familiar with the matter said on condition of anonymity.
The draft would add 23 AI-related technologies to a list banning or restricting their export, including advanced models, agents that carry out tasks with limited human direction, and technology used to design chips and run vast computing facilities.
A temporary requirement to register certain transfers took effect immediately.
The rules could impact how leading Chinese AI firms run advanced models on overseas data centers, structure international partnerships and handle foreign investment or ownership of AI assets.
DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.AI offer models to overseas customers through Web sites or cloud platforms. Some Chinese AI developers have also turned to overseas computing facilities to access advanced chips restricted from export to China.
Nvidia’s most advanced processors cannot be exported to China under US restrictions.
Researchers at major Chinese AI labs are seeking clarification on whether they can train or run their most advanced models on foreign-owned overseas servers, a person briefed on the matter said on condition of anonymity.
In a worst-case scenario, developers might have to maintain separate domestic and overseas versions of the same downloadable model, they said.
Beijing Dacheng Law Offices senior partner Liu Jing (劉晶), who participated in consultations with policymakers, said companies also wanted more clarity on the tests used to determine which models would be covered.
The draft specifies three tests: the computing work needed to train a model, with a threshold of 10 to the power of 26 calculations; its size, measured by at least 2 trillion parameters; or placing among the world’s top 10 in certain assessments of performance, use or efficiency.
Parameters are the numerical settings a model learns during training. The ranking test could cover smaller systems that excel at specialised tasks, but the draft does not identify which rankings would count.
Chinese law firm Han Kun in an analysis questioned how regulators would count the size of models that activate only some of their components for each task, and said one proposed chip design provision could reach beyond the most advanced products, because it lacks a minimum performance requirement.
The proposals are open for public comment until Nov. 15.
The Chinese Ministry of Commerce did not respond to a request for comment.
The rules could extend beyond model releases to corporate deals. Registration requirements, effective from Oct. 16, cover transfers that put Chinese technology under foreign ownership or control, including qualifying transactions already underway, a Fangda analysis found.
Beijing’s move earlier this year to order Meta to unwind its more than US$2 billion acquisition of Chinese-founded AI start-up Manus has already shown the risks facing foreign buyers.
Han Kun said that for computing centers, the draft provides simplified approvals for Chinese companies building and operating their own facilities abroad, but not expressly for transferring technology to foreign customers to build equivalent system.
The controls also cover methods for coordinating more than 10,000 AI chips.
Montufar-Helu said security concerns, including keeping powerful cyberattack capabilities and sensitive data in China, accompanied a commercial aim to retain valuable technological advantages.
Jincheng Tongda & Neal partner Yang Jingru (楊靜茹) described the emerging approach as a counterpart to US restrictions on China’s access to advanced technology and investment.
“The US controls the inflow of computing power, hardware and capital, while China is beginning to systematically manage the outflow of models and technological assets,” Yang wrote.

Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Legislative Yuan stiffens penalties on drug driving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:10 UTC
01:47:10 KST

The Legislative Yuan yesterday passed amendments to the Criminal Code significantly increasing penalties for drug-impaired driving, including raising the maximum prison term from three to five years and allowing capital punishment for repeat offenders who cause death within 10 years.
The amendments passed with support from opposition lawmakers, who hold a majority in the legislature, following a joint motion by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) to separate penalties for drug-impaired driving from those for drunk driving.
Previously, Article 185-3 of the Criminal Code covered penalties for driving under the influence of drugs, alcohol or other substances under a single provision. It did not provide for the death penalty.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
Under the amended law, drug-impaired driving carries a maximum prison term of five years and a fine of up to NT$500,000 (US$15,395), up from a maximum of three years in prison and a fine of NT$300,000.
If the offense results in death, offenders face at least seven years in prison and a fine of up to NT$7 million.
If it causes serious injury, they face five to 12 years in prison and a fine of up to NT$5 million.
Repeat offenders who commit another drug-impaired driving offense resulting in death within 10 years of a previous conviction or deferred prosecution for a drug-driving offense face the death penalty, life imprisonment or at least 10 years in prison, along with a fine of up to NT$10 million.
Repeat offenders whose offenses result in serious injuries face at least seven years in prison and a fine of up to NT$7 million.
Before the bill’s passage, TPP caucus secretary-general Hung Yu-shiang (洪毓祥) held a news conference to explain why the party proposed the amendments.
The caucus has long advocated tougher penalties for drug-impaired driving, particularly for repeat offenders who cause fatal accidents, and wanted the amendments to include the death penalty, Hung said.
The amendments were intended to deter drug-impaired driving, not to seek retribution, he said.
Separately, Democratic Progressive Party caucus secretary-general Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said the party supported a zero-tolerance approach to drug-impaired driving, including tougher prison terms and higher fines.
However, penalties should distinguish between intentional and negligent acts resulting in death, he said.
A zero-tolerance approach should not automatically entail the death penalty, despite what he described as its strong deterrent effect.
Meanwhile, a raft of stringent new penalties for driving under the influence of drugs are to take effect today, the Ministry of the Interior and the National Police Agency said.
In line with changes to the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例), first-time offenders caught driving under the influence of drugs face a fine of NT$120,000 if they were riding a motorcycle or scooter, or NT$150,000 if they were driving a car.
Those who refuse a police drug test may be fined NT$270,000 for a first offense.
Authorities can confiscate any vehicle involved in a drug-driving incident or if the driver refused a test.
Driver’s license regulations have also been severely tightened.
Anyone caught driving under the influence of drugs would have their license revoked and be barred from retaking the test for three years.
The amendment also introduces “preventive revocation,” allowing authorities to revoke the licenses of confirmed drug users for two years.
Repeat offenders caught within a 10-year period, as well as those who cause injury or death while driving under the influence of drugs, would face a lifetime license ban.
Those seeking to reapply for a license after a suspension must first complete mandatory anti-drug driving education or addiction treatment programs.
The new rules also introduce joint liability for passengers, stipulating that anyone aged 18 or older who knowingly rides in a vehicle operated by a driver under the influence of drugs faces a fine of NT$6,000 to NT$15,000.
To facilitate enforcement of the new regulations, police nationwide have been equipped with rapid saliva test kits, the agency said.

Q3 GDP growth hits 14.36%, highest in 48 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:04 UTC
01:47:04 KST

Taiwan’s economy grew by an estimated 14.36 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier, the highest growth for the quarter in 48 years, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.
The forecast was 2.94 percentage points higher than an August estimate.
It also marked the fourth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth.
Photo: CNA
DGBAS specialist Chiang Hsin-yi (江心怡) said stronger-than-expected exports and business investment were key drivers of the robust third-quarter growth.
On the export front, demand for artificial intelligence applications, high-performance computing and cloud services, as well as stronger orders for electronic components used in new consumer products, helped boost exports, Chiang said.
Higher prices for exported products also helped increase export value, she said.
Export demand also supported business investment, with real investment and changes in inventories estimated to have increased 26.36 percent in the third quarter, 4.26 percentage points higher than the previous forecast, she said.
Capital equipment imports, measured in New Taiwan dollars, rose 58.5 percent in the third quarter from a year earlier, including a 35.66 percent increase in semiconductor equipment, while investment in machinery, transportation equipment, intellectual property and construction also grew, the DGBAS said.
Meanwhile, exports from industries other than electronics and information and communications technology also grew at double-digit rates, indicating a gradual recovery in traditional industries in recent quarters, Chiang said.
On the domestic front, private consumption remained strong, helped by a recovery in the auto market and the wealth effect from Taiwan stocks reaching record highs, she said.
Real private consumption grew 5.37 percent in the third quarter, 0.01 percentage points above the August forecast.
It was the second consecutive quarter in which growth exceeded 5 percent, the DGBAS said.
The last time Taiwan recorded an extended period of double-digit growth was in 1986-1987, when the economy recorded high growth for six consecutive quarters as the government gradually eased capital controls and foreign exchange restrictions, contributing to economic liberalization and an economic upswing, Chiang said.
For the first three quarters, growth is estimated to have reached 14.22 percent, the highest for the period in half a century, the DGBAS said.

Photo: CNA
However, hours after Asif’s comments were published, the Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority reversed the decision, granting China Airlines and EVA Airways approval to use its airspace until March 27 next year.
The US Department of State on Thursday said it welcomed reports of the reversal.
An unnamed department spokesperson said Beijing is continuously escalating its efforts to isolate Taiwan and intimidate international partners.
These actions undermine the sovereign decisions of other nations, disrupt lawful international commerce, and threaten global peace and prosperity, they said, adding that international civil aviation relies on predictable and non-discriminatory technical rules.

Czechia eyes drone assembly in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:47:01 UTC
01:47:01 KST

Czech manufacturers are interested in setting up drone assembly lines in Taiwan, former Czech Chamber of Deputies president Marketa Pekarova Adamova told a forum in Taipei yesterday.
Adamova made the comments at the inauguration of the Global UAV Academy, an organization dedicated to international cooperation in drone supply chains, technological certification and pilot training.
The Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology said the Czech Republic is the largest importer of Taiwanese drones and uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) components.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Adamova, who transitioned to the defense industry after retiring from politics, said the Roman adage “si vis pacem, para bellum” — “If you want peace, prepare for war” — applies to a country’s relationship with its UAV sector.
Adamova introduced representatives of Czech-based drone, counter-UAV and autonomous interceptor makers that have plans to cooperate with Taiwan’s drone sector.
The companies include AVEC Systems, which makes autonomous interceptors and attack drones; Digitech Automotive, a software designer that has transitioned to UAV navigation systems; JISER, a NATO-certified counterdrone system producer; and Farpoint, which has an ongoing pilot-training collaboration with the academy, she said.
Twenty-four Taiwanese UAV pilots have already graduated from the collaboration, she added.
Farpoint is also working with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to open an office at the Asia UAV AI Innovation Research and Development Center in Chiayi, she said.
The Ukraine war has proven that conventional military doctrines are no longer adequate for meeting the rigors of modern warfare, she said.
UAV and counter-UAV systems proved to be valuable military capabilities, and the rapid evolution in technology and tactics has been rendering new systems obsolete within weeks of being fielded, Adamova said.
The Czech Republic is a significant contributor to Ukraine’s defense efforts, as the two countries are separated only by 300km, she said.
As a result, Czech industries have rich experience in developing battle-tested drones, software and navigation systems, compared with other manufacturers that can only test their platforms in labs, Adamova said.
Beyond warfighting, drones have many applications, such as critical infrastructure security, agriculture and logistics, she added.
Prosperity, democracy and livelihood lose all meaning if people cannot live in peace and security, which underscores the importance of Taiwan-Czech collaboration in drones, Adamova said.
Taiwan and the Czech Republic are like-minded countries with shared democratic values, and must work together to defend themselves against powerful foes, Adamova added.

Far right’s plans for Europe would benefit Xi, Putin and Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:59 UTC
01:46:59 KST

Following the Brexit referendum in 2016, then-National Rally president Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. The UK’s vote to leave the EU was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall,” she said.
Le Pen’s party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance, but as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.
Instead, Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, she and Alternative for Germany leader Alice Weidel outlined their visions of a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of cash and power. Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defense and common borrowing. Le Pen’s party proposes slashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60 percent over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.
Similar ideas have long circulated in far-right thinktanks, but they are now in the programs of parties that lead the polls in France and Germany — Europe’s historic engines of integration. Weidel has targeted 2029, when the next German election is due to take place, as the year in which a critical mass of anti-EU leaders can begin to effectively unravel the European project. By then, Eurosceptic ultra-nationalist parties could conceivably be in power in France, Italy and Poland.
Faced with plotting in plain sight and a putative timetable for action, the response of pro-European forces has been distinctly underwhelming. From the economy to the climate emergency and security, Europe faces challenges that can only be properly addressed through the greater pooling of resources, allowing it to punch its continental weight.
Former European Central Bank president Mario Draghi has warned that without an industrial policy to compete with China and the US, the continent faces an existential struggle. However, other than the beleaguered and soon-to-be-departed French president Emmanuel Macron, it has been hard to find any EU leader speaking with the same sense of urgency.
Le Pen and Weidel’s interventions should be treated as a wake-up call. The kind of Europe they envisage would be less than the sum of its parts, distracted and weakened by competing national interests. In relation to defense, the moves toward European strategic autonomy would be undermined. The green transition, in the absence of collectively agreed goals, would stall. Adopting such a direction of travel would be an act of continental self-harm, opening up vulnerabilities that Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and Russian President Vladimir Putin (and any “make America great again” successor to US President Donald Trump) would eagerly exploit.
As a pivotal period in the history of the EU approaches, the time to start making such counterarguments is now. The case for a strong Europe at a time of geopolitical volatility and anxiety is overwhelming, but it will need vigorous advocates as a battle for hearts and minds looms.
For the time being, to paraphrase poet William Butler Yeats, the pro-Europeans appear to lack all conviction, while their opponents are full of passionate intensity.
Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

US tells EU allies to cool it over Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

Pentagon officials have in the past few weeks asked several NATO countries to tone down their rhetoric regarding the threat posed by Russia, arguing that some statements by European leaders and officials have undermined continental security, four people familiar with the matter said.
Among the nations that have received messages urging them to keep public statements in check are Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
It was not clear if the messages, which were delivered in bilateral meetings, were conveyed to other European governments.
The US requests come as US President Donald Trump’s administration restarts an effort to press for a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year. The latest push has blended incentives for Russia — including sanctions relief — with pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked for comment, a Pentagon official said: “Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations.”
Among the comments that have drawn US officials’ attention are suggestions by European leaders that Russia is cornered and resorting to increasingly desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slows to a crawl, one of the people said.
Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, a key figure in an ongoing review of US troop levels in Europe, was one of the US officials delivering the message, the people said.
Reuters could not determine what other officials were involved.
None of the people, who include three European officials and a US official, suggested the advice was communicated in a confrontational manner.
The US messages reflect a debate within NATO regarding how to publicly address the threat of an increasingly assertive Russia.
Some Western officials have said that emphasizing the threat posed by Moscow could play into the hands of the Kremlin, which they say seeks to sow fear and undermine support for Ukraine.
Others said European governments must be transparent to show their electorates that sacrifice and resources are needed to keep Moscow at bay. That is especially true as Russia appears to accelerate a covert campaign of sabotage throughout the continent.
Russia has denied that it is pursuing such a campaign.
One of the people familiar with the matter said that Colby told a Baltic official recently that there should be no “poking” directed at the Russians.
The person said Colby pointed to Europeans publicly suggesting that Russia was “cornered like a rat” as an example of unhelpful rhetoric.
It was not clear what specific statement Colby was referring to. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal referred to Putin as a “rat in a corner” late last month, suggesting the Russian leader was resorting to sabotage efforts in Europe, as Russia had become increasingly bogged down in Ukraine.
“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” said a separate European official, describing the Pentagon’s recent private messaging. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.”
In a separate recent meeting, the Pentagon urged an Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its communications, according to a person briefed on the encounter, though the person did not say Pentagon officials complained about any specific statement.
The defense ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment, while NATO declined to comment.
One of the European officials said that the Pentagon’s advice, while cordial, was baffling, given that intelligence services in the Baltic states have in recent months consistently played down the probability of Russia testing NATO’s mutual defense provisions.
Other NATO intelligence services, by contrast, have publicly warned that Russia could dramatically ramp up its sabotage campaign in the near future.
Moscow has recently intensified its campaign of deniable attacks on NATO countries, Western intelligence officials have said.
On Wednesday, German prosecutors said two Belarusians were arrested for allegedly planning to set fire to a building or critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area.
Last month, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, allegations Moscow has denied.
At the same time, US officials have been discussing potential business deals with Russia as part of the Trump administration’s push for peace in Ukraine. Those efforts have drawn mixed reactions from European officials, many of whom are pushing for the Kremlin’s continued economic isolation.
Pentagon planners, meanwhile, are reviewing Washington’s force posture in Europe, a process that could see a sharp drawdown in the US’ troop presence on the continent.
US officials have said European NATO members need to assume more responsibility for their own defense, particularly as the US focuses on threats in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.

Vatican celebrates popemobile at exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

The Vatican is opening a celebration of the popemobile, the now-iconic vehicle that for nearly a century has let popes get close to the faithful at home and abroad.
The Vatican Museums on Wednesday unveiled a preview of the exhibition commemorating “A Century of the Popemobile,” featuring eight Mercedes-Benz versions of the car that popes have used since 1930. It officially opened to the public on Thursday.
Separately, Pope Leo XIV — a big car lover — met with top Mercedes-Benz executives and thanked them for their partnership with the Holy See.
Photo: AP
In his remarks, the Chicago-born pope said that the advances in automotive technology had accompanied the advances and evolutions of papal travel.
“Over the decades, the popemobile has evolved from a means of transportation into an instrument of encounter, enabling the pontiff to draw closer to the faithful during pastoral visits and public celebrations,” Leo said. “In this way, your work has helped facilitate the church’s mission of reaching out to people and bringing a message of faith, of hope and of charity to the world.”
The oldest car on display in the Vatican Museums exhibit was given to Pope Pius XI on May 23, 1930. The Mercedes-Benz Nurburg 460 featured a luxurious armchair upholstered in silk brocade and finishes of fine wood and metal.
It “was specifically built, designed and prepared for papal use, so much so that just by comparing it, you can see how it transitions from the serial to the unique,” said Sandro Barbagallo, curator of the Historical Collections Department at the Vatican Museums.
“From this point, it is clear how all the cars were then made, precisely to allow the pope to be seen, but to be seen and to see in total safety and, I would even say, comfort,” he said.
Later versions of the popemobile on view reflected the changing needs of a pope on the road, most importantly his need to engage with the faithful and — more recently — bless babies that were brought to him.
In 1960, Pope John XXIII was presented with the 300 d Landaulet, with a detail that foreshadowed change: The removable rear side windows allowed the future saint to reach out to those he met along the way.
In 1980, for St John Paul II’s visit to Germany, Mercedes-Benz developed the 230 G, which featured another major innovation: a tall, transparent dome at the rear, providing safety, but also guaranteeing a clear view for the millions of faithful gathered to see him.
In his remarks to the Mercedes-Benz executives, Leo recalled the electric popemobile they presented to Pope Francis in keeping with the Argentine pope’s ecological priorities.
“In this spirit, I encourage you to continue placing technological innovation at the service of human dignity, care for creation and the common good,” he said.

Protests, riots and the paradox of tolerance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:57 UTC
01:46:57 KST

On Sept. 21, a teacher shortage at a high school on the outskirts of Paris sparked student protests meant to express long-standing frustration over a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and outdated facilities. The protests gained further traction through social media and resonated with a wider audience. The French government’s heavy-handed response only intensified the conflict, while mutual accusations between politicians added fuel to the fire. Civic groups and other organizations joined the movement, and the protests spread nationwide.
However, some demonstrations turned into violent riots, with fires being set and causing collateral damage to innocent people and property. Among the losses was the 19th-century town hall in Limoges, whose clock tower, spire and roof collapsed in flames at the hands of masked protesters. In an interview with Reuters, one Limoges resident lamented, “It broke my heart. I saw Notre-Dame all over again, except this time it was our town.” Inspired by this example, students and other members of the public took to the streets in Milan, Italy, and other cities across Europe under the slogan, “Let’s do it like in France.”
In June 2023, Nahel Merzouk — a French 17-year-old of Algerian descent — was shot and killed after refusing to comply with a police traffic stop, sparking protests across France over the use of excessive force by law enforcement. Merzouk’s mother initially organized a peaceful protest in the place where her son died, but demonstrations in several cities soon spiraled out of control, resulting in arson and looting. Merzouk’s grandmother soon called for an end to the violence, accusing rioters of using his death as a pretext for damaging property and causing disorder.
In July, I visited several parts of France and spoke with police officers. One thing I observed is the way the media sometimes sensationalized — or even misrepresented — events. For example, videos that circulated online purportedly showing the Alcazar Library in Marseille being burned down were actually depicting a fire at the Central Post Office in Manila that had occurred months earlier. It is true that the library’s windows and doors had been the targets of Molotov cocktails, but the fires were quickly extinguished before they could spread inside the building.
Today, social media algorithms act as filters, creating echo chambers that reinforce pre-existing views. Generative artificial intelligence can conjure up almost any sensational scenario. Dramatic scenes — such as clashes between police and protesters or fires consuming buildings — are highly attention-grabbing. They might even draw more people into the fray, blurring the lines between peaceful protesters, opportunistic rioters and radical groups.
In poor countries, people struggle to meet even their most basic needs. In authoritarian states, public demonstrations often face severe repression. How should those of us living in a free and prosperous society view the unrest in France?
Austrian-British philosopher Karl Popper argued that the driving force of progress lies in identifying and correcting errors. When applied to society, this means that allowing for criticism and dissent offers a more effective way to address problems. Popper’s concept of the “open society” posed a serious challenge to totalitarianism. Yet, he also took an objective view of the global landscape and proposed the “paradox of tolerance” — the idea that tolerance without limit would ultimately lead to the extinction of tolerance itself. Therefore, we must defend a tolerant society against attacks by the intolerant. This is a lesson we should all take to heart.
Lin Ji-shing is a university professor.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:55 UTC
01:46:55 KST

Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) on Thursday said that revenue this quarter would increase from the previous quarter’s NT$197.06 billion (US$6.07 billion), driven by rising demand for its power and thermal management products amid robust investment in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Order momentum for this quarter remains high and is expected to extend into next year, supported by robust demand for AI data center-related products, Delta chairman Ping Cheng (鄭平) told an earnings conference.
Despite component shortages, power constraints, labor shortfalls and project delays, long-term AI data center demand and growth remain intact, Cheng said.
Photo: CNA
“I think no matter what [short-term] problems it faces, the trend remains unchanged,” Cheng said, adding that Delta remains optimistic about its long-term business outlook.
Data center and AI-related products accounted for about 50 percent of the company’s revenue of NT$539.7 billion in the first three quarters of this year, he said.
Capital expenditure among the world’s four major cloud service providers is expected to top US$1 trillion next year, driving global data center investment to US$1.5 trillion, Delta vice president Lanford Liu (劉亮甫) said.
Power electronics products accounted for 54 percent of Delta’s revenue last quarter, followed by infrastructure products at 33 percent, automation devices at 8 percent and mobility applications at 5 percent, the company said.
Delta reported net profit of NT$23.5 billion last quarter, down 6.5 percent quarter-on-quarter, but up 26.3 percent year-on-year.
The earnings results were the strongest for the third quarter in the company’s history.
Third-quarter earnings per share dropped to NT$9.04 from NT$9.68 the previous quarter, but were up from NT$7.16 a year earlier.
Gross margin fell to 34.08 percent last quarter from 35.64 percent the previous quarter and 34.87 percent a year earlier as component shortages and delays in customers’ data center construction plans pushed up inventory costs, Delta said.
Gross margin is expected to be no lower than last quarter, Cheng said.
Material costs have risen about 2 percent since the beginning of this year, Cheng said.
Delta is considering price hikes this quarter or next quarter due to higher material costs, he said.
Delta booked inventory write-down provisions equivalent to about 1.7 percent of revenue last quarter, mainly due to customer order adjustments, chief financial officer Yu Po-wen (余博文) said.
In its thermal solutions business, liquid-cooling products accounted for 13 percent of Delta’s revenue, or about NT$25 billion, last quarter and are expected to remain at a similar percentage for the rest of this year, Yu said.
Separately, Delta’s Singapore subsidiary on Wednesday approved a planned US$120 million capital injection into its wholly owned Malaysian subsidiary.
Delta plans to build a large production base in Malaysia and aims over about five years to expand its capacity to a scale comparable with its Thailand operations, Cheng said.

New rail opens vistas in Tainan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:46:55 UTC
01:46:55 KST

Tainan’s urban railway undergrounding project, which has been in the works for 16 years, reached a major milestone this month. The Railway Bureau of the Ministry of Transportation and Communications held a farewell event for the above-ground station on Oct. 17, and the first section of its underground successor opened for business the following day. The railway line that has long cut through central Tainan is set to fade from the city’s landscape.
Across the project’s full span of 8.23km, traffic barriers including level crossings, overpasses, underpasses and bridges are to be removed, reconnecting the eastern and western sides of the city.
However, the most important policy questions are yet to come. This includes how the freed up land is to be used, how the plans to turn the former railway corridor into a greenway are designed, how neighborhoods are reconnected, and how the new railway station is integrated with bus, walking and cycling links and the future metro system. Together, these factors would determine the long-term value of this major public infrastructure project for residents.
Current plans for the greenway envision cycle paths, pedestrian spaces and green areas. Done right, this corridor could reconnect residential neighborhoods, schools, shopping districts and public facilities that were previously separated by the railway. Design priorities should include continuous pedestrian routes, shade, nighttime lighting, accessible facilities, cycling routes and safe crossings at intersections. It should not be divided up into fragmented parking areas. Given Tainan’s hot summers, the choice of plants, tree canopy coverage and the provision of rest spots would also prove critical.
The city government could publish design plans for each section, construction schedules and records of public consultation, allowing local residents to understand the planned changes in advance. After significant levels of public investment, the space that is given back should be genuinely walkable and offer people a place in which to slow down; only then would the benefits of the underground railway be borne out in residents’ daily commutes, walks and shopping trips.
Tainan has long been dependent on cars and scooters for transportation. If people still have to drive themselves to get to the new underground stations, the benefits of the railway investment could be limited. The city government should review bus stop locations, transfer distances, taxi ranks, YouBike stations, bicycle parking and pedestrian crossings to ensure easy access to railway stations.
As Linsen (林森) and South Tainan (南台南) stations begin operating, and plans for the Tainan Metro network advance, Taiwan Railways could also become a key component of the city’s north-south public transport network. A unified transfer plan and passenger information system should be established now, with ticketing data being used to identify passenger routes and transfer needs. The value of major rail infrastructure increases with the degree of integration with surrounding transport networks; roads and bus services near the stations should be adjusted in tandem with the undergrounding project.
The government has tended to evaluate major infrastructure projects primarily in terms of construction progress, budget execution and opening dates. After the railway opens, more meaningful indicators would include travel time reductions, whether public transport use increases and conditions for pedestrians and cyclists improve, how the project affects local shopping districts and residents’ daily lives and public utilization of the completed greenway. The city government could publish these figures regularly over the next five to 10 years, allowing residents to see the tangible changes brought about by the underground railway.
The railway’s move underground gives Tainan a rare opportunity to reconfigure its public spaces. If transport, green space, cultural preservation, flood control, public transport and urban renewal can be planned together, the project’s legacy could extend far beyond an underground railway line. A truly successful effort to reconnect the city should allow residents on either side of the former railway corridor to coexist within the same urban space.
Roger Lo is a freelancer and Tainan resident.
