Feature: Rwandan honey producer eyes sweet opportunities in Chinese market ahead of CIIE
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:03:05 CST
01:03:05 KST

Grace Mbabazi, founder and chief executive officer of M&M Sozo Ltd., a honey-producing company based in Kigali's Kicukiro District, receives an interview with Xinhua in Kigali, Rwanda, Oct. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Ju Yinhe)
KIGALI, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Rwandan entrepreneur Grace Mbabazi has spent years producing and selling honey in the domestic market. Now, she is setting her sights on a market that once seemed beyond reach: China.
Her ambitions are gaining momentum thanks to the China International Import Expo (CIIE) and China's zero-tariff policy for 53 African countries, which offer new opportunities for Rwandan honey to reach Chinese consumers.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Mbabazi, founder and chief executive officer of M&M Sozo Ltd., a honey-producing company based in Kigali's Kicukiro District, said the CIIE had helped her company explore the Chinese market by providing direct access to Chinese buyers, importers, distributors and business partners.
Rwanda has participated in all eight previous editions of the CIIE since the expo's launch in 2018, with honey among its featured products. The country has also designated honey as its priority product under the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations' One Country One Priority Product initiative.
According to data released in 2022 by the Rwanda Agriculture and Animal Resources Development Board, the country has approximately 120,000 beekeepers operating across five major beekeeping zones, including Akagera National Park and Kigali City.
As M&M Sozo Ltd. prepares to showcase its honey products at the ninth CIIE, scheduled for Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, Mbabazi looks back on her first participation in 2024 as a valuable stepping stone toward the Chinese market.
Mbabazi said the expo gave her a rare opportunity to introduce her products to an international audience, raise brand awareness, engage with potential customers, importers, and distributors, and gain a better understanding of the Chinese market.
"Our experience at the CIIE showed that the expo can help local businesses build commercial partnerships and introduce products such as honey to Chinese consumers," she said.
Mbabazi highlighted the free exhibition booths, "green channel" arrangements for products exported to China, and other preferential measures available to exhibitors from Rwanda and several other African countries, saying these policies could help businesses reduce marketing and participation costs.
Such support enables her company to showcase its honey to Chinese buyers and international visitors while allocating more resources to product development, packaging, and business promotion.
She also described China's zero-tariff policy as "a big motivation," saying it offered Rwanda "a good opportunity to increase honey exports."
Mbabazi hopes to capitalize on the policy to "use the potential savings from eligible tariff-free imports to improve price competitiveness, negotiate attractive commercial terms, and reinvest in business expansion."
Her immediate goal is to build long-term relationships with importers and distributors in China, creating a reliable market for her honey, increasing export volumes, and raising the company's international profile.
Producing seven tons of honey monthly, the company now works with 36 permanent beekeepers as well as several outgrowers across various districts of the country.
Since its inception in 2018, the company has expanded its operations to almost all districts in the Eastern Province, working mainly with women and young people. Mbabazi aims to increase the number of beehives associated with the business from 5,000 to approximately 25,000 by 2028.
At this year's CIIE, the company plans to showcase two signature products, Sozo Pure Gold Honey and Sozo Pure Natural Honey, both produced in Rwanda. Mbabazi said the products stand out for their natural production process: the honey is collected straight from beehives and sold without heating, processing, or pasteurization.
"Our beehives are located in forests where no pesticides are used," she emphasized.
As the business grows, Mbabazi hopes to create greater economic opportunities for the beekeepers who supply her company. She said the prospect of higher earnings for beekeepers has reinforced the importance of accessing larger markets, including China.
Looking ahead, she hopes to establish a reliable and sustainable honey supply chain from Rwanda to China, increase export revenue, and build lasting business relationships with Chinese partners. ■

Ukraine Reports First Drone Interception of Russian KUB-2E Loitering Munition

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:02:57 UTC

Ukraine’s Posipaky drone unit shot down a Russian KUB-2E loitering munition in the Zaporizhzhia sector in what the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industries (NAUDI) described as the first confirmed interception of the weapon by a frontline interceptor drone.
The pilots used a General Chereshnia AIR interceptor, NAUDI said in a Facebook post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The General Chereshnia FPV team also reported the interception, congratulating the Posipaky unit.
“There is now one more page in our ‘Red Book’,” the team said, referring to its registry of rare or destroyed equipment.
Both statements included a short video of the engagement recorded by the interceptor’s onboard camera. Kyiv Post could not independently verify the footage’s time or location.
What is Russia’s KUB-2E?
The KUB-2E is a Russian-made loitering munition developed by the Kalashnikov concern. Russian forces use it against Ukraine, while the manufacturer also markets the system for export.
The weapon is designed to strike personnel, military equipment and drone operator positions. It typically works alongside a reconnaissance drone that identifies targets, with an operator using the munition’s onboard video feed to guide the attack.
The KUB family includes several variants with different payloads and ranges. According to the Vash Visnyk news outlet, the basic model carries a warhead weighing about 3 kilograms (6.6 pounds) and has a reported range of 25–40 kilometers (16–25 miles).
Su-57 Fighter Reportedly Burned Down at Russia’s Akhtubinsk Airfield
Other KUB-2E versions reportedly carry thermobaric warheads and have a range of up to 40 kilometers (25 miles).
Heavier models, including the KUB-10E and KUB-10ME, reportedly have ranges exceeding 100 kilometers (62 miles) and optical guidance systems. Their intended targets include lightly armored vehicles, artillery positions, command posts and personnel.
The family’s electric propulsion reduces its acoustic signature. Newer variants are also reported to have improved resistance to electronic warfare.
Interceptors also target Russian reconnaissance drones
Ukrainian interceptor crews have also downed Russian reconnaissance aircraft, including the ZALA Z-20, a drone reportedly worth about $200,000.
In early January 2026, a crew from the 55th Separate Artillery Brigade, Zaporizhzhia Sich, shot down a Z-20 using a General Chereshnia AIR interceptor.
The electrically powered Z-20 monitors the battlefield, identifies targets and adjusts artillery fire. It is also believed to help locate targets for Russia’s Lancet loitering munitions.
Its manufacturer, ZALA Aero, part of the Kalashnikov concern, claims the drone can remain airborne for more than six hours and transmit video over distances exceeding 100 kilometers (62 miles).
The General Chereshnia AIR interceptor has been used by dozens of Ukrainian units. According to the Brave1 defense innovation cluster, it had been credited with more than 300 confirmed interceptions of Russian reconnaissance drones by December 2025, including Orlan-10, ZALA, Supercam and Merlin models.

Pope Leo votes in US midterms in first known political ballot for any pontiff

Pope Leo has voted in the US midterm elections – the first time a sitting pontiff is known to have cast a ballot in any political election at any time in history.
Leo, who has clashed with the US president, Donald Trump, over several issues, submitted his vote by post in Chicago, where he was born, the Vatican said on Friday. Leo became the first American leader of the Catholic church last year after the death of Pope Francis.
The Vatican said Leo “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so”, including in Peru, where he lived for years as a missionary. “The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” the statement added.
Leo, who before being elected pope was known as Robert Prevost, reportedly made his request for the mail-in ballot on 3 October, registering at an address in New Lenox, Illinois.
That was 10 days before he had surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. The pontiff has gradually been resuming activities since being discharged from hospital on 17 October.
The crucial midterm elections are due to be held on 3 November.
Leo and Trump have clashed over the US president’s harsh immigration polices, with the pontiff describing them as “inhuman”.
Earlier this year, Trump lashed out in response to Leo’s criticisms of the US-Israeli war on Iran, calling the pontiff “weak on crime” and “terrible on foreign policy”. The US president also said Leo had only been elected pope because Trump himself was in the White House.
In response to the tirade, Leo said he was “not afraid” of Trump.
In his first key address to the US on the eve of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, Leo praised the country’s history of welcoming migrants, while urging Americans to live up to the ideals put forward in the declaration, in what was seen a further rebuke to Trump.
In an interview with the US broadcaster in late July, Leo expressed “great love” for his home country and its core principles of freedom, opportunity and welcoming immigrants but qualified that he just “happens to be American”.
Leo will travel to Latin America in November for an 11-day trip covering 10 cities. Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, told reporters at Rome’s foreign press association this week that a papal visit to the US was expected in the “not too distant future”, adding that the outcome of the midterms might influence whether the trip went ahead in 2027 or later.

Mood symptoms in bipolar disorder correlate with changes in sexual desire and distress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:00:10 UTC
01:00:10 KST

People newly diagnosed with bipolar disorder experience changes in their sexual desire and levels of sexual distress that closely track their shifting moods. A recent six-month study found that depressive symptoms were linked to lower desire and higher distress, while manic symptoms corresponded with increased desire. The findings were published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.
Bipolar disorder is a psychiatric condition characterized by extreme swings in mood, energy, and activity levels. People with the condition typically experience episodes of depression, marked by deep sadness, hopelessness, and lethargy. They also experience periods of mania or hypomania, which involve elevated mood, impulsivity, and unusually high energy. Between these distinct episodes, individuals might also experience daily fluctuations in their emotional state, a phenomenon known to mental health professionals as mood instability.
Doctors and therapists have recognized that these emotional highs and lows often spill over into patients’ sex lives. Bipolar disorder can increase the risk of sexual dysfunction, which involves difficulties in the phases of sexual desire, arousal, or orgasm. However, most previous research on this topic has relied on single snapshot surveys of patients. Medical researchers wanted to better understand how specific mood symptoms interact with sexual desire and sexual distress across a longer period.
The research team was led by Helle B. Krogh, a researcher at the Sexology Clinic at Copenhagen University Hospital in Denmark. The team designed a longitudinal study to observe how symptoms of depression, symptoms of mania, and daily mood instability related to sexual function. They also wanted to look at sexual distress, which involves the grief, worry, and frustration people feel regarding their sex lives. Assessing distress is a necessary step for clinicians when diagnosing sexual dysfunction, making it a highly relevant factor for patient well-being.
The study enrolled 236 adults between the ages of 18 and 68 who had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder within the previous two years. The participants were evaluated at three specific points over a six-month period: at the beginning of the study, at three months, and at six months. During these visits, clinical researchers used standardized interviews to rate the severity of each participant’s depressive and manic symptoms.
To measure daily mood instability, participants used a smartphone application called Monsenso. The app prompted them to rate their mood every day on a scale ranging from negative to positive. This allowed researchers to track emotional turbulence outside of the formal clinical visits.
At each of the three in-person visits, participants also completed detailed questionnaires about their sexual functioning and overall quality of life. The sexual functioning surveys measured their current level of sexual desire and any distress they felt about their sexual experiences.
When analyzing the data, the researchers found a consistent pattern linking depression to sexual difficulties. Higher scores on the depression rating scale were associated with decreased sexual desire and an increase in sexual distress. This held true even after the researchers adjusted their statistical models to account for the age and sex of the participants. Women in the study generally reported lower sexual desire than men, and older age was linked to lower desire.
Symptoms of mania showed a different pattern. The data showed that higher scores on the mania rating scale were associated with increased sexual desire. The researchers did not find an association between manic symptoms and increased sexual distress. This suggests that the heightened sexual desire experienced during manic or hypomanic phases is not typically perceived as distressing by the individuals themselves at the time.
The researchers noted that heightened sexual interest is a central feature of manic episodes, which aligns with these observations. The daily smartphone ratings provided another layer of information about the patients’ experiences. The researchers found that greater day-to-day mood instability was associated with higher levels of sexual distress. This indicates that even outside of full-blown depressive or manic episodes, daily emotional turbulence correlates with worse sexual well-being.
The researchers also discovered that a large portion of the variation in sexual desire and distress was due to individual differences between people. The statistical models showed that over 60 percent of the variance in the sexual outcomes was attributable to factors unique to each person, rather than just their clinical mood symptoms. This highlights that sexuality is highly individualized and influenced by many personal, social, and situational factors beyond a psychiatric diagnosis.
Quality of life was also measured during the clinical visits using a standardized survey from the World Health Organization. The researchers found that a better overall quality of life was associated with lower levels of sexual distress. However, quality of life scores were not statistically linked to the level of sexual desire itself.
The study has several limitations that provide context for the results. Because the participants were observed in their natural clinical treatment rather than subjected to a controlled experiment, the findings can only show associations. The data cannot prove that mood symptoms directly cause the changes in sexual function.
The study also excluded patients who were taking certain common antidepressants known to cause sexual side effects. This exclusion, along with the fact that many participants were in partial or full remission from their mood episodes, may have resulted in a sample with better overall sexual functioning than the broader population of people with bipolar disorder. The researchers noted that participants with more severe symptoms might have dropped out of the study before the six-month mark.
This attrition means the findings might mostly reflect the experiences of individuals who have relatively stable disease progression and are functioning well in their daily lives. Future studies would benefit from including a wider range of participants, particularly those with higher scores for manic symptoms. This would help determine if the patterns hold true during severe manic episodes.
The research team suggested that healthcare providers should regularly ask patients about their sexual health. Initiating these conversations could help patients manage sexual distress both during active mood episodes and during periods of relative stability.
The study, “The impact of affective symptoms and mood instability on sexual desire and sexual distress in newly diagnosed bipolar disorder: a longitudinal study,” was authored by Helle B. Krogh, Caroline Fussing Bruun, Jeff Zarp, Maria Faurholt-Jepsen, Lars Vedel Kessing, Annamaria Giraldi, and Maj Vinberg.

The messages, which include calls to loot shopping centres, were enough to prompt school heads to issue warnings to parents in Maastricht. Limburg police backed the warnings, according to local broadcaster L1 News.
Shopkeepers in The Hague have also started boarding up their windows as a precaution, as some messaging groups are calling for gatherings on the Malieveld and attacks on commercial centres nearby, according to Omroep West.
The protests in France, which have spread to Italy and Spain began over education and living standards among young people. Many of the demonstrations quickly descended into serious rioting, often with heavy police response.
There are similar concerns in Germany, where youth groups are preparing to protest over similar issues on Halloween.

EU lays out 45 billion euro spending plan for Ukraine in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:57:45 UTC
00:57:45 KST

The European Commission on Oct. 30 unveiled plans on how to disburse about 45 billion euros ($51 billion) next year under its Ukraine Support Loan, with the vast majority allocated to defense.
Roughly 31.7 billion euros ($35 billion) have been earmarked to support Ukraine's defense industrial capacity, according to the Commission's press release.
The rest — 13.3 billion euros ($14.8 billion) — would be split equally between two financial support mechanisms for Ukraine: the Ukraine Facility and the Macro-Financial Assistance, with the latter tied to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) support program.
Despite the loan, Kyiv still needs to bridge its estimated 70 billion euros ($78 billion) budget gap next year, as economic pressures of Russia's war mount.
"With today's proposal, we are providing Ukraine with much-needed predictability and helping maintain essential public services," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, adding that the topic is "high on the agenda" at the EU-Canada summit in Montreal.
"Together with our allies, we must also do everything in our power to mount pressure on Russia to stop its barbaric war of aggression."
The European Commission stressed that the budgetary support remains tied to conditions related to Ukraine's rule of law and anti-corruption reforms, as well as economic resilience and sustainability.
The Commission's proposal must now be approved and adopted by the Council of the EU, with member states making a final decision on the allocation of funds afterward.
The 45-billion-euro package is the second part of the EU's 90-billion-euro ($100 billion) loan approved in April, two-thirds of which is allocated for defense.
The first half of the loan, which is being disbursed throughout 2026, included 16.7 billion euros ($18.6 billion) in budget support and 28.3 billion euros ($31.6 billion) for defense industrial capacity.
As the loan does not cover all of Ukraine's needs for next year, Kyiv has already requested additional funding beyond the 90-billion-euro package.
Meanwhile, Kyiv's other partners are beginning to step up. In October, Norway pledged $9 billion for Ukraine, and the U.K. announced a $13 billion pledge, its largest ever.
Canada is also widely expected to join in, though the scope of its potential commitment remains unclear.

People Are Creating ‘Survival Guides’ to Cope With the ‘AO3 Apocalypse’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:57:35 UTC
00:57:35 KST

In a major blow to both the terminally online and the criminally horny, the fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) has temporarily shut down due to a “security incident,” according to an update posted on the site.
On October 29, an admin for AO3 posted that the website was “down for maintenance.” The statement said that it could take up to four weeks for service to be fully restored, though it was possible the site would be back up in a “degraded state” sooner, with some of its features disabled.
Though the original statement did not specify the reasons for the closure, subsequent updates said that a “security incident” had taken place, though “we are still in the early stages of response [and] determining its scope.” While the statement said that AO3 did not believe that its user database had been stolen, it urged users to exercise caution and change their passwords for the site.
Run by the Organization for Transformative Works, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving fandom communities on the internet, AO3 was founded in 2007 in part due to concerns about censorship and corporate interests overtaking fandom spaces. The website has 11 million users, according to a 2026 press release, and hosts more than 18 million original works. The explosive popularity of the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry TV series generated a surge of new interest last year, resulting in the publication of tens of thousands of stories featuring the show’s main characters, Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, on the platform.
Those reliant on AO3 for their daily dose of Destiel- or Dramione-inspired smut are not taking the news well. “No ao3 for possibly 4 weeks SOMEONE DO SOMETHING,” one Heated Rivalry fan account posted on X, tagging not just AO3 itself but also the official X accounts for the FBI, the CIA, and, for some reason, Uber Support. Other fans are compiling Google Docs of links to downloaded stories, touting them as “survival guides” for the “AO3 apocalypse” and organizing them by fictional character pairings, or ships. (Be warned, however: One such doc is difficult to load due to “heavy traffic” on the file.)
Others commented on the timing of the outage, pointing out that it coincides with “No Nut November,” the internet-based challenge that encourages people to abstain from masturbation throughout the month. “AO3 taking no nut november a little too seriously,” one person wrote.
A representative for the Organization for Transformative Works did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the chaos inspired by the site’s shutdown underscores the prominence of fan fiction in everyday lives, driving mainstream publishing trends and generating hundreds of millions of views. It also serves as the engine for the burgeoning vertical video industry, with streaming platforms constantly scouring fan fiction websites for works to adapt.
“All life forms dependent on AO3 are literally withering right now,” one fan wrote. “This is our 9/11.”

Sybiha: Kyiv ready to cooperate with African partners to prevent citizens being drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:57:30 EET
00:57:30 KST

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha expressed his readiness to cooperate with African partners regarding the situation involving the recruitment of citizens from those countries into Russia's war against Ukraine.
"Ukraine is ready to share relevant information and cooperate with African partners so that no more of their citizens are deceived, exploited and sacrificed for Russia's neocolonial war," Sybiha said on X social media platform on Friday, commenting on reports of citizens from African countries being recruited into Russia's war against Ukraine.
The foreign minister noted that many of them were lured under false pretenses with promises of jobs, education, and a better life. Others, according to available information, are currently considered missing or dead. Their families are trying to find out how their loved ones ended up on a foreign battlefield.
Sybiha said the governments of African countries can help prevent new tragedies by: investigate the activities of recruitment networks, warn citizens against deceptive job offers, and work together to determine the fate of those who have already been sent to fight in Russia's war against Ukraine.

DMWS Welfare Services for the armed forces: Supporting Veterans through VALOUR

Self-employment: another path to opportunity for armed forces families
Armed forces spouses and partners have valuable skills, experience and ideas. However, frequent moves, caring responsibilities and the demands of service life can make traditional employment routes difficult to sustain.
Self-employment will not be right for everyone, but it can be one option to explore alongside employment, training and other opportunities.
X-Forces Enterprise works with spouses and partners who have a skill to build on, an idea to test, or a sense that they want to work differently. Many do not think of themselves as entrepreneurs and may be unsure where to begin. This is where specialist support can help.
X-Forces Enterprise’s ‘Supporting the Unsung Hero’ programme gives armed forces spouses and partners a structured way to explore self-employment. After a self-employment discovery stage, participants can access:
- one-to-one mentoring from experienced business owners
- enterprise learning to build knowledge and confidence
- connections with others exploring a similar path
Participants can start with an idea, a skill, or a question, and the programme helps them identify their next step.
Ren Kapur MBE, founder and chief executive of X-Forces Enterprise, said:
  I want women in the Armed Forces community to know that they can explore a business idea without having everything worked out first. A conversation, some learning or the right mentor can help people understand what might be possible, and they do not have to work it all out on their own.
For more information, contact X-Forces Enterprise at info@x-forces.com.
LGBT veterans have 100 days left to apply for financial recognition
- LGBT veterans can apply for restorative measures, including financial recognition payments of up to £70,000
- non-financial recognition available includes an official letter of apology, replacement service items and a restoration ceremony
- nearly £60m has been paid to over 1,800 veterans so far, but more may be eligible
Veterans discharged or impacted by the ban on LGBT personnel in the armed forces have 100 days left to apply for the government’s restorative measures.
The measures were introduced following an independent review on the impact of the ban on LGBT personnel serving in the UK Armed Forces between 1967 and 2000.
The government is now issuing a final call to eligible veterans before the application deadline closes on 12 December.
What is a veteran?
Veterans are defined as anyone who has served for at least one day in His Majesty’s Armed Forces (Regular or Reserve) or Merchant Mariners who have seen duty on legally defined military operations. There are currently 2.4 million veterans in Great Britain.
There are 2.4 million veterans in Great Britain. 40% of veterans are 16-64 years old. The percentage of working age veterans is set to increase to 44% by 2028. 60% of veterans are over 65. 75% of veterans own their home or have a mortgage. It is estimated that 3% to 6% of those sleeping rough have served in the Armed Forces. 75% are healthy, 17% have fair health and 8% have bad health. Want to learn more? Tune in to our ‘being forces friendly’ podcast’.
Listen to our team of veterans talk about their experiences: transitioning from the UK Armed Forces and what the word ‘veteran’ means to them.

Defence Medical Welfare Service

Veterans Foundation
The Veterans’ Foundation was set up in 2016 to raise funds to help improve the lives of all within the armed forces community who need it. The funds raised are then donated to charities and organisations that have a real impact on those currently serving, veterans, and their families. These organisations support a range of needs, including mental health, physical therapy and rehabilitation, homelessness and education and training and more.
Charities and charitable organisations find it increasingly difficult to raise the funds they need to continue their vital and often life-changing work and rely on The Veterans’ Foundation for grants to support them. That was why retired Major General David Shaw set up The Veterans’ Foundation in 2016 and why it has grown to be one of the UK’s leading military charities.

Russian man who turned abandoned water tower into home fined 570,000 rubles for donating to Anti-Corruption Foundation
A court in Tomsk fined Tomsk radio host and IT manager Alexander Lunev 570,000 rubles for donating to the Navalny-founded Anti-Corruption Foundation.
The court convicted Lunev of financing extremist activity after he donated 7,000 rubles to the Anti-Corruption Foundation five years ago, when Russian authorities had already designated the foundation “extremist.”
Lunev pleaded guilty, saying he “hadn’t looked into the status” of the Anti-Corruption Foundation before sending the money. “Five years ago, I transferred seven thousand rubles to people I shouldn’t have sent that money to, people I shouldn’t have trusted in any way. That act eventually landed me in the cage where I am today,” he said in his final statement.
Lunev was released from custody after the verdict.
Alexander Lunev became known after buying a derelict water tower from the city administration in 2012 and turning it into a home. He moved into the tower in 2020 and relocated to the Czech Republic two years later. Lunev was detained and then arrested in August during a short trip to Russia.
Russian authorities declared the Anti-Corruption Foundation and other organizations linked to opposition politician Alexey Navalny “extremist” in June 2021.
By April 2026, Russian authorities had opened at least 225 criminal cases over donations to the Anti-Corruption Foundation, according to an estimate by the independent Russian news outlet Mediazona.

Poland approves first fast-track renewable energy zones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:56:05 UTC
00:56:05 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity.
The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.
The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years.
Pierwsze #OPRO już są! Sejmik województwa wielkopolskiego przyjął dziś pierwsze w Polsce plany OPRO. Obejmą one ok. 105,4 ha w gminach Lwówek, Rawicz, Słupca i Złotów.🔆
❓Czym jest OPRO?
✅To Obszary Przyspieszonego Rozwoju #OZE, czyli tereny, na których – już podczas ich…
— Marek Pogorzelski (@rzeczni_MKiS) October 26, 2026
Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.
Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days.
The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.
Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”.
The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.
Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.
EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.
Polish state mining firm JSW, which is the EU's largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland's biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year as it seeks to stem large financial losses https://t.co/EWP3rAVMaH
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026
Poland has long had one of Europe’s most polluting energy sectors. The country still produces around half of its electricity from coal, by far the higher proportion in the EU.
However, the share of renewables has grown significantly in recent years. It nearly doubled from 14.7% of the energy mix in 2021 to 29.4% in 2025. Onshore wind was the largest contributor last year, accounting for 14.2%, followed by solar at 12.1% and biomass at 1.8%.
Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for just 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).
Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty".

Himalayan Communities Are Relying on Centuries-Old Water Solutions In the Face of Climate Change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:55:56 UTC
00:55:56 KST

The word Laya describes the natural rhythm that has carried the people of the Himalayas through monsoons and drought for centuries. Across the peaks and glaciers, the populated mid-hills and the foothills, communities have harmonized their calendars to the pulsing of water.
Where annual rain falls in just four months, these master engineers funnel rooftop rainwater through handmade bamboo piping into gravel pits to recharge underground wells, maintaining them at the annual festivals. They adapt to the climate by unearthing ancient subterranean medieval stone spout networks for drinking, washing, and bathing.
But there’s another Sanskrit word used in Hindi called Pralaya, passed down through oral tradition like Himalayan myth. It means the melting away of places that no longer exist.
“Recent flooding in Nepal was a pralaya,” says hydrometeorologist and environmental scientist Ngamindra Dahal, chairperson of the Nepal Water Conservation Foundation (NWCF) and executive board member of the South Asian Meteorological Association. “We’ve never witnessed anything like it.”
Himalayans have fallen out of sync with nature at no fault of their own. As earth’s largest swath of ice outside the poles thaws from the unprecedented rapid global warming, high- and mid-mountain villages across eight countries of the Hindu Kush and Himalayan mountain regions have entered a new world of extremes: too little and too much water.
The Himalayas are losing glacier mass 65% faster than a decade ago. The impacts will be felt by 2 billion Asians across 12 major downstream river basins by 2050. And by 2100, it’s projected that 80% of glacier mass will be lost. The reality of dangerous cloudburst floods and water scarcity is, however, already being felt.
On Aug. 26, a 55 million-ton, 93-m.p.h. ice-rock avalanche triggered by a glacier collapse in Nepal near the Tibet border killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands more still missing. Meanwhile, the Nepali government will drain four massive glacial lakes to reduce the danger of yet another catastrophic flood.
The vulnerable, historically low-polluting country has been waiting for a response to its request for compensation from high-emitting nations for the damage created in part by this climate disaster. And on Oct. 22, Nepal became the first country approved for a provisional payout from the U.N.’s Loss and Damage Fund, securing over $21.6 million for recovery from the catastrophic floods. Meanwhile, with deepening uncertainty about the planet’s most basic natural resource, Himalayan people forge on charting their own solutions to save their homes by reviving ancient water systems, building artificial glaciers, and uncovering hidden flood risks.
“The Himalaya is often described as Asia's water tower, but that metaphor is dangerously passive if it makes the mountains sound like a stable reservoir. What the laya-to-pralaya concept clarifies is that the Himalaya is a living, dynamic system—and that climate change is compressing geological time,” says Dahal. “What once happened across generations may now happen within one.”
Reviving Lifelines
For centuries, perennial springs, or mool, have dictated how Himalayan communities live their lives. But that trusted relationship is breaking down. Still, resilient Nepali communities are adapting to the shifting environment of melting snow and ice and unpredictable monsoon rain by reclaiming historic infrastructure.
To combat water shortages often from erratic rainfall shifts disrupted by climate change, they’re reviving an ancient network of underground terracotta canals that channel water to sunken stone spouts, some chiseled as early as the 6th century. Known as hiti or dhara, these water systems connect to ponds that absorb monsoon rain, recharging the groundwater table to keep spouts flowing during dry season. In places like the Kathmandu Valley, local governments are actively restoring and rerouting this massive ancient spring network, originally engineered by the Licchavi and Malla dynasties and now threatened by climate change and rapid urbanization.
Through the NWCF and an intergovernmental organization protecting mountain environments and cultures called the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development, Dahal is replenishing water supplies by taking inventory of more recent drying springs to gauge a new baseline of water availability.
"A community may have adequate water in its landscape but lack the investment to bring it to households,” says Dahal. “Conversely, a community may have taps everywhere but an increasingly unreliable source.”
He’s teaching local communities how to revive and reroute their drying life sources based on changing water movement underground, by tracking seasonal flow rates, water quality, and geographic elevations. Once new water patterns are mapped, Dahal helps communities design localized water-sharing agreements and storage, and adapt household rainwater harvesting systems—in a grass-roots water governance model aligned with the Nepal government adaptation plan. “When a pipe breaks, you repair the pipe; when a tank collapses, you rebuild the tank,” says Dahal. “But when the spring itself stops flowing, repairing the infrastructure solves nothing.”
Hidden Risk
Up in Nepal’s Limi Valley, families are confronting a different kind of uncertainty. Tashi Lhazom recalls being 13, studying at a Kathmandu boarding school, when she received a phone call from her remote high-alpine village. On the other line her mother simply said, “You better study hard because you have nothing to eat here anymore.”
An avalanche had struck her 1,000 year-old ancestral valley—just two years after a massive glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), a sudden violent release of water from a melting glacial lake—and had taken with hundreds of the yaks that were her nomadic herding family’s generational livelihood. This went against everything Limi Valley indigenous villagers had known about trusting the mountain Gods.
“My people believed the Gods were angry with them for being greedy. That was their cultural rationalization,” explains Lhazom, now 26. When what villagers assumed was another catastrophic GLOF washed away bridges and a hydropower plant in the Limi Valley in May 2025, Lhazom was ready to do something about it.
“I couldn’t let the community blame itself for something it was not responsible when I knew it was those emitting greenhouse gases who were partially to blame,” says Lhazom, one of the first from Limi Valley to earn a college degree and now an activist among a wave of Gen Zs fighting climate destruction in Nepal.
She tracked down climate scientists and politicians, urging them to investigate the cause of the flood, until a field team finally agreed to come. After Lhazom directed them around closed flooded roads to local water sources, they trekked upstream, reaching glacial terrain at 17,000 ft. to learn the truth: It wasn’t a GLOF this time.
Instead, thawing permafrost—the ice that acts as glue to bind mountain rock—was without warning, draining trapped small “thermokarst” lakes, releasing massive volumes of underground water down the slope. As a result of their investigation, that 2025 Limi Valley flood was reclassified as Nepal’s first-ever recorded thermokarst lake flood.
After sharing drone footage, photos, and satellite images with the scientists who proved the flood mechanism, Lhazom became co-author of a September 2025 comment paper in the Communications Earth and Environment Journal alerting the world to this overlooked risk.
It led to an acknowledgement and warning in a July 2026 scientific paper about the increased risk of thermokarst lake floods due to climate change—not just in the Himalayas, but across Peru, China, and other high-alpine mountain environments. And from it, a newly defined dangerous hazard category, called Small Alpine Lake Outbursts (SALOs), emerged.
“Limi is fortunate enough to know they are in danger, but there are hundreds of ‘Limi Valleys’ across the Himalaya. There are still villages whose mountains have not been studied. They don't know if they are living in danger or not,” says Lhazom, whose 2024 film documenting the Limi Valley flooding, No Monastery No Village, was screened at Banff.
But most importantly to Lhazom, she was able to convince her Indigenous people of the Limi Valley that the flooding was not their fault. Since finally putting them on the map, Lhazom has been working to help secure government funds to resettle the remaining families away from danger on nearby ancestral land.
As Nepal’s politicians scramble after this year’s floods to reform the legal framework for disaster relocation, Lhazom is traveling high in the mountains to deliver relief for the victims among 33,000 now in need of permanent resettlement after being banned from rebuilding their homes along the permanently destabilized high-risk mountainside.
“The frozen water banks we know are melting, and that means flooding that can sweep an entire village away within a fraction of a second. Our water sources are getting thinner and fewer and that is a grave concern,” says Lhazom. “But what’s most heartbreaking for these mountain people is knowing they can never go home.”
Generational families have no choice but to accept the erasure of their ancient Indigenous settlements. “The mountain is more than land. It is our identity, our history. The water spirits we worship inspired our folk songs and Indigenous wisdom, and polluting means you are being disrespectful to the water spirits,” says Lhazom. “It’ll be a challenge to convince the people to live in safer places, but I don't want them to be in a place that could kill them.”
Growing Artificial Glaciers
Northwest of Lhazom’s home, in Ladakh, India, where –40°winds whip through a remote desert on an 11,500-ft. shelf in the shadow of the Himalaya’s highest northern peaks, the people rely on a single water source: melting glacial ice, now covered in soot from vehicles carrying adventure tourists acclimating in its capital of Leh.
The region’s unbearably beautiful and dry glacial-dependent settlements could become the next Himalayan ghost villages—joining the 2,000 already abandoned from drying glaciers, water scarcity, drought, and unpredictable monsoons in places like Spiti and the Uttarakhand, India, and the Upper Mustang of Nepal.
But here in the “Third Pole,” climate activist and mechanical engineer Sonam Wangchuk is blending modern technology with his traditional knowledge. In 2015, inspired by stories of his ancestors moving “parent” glaciers into a cave to make “baby” glaciers—based on the early work of “the Iceman of India”—Wangchuk developed the science to revive the ancient cultural practice of grafting glaciers. He grew new ice to reverse water scarcity in Ladakh.
He ran a mile a mile-long pipe from a glacier spring down a steep slope; at the bottom in the shade the water shot straight into the air and, in the dead of winter, froze. Over a month, the ice grew into a multistory conical artificial glacier fountain he called an ice stupa after the sacred Buddhist dome-shaped shrines. Rather than wasting down the mountain, his invention preserves a critical water supply for an extra month through June when farmers need it most for planting.
Word of Wangchuk’s ice storage traveled, and he built ice stupas in numerous Himalayan villages facing water scarcity, even allowing a community from Ladakh’s abandoned village of Kulum to return home.
Beneath this elegant solution lurked a critical flaw. The pipes feeding the stupas were freezing. But working with longtime colleague Surya Balasubramanian, who earned his PhD in Switzerland in ice reservoir behavior, Wangchuk last year brought the ice stupas back to life through automation. By integrating solar-powered, computer-controlled sensor networks and motorized valves, the water flow could be turned off remotely to prevent the pipes from icing, ensuring 80% of the incoming spring water is frozen and stored.
“We innovated a method to either spray water from fountains or drain the pipes using valves controlled by weather and pipeline sensors,” says Balasubramania, who in 2023 independently launched Acres of Ice to scale the ice stupas.
Today, they’ve built or supported 160 ice stupas across Ladakh, Nepal, Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan, Chile, and Pakistan, each standing up to 12 stories and capable of storing 3.2 million gallons.
But the fight may never be over for Wangchuk, who knows the temporary nature of his adaptation strategy won’t outlive the glaciers. He is now testing a new application: sourcing water for his stupa from a dangerous glacial lake to help prevent it from collapsing and sending a massive GLOF wave down the mountain—and using natural refrigeration to refreeze the lakes.
With the growing threat of climate-induced glacier collapse, intensifying monsoons, and prolonged dry spells, the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region is nearing a tipping point. As global temperatures rise, the people who have learned to adapt to harsh conditions for centuries have little control over the destabilization of their ancestral homes. Still, they look to nature for a way forward through simple innovation to make every drop of water count. The question is: Will it be enough?
“There’s very little that can be done at this point to protect against glaciers in vulnerable places in the Himalayas, so these communities suffer and pay the price for what the rest of the world does,” says Wangchuk. “The recent avalanche in Nepal is an alarm bell for the rest of the world to mend our ways on this planet.”

US-Russia cooperation in Arctic: Why energy-hungry economies have big hopes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:55:52 UTC
00:55:52 KST

US-Russia cooperation in Arctic: Why energy-hungry economies have big hopes
Speaking at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow on October 27, President Vladimir Putin warned that excluding Russia from global gas markets would raise costs for consumers. He also revealed discussions with potential American partners for exploring cooperation in Arctic gas development. This is happening even as restrictions on Russian energy projects remain in place.
Putin’s remarks come amid continued disruption to LNG supplies. QatarEnergy has extended the suspension of certain deliveries into December, while India’s LNG import bill rose 23% to $8.5 billion during April-September, despite volumes increasing by just 4.4%.
For import-dependent economies such as India, the question is whether prospective Arctic cooperation could eventually expand supply options, or whether sanctions, pricing and transportation constraints will keep that possibility beyond commercial reach.
Arctic gas cooperation meets commercial reality
Russia’s interest in Arctic cooperation extends beyond developing its vast gas reserves. Following Putin’s October 27 remarks, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak clarified that discussions with Washington concerned potential joint development of gas fields and LNG liquefaction facilities, including opportunities involving Russian infrastructure.
One possible example has already surfaced. Russia’s Novatek has acknowledged agreements to provide technology for the proposed $25 billion Polar Train LNG project in Alaska. The venture aims to use Russian liquefaction infrastructure for American gas exports, although its implementation remains subject to regulatory approvals.
Russia and the US compete for LNG buyers, yet Arctic development could give their energy companies reasons to work together. Russia could find opportunities to deploy its Arctic expertise and attract investment, while American developers could benefit from technology and infrastructure suited to challenging northern conditions.
Yet commercial interest alone cannot overcome the obstacles facing Arctic LNG development. Washington sanctioned Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project in November 2023, subsequently extending restrictions to companies and vessels involved in supplying equipment and transporting LNG from the project.
In September, the Novatek-led Arctic LNG 2 project sought approximately $1 billion in damages from South Korea’s Hanwha Ocean in an arbitration dispute over cancelled contracts for specialized ice-class LNG carriers, highlighting the shipping complications facing Russian Arctic gas development.
The regulatory environment remains equally complicated. On October 16, President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act, but the decision did not automatically remove restrictions imposed separately on Russian LNG projects.
Beyond regulatory approvals, Arctic operations depend on a limited fleet of specialized carriers capable of navigating ice-covered waters. Seasonal conditions further restrict their deployment, making transportation capacity a critical consideration for new projects.
India’s LNG security faces an Arctic test
India’s response to recent LNG disruptions offers an indication of how importing economies may approach future supply arrangements. According to Kpler data for the month of October, the US, Oman and Nigeria accounted for 68% of India’s LNG imports between March and September, against 25% a year earlier. Qatar’s share fell sharply before shipments began recovering this month.
India’s changing LNG suppliers expose a distinction between diversifying sources and reducing exposure to international prices. With more than a third of its LNG reportedly sourced through spot purchases, Indian buyers remain exposed to price fluctuations even when physical supplies are available. Adding Russian Arctic LNG to India’s supplier portfolio would not necessarily change that exposure unless the contracts offered a different pricing structure or greater protection against international price swings.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects India’s LNG requirements could reach 64 billion cubic metres annually by 2030, with the gap between contracted supplies and projected demand widening after 2028.
That gap could influence how Indian importers negotiate their next generation of LNG contracts. Long-term agreements offer greater supply certainty, while shorter commitments provide flexibility when demand or prices change. The balance between them will become increasingly important as India seeks to expand natural gas consumption.
Transport economics add another dimension. Analysis by Reuters in May estimated that shipping LNG from Russia’s Yamal project to India’s Kochi terminal via the Northern Sea Route could cost approximately $3.80 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), compared with $2.60-$2.70 through the Suez Canal using transshipment facilities at Murmansk.
In August, the Indian authorities announced plans for a joint Russia–India pilot voyage along the Northern Sea Route in 2027, alongside a bilateral cooperation agreement that is being negotiated. In September, Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov confirmed these plans, stating in the future, Russian-Indian shipments along the NSR could reach 5 million tons annually.
The proposed voyage could help establish whether the NSR offers practical advantages for India-bound cargoes. For LNG, however, that assessment would require more than a successful transit, including evidence of year-round operating reliability and the costs of deploying specialised vessels.
Asia’s LNG market confronts a new supply equation
China offers an early indication of how Arctic LNG is entering Asian markets despite Western restrictions. According to S&P Global Energy, Chinese imports of Russian LNG increased nearly 25% during January-July 2026, supported partly by discounted Arctic LNG 2 cargoes. Reuters reported in June that Beijing was preparing a second receiving terminal for the sanctioned project’s shipments.
Meanwhile, Kpler estimates cited by Reuters on October 22 suggest Asian LNG arrivals could reach 23.31 million tonnes in October, their highest level in three months despite elevated prices.
Yet stronger imports do not necessarily signal sustained demand growth. The IEA reported that Asian spot LNG prices averaged $17.50/MMBtu in the second quarter, up 45% year-on-year, and projected a 0.5% decline in regional gas consumption during 2026 as higher prices encouraged fuel switching and reduced industrial demand.
China’s experience contrasts with that of other Asian importers. On October 1, Britain exempted certain Russian LNG shipments to Japan and South Korea from its sanctions restrictions until March 2028, but only for Sakhalin-2 supplies under existing contracts. India, meanwhile, declined an offer of sanctioned Russian LNG in May, according to Reuters, while remaining open to permitted cargoes. These differences show how sanctions compliance and contractual commitments can shape Asian buyers’ access to Russian gas, regardless of the availability of additional supplies.
Prospective US-Russia cooperation could bring additional Arctic gas into international trade, but new production alone would not redraw global LNG supply patterns. For India and other importing economies, the larger question is whether future projects can offer access on terms that improve their existing procurement choices. The Arctic’s next commercial breakthrough may depend as much on reaching buyers as on producing gas.

Residents leave Russian-occupied Oleshky amid local ceasefire

The White House said US first lady Melania Trump helped negotiate the ceasefire and coordinate the humanitarian mission.
Some residents have been evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and are heading towards Ukrainian-controlled areas, a Ukrainian lawmaker announced on Friday, as a major ceasefire entered its fourth day.
"The Ukrainian delegation, along with the evacuated residents of Oleshky, set off for Anapa. From there, they will fly to Belarus and then travel home by bus," said Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia.
A convoy of 25 buses and several ambulances arrived in the war-torn city earlier on Friday, bringing food and medicine and helping residents who wished to leave.
“At this moment, the humanitarian operation is underway in Oleshky,” Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an post online. Budanov is not part of the Ukrainian delegation in the city.
Officials from Ukraine and Russia have worked together on the rare humanitarian mission, offering a brief moment of cooperation amid the ongoing war.
"We are completing our humanitarian mission in Oleshky," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said in a video on Telegram, adding that a "convoy with those who are going to the territory of the Russian Federation is heading to the territory of the Russian Federation".
Around 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to local authorities and volunteers.
The local ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region is expected to remain in place until Sunday evening.
“Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will have the opportunity to do so safely,” Russia and Ukraine said in separate, identical statements. “Those who choose to stay may remain and will receive all the humanitarian support they need.”
Although Ukrainian-controlled territory is just a few kilometres across the Dnipro River from Oleshky, evacuees will have to travel hundreds of kilometres through Russia and Belarus before entering northern Ukraine, according to Ukrainian public television. The exact evacuation route has not been disclosed.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said on X that he will "personally continue to coordinate the humanitarian mission."
Despite the local ceasefire, fighting on Friday continued in other areas. Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed to have intercepted more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine reported Russian strikes involving ballistic missiles, other missiles and dozens of drones.

EU to fast-track €45 billion for Ukraine amid acute financial crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:54:54 UTC
00:54:54 KST

In 2027, the EU will provide Ukraine with €32 billion in military aid and €13 billion in budget support. But more funds will be needed as Russia escalates.
The European Union intends to accelerate the disbursement of its €90 billion support loan to Ukraine as the country faces a financial crunch amid Russia's all-out escalation and blockade in the Black Sea.
The loan is split evenly: €45 billion for 2026, with payments underway, and €45 billion for 2027. Initially, the credit was meant to last until the end of next year, but the brutality of the war has upended the calculation.
As a result, Brussels will concentrate funds in the first half of 2027 to avoid a cut-off of assistance that could have catastrophic consequences on the ground.
The second €45 billion envelope will allocate €31.7 billion for the military and €13.3 billion for the budget, according to a strategy published on Friday by the European Commission.
The €31.7 billion will be paid out gradually as Kyiv submits new contracts for weapons. The submissions can begin this year to ensure timely deliveries in 2027.
The €13.3 billion will be conditional on reforms, some of which relate to Ukraine's accession process. EU leaders have urged the country to keep the legislative pace on track.
A €3.7 billion payment has already been delayed.
"We are providing Ukraine with much-needed predictability and helping maintain essential public services," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Together with our allies, we must also do everything in our power to mount pressure on Russia to stop its barbaric war of aggression."
Ahead of the announcement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked Brussels to speed up disbursements.
"The sooner we start receiving the corresponding tranches for our drone production, air defence procurement, budget support and other vital expenditures, the better our position in 2027 will be," he said.
In the meantime, the Commission is searching for ways to fill the €70 billion shortfall that Ukraine faces next year, which will require fresh funding on top of the existing loan.
Commission officials insist the bloc will cover no more than two-thirds of the gap, roughly €46 billion, with the remainder to be handled by other allies. Joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunnerto plug the hole.
An internal document seen by Euronews identifies three main reasons for the deficit.
First, the prolongation of the war, now well into its fifth year. When Brussels designed the €90 billion loan, it did so under the assumption the conflict would end sometime in 2026. The premise, which raised eyebrows last year, has now come apart.
Second, the intensification of Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure and the blockade of the Black Sea, which are "weakening economic activity and Ukraine's capacity to raise domestic revenues", further compounding its reliance on global donors.
Third, the decrease in assistance from non-EU allies. The document says that if all NATO allies deliver on their pledges made at the summit in July, the gap in military aid will be reduced by up to €13 billion next year.
Ukraine's financial needs, the document adds, will be "largely determined" by the ability to resist Russia's airstrikes, which need costly US-made Patriot interceptors.
Kyiv has accused Washington of delaying Patriots that have been paid for with European money. The impasse has been linked with US President Donald Trump's insistence that Ukraine cease attacks on Russia's oil refineries, claiming they raise global fuel prices.
On Friday, a Ukranian drone attack was reported at the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Russia's Samara region.

NATO reconnaissance aircraft spends over seven hours over Black Sea

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. A US-registered NATO reconnaissance aircraft spent more than seven hours flying over the Black Sea on Friday, a source in air traffic control services told TASS.
The aircraft, a Bombardier ARTEMIS II, regularly conducts surveillance flights over international waters in the southern Black Sea, spending hours flying back and forth between the western and eastern parts of the region.
"The aircraft was spotted in the area for the first time this week, spending just over seven hours there in total," the source said. He noted that during several passes, the aircraft flew almost as far as the Romanian-Ukrainian border, making repeated loops over the surrounding area.
According to the source, the aircraft has since returned to its home base in Constanta, Romania.
"Earlier this week, the Bombardier ARTEMIS II was also spotted near the Kaliningrad Region, flying along its perimeter while remaining in Polish and Lithuanian airspace. It was also observed over the Mediterranean Sea," the source added.
He further noted that in late July, the aircraft set what could be considered a record by spending nine hours over the Black Sea. On October 7, it was spotted over the sea alongside a Swedish Air Force Gulfstream S102B Korpen radar reconnaissance aircraft.

Fighters of the 1st Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine "Azov" struck more than 100 Russian trains carrying fuel and other supplies for occupying forces, the corps reported on social media on 28 October. The strikes disabled locomotives, fuel tank cars, and other equipment, the statement said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 16 October that seizing all of Donetsk Oblast remains one of Russia's main tasks. Azov notes that these strikes help "destroy" Russia's offensive capabilities.
Small Ukrainian drones strike Russia's 100-ton locomotives
Azov emphasizes that neither mobile fire groups nor electronic warfare systems can protect Russian logistics routes.
"The enemy is doing its utmost to create an image of successfully capturing settlements, but is unable to protect key railway stations through which the fuel supply chain runs toward the front," Azov said.
The rail hubs hit had carried Russian military trains to the fighting in Donbas and southern Ukraine, Defense Express reported on 29 October. The count of more than 100 trains covers Azov's operations over the past four months, the outlet said.
The mass of any diesel locomotive exceeds 100 tons, yet the Ukrainian military struck these large Russian targets using small UAVs, the outlet also notes.
Donations helped make the strikes possible
Donations and the work of the Come Back Alive foundation contributed to the operation's results, Azov said. In particular, the foundation provided the military with 440 Starlink Mini terminals, the corps added.
Azov announced Operation Hell back in the summer
On 2 July, the Azov Corps announced Operation Hell and released the first footage of strikes on Russian railway equipment. The video shows a strike on a diesel locomotive that was likely used by Russian forces for military logistics.
The corps said the strike was part of a carefully planned operation and promised details soon.

New Jersey Governor Weighs Blocking Russian Diesel Shipment From State Port

New Jersey Governor Weighs Blocking Russian Diesel Shipment From State Port
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill stated that she is considering blocking a shipment of Russian diesel from arriving at a port in the state, KYW Newsradio reported on October 29.
The Trump administration announced a deal with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel to US and global markets. UNITED24 Media reported that the arrangement included an initial shipment of more than 300,000 tonnes, with larger deliveries expected to follow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a statement to KYW Newsradio, Sherrill commented on US President Donald Trump’s fuel agreement with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, arguing that it has failed to reduce energy costs for American consumers.
“Donald Trump isn’t doing anything to bring down gas prices, diesel prices, or costs,” Sherrill stated. “Instead, he is lining Vladimir Putin’s pockets at the expense of American consumers and our democratic ally Ukraine.”
The diesel volumes involved are unlikely to materially lower US fuel prices. UNITED24 Media calculated that the initial 300,000-tonne shipment would cover less than two hours of global diesel demand, while analysts described the expected effect on prices as marginal.
Sherrill stated that her administration is examining possible steps to prevent the shipment from entering New Jersey.
“Make no mistake: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin is corrupt and illegal, and I am evaluating options to stop it from arriving at a port in New Jersey,” she told KYW Newsradio.
The shipment is also facing pressure from Congress. US Senator Richard Blumenthal urged the Agioi Fanendes, a Malta-flagged tanker carrying around 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel toward New York and New Jersey, to turn around, arguing that a presidential license cannot override the 2022 federal ban on Russian energy imports.

Dockworkers launch global strike against Israeli and US military shipments (VIDEOS)
Dockworkers across five continents have launched a coordinated anti-war strike, targeting Israeli arms shipments, US military cargo, and the growing militarization of civilian ports.
Organizers say more than 25 unions are mobilizing across 113 ports in 22 countries and regions on Friday in an unprecedented international action. The campaign includes 24-hour strikes, shorter walkouts, blockades, and solidarity rallies.
Major European ports joining the action include Genoa, Marseille, Le Havre, Hamburg, Valencia, Barcelona, and Piraeus. Beyond Europe, protests are planned at Tangier Med in Morocco, Nhava Sheva and Chennai in India, and Oakland and San Francisco in the US, with further actions across Türkiye, Cyprus, Sweden, Denmark, Ireland, Portugal, Brazil, Mexico, and Australia.
France’s CGT Ports et Docks has called 24-hour strikes across 24 ports, while Italy’s USB has declared a nationwide general strike, with protests in more than 40 cities. Unions in Germany, Greece, Spain, India, and the US are also taking part.
Dockworkers at the port of Piraeus, Greece, walked off the job as part of a global day of action, with protesters in more than 100 ports worldwide striking against the arms trade with Israel.

— Press TV 🔻 (@PressTV) October 30, 2026
Dockworkers at Piraeus, Greece’s largest port, were among the first to join the action, with a three-hour stoppage scheduled from 08:00 to 11:00 GMT. Other Greek maritime unions announced 24-hour strikes affecting seven ports, threatening ferry services to the country’s islands.
Dockworkers across 21 major ports in Europe and the Mediterranean shut down operations in a coordinated day of action. Under the call “Port Workers Do Not Work for War,” 
They blocked arms shipments and demanded a full trade and arms embargo on Israel. pic.twitter.com/43Srp1pYE5
— The Resonance (@Partisan_12) February 7, 2026
Videos of demonstrations and gatherings at other ports have emerged online, although the full extent of the disruption to shipping operations remains unclear as actions are taking place at different times.
What do the dockworkers want?
The unions demand a halt to weapons, ammunition, military equipment, and troop shipments through commercial ports, targeting both Israeli and US military supply chains. They also oppose turning civilian ports into military hubs and diverting public funds into rearmament while workers face stagnant wages, job insecurity, and worsening conditions.
Protesters gather outside Tilbury Docks in the UK, urging dockworkers to join an international mobilisation involving over 100 ports in solidarity with Palestine and against arms shipments to Israel. pic.twitter.com/7fulNOmU82

“From planes to tanks, guns to bullets, explosives to ammunition, uniforms to boots, our ports have become replenishing and forwarding bases for war and genocide,” the organizers said at a press conference on October 15 in Rome.

The unions accused governments and shipping companies of keeping military supply routes open despite the Gaza ceasefire announced over a year ago, which they say has been rendered largely meaningless by continued Israeli strikes.
‘No Harbour for Genocide’, the campaign coordinating the action, claims that it tracked 315 shipments of components for Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems through 56 ports in 29 countries over 14 months. It says it identified 3,400 shipments of US military cargo through 67 ports in 42 countries over ten months. The group also says US military cargo volumes at some European ports rose as much as tenfold following the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran. The figures have not been independently verified.
Organizers estimate the action could delay 40,000 containers carrying cargo worth over $2 billion, potentially costing shipping companies up to $43 million.
Is it the first strike of this kind?
Dockworkers have challenged military shipments for years, though resistance was largely scattered and localized. Since 2019, workers in Italy, Greece, Morocco, and France have staged sporadic blockades and stoppages, targeting arms shipments to Israel, US bases, and other conflict zones.
The movement gained momentum in late 2025 after Israel intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla, a 40-plus-vessel convoy attempting to deliver aid to blockaded Gaza. Hundreds of activists were detained, sparking strikes and port blockades across Europe. The flotilla campaign also pledged to join the action on Friday with “coordinated, strategic actions on the water.”
