What Tokayev’s Economic Agenda Means for Kazakhstan’s International Partnerships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

For Kazakhstan, a country linking China and Europe while sharing a long border with Russia, infrastructure is never entirely a domestic matter. Railways determine how goods move across Eurasia, electricity supplies shape industrial investment, and the ability to process minerals affects the country’s place in international supply chains. These connections offer a useful way to read President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s October 28 State of the Nation address, which was mostly about economic development but had also important implications for foreign relations.
Tokayev began by warning of deepening mistrust among major powers and a more unpredictable international environment. Rather than proposing a new diplomatic alignment, he emphasized a stronger economy, modern infrastructure, technology, and effective institutions. For Kazakhstan’s longstanding balanced and multivector foreign policy, the underlying logic is that domestic capacity can widen the scope for cooperation with different partners at the same time.
The most visible proposal was the nationwide “People’s Construction” program, backed by 6.5 trillion tenge (approximately $14 billion) from the National Fund through 2029, including 1.5 trillion tenge earmarked for early social projects. Roads, utilities, housing, and public facilities are central to the plan. Tokayev also proposed a higher minimum wage and new healthcare facilities. These measures principally address domestic needs, but more reliable services and regional infrastructure can also reduce costs for investors and make industrial projects more viable outside the largest cities. The president’s insistence that public spending mobilize private capital, rather than substitute for it, gives the initiative an international dimension.
The clearest connection between domestic investment and foreign relations is transport. Tokayev said the Bakhty-Ayagoz railway should enter service in 2027, adding 20 million tons of capacity on routes toward China. Construction has also begun on an Aral-Caspian corridor intended to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by roughly 1,000 kilometers. Both projects respond to an established demand for more dependable links between Asian production centers and European markets. In February, the World Bank approved an $846 million guarantee designed to mobilize $1.41 billion in commercial financing for Kazakhstan’s rail network along the Middle Corridor.
The geopolitical value of these routes lies in their usefulness to multiple economies. China gains additional westward capacity, European businesses gain another option for moving goods, and Kazakhstan can expand its role in services surrounding that trade. Tokayev’s call for freight consolidation centers, logistics operators, and factories near transport junctions suggests an ambition to capture value beyond transit fees. Yet the route’s performance will depend not only on Kazakh construction but also on ports, customs procedures and coordination with Azerbaijan, Georgia, and other corridor partners. Greater connectivity is a regional undertaking, not simply a national project.
The same logic applies to data. On October 15, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan inaugurated a 380-kilometer fiber-optic link beneath the Caspian Sea, designed to carry information between Central Asia and Europe. Mentioned again in the address, the cable shows how physical and digital connectivity can reinforce one another. Reliable cross-border data links matter to cloud services, financial transactions, and the data centers Kazakhstan wants to attract.
China’s role is notable in other spheres too. At a September China-Kazakhstan investment forum, Tokayev described a portfolio of 260 joint industrial projects valued at more than $62 billion, spanning manufacturing, metallurgy, agriculture, and energy storage. Its composition indicates how the relationship is developing from commodity trade and transport toward local production and technology. The address’s emphasis on manufacturing capacity and domestic suppliers is consistent with this direction.
Energy provides a second intersection between internal requirements and external partnerships. Kazakhstan generates about 123 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually but still faces shortages. Tokayev set a goal of achieving a sustained surplus by 2029 through new generation, modernized grids and a broader mix of energy sources. Russia is an established partner in this sector. During President Vladimir Putin’s May visit, the two countries signed a nuclear power agreement and arrangements for Russian export-credit financing. Chinese companies have also proposed nuclear cooperation, including technology transfer and specialist training, as Tokayev noted in the address.
These projects are significant because a nuclear partnership can encompass engineering, fuel services, training and maintenance over decades. They should not, however, be mistaken for an immediate solution to the 2029 electricity target: the first planned reactor is not expected to begin operating before the following decade. In the nearer term, grid upgrades and other generation projects will remain decisive. For Kazakhstan’s partners, a more dependable power system would also improve the prospects for energy-intensive manufacturing, mineral processing and computing infrastructure.
Critical minerals offer another area in which domestic reforms can produce international effects. Tokayev called for modern geological exploration, better access to geological data, long-term financing and offtake arrangements, alongside consideration of a dedicated mechanism for nonferrous and rare-earth metals. The objective is to develop processing and other parts of industrial value chains. This meets interests expressed by both Western and Asian partners, although turning resource potential into competitive production will require technology, investment and skills.
During Tokayev’s June visit to Brussels, EU leaders identified critical raw materials, energy, transport and digitalization as priorities for expanded cooperation. As Kazakhstan’s largest trading and investment partner, the EU has a particularly strong interest in the development of these sectors. The United States and Kazakhstan have also agreed to cooperate on mineral supply chains, including a proposed American-backed tungsten mining and processing project. These relationships have distinct commercial purposes, but each could support Kazakhstan’s stated goal of producing more value domestically. They complement its established energy and industrial ties with Russia and China rather than necessarily displacing them.
Technology is becoming a further point of international engagement. The address highlighted two operating supercomputers, another planned before year’s end, and efforts to apply artificial intelligence to agriculture, industry and public services. In June, Kazakhstan joined the U.S.-backed Pax Silica initiative and signed an AI Opportunity Partnership statement, connecting cooperation on computing, semiconductors, energy, critical minerals and research. On October 23, Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana and met Tokayev. Nvidia’s own account of the visit described planned computing investments and potential applications in mining, agriculture and industrial automation. These developments give the digital agenda a tangible international dimension, although the economic benefits will depend on adoption by ordinary businesses as much as high-profile infrastructure.
The final link is institutional. Tokayev acknowledged weaknesses in investment coordination and proposed a larger role for the Baiterek development holding, a new civil code, adjustments to tax rules and an English common law-based investment court in Alatau. Such changes will matter to foreign partners only insofar as they create predictable conditions in practice. The same is true of financing: public construction spending can initiate projects, but sustained industrial cooperation requires viable businesses, long-term credit and confidence in dispute resolution.
The address did not signify a departure from Kazakhstan’s established diplomatic approach. It suggests rather how that approach might acquire greater economic substance. China’s industrial and transport links, Russia’s energy cooperation, the EU’s connectivity and raw-materials partnerships, and emerging U.S. ties in minerals and artificial intelligence each intersect with priorities set out by Tokayev. Delivery remains the essential test. If infrastructure is completed, power becomes more reliable and investment rules improve, Kazakhstan could become a stronger participant in the production, services and technology networks that connect Eurasia.

Mossad to assist Shin Bet probe into suspected foreign election interference, i24NEWS understands

Mossad to assist Shin Bet probe into suspected foreign election interference, i24NEWS understands
Israel’s foreign intelligence agency will focus on intelligence relating to Qatar; elections committee says probe has no impact on final results
The Mossad was set Friday to assist the Shin Bet’s investigation into suspected foreign interference in Israel’s election, focusing on matters within its authority, particularly intelligence relating to Qatar, i24NEWS understands.
The investigation followed a briefing in which Shin Bet chief David Zini presented classified information to Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg. Sohlberg ordered a probe into suspected foreign funding and election bribery, requesting findings within a week.
The Shin Bet said the information was gathered independently and did not originate with a political party. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot and opposition leader Yair Lapid were briefed on the investigation.
The Central Elections Committee stressed that the investigation had no impact on the final election results and did not target any particular sector. Its findings will be submitted to Sohlberg to assess their scope and implications.
Qatar issued a statement categorically denying interfering in the election, saying it would "not serve as a scapegoat for Israeli politicians." Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas also denied his party had any connection to the matter.

Poland's coalition politicians slam opposition leader's EU exit remarks
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
16:02:51 CET
00:02:51 KST

Poland's coalition politicians slam opposition leader's EU exit remarks
Poland's ruling coalition politicians on Thursday condemned the suggestion by the leader of the main opposition, Law and Justice (PiS) party, Jaroslaw Kaczynski, that Poland could initiate formal EU withdrawal negotiations as a high-stakes pressure tactic to force institutional changes within the bloc.
Reacting sharply on X, Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that the very future of the country's Western integration is now up for debate.
"Jaroslaw Kaczynski has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the conditions of leaving the European Union," Tusk wrote on Thursday morning. "This is precisely what is at stake in today's fierce struggle in Poland. A tough battle—and I do not intend to lose it, even if not everyone plays on my side."
Kaczynski countered on X later that day, writing that "Tusk, as usual, is lying." He added that "the European Union is needed, but it requires thorough reform," attributing the bloc's current crisis to the past governance of former German Chancellor Angela Merkel and Tusk himself during his tenure as European Council President. Kaczynski declared that PiS wants an EU focused on lowering energy prices, strengthening security, and eliminating unnecessary bureaucracy for ordinary citizens. "We will restore the European Union to its citizens," Kaczynski wrote, adding that allowing the current systemic crisis to continue is what truly threatens Europe's future.
Earlier on Thursday, PiS Vice-Chairman Przemyslaw Czarnek also said that the party has no plans for Polexit, clarifying that Kaczynski's remarks were aimed entirely at the necessity of reshaping and reforming the face of the EU.
The political firestorm follows Kaczynski's speech at the Krynica Forum 2026, a major political, economic, and geopolitical conference held in southern Poland on Wednesday. There, Kaczynski expressed his "deep conviction" that the European Union requires fundamental changes. In addition to shifting public opinion and drafting a new treaty with delayed implementation, the opposition leader proposed a "hard and risky" approach using the exit clauses of the Treaty on European Union
"It all begins with negotiations, and simply starting these negotiations," Kaczynski told the forum, referring to the EU's treaty provisions for member state withdrawal. "It is a hard method, a risky one, but things are really so bad... that it is worth employing such a method if others fail." He admitted that the strategy would require immense determination and aligning positions among like-minded member states whose views, particularly on Eastern policy, remain far apart.
Senior coalition figures swiftly linked Kaczynski's remarks to a broader pro-Russian and anti-Western agenda, tying the opposition's actions to far-right, Euroskeptic Confederation of the Polish Crown leader Grzegorz Braun. The row comes amid public friction over whether President Karol Nawrocki should invite Braun's faction to the upcoming National Security Bureau (RBN) meeting on November 3.
Special Services Coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak criticised Kaczynski for entertaining EU exit talks "at such a sensitive moment for our security", adding that "even Kremlin dreamers would not have predicted a significant Polish politician speaking directly against Poland's interests." Government spokesman Adam Szlapka said that "Kaczynski is implementing Braun's agenda, and we all know whose agenda Braun implements."
Speaker of the Sejm, lower house, Wlodzimierz Czarzasty said that while Nawrocki normalises the "pro-Russian Braun", Kaczynski is "familiarising the public with the topic of Poland leaving the EU," concluding: "They are moving East. We are staying."
Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the rhetoric follows the opposition's recent votes against the EU's SAFE programme, a loan fund providing up to EUR 150 billion for defence industry investments, which President Nawrocki vetoed in March. Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the EU must be reformed "where improvement is needed, not threatened with an exit," demanding that PiS and Confederation explicitly state ahead of the parliamentary elections whether they want Polexit.
Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned that leaving the EU would trigger severe everyday consequences, including "a customs border with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Lithuania, passport controls at airports, and an end to EU subsidies for farmers and investments." New Left MEP Joanna Scheuring-Wielgus and Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak echoed these concerns, with Klimczak warning that the UK's severe post-Brexit national losses should serve as a stark warning to Poland. (PAP)

Kazakhstani stranded on arrested tanker in India, seven sailors head home

Kazakhstani stranded on arrested tanker in India, seven sailors head home
The first crew members from the vessel MT UNITY, detained in India, are heading home. A Kazakh citizen remains among the sailors still aboard. Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry has said when he will be able to return home, Qazinform News Agency reports.
On Oct. 29, seven crew members — six Russian nationals and one Egyptian were disembarked from the vessel and transferred to Bhubaneswar, the capital of India's Odisha state. They are scheduled to depart for their home countries on Oct. 31.
The tanker had a crew of 23 people: 20 Russians, two Egyptians, and one Kazakh citizen.
According to Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry, visa processing and repatriation arrangements for the Kazakh national are currently being resolved, and the Embassy in India is keeping the situation under control.
"Efforts are underway with India's Ministry of External Affairs and other authorized agencies to ensure the repatriation of our citizen," the ministry said in a statement. "The Indian court has ruled to allow a crew replacement for the detained vessel. Efforts to process visas and arrange repatriation are underway."
The Cameroon-flagged tanker MT Unity has been under arrest near Paradip Port since May 11, 2026, following a commercial dispute involving financial claims by a local fuel supplier against the shipowner.
The crew was stranded aboard for months. According to Indian media reports, the sailors faced severe shortages of food and drinking water. The crew also faced delays in wage payments.
On 17 September 2026, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the detention and sent a diplomatic note to India’s Foreign Ministry requesting assistance in resolving the situation.

CineCrossroads: Five films to make your Halloween weekend unforgettable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:01:15 UTC
00:01:15 KST

CineCrossroads: Five films to make your Halloween weekend unforgettable
With Halloween arriving this weekend, CineCrossroads presents a special selection of five films that explore the holiday from different angles. From supernatural terror and a genre-defining classic to gothic suspense, playful comedy and family animation, this edition offers something for every kind of Halloween viewer. Qazinform News Agency wishes you an enjoyable and suitably spooky viewing experience.
Movie of the week: Other Mommy (2026)
This week’s main release is Other Mommy, a supernatural horror film directed by Rob Savage and based on Josh Malerman’s novel Incidents Around the House.
The story follows Bela, a young girl whose family home is invaded by a sinister entity she calls Other Mommy. Appearing in the shape of Bela’s mother, the creature tries to gain the child’s trust while gradually tightening its hold over the household.
Jessica Chastain takes on a disturbing dual role as Bela’s mother and the entity imitating her. She is joined by Jay Duplass and Arabella Olivia Clark, while filmmaker James Wan serves as one of the producers.
Rather than relying only on sudden scares, Other Mommy draws its tension from a fear familiar to many children: the possibility that something frightening may be hiding inside an apparently safe home. Its domestic setting and unsettling central figure make it an appropriate choice for viewers seeking a chilling start to the Halloween weekend.
Classic pick: Halloween (1978)
No Halloween selection would be complete without John Carpenter’s Halloween, one of the most influential horror films ever made.
The film follows escaped killer Michael Myers as he returns to the fictional town of Haddonfield on Halloween night. There, teenager Laurie Strode, played by Jamie Lee Curtis, gradually realizes that a silent masked stranger is following her.
Carpenter creates suspense through patient camerawork, carefully framed shadows and an unforgettable minimalist score. Much of the film’s power comes from what remains unseen. Quiet streets, darkened houses and empty doorways become sources of danger long before violence occurs.
More than four decades after its release, Halloween remains a model of economical filmmaking. Its imagery and music have become inseparable from the holiday itself, making it an essential classic for anyone interested in the history of horror cinema.
Gothic pick: The Others (2001)
For viewers who prefer atmosphere to bloodshed, Alejandro Amenábar’s The Others offers an elegant and haunting alternative.
Nicole Kidman stars as Grace, a deeply religious mother living with her two children in an isolated mansion shortly after the Second World War. Because the children suffer from an extreme sensitivity to sunlight, the curtains must remain closed and every door must be locked before another is opened.
When unexplained footsteps, voices and strange figures begin appearing in the house, Grace becomes convinced that the family is no longer alone. Yet the truth behind the disturbances proves far more complicated than she expects.
With its candlelit rooms, heavy fog and growing sense of isolation, The Others captures the spirit of a traditional ghost story. Its restrained approach and carefully constructed mystery make it an excellent Halloween choice for audiences who enjoy psychological suspense.
Horror comedy pick: What We Do in the Shadows (2014)
Halloween does not have to be entirely frightening. Taika Waititi and Jemaine Clement’s What We Do in the Shadows turns a household of ancient vampires into the subjects of a mock documentary.
The vampires share a home in Wellington, New Zealand, where their supernatural abilities do little to solve ordinary domestic problems. They argue about cleaning, struggle to enter nightclubs without an invitation and attempt to understand contemporary fashion and technology.
The film affectionately parodies familiar vampire traditions while giving each of its immortal characters a distinct and surprisingly relatable personality. Its humor comes from placing legendary creatures in mundane situations, without losing sight of the darker mythology surrounding them.
Inventive, quotable and consistently charming, What We Do in the Shadows is ideal for viewers who want costumes, creatures and Halloween atmosphere without an evening of intense scares.
Family pick: ParaNorman (2012)
The final recommendation is ParaNorman, a stop-motion animated adventure that combines ghosts, zombies and witchcraft with a compassionate story about fear and prejudice.
Norman is an eleven-year-old boy who can see and speak with the dead. His unusual ability makes him an outsider in his small town, but it also leaves him as the only person capable of stopping an old curse when the dead begin rising from their graves.
Although the film embraces spooky imagery, its monsters are never quite what they initially appear to be. Beneath the supernatural adventure is a thoughtful message about misunderstanding others and the harm caused when fear turns into cruelty.
With its detailed animation, lively humor and emotional depth, ParaNorman is a strong choice for families with older children. It provides plenty of Halloween excitement while ending this special edition on a warm and meaningful note.
Whether the weekend calls for supernatural terror, classic suspense, gothic mystery, vampire comedy or animated adventure, these five films offer different ways to enter the Halloween spirit.

Nations struggle for deal as UN’s COP17 nature talks go down to the wire

Nations agree on push to get nature goals on track at UN summit
- Nearly 200 nations approved key UN biodiversity texts in overtime at COP17 in Yerevan, after two weeks of tense talks aimed at reversing nature loss by 2030.
- Countries still face major gaps on targets, including protecting 30% of land and oceans, cutting pollution, and raising conservation finance. The UN says the world needs US$700 billion more a year.
- Talks were dogged by disputes over harmful subsidies, new funding sources, the weak Cali Fund, and attacks on science. Leaders and indigenous groups urged urgent action, and the next summit host may be Panama or Ecuador.
AI generated
YEREVAN – Nearly 200 nations on Oct 30 adopted hard-fought agreements at a UN biodiversity summit aimed at putting the world back on track in efforts to halt nature’s destruction by 2030.
The outcome, however, came with disappointment over missed opportunities to address humanity’s destructive toll on nature.
Delegates cheered as the crucial texts were approved in overtime, but celebrations were tempered by acrimonious debates and regret over limited progress on some of the most contentious issues.
The COP17 summit in Armenia sought to revive a landmark commitment to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 after global efforts to meet that goal fell short.
Over two bruising weeks in Armenia’s capital, Yerevan, nations were urged to correct course to keep the pact alive and protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on earth.
“And that’s it. Perfect,” said COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan to applause, as he brought down the gavel on the documents, the final versions of which were not immediately available.
The world adopted a historic pact in 2022 setting ambitious targets to halt biodiversity loss by 2030. But ahead of the summit, the UN warned that countries would fail to meet the goals unless they urgently correct course.
Most of the objectives are falling short, including targets to protect 30% of earth’s land and oceans, tackle pollution, and provide poorer countries with greater conservation finance.
A draft COP17 text had called on countries to “accelerate” efforts to keep the pact alive.
The much-anticipated text stressed that “increased action” was needed to tackle the root drivers of nature loss.
Highlighting the disagreements that dogged the talks, the document proposed various options to achieve the 2030 goal. It was not immediately clear which of those options made the cut.
The text “needed to respond to the irrefutable evidence that we are off track for our 2030 deadline, and while not particularly exciting or detailed, it’s good news that countries could reach agreement”, Catherine Weller from Fauna and Flora told AFP.
Kirsty Leong, of WWF International, told AFP the “outcome has its strengths and weaknesses but, on balance, it’s a good outcome”.
‘Weak terms’
During negotiations, countries wrangled over reforming subsidies and other incentives that encourage activities harmful to nature, such as fossil fuel use, intensive agriculture and overfishing.
Governments had pledged to reduce this spending but made little progress, with an estimated US$2.4 trillion (S$3.1 trillion) still flowing every year to harmful subsidies.
An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International said it was crucial that spending was switched to nature protection and restoration.
“Even though the agreed decision text expresses it in weak terms, COP17 saw important political momentum to address harmful financial incentives – including subsidies – and that’s urgently needed,” she told AFP.
A separate row revolved around finding new cash sources to fund conservation efforts around the globe – a hot-button issue with public budgets under strain amid an energy crisis and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
To restore degraded ecosystems, save endangered species and conserve forests, wetlands and other vital natural habitats, the world needs an estimated US$700 billion more every year than it currently spends. The European Union led a charge for wealthy emerging economies such as China to join in paying for global conservation efforts, a contentious issue at COP17.
In a sign of possible compromise, another draft text that circulated on Oct 30 invited countries outside the developed country donors to voluntarily join the group. It did not compel any country to contribute to biodiversity finance but asked for volunteers to “signal interest”.
Science under attack
Efforts to refine the lacklustre Cali Fund – a UN mechanism for sharing profits from corporations that use genetic data from plants and other organisms – also proved difficult.
The fund set out to raise US$1 billion a year for conservation in developing countries when it was launched in early 2025. So far, it has attracted around US$10,000.
Nations have also feuded over key scientific reports, with a handful of countries accused of stonewalling efforts to accept the benchmark findings of a UN-backed biodiversity body.
“The attacks on science have bothered me a lot,” French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.
Around 70 ministers joined the negotiations this week, in an effort to nudge things along, while indigenous leaders and civil society activists appealed to nations to act with greater urgency.
At the last biodiversity summit in Colombia in 2024, talks ran overtime as nations haggled over conservation finance and ended without a deal. Negotiations resumed in Rome in 2025 where an agreement was reached.
The COP17 summit was also expected to decide on Oct 30 whether Panama or Ecuador will host the next biodiversity summit in 2028. AFP

Halis Sünnetci
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Romano Floriani Mussolini, the great-grandson of Italian fascist dictator Benito Mussolini, scored his first goal for Lazio in a 6-2 victory over Sassuolo on Tuesday, helping the Rome-based club move provisionally to the top of Serie A.
The 23-year-old right-back converted a low cross from Kenneth Taylor in the 16th minute to put Lazio 3-1 ahead, with the goal initially ruled out for offside before being awarded following a video assistant referee (VAR) review.
It was his first goal for Lazio and his first in Italy's top flight, having previously scored in Serie B while on loan at Juve Stabia.
"I'm really happy to have scored that first goal, but even more so about this win, which is crucial for us," Floriani Mussolini said after the match.
Lazio's 6-2 victory over Sassuolo, which saw the hosts reduced to 10 men in the first half, extended their unbeaten Serie A run to nine matches, leaving them level with Inter Milan on 25 points at the top of the standings. 
Mussolini's family legacy and Lazio's far-right history
Floriani Mussolini's family background has attracted attention throughout his career, particularly because of Lazio's historical association with far-right supporter groups.
The 23-year-old is the son of former Italian politician Alessandra Mussolini and a great-grandson of Benito Mussolini, who ruled fascist Italy from 1922 to 1943.
Sections of Lazio's organized supporters have been associated with far-right politics since the 1970s, with the club's Curva Nord later becoming particularly linked to the Irriducibili, a group founded in 1987 and known for its far-right ideology and controversies involving fascist symbols and racist behavior.
Floriani Mussolini, who developed through Lazio's academy before loan spells at several Italian clubs, has sought to keep his football career separate from discussions about his family history.
"My surname has never caused me any problems and, from my point of view, the less said about it, the better," he said in July 2025, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
"I'm here to express myself on the pitch, nothing else."
His first senior goal, scored while playing for Juve Stabia in December 2024, also sparked controversy after some supporters appeared to perform fascist salutes during the celebrations.
The Italian Football Federation opened an investigation into the incident, while Juve Stabia denied the allegations, saying supporters were raising their arms as part of a customary goal celebration.

Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Swiss components also found in new Russian weapons
Ukraine has now named 11 Swiss companies whose components have been found in Russian drones and missiles.
What new discoveries have the Ukrainian authorities made?
The Ukrainian military intelligence service, HUR, regularly publishes details of electronic components found in the wreckage of Russian weapon systems in a publicly accessible database. Findings from spring, September and October of this year show that Swiss components continue to be used in new or upgraded Russian drones, missiles and cruise missiles. Ukraine has identified components from 11 Swiss companies. Swiss components have also been found in North Korean ballistic missiles fired at Ukraine.
How important are these parts for Russian weapon systems?
Very important, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s adviser on international sanctions, speaking to Swiss public broadcaster SRF. According to Vlasiuk, 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain parts from Swiss companies. The electronic components supplied by Swiss firms are mass-produced industrial goods. They are used as microcontrollers in the control systems of missiles and drones, in the processing of satellite navigation data, as voltage converters, as sensors or as memory chips.
These components are not military equipment, nor are they dual-use items
And yet these electronic components are of military use. Countries are still struggling to define these goods in a uniform manner, as they have hitherto regarded them as civilian products. With changes in the nature of warfare – for example, the widespread use of low-cost drones – these mass-produced goods are becoming strategically significant. Together with the G7 countries, the EU has placed these goods on a joint sanctions list. Switzerland has adopted this sanctions list. As a result, Swiss companies are also no longer permitted to sell them to Russia.
What is Switzerland being accused of?
Switzerland is not doing enough to prevent shipments to Russia. This is the criticism levelled by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president. He is calling on the Swiss government to involve the law enforcement authorities and to strengthen the export control bodies. He is dissatisfied with Switzerland’s responses to date. Sanctions regimes have evolved, as has Russia’s ability to circumvent them, he says, adding that Switzerland cannot simply stick to the logic that there are no production facilities in Switzerland and that it does not export to Russia. That is not enough.
More
Swiss Army combines horses and high-tech drones
What does the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) say?
SECO is aware of the issue regarding the components, the State Secretariat stated in response to an enquiry. It explains that, in most cases, the goods are not produced in Switzerland. Consequently, no exports take place. The export of these goods from Switzerland – including indirectly – to Russia is prohibited. Swiss companies are obliged to comply with certain due diligence requirements. This includes, in the case of exports or sales to third countries, contractually prohibiting the re-export of these goods to Russia. The effective and comprehensive enforcement of sanctions against Russia is a priority for the government, SECO writes.
What is required of companies?
They should take a closer look. Particularly when selecting their distribution partners and intermediaries, says Vladyslav Vlasiuk. He cites the example of the Dutch company NXP. A few years ago, this company attracted even more negative attention than the Swiss firms. By 2026, NXP electronic components were almost entirely absent from Russian weapons.
The Ukrainian government lists 11 manufacturers based in Switzerland, two of which belong to the same group. We have asked the four companies with the most entries in the Ukrainian database for their comments:
STMicroelectronics: The company is headquartered in Plan-les-Ouates (canton Geneva). It emphasises that the use of its products for purposes other than those for which they are intended is neither authorised nor tolerated. The company has a comprehensive global compliance programme that includes training, procedures and guidelines for all sales channels. Since the end of February 2022, STMicroelectronics has taken measures to implement all sanctions packages and export control measures imposed by the EU, the US and other partner countries against Russia and Belarus. The company says it no longer conducts any business in Russia.
u-blox: In its statement, the Thalwil (canton Zurich)-based company condemns Russia’s attack on Ukraine in the strongest possible terms. Upon the outbreak of war, the company suspended all cooperation and deliveries to Russia and Belarus; sales to countries in the Eurasian Economic Union were subsequently halted as well. Since 2021, u-blox has also been working with the organisation Conflict Armament Research (CAR) to investigate how its own components ended up in drones used in the war in Ukraine. On the basis of this collaboration, it says several companies involved have been identified and blacklisted.
Traco Power: The company, based in Baar (canton Zug), points out that its products are electronic components for civilian industrial applications which are not listed in any dual-use regulation and are not intended for military purposes. Until the sanctions came into force, the company had supplied the Russian market exclusively via closely monitored authorised distribution partners. With immediate effect from February 28, 2022, Traco Power says it ceased all deliveries and business relations with Russia – including those via third countries. Any of the company’s components that may be found could therefore under no circumstances have originated from deliveries made after the sanctions came into force. The company says it conscientiously and strictly complies with all applicable regulations, embargoes and sanctions.
TE Connectivity (Schaffner / Axicom): TE Connectivity states that it complies with all export controls and sanctions applicable worldwide and has therefore fully complied with all sanctions imposed following the Russian invasion. Since these came into force in March 2022, the company has not supplied any products to Russia from any of its sites. TE Connectivity says it is committed to a business policy that excludes both direct and indirect deliveries to Russia or other sanctioned countries. These guidelines are communicated to its distribution partners, who are also expected to comply strictly with them.
So why are Swiss components still finding their way into Russia?
There are many indications pointing to China. Research and investigations by thinktanks, NGOs and the media show that intermediaries and distribution partners from China are supplying the goods to Russia. Some Swiss companies have their products manufactured in China.

NASA’s Swift telescope will face a fiery demise after a failed rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

NASA’s Swift telescope will face a fiery demise after a failed rescue
During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable
For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s science tenure is ending, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. The Swift spacecraft is falling uncontrollably, destined to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in just a few days.
The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.
“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”
Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.
Swift is doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.
Glimpsing gamma-rays
When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.
Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.
“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”
Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.
That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.
Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.
Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.
Beyond gamma-rays
As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.
“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.
Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.
Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”
A grand finale
A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”
Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.
And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.
“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

I Spent 30 Minutes With Apple’s CEO. Now I Know Why John Ternus Got the Job
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules.
A few minutes after the presentation, I sat down with Ternus, for the second time in two days. Steve Jobs used to grant me an audience after his famous keynotes, too. Ternus isn’t Jobs, of course, nor is he supposed to be. But who is he?
I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.
That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.”
Ternus has so far been defined by his product prowess. “John innately has a great sense for great products, and that’s what Apple is,” says Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing and a 40-year company veteran. “You can’t teach that.” In one sense Ternus’ ascension is similar to that of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, another lifer promoted to the top post. But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity. That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice.
The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration.
Ternus’ key collaborator is probably Johny Srouji, the architect of the company’s custom silicon, an initiative that’s driven many of the company’s innovations in the past decade. Srouri says that their relationship will be even closer, as Apple has merged its hardware engineering and technology organizations with Srouji at the top, reporting to Ternus. “John is going to be a great CEO,” he said. “He's a product guy at heart, but Apple's secret weapon is the DNA, the culture, which is not going to change. Remember, John has been here for 25 years. It’s not like he's going to come and everything's going to be different.”
Being Apple’s CEO encompasses much more than products—there’s a $100 billion business in services, a huge infrastructure, and the general mishegoss of running a giant corporation. I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I'm super passionate about it.”
Like it or not, the CEO of a $4 trillion company has to be involved in policy and politics. It has been widely reported that as executive chair, Cook will still conduct some of Apple’s high-level policy duties, including the equivalent of stuffing gold-plated binkies in the presidential mouth. Ternus implies that the reality is more nuanced. “Tim is available to help wherever I ask him, and it's great to have him in that role,” he said. “He obviously has a ton of relationships he's developed over the years, and of course, I'm building new relationships in this role as well.” One relationship he has yet to build: the president. Ternus has yet to meet Donald Trump.
Then there’s the one thing that could possibly disrupt the way Apple has run its business for the past 50 years. Ternus is taking over the company during what may be the biggest technological shift ever. I suggested to Ternus that history may judge him on how he handles AI. I spelled out for him a couple of narratives people spin about Apple. One is that Apple has been hobbled by a failure to develop its AI product Siri, and even after an update it’s still in catch-up mode. The other is that Apple is smart to avoid the high cost of developing a frontier model and that the strategy of organically putting AI into its products, with a focus on privacy, will pay off in the long run.
“Everyone has an opinion—I really like where we’re at,” he said. “I would hope people recognize that the work we do is building incredible products that make their lives better. We’re absolutely going to leverage AI to do that. We don't want to ship AI for AI's sake. When we're doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”
That assumes that AI, as powerful as it is, will wind up as a “normal” technology, organically integrated into our current gadget-sphere. Another school of thought is that AI is an apocalyptic disruptor that will shred the current ecosystem. In that vision, all those cool apps Apple supports will be subsumed by AI-concocted agents generated from prompts, or even autonomously. Ternus doesn’t buy that scenario. “That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do,” he said.
When I asked whether he’s in favor of AI regulation, he replied, “We all read the stories and think about it from a cybersecurity standpoint—clearly these models are very capable of doing things. Our focus is on making sure that our products are secure and safe, and protecting the users' information.”
His non-answer shows that he might well be on the way to mastering political communication. But policy will never be the focus of John Ternus. He is, and probably always will be, the product-guy CEO. Before we ended our conversation, Ternus had one question for me: “What did you think of the logo?”

‘I Won’t Hold Back’: Estonian PM Refuses to Soften Criticism of Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:59:20 UTC
23:59:20 KST

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said on Friday, Oct. 30, that he would not soften his criticism of Russian President Vladimir Putin after a report that Pentagon officials had urged Baltic allies to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Speaking to Delfi, Michal said Estonia would maintain its position and continue speaking openly about the Russian threat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I won’t hold back. Putin is a dictator who kills women and children,” he said.
Michal added that Putin would continue doing so until he was forced to change course.
Appeasing dictators brings humiliation without preserving freedom, Michal argued. Estonia and its Baltic neighbors would continue warning about the threat posed by Russia, he said.
Michal said he had not personally received a US request to moderate his language. The issue did not arise when he last met President Donald Trump in Ankara during the summer, he added.
He noted that domestic critics accused his government of being insufficiently assertive, even as reports suggested the US wanted greater restraint.
Pentagon reportedly urges restraint
Reuters reported that Pentagon officials had privately asked several NATO allies, including Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to tone down their rhetoric about Russia.
Four people familiar with the discussions told Reuters the requests were made during bilateral meetings in recent weeks. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby was among the officials involved.
Zelensky Ready to Discuss Territory With Putin, Sybiha Says
One source said Colby advised a Baltic official against “poking” Russia and cited descriptions of Moscow as cornered and increasingly desperate.
Michal had called Putin a rat in a corner in September, linking Russia’s difficulties in Ukraine to suspected sabotage in Europe. Reuters could not establish whether Colby was referring specifically to those remarks.
The sources described the conversations as cordial. The Pentagon declined to discuss private exchanges between allies, and NATO also declined to comment.
The reported appeals to Baltic governments come as Washington reviews its military presence in Europe and presses European allies to take greater responsibility for their defense.
Estonia backs continued pressure on Russia
At an October summit in Brussels, Michal backed Ukrainian refinery strikes despite US pressure on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil production.
“The faster all the Russian refineries and ability to sell energy will be blown to smithereens the better,” Michal said at the time.
His comments came as European leaders discussed additional financial support for Ukraine and relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated following Trump’s diesel agreement with Russia.
On July 7, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Michal signed a Drone Deal agreement on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara. Zelensky thanked Estonia for its military and humanitarian assistance, as well as its diplomatic support for Ukraine’s EU and NATO ambitions.
Allies debate how to describe the threat
Some believe emphasizing it risks amplifying the fear Moscow seeks to spread; others argue that frank warnings help explain the need for greater defense spending and continued support for Ukraine.
Western intelligence officials have warned of an expanding Russian sabotage campaign in Europe. Moscow denies conducting such a campaign.
Michal said a clear assessment of the threat was essential to preparedness and warned that Ukraine faced a difficult winter.

Russia’s Sevmash Shipyard presents nuclear sub building innovative solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:59:05 UTC
23:59:05 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. A representative of the Sevmash Shipyard, a subsidiary of the United Shipbuilding Corporation (USC), has presented an innovative solution for the construction of modern nuclear submarines at an international research and practical conference in Nizhny Novgorod, the shipyard’s press service reported.
The new solution will save an estimated 81 million rubles ($1.004 mln), it said.
"Sevmash Shipyard representative Igor Kalemintsev demonstrated an innovative development for the construction of fourth-generation nuclear submarines with an economic savings of over 81 million rubles at the international workshop titled ‘Modern Technologies in Shipbuilding and Aviation Education, Science, and Production.’ The event is taking place in Nizhny Novgorod from October 28-30," the press service said.
It specified that Kalemintsev, head of a department at the Sevmash Design Bureau, presented modern technologies for installing equipment and structures using polymer materials. The development includes a unique method for securing mechanisms to the foundation, protected by a Russian patent. He demonstrated practical solutions aimed at improving the efficiency of equipment installation, introducing modern materials, and optimizing production processes in the construction of fourth-generation missile-carrying submarines.
The press service emphasized that the practical application of this design and technological solution has already been confirmed by its successful use in the construction of Yasen-M and Borei-A class nuclear submarines at the shipyard. The technology has been approved by the USC’s Malakhit and Rubin design bureaus, as well as by the Defense Ministry’s Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Technology Center.
"This development significantly reduces the labor required for installation work and ensures the reliability of the structures. The innovative solutions implemented can also be applied to the construction of other vessels in the domestic shipbuilding industry. The assembly unit, which involves securing mechanisms to the foundation using flowable plastic, has been registered as an invention by the Federal Service for Intellectual Property and has been granted a patent. Labor savings per order range from 800 to 2,200 standard hours," the company stated.
Sevmash added that, due to the reduction in the labor intensity of installation work, the total economic benefit from using these components and technology in the construction of nuclear submarines exceeds 81 million rubles.

NEW DELHI: Former Union minister Kapil Sibal on Friday referred to the alleged use of pellet guns against student protesters by security forces in Delhi, saying that the Congress government had "never used" pellet guns or resorted to lathi-charge against demonstrators, unlike the current BJP-led government.His remarks came a day after Union minister Kiren Rijiju shared a video from 2011 featuring Sibal, who was then a Union minister, addressing a press conference on the India Against Corruption movement, which had challenged the Congress-led UPA government.In the video, Sibal, who is no longer associated with the Congress, had said, “Right to protest is not the right to protest at the place of your choice.”
Sharing the clip, Rijiju called Sibal a “Dimagi Naxal” and remarkeed that the senior advocate had exposed the Congress's “secrets” and “thoroughly torn Rahul Gandhi to shreds”, referring to the Congress MP and Lok Sabha leader of the opposition.In a subsequent post, Rijiju questioned whether any "new laws" governing protests had been introduced since 2014, when the BJP came to power.
Hitting back at Rijiju at a press conference in Delhi, Sibal first questioned the former law minister’s legal experience.“I wish I could have seen him somewhere in court -- in my 50-odd years at the courts, at least I have not seen him in the corridors of the court,” he remarked, accusing the BJP MP of criticising others without understanding the facts.
Rejecting the claim that the UPA government had opposed protests, he challenged the minister to cite instances when the Congress-led government had used pellet guns or resorted to lathi-charge against demonstrators.“We never ensured that people don’t protest. In fact, on one occasion… in a Cabinet meeting this issue was discussed, and my colleagues said, ‘Look, this is a right under the Constitution, you cannot interfere with this right, this is a constitutional right,’” Sibal added.He also highlighted the role of protests in India’s Independence movement, arguing that they could lead to another form of independence.Criticising Rijiju’s handling of parliamentary affairs, Sibal remarked, “As far as Parliamentary Affairs is concerned, we know how he (Rijiju) runs Parliament. That is his expertise: to ensure that the voice of the opposition is not heard for which he should get a medal of some kind.”“They don't allow us to raise the issues we want to raise. They don't allow us to protest. They pass bills without a discussion. They are unconcerned with parliamentary procedures. The manner in which Parliament was functioning was unprecedented in India’s history,” he added.
Sibal further stated that the Congress would allow Rijiju to speak if he found himself in the opposition in the future: “Rijiju ji, please remember: history repeats itself.”Clashes broke out between student protesters and security forces in Delhi on July 20 as demonstrators marched towards Parliament, demanding the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG paper controversy. The Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force were accused of using pellet guns to disperse the protesters and stop their march.Pradhan resigned on July 25, bringing the protests to an end.

Russia has accumulated sufficient winter-grade diesel stocks — Novak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:58:16 UTC
23:58:16 KST

MOSCOW, October 30. /TASS/. Russia is accumulating sufficient volumes of winter-grade diesel fuel within its system, with all processes tracking the production schedules of domestic refineries, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"It is sufficient. It is naturally in line with the enterprises' production programs," Novak said, when asked about the accumulation of winter-grade diesel and its production adjustments.
Winter-grade diesel differs from summer fuel due to its lower pour point and improved filterability, allowing for its use in low temperatures without losing fluidity or clogging fuel filters. With the onset of cold weather, production shifts toward winter-grade fuels, and reserves are built up within the system to ensure an uninterrupted supply for transport, municipal machinery, and industrial enterprises throughout the heating season.

Russia’s Starlink Rival, Rassvet, Draws Ukrainian Sanctions Against Its Developers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:56:58 UTC
23:56:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Starlink Rival, Rassvet, Draws Ukrainian Sanctions Against Its Developers
Ukraine has imposed new sanctions on Russian companies and individuals involved in developing the Rassvet satellite communications system, which Moscow intends to use in its war against Ukraine, as well as dozens of vessels operating as part of Russia’s shadow fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the corresponding decrees, according to Ukraine’s Presidential Office on October 30.
The sanctions targeting the Rassvet project cover 10 companies and 19 Russian nationals associated with their activities.
“The Russian Federation seeks to establish a satellite system similar to the Starlink network that would enable it to command troops and target and control attack drones, including ‘shaheds,’ and missiles in real time. The deployment of this system could help Russia not only maintain continuous real-time control of its weapons in Ukraine but also pose threats to other countries,” the statement read.
The sanctioned entities include Bureau 1440, the main developer of the Rassvet project, and its affiliate Labs 1440, which produces spacecraft solar panels. The list also includes FAB Rassvet, a manufacturer of communications satellites and terminals, and Belarus-based Aerospace Instruments, which develops aerospace components.
Other sanctioned companies are 5S Group, which supplies industrial equipment and computers to Russia, including technology used in work for Bureau 1440, and Aquamash Production Association, a manufacturer of precision metal parts.
Also on the list are El-Optics, a supplier of optical and telecommunications equipment, Elesar Group, which imports foreign electronic components, and Small Spacecraft, a developer of satellite communications technology.
Russia’s efforts to develop its own satellite communications network come amid restrictions on its access to Starlink services used in military operations.
In early February, Starlink CEO Elon Musk disabled terminals that were not registered on Ukraine’s approved “whitelists,” following a request from former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Following the restrictions, Ukraine’s General Staff reported a significant decline in Russian assault operations, with 56 attacks recorded on February 5, down from approximately 80 to 110 on previous days.
The latest measures follow findings published by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR), which identified 49 companies in Russia and Belarus in developing Rassvet, Moscow’s planned alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network.
On October 28, HUR released the findings through its War&Sanctions portal, reporting that 23 of the identified organizations, including Russia’s state space corporation Roscosmos, remain outside international sanctions.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the project involves companies specializing in technology, microelectronics, aerospace manufacturing, and scientific research, alongside organizations affiliated with Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Another Russian Su-57 Goes Up in Flames—Fourth Loss or Damage Case of 2026
A Russian Su-57 multirole fighter reportedly caught fire and burned at the Akhtubinsk airfield in Russia’s Astrakhan region on October 29. Marking what could be the fourth known Su-57 loss or damage incident this year, Militarnyi reported on October 30.
The report cited the Telegram channel “Absolutely Reliable Source,” which published satellite imagery of the airfield.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to preliminary information, the fighter caught fire after an abnormal incident during engine startup.
If confirmed, the Akhtubinsk fire would add another aircraft to an unusually costly year for Russia’s small Su-57 fleet.
On April 25, Ukrainian drones struck two Su-57 fighters at the Shagol airfield in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region.
Another Su-57 was lost on July 23 in the Moscow region after it was reportedly shot down by a Russian BARS Moscow air-defense crew in a friendly-fire incident.
The latest case would therefore represent the fourth Su-57 known to have been destroyed or damaged in 2026.
The Su-57 is Russia’s most advanced multirole fighter, designed to engage aerial, ground, and maritime targets. The aircraft can reach speeds of roughly 2,600 kilometers per hour and carry guided weapons, including air-to-surface missiles.
Serial production of the Su-57 is carried out at the Komsomolsk-on-Amur aircraft plant in Russia’s Far East.
Earlier, Ukraine destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers in a Neptune missile strike on the Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region.

Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to cast ballot in US election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to cast ballot in US election
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 - Pope Leo XIV cast a ballot by mail in the US midterm elections, the Vatican press office said on Friday, a historic first for the American-born pontiff.
"In keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago," the Vatican said. "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes."
The Vatican did not say which candidates Leo had voted for.
Leo, 71, was born in Chicago and is the first American-born pope. He registered to vote in Illinois under his birth name Robert Francis Prevost and requested a ballot on October 3, the Chicago Sun-Times reported on Thursday, citing the Will County Clerk's office.
President Donald Trump's sagging popularity is hurting his fellow Republicans' chances of holding onto their majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 election, with the public unhappy about the high cost of living and the Iran war.
Trump repeatedly criticized Leo early in the new pope's tenure, calling him "weak" and "terrible" on crime.
The pope said in March that God rejects the prayers of those who start wars and have "hands full of blood." In April, he termed Trump's threat to destroy the Iranian civilization as unacceptable and previously declined to join the US president's so-called "Board of Peace" initiative for Gaza.
Leo has also urged a "deep reflection" on the way migrants are treated in the US.
Voters in the solidly Democratic state of Illinois will select a successor for retiring US Senator Dick Durbin and choose whether to re-elect Governor JB Pritzker.
Leo was elected to lead the 1.4-billion-member Church by the world's cardinals in May 2025.
The pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on October 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Doctors say he will not need further therapy.
He is set to travel to South America next week. REUTERS

G20 foreign ministers' meeting kicks off in US amid global tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:56:26 UTC
23:56:26 KST

A G20 foreign ministers’ meeting kicked off in the US on Friday, bringing together top diplomats from the world’s leading economies for two days of discussions of pressing global economic challenges, geopolitical tensions, and international security issues.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting the gathering in the Southern city of Atlanta, Georgia, where the main focus will be on economic growth, energy and food security, freedom of navigation, and the resilience of global supply chains.
The meeting comes against the backdrop of ongoing international conflicts, including the war in Ukraine and tensions involving Iran, which continue to raise concerns about regional stability and their impact on the global economy.
The meeting began directly with Rubio's opening remarks, without a family photo ceremony.
The absence of the traditional photo came after several European officials indicated they would not appear alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the gathering, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul was asked whether he would participate in a group photo with Lavrov.
“I assume there will be no family photograph at all,” he said, adding that European partners would not appear in a picture alongside the Russian foreign minister. “There is no normality with Russia,” Wadephul said.
Addressing the opening session, Rubio urged G20 members to work together to tackle interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, warning of growing threats to global energy and food supplies, international trade, and freedom of navigation.
Rubio described the current period as a “moment of choosing,” saying the challenges facing the US also have implications for the rest of the world.
'Series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises'
“We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order,” said Rubio.
He identified disruptions to global energy and food supplies, supply chains, trade, and freedom of navigation as major challenges requiring a coordinated response.
Rubio called on G20 partners to strengthen economic resilience, safeguard markets, and protect the economies that depend on them.
He also stressed the role of foreign ministers and political leaders in coordinating responses to emerging crises and protecting shared interests.
“By translating our shared interests into practical cooperation and real action, we can reinforce global stability and, more importantly, deliver meaningful results for our citizens,” he said.
Rubio said the assembled officials faced a busy two-day agenda, with the opening plenary session focusing on freedom of navigation and food security.
Issues Turkish foreign minister expected to address
Participants include Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Lavrov.
Fidan is set to address the situation in the Gaza Strip, tensions between the US and Iran, and the importance of safeguarding strategic maritime routes. He is also expected to underline Türkiye’s diplomatic efforts to promote regional security and stability.
Lavrov, who is leading the Russian delegation, is expected to call for greater economic cooperation and equal dialogue among G20 members. Moscow has also criticized Washington’s decision to exclude South Africa from the G20 process, calling for its membership rights to be restored.
US President Donald Trump earlier announced that South Africa would not receive an invitation to the 2026 summit. The decision followed Washington’s boycott of the Johannesburg summit and stemmed from Trump’s claims of persecution of white farmers in South Africa.
The Group of Twenty (G20) is an international forum bringing together the world's major advanced and emerging economies to discuss and coordinate global economic policies and address key international challenges.
Established in 1999 in the aftermath of the Asian financial crisis, its membership now consists of 19 countries and the European Union and the African Union, which joined in 2023.

Two ‘Non-Hostile’ Deaths Raise Iran War Toll to 23
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:56:16 UTC
23:56:16 KST

Two Airmen supporting the U.S. conflict against Iran died this month in “non-hostile” incidents, according to the official count recently updated by the Pentagon.
The Pentagon has not publicly identified the two Airmen nor said where their deaths occurred, but both were assigned to U.S. Central Command, U.S. officials said. Listing a death as “non-hostile” means the cause was something other than direct military action.
One of the deaths was described as the result of “illness/injury.” That Airman died in the United States after being medically evacuated due to an illness, U.S. officials said. The other death’s cause is listed as “pending,” according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS. The Airman died in the Middle East and the cause is under investigation, the officials said.
The deceased service members, both men, were mid-to-senior enlisted personnel, between the E-5 and E-9 paygrades. Statistics indicate one was 31-35 years old and the other was older than that, according to the database, which is current as of Oct. 29.
At least 23 U.S. service members have died during the conflict with Iran. Fifteen of those occurred during Operation Epic Fury, the initial strike campaign against Iran that the Trump administration says lasted until early May. Eight more have died during operations that followed. The Pentagon has used “Overseas Operations” to refer to its ongoing military pressure campaign and blockade of Iran.
Iranian missile and drone attacks attacks have killed U.S. personnel at Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia, and Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan. Some deaths have also been caused by accidents. Six Airmen were killed in a mid-air collision between two KC-135 Stratotankers over Western Iraq on March 12, when one of the tankers crashed, killing its crew.
At least 865 service members have been wounded in action since hostilities kicked off on Feb. 28. The vast majority are attributed to “hostile” acts, including 64 Airmen.
A shaky ceasefire is now in place between the U.S. and Iran, and the U.S. has maintained a blockade of the country since early April.
The Trump administration is weighing its next move and the Wall Street Journal reported Oct. 28 that President Donald Trump met with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, and U.S. Central Command’s Adm. Brad Cooper U.S. Central Command boss Adm. Brad Cooper on military options beyond the blockade. Trump later hinted at future action, saying during a mid-term campaign event, “We may do another little Epic Fury.”
