Europe facing gas price shock – Gazprom chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:55:52 UTC
23:55:52 KST

Europe facing gas price shock – Gazprom chief
European gas prices could more than double as depleted reserves threaten winter supplies, Gazprom CEO Aleksey Miller has warned.
Wholesale prices have already reached their highest level in nearly four years, briefly exceeding €97 ($108) per megawatt-hour on Monday. December gas futures climbed another 3.1% on Friday to around $1,164 per thousand cubic meters, according to London’s Intercontinental Exchange.
Miller pointed to unusually low gas reserves across the EU, noting that Germany, the bloc’s largest consumer, has filled just 61.6% of its underground storage capacity.
”Given the series of historic record lows Europeans have set in filling underground gas storage facilities [...] we can expect gas prices in Europe to peak at $2,500 per thousand cubic meters in the event of a cold winter,” he said.
Norwegian energy giant Equinor has echoed concerns over another price shock. CEO Anders Opedal said on Wednesday that European gas reserves were at their lowest seasonal level since 2011, leaving the bloc exposed to further price spikes as it competes with Asian buyers for liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The US-Israeli war on Iran has further strained supplies, disrupting shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, which previously handled around a fifth of global LNG trade. Deliveries remain roughly 80% below pre-conflict levels.
EU gas storage facilities were 74.62% full as of October 25, well below seasonal averages, with some member states already drawing on reserves as temperatures fall.
Germany has been particularly hard hit. Gas tariffs for new household customers have jumped 55% this year, according to comparison website Verivox. High energy costs have forced some European fertilizer, chemical, and steel producers to cut output, Reuters reported.
In September, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen warned that the bloc faced its worst energy crisis since 2022, when wholesale gas prices exceeded €300 per megawatt-hour.
Despite mounting supply concerns, Brussels is pressing ahead with plans to eliminate Russian gas imports. Long-term LNG deliveries are set to be banned from January 2027, with remaining pipeline supplies scheduled to end later that year.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned the EU’s energy policy as “suicidal.” Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev argued last week that restoring economic cooperation with Russia “will be inevitable.”

Cambridge, MA council to divest from firms linked to Israel army

Cambridge, MA city council votes to divest from firms 'complicit in Gaza genocide'
The city council in Cambridge, Massachusetts, voted 5-4 on Wednesday in favour of divesting public funds from companies complicit in Israel's genocide in Gaza.
"Our retirement funds should not be invested in companies that profit off of killing people," Cambridge City Councilor Ayah Al-Zubi, who voted in favour of divestment, told NBC Boston.
The vote will impact the council's public investments, including for pensions. The vote will impact at least $24 million of investments, according to campaign group Cambridge for Palestine.
The firms targeted by the new policy include Palantir Technologies Inc., Elbit Systems, Lockheed Martin, GE Aerospace, and Boeing.
"Our wins are one small step in the much larger international struggle for Palestinian liberation," Cambridge for Palestine said in statement after the vote.
The policy order stated that "Israel is committing genocide in Gaza", and said Israel's treatment of Palestinians "amounts to apartheid" — positions held by UN experts and leading rights groups.
Orphan Black and She-Hulk: Attorney at Law star Tatiana Maslany celebrated the news with an Instagram post captioned "Hell yes @cambridgema4palestine !!!!!!!!!!"
However, the council voted down a boycott of companies complicit in the genocide for city contracts. Vice Mayor Burhan Azeem, who voted in favour of divestment, was the deciding vote against the boycott.
Cambridge follows three other Massachusetts councils -- Medford, Northampton and Easthampton -- in divesting from complicit companies. Neighbouring Somerville City Council is set to vote on similar action in November.
Cambridge, part of the Greater Boston area, is home to two of the world's top universities, Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
Last year, Harvard University faced a legal battle with US President Donald Trump after the president cut funding for the Ivy League institution and blocked visas for international students.
The president claimed the university is an "antisemitic, far left institution", following pro-Palestine protests on campus.
In July 2025, a Boston judge blocked Trump's attempts to bar foreign students from studying at Harvard.

Strikes on camp in Ethiopia kill at least 15, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:54:40 CET
23:54:40 KST

NAIROBI, Oct 30 (Reuters) - At least 15 people, several of them children, died in a series of drone strikes that hit a camp for displaced civilians in Ethiopia’s Amhara region, two sources involved in a rescue operation said on Friday.
It was not clear why the camp was targeted or who was behind the attack, but the strikes highlight continuing clashes in the area despite a lull in the heavy fighting that erupted last month between an alliance of rebels from northern Tigray region and the government in Addis Ababa.
“There were around five explosions. Then … we started collecting bodies,” a community representative involved in the burials told Reuters, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The representative said they helped bury 13 people at the camp, which is known as Jari 2 and is home to more than 1,700 people who fled previous violence.
Two of the injured later died at a hospital in Hayk, a town 17 km (10 miles) away.
A spokesperson for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A local official said they were aware of the incident and were helping get medical treatment to 36 people who had been injured.
A man who lost a family member described seeing a drone circling overhead on Wednesday and then returning on Thursday.
“Then finally it hit the camp … three times,” the relative told Reuters. “Their body parts were scattered everywhere. We collected and buried pieces of their body parts.”
NO FIGHTING IN THE AREA WHEN CAMP HIT
A resident of Hayk who was helping provide shelter to survivors also said 15 people had been killed. “Those from the camp are now sheltering in a school,” the resident said.
The dead included five children, according to the two sources involved in the rescue.
The relative of one of the victims said they had seen at least 10 injured children under the aged of five receiving treatment.
All three sources said there had been no fighting in the area when the strike took place, but members of the Amhara Fano National Movement, which is part of the rebel alliance spearheaded by fighters from Tigray, had been nearby.
Government troops have driven back the rebel alliance since their offensive was launched on September 23.
They retook the capital of Tigray region earlier this month and advanced towards the border with Eritrea, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebellion by sending troops over the border.
Eritrea denies the accusation and says Addis Ababa’s allegations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a “declaration of war”.
Given the web of interconnected conflicts in the Horn of Africa, with neighbouring countries and powers further afield backing their respective proxies, experts have warned that war in Ethiopia could trigger a broader conflict in the region.
(Reporting by Nairobi Newsroom; Writing by David Lewis; Editing by David Holmes and Ros Russell)

Dockworkers strike in Europe and beyond against arms shipments, war deaths
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:54:20 CET
23:54:20 KST

By Valentini Anagnostopoulou
ATHENS, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Dockworkers went on strike across Europe and beyond on Friday, disrupting shipping and ferries as they protested against the use of their ports for arms shipments and the number of seafarers killed in wars from the Gulf to the Black Sea.
Strikers across 113 ports in 22 countries also called for pay rises, better working conditions and the right to have doctors on board vessels crossing war zones.
“We will not work for their wars, and we will not become food for their cannons,” Apostolos Kypraios, head of the Greek union of merchant marine engineers, told Reuters during a rally at the Greek port of Piraeus.
‘SEAFARERS HAVE SUFFERED MANY CASUALTIES’
“We have felt it first hand, and our families have felt it too, living with the anxiety of whether a colleague will get back home,” he added.
More than 25 unions have now backed the strike originally called in Italy, France, Greece, Spain’s Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco.
On Friday, it covered major shipping hubs in Piraeus, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras and Genoa, as well as Morocco’s Tangier Med and India’s Nhava Sheva.
“Seafarers have suffered many casualties — numbering in the hundreds — including both the dead and the severely injured,” the Greek seafarers’ union PENEN said in a statement.
It said there had been 28 attacks on vessels in the Gulf in the first 21 days of October, a record since the start of the Iran war.
It said there had been 570 attacks confirmed in the Black Sea so far this year, leaving 40 seafarers dead and hundreds wounded.
A series of strikes in the western Black Sea has raised concerns about the widening scope of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Cargo operations were disrupted in Piraeus and ferry services to Greek islands were suspended, as about 3,000 dockworkers and seafarers joined the walkout.
Representatives of India’s WTWFI union said about 15 Indian seafarers had died as a result of the Iran war, with many more stranded at sea as waterways were blocked.
A group of dockworkers and other activists, called ‘No Harbour for Genocide’ and campaigning to stop military cargo from reaching Israeli ports, said on Friday the protest would halt some 52,000 containers and snarl cargo worth $2.8 billion.
Reuters was not able to independently verify the impact.
In May 2026, dockworkers’ unions from over 35 European countries published the so-called Istanbul Declaration demanding that port facilities not be used to transport weapons destined for war zones.
Dockworkers said they were also worried about the rising cost of essential goods and energy, stemming from the ongoing conflicts.
“We can’t even afford to fill the car with fuel to get to the supermarket,” George Gogos, head of the Piraeus port dockworkers’ union, said.
(Reporting by Valentini Anagnostopoulou in Athens, Sybille de La Hamaide in Paris; Writing by Angeliki Koutantou; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

Top Swiss court upholds landmark Liberia war crimes ruling
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:54:20 CET
23:54:20 KST

By Emma Farge
GENEVA, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The top Swiss court on Friday confirmed a guilty verdict against a Liberian warlord, upholding his 20 year sentence in the country’s first ever war crimes trial.
Alieu Kosiah, who fought in the 1990s against then-president Charles Taylor’s army during Liberia’s brutal civil war, was originally sentenced to 20 years in prison in June 2021 for rape, murder and cannibalism.
An earlier appeal was rejected in 2023 by the Federal Criminal Court and the dismissal of his second appeal by Switzerland’s highest tribunal the Federal Supreme Court published on Friday closes the case.
“This is a landmark decision, made possible by the courage of these victims, who have written a page of legal history,” said Alain Werner, Director of Civitas Maxima, an NGO representing victims in this case.
However, the court reversed a parallel conviction for crimes against humanity on the grounds that the law on this crime introduced in 2011 cannot be applied retroactively.
(Reporting by Emma Farge, Editing by Friederike Heine)

Spanish police arrest suspected founder of ‘Blocus’ group linked to looting
Italy
Unknown Publisher

By Mireia Merino
MADRID, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Spanish police said on Friday they had arrested the suspected founder and main promoter of the local “Blocus” chapter, a group accused of using social media and online channels to exploit student protests and demonstrations as a cover for looting and violence.
The arrest followed a wave of anti-establishment protests organised through social media under the “Blocus” banner and the slogan “Instituts Indignats” (Indignant High Schools), an apparent reference to the “Lycees Indignes” movement that has mobilised young students across France in recent weeks.
Six other people linked to the group have been arrested in Spain, the Interior Ministry said.
The male suspect is accused of creating and administering Telegram groups used to coordinate their actions and of disseminating a video featuring a hooded individual claiming to be the movement’s leader.
POLICE PREPARING FOR FURTHER DEMONSTRATIONS
He presented himself on social media as the person responsible for Blocus in Spain, investigators said.
Telegram groups linked to the group, some with thousands of members, have been repeatedly shut down for violating the messaging platform’s terms of service. Messages posted in the groups encouraged participants to wear black clothing and Halloween masks on October 31 and, in some cases, promoted looting and vandalism.
The investigation is linked to unrest in Barcelona on October 24 in which around 500 people took part, according to the Civil Guard police force.
Violence during the protests led to the arrest of 132 people including 83 minors and 49 adults, Catalan police said.
Police said they were still investigating while preparing security deployments for further demonstrations planned for October 31, mirroring similar calls for action seen in France, as they sought to identify and close channels used to coordinate the unrest.
Investigators are also examining the spread of false alarm messages on social media. Madrid’s Metro operator said on Thursday that reports circulating online of a bomb threat were a hoax.
(Reporting by Mireia Merino; Additional reporting by Emma Pinedo and Victoria Waldersee; Editing by David Holmes)

Police watchdog to investigate Met’s handling of Meghan warning letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:53:26 UTC
23:53:26 KST

Scotland Yard faces an independent investigation into its failure in 2019 to pass claims alleging wrongdoing by Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex, to law enforcement agencies overseas.
The force had referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) over its handling of a letter written by Markle’s former wife, Roslyn Loveless. Markle, 82, is now facing claims of child sexual abuse in the Philippines, which he denies, and is under investigation by authorities there.
On Friday, the IOPC decided to use its formal powers to launch an investigation into the Met. The police watchdog views the claims in the 2019 letter as potentially alleging serious offending.
Its investigation will look at who in the Met made decisions such as not to pass on the claims to police forces in countries where wrongdoing by Markle was alleged, and whether police policies and procedures were followed.
An IOPC spokesperson said: “Following a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, we have decided an independent investigation is required into its failure to pass on allegations of serious offending, contained in a letter it received in 2019, to relevant overseas authorities at the time.”
The Met had announced on Thursday its voluntary referral to the IOPC about the handling of the 2019 letter. It also referred whether its decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duchess of Sussex could have been a breach of data rules because it contained sensitive information. The IOPC has decided it will not investigate that.
The contents of the letter are understood to have played a part in Meghan’s estrangement from her father. The Guardian understands that the long letter made claims about Markle’s activities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.
The Met has said it did not investigate because the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas. But for seven years it did not pass on details to the countries affected, and it is only now sending details of the letter to the FBI in the US and law enforcement in the Philippines, where Markle lived until May, as well as Thai counterparts.
Markle, now in the US, has admitted paying for sex but denies possessing material that would be illegal. On Saturday, the Philippine interior minister, Jonvic Remulla, told the Guardian that all signs pointed to Markle being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” and that a full forensic investigation would give a “definitive picture”.
Investigators in the Philippines are examining digital images alleged to belong to Markle and alleged to have been found at his former home in the south-east Asian country.
Meghan’s half-brother, also called Thomas, reported to Philippine authorities last week the alleged discovery of child sexual abuse images. Footage on Thursday showed Markle Jr present as Philippine officials started gathering material to examine.
On Friday the Daily Mail claimed that a garage close to where Markle Sr lived in Mexico, before moving to the Philippines in 2025, contained material the paper characterised as child sexual abuse images.
It said it had reported its alleged find to the FBI.
The scale of embarrassment for the Met will depend on whether investigators in the Philippines assess that the allegations relating to child sexual abuse images have any credence.
On Thursday, the Met commander Adam Slonecki, who leads its protection command, said the letter had been sent in 2019 to the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre. “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom,” he said.
“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”

North Korean hackers linked to Russia suspected in Binance crypto exchange hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:53:21 UTC
23:53:21 KST

A North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor, or Lazarus Group, may be behind the theft of more than $6 billion from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange, according to analytics firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis, the BBC reported.
The independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo notes that the group may have ties to Russia. A UN Security Council panel of experts said in a report published in March 2024 that Lazarus Group is “very active in the Russian Federation” and retains access to Russian systems. In 2025, cybersecurity researchers found that Lazarus had routed internet traffic through servers in the Russian village of Khasan, on the border with North Korea.
A preliminary review by Binance found that the attackers gained access to its system by hacking the laptop of one of its engineers. The exchange also discovered “additional points of breach.”
Binance announced that about half of the stolen funds have been frozen, but a significant portion remains in the hackers’ hands. The exchange has pledged to reimburse customers for their losses and has set aside $6.34 billion of its own funds for that purpose, and it announced that it has already begun returning the assets.
Experts consider the Binance attack the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The previous record belonged to the Bybit exchange hack in February 2025, when hackers stole about $1.5 billion. TraderTraitor was also blamed for the Bybit hack.

Bulgaria signs agreement to join NATO air defence initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:49:39 UTC
23:49:39 KST

Friday 30 October 2026 16:14
Friday, 30 October 2026, 16:14
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Bulgarian Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov signed an agreement on Friday enabling Bulgaria to join a NATO initiative to develop defences against low-flying air threats, including drones and cruise missiles.
The initiative provides a framework for allies to jointly acquire, develop and deploy air defence capabilities. It aims to improve protection against threats flying below 150 metres, including glide bombs, by developing systems to detect, identify, track and counter them.
NATO said the project was established in February 2025, with the initial participants signing a memorandum of understanding in July 2026. Bulgaria’s participation would improve interoperability and bring cost savings and operational benefits, the alliance said.
The accession document will be submitted to Bulgaria’s parliament for ratification.

Putin open to phone call with Zelensky, Ukraine suspects a Kremlin trap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:47:37 UTC
23:47:37 KST

The Kremlin is seeking to avoid a face-to-face meeting between President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin by proposing they speak by phone instead, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
The apparent move comes as Kyiv insists the two leaders should meet in person to address the most pressing issues in negotiations, including Russia's territorial demands and security guarantees. Such a meeting would be their first since 2019.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Oct. 30 that Putin was "open to dialogue with everyone." Asked whether the Russian leader would speak with Zelensky by phone, Peskov added that "no one has called yet."
The comments came as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi, which Kyiv sees as a possible starting point for a meeting between the countries' leaders.
Ukrainian officials privately suspect Moscow is trying to arrange a phone call that they believe would achieve little while avoiding the prospect of a face-to-face meeting.
"They've already tried to do this over the phone," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
read also
Meeting or a call?
Kyiv has long pushed for a direct meeting between Zelensky and Putin.
The two leaders last met in person in Paris in December 2019 during the Normandy Format talks mediated by France and Germany. They have not held direct talks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine has made several attempts to arrange a meeting since then.
Zelensky invited Putin to Istanbul for talks on May 16, 2025, proposing a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump to advance peace efforts. Putin declined to attend and instead sent a delegation led by a low-level presidential aide, Vladimir Medinsky.
After meeting Putin in Alaska in August 2025, the U.S. president said he was working to arrange a meeting between the Russian and Ukrainian leaders.
Trump later said Putin was reluctant to meet Zelensky because "he doesn't like him."
Now, every time the Ukrainian side raises the idea of a meeting at the level of leaders, the Kremlin challenges the Ukrainian president to come to Moscow for it. Zelensky has called for Putin to meet him in a neutral location.
Kyiv continues to argue that only direct talks between the leaders can produce meaningful decisions on the most difficult issues. Ukrainian officials say the Russian representatives sent to negotiations do not have the authority to make such decisions.
"Territorial issues can only be discussed by the leaders of the countries at war, and only at their level," Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 27. "No one else has the authority to do so."
Territory remains one of the main obstacles to an agreement.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the parts of Ukrainian Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts that Russian forces have failed to capture. The strategically important regions in eastern Ukraine remain central to the negotiations.
Ukraine, by contrast, has called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
Several people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent that Washington supports the idea of a leaders' meeting and that Trump could help arrange one.
The G20 summit in Miami in December could serve as a possible venue, the people said. Under this scenario, if Putin accepts Trump's invitation to attend, Zelensky could also travel there to meet the Russian leader.
Kyiv warns against sidestepping direct talks
As Ukraine pushes for a meeting, its officials believe Moscow is trying to undermine the effort by offering alternatives that would not require Putin to meet Zelensky.
One senior Ukrainian official questioned whether a phone call could resolve the issues at stake without U.S. involvement.
"Well, what do we want? To reach a final decision on key issues and security guarantees," the official told the Kyiv Independent. "Is it possible to do this over the phone — and only over the phone — without the U.S.? No."
"We need a trilateral format with the U.S., plus some involvement from the Europeans... But they're like, 'Well, just go to Moscow,' or call us, but what good will a phone call do?"
Ukrainian officials fear that Moscow's insistence on a phone call could give it another reason to walk away from negotiations without making meaningful commitments. They argue a meeting with third parties would better address the disputes.
Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. plan to hold talks in Abu Dhabi in November, focusing on steps to de-escalate the war. Moscow has signaled readiness to resume negotiations with Kyiv after a pause of more than eight months.
Zelensky said the planned technical talks should seek concrete progress on de-escalation, including an energy and maritime ceasefire, prisoner exchanges, and discussions about a possible trilateral meeting between the leaders.
"We hope for a result regarding energy and at sea, an exchange of prisoners, and a discussion of the possible format for a trilateral meeting at the leaders' level."
Kyiv does not expect working-level negotiations alone to end the war.
Ukrainian officials say Putin must take part in the process himself if the talks are to produce actual decisions.
"Putin needs to come out of his bunker and take part in the trilateral talks," the senior Ukrainian official said. "And personally confirm that he is ending the war."

Denmark set for unusually mild but cloudy weekend with rain on Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:46:18 UTC
23:46:18 KST

The Danish government hopes to allow wolf hunting as early as 2027. Researchers will now determine how large the country’s wolf population needs to be to remain viable.
Denmark is taking another step towards allowing wolves to be hunted, after EU rules protecting the species were relaxed last year.
The government has commissioned work to determine how many wolves Denmark needs to maintain a stable and viable population in the long term.
At the same time, authorities want to introduce more precise monitoring using DNA to identify individual wolves.
Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of the Social Democrats said the scientific work could pave the way for hunting as early as 2027.
“We need a population model in place. It is a step towards being able to regulate – that is, hunt wolves in Denmark,” he said.
The Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV) will put the development of the population model out to public tender. A separate tender will cover individual monitoring of wolves.
At least 49 adult wolves
Denmark does not currently have an exact count of its wolf population.
In spring 2026, researchers from the Natural History Museum Aarhus and Aarhus University estimated that there were at least 49 adult wolves in Denmark.
The government now wants a more precise assessment based on DNA, making it possible to identify individual animals.
“We need a scientific count of the wolves, and we need a model for a minimum population,” Rabjerg Madsen said.
Once that work has been completed, the government hopes it will provide the scientific basis for introducing regulated hunting.
EU rules on wolves were relaxed in 2025
Wolves remain protected under EU law, but their protection status was changed in 2025.
The species was moved from Annex IV to Annex V of the EU Habitats Directive, changing its status from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
The change gives EU countries greater flexibility to manage their wolf populations, including through hunting.
However, it does not mean Denmark can simply introduce unrestricted wolf hunting.
Any hunting or population management must be compatible with maintaining the wolf at what EU rules call a “favourable conservation status”.
Determining that status involves more than simply counting wolves. Authorities must also consider factors including the population’s geographical range, habitat and long-term prospects.
The population model being commissioned by the Danish authorities is expected to be ready during 2027.
Minister hopes for hunting in 2027
Rabjerg Madsen said his ambition is to allow wolf hunting that same year.
“It is my ambition that we can have wolf hunting in 2027, because that is when we will start getting the numbers,” he said.
“My expectation is that they will show that we have a viable wolf population and that we therefore can have hunting of the wolf.”
Asked whether he was anticipating the researchers’ conclusion before the calculations had been made, the minister said the outcome would have to remain within the scientific and international rules governing Denmark.
“I have been very careful to say that it is my assessment and hope that we have a viable wolf population, so that we can have wolf hunting within the scientific boundaries we are committed to by international rules,” he said.
Individual wolves can already be killed under certain circumstances in Denmark. This can include wolves that repeatedly attack livestock protected by approved wolf-proof fencing or animals that display an abnormal lack of fear of humans.
Sources: Ritzau, European Commission and Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV)

Spanish train was traveling up to 200 km/h before deadly collision, investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:46:10 UTC
23:46:10 KST

A high-speed train was traveling at between 160 and 200 kilometers per hour when it crashed into a stationary train in central Spain on Wednesday, killing at least 69 people.
The findings come from a preliminary investigation into the collision in the Castile-La Mancha region, according to Reuters.
Spanish authorities have also received reports of 64 missing people, although it remains unclear how many are among the unidentified victims.
So far, 49 autopsies have been conducted, with five victims identified, including three women and two men.
Esther Padilla, a spokesperson for the regional government, provided the figures to Spanish broadcaster TVE, Reuters reported.
The accident occurred when a high-speed train operated by state-owned Renfe, carrying 397 passengers, struck the rear of a stationary train operated by private company Iryo.
The Iryo train had 147 passengers on board. The force of the collision sent several carriages down an embankment.
According to Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente, several trains had been stopped because of a malfunction in the automatic signaling system.
However, the Renfe train was subsequently authorized to continue, despite another train remaining stationary farther along the tracks.
“A series of errors, instructions, and actions ultimately led to the collision,” the preliminary investigation stated, according to Reuters.
Spain began three days of national mourning on Thursday following one of Europe’s deadliest railway disasters this century.
The tragedy follows another train accident earlier this year that killed 46 people.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described it as “unacceptable” that the country had experienced two major railway disasters within a single year.

WATCH — Germany's dual Asia strategy: Courting China, building alternatives
Two German leaders, two parallel missions across Asia.
While President Frank-Walter Steinmeier sought to reinforce ties with China in Beijing, Chancellor Friedrich Merz toured Japan, South Korea and Singapore, promoting closer cooperation among what he calls the world's "middle powers."
Together, the visits highlight Berlin's effort to lower risks without decoupling from China.
Watch here for all the details
Fuel tax cut helps bring German inflation down to 2.8%
Germany's annual inflation rate eased to 2.8% in October from 3.3% in September, with economists pointing to the government's fuel tax cut as the main reason.
Preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office showed energy prices rose 12.2% compared with a year earlier, down from 14.9% in September. Services inflation slowed to 2.5%, while food inflation remained at 0.4%.
"The decisive factor was the fuel tax cut," said Silke Tober of the Macroeconomic Policy Institute. The reduction took effect in October and runs through December, although rising crude oil prices partly offset the savings at the pump.
ING bank economist Carsten Brzeski said higher energy costs had yet to feed through into broader price increases. Unlike during the 2022 energy crisis, consumers were unwilling or unable to absorb substantially higher prices, he said.
But economists warned the relief could prove temporary. "Gas and oil prices have risen significantly again in recent weeks," said Stephanie Schoenwald, an economist at Germany's state-owned development bank KfW, citing continuing conflicts and lower inventories.
What did Steinmeier's trip to China achieve?
German President's Frank-Walter Steinmeier latest trip to Asia was intended to provide more clarity. Amid a delicate period, Steinmeier sought a balancing act in China between respect and criticism.
It was a state visit of a kind rarely seen today. For four days, Steinmeier traveled across the country: from Hefei, where the German automaker Volkswagen's China operations are headquartered, through historic villages and the imposing landscapes of the Yellow Mountains. He also visited several points of interest of Chinese history, art, and science, and finally, he headed to Tiananmen Square in the heart of Beijing's political center.
Diplomatic detours
Steinmeier—who is set to leave office in March 2027— spoke as a statesman and diplomat on matters of German and European interest. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Steinmeier have known each other for many years, so in this respect, the president was the right man to address even the most difficult issues as a European.
This political balancing act between respect and criticism did not trigger any visible outrage in Beijing.
When he spoke with Chinese leaders about their subsidies for exports to Europe and the related issue of the trade deficit, Xi replied: "I am ready to work together to open a new chapter in the comprehensive strategic partnership between our two countries and to advance the development of global governance."
Europe's economic crisis also weakens China
Just how much willingness lies behind the push for a strategic partnership will become clear during further negotiations between the EU and China.
Xi Jinping seems to understand that a persistent trade deficit with Europe could also become a problem for his country, as an economic crisis in Europe could further strain China's economy.
As "the world's second- and third-largest economies," China and Germany also bear "an important responsibility for the development of relations between China and Europe, as well as for stable growth in the global economy," Xi Jinping said. While that may not sound like a breakthrough yet, it certainly sounds like an understanding.
China remains silent on the topic of international order
In contrast to his economic arguments, Steinmeier's political appeals for Beijing to assume more responsibility for the international order fell on deaf ears.
The German president addressed global conflicts and wars on several occasions in Beijing, including Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine. But he received no responses in official statements.
That same evening, the news channel of the Chinese TV network CCTV aired a report that merely covered Steinmeier's visit to a well-known astrophysics institute.
There was no mention of the call for China, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, to do more to promote world peace.
WATCH: 65 years of Turkish guest workers in Germany – A life between two cultures
Mitat Özdemir is one of more than 870,000 Turkish workers who were recruited to Germany by a government program between 1961 and 1973. He dealt with tough factory work, language barriers and cultural differences.
Six decades later, he and his family still live in Germany. How did the program from back then shape their lives and modern Germany?
Merz at DMZ says he hopes Korea can reunify like Germany did
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.
North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.
In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.
"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.
"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he said, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.
North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state."
Munich: Vandals smash Manchester United memorial
A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.
The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.
The plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.
The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.
Munich police said the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.
"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories."
The Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same day. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.
The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.
IN DEPTH: Germany takes cautious approach to Israeli election results
German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

Carmaker Audi's profits plunge in 3rd quarter
Profits of German luxury car brand Audi for the third quarter came plunged 87% year-on-year to €95 million ($106 million), the Volkswagen subsidiary reported on Friday. This is a drop from €718 million seen in the same quarter last year.
The drop comes amid weak demand in China, and US tariffs.
"Market and competitive conditions have become significantly more difficult in the third quarter," Audi chief financial officer Jürgen Rittersberger told journalists on a call.
"That all shows that we need to intensify measures and set clear priorities," he added.
Overall in the first nine months of 2026, Audi's profits have dropped 41% to €1.22 billion.
The carmaker trimmed its 2026 profit outlook down to 3 to 5% for the year, down from the previous 5 to 7%.
Audi's sluggish numbers represent more bad news for the 10-brand Volkswagen Group, which on Thursday reported its largest quarterly loss in more than a decade, at nearly €6 billion.
Holocaust 'stumbling stone' ban to remain in Heidenau
A ban on new Stolpersteine ("stumbling stones") to commemorate victims of the Holocaust in the eastern German town of Heidenau will be upheld after five petitions against the measure were thrown out.
Local councilors from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voted together in September to pass the controversial ban on new stones being laid in the town in Saxony, near Dresden.
Petitions against the measure were submitted from across Germany — as well as one from the Netherlands — calling for victims of the Nazi regime to continue to be remembered in Heidenau by way of the small metal plaques embedded in pavements.
"Not everybody has to like the stumbling stones but everyone should have the possibility to lay one in public," one councilor, Michael Schürer, told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), criticizing the rejection of the petitions.
The initiators of the Heidenau ban had argued that, while remembering Holocaust victims remains essential, the placement of Stolpersteine leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring victims at a local cemetery instead.
The decision of the local Heidenau CDU to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion sparked a nationwide scandal and furthered the debate over the conservatives' commitment to the political "firewall" against the far right.
Chinese President Xi lauds 'new chapter' of Germany-China ties
Ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier lauded China's role as a global technological and economic power, while emphasizing the responsibility that comes along with it.
"We both bear responsibility for the international order and for the conditions under which states in this world maintain and shape their relations," Steinmeier said.
President Xi praised what he called an "all-dimensional strategic partnership" between China and Germany, calling for new cooperation based on stability and mutual benefit.
"This new paradigm sends a positive signal to the world: we favor openness over closure, and cooperation over confrontation," Xi said during opening remarks, emphasizing the start of a "new chapter" in Germany-China ties.
Xi added that he hopes Germany and the European Union will stick by a "rational, pragmatic and friendly" China policy, adding that cooperation outweighs competition and consensus outweighs differences in China-EU relations.
The EU has a massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.
Brussels has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Germany with its export based economy, the EU's largest, is hit hard by China's manufacturing surplus flooding global markets.
Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.
Nonetheless, "differences and problems can always be resolved," the Chinese president said.
IN DEPTH: 65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty
On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.
Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.
German president in Beijing addresses trade tensions with China
While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.
In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.
Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.
At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."
Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.
Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.
Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.
Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Merz in Seoul calls for new trade order, says supply chains cannot become 'political pawns'
During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.
Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.
"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.
"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."
During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.
In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.
The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).
"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.
"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.
"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."
Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.
"There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ourselves off from other nations," Merz said.
"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.
Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."
Additional reporting by Nina Haase

There was no mention of the call for China, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, to do more to promote world peace.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.
North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.

Munich: Vandals smash Manchester United memorial
A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.
The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.
The plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.
The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.
Munich police said the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.
"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories."
The Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same day. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.
The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.

Holocaust 'stumbling stone' ban to remain in Heidenau
A ban on new Stolpersteine ("stumbling stones") to commemorate victims of the Holocaust in the eastern German town of Heidenau will be upheld after five petitions against the measure were thrown out.
Local councilors from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voted together in September to pass the controversial ban on new stones being laid in the town in Saxony, near Dresden.
Petitions against the measure were submitted from across Germany — as well as one from the Netherlands — calling for victims of the Nazi regime to continue to be remembered in Heidenau by way of the small metal plaques embedded in pavements.
"Not everybody has to like the stumbling stones but everyone should have the possibility to lay one in public," one councilor, Michael Schürer, told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), criticizing the rejection of the petitions.
The initiators of the Heidenau ban had argued that, while remembering Holocaust victims remains essential, the placement of Stolpersteine leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring victims at a local cemetery instead.
The decision of the local Heidenau CDU to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion sparked a nationwide scandal and furthered the debate over the conservatives' commitment to the political "firewall" against the far right.

German president in Beijing addresses trade tensions with China
While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.
In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.
Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.
At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."
Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.
Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.
Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.
Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Merz in Seoul calls for new trade order, says supply chains cannot become 'political pawns'
During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.
Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.
"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.
"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."
During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.
In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.
The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).
"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.
"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.
"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."
Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.
"There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ourselves off from other nations," Merz said.
"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.
Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."

Russia’s return to international ice hockey could reshape 2027 World Championship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:45:54 UTC
23:45:54 KST

Germany’s ice hockey federation has warned that Russia’s reinstatement to international competition could have major consequences for the 2027 Men’s World Championship, which Germany is scheduled to host.
The warning follows a Friday ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), which cleared the way for Russia’s return to international ice hockey.
A three-member CAS panel found insufficient evidence to support the safety and security concerns cited by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) to justify Russia’s exclusion.
“Allowing Russia to participate will have significant consequences in terms of security, politically and economically for us as hosts,” the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) said in a statement.
The federation reiterated its opposition to Russia’s reinstatement, saying it had communicated that position to the IIHF and during the CAS hearing.
Germany’s organizers said they would assess the ruling alongside the IIHF before determining their next steps.
The decision could also affect which countries compete in the tournament.
Henrik Bach Nielsen, chairman of the Danish Ice Hockey Union and a former senior IIHF official, said Russia and Belarus were previously guaranteed a return to their original competitive level if their suspensions ended.
Both countries competed in the top division before being excluded following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
“When they were excluded, it was decided that if Russia and Belarus returned, they should return to the level they were at when they were excluded,” Bach Nielsen said.
According to Bach Nielsen, reinstating both teams could mean Ukraine and Kazakhstan lose their recently secured promotions to the top division.
The final tournament lineup remains subject to further decisions.

Nearly two million Danes register organ donation preferences as numbers surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:45:43 UTC
23:45:43 KST

The Danish government hopes to allow wolf hunting as early as 2027. Researchers will now determine how large the country’s wolf population needs to be to remain viable.
Denmark is taking another step towards allowing wolves to be hunted, after EU rules protecting the species were relaxed last year.
The government has commissioned work to determine how many wolves Denmark needs to maintain a stable and viable population in the long term.
At the same time, authorities want to introduce more precise monitoring using DNA to identify individual wolves.
Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of the Social Democrats said the scientific work could pave the way for hunting as early as 2027.
“We need a population model in place. It is a step towards being able to regulate – that is, hunt wolves in Denmark,” he said.
The Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV) will put the development of the population model out to public tender. A separate tender will cover individual monitoring of wolves.
At least 49 adult wolves
Denmark does not currently have an exact count of its wolf population.
In spring 2026, researchers from the Natural History Museum Aarhus and Aarhus University estimated that there were at least 49 adult wolves in Denmark.
The government now wants a more precise assessment based on DNA, making it possible to identify individual animals.
“We need a scientific count of the wolves, and we need a model for a minimum population,” Rabjerg Madsen said.
Once that work has been completed, the government hopes it will provide the scientific basis for introducing regulated hunting.
EU rules on wolves were relaxed in 2025
Wolves remain protected under EU law, but their protection status was changed in 2025.
The species was moved from Annex IV to Annex V of the EU Habitats Directive, changing its status from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
The change gives EU countries greater flexibility to manage their wolf populations, including through hunting.
However, it does not mean Denmark can simply introduce unrestricted wolf hunting.
Any hunting or population management must be compatible with maintaining the wolf at what EU rules call a “favourable conservation status”.
Determining that status involves more than simply counting wolves. Authorities must also consider factors including the population’s geographical range, habitat and long-term prospects.
The population model being commissioned by the Danish authorities is expected to be ready during 2027.
Minister hopes for hunting in 2027
Rabjerg Madsen said his ambition is to allow wolf hunting that same year.
“It is my ambition that we can have wolf hunting in 2027, because that is when we will start getting the numbers,” he said.
“My expectation is that they will show that we have a viable wolf population and that we therefore can have hunting of the wolf.”
Asked whether he was anticipating the researchers’ conclusion before the calculations had been made, the minister said the outcome would have to remain within the scientific and international rules governing Denmark.
“I have been very careful to say that it is my assessment and hope that we have a viable wolf population, so that we can have wolf hunting within the scientific boundaries we are committed to by international rules,” he said.
Individual wolves can already be killed under certain circumstances in Denmark. This can include wolves that repeatedly attack livestock protected by approved wolf-proof fencing or animals that display an abnormal lack of fear of humans.
Sources: Ritzau, European Commission and Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV)

Christa Pike describes pain and confusion after surviving failed execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:45:38 UTC
23:45:38 KST

American death row inmate Christa Pike has spoken publicly for the first time about her failed execution in Tennessee, describing persistent physical and emotional pain after surviving two doses of a lethal drug.
The 50-year-old was scheduled to be executed on September 30 but survived two injections of pentobarbital, according to Sky News.
“Several days later, I woke up alone in a hospital – confused and in pain. Since that night, there has not been a single moment where I have been free of pain,” Pike said in a written statement obtained by Sky News and other media outlets.
“My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still have difficulty speaking. And the pain is not only physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” she added.
Pike was convicted of murdering her 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in 1995 alongside her boyfriend. She was 18 at the time.
She was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Her execution was initially delayed for several hours after an appeals court ordered a postponement.
The U.S. Supreme Court later overturned that decision, allowing the execution to proceed at a high-security prison in Nashville.
However, Pike remained alive after receiving two doses of pentobarbital.
Journalists witnessing the procedure reportedly heard her snoring loudly behind a curtain.
According to her lawyers, Pike was subsequently taken by ambulance to a hospital for treatment.
Until now, her lawyers had spoken publicly on her behalf about the failed execution.

Subsequent police searches led to the discovery of additional bags containing other body parts.

The suspect was arrested on Oct 27.
“The exact course of events and the background to the crime are the subject of ongoing investigations,” the statement said.
“To date, there is no evidence of a politically or religiously motivated homicide.
“In the course of the investigation, the suspect showed signs of psychological disorders,” the statement added. AFP

Russia has damaged more than 800 Ukrainian energy assets since September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:43:49 UTC
23:43:49 KST

Russia has carried out more than 350 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since September, damaging more than 800 pieces of equipment, Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said on Friday.
The strikes are increasing pressure on the country’s power system as the heating season approaches. Ukraine is stepping up efforts to protect energy facilities while expanding generation capacity to reduce the impact of further attacks on an already crippled system after years of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Speaking during a question-and-answer session with the government in parliament, Shmyhal said the damaged equipment included facilities at substations and power generation sites.
He said a second level of physical protection had been built for 235 transformers. According to the minister, only one piece of protected equipment had been hit by a ballistic missile over the past six months.
"Without this protection, restoring energy facilities under the current intensity of Russian attacks would take months," Shmyhal said.
Alongside protecting existing infrastructure, Ukraine is working to expand its electricity generation capacity through smaller, decentralized power plants.
On Oct. 29, the government approved the mechanism and terms for providing almost Hr 939 million ($20 million) in loan financing from the Finnish-Ukrainian Investment Fund to state-owned energy company Ukrnafta.
The funding will support four projects to install gas-engine power plants in the western Ivano-Frankivsk and Lviv oblasts, adding around 60 megawatts of capacity to Ukraine’s power system, Shmyhal reported.
The money will cover the purchase of the power plants and related equipment, as well as installation, testing and commissioning. The loans were raised for Ukraine’s state budget under a framework agreement between the Ukrainian and Finnish governments signed in November 2024.
The projects are part of broader efforts to develop distributed generation, spreading electricity production across multiple locations rather than relying solely on large power plants.

It provided no details about the tankers’ identities, their flags, the precise cause of the incidents or the condition of their crews.
The reports came as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday to continue efforts to broker an agreement between Iran and the United States.
Uncertainty over the number of tankers damaged
In a separate incident whose possible connection to the Guard’s claims remains unclear, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, or UKMTO, reported that a small boat approached an oil tanker Thursday evening and attached two explosive devices to its hull above the waterline.
The devices detonated, sparking a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel.
The Financial Times identified the tanker as the Louise 1.
The incident occurred about 25 nautical miles (46 kilometers) northeast of Khasab, Oman.
UKMTO said the fire had been extinguished, all crew members were safe and no environmental pollution had been reported. The tanker subsequently resumed its voyage toward its next port.
The attack appeared to mark the first reported successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S.-Iran war began in February 2026.
It was not immediately clear who was responsible or whether the attack was connected to the Guard’s latest claims involving two tankers.
Separately, Oman’s Maritime Security Center reported Friday that the Royal Navy of Oman had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel that came under attack and caught fire about 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam.
The center said the crew members received necessary medical care but did not identify the vessel or those responsible for the attack.
It remained unclear whether the incident was connected to other reported attacks on tankers in the strait.
The Guard’s latest statements followed claims Thursday, Oct. 29, that three tankers had struck naval mines along the strait’s southern route, triggering explosions and fires.
Iran’s regular military also reported Thursday that another tanker had caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
According to Agence France-Presse, Iranian officials claimed that all four vessels had been operating in prohibited and unsafe areas.
However, it remained unclear whether the two tankers mentioned in Friday’s Guard statement were additional vessels or were among those involved in the incidents reported Thursday.
U.S. Central Command disputes Iranian claims
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz’s main shipping lanes had been cleared of Iranian naval mines.
He also claimed that Iran’s navy had been destroyed and that Revolutionary Guard forces were no longer operating in the waterway.
Cooper said U.S. forces remained in the region to keep major shipping routes open and secure.
CENTCOM also rejected a claim made Thursday by the Revolutionary Guard that it had taken control of an American MQM-170 Outlaw drone in the western Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian sources, meanwhile, reported Friday that an American unmanned surface vessel had been destroyed in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military had neither confirmed nor denied that report at the time of publication.
The growing number of maritime incidents comes amid a continuing dispute between Washington and Tehran over the routes used by commercial shipping through the strategic waterway.
Iran has demanded that vessels coordinate their movements with Iranian authorities and use routes closer to the strait’s northern shores. Ships seeking to avoid Iranian control have instead used the southern route.
Qatari mediators return to Tehran amid threats of renewed U.S. strikes
Diplomatic efforts to prevent another major escalation in the U.S.-Iran war are continuing alongside mounting military tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.
CBS News, citing a source familiar with the negotiations, reported signs of progress and said Iran was expected to respond to a revised proposal from Qatari mediators by the end of the week.
The diplomatic initiative is aimed at preventing a resumption of large-scale U.S. strikes against Iran, a possibility President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised in recent weeks.
Axios reported that Qatari-led mediators were seeking common ground on issues including inspections of Iran’s nuclear facilities and sanctions relief.
However, disagreements persisted over the conditions for formally opening negotiations.
Axios also reported that the United States and Israel were considering options for extensive military strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.
The Associated Press reported Thursday, citing two diplomats, that Washington had warned several regional allies about the possibility of renewed U.S. attacks on Iran and potential Iranian retaliation, although Trump had not made a final decision.
Trump, speaking Friday to a Kansas City radio station, said the war with Iran would end "soon," but did not specify whether that would be achieved through a diplomatic agreement or military action.
The U.S. president reiterated that Washington wanted guarantees that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.
His remarks came as there was still no clear indication that Tehran and Washington had reached an agreement on the conditions for ending the war, while the possibility of renewed large-scale military strikes remained on the table.

UK probes Meta over 'exploitative' new terms for media as global pushback mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
14:43:02 UTC
23:43:02 KST

Britain's competition watchdog has opened an investigation into whether Meta was imposing "exploitative" new terms allowing it to use media content for its own products, including AI, without giving publishers adequate choice.
The UK's competition watchdog has launched an investigation into whether Meta is imposing "exploitative" new terms that allow it to use publishers' content for its own products, including AI, without giving media organisations adequate choice.
The probe will examine whether the "terms and conditions" from the US technology giant "unfairly harm news publishers and other content businesses", the Competition and Markets Authority said in a statement.
The CMA said the new terms, which the Facebook and Instagram parent had planned to introduce on November 20 before putting it on hold, could amount to an abuse of its dominant position in the market.
The watchdog will determine whether "Meta is abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers".
Meta's new terms could allow it to access and use content from news publishers' websites to develop and provide its own products, including its AI features.
A Meta spokesperson said "we've already committed not to change our terms without consulting publishers and other stakeholders".
"We welcome the opportunity to explain our approach to the CMA," they added.
Thousands of UK businesses rely on Meta to reach customers and audiences, meaning an unfair imposition of the new terms could breach competition law.
"We've heard concerns from news publishers and other businesses and are acting swiftly to investigate whether Meta's proposed changes may breach competition law," said CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell.
European pushback
The British governments effort follow hot on the heels of action taking place across Europe and around the world against Meta's proposed new rules and its practices in general in using media content.
Since May this year, more than 340 local and national news sites including the Guardian, the New York Times and USA Today have blocked internet archive crawler bots to prevent them from collecting data for training AI models.
A Norwegian court this week temporarily banned Meta from enforcing the new user terms after ten media outlets argued it would threaten their rights to their content.
And in France, the country's appeals court rejected on Thursday an attempt by Meta to overturn an order to negotiate in good faith with French media over rights payments for information used on its social networks.
In two rulings, the Paris Appeals Court found that Meta's conduct had caused "serious and immediate harm to the press sector" in France, affirming the position of the country's anti-monopoly body.
The regulatory authority in July ordered the parent company of Facebook and Instagram to "negotiate in good faith" with French media on neighbouring rights payments — a form of copyright payments for use of information on social media platforms.
It said Meta's conduct could be considered "abuse of a dominant position".
Two associations of media groups had complained to the Competition Authority following a lack of progress in talks to renew deals of neighbouring rights payments.
The regulator noted that Meta was continuing to use the content of the media groups but not making payments to them since their deals lapsed.
The Paris Appeals Court found that Meta had in the negotiations with publishers provided only fragmentary, opaque and unverifiable data about its use of media content.
The DVP association of publishers, of which AFP is a member, called the rulings a "major development" and urged Meta to fully meet its obligations to media.
A Meta spokesman said "we are disappointed with the Paris Appeals Court ruling" and was considering what steps to take.
Meta is in the midst of another battle with media over new user terms and conditions that force professional users to give it the right to collect content -- including content behind a paywall -- and use it for AI training among other things.
The company is also facing mounting global pushback against its platform designs and features, especially amid claims of harms against children and teenagers, and is back in court in the US later this month alongside Snap.

Unknown Publisher
