Strikes on camp in Ethiopia kill at least 15, sources say
NAIROBI, Oct 30 - At least 15 people, many of them children, died in a series of drone strikes that hit a camp for displaced civilians in Ethiopia's Amhara region, two sources involved in a rescue operation said on Friday.
It was not clear why the camp was targeted or who was behind the attack, but the strikes highlight continuing clashes in the area despite a lull in the heavy fighting that erupted last month between an alliance of rebels from northern Tigray region and the government in Addis Ababa.
"There were around five explosions. Then ... we started collecting bodies," a community representative involved in the burials told Reuters, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue.
The representative said they helped bury 13 people at the camp, which is known as Jari 2 and is home to more than 1,700 people who fled previous violence.
Two of the injured later died at a hospital in Hayk, a town 17 km away.
A spokesperson for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment but a local official said they were aware of the incident and were helping get medical treatment to 36 people who had been injured.
A resident of Hayk who was helping provide shelter to survivors also said 15 people had been killed. "Those from the camp are now sheltering in a school," they said.
The dead included five children, the two sources said.
Both sources said there had been no fighting in the area when the strike took place, but members of the Amhara Fano National Movement, which is part of the rebel alliance spearheaded by fighters from Tigray, had been nearby.
Government troops have driven back the rebel alliance since their offensive was launched on September 23.
They retook the capital of Tigray region earlier this month and advanced towards the border with Eritrea, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebellion by sending troops over the border.
Asmara denies the accusation and says Addis Ababa's allegations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a "declaration of war".
Given the web of interconnected conflicts in the Horn of Africa, with neighbouring countries and powers further afield backing their respective proxies, experts have warned that war in Ethiopia could trigger a broader conflict in the region. REUTERS

Christa Pike describes 'pain in my mind and in my soul' in first statement after failed execution
Unknown

Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during her attempted execution on 30 September. She was sentenced to death for torturing and killing her classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when she was 18.
Christa Pike said she has been in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month, but remains grateful for the love and support she has received.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said in her first public statement, released through her attorneys on Friday.
Pike dictated the statement to her legal team from the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she is being held.
Pike said she entered the execution chamber prepared to die peacefully, only to wake up alone and confused in a hospital bed. The 50-year-old added that she had never imagined living beyond her scheduled execution date.
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.
Pike also criticised the handling of her execution attempt, while expressing sympathy for her victim’s family.
"I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike said.
Pike’s lawyers have called on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment.
However, Lee told reporters this week that he expected her sentence to remain unchanged unless the courts ruled otherwise.
“I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
The governor has ordered an investigation into the failed execution and postponed the state's other lethal injection scheduled for this year.
She was initially hospitalised following the failed execution before being transferred back to prison.

Pope Leo casts US midterm ballot after row with Trump
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV, the Catholic Church’s first US-born pontiff, has voted in the United States midterm elections, submitting his mail-in ballot in Chicago, the Vatican said on Oct 30.
It is the first known time a pope has voted in a political election.
The head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, who has clashed with US President Donald Trump, believes in “the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes”, the Vatican said in a statement.
The Chicago-born pontiff “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so”, the Vatican said.
“The Holy See Press Office confirms that, in keeping with this longstanding practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago,” it added.
A rift earlier in 2026 between US President Donald Trump and the Pope sparked global headlines.
Leo and Trump repeatedly clashed over papal criticism of the harsh crackdown on immigration in the United States and of the war on Iran, with Trump calling the pontiff “weak” on crime and “terrible” on foreign policy.
The Pope said he was “not afraid” of Trump.
The crucial US midterm elections are scheduled to be held on Nov 3.
Robert Francis Prevost, as he was known before his election to the papacy, spent nearly two decades as a missionary, then bishop, in Peru, and has both US and Peruvian citizenship.
“The Holy Father has also confirmed that, during his years of residence in Peru, he exercised his right to vote whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Vatican said. AFP

Somali pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel

Breadcrumb
Somali pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel
Armed pirates have hijacked an Iranian fishing boat off the northeastern Somali coast, the European Union Naval Force and security sources in Puntland said on Saturday.
Somali piracy has seen a resurgence, with at least 15 attacks reported since April, the highest number since 2013.
The vessel, named Azini, was seized at 0900 GMT on October 29 off the Somali coast, between the coastal towns of Bandar Beyla and Xaafun in the semi-autonomous region of Puntland, according to an alert from the EU's Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO).
AFP news agency reported, citing Puntland security officials that the hijacking was conducted by eight gunmen from a remote coastal area near Bandar Beyla carried out the attack.
"There were two Somali guards on-board but they were outnumbered and overpowered by the pirates," a security official said adding: "They were fishing close to shore, which made them vulnerable to a hijacking."
A second security source said 21 crew members, excluding the two Somali guards, were aboard, while the MSCIO did not specify the number, saying their safety was "unknown".
Four more gunmen later boarded the vessel, bringing the total number of pirates aboard to 12, security officials said.
"After they took the fishing boat, they went further out to sea," a Puntland security official said.
Azini is the third Iranian fishing boat to have been hijacked off the Somali coast since July.
The MSCIO warned that the vessel could be used as a "mothership" to carry out "further piracy attacks".

Pentagon facing up to $15 bn in Iran war base damages – WSJ

Pentagon facing up to $15 bn in Iran war base damages – WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted up to $15 billion in damage on military installations hosting American forces across the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing sources and its own satellite imagery analysis. The massive destruction adds to the Pentagon’s mounting war bill, which has already reached nearly $50 billion.
The newspaper’s analysis identified a total of 274 damaged structures across 24 installations with an American military presence. At least 119 buildings at 13 installations were damaged in the opening two weeks alone; the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was among the hardest hit. Tehran launched a retaliatory wave of strikes following the unprovoked US-Israeli attack which started the conflict on February 28.
An unnamed US official familiar with the matter told the WSJ that the Pentagon estimated damage to bases from Iranian strikes – which became increasingly precise as the conflict escalated – at a minimum of $5 billion. Another WSJ source suggested that the number could potentially be as high as $15 billion.
Many installations are shared with Washington’s regional allies, meaning they could potentially pay for some of the damage, the report says, adding that the Pentagon may elect not to restore some infrastructure at all.
In particular, Washington is reportedly considering pulling back from its installations in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia so that its personnel would be out of reach. Tehran has previously demanded a full-scale US military withdrawal from the region as a prerequisite for sustainable peace.
Iran, meanwhile, has been rapidly restoring missile facilities and recovering buried weapons stockpiles, the report adds, noting that the military build-up comes as US President Donald Trump is considering further strikes despite shortages in American interceptor inventories.
However, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has been dismissive about Tehran’s military potential, saying in August that “They still have some capabilities, but it’s nowhere near what it was at all.”
Meanwhile, Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, a member of the Foreign Relations Committee and the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, accused the administration of seeking to “mask the true cost of the war” after being denied access to Qatar’s Al Udeid Air Base, where the WSJ identified at least a dozen damaged buildings. The Pentagon said that the ban was due to regional travel restrictions.
According to the Pentagon’s latest estimate provided to Congress, the Iran war has cost $47.1 billion through October 16, excluding base damage. The figure includes roughly $29 billion to replace expended munitions, $11.9 billion in operational expenses, and $6.1 billion in equipment losses.
As for the casualties, the US military now acknowledges 23 deaths linked to Iran war operations, including 11 from enemy fire, and 865 wounded.

Study finds the “bowing effect” on attractiveness is cultural, not universal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:00:42 UTC
23:00:42 KST

People in Japan tend to view a face as more attractive when the person performs a traditional bow, and this boost occurs regardless of the individual’s racial appearance. Observers in the United States, on the other hand, show little or no reaction to bowing, suggesting that cultural habits rather than universal body language explain the effect. The findings, published in Japanese Psychological Research, provide evidence that social etiquette can shape how aesthetic qualities are judged.
Bowing is a physical gesture that involves lowering the head and bending the upper body forward. In Japan, it serves as a customary greeting used to show respect, express gratitude, or offer an apology. The gesture can range from a slight fifteen-degree tilt when greeting someone in passing to a thirty-degree bow of respect for a senior colleague, or a deep forty-five-degree bend reserved for heartfelt apologies or profound thanks.
The research, led by Takayuki Osugi of Yamagata University, builds on earlier findings showing that tilting an image forward to simulate a bow increases perceived facial attractiveness among Japanese raters. Psychologists suggest that this reaction occurs because bowing activates cognitive schemas, which are mental frameworks that organize knowledge and expectations. In this context, the gesture triggers cultural associations with politeness and submissiveness, or non-threatening social deference. In Japanese society, these traits encourage a favorable overall impression that spills over into aesthetic judgments, a pattern known as a halo effect.
In related work, an experiment exploring head orientation found that downward head tilts increased perceived femininity and attractiveness for female faces, whereas upward tilts increased perceived masculinity. That earlier work examined vertical head motion as an evolutionary cue related to physical height and biological sex differences. In contrast, Osugi and his team approached bowing as an intentional, culturally learned greeting intended to communicate social respect.
One competing explanation holds that lowering the head is a universal signal of submission, observed across non-human primates, which would predict that bowing boosts attractiveness in any culture. Testing American observers offered a way to distinguish that account from a culturally specific one. In addition, past studies on the bowing effect relied almost entirely on East Asian faces shown to Japanese observers. Because the raters and the faces shared the same ethnic background, it was difficult to tell whether the boost occurred because the gesture was culturally familiar or because people were observing members of their own group.
To investigate, the researchers developed three-dimensional computer-generated models representing four racial appearances: East Asian, European, South Asian, and African. Both male and female models in their twenties were created with varied hairstyles and everyday clothing. In an initial setup phase, independent groups of Japanese volunteers rated the static appearance of these faces on a scale from 0 (unattractive) to 100 (attractive) so the team could select models with average baseline attractiveness scores of roughly 42 points.
Experiment 1 focused on Japanese participants recruited through an online crowdsourcing platform. Across six sub-experiments, each testing different combinations of model gender and race, between 45 and 49 participants evaluated faces under three movement conditions: a 1.5-second long bow, an immediate short bow, and a static upright control condition. About half of the Japanese participants took part in more than one sub-experiment, though the sub-experiments ran intermittently over roughly three years. A follow-up analysis accounting for repeated participation produced the same pattern of results.
Japanese observers consistently awarded higher facial attractiveness ratings to bowing models than to standing-still models across all sub-experiments. For instance, when rating female European models, the average score was 43.2 for the static condition, 51.1 for the short bow, and 59.0 for the long bow. Across the different model types, scores rose by roughly 6 to 12 points for short bows and 15 to 28 points for long bows compared to static faces. Across all tests, holding the bow longer produced higher ratings than a brief bow, and the interaction between the motion condition and the model’s racial appearance was not statistically significant.
In Experiment 2, the researchers presented the identical video sequences and rating tasks to American participants recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Between 30 and 40 American participants completed each sub-experiment. Participant overlap was minimal in this group, ranging from just one to seven participants across sub-experiments.
American participants showed minimal change in their attractiveness ratings when models bowed. Some differences did reach statistical significance, but the gaps were small, typically under three points on the 100-point scale, compared with gains of 15 points or more among Japanese raters. In female European model tests, for example, American ratings averaged 56.5 for the static pose, 57.4 for the short bow, and 56.9 for the long bow. A direct statistical comparison between the two national samples confirmed that the attractiveness boost from bowing was robust among Japanese participants but essentially absent among American participants.
The authors then conducted Experiments 3 and 4 to test whether the bowing effect generalizes across different levels of baseline physical attractiveness. These follow-up experiments also addressed a potential confound: all initial attractiveness ratings had been completed by Japanese university students, leaving it uncertain whether American raters would judge the facial aesthetics of the models similarly. In Experiment 3, 49 Japanese participants evaluated female East Asian models and 48 evaluated male East Asian models, with faces categorized as either distinctly attractive (averaging around 55 to 58 points) or less attractive (averaging around 28 to 30 points).
Bowing increased attractiveness scores for both attractive and less attractive faces among Japanese raters. For less attractive female models, scores rose from 33.3 when standing still to 42.0 for a short bow and 49.0 for a long bow. For highly attractive female models, scores rose from 48.0 when standing still to 54.3 for a short bow and 62.7 for a long bow. Holding the bow longer produced a steady enhancement regardless of baseline looks, though a brief bow provided a slightly smaller relative lift to already attractive faces.
To evaluate American aesthetic perceptions and task engagement, Experiment 4 presented the same high- and low-attractiveness models to 35 American participants for female models and 32 for male models. The participants easily distinguished between the two tiers, giving high-attractiveness female models an average score around 65 points and low-attractiveness models around 44 to 45 points. Within each tier, bowing motion produced almost no change in ratings, and though a small overall effect of motion appeared for male models, no individual comparison held up after correction. These results indicate that American viewers were paying close attention and evaluating facial aesthetics normally, yet simply did not factor the bowing motion into their judgments.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The researchers did not record how much exposure individual American participants had previously had to Japanese culture, anime, or travel. While some participants might have had passing familiarity with bowing etiquette, measuring this background would likely have highlighted the cultural divide even further.
The authors also did not collect race-related demographic information from the American sample, meaning future studies will need to examine whether an observer’s own racial background interacts with the racial appearance of the bowing person. Additionally, participants completed the tasks on their personal computers, so screen size, resolution, and viewing distance were not standardized. Live interpersonal encounters also involve vocal tone, body posture nuances, and spontaneous eye contact that digital avatars on computer monitors cannot capture.
The study, “Effect of Bowing on Facial Attractiveness of Other Races,” was authored by Takayuki Osugi and Jun I. Kawahara.

More than 5,000 people have died from Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo since an outbreak was declared in mid-May, according to a Health Ministry update.
The cumulative number of cases has reached 10,351, the ministry said on Saturday, as authorities battle the country’s largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak on record.
Eight provinces have been affected: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, South Ubangi and North Ubangi.
The outbreak is the second-largest globally, after the 2014–2016 epidemic in West Africa.
Call for stronger measures
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) called on Friday for stronger measures to protect frontline workers after two young Congolese doctors died from Ebola earlier in the week in North Kivu and Ituri provinces.
Gaps in early detection and contact tracing remain among the main obstacles to stopping transmission, according to health authorities.
Only about 12 percent of confirmed cases have been identified among previously known contacts, while many deaths have occurred in communities, authorities said.
